en: The First Chapter, titled "The Great Assembly," from the *Vāstuśāstra* composed by the Emperor of Emperors, the illustrious Bhojadeva, also known as *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*. May that God, the architect of the three worlds, whose crest is marked by the bud of the young crescent moon, protect you—he by whom this entire universe was designed in its totality, even without any prior cause for such design. (1)
Happiness, wealth, prosperity, and progeny are always dear to men;
for their complete attainment, every auspicious mark is beneficial. Whatever possesses a censured characteristic, however, brings about their ruin.
Therefore, everything that possesses auspicious characteristics is to be accepted:
the region, the city, the dwelling, the assembly hall, the residence, the seats,
and whatever else of this nature— each of these is considered conducive to prosperity.
Without the science of architecture (vāstuśāstra), there can be no determination of its characteristics;
therefore, out of compassion for the world, this treatise is proclaimed.
Now, once upon a time, [he approached] the lotus-seated one, the cause of the world's birth...
The Earth, bewildered by great fear and with eyes startled, approached;
having bowed down to the Grandfather, the Lord of all the gods who were prostrate in salutation, the Sustainer of Beings spoke thus to him with a faltering voice:
6–7. Having bowed down to the Lord of all the gods who were prostrate in salutation, the Sustainer of Beings spoke thus to the Grandfather with a faltering voice:
"O Blessed One, I have been oppressed by this Pṛthu of vast splendor;
having come to you for refuge, protect me from him.
While she was speaking thus on the earth, Pṛthu then appeared.
With his heart freed from agitation, he bowed down to Brahmā. Then,
with a voice deep and resonant like a gentle sound, he spoke to him,
making the swans accompanying him suspect it to be the roar of a rain cloud.
"O Lord of the worlds, by you I have been made the sovereign of the world;
and all beings have been established under my control.
Yet, O Lord of the Universe, this [earth] has at times remained outside my subjection."
"I shall now level her heaps of stones," [he thought].
Meanwhile, having become a cow, she fled while being pursued by my bow;
desiring to milk her, I too followed her for a long time across the earth. (12-13)
Wherever she goes, she sees only me;
finding no protection elsewhere, she has come to you unprotected.
Within her, the distinctions of caste, stage of life, and station shall be established.
"And this [earth] is difficult to traverse, being crowded with many ranges of mountains;
how shall I manage this upon it? Thus my mind was filled with doubt.
Then, having been thus addressed by Pṛthu, the Lord born from the lotus spoke.
Having made the earth free from fear, he spoke to him, awakening his understanding:
"O protector of the earth, this great earth, having been protected according to the law, shall become yours to enjoy once it has produced and yielded its crops. (17)
And whatever arrangement of places and so forth may be desired by you,
this teacher of the gods, the promoter of all accomplishments,
the son of the lord Prabhāsa, and the nephew of Bṛhaspati, [will provide it]. (18–19)
With a mind intent on conquering all, Viśvakarman will accomplish everything;
O King, he shall construct Amarāvatī for Mahendra.
Furthermore, other beautiful cities have been created by him for the sustainers of the worlds.

Having seen this form, which you have made your field of action, together with its mountains and trees, he will establish the settlements of villages, towns, and cities. Therefore, my child, go from here out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
O Earth, free from fear, you too must act for the pleasure of Pṛthu;
whenever remembered by the king out of a desire to do what is pleasing, you, being meritorious, shall be remembered.
O Viśvakarman, you too shall accomplish all of this.
Having spoken thus, when the Lord of Creatures had departed for his own abode and the king had taken refuge on the joyful earth, [the sage remained].
Viśvakarman quickly arrived at the snowy mountain, which was surrounded by playful celestial nymphs.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Great Assembly," in the *Vāstuśāstra*—also known as the *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*—composed by the great king of kings, Śrī Bhojadeva.
Now begins the second chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Viśvakarman and His Sons."
Then, on the back of the snowy mountain, in a cave-dwelling as lovely as jewels and frequented by *siddhas* and celestial nymphs, where the moon shone with pure radiance,
they remembered the Omniscient One as he sat upon a wide seat.
The four mind-born sons of Viśvakarman arrived:
Jaya, Vijaya, Siddhārtha, and the fourth, Aparājita.
Having approached that sage, they bowed their heads with palms joined in reverence.
The sage said to them: "O children, it is known to you that in the past the Brahman of the dwelling-place always pervades the entire universe;
then, righteous action leads to the attainment of one's own desires and to the protection of the worlds."
Having established this conceptual framework, he became the guardian of the world (Lokapāla).
"I too have been commanded by this Self-born Lord of the Universe, born from the lotus, for the purpose of arranging the worlds. (5-6)
Then, out of my own creative intelligence, I fashioned delightful cities, gardens, and assembly halls for the gods, asuras, serpents, and others;
and having gone to the earth, O sons of King Vainya, I acted out of a desire to do what was pleasing to you.
"I shall establish cities, villages, market-towns, and so forth, each separately.
In this entire task entrusted to me by Viśvasṛj,
it is my firm resolve that you must provide full assistance."
Since the rays of the sun, who has risen to illuminate the three worlds,
provide assistance in the destruction of darkness,
I shall myself build a city for Pṛthu as his residence.

"Having returned once more from all four directions, you four should establish various settlements— wonderful cities, villages, and market towns— that are exceedingly beautiful and provide refuge for ordinary people. ||11-12||
In the intervals between roads, oceans, mountains, and likewise rivers,
fortresses must be constructed for the sake of pacifying the fear of kings. [One should also consider] the castes, natural features, houses, and locations according to their characteristics.
These [duties] must be observed in every village, every city, and every town. Having thus properly instructed his sons on these matters—
which constitute the essential meaning and are neither obscure nor redundant— [he spoke].
With his mental state satisfied by the weight of his thighs placed upon [his father's] lap,
the son of Prabhāsa, skilled in policy, departed in silence.

(15) Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Dialogue with Viśvakarman’s Son," in the *Vāstuśāstra* composed by the illustrious Mahārājādhirāja Śrī Bhojadeva, also known as the *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*.
Now begins the third chapter, titled "The Question.
Then, having heard that speech of Viśvakarman called "Victory" regarding them, he spoke with palms joined in reverence, in a voice that was affectionate and deep. (1)

O Lord, that you choose us as your companions even though you are the sole treasury of wisdom— because of this, we do not hold ourselves in high esteem. Therefore, now, for the sake of our welfare and that of all creatures, O Master...
You possess immeasurable power; you ought to explain everything.
When the world had become a single ocean and had reached dissolution, how did the great elements, the celestial cities of the immortals, and the luminaries arise?
What is the form, what is the support, and what is the measure of the earth?
What are its extent, circumference, and thickness?
By what heights, widths, and lengths are which mountains considered principal on it?
How many years are said to be [the lifespan] of the continents, rivers, and oceans?
What are the individual movements of the sun, moon, planets, and constellations?
Furthermore, what is the distance stated between these [heavens] above the earth and among themselves?
Upon what support does the wheel of light revolve in the sky, and who causes it to turn?

How do the great elements maintain their stability, positioned above and below in this world? By what regulations of the laws of the ages (yugas) were the various modes of worldly conduct established in the beginning?
And who was the first among the kings? How [did it happen] for the planets and the social orders (varṇas)?
How many countries and how many divisions of the earth have been described separately? Where and how should the arrangement of the inhabited regions be made?
By what manifest signs— such as sound, touch, smell, color, and taste—
are the grounds of cities indicated as auspicious or censurable?
And by what procedure should the establishment of a city on a mountain be carried out?
What is the fruit when this [fortress] is well-established, and what again when it is poorly established?
Of how many kinds is a fortress, and what is the sequence of fortification works? What is the irreproachable layout of the foremost city, and what is censurable? (12-13)

And what is the rule for the sequence established by the authorities here regarding the construction of the enclosure wall, the gate-tower, the watchtower, the moat, and the rampart; as well as the exit from the courtyard, the gates, the main streets, the turrets, and so forth? 14.14-15ab.

What is the specific division by means of streets, crossroads, and roads? What are the measurements, configuration, boundaries, fields, directions, and paths? And how should the settlements of cities, villages, and market towns be established individually? (15–16)
Within the city, by what sequence of materials and components,
in which location, and in what manner should the installation of Śakra’s banner be performed?
Furthermore, how should it be done for that appointed [banner] every year?
For the welfare of the world of men, a great festival must be ordained.
In which houses here, and in which directions, and with which internal and external portions, should which various deities be installed? || 18-19 ||
By what various vehicles, retinues, complexions, forms, and ornaments;
by what gods, garments, ages, costumes, weapons, and banners; and by what measurements, postures, numbers, heights, and characteristics [should they be represented]? (20)
To whom do the palaces belong, or which ones would they be among the gods and the twice-born? Where in the city would there be a gatehouse protected by walls and moats?
Where would the water-chambers be between the pairs [of buildings], and where would the kitchen be? 21–22.
With storehouses, armories, treasuries, and dwellings;
with places for exercise, dancing, music, bathing, and fountain-houses (dhārāgṛha);
and with separate quarters for beds, residences, theaters, and mirror-halls. ||23||
With pleasure-pavilions, swing-houses, and inner-apartment chambers;
with gables, rotating turrets, balconies, and porticoes;
and with Aśoka groves and vine-covered bowers.
With ponds, artificial mountains of wood, and variegated flower-paths—
with these and other diverse features suited for forest retreats—
he constructed a mountain-like form fashioned from materials for the purpose of measuring and weighing.

How should the residential quarters for kings be situated according to their respective divisions? Reaching which specific divisions should the residences of the domestic priest, the commander of the army, the chief minister, and the astrologer be located within the royal palace? (27–28)
In the pure directions and in certain divisions of the quarters,
the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras should dwell together with those born of their own or intermediate castes;
likewise those who subsist by agriculture, trade, crafts, arts, and commerce.
And how and where should men who rely on violence be settled?
What kind of dwellings should they have, and how many are there? Or by what means do they obtain grain for their livelihood, and through what systems of entry and water management? (30–31)
How many kinds are the primary seats (dhiṣṇya), and what are the primary substances?
What is the cause of all these, and what is their sequence? Which substances enter into conjunction with which others?
Which things do not attain union (yoga), or by what means, and where does a man dwell?
What is the desired work with bricks, how many times has the earth been proclaimed, and what is the sequence of their preparation by means of fire, water, and wind? (33–34)
Which trees are praised for the purpose of building houses, being like the preceptor, the color, the banner, the earth-lord, and his servants? And which are censured?
[The defects] arising from their cutting, their sap-flow, sounds, the falling of directions, and those within the womb [of the tree]. 35.
How is it understood that the agency of the agent and so forth is auspicious or inauspicious?
(36) How can there be a means of valid cognition for those [images] purified by carving and cutting? Having first brought [the wood], where is the place for the placement of the logs? (37)
In general, which specific types of ground are proclaimed to be endowed with all excellent characteristics according to their respective classes?
What is the procedure for extracting splinters, and what is the nature of the work of preparing the ground?

How should the determination of the directions, the marking out of the site, and the consecration be performed? What is the measurement for the foundation pillar, and what is the ritual for laying the stones?
How is the dwelling divided by the distribution of halls and porticos? ||39-40||
What are the measurements for the walls and the heights of the pedestals?
How are they to be proportioned with the colors, the girdles, and so forth, as well as for all the pillars along with the door-pillars and seats? 41.
What is the prescribed measurement for the planks used in the construction of the *nāgavīthī* (serpent-path) supports, those with neck-protrusions (*kaṇṭhavinirgama*),
as well as for the *jayantī*, the *saṅgraha*,
the *tulā*, and the *vāstu*? ||42-43||
What should be the heights of the various storeys according to one's own measurement?
What should be the construction of the windows, the pigeon-cotes, the ledges, and the lattices?
Likewise, what are the pillars, the projections, the cornices, the animal-heads, and the beams?
What are the dimensions proclaimed for the inner-living-beings (sāntaḥprāṇi) and the head-arches (śirovaṃśa)?
How many are the *chādyaka* and *udaya* elements, and what is the sequence of the circular *chādyaka*?
How are the operations for the triangular, semi-circular, and *lupā* elements performed? (45–46)
What is the nature of their parapets and cornices, and what are the types of supports?
What are the various classifications for the tops of palaces, and whatever else there may be regarding palaces, mansions, and so forth? ||47||
What is the measurement for that which is attached to the wooden frames?
(48) In houses with four wings, the measurements for the halls and verandas—whether larger, medium, or smaller—are determined by the wooden molds used in the construction of the frames. (49)

How and how many types of houses— consisting of one, two, three, or four wings— are to be designed according to their various combinations? And how do the numbers sixteen, sixty-four, eighty-one, and one hundred arise through their divisions?
How could there be a division of words here, and how can there be an immortal state?
How is it that the first [portion] consists of nine words, while the last consists of a thousand?
In which specific major and minor limbs did those who were stationed remain?
How are these gods stationed within the body?
In which substances, when they are located therein, would pain arise in the head, lineage, eyes, belly, heart, crown, or vital organs (marmas), and for whom? (53)
In the commencement and entry of a building site, in journeys, and in installations;
how is the auspicious or inauspicious to be known through messengers, dreams, omens, and the like?
And likewise in the works of artisans, in paintings, and in the craft of modeling? ||54-55||
What is appropriate and what is inappropriate to be joined in royal palaces and other such places?
How is the characteristic of the hand, its measurement, and its names known?
What would be the mark of fire regarding oblations, and what is the characteristic of that which is employed?
In what manner should the bali-offering for the various castes be performed in due order?
By what rite should the entry into the house be conducted?
And [what is to be done] when it has fallen, cracked, decayed, been scorched, or struck by lightning?
When buildings are submerged, destroyed, shattered, or collapsed;
when honey is found in an anthill; and when wood has begun to sprout—what fruit arises from these, where does it occur, what is the rite of atonement, and what is the prescribed procedure?

"Thus, you whose mental disposition is moistened by no small measure of compassion for us, ought to explain in due order all these various types of architectural prescriptions— those pertaining to dwellings, as well as those constructed upon separate foundations.
Thus ends the third chapter, on the inquiry (*praśnādhyāya*), in the *Vāstuśāstra* composed by the great king of kings, the illustrious Bhojadeva, also known by the title *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*.
Now begins the fourth chapter, on the creation of Mahat and the rest.

Having heard these words of Jaya, Viśvakarman spoke with a voice as deep as the roar of thundering clouds: 1. "Having heard these words of Jaya, Viśvakarman spoke with a voice as deep as the roar of thundering clouds."
Excellent, my child! This question you have raised with your perfectly pure wisdom is like a sun to the lotus-forest of the science of architecture (vāstuvidyā).
Therefore, having placed this collection of questions in your heart—
Listen with attention as I relate what was spoken by Brahmā:
This entire universe had been reduced to a single ocean by the Samvartaka and other winds, which released waters that consumed everything scorched by the fire at the end of the Yuga. ||3-4||
Then, when that [world] had become shrouded in darkness,
Hari, having taken the entire universe into his belly, lay asleep upon the waters, reclining on a couch of serpent coils. Then, from his navel, there arose a lotus, and upon it he sang.
The glorious lord of the gods, the four-faced one, who is the foundation of all knowledge,
once set his mind upon the creation of progeny;
for that purpose, he first created the Mahat for the sake of the universe.

From this [ahaṃkāra], the mind arose as threefold; from the *sāttvika* [ahaṃkāra] came the senses, and from the *rājasa* also [the senses]; and from the *tāmasa* came the subtle elements (*tanmātrāṇi*). From those, the five great elements (*mahābhūtāni*) appeared in succession.
The elements beginning with space (vyoman) and ending with earth (dharā) are each endowed with their respective qualities.
Furthermore, the relationship of superior and inferior among them is correctly stated as follows:
first is earth, then below that is water, and below those is fire.
Below that is the wind, and from there comes space (kha), which provides room;

this ether (viyat) resides within the source of the elements (bhūtādi), and it too is surrounded by the Great One (mahat). The Great One enters the manifest (vyakta), and the manifest, in turn, enters the unmanifest (avyaktaka).
The manifestation of the elements arises through the relationship of the grasped and the grasper;
likewise, the relationship of the support and the supported, as well as persistence and destruction, exist according to their true nature.
Having thus created the great elements along with their qualities, the Lord [proceeded] from there. ||12-13||
Furthermore, at the time of creation, he properly directed his mind toward the material world;
with his mind, he brought forth gods, asuras, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, pannagas, nāgas, sages, and apsarases.
The sun and the moon were born as his two eyes, capable of traversing the sky;
from his limbs the circle of the constellations was produced, and from his five sense organs the five planets and stars came into being. ||15-16||
Furthermore, they know the state of being a planet (grahatva) to be due to their seizing (grahaṇa) by means of the senses;
for those who bear the marks of Indra’s bow, who are adorned with circles of lightning,
and who carry terrible thunderbolts, their origin was from the hair of Śiva as he released the waters.
By his will, he manifested, filling the entire universe.
Then there arose the fierce wind, the purifier of the three worlds, blowing horizontally;
and by that fierce wind, [the dust] was stirred up and heated from above by the rays of the sun.
The water, having been dried up by the winds, attained density;
above that ocean, the body of Viṣṇu, coiled below,
assumed the form of Ananta with his bowstring and supports the entire earth.
In those various regions where water had not been heated by the rays of the sun,
nor dried up by the winds, there the oceans came to be;
masses of great ocean waves were cast about by fierce winds.
Wherever they formed a single mass, there the earth became impassable;
then, for the sake of stability, it was spread out by them like a hide, and this earth was heaped upon those various spots with mountains like stakes. (23)

From the outpourings of the mountains that had increased in size, there arose rivers distinguished by their various courses; flowing toward lower ground, they became beloved daughters of the ocean and issued forth from the edges of the earth,
reaching the limits of the sea.
Wherever there were waters, there appeared islands of diverse forms;
with its rivers, oceans, and islands, and with all its mountains clearly demarcated,
the entire earth thus became manifest, supporting all living beings.
That Lord created, beneath the earth, the hells beginning with Raurava as a place for those of evil deeds to experience the fruits of their own actions, together with the four classes of beings:
the viviparous, the oviparous, the soil-born, and the sweat-born. ||27-28||
Thus he created the fourfold host of beings, both moving and stationary, in the world. Among them, those born from a womb are twofold: humans and animals.
Of these, seven were domestic and seven made their abodes in the forest.
Man, cow, horse, donkey, goat, ram, and mule—these seven are proclaimed to be solely devoted to living in villages.
Lion, elephant, camel, buffalo, śarabha, gayal, and monkey—[these seven are forest-dwellers]. ||30-31||
"O child, these seven living beings who range in the forest have been created;
yet, because of his discernment between dharma and adharma, a man among those in the villages is superior.
Among those who roam the forest, the lion is the best by virtue of his valor, strength, and other qualities."
Suparṇas, serpents, insects, and even those that are ants—
these are proclaimed as the fourfold beings born from eggs. Furthermore,
creatures such as worms and lice are produced from moisture and hair.
All those born from sweat were created by Prajāpati;
having become fivefold as plants (udbhijja), they are designated as the immobile beings (sthāvara). These are trees, creepers, shrubs, bamboos, and the various species of grasses.
The state of having a concealed internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), not abandoning one's own place,
and the capacity for what has been severed to grow again— these are their three specific qualities (*vaiśeṣika-guṇa*).
This *gāyatrī* is known as the "Elemental" (*bhūta-saṃjñā*) and possesses twenty-four joints (*parvika*).
Having known this meritorious [knowledge], a person becomes a recipient of heaven.
This existence (bhava), consisting primarily of the world, earth, water, fire, wind, and space, has been described by you;
now, O child, listen to me as I explain the determination of its measurement according to Vaṃsumatī. 38.

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Conjunction of the Great [Elements] and so forth," in the *Vāstuśāstra* composed by the Emperor of Emperors, the illustrious Bhojadeva, also known as the *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*.
Now begins the fifth chapter, the "Description of the World" (*Bhuvanakośa*).
Hereafter, I shall describe to you the entire earth in its proper sequence.
O child, [I shall describe] its diameter, circumference, and also its thickness clearly.
Its diameter is declared to be one hundred million yojanas,
and the thickness of the earth is likewise nineteen hundred thousand [yojanas].
The circumference of the earth is proclaimed to be three times its diameter, up to the fifth part of that diameter;
the circumference of the earth is thirty-two crores and sixty lakhs of yojanas.
"Eighty thousand yojanas is its extent proclaimed;
two lakhs and twenty thousand yojanas— thus,
my child, has the thickness of this earth been described to you."
They know that the measurement of each subsequent element— beginning with water and extending up to the Great Principle (mahat) and the Earth— is a hundredfold greater than the one preceding it.
This earth, situated within the waters and other elements, is shaped like a wheel, possessing a circular form.
These others as well, which successively seize the beauty of the other vessels situated within the [great] vessel,
are the measures of these elements beginning with earth that have been declared by you.
Now, however, the arrangement of the islands and so forth within the ocean is being stated again.
Situated in the midst of all seven continents and oceans,
Jambūdvīpa is circular and extends for one hundred thousand [yojanas].
There are the Himālaya mountain, the one called Hemakūṭa, Niṣadha, and the one designated as Nīla.
These six are the Kulaparvatas here: Śveta and Śṛṅgin. To the north of this mountain, whose slopes are marked by snow, all the mountains extend from east to west as far as the ocean.

Between the Nīla and Niṣadha mountains lies the glorious and great mountain Meru, the navel of Jambūdvīpa, circular and crowded with Puṇyajanas. To the north and south of Meru, on its eastern side, is the Mālyavat mountain.
To the west of Mount Sumeru lies the mountain Gandhamādana, frequented by perfected women, extending as far as the Nīla and Niṣadha ranges, crowded with hosts of gandharvas,
and equal in length to Mālyavat. (13) The mountain Gandhamādana is equal in extent to Mālyavat.
On both sides of the central mountains stand Himavat and Śṛṅgavān;
their height is two thousand five hundred yojanas.
At the two ends are the earth-supporting mountains Śveta and Hemakūṭa.
The height of each one of those two [mountains] is five hundred yojanas;
Niṣadha, Nīla, Mālyavat, and Gandhamādana—
these four are each individually five thousand yojanas in height.
These eight lords of mountains are each two thousand [yojanas] in width;
they extend downwards for half their height, being joined together with Meru.
The total height of Meru is eighty-four thousand [yojanas]. ||17-18||
It is sixteen thousand [yojanas] in depth below and thirty-two thousand in breadth at the top;
the great Jambu tree stands in the middle between Sumeru and Niṣadha.
Because of its presence on this island, it is known by the name Jambūdvīpa.
This Himavat mountain is covered on all sides with peaks consisting of snow-stones;
great piśācas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas dwell here.
This mountain range is called Hemakūṭa because of its peaks made of gold.
The Niṣadha mountain, which resembles a mass of light from the rising sun and is constantly frequented on all sides by Cāraṇas and Guhyakas,
is there where Śeṣa, Vāsuki, and Takṣaka dwell in happiness.
Sumeru, whose mountain caves are made of jewels, has the form of the pericarp of a golden lotus.
Here dwell the thirty-three immortals together with the Apsarases.
The blue mountain Nīla is adorned with peaks set with lapis lazuli.
There, the celestial rishis, constant in their austerities,
maintain their abode; that mountain is white, surrounded by golden peaks that scrape the heavens, and there dwells those who pride themselves on the strength of their arms, the enemies of the gods.
Consisting of sapphire and possessing the luster of a peacock's tail, the great mountain Śṛṅgavān stands vast on the outside; it is the abode of the ancestors, with its lofty peaks,
situated to the south of the Himālaya and surrounded on the other side by the salt ocean.
The first region, named Bhārata, is shaped like a bow;
it lies between the mountain that is the abode of frost (Himavat) and the Hemakūṭa mountain. Between these two, the second region is said to be named Kiṃpuruṣa.

Between the mountain Hemakūṭa and the mountain Niṣadha lies the third and most excellent region, known as Harivarṣa. It is situated between the Niṣadha mountain, the Nīla mountain, and the Mālyavat and Gandhamādana mountains.
The fourth continent, situated between these four, is Ilāvṛta;
it lies to the north of the Nīla mountain and to the south of the Śveta mountain. The fifth continent, known as Ramyaka, is exceedingly delightful.
Between these two kings of mountains here, Śveta and Śṛṅgavān,
lies the sixth [region], the beautiful Hairaṇyaka, which possesses a double expanse of golden light.
It is situated to the north of Śṛṅgavān and to the south of the salt ocean.
To the north, they declare the region named Kuruvarṣa; situated between the Nīla and Niṣadha mountains, in the eastern part of the Mālyavat mountain,
the eighth region, Bhadrāśva, is said to extend as far as the eastern ocean.
To the west of Mount Gandhamādana and extending eastward to the western ocean, the teachers declare the ninth region to be Ketumāla. Thus, these nine regions have been described by me to you. (35–36)
Now, furthermore, determine their measurement:
they maintain that Ilāvṛta here is thirty-four thousand yojanas in extent, square in shape on all four sides. (37)
The two regions situated in the east and west are equal from north to south;
they extend slightly more than thirty-one thousand [yojanas] from east to west.
Those other six regions mentioned are smaller than these.
Each of those is considered to be nine thousand [yojanas] in extent.
In the region of Kimpuruṣa, the women and men subsist on the fruit of the Plakṣa tree;
they live for ten thousand years, possessing the luster of naturally occurring gold.
In Harivarṣa, men and women dwell subsisting on sugarcane juice;
they live for ten thousand and one thousand years, possessing the luster of silver.
Likewise, in Ilāvṛta, the men have the brilliance of rubies.
Subsisting on the juice of jambu fruits, they live for eleven thousand years.
On this region covered by the slopes of Meru, the rays of the stars, sun, and moon do not reach;
rather, these beings dwell here having created their own illumination with the radiance from their own bodies.
In Bhadrāśva, men have the pure luster of the interior of a white water-lily;
they subsist on the fruit of the blue mango and live for ten thousand years.
In Ketumāla, embodied beings are dark-complexioned like a blooming blue lotus.
The lifespan of those who subsist on breadfruit (panasa) in [the region of] Śveta is ten thousand autumns.
In the delightful Ramyaka, the people eat the fruit of the banyan tree (nyagrodha);
the measure of their lifespan is declared to be the same as in Harivarṣa.
In the region of Hiraṇyaka, men and women of dark complexion live for ten thousand years,
all subsisting on lakuca fruit;
in the Kuru lands, men together with their wives live by means of trees that grant all desires.
In these regions, all the inhabitants— possessing the luster of fair-complexioned celestial children and numbering ninety-five thousand (sapāda-ayuta)— are entirely devoted to meritorious deeds;
they are forever happy, being liberated from sorrow, disease, old age, fear, and anxiety.
All [the regions] were strewn with forests bent under clusters of blossoms,
along with rivers emerging from the earth and various lofty trees;
and on the outside was the salt ocean, garlanded with rising waves.
This Jambudvīpa, surrounded by a garland of oceans, has been described by me to you.
Here, within these twelve seas, the mountains are situated separately;
in each direction there are three, their surfaces covered by vast waves.
Maināka, Balāha, and Cakra are on the south;
Nārada, Varāha, and Saumaka are on the west; and in the northern quarter, there are three: Droṇa, Kaṅka, and Candra. (53–54)
Dhūmraka, Dundubhi, and Sārdra—these are in the east;
they are a thousand yojanas long and half that in height.
These mountain-bearers are submerged halfway in the ocean and are broad across.
All these islands are frequented by gods, their heights kissing the sky;
they are ablaze with medicinal herbs and possess lovely, variegated trees and creepers.
They are, in order: Śāka, Kuśa, Krauñca, and Śālmali.

Gomeda and the one called Puṣkara—these six are situated on the outside; they are surrounded by the oceans of milk, clarified butter, curds, wine, sugarcane juice, and sweet water, respectively. These [oceans] stand encircling the islands beginning with Śāka in due order.

All of them are equal in size to their own respective islands, according to their sequence. These islands, beginning with Śāka, are double the size of Jambūdvīpa in successive order; and the oceans likewise [double in size]. (59–60)
In the Śākadvīpa, there are seven mountains; among them are Udaya, Jaladhara, Nāraka, Raivata, Śyāma, Rājata, and Ambikeya.
Their width is four thousand [yojanas], and their height is half that.
And half of that is the region of land frequented by divine sages;
outside of those circular regions, which are like islands, these seven Varṣas are situated in succession; I shall describe them to you.
And [he saw] the Kumāra named Jalada, Sukumāra, Maṇicaka,
Kusumottara, Modākī, and Mahādrumavana;
then Kuśa, Vidrumahemākhya, Dyutimān, and Puṣpavān.
Kuśeśaya, Harikṣmābhṛt, and Mandara are the boundary mountains (kulācala).
Each of them is said to be eight thousand [yojanas] in width.
Their height is half of that, and their depth below the surface is half of that height.
Udbhida, Veṇuvatsa, Sarāla, Lambana, Varṣa, Śrīmat, Prabhākṛt, Kapila, and the one named Pannaga;
on Krauñca are Krauñca, Andhakāra, Deva, Govinda, and Vāmana.
Dvividha and Puṇḍarīka—these are the seven mountain ranges [of the central region].
Their width is ten thousand [yojanas], their height is half that, and their depth below the surface is half of that again.
Beyond these, however, lie the [seven] Varṣas.
In Śālmali-dvīpa, there are seven mountains known as Kuśala, Aṣṭavarṣa, Parāpata, Manonuga, Munivarsa, Andhakāra, and the seventh is Dundubhi. They are red, yellow, and white respectively.
Their width is said to be thirty-two thousand [yojanas].
Their height is half that, and their extent on the earth is half of that again.
The regions situated there are Śāntabhaya and Vītabhaya. ||71-72||
On Gomeda, however, there are two mountain-supporters (bhūdhara) named Sura and Kumuda;
they are sixty-four thousand yojanas in extent,
their height is half that, and their depth below the surface is half of that again.
In the center of this [continent] is declared the region named Dhātakīkhaṇḍa.
On Puṣkaradvīpa there is a mountain called Mānasottara;
outside of this [mountain] is the region known as Mahāvīta.
This mountain extends for eighteen thousand [yojanas] and is frequented by gods, siddhas, and ṛṣis;
its height is half its width, and its depth below ground is half that again.
"O child, the cities of the lords of the gods have been established by me here:
Aindrī in the east, Vasvokasārā, then Saṃyamanī in the south, Prācetasī in the west, and likewise Sukhā and Vibhā in the north. (77–78)
For the sake of protecting the Dharma, four [guardians] reside in each of these four [continents];
likewise, for the sake of maintaining the order of the world, they stand as separate sustainers of the world.
Beyond the ocean of sweet water stands the Lokāloka mountain, which is twice its size.

Twice as wide as the expanse of the Ocean of Sweet Water (Svādūdaka), it is also twice as high; it extends one hundred thousand yojanas above and fifty thousand yojanas below. Furthermore, it measures five krośas in each direction and nine hundred thousand yojanas [in circumference]. ||80-81||
And likewise, half of a *niyuta* from the center of Meru is the distance to its end;
this [mountain] has half its body illuminated by the rays of the sun, and it is further covered by a portion of land equal to that. (82)
"O sinless one, these elemental coverings of the earth are situated below it,
and likewise, O child, they are established above the earth on its exterior; thus has the entire configuration of the earth been described to you."
Henceforth, I shall describe the positions and movements of the sun and the other [planets].
The sun, the moon, the lunar mansions (dhiṣṇya), Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn,
as well as the Seven Sages (Saptarṣis) and Dhruva, are situated above the earth in this order.
Four [thousand] and two [thousand], and likewise from that earth up to Sūryanandana;
thus there would be six intermediate spaces of one hundred thousand each.
As for the other remaining intervals between the planets, they follow in sequence. ||86-87||
Each of those four [regions] is said to measure two hundred thousand [yojanas].
Between the earth and the pole star (Dhruva), the height of the three worlds is proclaimed to be fourteen million yojanas.

Above Dhruva, the distances between Maharloka, Janaloka, Tapoloka, and Satyaloka increase successively by one, two, four, and eight crores [of yojanas]. Those worlds situated above Satyaloka extend downward as far as the shell of the cosmic egg (aṇḍakarpara). ||89-90||
Their total number shall be one koṭi along with fifty niyutas;
then the yoga of the veils (āvaraṇa) for this [deity] was ordained by the Lotus-born One.
Just as it is below, so it is manifested outside, and likewise in sequence above.
The sun is situated in the Pravaha wind, and the moon in the Udvaha;
the constellations are in the Saṃvaha, while the planets are in the Āvaha;
the Seven Sages (Saptarṣis) are in the Parivaha, and Dhruva is in the Parāvaha.
These seven Maruts cause those [luminaries] to revolve clockwise;
Dhruva stands in the center of Mount Sumeru, having become a cloud. This entire wheel of luminaries, thus bound together, revolves in this manner.
The best of chariot-warriors, the lord of the luminaries, constantly revolves upon his seven-horsed, single-wheeled chariot made of radiant light;
he causes night in Ketumāla and sets in the land of the Kurus.
And as the sun moves toward the auspicious midday in Bhārata,
that lord of the day traverses in a single moment twenty-seven thousand, six hundred,
and twenty-eight parts of yojanas. (97)

The sun traverses by the *kāṣṭhā* [measure] a distance of as many *yojanas* as there are qualities (*guṇa*)—that is, three—multiplied by the delights of the path (*adhvananda*), which is nine; thus, it moves four *navāṃśakas* (or thirty-six degrees). The lord of the lotuses (the moon) traverses a distance numbered by fire (three), fire (three), Vasu (eight), Indra (four), and earth (one); that is, eleven *navāṃśakas*. 98–99.
The sun traverses three parts of a yojana with a single *kalā*, and it moves across the sky at a speed numbering [the sum of] ether, space, void, earth, horses, twice, and fire, [that is, 360],
in one *muhūrta*.
By this path of motion,
as the sun travels through the middle of Puṣkaradvīpa, its course consists of nine hundred million, fifty thousand, and ninety-seven lakh days and nights. ||101-102||
Furthermore, by means of the celestial vault, one should determine the rising from one rising to the next;

thus has the motion of the intensely radiant sun been correctly described. One should likewise determine the motion and the longitudinal distance (bhoga) of the moon, planets, and lunar mansions relative to the sun.
"O sinless one, the measure of a day and night has now been declared to you;
by means of this, one may calculate the fortnights, months, seasons, years, and so forth for the sake of worldly convention.
Thus has this [system] of the islands, mountains, and oceans been described.
The entire arrangement existing upon the circle of the earth, as well as the course of the sun, has been described as the measure of the universe;
now, listen again as the characteristics of the ages (yugas) are being proclaimed here. 105

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Treasury of the World" (*bhuvanakośādhyāya*), in the *Vāstuśāstra* composed by the great king of kings, the illustrious Bhojadeva, also known as the *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*.
Now, immediately following this aforementioned creation of beings, this world became filled with progeny along with the immortals. (1)
In the Kṛta age, men were like the gods, free from grief, disease, arrows, and terror; they possessed perpetual youth.
They [dwelt] in the bowers of the mountains, by the rivers, and at the lakes.
And they sported with the deities in various wonderful forests. Sometimes, leaping up with ease along with the immortals,
those unimpeded ones moved about like gods in heaven.
All were clothed in variegated garments and adorned with diverse ornaments;
their trees were like celestial chariots and resembled the wish-fulfilling kalpa-trees.
Together with women who were lovely and wore wonderful jewelry, [they stood] with women likewise adorned.
Then they made their dwellings and their sports among the wish-fulfilling trees (kalpadrumas).
Free from the sufferings of hunger and thirst, they all lived for ten thousand years;
with bodies as radiant as jewels, they at times fed upon the essence of the earth.
At that time, they were devoted primarily to pleasure, taking food and engaging in recreation according to their own will;
their minds were purified by the acceptance [of the truth] and the destruction of their physical bodies.
In this place, the sun does not burn fiercely, nor does a powerful wind blow.
The nights were beautiful with the clearing of the frost and adorned by the full moon; the clouds, dark as crushed and glossy collyrium, accompanied by lightning and deep rumbling,
were not harsh with thunderbolts, yet possessed the loveliness of braided tresses.
The forest-dwellers there possessed mango-tree sprouts that served as mirrors for the beaks of intoxicated female cuckoos, and these trees were always laden with the fullness of flowers and fruit.
In this land, there was but one caste— the first-born— and there was but one Veda.
The spring season alone was the friend of the flower-armed god [Kāma].
Though they all possessed beauty, learning, pleasure, and sovereignty, because of their equanimity, there was no distinction among them as superior, inferior, or middling. (12–13)
There were no villages, towns, cities, fields, or threshing floors;
nor was there any fear of gadflies, mosquitoes, or carnivorous beasts, nor of the planets and such.
Even though they possessed enjoyments obtained from the wish-fulfilling trees, they did not have a master over them.
In former times, while they were dwelling here in this land of Bhārata-varṣa together with the gods, a very long period of time passed for those who possessed divine splendor,
as a result of their living together for a thousand years without knowing the true extent of his power. ||15-16||
Then, by fate, contempt for the gods arose among them;
though they were worthy of worship and all-knowing, they were not honored.
Taking that Kalpavṛkṣa tree, the denizens of heaven flew up to the sky.
The power of ascending to heaven and the divine state associated with it, as well as the supreme essence on earth and the earthly essence itself, returned;
he did so remembering those various wish-fulfilling trees and those pastimes with the gods. ||18-19||
Those whose minds were intent on what was harmful lamented excessively in many ways.
Then, as they were lamenting profusely for the sake of their own food,
parpaṭaka appeared upon the earth for the purpose of saving their lives.
By that very earth, while they were thus preserving their lives,
they made their dwelling among other trees in the absence of the Kalpa-trees. Then, even as they looked on, once, due to the exhaustion of their merit— ||21-22||
And due to the reversal of time, even the earth-crust (parpaṭaka) disappeared;
then, when the crust had vanished,
rice grains grew on the earth without being tilled, free from husks, awns, and broken grains.
Then, with that rice of śāli grain and its delicious condiments,
they attained supreme satisfaction, their minds filled with contentment.
Fearing its destruction, they [hid] the śāli grains beneath the trees.
They made great heaps [of grain] and established fields for them;
from that, greed was born, preceded by envy and malice.
Thereupon, the god of love (Manmatha) gradually set foot here and there.
Then, through the attainment of sexual union, as they maintained their supreme state of being,
the horse of passion became exceedingly agitated toward women due to the destruction of their fortitude; immediately thereafter, there arose many causes for the cultivation of wives as fields.
The pairs of opposites (dvandvas) became individually rooted solely in affliction;
then, as those who had not conquered their own selves began to destroy the boundaries established by themselves,
that discipline reached the state of mere husks among the undisciplined and ill-fated.
As their passion increased, that state of possessing a meritorious reputation vanished. The production of impurity occurred through the consumption of grain with its husks;
then, when the stockpile of husked grain was exhausted and consumed, [the situation changed].
For those who wore garments of rags and bark and subsisted on bulbs, roots, and fruits,
the six seasons beginning with spring arose through the passage of time. Consequently, their bodies became afflicted by humors, diseases, and grief.
And his mind was afflicted by desire, anger, envy, dejection, malice, and the like;

there was great suffering born of the divine (ādhidevika), such as heat, cold, and water; and there was also suffering born of the elemental (ādhibhautika), arising from predatory beasts, wild animals, and so forth. (33–34)

Thus, afflicted by the threefold suffering, they— finding no pleasure in trees— constructed houses with paved floors for the sake of protection against sexual union and other such acts, as well as for the warding off of snow, mist, cold water, wind, and other calamities.
With their minds afflicted by grief, they cut down other trees with stones;
remembering those houses which resembled wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpadruma*),
they constructed dwellings of one, two, three, four, seven, and ten rooms.
The sounds of those householders, who were joyful as they waited for their appointed time, reached them from within the enclosures and moats that were concealed by grass and other vegetation.
Thus, in these houses of theirs— which dispelled the cold, the wind, and the heat with water— those [ascetics] dwelt.
With their minds filled with joy and having long since cast away all calamities, they dwelt in happiness. 39.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Section on Sahadeva," in the *Vāstuśāstra* composed by the great emperor Śrī Bhojadeva, also known as the *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*.
Now begins the seventh chapter: "The Classification of Castes and Stages of Life."
Then the Grandfather (Brahmā) arrived together with the hosts of immortals,
bringing King Pṛthu to sever the suffering of mortals.
That Lord spoke to them, as Vāsava does to the Maruts:
Bearing the rod of punishment over the wicked with power like a world-protector (lokapāla),
a lion among enemies scorched by his majesty and possessing the prowess of a lion—
this Pṛthu has been consecrated by me into the sovereignty over you all.
"This king shall be the protector of all the virtuous, the destroyer of those with evil intent,
and by his conduct, the remover of your fear.
You must remain dependent upon him in accordance with my command."

"He shall establish for you, through his policy, the stability of the four castes and the stages of life. Having spoken thus, when Brahmā had departed, they approached their protector and, being distressed, said out of their sorrow: "O Lord, protect us from this suffering!"

"O Lord of the Earth, protect us who have been abandoned by the celestial wish-fulfilling trees, whose minds are exhausted by the affliction of dualities, and who are submerged in an ocean of calamity.
Then Pṛthu said to them, "Do not fear; remain in comfort."
"I shall remove your sufferings and I shall bring about your happiness.
Thereupon, he divided the four castes and the stages of life. Among them, those who were devoted to the Vedas, of good conduct, and with senses restrained—
At that time, those Brāhmaṇas were wise and pure;
their duties consisted of sacrificing, studying, giving gifts, officiating at sacrifices for others, teaching, and receiving gifts.
With the exception of the last three, these duties were common to both the Kṣatriyas and the Vaiśyas.
Those who were brave, possessed of great energy, worthy of providing refuge, and capable of protection;

those with firm and well-proportioned bodies—these were the Kṣatriyas who existed here. Valor, the preservation of the world, the distribution [of justice], and resolute determination [were their qualities]. (11–12)

For those whose natural skill lies in the acquisition of wealth, this dharma— which brings about auspicious results— was also prescribed. He made those Vaiśyas endowed with faith, dexterity, and compassion.
Medicine, agriculture, commerce, architecture, and the rearing of livestock—
this is declared to be the duty of the Vaiśya, as well as his work involving fire.
Those who are not excessively proud, not overly pure, and who are backbiters [are also among them].

Those born of the Śūdra caste, who are not excessively devoted to dharma, have their declared duties as follows: subsisting by the commencement of various arts, craftsmanship, the rearing of cattle, and service to the three other castes. ||16||

"The student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and likewise the ascetic—thus have the four stages of life (āśramas) been distinguished by him separately. Service to the teacher, living on alms, the performance of vows, and the tending of the sacred fire [are the duties of the student]. ||17-18||

Vedic study, ritual ablution, worship of the sacred fire, guests, and deities, subsistence by one's own prescribed means, self-restraint, marriage with those not of the same lineage as one's ancestors, and approaching one's wife only during her season— this is the dharma of the student (brahmacārin). (19)

Aversion toward the wives of others, a disposition toward favoring others, and desisting from improper acts—this is the dharma prescribed for householders. Honoring deities and guests, celibacy, and dwelling in the forest [are likewise prescribed]. ||20-21||
Wearing bark, skins, matted hair, and rags; sleeping on the ground; emaciating the body through fasts, vows, and restraints;
and subsisting on food grown without cultivation—this is the dharma for those dwelling in the forest.

Detachment, mastery over the senses, abandonment of anxious thought, tranquility, possessionlessness, and freedom from worldly undertakings are always remembered as the duties of an ascetic. Likewise, forbearance, dependence upon the guru, purity, and constancy in self-study [of the scriptures] are required. ||23-24||
Purity in worldly dealings—this is declared to be the duty of a female disciple.
Purity of speech, mind, and body, service to her husband, forbearance, worship of those worthy of her husband's worship, and cleanliness are the duties of a woman. (25)
Having thus properly established the social classes and stages of life,
and having divided those classes according to their origins, Vainya proclaimed their respective duties; he then specified for each of them their distinct means of livelihood and occupations.
"For you who remain steadfast in your own dharma, there shall be happiness in both worlds;
but for him who, out of delusion, transgresses this established order and ordains otherwise, I, enraged like Yama, shall mete out my punishment. (28)
"For you who are engaged in your respective duties,
I shall provide dwellings in villages and towns, as well as cities, for the sake of your livelihood.
Having spoken thus to them with his ten million bows, King Pṛthu then—
He of vast prowess rendered the earth uneven;
because of that affliction, the earth, having become a cow, was on the verge of perishing, yet by his command she yielded crops well for the welfare of all beings. (31)

By him were laid out the divisions of cities and other settlements among the mountains, within the rivers, and in level open spaces. By him this earth was ploughed with the tips of the ploughshares and sown with grains according to the prescribed rites.
"The earth is made to yield its crops by the Blessed One at the arrival of the clouds"—
thus was the first origin of the king described,
together with dharma and the distinctions of the stages of life (āśrama) and social classes (varṇa).
The activities of agriculture have also been declared and shown to you in their entirety, O child; now hear concerning the classification of lands according to regions.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Classification of Castes and Stages of Life," in the *Vāstuśāstra* composed by the great emperor Śrī Bhojadeva, also known as the *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*.
Now begins the eighth chapter, titled "The Examination of the Grounds. O King, the regions and the lands within those regions shall now be described to you in brief;
their number and their divisions will be told—listen attentively. (1)
Country may be of three kinds, according to its being arid (jāṅgala), marshy (anūpa), or intermediate (sādhāraṇa).
Now, the characteristics of each of these three are described as follows:
[A jāṅgala country] is characterized by water located at a distance, is largely saline soil, and has short, thorny trees.
The *jāṅgala* region has rough, hot, and fierce winds, with black soil.
The *anūpa* region is low-lying, abundant in water, moist, rich in fish and meat, cold, full of rivers,
lush, elevated, and densely wooded.
Furthermore, that region which possesses the characteristics of both [the Jāṅgala and Anūpa] types, being neither too cold nor too hot,
is called "common" (sādhāraṇa) by those expert in regions.
[This applies to] the three types of regions, such as the Jāṅgala, according to their own specific characteristics.
The sixteen stages (bhūmis) should be understood according to their classification as follows:
Bāliśasvāminī, Bhogyā, Sītā, Gocararakṣiṇī, Apāśrayavatī, Kāntā, Khanimatī, and Ātmadhāriṇī. ||6-7||
A city adorned by merchants, abundant in wealth, capable of destroying enemies, possessing guilds of men, able to withstand neighboring vassals, having a divine mother (a temple),
provided with grain and elephant forests, and well-protected— these are the sixteen [qualities].
The earth has been described by its various names; now its characteristics shall be told.
O gentle one, that land which can be governed even by a foolish ruler would be a territory presided over by a foolish master. (9–10)
That land where men of abundant wealth pay excessive taxes, such as shares of produce and enjoyments, is called "bhogya" (enjoyable) in this context. In that [land],
there are rivers and streams, and mountains either in the midst or on the outskirts.
That pasture-ground (sītā) which has its field boundaries clearly demarcated is called *gocararakṣiṇī*.
Because people may enter it out of fear when encountering rivers, mountains, forests, and the like, it is called *apāśrayavatī* due to its suitability for providing refuge to people. ||12-13||
The earth, enchanting with its forests, groves, mountains, rivers, and thickets, delights embodied beings; she is celebrated as "Kāntā" (the Beloved).
In her, metals such as gold and others are always produced.
They say that land abounding in salt mines is called *khanimatī*.
That land which cannot be excessively favored with troops, treasury, edicts,
and so forth, yet is inhabited by prosperous people, is known as *ātmadhāriṇī*.
That land where the buying and selling of merchandise are successfully carried out repeatedly is called "Vaṇikprasādhitā" (cultivated by merchants), for it is frequented by traders.
[It is also characterized] by Śāka, Aśvakarṇa, Khadira, Śrīparṇī, Syandana, and Asana trees.
The earth is "rich in resources" (dravyavatī) when it is endowed with bamboo, cane, reeds, and the like.
That earth is "a slayer of friends" (amitraghātinī) where the provinces are well-organized, where the subjects have abandoned their martial prowess, and where even friends fall into discord.

In that land there are no base sycophants who take refuge in forts or remote borderlands; it is a territory inhabited by people of disciplined conduct, including members of the guilds. Furthermore, the neighboring kings show no hostility toward its secret counsel or its military prowess.
That land which people cultivate on all sides by means of water from rivers and other sources is known as *śakya-sāmantā*.
That land where the owners of the fields live by means of the waters of rivers and the like, without depending on rainwater, is called *devamātṛkā*. ||21-22||
That land where seeds sown without effort yield an abundant harvest,
and whose fields are tilled and well-prepared, is called *dhānyaśālinī*.
That land which has mountains on its borders and is endowed with elephant forests is [known as *hastinī*].
That vast earth, possessing elephant forests and increasing the strength of its mountain-like kings,
is ever difficult for enemies to overcome due to its ruggedness;
protected by uneven mountains and rivers, that land is known as "Well-Guarded" (Surakṣā).
The sixteen stages have been declared exactly as they are according to their divisions;
now we shall describe others, such as those of the inhabited regions, which possess mixed characteristics.
[26] They are covered with groves, shrubs, trees, and creepers, shimmering with the flow of mineral ores.
They were embraced on all sides by mountains with vast crags,
and were surrounded by rivers of sweet water, lovely with their descent at sacred fords,
and featuring riverbanks abounding in various trees. ||27-28||
They were graced by forests beautiful with the warbling of cuckoos, frequented by bees intoxicated by honey, and rich in various fruits and flowers;
[forests] captivating with the humming of bees drawn to rows of blooming blue lotuses.
They were adorned with lakes, divine ponds, and other water bodies filled with abundant water;
and they were surrounded by level, fragrant, sweet, cool,
and beautiful fields with unbroken boundaries that yielded abundant crops.
Adorned with pastures free from thorns, stones, and ant-hills, abundant in fodder and fuel, and demarcated by clearly defined field boundaries;
the lands were beautified by these grazing grounds situated amidst the oceans of grass upon the dry plains.
Those [rivers] whose waters are nearby, sweet, and cool are praised;
those which are unassailable by the wicked, as well as those endowed with many resting places, and those which delight the mind that has been cleansed of agitation and fear. ||33-34||
Upon such lands endowed with these qualities, he should settle the districts,
as well as market towns, villages, cities, and so forth, each in its proper place.
These should be situated at the foot of mountains and provided with their respective individual ramparts.
Four types of fortunate grounds have been described as causes for fortresses:
[1] A mountain fortress (giridurga) consists of level-backed ground on a watered mountain, which is difficult to ascend and, at its extremity, cut off like by a chisel. ||36-37||
In a watery forest densely covered with thorny trees,
where the path of entry is hidden and the ground is difficult to traverse, it is known as a "fortress rooted in the earth" (bhūmūladurga).
On islands with sweet water, where the interior waters are deep and the exterior is vast, [it is known as a fortress surrounded by water].
The earth should have delightful open spaces and be protected by water-fortifications;
it should be lush, substantial, pure, and possess clockwise-flowing water-bodies;
it should abound in water, be covered with trees, dense, and slope toward the east and north.

Dūrvāsas, moreover, [described those hermitages] as being surrounded on all sides by medicinal herbs, muñja grass, kuṇḍa grass, kuśa grass, and bark-fibers, with waters that were sweet, clear, and still;
they were further adorned with sacrificial sites for the Vāstu-rite, temples of the gods, groves, and gardens.
Those lands which are adorned on all sides by the sites of tanks and ponds,
which provide comfort to vehicles and grant pleasure to couples,
are praised for the sake of a city as they generate prosperity.
The earth becomes fragrant with these— saffron, agallochum, camphor, spṛkkā, cardamom, sandalwood, and so forth— whether mixed together or used separately;
likewise with white water-lilies, trumpet-flowers, lotuses, jasmine, campaka, and blue lotuses.
Likewise, with other fragrant flowers produced on land and in water;
she possessed the scent of cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, honey, and clarified butter;
and her fragrance was equal to that of wine, mādhvīka liquor, and the ichor of elephants.
With the fragrance of rice-flour and likewise the fragrance of grain,
the earth possesses such a scent that is praised by all castes;
the earth is white, red, yellow, and black in sequence.
For it is beneficial for all the castes, beginning with the Brahmins;
it is sweet, astringent, bitter, and pungent in that order, or else,
according to the taste of the castes, it is recommended as sweet for all of them.

That earth which is cold at the onset of heat and warm at the onset of cold, and which possesses both the touch of heat and cold during the rainy season, is praised. When the sounds of the mṛdaṅga, vallakī, flute, and dundubhi drums are identical [to one another], [it is auspicious].
And those whose sounds are equal to two, four, or seven oceans are auspicious grounds.
Now we shall describe the characteristics of inauspicious grounds, which are to be avoided for the purpose of establishing cities and other settlements. (51-52)
It was filled with ashes, charcoal, potsherds, bones, chaff, hair, poison, and stones; it was overgrown with mouse-hills and anthills, and strewn with gravel.
It was parched, sprouting [unwanted weeds], low-lying, treacherous, full of holes, and saline.
That river which flows counter-clockwise, lacks substance, and has uneven elevations;
where the trees are bitter, thorny, sapless, withered, and fruitless;
and which is swarming with carnivorous birds and teeming with worms and insects—[such a river is inauspicious]. ||54-55||
In that [city], even well-prepared foods, edibles, drinks,
and delicacies go to ruin at that very moment along with the sounds of musical instruments;
one should abandon even such a city where the river flows in the opposite direction.
For even after a long time, that [impurity] returns there once again.
One should abandon this earth, which shares the same odor as fat, blood, marrow, feces, urine, filth, insects, birds, oil, and corpses. (57–58)
The earth that is always smoke-colored, or of a mixed color, or discolored,
or rough in appearance, does not bestow what is desired.
Furthermore, ground that is bitter, sour, or salty in taste [is likewise unfavorable].
One should abandon that [ground] which causes hatred among the people during the settling of a city.
One should also abandon that which has a rough and harsh touch, which is always hot or cold, and whose touch is unpleasant to the senses.
"The sound of jackals, camels, horses, donkeys, and dogs, as well as the roar of mountain torrents and the harsh noise of broken vessels, are not desired.
Thus has the earth been described according to its auspicious and inauspicious qualities by means of its scent and other attributes.
When the earth being ploughed by the ploughshare brings up a piece of wood, one should know there is danger from fire; if it is a brick, there will be the arrival of wealth;
if it is stones, there is prosperity; but if it is bones, there is the destruction of the family.
One should predict fear from thieves among all reptiles.
Land that is not saline, rich in grass, moist, and sloping toward the north is praised;
likewise, land sloping toward the east or northeast, or sloping in all directions, and having a surface like the belly of a mirror [is also excellent].
On an auspicious day, having fasted, bathed, and purified himself, wearing white garlands and garments,
he should have the Brahmins recite benedictions and worship the deities of the site;
then he should cause a pit to be dug in the middle of that ground, measuring one cubit in depth.
Then, having extracted that earth, one should fill it back with that very same soil.

Earth that exceeds the amount excavated is said to be excellent; that which is equal to it is middling. Earth from which the excavated soil has been discarded is inferior; it is not recommended for men.
When, while digging a pit,
gems, conch shells, coral, and the like are seen within that earth, then that ground is most excellent;
indeed, even that ground is praised from which the dust of the excavation originates.
Having filled the excavation with water, free from husks, hair, stones, charcoal, ashes, and fragments of bone, one should walk a hundred paces away;
if the water remains upon one's return, then that ground is "all-yielding" (sārvakāmikī).

If [the earth] has abandoned only its middling quality, it would be of intermediate nature; if it has abandoned even more than that, it is inferior. The earth upon which white flowers and other garlands, having been left overnight, do not wither—being of whatever color they were—is a giver of desired things in that very color.
Or one should light lamps in the directions starting from the north of the pit;
that direction in which the light remains for a long time indeed bestows the desired [result] corresponding to its color.
Thus, the characteristics of city sites have been described in their entirety.
These very same [auspicious] sites are traditionally held to be beneficial for market towns, villages, and hamlets;

they are always conducive to the welfare of those belonging to the social orders who abide in their respective duties, as well as for military camps, palaces, sacrificial enclosures, and grounds. (75–76)
Thus, by means of these and other such [characteristics], these auspicious grounds endowed with favorable marks have been described for the purpose of building cities and the like;
beyond these, [the ground] may be conceived in many ways.
We shall now describe the measurement of the hand, even though it exists in three ways.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "Examination of the Ground," in the *Vāstuśāstra* composed by the Great Emperor, the illustrious Bhojadeva, also known as the *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*.
Now begins the ninth chapter, titled "Characteristics of the Hand."
It is the cause of all structures, the foundation of all activities, and the sole basis for determining measurements, proportions, and divisions;
for from it arise the circumference, height, width, and length.

Having understood the distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior, one is no longer deluded. Now, the characteristics of that hand— of all three types as revealed in the scriptures— are being correctly explained along with their definitive conclusions.
Eight *reṇu*s make one hair-tip (*vālāgra*); eight of those make a nit (*likṣā*);

eight of those make a louse (*yūkā*); and from eight of those comes the middle of a barley-corn (*yavamadhyam*). There are seven, six, or eight barley-corn breadths (*yavodara*) in a finger-breadth (*aṅgula*).
The hand consists of twenty-four of those [units], divided into superior, medium, and inferior sizes.
The hand should be made by one who understands it to consist of eight joints;
half of the hand has four joints, and the remainder should be divided into finger-breadths (aṅgulas).
In that [thumb], there should first be three joint-lines adorned with flowers;
one should not place flowers on the remaining lines of the fingers.
Here, in the middle of this half, the fifth finger should be divided into two parts.
The middle [section] should be made threefold, the eighth [part] fourfold, and then the twelfth [part].
A cubit (hasta) measured by its own fingers (svāṅgula) is desired as the unit of measurement (aṅgula);
its thickness should be one and a half or double that, or half of that again.
The classification of the types of hand-fists has been described according to the differentiation of the fingers; now we shall explain the woods for its construction and the presiding deities.
[10] Woods such as Khadira, Añjana, and Vaṃśa—smooth, firm, and beautiful—are recommended.
And it should be desired that the wood be full of essence for the fashioning of a hand-guard (hastaprakalpana).
Wood that is knotted, light, burnt, decayed, cracked,
unstable, or infested with hollows is not fit for a hand-guard.
Now, regarding these three types [of diagrams], the deities within the boundary lines (parvarekhā) are to be known starting from the center; I shall state those nine in sequence:
Brahmā, Agni, Yama, Viśvakarman, and the Lord of Waters (Varuṇa).
Vāyu, Kubera, Rudra, and Viṣṇu, the Lord of the World, are at the forefront.
In the distribution of building materials and especially regarding vehicles, one should determine the measurement from whichever direction one begins and assign the deities accordingly. ||14-15||
When [the asterism] is pierced by planets, occupied by malefic substances, or afflicted by deities,
one should predict the results as stated for each respective station of the gods:
headache, burning by fire, death, or the execution of the architect.
Diarrhea, a wind-related disease, loss of wealth, fear of the king,
and great affliction of the family— these are the defects that arise respectively from the oppression of Brahmā and the other [deities] by the agent and the performer of the rite. (17–18)
When one places the hand between the Brahma-fire and the Anala-fire,
there will be the attainment of sons for those who have undertaken their duties;
the successful completion of their work shall endure as inexhaustible enjoyment.
If Brahmā and Yama hold the hand between them, the builder and the artisan shall perish before long.
If the measuring cord is held between Viśva and Anala, [the same occurs]. ||20-21||
In the case of a good deed, when the middle and the end are accomplished, there is prosperity for the city;
one should designate the middle as being between Yama and Jalada.
Pavana and Viśvakarman are the support between both.
But when an auspicious work there bestows all desires,
one should designate it as "middle" between the "cloud" and the "giver of wealth.
When, among these, the "calf's hand" is held there— ||23-24||
There will be no doubt that there is fear of drought in the world and the destruction of the country;
however, if one holds the Rucihasta [mudrā] between Rudra and Pavana,
for that fortunate person there will be success in his undertakings, without a doubt.
When the hand extends between Viṣṇu and Dhanada,
various enjoyments indeed arise for that man; now,
the distinction of names for these, beginning with Jyeṣṭha, is prescribed.
That substance by which something is measured is also declared [to be a measure].
A hand that is specifically long, fashioned from eight barley-corns and eight finger-breadths, is called the "Jyeṣṭha-hasta" (the superior hand) by the learned; it is designated as the "Prāśaya."

Furthermore, that which is calculated here by experts using seven barley-grains as the unit for finger-breadths (aṅgula) is known as the "middle hand" (madhyama-hasta), which is considered the standard (sādhāraṇa).
Since the word "mātra" is said to mean "small," and since the "hand" (hasta) is also called "śaya" [in this context]. ||29-30||
Therefore, that hand which measures six barley-corns and six finger-breadths (aṅgulas) shall be the measure of the womb (mātrāśaya).
[This applies] to the divisions of length and width in villages, towns, cities, and the like;
as well as in temples, houses, moats, gates, streets, assembly halls, and so forth.
Their roads and exits, the boundaries and intervals between fields,
the portions of forests and groves, the divisions between different regions,
and even the measurements of the paths in yojanas, krośas, and gavyūtis— [all these he knew].
The reservoirs of water, as well as pits, trenches, and ditches, must be measured by their depth;

likewise, the height of their foundations from the base, the extent of the water areas below ground level, and the measurements for the determination of swings, water-weapons, and other such implements [must be determined]. 34.1–2.
One should construct dwellings excavated from rock with internal passages for subterranean tunnels;
one should also design common courtyards and pathways,
as well as weapons, bows, staffs, vehicles, beds, and seats.
The measurements for wells and tanks, for elephants, horses, and men;
for water-wheels, sugarcane presses, yokes, sacrificial posts, and plows;
as well as for the tools of artisans, umbrellas, banners, and musical instruments—[all these were established]. 37.
One should measure the small stools, religious implements, cloth, vessels, and so forth, as well as the *nalva*, staffs, and measures, by means of the *mātrāśaya-hasta*. Furthermore,
the definition of the *hasta* is said to consist of three distinct types.
Now, the differentiation of the designations for the measures of length is set forth:
one *aṅgula* shall be a *mātrā*, and two *aṅgulas* are said to be a *kalā*.
Three *aṅgulas* they call a *parva*, and four *aṅgulas* would be a *muṣṭi*.
The *tala* consists of five [finger-breadths]; the fingers and toes of the hands and feet consist of six;
the *diṣṭi* consists of seven; the quiver (*tūṇi*) is desired at eight finger-breadths;
the *prādeśa* consists of nine of those; and the *śyatāla* is ten finger-breadths. ||41-42||
Gokarṇa is eleven vitastis; dvādaśāṅgula is twelve aṅgulas. That which is designated as pāda consists of fourteen aṅgulas.
Ratni would be twenty-one [aṅgulas], while aratni is measured by one kara.

It is proclaimed that forty-two *kiṣku*-fingers constitute a *vyāma*, and likewise, eighty-four fingers constitute a *puruṣa*. A bow (*cāpa*) consists of ninety-six fingers, as does a pair of *nāḍīs*. ||44-45||
One hundred and six daṇḍas measure one nalva, which is thirty cubits (dhanus) in length;
a krośa is known to be one thousand dhanus, and two of those are understood as a gavyūti.
Those who know measurement maintain that four gavyūtis constitute a yojana.
One, ten, a hundred from this, then a thousand, and after that ten thousand (ayuta);
[then] a hundred thousand (niyuta), a million (prayuta), from that a ten-million (arbuda), and also a hundred-million (nyarbuda);
[then] a billion (vṛnda), ten-billion (kharva), a hundred-billion (nikharva), a trillion (śaṅku), ten-trillion (padma), and a hundred-trillion (amburāśi). ||47-48||
From that, there should be the middle, the last, the beyond (para), and the further-beyond (apara);
and thus the "ten-millionth" (parārdha) should be known, each increasing tenfold over the preceding one.
These twenty places of enumeration have thus been declared.

Now the measurement of the number of time-units is being stated: 50. A single blink of the eye is a *nimeṣa*; fifteen of those are known as a *kāṣṭhā*; thirty of those are a *kalā*; and thirty of those are a *muhūrta*. Thirty of those [muhūrtas] constitute a day and night. 51.
One should know that this triad [of breaths] occurs thirty times in succession;
furthermore, fifteen such days and nights are called a *pakṣa* (fortnight).
Two *pakṣas* constitute a month (*māsa*), and from two months, a season (*ṛtu*) arises.
Three seasons constitute an ayana, and two ayanas constitute a year;
this time is said to be tenfold by the best among those who know time.
Thus has all this been stated here with precision regarding the measurement of the kara, and the calculation of time has also been correctly explained.
We shall describe here the division of the city by means of the paths for the inner apartments, the countryside, and the abodes of the gods.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Hand," in the *Vāstuśāstra* composed by the great king of kings, the illustrious Bhojadeva, also known as the *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*.
Now begins the tenth chapter: "The Settlement of Cities."
Now, the measurement of each of the three types of cities is described,
along with their walls, moats, watchtowers, gates, streets,
and roads. Among them, the largest city is held to be four thousand dhanus in extent.

The middle [size] is two thousand [units] by one thousand in width; the inferior is one thousand [units] by one thousand in width. One should make each dimension—whether with an eighth part added, a quarter added, or half added—equal in length and breadth, forming a beautiful square.
One should fashion the entire city by means of what is called the sixty-four squares;
one should make it consist of sixteen compartments (dviraṣṭakoṣṭha), with six paths and nine courtyards. When the field has been made square, [the lines] run from east to north.
Its rafters should be made with three [units] each, separated by one-fourth [of a unit].
When this [mandala] is divided into six rafters and provided with sixteen squares,
an auspicious royal road should be made, resting upon the central rafter.
The army of the superior [king] should consist of twenty-four thousand units;
that of the middling, twenty thousand; and that of the inferior, sixteen thousand.
This applies to the fourfold army, as well as to the citizens and the king himself.
This [space] should be made unconfined and level, free from grass and pebbles.
Two great thoroughfares (mahārathyā) should be constructed between the two rows of bamboo enclosures;
these should measure twelve, ten, and eight cubits respectively for the three [classes], starting with the highest.
The work situated in the center of the lotus consists of the fourfold path of the vehicles;
in these cities beginning with Jyeṣṭhā, that lotus measures four cubits.
The side-street is half the length of the main road, or increased by two [cubits].
The remaining streets should be laid out according to measurement at half that size. On both sides of the fourfold carriage road, two pedestrian paths each should be constructed,
situated at the end of every eight paces.
In the superior [type], those two [gateways] should be three cubits; in the middling, they are reduced by half a cubit;
and in the inferior, they should be less than the middling by half a cubit.
Furthermore, two other gateways for the bells should be constructed within the interior of the city.
