Endowed with the qualities of a royal road and conforming to the prescribed measurements, seventeen paths are said to extend from east to west;
likewise, others of the same measurement should extend from south to north. ||14-15||
One who knows the ritual procedure should establish the ground for the rampart all around, outside the path of the bell, according to the measurement of the path of the bell;
and then, outside that ground, according to the measurement of the great carriage road.
Three moats should be constructed together with the intervening spaces between the widths of the ditches. The excavation should be made leaving out one-third, or even half, of the width;
it should be equal to the full width at the base, and likewise at the top.
One should construct a rampart on one's own ground using the earth excavated for the moat;
it should have a raised center, be shaped like the back of an elephant, and be struck with the foot by those of noble lineage.
Then, using the earth brought up from the moat, which exceeds the amount required for the construction of the rampart—

One should first fill up the low-lying areas of the ground and bring them to a level state. Having thus cleared the three moats on all sides, one should construct a firm foundation, properly bound together with stones or bricks.
Filled with water flowing through its channels, full of the waters of the Ganges,
enchanting with its various lotuses, and possessing outlets for the discharge of water at its grasp-points;
then, on all its sides, [he saw] female bees intoxicated by the fragrance.
One should establish gardens of *sumana* trees as delightful dwellings;
furthermore, its outer perimeter should be arranged in every direction,
enclosed by tree roots, networks of creepers, and even thorns.
One should construct a formidable rampart rising above the embankment, built with large stones and slabs in the center, or made of baked bricks;
it should be twelve cubits in height for the superior type, while the middling type stands at ten cubits.
The width of the smallest [type] should be eight cubits; thus it is threefold.
The largest is praised as being seventeen cubits in height, the middle fifteen, and the last thirteen.

They desire the height of the enclosure wall to be neither more than seventeen cubits nor less than thirteen; nor should it be measured by an even number of cubits. From top to bottom, it should be properly increased by two finger-breadths for every cubit of length.
Or, for that [structure] whose width at the base is twelve cubits,
its head (the pinnacle) should be ten cubits wide;
the *kapiśīrṣa* (lion-head ornament) should be one cubit high, and the *kāṇḍavāriṇī* (water-channel) should be two cubits.
Towers should be constructed upon that rampart in every direction, reaching from the ears [of the wall] up to the gateway and joined with the corners;
they should be two stories high, extending above the parapet, and equal in height and width to the rampart itself.
One should then construct gateways at half that distance, provided with watchtowers (aṭṭālaka).
There should be a distance of one hundred cubits between each successive watchtower;
in this way, the city shall be impregnable to infantry, cavalry, chariots, and elephants.
One should construct a walkway with moving doors, easy to ascend, provided with a railing, equipped with stairs, furnished with turrets, and adorned with lion-heads;
it should be situated on the royal highway and great thoroughfares in all four directions.
One who knows the science [of architecture] should provide three gates for each of the three [sections] in the city. The four great gates on the royal road should extend nine cubits in width;
they should be eight or seven cubits [in height], less than twice that [width] by three cubits.

One should construct a gate supported by a great carriage-road, measuring six, five, or four cubits in height, and less than one and a half, one, or half a cubit respectively in width; furthermore, one should build firm watchtowers at all the great gates.
The gates should have firm bolts, Indra-kīlas, and be provided with door-panels and cross-bars.
The hall should be equal in width to the royal road and extend out from the main gate;
half of that should be the interior courtyard, and the width of those two [the hall and courtyard] is recorded as being half again.
Having laid out the square [mandala], one should fashion a gateway extending from the mouth [of the central deity],
with paths established at three-quarters of its width, provided with two crucibles (mūṣā),
having four doors within the inner wall, and commensurate with the great door.
One should decorate the edges of the compartments for the decorative panels with wooden ornaments.
At each door, there should be two *śālā* (architectural projections) on both sides, and two *mūṣa* (ornamental niches) at each door;
these should face one another, measuring two cubits in width and twice that in height.
The middle section of the cloth for the wood and the beeswax should be five cubits high;
likewise, a second ground should be made, elevated by the remaining height of the door.
One should fashion that [second ground], excluding the outer door, as previously described.
It was joined at the front with windows capable of resisting frontal assaults;
then, having fixed a third floor above the great gate,
it was provided with a gateway for blocking access, a watchtower, and a circumambulatory path.
One should construct above that [the city] everything other than the pillars and the altar;
it should be equipped with nets of traps, *śataghnī* engines, missiles, weapons, and various implements.
One should design these for the sake of the city's prosperity, beauty, and protection.
It should have large gates surrounded by walkways with three floors.
From the southern side of the main gateway, one [gallery] should rise and extend toward the left, reaching as far as the second side, situated on the exterior. ||47-48||

A second enclosure wall, however, should be constructed on its left side, starting from that very point and extending until its completion; outside of it, there should be a rampart. And the space between these two should be equal in width to the royal highway.
In this case, however, it should be done here with an excellent opening for the mouth (the main gate).
Having repeatedly observed rivers, mountains, and reservoirs suitable for enjoyment, one should construct side-gates (winged gates) here and there according to one's own desire. ||50-51||
In the city, one should construct water-illusions concealed by stone or wood;
these, filled with water, should be two cubits or at least one cubit in height, arranged so as to be circumambulated.
Furthermore, there should be [statues] with severed ears, distorted ears, the "thunderbolt" (vajra), and the "needle-mouthed" (sūcīmukha).
That city which is circular in shape like a fan, or shaped like a bow,
or which is equal to two carts in width and twice as long,
or which has its serpent-wheel situated in the intermediate directions— that city would be censurable.
One should predict that people living in a city where ears have been cut off will face fear from thieves,
or from diseases, or from other such calamities; furthermore,
there will be enmity with their masters, universal reproach by the people, and childlessness.

A very short lifespan arises for the inhabitants of the city of Vikarṇa. Furthermore, a person living in the city bearing the form of a thunderbolt (Vajrākṛtidhara) encounters defeat by women, poison-diseases, and various kinds of dissensions. ||56-57||
Afflicted by the disease of hunger, living beings go to their destruction while dwelling forever in that city shaped like the point of a needle;
abandoned by their master and deprived of all accumulations, they perish on every side. (58)
People who take refuge in the Vṛtta-pura will be born with very short lifespans.
In the city shaped like a fan, people will be speakers of untruth, short-lived, afflicted by wind, and of fickle minds. (59–60)
A city shaped like a bow will certainly have a population that is joined with women of ill conduct and likewise abounds in many eunuchs; there,
fear of disease, grief, fire, and thieves arises among the people.
A city that is laid out in the shape of two oxen drawing a cart brings failure to undertakings, causes fear to Brahmins, creates dissension among kinsmen,
and results in the destruction of the citizens, their lord, as well as the elephants and horses. ||62-63||
That city, which is situated somewhere with a double-length configuration, may be attacked and occupied by powerful enemies.
Therein lie the destruction of people, the ravages of fire, and perils arising from women.
It becomes pure for one who is confused about the directions, yet it does not depart from that state.
People afflicted by the fear of weapons, wind, demons, fire, spirits, and yakṣas, as well as those tormented by disease, perish when they fall into the crooked hands of serpents. (65–66)
Since such sites as these were previously declared by the Purāṇas to be inauspicious,
he should not establish a city for them even at a single such location. If even a single site among these is occupied through negligence, [the king will suffer].
Then the kingdom would be oppressed by hunger, enemies, fear, and death. Therefore,
a master architect who knows the scriptures should, with a mind intent on diligence,
lay out a beautiful city exactly as it has been described.

One should perform a propitiatory rite (śānti) during the construction of altars, on the occasion of a procession, in the consecration of temples, during works related to rivers, under the Maitra nakṣatra, and during periods of exhaustion; likewise, when performing a sacrifice, entering a city,
or during the installation [of images], the wise man, being self-restrained, should do so.
One should perform the *abhyudayika* rite or whatever else may be necessary;
for any action performed by those who are impure constantly causes fear in the city, shortens life, fails to bring prosperity, and results in the death of the king. 71–72.
That which is prescribed by those ignorant of the scriptures, that which is performed by those lacking the defining marks,
and that which is done by those who are impure— such work is inauspicious and devoid of fruit.
[This applies] to the architect, the astrologer, and likewise to the priest who knows the scriptures.
The king, being consecrated, should perform his duties in the city and in rites for peace.

The domestic priest should offer oblations into the fire, and the astrologer should provide a firm [prediction]. The chief architect should present the sacrificial offering and arrange for the rite of pacification. ||74-75||
Then, in that city where the gods stationed at the vital points were constantly worshipped by the citizens as they stood at the crossroads,
there existed the fourfold science of architecture and the eightfold science of medicine. (76)

The science of archery with its seven branches, and astronomy, were received from the abode of Kamalā; furthermore, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra never abandon that city, along with all the general characteristics, portents, and omens.
This division of the city has been correctly described;
they say a *kheṭa* (market town) has half that [city's] diameter, and a village (*grāma*) half of that again.
They declare that a *kheṭa* is one *yojana* from the city, and a village one *yojana* from the *kheṭa*.
The distance between one village and another is declared to be one *gavyūti*.
The boundary of a district is two *krośas*, while that of a city is half of that.
The boundary of a *kheṭaka* is half the boundary of a city, and for a village, it is recorded as half the boundary of a *kheṭaka*.
The width of the road leading to the city gates is recorded as thirty dhanus;
for a *kheṭaka* (market town) it is twenty, and ten is shown for a village.
Nine thousand and ninety villages are proclaimed [to exist].
The wise know that even sixty-four villages constitute a superior kingdom;
likewise, five thousand villages, three hundred,
and eighty-four villages are declared to be a middling kingdom.
One thousand villages,
as well as five hundred, and forty-eight— these are said to constitute the smallest kingdom among the large,
medium, and small [kingdoms], according to their respective numbers.

Having divided each [of these] ninefold, the wise man should distribute them according to rule. When the kingdoms have been thus divided, the one who knows the ordinances should establish seven cities in each of them, according to the tradition. || 86-87 ||
The division, the authority, and the characteristics of the first [caste],
as well as its birth, color, and residence, are here described exactly as they are.
Goldsmiths and those who live by fire likewise reside in the south-eastern quarter.
One who knows the rules should settle other laborers as well;
to the south of the houses of the Vaiśyas, the gamblers, the cheats, and the usurers,
he should establish the dwellings of actors and dancers.
He should station pig-breeders, distillers of spirits, hunters, fishermen,
and those authorized for the suppression of criminals in the southwestern quarter (the direction of Nirṛti). Likewise,
he should station those who possess skill in charioteering and those who are proficient in weapons.
He should station all those in the western direction (the quarter of Varuṇa) within the city;
and those who are authorized for ritual duties as well as the attendants and the vintners—he should station all of them in the northern direction (the quarter of Vāyu). ||92-93||
One should establish residences for ascetics and likewise for those who have Brahman as their calf, as well as assembly halls,
water-stations, and meritorious guest-houses in the direction of the Lord of Wealth (the North).
Furthermore, there should be those who sell ghee and those who sell fruits.
Those stationed in the northeast of the city are praised.
A wise king should station the commanders of the army and his principal officers in the eastern part of the force, and likewise station the various kinds of troops in the southeast.
In the southern direction, he should station the guild-leaders; likewise, in the south-eastern quarter, he should appoint the great officials of the realm;
and in the south-western direction, he should station the treasury-keepers, high ministers, guides, and artisans.
One should appoint navigators in the direction of the Lord of Waters (the west);
one should appoint the commanders of the army along with their leaders in the quarter of Vāyu (the northwest);
and one should station the domestic priests and astrologers in the northern direction.
O gentle one, the Brāhmaṇas should be placed in the northern quarter, the Kṣatriyas in the direction of Indra (the east);
the Vaiśyas and Śūdras should be stationed in the south and west respectively;
and merchants, physicians, and chief officials should be settled in all four directions.
One should especially station the forces in the four directions.
Outside the city, in the east, the wise architect should establish the sites for the Liṅgas; likewise, in the south, he should establish the cremation grounds at their respective locations.
Just as the distribution has been prescribed for every direction in the city,
so it should be in the villages, the hamlets, and the encampment of the army.
The two [gates] facing the city should be made complete in their parts and highly prosperous.
At every gate, the auspicious Lakṣmī and Vaiśravaṇa, with gentle countenances,
gaze upon the kingdom, the town, the village, or the great capital. Therein, one should predict the attainment of health and wealth, as well as victory for the subjects.
Bound by the fetters of afflictions, people would become mutual slayers according to the [karmic] threads;
they would not even perceive the village, the hamlet, the city, or the kingdom,
just as those deities who are stationed in every direction within the city.
Beyond that, we shall describe them in relation to the outer and inner grounds.
Beginning from the four directions and extending to the end of the ramparts and moats, at intervals of one hundred and fifty bows, or even two hundred bows, outside [the city]. ||107-108||

One should construct the dwellings of the thirty gods in their proper order upon pure and irreproachable ground measuring a hundred bows [in length], together with their respective palaces and the houses of their attendants.

One should construct beautiful and variegated forests facing the city; one should arrange the dwellings of the gods both inside and outside the central axis of the city, which extends from south to north and passes through the middle of the conceptualized city.
One should place those facing west in the eastern direction and those facing east in the direction of Varuṇa (the west).
On its southern and northern sides, one should place the lineage members in a clockwise manner.
One should not place them facing south, nor even the gods facing north.

Together with the Caityas, Śānis, Sabhās, Yakṣas, and Mātṛs, these deities who occupy the primary directions have been correctly described. Now we shall explain those who reside in each of the outer directions.
The abode of Viṣṇu, the Lord of the Day (the Sun), and the Thousand-eyed One (Indra),
as well as that of Dharma, should be constructed in the eastern direction;
likewise, those of Sanatkumāra, Sāvitrī, the Maruts, and Māruta.
One should construct the dwelling in the south-eastern quarter.

To the south [should be] the house of Gaṇeśa, the Mothers, and the Bhūtas; to the south-west, the abode of the Lord of the Dead (Yama); and in the south-west (Nairṛta) direction, there should be the temple of Bhadrakālī and the shrine of the Pitṛs.
One should establish the abode of Sāgara, of the rivers, of Viśvakarman the lord of artisans, and of Prajāpati Varuṇa in the western quarter;
the dwelling of the hooded serpents should be constructed in the northwestern direction.
Right here, the temple of Śanaiścara and that of Kātyāyanī should be established;
likewise, the temples of Viśākha, Skanda, Soma,
and the Lord of the Yakṣas should each be constructed separately, situated in the northern direction.
In the north-eastern direction, one should construct a delightful temple for Maheśa, the teacher of the world, as well as for Śrī and Agni;
[and likewise] for the rivers and oceans all around the city.
In forests and on mountains, every place is dear to the Lord of Umā.
That city in which the best of gods are thus established within their respective quarters, having attained perfect prosperity, rejoices for a long time. (122-123)

Even if it is far from the city, in all directions, deities facing outward are praised, not those with their backs turned. If, however, on that plot of land, a bamboo fence is constructed, then it is considered "with its back turned. (124)

Then, one who knows that [deity] should perform this rite as prescribed in the scriptures. One should paint the god on a wall facing the city, clearly manifest in form, accompanied by his specific dress, color, ornaments, weapons, and vehicle. 125–126.
There is no fault in [using] wood from the *vaikaṅkata*, *śamī*, and *bilva* trees, or from milky and thorny trees, when they are situated inside water-wells or fire-houses;
this rule has been declared for those [trees] that have taken refuge near a shrine, but not for those that grow within a village.
Therefore, the gods should be depicted facing all directions in paintings.

Whatever arrangement has been prescribed for the abodes of the gods outside the city, that same arrangement should be made inside as well, each deity occupying its own respective direction. ||128-129||
In the center of the city, the temple of the Lotus-born (Brahmā) should be constructed;
likewise the residence of Indra, and similarly those of Balarāma and Kṛṣṇa.
[One should also establish] the Mothers, the lords of the Yakṣa hosts, the Śivakas, and the multitudes of Bhūtas.
Even without houses, one should construct courtyards and roads within the city.
The king, desiring prosperity, should establish those who live by their castes, stages of life, trade, and crafts in their respective quarters, and likewise the gods. 131–132.
When one possesses a temple and is endowed with devotion, desire, and capacity, if one wishes to have another temple built, the wise person should not cause distress to the former.
This applies likewise to every neighboring house, every village, and every temple.

One should also construct [a temple] for each city, but not exceeding the proportions of the original measurement. If another temple is built to the east of the original palace— whether that of Rudra, Soma, or Brahmā— it will cause suffering for the twice-born.
If another superior mansion [asterism] is formed for Vahni (Agni), Vācaspati (Bṛhaspati),
or the domestic priests (purodhas), one should certainly know that there is fear for the astrologers (jyotirvids) as well as for the Lord of Wealth (Kubera),
the Lord of the Immortals (Indra), Yama, or Varuṇa. ||136||
If a residence larger than [the king's] is constructed, one should know that there is danger for the lord of the earth.
(137) If another residence larger than the commander’s quarters is built within his dwelling, suffering will certainly arise for the general and his forces. (138)
If a house is built that exceeds the dimensions prescribed for Prajāpati or for Hari,
it will lead to the bondage and destruction of both the builder and the one who commissioned it.
This is even more so if another house is built that exceeds the proportions prescribed for Gaṇeśa, Yakṣas, or the Serpents.
Then there shall be constant and great danger to the components of the army.
If deities bearing feminine names are afflicted by [the construction of] houses, they then cause distress to the principal women of the city. (140–141)

When all the former temples were oppressed by other [shrines], or when those belonging to that [sect] were oppressed by other shrines, or by those oppressed by shrines; and when dwellings were built with deficient or excessive dimensions, or were poorly situated—[then calamities occurred]. (142)
There would be suffering for the builder and the one who commissioned the work, and likewise no honor for him [the deity].
One should not construct [a temple] that is excessively large, nor one that is too small, nor a residence for the gods;
and one should build a city that is not dependent [on another], nor one dependent on the divisions of the Vedha.

One should construct the divine abodes with nine, six, and three squares as the intervals for the superior, middling, and inferior types; otherwise, it leads to defects. This rule has been declared by the gods themselves regarding their own dwellings.
One may freely construct a celestial abode outside one's own residence.
This rule is recorded as being common to all cities, all villages, and all market towns. 146–147.
Thus has been described the arrangement of the positions of the deities of the quarters as they approach the city;
now we shall explain the distribution of the household deities.
[This concludes the section] endowed with the correct distinction between auspicious and inauspicious results.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, on the "Laying Out of Cities," in the *Vāstuśāstra*—also known as the *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*—composed by the great king of kings, the illustrious Bhojadeva.
Now begins the eleventh chapter, titled "The Division of the Three Types of Vāstus."
Then, when the field has been made square and divided into nine parts,
Brahmā of great splendor is to be placed in the center, occupying nine squares.
Immediately adjacent to him in the east, Aryamā is said to occupy six squares.
In the southeast corner, both Savitṛ and Sāvitra occupy one square each.
Immediately following Brahmā in the south, Vivasvat occupies six squares.
In the southwest corner, both Jaya and Indra are said to occupy one square each.
Then Mitra occupies six squares in the direction of the lord of waters (the north).
Both Yakṣman and Rudra occupy one square each in the west and the north-west respectively.
Then, with six squares, Niścala Pṛthivīdhara occupies the north.

Āpa, Apavatsa, Padika, Īśa, and Diggata—thus the deities residing within have been described; now we shall speak of those situated outside. Their positions should be known as proceeding clockwise, starting from the northeast (Pūrvottara) and so on.
Agni, followed by Parjanya, Jayanta, and Indra;
Ravi, Satya, and Bhṛśa—these are the [eleven Rudras]. After them is Nabhastha, and from him Anila; then Pūṣan, Vitatha, Gṛhakṣata, and Yama.
Then Gandharva, Bhṛṅgarāja, Mṛga, and the Pitṛgaṇa;
then Dauvārika, Sugrīva, Puṣpadanta, Jaleśvara,
the Asura named Śoṣa, and thereafter Pāpayakṣmā.
Roga, Nāga, Mukhya, Bhallāṭa, Soma, Caraka, and Aditi— the mother of the Daityas— these are the deities of the quarters.
They are positioned outside in sequence, belonging respectively to Agni, Vāyu, the Pitṛs, and Vyādhi.
Carakī, Vidārī, Pūtanā, and the sinful Rākṣasī—these have no movement of their feet;
they possess only a fixed station.
Now we shall describe the movement of the feet of those celestial dwellers who reside outside [the city]. || 11-12 ||

Among them, eight are lords of bipeds: Jayanta, Bhṛśa, Vitatha, Bhṛṅga, Sugrīva, Śoṣa, Mukhya, and likewise Āditi. Those remaining among these, who are outside [the inner group], are the gods who possess four feet.
The sequence of the deities' positions is declared in the eighty-one-square grid.
When the field has been made square and divided into ten parts, it becomes a hundred-square *vāstu*; we shall now describe the stationing of the immortals therein as well.
In the center of the site-plan consisting of one hundred squares, Pitāmaha occupies one square multiplied by twice eight (sixteen). Aryaman occupies four squares;
likewise do Vivasvat, Mitra, and Pṛthivībhṛt.
Indeed, the wise desire their enjoyment just as [they desire] that of Aryaman.
Those foremost of gods beginning with Savitṛ and ending with Āpavatsa who have not been mentioned—
just as in the case of the eighty-one [deities], so too is their enjoyment eightfold.
Agni, Antariksha, Pavana, Mriga, the Pitris, Roga, and Aditi—
these stand outside as the possessors of one and a half padas each.
These twenty-four supreme deities, beginning with Parjanya, have been described.
Those ending with Āditya are the two-pada [deities]; the remainder has been established previously.
When the field has been made square and divided into eight parts as before, the Vāstu site consists of sixty-four squares, being formed by sixty-four padas. ||20-21||
Within this [diagram], the Grandfather (Brahmā) occupies four squares;
the gods beginning with Aryaman occupy two squares each in the middle squares. There are eight in the intermediate directions and eight on the outside, situated in the eight corners.
All those gods who are present here are recorded as occupying half a square (padārdhabhuj).
Furthermore, Parjanya, Bhṛśa, Pūṣan, Bhṛṅga, Dauvārika,
Śoṣa, Nāga, and Āditi occupy one and a half squares (adhyardhapadaspṛśaḥ).

In the sixteen external [deities] beginning with Jayantī and ending with Carakī, who are celebrated here among the deities, each occupies two squares. One should lead the vein upward from the square of Agni (fire) to the end of the square of the Pitṛs (ancestors).
One should bring her, named "Disease," out from the outer quarters;
one should lead Bhṛṅga to Dvināman, and from Bhṛṅga, one should bring Sugrīva. Then one should cause him to go to Aditi and cause Dvināman to enter.
Having led [the breath] from the solar station to the southern one, one should then bring it to the watery (vāruṇa) station;
thence one should lead it to the lunar (saumya) station, and from there one should bring it to the solar (āditya) station.
Having brought it from Bhṛśa to Vitatha, and then from Vitatha to the one called Śoṣa—
Having brought the principal [line] from the Śoṣa, one should lead it back again from there very strongly.
(29) With those divisions specified here according to their respective numbers, the wise man should divide the entire site for sacrifices, gods, and men. (30)
Even by all these gods, he who has his sorrows dispelled is thus beheld with an excess of joy; for even in their entirety,
these lotus-petal-eyed ones gaze upon him.
"One beholds these with an expanded eye.

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Division of the Three Vāstus," in the *Vāstuśāstra* composed by the Great King of Kings, the illustrious Bhojadeva, also known by the name *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*.
Now begins the twelfth chapter, titled "The Classification of the Channels (*nāḍī*) and the Veins (*sirā*), etc."
Now, the smallest site is said to have sixteen squares;
it consists of sixteen cells, and therein we shall describe the deities.
The principal deity, the best of gods, occupies one square situated in the center.
The four-faced Brahmā fashioned it with four quarters of a foot [of the meter].
These four supreme gods— Aryaman, Vivasvat, Mitra, and Kṣmādhara— are the enjoyers of half-portions of a foot.

The eight deities beginning with Savitṛ and ending with Apavatsa, who reside in the corners of the Creator’s [mandala], have arms measuring four units; they are gods possessing the brilliance of the sun. These deities are stationed in the corners starting from the southeast (Agni) in successive order.
Those eight, beginning with Āditya and ending with Parjanya, who are the foremost among the gods, have been designated by the wise as having an eighth share;
they are proclaimed here by the learned as enjoyers of a fourth part [of the sacrificial offerings]. ||5-6||
The deities situated outside, such as Carakāntā, Jayantā, and others—
for all sixteen of them— their enjoyment is prescribed to be half a square (ardhapadika).
When the field has been made square and divided into thirty-three parts:
One should set aside two final rows and a half-row for the sake of the Carakī and other [deities].
Then, one should leave a path (vīthikā) of half a square in between;
thereafter, one should divide the site (vāstu) in the center by twenty-seven squares.
Seven hundred and twenty-nine words [make up the mandala];
therein, within the womb (garbha), there would be the Svabhū square consisting of eighty-one words.
Furthermore, there are eight separate squares of eighteen words each, beginning with the *capa*.
The first [section] for Aryaman consists of four sets of fifty-four squares.
The external deities, beginning with Īśa and ending with Aditi, occupy nine squares each.
This arrangement of regions is called the thousandfold Vāstu.
Now, it is said that for the purpose of a circular temple (vṛttaprāsāda),

there is a circular site (vṛttavāstu) divided into sixty-four parts, while another is divided into one hundred parts. When the diameter of the circle is divided into eight parts, there are intervals of one part each.
One should construct four enclosing walls (paridhis), with the middle circle consisting of two parts. The outer circular band (vṛttavalaya) should consist of twenty-eight parts;
the inner circular band should be formed by successively omitting eight-eighths (one-eighth) of those parts.
When this is done, that four-footed [area] of Brahmā will be in the center.
Thus, the circular site-plan (vṛttavāstu) consisting of sixty-four squares has been described.
When the diameter of the circle is divided tenfold, there are intervals of one square each.
Five enclosing walls (paridhis) should be made, with a circular space in the center occupying two parts.
Then, one should divide the outer ring into thirty-six parts;
by this arrangement of sixty-four squares, there shall be a hundred-vāstu diagram.
The contraction of the deity-syllables for these two is like that of the square;
likewise, other [shapes] should also be made by the wise according to the requirements of the task—
whether triangular, hexagonal, octagonal, or sixteen-sided— just as with the circle.
The division of the site (vāstu) into squares is performed in the circular, square, and semi-circular forms.
Among these, the single Puruṣa is conceived in many ways;
once every layout has been divided, one should then observe [the deities].
The body of this Vāstupuruṣa possesses qualities and defects;
[the parts are] the mouth, the head, then the ears, the eyes, the palate, the lips, and the teeth in sequence;
the chest, the throat, the two breasts, the navel, the penis, the testicles, and then the anus.
One should fashion the two upper arms, the forearms, the hands, the buttocks, the thighs, the shanks, and the two feet;
by this means, he becomes possessed of a human form. Likewise, one should fashion the veins, the primary bones, the secondary bones, the joints, and the sub-joints.
Furthermore, the vital points (marmas) located within the body of the building are like those of a great bamboo;
those channels situated in the ears are proclaimed to be the veins (nāḍīs).
The measure of that [channel] is proclaimed to be one-sixteenth part of the base (pada).
The two great bamboo-lines (vaṃśas) are those running east-west and north-south, situated in the middle;
the measurement for these two is stated to be one-fifth of the square.
These are designated as the "bamboos" in this context, which are the lines extending from the mouth [of the mandala]. ||26-27||
Those lines which extend horizontally are proclaimed as the *anuvamśas* (transverse veins);
the points where these intersect are declared to be the *marmas* (vital points).
They say that those which are situated in the middle of the feet are the *upamarmas* (subsidiary vital points).

The eighth, tenth, twelfth, and sixteenth parts measured from the foot (pada) are the desired dimensions for the beams (vaṃśa) and other components in their respective order. The joint that occurs at the eighth beam is designated as the "sandhi" (joint).
Furthermore, those which are declared to be the secondary parts (aṅga) of those [primary parts] are called the *anusandhis*.
The measure of the *sandhis* is said to be equal to the tip of a hair;
the measure of the *anusandhis* is declared to be half of that.
Having diligently abandoned these [defects], the master builder, an expert in the science of architecture,
should always carefully lay out the materials; he must not cause any obstruction to a large beam by means of any material whatsoever.
Furthermore, in other cases, one should abandon the substance in the middle sections of the bamboo;
if it is occupied by a large bamboo, the death of the master is certain.
One should know that fear arises from the heat of the year and from the oppression of the bamboos.
The secondary vital points lead to disease; the vital points lead to the ruin of the family.
When the veins are pressed, they cause agitation and the loss of wealth;
when the joints are pierced or the secondary joints are pressed, strife shall arise.
Therefore, one should observe all these [vessels] when they are compressed;

having understood the veins (sirās), along with the subsidiary vessels (anusirās), the channels (nāḍīs), and the primary and secondary bone-tubes (vaṃśānuvaṃśas) within the body of Vāstu, as well as the vital points (marmans) and their respective fruits, one should avoid piercing them with effort—he who does so meets no calamity. (37)

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Options Regarding the Piercing of Channels, Main Stalks, Sub-stalks, Veins, Sub-veins, Vital Points, and Sub-vital Points," in the *Vāstuśāstra* composed by the Great Emperor Śrī Bhojadeva, also known as the *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*.
Now begins the thirteenth chapter, "The Piercing of Vital Points" (*Marmavedha*).
[It concerns] that which consists of eighty-one squares, as well as that which consists of one hundred squares.
Regarding the sixty-four squares of the site-plan (vāstu) which have been declared here in three ways:
we shall now explain how one should divide them,
as well as their vital points (marmāṇi), which are also described herein.
A wise person should divide the site of the king’s residence and the dwellings of those belonging to the various social orders (varṇa) into eighty-one squares;
likewise, there are various palaces and diverse pavilions here.
The wise man should measure them by dividing them into a hundred squares.
Furthermore, one should divide that which consists of sixty-four squares into [the same units] for royal camps,
villages, market towns, cities, and so forth.
There are thirteen gods within and thirty-two on the outside;
their locations, vital points (marmas), veins, and bones are therein—
at the mouth, the heart, the navel, the head, and likewise the two breasts.
They declare that there are six great vital points (marmas) for this person of the site:
the junctions of the primary and secondary axes, and those which are the centers of the squares;
these are the locations of the deities within the initial sixteen-square grid.
Furthermore, the locations of the deities and the junctions are found within grids of sixty-four squares,
as well as in those of eighty-one squares and even those of one hundred squares;
in all four of these divisions, there are channels (sirās) extending in the four directions.

Those vital points (marmas) have been described, as well as those which are at the center of the doors. Whether by the middle of the width of the wall or by the middle of the timber, that vital point which is afflicted therein in the house— the result of that is now stated.
They say that from the crushing of vital points (marmans) by means of doors or even walls,
a householder suffers misfortune or the ruin of his lineage.
Through pillars there may be the destruction of the master, and through scales, the destruction of his wife.
Through the *jayantī* stars, there is the killing of a daughter-in-law; through the *saṃgraha* stars, the destruction of kinsmen.

When the body [of a planet] occupies the vital points (*marmasthāna*) of the body [of a sign], the body of the master is oppressed. Those who know this declare that the *sandhipāla* stars cause separation from friends.
One should predict the loss of wealth from *nāgapāśas*, the destruction of friends from *nāgadantas*,
and the ruin of servants from *kapicchakas* situated at the vital points (*marmas*).
There should be six wooden beams, hollows, windows, and openings for observation.

These [cracks], occurring in the middle of vital points (marmans), bring about the loss of wealth. Through cracks at the doors, the materials [of the structure], the scales, the pillars, the pegs, and the windows, as well as those afflicted in the middle of the doors, there arise afflictions from hosts of diseases and the loss of wealth. ||16-17||

The wise declare that there is fear of punishment from the king and suffering from one's husband when [the house] is pierced at the middle of the door-posts or even in the middle of the six wooden beams;
they know this very same result occurs when it is pierced by iron, wood, and other such materials.
A bed arranged along the length of the house destroys the family of householders.
Elephant-tusk supports fixed upon the canopy of the husband’s bed bring about his ruin.
Furthermore, those elephant-tusk supports that are pierced by windows or pillars [are likewise inauspicious].
They bring fear of weapons to the master, or else they cause the danger of thieves;
they lead to the destruction of wealth and grain, as well as to sorrow and strife.
Furthermore, a door situated in the middle of the house leads to the corruption of women.
If even one of these substances should strike a major vital point (mahāmarmā),
it may lead to the destruction of all the householder's possessions or even to his death.
These substances include fine cloth, bamboo pointing upwards, bottle gourds, and Indra-kīlaka.

Even when there is a piercing (vedha) of cities, palaces, or houses, these [planets] do not cause harm. Thus, this distinction resides in the syllables of the names of gods, kings, and excellent men; likewise, a piercing (vyadha) occurs when it reaches all the vital points (marmas) within the words.
The respective fruits of each [of these] have been correctly stated;
now we shall describe here the division of the limbs of the Vāstupuruṣa.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "Piercing the Vital Points" (Marmavedha), in the Vāstuśāstra composed by the Great King of Kings, the illustrious Bhojadeva, also known as the Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra.
Now begins the fourteenth chapter, the determination of the deities of the limbs of the person and so forth:
"With these variously distributed terms for the deities, the diligent architect should thus fashion the human form of the site. (1)
Fire is declared to be his head; Diti and Ambudādhipa (Varuṇa) are his two eyes;
Jayanta and Aditi are his two ears; and Vāyu is situated in his mouth.
The Sun is on his right arm, and the Moon is established on his left.
Mahendra and Caraka, along with Apavatsa, are stationed upon his chest;
Aryaman is on the right breast and Pṛthivīdhara on the left.
Yakṣman, Roga, Nāga, Mukhya, and Bhallāṭa—these [are the others].
The gods have taken refuge in his left arm:
Satya, Bhṛśa, Nabhas, Vāyu, and Pūṣan;
thus, five dwellers of heaven have resorted to this arm of his on the right.
Sāvitra and Savitṛ, as well as Rudra and Śaktidhara—these four preside over the *kalās*. Svabhū is in the hands and the heart;
Vitatha and Eka-kṣata are situated on his right side.
Furthermore, on his left side stand the two deities named Śoṣa and Asura;
both Mitra and Vivasvat are situated upon his belly;
and the two deities named Indra and Jaya are located in the middle of his penis.
Yama and Varuṇa reside respectively in the right and left thighs;
Gandharva and Bhṛṅga, along with the two Mṛgas, are in the two shanks;
and the doorkeepers Sugrīva and Puṣpa, as well as the Pitṛs, have taken refuge in the feet. ||9-10||
One should know that the head of the eighty-one-square site rests upon the division of the eastern direction,
whereas the sixty-four-square site rests upon the Māhendrī direction.
From the eighty-one-square site is born the Vāstu known as the hundred-square.
That which consists of sixteen parts arises from sixty-four parts.
He who stands in the midst of the gods, born from the lotus of Brahmā,
is the thousand-faced Lord of the worlds, whose power is inconceivable.
This fire which has been mentioned here is Hara, the destroyer of all beings;
and this one named Parjanya, the lord of the clouds who brings rain,
is the venerable sage Kaśyapa, known by two names, Jayanta.
Mahendra is the lord of the gods and the crusher of the Danujas;
they further desire Āditya, the radiant Vivásvat.
Satya is Dharma, who benefits all beings; Bhṛśa is Kāma, the god of love. ||15-16||
The deity remembered as Antariksha is declared to be the sky;
Maruta is designated as the wind, and Pushan is remembered as the host of mothers (the Maruts).
Adharma shall be known by the name Vitatha, the peerless son of Kali.
Furthermore, Gṛhakṣata is the son of Soma (Candra) and is known as Budha. The illustrious Yama, the son of Vivasvat, is considered the lord of the departed;
and the divine Gandharva is proclaimed to be the venerable Nārada. ||18-19||
In this context, they call Bhṛṅgarāja the Rākṣasa, the son of Nirṛti;
that infinite deer which is here is also said to be the Self-born Dharma.
He is declared to be the primordial Prajāpati, the Creator, Manu, and Sugrīva.
Puṣpadanta, however, shall be the son of Vinatā, possessed of great speed. Varuṇa is celebrated as the lord of the waters and a guardian of the world (lokapāla).
Rāhu is an asura, the crusher of the sun and moon, and the son of Siṃhikā.
This illustrious son of the Sun, Śanaiścara, is Śoṣa;
he is declared to be Pāpayakṣmā, Kṣaya, and the disease known as Jvara.
The glorious Nāga Vāsuki is the sovereign of the serpents.
Tvaṣṭṛ is known here by the name Mukhya, and he is also designated as Viśvakarman.
Candra is called Bhalvāṭa, and Kubera is named Soma. Caraka is known as Vyavasāya, and Śrī is designated here as Āditi.

Here, Śarva is said to be Diti; he who bears the trident and has the bull as his emblem is Himavat, and the waters are called Āpa; Umā is remembered as Āpavatsa. Aryaman is the Āditya, and Sāvitra is said to be the Mother of the Vedas.
Here, the goddess Gaṅgā is proclaimed by the wise as Savitrī;
that Mṛtyu, the taker of bodies, is remembered as Vivasvat.
He who is named Jaya, the wielder of the thunderbolt, is Indra, the powerful Hari.
Mitra is Haladhara, Mālī; Rudra is declared to be Maheśvara. Rājayakṣmā is called Guha, and Kṣitidhra is said to be Ananta.
Carakī, Vidārī, Pūtanā, and Pāparākṣasī—
For these are known as the attendants of the deities born from the womb of the Rākṣasas.
Thus has this glossary (nighaṇṭu) of the deities of the dwelling been proclaimed.
[The syllable] *kṣo* is on the head; *ho* is between the eyes; *so* is on the nose; and *ṣa* is on the chin.
The letter Śa is in the throat; Va should be at the heart; Lakāra is located in the region of the navel;
Repha is in the bladder; Yakāra is in the penis;
Ma is in both the testicles; Nakāra is in the thighs; Ñakāra is situated in the kneecaps.
The syllable *ṅa* is at the end of the two ankles, and the syllable *pa* is said to be on the soles of the feet.

(33) Thus have been correctly described the limbs of the Vāstupuruṣa, as well as the distinctions between the names of the deities of the Vāstu-squares and the sixteen syllables assigned to the members of the Vāstu. Now, we shall describe the layout of the city according to the presiding deities. (34)

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Letters and Limbs of the Person and the Deities," in the *Vāstuśāstra* composed by the Great King of Kings, the illustrious Bhojadeva, also known as the *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*.
Now begins the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Royal Residence.
Once the layout of the city has been established, based upon the sixty-four squares—
It was provided with appointed moats, halls, gate-towers, and watchtowers;
its streets were well-laid out and its courtyards were distributed all around;
and shrines for the deities were established in their proper order, both within and without.
On ground sloping toward the east or north, or otherwise elevated toward the eastern door,
one should take a friendly stance that bestows fame, prosperity, and victory—
a square, level, and auspicious position attained according to the sequence of the castes.
One should construct the king’s palace situated toward the western direction from the center of the city.
In difficult terrains, it may be built according to the requirements of the ground, even in other directions;
or it should be constructed in any one of the positions belonging to Vivasvat, Bhūdhara, or Aryaman.
When joined with forty-three [thousand], the largest [city] shall be two hundred bows;
the medium one, one hundred and sixty-two; and the smallest, one hundred and eight.
In the largest city, the king's residence should be constructed as the largest.
A middling task should be performed for a middling [fortress], and an inferior one for an inferior one.
It should be protected by walls and moats, beautiful in appearance on all sides,
and provided with turrets, gateways, and very firm watchtowers.
The royal palace should be constructed by dividing [the site] into eighty-one squares;
the gateway of the building, facing north, should be situated along the main royal road. By this same method, it should also be constructed when resorting to other directions.
The gate of this [city] situated at the Bhallāṭa site is desired as the Gopura gate;
it bestows desired fruits when its width and height are commensurate with those of the city gate.
For one established on a mountain, they desire the Mahendra gate. ||10-11||
In the south (Vaivasvata) one should place Puṣpadanta, and in the southeast (Aryaṇī), Gṛhakṣata;

in the other [directions] following these, one should then arrange the others in their respective clockwise positions. In this manner, one should likewise assign the other doors in their own directions.
And for the sake of facing all [the quarters], gate-towers (gopura) are recommended;

or else, the side-gates (pakṣadvāra) should be set at a distance of one-twentieth part from the city gates of that [fortress], O Sugrīva, in the case of those named "Victorious" (jayanta) and "Foremost" (mukhya). ||13-14||
Likewise, one should perform circumambulations in the false [directions] as a result of delusion;
when the site has been divided and arranged like a city with rows of divine abodes,
there, in the place of the Maitra-pada, for the purpose of the king’s residence—
A palace facing the east should be constructed according to the rules for the conquest of the earth (Pṛthivīñjaya). Whether it be the Śrīvṛkṣa, the Sarvatobhadra, or another such as the Muktakoṇa,
the king may have whatever auspiciously characterized palace he desires built.
It should also be provided with workshops for the management of various tasks.
Therein, in the eastern direction, there shall be a building situated on the site of the Sun (Ādityapada),
serving as the court of justice for the administration of dharma and the examination of legal disputes.

The storehouse should be situated in the Bhṛśa direction, and the aviary for deer and birds should be in the Ambara direction. One should establish the kitchen in the Kakubha direction relative to the fire (Agni), the assembly hall and its dependencies in the Pūṣan direction, and the dining hall in the same.
The hall for music should be in the direction of Savitṛ, and the panegyrists (vandins) should be stationed in the direction of Savitṛ.
One should place shields and weapons suitable for them in the Vitatha quarter;
and one should establish the workshops for gold, silver, and other crafts in the Gṛhakṣata quarter.
To the south, on the right side, one should arrange the defensive enclosure and the storehouse.
In the region of Gandharva, there should be theaters for performances and music, as well as the residence of the Vasus.
Furthermore, in the region of Vaivasvata, stables for chariots and likewise for elephants should be constructed.
One should also cause a pond to be constructed situated in the northwestern part;
and one should establish the location of the harem within the enclosure of the ramparts, outside the positions of Sugrīva and the Gandharva in the northwest.
In the one named Jaya, one should construct the gateway of the gopura facing north;
the architect must likewise build the temple facing west,
as well as pleasure-pavilions, swings, and the abode of the Kumārīs in the Bhṛṅga [corner].
They desire the king’s inner apartments when the deer is in the ancestral forest,
but they know the assembly hall of the king’s women to be Indra’s station. Sugrīva’s station is adjacent to it, and Ariṣṭāra bestows what is desired.
To the rear of the gatekeeper Sugrīva’s ancestral residence shall be the enchanting Aśoka grove;
here also shall be the bath-houses with cascading streams and vine-cloistered bowers. (28–29)

One should construct wooden and stone structures, ponds, and well-laid-out flower avenues; at Puṣpadanta, there should be a workshop for mechanical arts and a flower-house. At the site of Varuṇa, one should build ponds and drinking halls.
The master builder should establish a granary in the Asura region, but an armory in the Śoṣa; he should establish a treasury for the sake of prosperity in the one called Raudrākhyā,
and a building for mortars, stones, and machines in Pāpayakṣman.
They say that even the work of woodcraft leads to well-being for one afflicted by pulmonary consumption (rājayakṣman).
For a disease, the site of a medicinal herb is auspicious in the direction from which the wind blows.
The wise recommend the location of elephants at the footprint of an elephant.
In the principal [quarter], there are the gymnasium, the theater, and the picture gallery (34).
Likewise, the cow-pen and the dairy are located in the area named after Bhallāṭa;
in the northern region, the station for the priest of Soma is desired (35).

And here, on the mountain, there shall be the king’s consecration hall, as well as places for charity, study, and peace; there shall also be the chamber for the fly-whisk, the umbrella, and the council hall.
Furthermore, the lord of men, remaining here, shall oversee the affairs of those who have business before him.
The stable for the horses should be constructed on the northern side;
it should be properly oriented toward the south, like the Mahīdharapada [stupa], and the stables for the king's horses should be made everywhere according to the layout of his palace. ||37-38||
To the south of the entrance should be the quarters for those with tusks (elephants), and to the north,
he should provide dwellings for the princes known as the *carakas*.
Right here, he should also establish schools for their acquisition of knowledge.
One should establish the residence for the king’s mother in the place of Aditi.
In this very location, they know that there should be separate palanquins, beds, seats, and houses;
even the arrangement of dwellings for the king’s elephants is recommended here.
In this very place shall be a site for the consecration of horned beasts;
and at Āpavatsapada, there shall be reservoirs of clear water, resounding with the cries of swans, cranes, and saras cranes, and filled with forests of blooming lotuses.
The residence for paternal uncles, maternal uncles, and others should be in the south-eastern quarter (the place of Diti).
Furthermore, O Lord of the Earth, for other vassals as well,
there should be a raised pillar-platform in the north-eastern direction or in the place of Agni (the southeast).

A beautiful temple with well-joined jeweled floors should be constructed for Parjanya; in his position, a house for an astrologer is desired. For Jaya, a victory-bestowing residence for the commander-in-chief should be established.

Relying on the wall at the gate, the position of Aryaman (the Sun) is praised; here, the end of the work involving weapons and the weapons themselves are located. One should cause the place of Brahmā, marked by Indra’s banner, to be enjoyed by men in the southeast.
In that regard, the houses and dwellings should be unattractive and conducive to discomfort;
they should be adorned with windows and pillars and constructed according to one's desire.
The assembly hall should be situated according to the cardinal directions for the protection of the royal residence.
Everywhere, either facing the king’s palace or situated at its rear, a hall for horned animals (elephants) should be constructed;
such a site is like unto the abode of the gods. This is the primary [instruction].
He who always practices this exactly as it is,
that king— having destroyed the ranks of his enemies by the strength of his arm— rules over this earth, which has the seven oceans for its girdle. (50)
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Royal Residence," in the *Vāstuśāstra* composed by the Great Emperor Śrī Bhojadeva, also known as the *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*.
Now begins the sixteenth chapter, titled "Entering the Forest.
For the purpose of a dwelling, one should duly procure timber either from the east or from the north.
One should indeed march against those [planets] situated in their own mansions (dhiṣṇya) that move slowly or swiftly;

likewise, fasting should be observed under them. Cutting and piercing should be performed under the fierce planets, while entry [into a city] should be undertaken under the stable ones; the commencement of new works is commended under the moving planets.
Having gone to an auspicious and pure place, he should then cause a dwelling to be constructed. Having established his workshop there, he should satisfy the laborers with food and drink.
With his retinue well-nourished and contented, he should fast throughout the night.
Having laid down his weapons, he should then examine a tree suitable for a dwelling.
[He should avoid those] growing in front of a city, a cremation ground, a village, on a road, in a lake, at a shrine, or in a hermitage;
nor those growing within a field, a grove, or on a boundary, nor those growing on uneven ground or in a depression. 4–5.
One should avoid trees that grow on lands possessing bitter, sour, pungent, or salty tastes,
as well as those growing in pits, on uneven ground, or on firm, solid soil;
having carefully observed the color, sap, bark, and other characteristics of the trees.
One should recognize these two types among them and abandon both the young and the old.
The age of the heartwood of trees is recorded as three hundred years;
one should take [the wood] after sixteen years and until the limit of one hundred and fifty years.
Just as the loss of vigor in men occurs through the passage of age,
so too does it occur in trees; thus they become perforated by holes, with leaves falling away,
brittle, hollow, covered with insects, and rough-barked.
Therefore, one should avoid these trees, as well as those that are withered at the top;
one should likewise shun trees that are crooked, rough, scorched, or poorly situated,
as well as those with broken branches or those possessing only two or one branch.
Those inhabited by others, those wounded by lightning strikes, winds, and rivers, those with resinous exudations tied in knots, those providing refuge for bees and snakes,
those clustered together, those fallen from their places, and those surrounded by powerful honey-bees— [he avoided them all].
Likewise, they saw those [trees] defiled by birds feeding on flesh and impure substances, covered with spiderwebs, rubbed by wild animals, and scarred by elephants;
with very large trunks at their bases, they served as landmarks for the road. ||13-14||
One should abandon trees that bear flowers and fruit out of season, those afflicted by diseases,
those that serve as dwellings for owls, and others of a similar nature.
[Likewise, one should avoid] the khadira, bījaka, sāla, madhūka, śāka, and śiṃśapā trees.
The Sarja, Arjuna, Añjana, Aśoka, Kadara, Rohiṇī tree, Vikaṅkata, Devadāru, and likewise the Śrīparṇī tree—
these are declared to be the Kuṭumbins (householders), which bestow nourishment as well as life. ||16-17||
Among trees, those that are observed to possess the capacity to bear heavy loads are likewise recommended for house-construction work according to their suitability—
such as the Karṇikāra, Dhava, Plakṣa, and Kapittha, which have irregular leaves. (18)
The śirīṣa, udumbara, aśvattha, śelu, nyagrodha, and campaka;
the nimba, āmra, kovidāra, akṣa, and vyādhighāta—these are censured.
They are not desired for household tasks because they are givers of what is undesirable. ||19-20||

Thorny trees with sweet fruit, milky trees, and those that are fragrant— cattle will certainly perish when these are present. Furthermore, when the shadow is invariably observed to be equal in measure to the height of a person, [it portends misfortune].
At that time, the shadow of a tree should be grasped; that tree shall be the measure [of the distance].

One should observe a constellation upon the tree in the eastern direction of that site. One should designate as born there the person whose name begins with the first letter of the lunar mansion (nakṣatra) situated there. ||22-23||
Having recognized that tree of his master to be secure and truly effective—
without knots or hollows, supple, straight, endowed with solid heartwood,
thick-trunked, green-leaved, and well-rounded— he should worship that tree.
Then, having gratified the twice-born and had them pronounce blessings,
the architect should offer a bali-oblation at the onset of night with cooked and uncooked meats, likewise with offerings for the spirits, spirituous liquors, perfumes, incense, and garlands.
"May all beings who dwell in these trees depart;
I shall perform my ritual meditation, so let there be a change of residence for you.
Be blessed, auspicious, a bringer of prosperity, and a promoter of the increase of progeny."
May the Candras, the Nīlayamās, the Sūryas, the Rudras, and likewise the Nalas;
may the quarters, the rivers, and the mountains, together with the ṛṣis, protect you!
If one who has been consecrated with mantras speaks in a human voice or trembles, [he shall be overcome]. ||28-29||
That tree which has withered sprouts and flowers should likewise be abandoned.
Then, having looked toward the sun and circumambulated the tree, the cutter, standing facing north,
should proceed while reciting words of auspiciousness from the Brahmins.
One should cut down a tree facing east with weapons whose blades are smeared with honey.
If, while the tree is being cut, there occurs a flow of blood,
or shaking, or even a sound, then death shall come to the householder.
Alternatively, if a tree exudes curd, honey, milk,
and ghee while being cut, one should then know that there is bondage and disease for the householder. If a dark, oily sap flows excessively from it, [one should likewise know this].

Fragrant, slightly sweet, and astringent—such a tree is praised. A fall toward the east from an auspicious tree is most excellent; a fall toward the north accomplishes one's undertakings. However, if it falls toward the south or the west, one should perform a rite of pacification and then abandon the tree.
Fear arises from one's kinsmen when a tree falls while crushing another; however,
that wind which is remembered as blowing when a tree has its roots severed and falls far away, or when it shrieks excessively, is considered a bringer of auspiciousness.
The sight of a donkey, a camel, jackals, or a serpent portends the cutting off of one's work, obstacles to the task, or imprisonment with fetters.
Likewise, the sight of a plow, a discus, a banner, a lotus, a flagstaff, an umbrella, and so forth [is auspicious]. (37–38)
Or, seeing a *śrīvṛkṣa*, a *vardhamāna*, or similar auspicious signs brings good fortune;
however, if it is lifted up after being cut, there will be loss for the head of the household.
If it is cut and then thrown away, there will be total ruin on all sides.

Just as when the characteristics described for a single tree are observed in its uprooting, a wise man should recognize the remaining trees as being free from defects; he should properly select that tree which is straight and growing in the natural direction. ||40-41||
One should cut [the tree] at a height increased by one-half or one-tenth of its auspicious portion;
such a tree, possessing a swelling at the top and a hollow in the middle, is known as "pregnant.
Its circles [of growth] should be understood even when it is being cut down at that very moment.
One should know that a frog appears when there is a madder-like luster, and a mouse when it is tawny-colored (43).
Likewise, a monitor lizard appears when it shines yellow, and a snake when it is long, white, and extended.
Honey appears when the luster is like molasses, and a chameleon when it is reddish (44).
One should predict rain within a circle that resembles a house-lizard, a pigeon, a mongoose, the scum of clarified butter,
red arsenic, a weapon, or the luster of a lotus or blue water-lily; likewise,
in a circle with the color of a polished sword-blade or a bamboo staff.
If the shape or the color of a snake is clearly visible [on it],
one should unhesitatingly designate that tree as being "pregnant" with a snake.
There is danger from thieves in a honey-tree, and danger from water in a water-tree.

One should know that there is fear of poison from a snake, and fear of fire from a stone; likewise, one should recognize a place as being afflicted by goats, sheep, cows, buffaloes, camels, donkeys, and the like,
or as being pregnant with a monitor lizard, a gaudhera, a frog, or a chameleon.
Furthermore, those who know the science of architecture maintain that a mouse portends either death or [the ruin of] the house;
other wise men say that by this very sign, one may predict affliction to the dwelling, provided there is safety and no obstacles, and if its arrival was unimpeded. (49–50)
At that time, one should predict security and abundance within the forest regions.

A householder who knows the ritual procedures should worship with the prescribed method of offering wealth when riches have arrived; likewise, a king should worship radiant wealth that bears the signs of the thunderbolt weapon and the banner. 51.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "Entry into the Forest," in the *Vāstuśāstra* composed by the Great Emperor Śrī Bhojadeva, also known as the *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*.
Now begins the seventeenth chapter, titled "Description of Indra’s Banner. [It was composed] for the sake of accomplishing the goals of the gods and for the destruction of the enemies of the gods.
Just as Brahmā spoke regarding the raising of Śakra’s banner, so it is now told:
Then the Lord born from the lotus, the master of speech, addressed the Blessed One: "How are the enemies of the gods not to be conquered by Indra?"
He said, "Gather together and make a banner of all kinds of jewels;
having consecrated it with incantations for sorcery, carry it aloft,
fixed upon the top of the machine and properly equipped with hundreds of birds."
Leading at the head of the divine army, you shall conquer your enemies.
Indra gave him an unassailable banner of celestial form, which, though possessing a thousand streams, was like a single [flame] that brings an end to the host of foes.
This effort is ordained for the purpose of increasing his vigor,
so that by this deed Śakra might conquer all his enemies without exception.
Then, desiring victory, he quickly created a banner with his mind.
Mounted upon that chariot, Hari deluded his enemies.
Beholding him, the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Viśvedevas, as well as the Aśvins and the Maruts, adorned themselves with ornaments.

This radiant banner swiftly robbed the enemy forces of their luster, vigor, physical form, activity, and even their strength as they watched. Having honored him, the Lord of the Gods [conquered] those powerful enemies.
In three nights, the powerful one conquered in battle by force with his thunderbolt.
Then, being pleased on the twelfth lunar day of the month of Ṛkṣa,
that slayer of Bala consecrated him after he had obtained the sovereignty of the three worlds.

Having worshipped all the worlds and being honored by all the worlds, the slayer of Vṛtra, having worshipped the banner, praised it with these words. Then, beholding that banner nearby, Vāsava spoke to it:
"O Indra, the worlds shall perform your worship by means of the Indradhvaja,
while the protectors of the earth observe the omens according to the scriptures.
From that time forward, he (the banner) has been endowed with all auspicious characteristics in the world."
Due to the granting of a boon by Indra, the Śakradhvaja is worshipped by kings;
difficult-to-access sanctuaries, fire-chapels, and altars have been constructed.
There are various vessels for cooking and whatever foods and drinks there may be.
These should be placed before the gateway, or one may arrange others;
if there is a desire to conquer invincible enemies in battle,
or to attain splendor, strength, and fame, then one should have a banner of Indra fashioned.
Having installed Purandara either in the army or in the city,
by the kings for the sake of victory and for the purpose of pacification,
the procedure for the raising of Śakra’s banner [is as follows] for the rulers of the earth.
They shall perform it correctly and in its entirety, as it is now being set forth.

Then, the wise one, having brought the materials from the forest according to the previous procedure, should worship them with water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), and so forth, and adorn them with perfumes and garlands. ||19-20||
Having honored the twice-born in a pure place, being perfectly composed,
he should carefully cause [the line] to be drawn with its end pointing east or north;
or else, the master of the site, being skilled in his work, should do so for the city facing east or north.

He should have all the mechanical devices, beginning with the flagstaff, constructed by artisans. The best [flagstaff] should be thirty-two cubits; that which is twenty-eight is the middle measure, and that which is twenty-four is the lowest.
The width and length of the base for each pillar shall be half a finger-breadth (aṅgula).
At the top, the diameter shall be half of that at the base, or one-third of it; this applies to all [pillars].
The capital (kuṣya) is desired to be less than one-eighth of the width of the base of the flagstaff (dhvaja).

The thickness [of the base] should be half the width, and its length three times its thickness. The platform for the circular path (bhramapīṭha) should be as thick as the width of the flagstaff, extended by the thickness of the legs, and with a length of one and a half [the width]; this brings auspiciousness. ||25-26||
The piercing should be equal to the width of the flag-staff and situated upon the revolving pedestal.
The two eyes should be circular with a circumference exceeding the tip of the staff, and they should extend for twice the length of the tip.
The feet should be made thick according to the thickness of the revolving part and as wide as the width of that revolving part.
In the case of piercing with those [measures] according to the rule, these two [pillars] should be twice as high as the width of the base.
One should fashion a pedestal here from one-fourth of the length of the flagstaff;
it should be supported by pillars at both ends and established upon a central platform.
It is firm, provided with two doors for the suppression of that seat,
facing east, very secure with bolts, and capable of withstanding disturbances from the south and north;
its width is half the span of the banner-staff (ketu), and its height is one-eighth of its length.
The residence of the Wielder of the Thunderbolt (Vajrin) should have a length equal to its width at the center.
The wrestler, the pedestal, and the feet [of the image] are the two arms extending from the pillars;
Śakramātā and the maidens are as wide as the expanse of the banner.
The lower portions of all [the tiers] should be made four times their own width,
or five times, or sevenfold from the base;
this is declared to be the rise of the kanyās, which is three times one-sixth [of the total height].
Indramātā, however, should be greater than all of them by one-eighth part.
The piercing (vedha) should be seven parts of its own width, starting from the emergence of the kanyaka;
the piercing should be square and well-proportioned for the lakaṭa.
The two piercing-edges (nirvedhāvasya), situated seven parts apart from the upper and lower [ends],
should be fashioned with another needle-penetration according to the measurement of the needle's size.
The needle should be one-third of the width of the maiden (kanyā) in breadth.
Three-quarters of a cubit thick, made of beautiful wood, and firmly joined;
with a width equal to that of a young girl and a circumference twice as great—one should then construct the machine after understanding this outer and inner measurement. ||37-38||
Beneath those two, the two mṛgālis should be half that size and as wide as the needle; a line should be drawn across the field for the junction of the two needles.
The *lakaṭa* should be half the width and length of the base of the temple with its pillars.
One should properly and firmly join the two axles to the arms and the axle-piercing [sockets].
The construction of all five types of carts should be identical;
having fashioned the mechanical parts in their proper sequence, one should install them all.
In the month of Āśvina, during the bright fortnight, on the first lunar day (pratipad),
when the planets were fixed in their rising and the constellation of Viśākha was aspected by the gentle planets,
and amidst the sound of all kinds of musical instruments played by the people of the city and the countryside— ||42||
Having removed the mechanical devices and the staff, one should lead it to the water from the workshop.
There, the master builder himself should bathe the staff— which is adorned with variegated protective amulets and smeared with clarified butter— using powders and all medicinal herbs.
Having lifted it from the reservoir amidst the clamor of people’s voices,
one should place the wooden elephant with its front end raised, facing eastward;
then, having covered it with unwashed garments as desired and having worshipped it with garlands and other offerings.
Having scattered the sacrificial offering (bali) in all directions, he should cause the twice-born to pronounce benedictions.
Then, having been worshipped there at the three junctions of the day by all the subjects,
he should cause the pillar to remain for five days, guarded by men bearing bows.
On that very day, O Indra, one should cause all the mechanical devices to be washed like sacrificial posts, clothed, and brought into the location of the deity's station.
Then, at the site marked for the flagstaff, [one should prepare] a space measuring one-eighth of the length of the staff.
Then, on two auspicious squares situated in the cardinal directions, each half as wide [as the central area] and extending eastward,
having divided them into eighty-one sections,
one should then duly install all the deities in their respective places in sequence.
In the eastern middle, on the Maitra square, and from the center of that toward the direction of the Maruts,
one should place a *malla* of depressed measurement at the corner of the foot.
[Likewise] in the two intermediate corners of the wind (northwest and southeast), between the two pairs of feet of the chief *bhṛṅga*.
One should fix the two pillars and place the pedestal (pīṭhī) between them.
The pedestal should extend from the pair of arms; there, by means of the connection at the tip, one should erect the two pillar-supports (stambhinī), each resting on a separate pair of Brahma-padas.
In this [mandala], one should place two pairs of *pratikṣobhas*, each resting upon a pair of arms;
one should position them on the outside at the terminal points of the two *maitras*.
Having identified the front of the *mallas* in the east, one should arrange the upward movement of Śakra in due order.
One should join the two unbroken "wandering feet" (bhramapāda) accompanied by the circular movement (bhramaṇa).
To the west of the wrestler (malla), one should establish the auspicious Bhadrā, who rests upon the quarter of Varuṇa; from the low point, one should place the mother of Śakra.
There should be those known as Nanda, Upananda, Jaya, and Vijaya, who respectively occupy the positions of Parjanya, Antarikṣa, Dvāra, and Yakṣman; then,
when all the maidens have been assigned their places according to their divisions.
Three sets of three [syllables] should be applied externally for the sake of firmness.
Casting away all material substance, one should meditate upon the deities of the words;
that substance attains the name of those [deities] and receives the worship directed toward them.
One should construct a pair of side-frames on both sides of the girl's body, level with the surface of the pedestal, joined by iron pegs and following the contours of the body; then,
having relied upon that pair of side-frames and the pedestal above for support, one should proceed with the grasping.
One should fasten it with iron pegs to ensure the immobility of the machine.
When the work on the machine is completed, according to the injunctions of the scriptures,
one should place the Lord of the Thirty-three (Indra) in his own station during the asterism of Indra.
For one who has bathed according to the rules, is clothed,
anointed with fragrant substances such as sandalwood, and honored with flowers,
[the rite should be performed] during the three muhūrtas beginning with Rauhiṇa, or during the Maitra or Vajrin [muhūrtas] of Indra.
They welcome the entry when the instruments have been honored.

Whether it be the architect or the priest, being pure, bathed, and composed, he should gratify the Brahmins—who have been worshipped with perfumes and garlands—with sacrificial fees and other gifts. ||64-65||
Then, with auspicious sounds and the resonance of musical instruments, and with cries of "Auspicious Day! and "Victory!", they should lift him up with concentrated minds;
all the citizens, adorned with ornaments, were filled with joyful hearts.
Free from disease, strong, capable, and endowed with natural excellence,
let the Sūtas and Māgadhas, with virtuous minds, praise him with hymns;
let the panegyrists honor him, and even the courtesans attend upon him.

The lord of men, accompanied by his army, ministers, citizens, and country-folk, should follow him as he enters his own abode, while men raise loud and resonant shouts of joy. If the men [are thus]: 69.
If they should joyfully lift up or carry the Lord of the Gods,
then the king becomes victorious and the subjects rejoice;
there is happiness in the kingdom and delight in the city, and all calamities perish.
If, having risen with difficulty, he leaves his bed out of respect for him,
then the king falls into great dejection.
Stumbling, distressed, miserable, and sighing at every step—
When the banner falls to the ground, diminished on one side, those who experience distress will surely suffer the loss of their country. At that time,
there will be neither abundance of food nor security, nor victory for the king.
If this [mirror] is torn, broken, or falls, or if it is entirely upturned, there will be for the king either the loss of his realm or the destruction of his sons, or death. Furthermore,
from the theft or the falling of garments, ornaments, and garlands, [the same results follow].
The destruction of such objects certainly befalls the citizens.
When entering the city, it becomes silent or lusterless;
or upon the elevation of Śakra, it then meets its destruction.
Having quickly and without obstacle brought Śakra to his own place,
one should install him as before on his own bed, facing eastward;
and there, under that very constellation, one should perform [the rite] for the Lord of the Immortals while he is seated upon the bed.
Regarding the conjunction in the Bhrama and Kuṣya [houses] as it is determined by their respective portions:
if the banner, while being joined to the Kuṣya, falls to the ground, then the displacement of the king from his position will certainly occur. ||79-80||
When Śakra revolves to the left during the conjunction with Kuṣya, then there shall be death for the architect; and if it occurs on the right, there will be a collapse.
If that staff should somehow attain its own piercing, it would be through great difficulty.
Then, for a negligent king, a great calamity arises.
(82) If the banner of Indra, having been extracted and joined, should break apart, then the alliance of the king with his vassals will fall asunder. (83)
If, when being joined on all sides, it cracks, breaks, or becomes damaged,
then from that breaking comes disease for the king, and from its cracking, the death of a woman.
That which is uncracked, not overturned, without defect, and not delayed—
If the banner of Vāsava (the Indra-dhvaja) attains its proper placement according to the rules,
