then the king— accompanied by wealth, servants, women, offspring, feudatories, and followers— becomes free from fear, strong of limb, and prospers. (85–86)
Even for the wielder of the thunderbolt (Indra), who remains on his bed and is guarded with great effort,
one should apply all his limbs— the Kuṭanyā and others—
[to the following]: Aindra, Balāka, Yakṣeśa, Sarpamāda, and the one called Digāhva.

The peacock, the head of Indra, and the eight-petaled lotus—these should be fashioned according to their respective proportions, endowed with clearly defined forms. The joints between these parts should be made of cloth and correspond to the names of those [intervals]. ||88-89||
One should wrap this banner with strong, split bamboo strips from the base to the tip,
and with thick, non-loose cords;
its width shall be one-third of the height of the banner-staff including the foot.
The height of the Śakrapiṭaka should be half of that;

having established the eight directions within this [structure] separated by the beams (vaṃśa), one should then place the four lords of the directions upon it according to their respective quarters. ||91-92||
When the fifth part has been set aside for the vajrin-piṭaka,
one should place the remaining parts— each reduced by an eighth— in their proper order;
the balākā and the others should be extended [in width] and [the measurements] reduced by a quarter in height.
The meters possess their own respective colors and are full of beauty.

The success or failure resulting from the inversion of the break (bhaṅga) and the fall (pāta) arising from the *piṭaka* [defect] are proclaimed to cause excessive suffering, pain, and death for each individual case. ||94-95||
For the inner apartments, the ministers, the subjects, the army, fame, the earth, the royal splendors,
the king, and the kingdom—
there are eight well-twisted cords, each having a width equal to one-sixth of a banner-staff (ketu).

The banners should be made firm, three times as long as their width, and strong. On the day preceding [the festival], one should carefully erect the auspicious celestial banner (amaradhvaja), which has previously been covered with cloths and accompanied by courtesans. ||97-98||

It is auspicious, marked with the sun, moon, planets, and stars, adorned with bamboo, shrubs, and the head of Indra; it possesses eight necks and three strands, and is equipped with a staff, a cord, and a mirror;
it is rich with grain, fruit, and flowers, and is decorated with fine cloth.
One should fashion a banner-cloth that is firmly fastened with eight continuous ropes, variegated and well-constructed;
this is for the sake of providing omens for the people and for the beauty of the banner itself. ||100-101||
Upon this mountain, the entire world— including its cities, towns, groves, gandharvas, gods, and asuras— is depicted, filled with trees;
it is bound at the tip of the banner by rays of light and well-established upon the ground.
One should install that [image], free from delusion, resting upon its lower portion.
Accompanied by joyful songs, instrumental music, and dancing actors,
a vigil (jāgara) should be performed before it throughout that entire night.
Then, when the sun has risen, the domestic priest, with his senses restrained,
should perform the encircling of the fire to the northeast of its base.
Having performed the smearing of that site, he should then proceed with the tracing of lines and the sprinkling of water.
Having consecrated and spread darbha grass, he should kindle the fire there.
Therein [he should place] vessels for the clarified butter, the clarified butter itself, perfumes, flowers,
materials to be recited over, and fuel-sticks made of palāśa wood.
O Indra, having brought together two golden ladles (sruc and sruva), a portion of food, and sacrificial offerings (bali),
one should then offer all of this into the fire for a king who is endowed with sons, wives, cattle, wealth, and an army. 108.

When the fire is kindled by itself, it is praised if it possesses a pleasant sound, great flames, and is oily; it is auspicious when it is radiant, fragrant, and drives away the sacrificer's misfortunes through mantras that bring about victory and peace. ||109-110||
Having the brilliance of molten gold, the hue of lac, and the color of the *kiṃśuka* flower;
possessing a luster equal to coral, red pearls, the *aśoka* tree, and the cochineal insect;
[adorned] with banners, goads, houses, umbrellas, sacrificial posts, walls, and arches. ||111||
A fire with even flames, praised by other auspicious signs,
glossy, with a clockwise-pointing crest, smokeless, vast,
and burning brightly for a long time, is said to bestow abundance and security. (112-113)
Smoke-colored, discolored, harsh, yellow, or blue; flickering, making a terrifying sound, with flames curling to the left, or small;
with dim light, devoid of brilliance, smelling of blood and fat, and emitting sparks—[such fire is inauspicious]. ||114||

If the fire, enveloped in smoke and accompanied by foam, bends toward the oblation, it brings victory. However, if the fire burns the spread of darbha grass, the other implements of the homa, or the very offerings being poured, one should predict loss.

If the throne is pulled toward the house while it is being consumed by fire, there will be destruction of a portion of the land; however, from its extraction [to a safe place], there shall be gain. Furthermore, that which is deep on all sides increases the prosperity of kings.
One should predict victory in whichever direction the flames go.
They declare that ghee which is discolored, impure, foul-smelling, or infested with flies and rats portends the loss of sovereignty; so too does that which is offered into ashes. (118–119)
Fuel that is deficient or excessive in size, split, eaten by woodworms,
or fallen from trees broken by wind brings about the destruction of one's wealth. Likewise, fuel that is hollow, covered in blossoms, broken at the tip, or mixed with grass leads to misfortune.
Darbha grass that is difficult to cut likewise causes distress; seeds that are spoiled,
covered in dust, damaged by insects,
or those that are undernourished lead to the destruction of the seed.
A garland that is foul-smelling, withered, neither yellow nor white,
or one that has been gnawed or eaten by insects, leads neither to victory nor to prosperity.
Likewise, those that are leaking, uprooted, fierce, torn, or split do not bring success.
They say that vessels of clarified butter cause famine and disease when they are impure,
fallen [to the ground], defiled by flies or insects, offered to a *bali* sacrifice,
given to one who eats the food of Indra, or possessed of hair. (124–125)
All the aforementioned forms, such as clarified butter and the rest, in their respective order,
bring about fear for both the kingdom and the city.
Having offered perfumes, garlands, and other items to the deities according to their directions—
Then the domestic priest or the architect, with a joyful heart,
should cast the bali offering in the south-western quarter toward the preeminent brahmins who have assembled there—
men endowed with good character and conduct, and well-adorned with abundant perfumes and garlands.
[He should choose] elders who are devoted to the six duties, friends who have mastered the Vedas,
who are pleasing to the mind, full-limbed, capable in every respect, pure, dressed in white garments, handsome, mostly fair-complexioned, and endowed with strength.

One should join with gifts as desired— or with eight hundred— those who are not shaven-headed, those with matted hair, eunuchs, initiated ones, the diseased, and the emaciated; then, with flowers and unbroken grains, one whose mind is pleased should cause them to pronounce a blessing.
And they shall consecrate you with eight very firm jars filled with water, well-adorned and drawn in circular patterns at the base,
while the best of the twice-born offer praises with victorious mantras and hymns.
The lord of the earth should proclaim this throughout the kingdom by means of these [messengers] and by himself;
he should effect the release of all prisoners and utterly abandon violence,
and indeed, he should endure the faults of his subjects for ten days.
Well-dressed, adorned, bathed, and diligent in right conduct,
the pure king, together with his army, should await the raising of the banner. Fasting, pure, bathed, self-restrained, and having conquered his senses, he should remain watchful.
With palms joined in reverence, the architect (sthapati) should recite this mantra:
"Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, Vāguli, O crusher of all demons, svāhā!
Just as you arose when the battle between the gods and the asuras had commenced..."

"O Lord of Gods, arise thus for the victory of the king, being duly honored. Having spoken thus and performed a circumambulation of him, the architect should cause the hoisting of the flagstaff for the King of the Gods. (137-138)
[He was followed] by well-adorned citizens and countryfolk, as well as by disciplined attendants wearing white, pure garlands, garments, and ointments; accompanied by lutes,
cymbals, conchs, *nandis*, kettledrums, and *gomukhas*.
With other joyful musical instruments being played with great sound,
and with singers and dancers singing and dancing,
there arose the exultant, intense, and rising clamor of elephants, chariots, and horses.
With the sounds of those musical instruments and the cries of "Auspicious Day," one should raise the banner when it has been pulled up by strong ropes;
as it is being raised with effort and reaches its height.
He observed the omens of kings, birds, vehicles, and so forth—
[omens] characterized by the enjoyment provided by procuresses, radiant with banners and mirrors,
displaying the vivid splendor of variegated cloths, and adorned with the qualities of the sun and moon.

The Lord of the Gods, whose garlands and ornaments had not fallen, whose parasol remained unshattered upon his head, whose limbs were neither trembling nor broken, who had not strayed from his direction,
whose head was level and properly aligned, and who was uninjured and undisturbed— [he saw him].
Arising from a straight path that is neither delayed nor wavering—
such is the emergence of Śakra’s thunderbolt for a king, which brings victory and provides security,
health, and abundance for the people of both city and countryside. ||146–147||
When the banner of Śakra rises toward the eastern quarter, it bestows prosperity upon ministers, astrologers, kṣatriyas, kings, and those dwelling in the east.
When it moves toward the southeastern direction, those who live by fire prosper.
When the banner of the enemy of Namuci moves toward the southern direction, the accomplishment of undertakings already begun arises without effort;
at that time, there shall be abundance of honor, grain, and wealth for the world of Vaiśyas. ||149-150||
For one who takes refuge in the western quarter (Nairṛtī), all hopes and prosperities arise most excellently;
likewise, the pregnancy shall not be in vain, nor shall there be fear of execution or imprisonment.
O Śūdra, for one who takes refuge in this southern quarter (Prācetasī), victory shall come to pass.
When Ketu enters the quarter of Vāyu, there shall be no fear of hunger, thirst, or fire, and desirable rain shall fall;
there will be an abundance of trees, crops, and fruits, as well as an increase in four-footed animals and the cessation of disease. ||152-153||

When [the planet] has gone to the northern direction, there shall be prosperity for all four castes; especially for the best of the twice-born, as well as sacrifices, will succeed. When it has resorted to the eastern quarter, the king becomes devoted to dharma.
There shall be prosperity for the country and likewise for the heretics (pāṣaṇḍins).
If Śatakratu (Indra) should move forward even slightly, drawn by a rope,
then the expedition of that king who desires victory will be successful.
If the banner, having pierced through the ground, finds firm footing,
then the king conquers the earth together with its mountains and forests;
such is the fruit declared for the unimpaired banner of the wielder of the thunderbolt as it moves toward the quarters.
All of that has been stated again as being the opposite for the *vyaṅga* [the defective]. Furthermore:
"If Śatakratu (Indra), though previously well-adorned, were to be joined [to a body] while being hoisted by a rope-mechanism, or even if he were slightly raised and remained halfway up," (158–159)
If it falls upon the bed, or on the ground, or into one's lap,
then it shall destroy the king, the queen, or the prince. Or, if while rising or half-risen, it becomes agitated or trembles, [the same result follows].
If [the enemy] should go to another place or move about in some way, then the king is challenged; he may even fall from his position, and his realm will undoubtedly depart out of fear. ||161-162||
When any one of the eight ropes is pulled and then snapped, that shall certainly signify the death of a minister;
likewise, if it breaks while being raised at its base, middle, or top, the same result follows. (163)
Then he gradually slays the city-dwellers, the army commanders, and the kings.
If the umbrella, the sun, the bamboo thicket, Indra, the head, the throat, or the cord fall to the ground, or if Indra himself does so, then he slays the lord of the earth. (164–165)
The king meets his death by those [omens] that are broken, falling, or shaken;
by those that are unbroken yet shaken, the army goes to its destruction.
Gradually, mirrors, banners, the moon, and stars shall destroy them.
The wives of the minister of the king, the lord of the army of sight, fall [from their celestial state].
By means of these— garlands, ornaments, vehicles, weapons, garments, fruits, and food—
which have fallen from the royal banner, those very things of the king go to destruction.
The ancient sages have declared that in whichever direction the basket of Śakra or the palace of Śakra falls from its peaks, there will be misfortune;
for in that sequence, the bolts of the deer-like side-glances of women are broken.
Affliction arises for courtesans, kings, merchants, and guards.

(170) Or, if the *malla*, *mātṛkā*, and *kumārikā* [omens] are broken by the *bhrama* and *akṣapāda* [omens], they will destroy the kingdom of the king, his beloved, his mother, and his sons, respectively. (171)
If a thunderclap, a lightning bolt, or a meteor should fall upon the banner,
then one should predict fear of drought for the king and his defeat.
If flies swarm like honeybees over the raised honeycomb-like canopy of Indra’s banner, [the same result follows].

If flies or birds should circle around the enemy there, one should predict his death within six months; however, if they move from the side of Hari toward the exterior and perform a circumambulation, they indicate that death has already occurred.
If vultures, hawks, and pigeons settle upon the top of the banner,
then they bring about famine, war, and the destruction of kings. If ospreys, owls, and crows settle upon the banner, [the same results follow].
Then, in due course, they would slay the king’s ministers, sons, and domestic priests.
Or, if a peacock or a swan should take refuge with Indra, then a son endowed with all auspicious marks would be born to the king. (176–177)
If a wheel, a crane, or a female swan alights upon the banner,
then the king obtains an exceedingly beautiful wife.
Through birds there shall be good rain, and through aquatic creatures that feed on fruit, there shall be abundance of food.
If those who eat excrement appear, there will be famine; if those who eat flesh appear, there will be fear.
If the foremost gods, yakṣas, and nāgas are depicted on a painted cloth, endowed with various forms and equipped with vehicles, weapons, and ornaments— ||179–180||
The eight directions were personified, and throngs of Apsarases danced;
the planets, stars, clouds, swelling rivers, and oceans were present,
as were ponds covered with lotuses and lakes filled with swans.
Forests and groves adorned with fruits and flowers;
temples of the gods, ancient gate-towers, and cities; and exceedingly brilliant palaces provided with beds and seats. (182–183)
The kings, their servants, and those possessing troops and vehicles were delighted; the citizens, the people of the countryside, and the children engaged in play were joyful;
and the four castes, along with actors, dancers, and artisans, were filled with gladness. (184)
Mountains bearing cow-pens, creepers, thickets, trees, and medicinal herbs;
herds of deer and flocks of birds; all auspicious and propitious things; lands with diverse pastures and soil; and birds that subsist on fruit—[these are favorable]. ||185-186||

When these [images] shine according to their proper placement, then one should predict peace, health, abundance, and victory for the king in that region and city as well. However, if they are crushed, fallen, broken, destroyed, or stolen— [The rest of the verse follows: ...then one should predict the opposite. If the image of the Lord of the World (Lokanātha) is broken, one should predict the death of the king; if it falls, the destruction of the city; and if it is stolen, the ruin of the kingdom. If the image of the Goddess (Devī) is broken, there will be a great famine; if it falls, the death of the queen; and if it is stolen, the ruin of the kingdom. If the image of the Yakṣa is broken, there will be a great epidemic; if it falls, the death of the minister; and if it is stolen, the ruin of the kingdom. If the image of the Nāga is broken, there will be a great drought; if it falls, the death of the chief priest; and if it is stolen, the ruin of the kingdom. If the image of the Planet (Graha) is broken, there will be a great war; if it falls, the death of the commander-in-chief; and if it is stolen, the ruin of the kingdom. If the image of the Rākṣasa is broken, there will be a great pestilence; if it falls, the death of the astrologer; and if it is stolen, the ruin of the kingdom. If the image of the Vidyādhara is broken, there will be a great fire; if it falls, the death of the treasurer; and if it is stolen, the ruin of the kingdom. If the image of the Gandharva is broken, there will be a great loss of cattle; if it falls, the death of the physician; and if it is stolen, the ruin of the kingdom. If the image of the Kinnara is broken, there will be a great loss of grain; if it falls, the death of the messenger; and if it is stolen, the ruin of the kingdom. If the image of the Piśāca is broken, there will be a great fear of thieves; if it falls, the death of the gatekeeper; and if it is stolen, the ruin of the kingdom. If the image of the Bhūta is broken, there will be a great fear of spirits; if it falls, the death of the cook; and if it is stolen, the ruin of the kingdom. If the image of the Siddha is broken, there will be a great fear of poison; if it falls, the death of the charioteer; and if it is stolen, the ruin of the kingdom. If the image of the Cāraṇa is broken, there will be a great fear of weapons; if it falls, the death of the bard; and if it is stolen, the ruin of the kingdom. If the image of the Apsaras is broken, there will be a great fear of women; if it falls, the death of the female attendant; and if it is stolen, the ruin of the kingdom. If the image of the Vidyā is broken, there will be a great fear of spells; if it falls, the death of the sorcerer; and if it is stolen, the ruin of the kingdom. If the image of the Mantra is broken, there will be a great fear of incantations; if it falls, the death of the reciter; and if it is stolen, the ruin of the kingdom. If the image of the Mudrā is broken, there will be a great fear of obstacles; if it falls, the death of the ritualist; and if it is stolen, the ruin of the kingdom. If the image of the Dhyāna is broken, there will be a great fear of distraction; if it falls, the death of the meditator; and if it is stolen, the ruin of the kingdom. If the image of the Samādhi is broken, there will be a great fear of delusion; if it falls, the death of the yogin; and if it is stolen, the ruin of the kingdom. If the image of the Prajñā is broken, there will be a great fear of ignorance; if it falls, the death of the scholar; and if it is stolen, the ruin of the kingdom. If the image of the Upāya is broken, there will be a great fear of attachment; if it falls, the death of the benefactor; and if it is stolen, the ruin of the kingdom. If the image of the Karuṇā is broken, there will be a great fear of cruelty; if it falls, the death of the protector; and if it is stolen, the ruin of the kingdom. If the image of the Maitrī is broken, there will be a great fear of enmity; if it falls, the death of the friend; and if it is stolen, the ruin of the kingdom. If the image of the Śīla is broken, there will be a great fear of transgression; if it falls, the death of the observer of vows; and if it is stolen, the ruin of the kingdom. If the image of the Kṣānti is broken, there will be a great fear of anger; if it falls, the death of the patient one; and if it is stolen, the ruin of the kingdom. If the image of the Vīrya is broken, there will be a great fear of sloth; if it falls, the death of the energetic one; and if it is stolen, the ruin of the kingdom. If the image of the Dāna is broken, there will be a great fear of poverty; if it falls, the death of the donor; and if it is stolen, the ruin of the kingdom. If the image of the Śraddhā is broken, there will be a great fear of doubt; if it falls, the death of the faithful one; and if it is stolen, the ruin of the kingdom. If the image of the Vīrya is broken, there will be a great fear of indolence; if it falls, the death of the diligent one; and if it is stolen, the ruin of the kingdom. If the image of the Smṛti is broken, there will be a great fear of forgetfulness; if it falls, the death of the mindful one; and if it is stolen, the ruin of the kingdom. If the image of the Mati is broken, there will be a great fear of confusion; if it falls, the death of the intelligent one; and if it is stolen, the ruin of the kingdom. If the image of the Gati is broken, there will be a great fear of wandering; if it falls, the death of the traveler; and if it is stolen, the ruin of the kingdom. If the image of the Jñāna is broken, there will be a great fear of ignorance; if it falls, the death of the wise one; and if it is stolen, the ruin of the kingdom. If the image of the Satya is broken, there will be a great fear of falsehood; if it falls, the death of the truthful one; and if it is stolen, the ruin of the kingdom. If the image of the Dharma is broken, there will be a great fear of unrighteousness; if it falls, the death of the upholder of Dharma; and if it is stolen, the ruin of the kingdom. If the image of the Artha is broken, there will be a great fear of loss; if it falls, the death of the seeker of wealth; and if it is stolen, the ruin of the kingdom. If the image of the Kāma is broken, there will be a great fear of desire; if it falls, the death of the lover; and if it is stolen, the ruin of the kingdom. If the image of the Mokṣa is broken, there will be a great fear of bondage; if it falls, the death of the seeker of liberation; and if it is stolen, the ruin of the kingdom. If the image of the Buddha is broken, there will be a great fear of saṃsāra; if it falls, the death of the follower of the Buddha; and if it is stolen, the ruin of the kingdom. If the image of the Dharma is broken, there will be a great fear of the teachings; if it falls, the death of the student of the Dharma; and if it is stolen, the ruin of the kingdom. If the image of the Saṅgha is broken, there will be a great fear of the community; if it falls, the death of the monk; and if it is stolen, the ruin of the kingdom. If the image of the Guru is broken, there will be a great fear of spiritual failure; if it falls, the death of the teacher; and if it is stolen, the ruin of the kingdom. If the image of the Devatā is broken, there will be a great fear of divine wrath; if it falls, the death of the worshipper; and if it is stolen, the ruin of the kingdom. If the image of the Tīrthika is broken, there will be a great fear of heresy; if it falls, the death of the heterodox teacher; and if it is stolen, the ruin of the kingdom. If the image of the Śramaṇa is broken, there will be a great fear of worldliness; if it falls, the death of the ascetic; and if it is
If it burns, an inauspicious omen must be declared according to the specific birth-sign and the direction;
whether the painted cloth remains standing or has fallen upon the ground, there will be a calamity for the king and his realm. (188-189)
If every ornament shines throughout the festival,
and the king remains unharmed and undisturbed, then he shall conquer the entire earth while the troupes of actors and dancers dance and recite. (190)
In an auspicious [dream], an auspicious result should be predicted; in the other case, an inauspicious one.
Those groups of elephants and horses that are joyful, auspicious, well-attired, well-behaved, and adorned—among them, one should certainly predict an auspicious outcome. (191–192)
One should predict disaster among those men or women who seek misfortune, who are deformed, and whose minds are dejected; likewise,
elephants with temples flowing with rut, as massive as great clouds.
Not dejected and independent, bringing victory to the king;
scratching the earth with their right hooves and joyful in heart, the horses, as they neigh, also proclaim the king's triumph. (194-195)
If rain accompanied by lightning and thunder occurs then,
one should know that there will be victory for the lord of the earth, as well as abundance of food and security.
Now, when the tenth day has arrived at midnight during the asterism of Rohiṇī—
Sages desire the downfall of Śakra every year.
Therefore, when the assembly has concluded and the banner of Indra has been re-established, one should perform the ritual service with water using fragrant waters and flowers. 197–198.
When people play with impure rags, ashes, hair, bones, or mud,
then famine arises.
When the brahmins see the banner of Indra falling in the eastern direction, they should remain vigilant.
There will be abundance of food, security, and health; otherwise, the opposite shall occur.
Now, the specific details regarding the flag-pole as described in the *Aṣṭāṅga* are being told:
to the east of the city of Brahmapura, the station of Indra is ordained. ||200–201||
Its measurement is declared to be by the hand with its span;
it is sixty-four [units] in length and square on all sides.
One should divide the field into eighty-one parts according to their proportions.
One should determine the length of the flagpole according to half the measurement of the field.
Thereafter, an increase should be prescribed by the wise at the rate of one finger-breadth for every cubit;
or in some cases, the increase of the Indra-flag may be half a finger-breadth.
The increase should be applied until it is equal to the field in finger-breadths (aṅgulas);
thereafter, one should again employ that which was the original measurement.
The measurement of the ketu [flagstaff] should be forty finger-breadths.
The wise should increase its height by two finger-breadths each year.
A discerning person should fashion the Brahmāvarta at the station of Brahmā;
immediately to the east of Brahmā should be the deity Aryaman.
There, the two feet of the machine are six padas in height;
on its western side, the deity Mitra resides.
From that point onward, the left piercing of the machine becomes inclined.
It should be sloping from east to west; this is remembered as the rule for the mechanical device (yantra).
On the western side of the device, Varuṇa is the presiding deity.
At the end of Varuṇa’s position, there are two young girls situated on the bamboo pole.
Having dug four cubits deep and ten cubits high,
O Rudra, the well should be constructed in that place, and the Kumārī [image] should be well-established there.
The fourth [tithi] occurs during the conjunction with Soma, and the fifth during the portion of Āpa.
"The sixth [line] is in the portion of Savitṛ, and the seventh is in the portion of Yama.

(212) Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "Description of the Indra Banner," in the *Vāstuśāstra* known by the alternative name *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*, composed by the Great King of Kings, the illustrious Bhojadeva.
Now begins the eighteenth chapter, titled "Designations of Cities and Other Settlements."
Nagara, mandira, durga, puṣkara, sāmparāyika,
nivāsa, sadana, sadma, kṣaya, and likewise kṣitilaya— these are synonyms for city.
They know that city where the king resides as the capital (rājadhānī).
Others beyond these are designated as branch-cities (śākhānagara).
They say that a branch-city itself is called a karvaṭa when it resembles a city;
a karvaṭa deficient in qualities here is called a nigama.
A village (grāma) is that which is smaller than a market town (nigama); it is called a "village-like" settlement (grāmakalpa) when it consists of houses.
A small herd-pen for cattle is called a goṣṭha, whereas a larger one is a goṣṭhaka.
That place where kings hold court is known as a pattana (a fortified city).
That city, filled with many prosperous merchants, is called a *puṭabhedana*.
Where people construct small huts from leaves, branches, grass, and stones, the Pulindas make their dwelling; such a place is a *pallī*, while a smaller one is a *pallikā*.
Excluding the city, everything else is known as the countryside (janapada).
Together with the city, the entire realm is called a kingdom (rāṣṭra), a region (deśa), or a province (maṇḍala).
A dwelling place is considered to be an abode (āvāsa), a residence (sadana), a home (sadma), a habitation (niketa), or a palace (mandira).
Saṃsthānam, nidhanam, dhiṣṇyam, bhavanam, vasatiḥ, kṣayaḥ, agāram,
saṃśrayaḥ, nīḍam, geham, śaraṇam, ālayaḥ,
nilayaḥ, layanam, veśma, gṛham, okaḥ, and pratiśrayaḥ [are synonyms for a dwelling]. ||8-9||
That which is the upper floor of a house is proclaimed to be a *harmya*;
the path for ascending it is called a *sopāna*.
Where an ascent between two pillars is constructed of wooden beams, that is [a *sopāna*].

That is called a ladder (niḥśreṇī) because it consists of broad steps. That which is covered with wooden beams is known as a wooden frame (kāṣṭhaviṭaṅka); a mansion plastered with lime is a palace (harmya), a stately house (saudha), or a paved floor (kuṭṭima).
That which is covered with palm leaves, plantain leaves, and so forth for protection against the rain is known as *abhigupti*; situated within and above the entire house, it is [the roof].
A window (*vātāyana*), however, is said to be an opening in the walls for looking out.
That which is a small opening for the passage of air is indeed called an *avalokanaka*. The aperture in the middle of the palace (*harmya*) is known as a *loka*;
that which forms the enclosure of the palace is the *kaṇṭha* of the palace floor.
The *vitardikā* is a wooden railing that runs all around the base of the roof-covering;
those [carved] animals on its pillars are called *īhāmṛgas*.
A *niryūha* is the projection of wooden beams from the area of a palace building.
A wooden plank that has emerged from a cut in the timber is known as a *valīka*.
That which is covered on four sides is called a *catuśśāla*;
they say that with three [sides covered] it is a *triśāla*, and with two it would be a *dviśālaka*.
A house with a single hall covered by one roof is called a *gṛha*;
however, when a single hall covers the entire structure, that is traditionally known as a *śālā*.
Furthermore, that which is in the middle of the halls is a pond or a lotus-pool (*puṣkariṇī*).
Furthermore, that which is completely enclosed is called a *garbhagṛha* (inner chamber).
When a place for many people is arranged within a house with three walls, they call that an *upasthāna*; it may also be a small *upasthānaka*. ||20-21||
That very same structure is a *prāsāda*, while a small one is known as a *prāsādikā*.
That which is a long *prāsādikā* is designated as a *valabhī*.
As for that which is a *valabhī* at the front of a hall (*śālā*), they call it an *alinda*.
A *valabhī* without a hall (*śālā*) is called a *valabhī*.
Those with very small four-walled enclosures are considered *apavarakas*.
The interior space within a house is known as the *śuddhānta*.
That which people know as a street (pratolī), where one might dwell like a tunnel (suraṅgā),
is called a "kakṣā" by those who know it— the intermediate space within a house. Likewise, that which is called a reception hall (upasthānaka) and those which are inner chambers (apavarakas).
That which is the neck of the rooms is called the *kaṇṭha*, while the wall and its accumulation is the *bhitti*. That which is the hall for food is called the kitchen (*mahānasa*).
And that which is covered at the location of the door is called the door-chamber (*dvārakoṣṭhaka*).

They call "entrance" (praveśana) the exit through the door; the place for the exit of water should be known as the "water-circulation" (udakabhrama). That which is the courtyard of the house, they call the "house-precinct" (bhavanājira).
The courtyard of a forest is called *vanājira*, and the courtyard of a hermitage is *āśramājira*.
Experts call that which is situated beneath the northern *udumbara* tree, between two walls, and serving as the support for the door-panels, by the name *dehalī*. (29–30)

*Kapāṭa* refers to a door-panel (*dvārapakṣa*) as well as the two leaves of a door (*kapāṭapuṭa*). *Pakṣa*, *pidhāna*, *āvaraṇa*, and *dvārasaṃvaraṇa* likewise denote the same. *Kapāṭa* and *saṃpuṭa* are both terms for that pair of door-panels (*kapāṭayugala*).
A *kalikā* intended for the purpose of securing a door is known as an *argalā*.
If it is long in measurement, it is called an *argalasūcī*.
In ancient cities, however, that which serves to ward off elephants is called a *parigha* or a *phaliha*.

That wooden panel which is perforated on all sides with holes resembling lattice windows is called a *gavākṣa* (lattice window), and it is also termed a *jāla* (net). [It is used] at the gate of a palace,
at the door of a house, and likewise for looking out from a palace.
On the back of the inner wall, however, there may be a beautiful structure;
on both its sides, two planks are raised, joined one above the other in the shape of two half-moons. ||35-36||
Just as there are two entrances in this [mandala] with great lower lips joined by the foremost [deities],
and a circle in the form of a star at the junction above them—
that is called the *toraṇa*, and it is adorned by that.
There should be a golden arch and likewise a jeweled arch;
this flower-arch is also made with flowers and the like.
That which is the letter-like form at the top of the arch is called the "lion's ear" (siṃhakarṇa).
The ground areas for moving about within the house are known by the name *saṃyamana*.
Whatever is situated at the side of the house, they know that as a *saṃyamana*.
Alternatively, [the part] of the wall or of the wooden [structure] that is bent like the tip of a wave—
That row of swans is the water-channel (praṇālī) for the discharge of water from the palace;
that which is called the enclosure wall (prākāra) is the neck of the courtyard. That which is near the main gate is here called the side-door (pradvāra). ||41-42||
If there is a place at the base of the door that is built with bricks—
whether it be long or short— that is desired as the *āsthalaka*.
The ground for urine is called *amedhya*, while that for feces is likewise called *varcaska* or *avaskara*.
The area common to the house and its wall, extending outside, is considered the *parisara*.
That which is spacious and elevated is called a *veśma* (palace); when this same structure is contracted, it is termed an *aṭṭālaka* by those who know [the terminology]. ||44-45||
That very same [structure], when extremely compact, is called an *aṭṭālī*;
however, they know that *aṭṭālī* which is not very high to be an *aṭṭālikā*.
It is surrounded by wooden pipes with apertures through a single channel.
Where water flows on the surface of the roof by means of a wooden channel;
where the forms of pillar-heads are supported by the bases of the wood;
and where there are hollows with great effort [made] through the openings at the ends of wooden tubes.
Then, from the breasts, noses, mouths, and eyes of those forms—
some stationed in various places, some bull-like, some monkey-like, and some fanged—
he rained down from all sides through the fine, intervening apertures he had created.
That is called a *dhārāgṛha* (shower-house), bearing such names as *dhārāgāra* and so forth.
That house whose walls are covered with bronze, iron, or silk cloths, polished until they are as stainless as mirrors, is known as a *darpaṇagṛha* (mirror-house).
They say that what is other than the main gate here is the side-gate (pakṣadvāra);
they know that gate which rests upon the rampart in the city as the gopura. And those which have gone out, being elevated at intervals within the rampart, [are likewise known].
These are called *upakāryās*; *aṭṭālakas* are considered to be secure watchtowers (53).
Structures for storing timber and halls are known as city enclosures (*purī-saṃvaraṇa*). Those situated along the rampart are *anupālas*, while those on the rampart itself are *upaniṣkalas* (54).
That which is a pleasure-house within a grove is called an *udyāna*;

a pleasure-house on the bank of water is a *jalodyāna*, while one situated in the middle of the water is a *jalaveśma*. That which is described here as a pleasure-house (*krīḍāgṛha*) is also termed a *krīḍāgāra*.
It is called a "monastery ground" (vihārabhūmi) or a "pleasure ground" (ākrīḍabhūmi).

It is also termed a "divine abode" (devadhiṣṇya), a "station of the gods" (surasthāna), a "shrine" (caitya), a "temple" (arcāgṛha), a "sanctuary of the deities" (devatāyatana), and likewise a "house of the wise ones" (vibudhāgāra). ||56-57||
That which is a concealed place for a great multitude is called a *sabhā* (assembly hall) or a *śālā* (hall);
furthermore, those who are experts in the layout of dwellings call a cowshed here a *goṣṭha*.

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "Designations of Cities, Market Towns, Villages, Houses, and Temples," in the *Vāstuśāstra* known by the alternative name *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*, composed by the great king of kings, the illustrious Bhojadeva.
Now begins the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Rules for the Four-Walled House.
We shall now describe the dwellings for kings, army commanders, and ascetics—
both those that are auspicious and those that are inauspicious— in their entirety and in due order.
One hundred and eight houses with a single hall are recorded;
fifty-two with two halls, and seventy-two with three halls.
As for those houses with four halls, there are two hundred of them.
The wise should understand that there are six thousand five hundred;
likewise, there are twenty-five thousand six hundred and ninety-six houses with six halls. ||3-4||
For the one-winged (ekaśāla) buildings with eight components, fifty varieties are proclaimed;
for all the two-winged (dviśāla) types, however, there are five hundred subdivisions.
And for each of the three-winged (triśāla) types, one hundred varieties have been described.
There are eight hundred and forty-two four-winged halls (catuḥśāla).
Thus, there are sixteen thousand, seven hundred and ninety-two, and sixteen less four hundred [additional units]. (6–7)
By calculation, there were seven-hall houses numbering sixty-five thousand five hundred;
furthermore, there were thirty-six other eight-hall houses.
Two hundred and sixty-two thousand one hundred [houses],
and forty-four [houses] with nine halls;
likewise, ten million forty-eight thousand.
There are one thousand and sixty-five halls,
twenty known as "conjoined" (saṃyukta) through the combination of two houses,
and thirty-two houses here through the combination of two houses. 11.232–233ab.
Likewise, there are fifteen other types of *halaka* as well:
the *gṛhamālā*, the *saṅghaṭṭa*, the *gṛhanābhi*, and the *gṛhāṅgaṇa*;
the *udbhinna*, the *bhinnakakṣa*, the *nilīna*, and the *pratipādita*. ||12-13||
There are also eight other varieties for those of the highest caste;
their characteristics, names, and configurations are now set forth.
For those of the castes, the four-winged (catuḥśāla) house should be measured at thirty-two cubits.
The commander-in-chief has sixty-four [wives], and the domestic priest likewise.
There are one hundred and eight of the best kings;
these [groups] respectively decrease by four, six, and eight, and the fifth group is distinct from each of these.
One should clear the middle-sized houses with the smallest ones in due order;
O King, these houses for men lead to prosperity.
One should clear the larger houses with the middle-sized ones, just as before.
These [dimensions] serve as the abodes for the pleasure-chambers of kings.
The length of the houses of Brahmins should be one-tenth greater than their width;
for the houses of the three classes beginning with the Kṣatriyas, it should be increased by eight, six, and four parts respectively.
In this [temple], the length should be equal to the width according to the sequence;
there should be an increase in the houses of the Vaiśyas and Śūdras, as well as in the central and principal [sections].
One should carefully place all the pillars outside the ear-line (karṇasūtra).

Of the sixteen types of *dhāma* (sanctuaries) measuring sixteen cubits, there is an increase of four for each subsequent type; their halls (*śālā*) should be one-fourth as wide as they are long. For all these dwellings, the portico (*alinda*) shall be half the width of the hall.
In that [central hall], it should be sixteen cubits;
or else, by two-fifths [of the total width] for the two rear chambers, and by three-sevenths for the two outermost chambers;
in those two final chambers, it should be four and nine-tenths [cubits].
The length of the hall in the sixteen- and other types [of temples] should be five, six, seven and a half, or eight cubits;
or it may be ten cubits plus one-tenth of the width, increased by seven cubits. ||24–25||
The width of the hall for the most excellent dwellings has been declared here;
the measurement of the porch (alinda) for all dwellings has already been stated previously.
That which remains of the hall and the porch together is indeed the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha).
The wise desire the length of the hall to be measured by the crucible (mūṣā).
The diagonal measurement (avakosimā) for all [halls] should be equal to the width of the hall.
In the cardinal directions, the hall is situated in the building; in the intermediate directions, it corresponds to the ears.
That which is called the *karṇaśālā* should be known as the *avakosimā*.
That which lies between the *alinda* and the *śālā* is remembered as the *mūṣā*.
Having first fixed the eastern door, the first *mūṣā* is situated to its north.
They say that "mūṣā" means "bhadra"; one should determine its number. As many houses as there may be in the mūṣā, so many are called "bhadra.
Whether auspicious or inauspicious, situated in the direction of Indra (the east) or resorting to the direction of Yama (the south), [the result depends on] the "bhadra" within the "bhadra. ||30-31||
Some call them *alindās* when they are situated in the west, between the peaceful and the unpeaceful, or between the auspicious and the inauspicious; others know them as *mūṣās*;
some sing of them as *bhadras*, and others as *parisarās*. (32)
Those crucibles which follow the sequence of one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, and eight are designated here as *pravahaṇas* for houses; among them,
the first ones are auspicious, while those following thereafter are inauspicious.

Having first placed eight gurus according to their names and qualities, and because they give rise to auspicious and inauspicious results, one should then place a *laghu* beneath the first guru; thereafter,
one should arrange the remaining [syllables] as above.
One should fill the beginning with long syllables (gurus) until all [the syllables] become short (laghus).
In the first row, there is one long and one short syllable in sequence;
from that point on, however, these [syllables] double in each subsequent row.
In a four-winged mansion (catuḥśāla), there are two hundred and fifty-six varieties of floor plans (mūṣābheda) through the arrangement of various components such as the vestibule (alinda),
the passage (vīthī), the upper gallery (pragrīva), the turret (niryūhaka), and the window (gavākṣaka).
This [variety] is manifold due to the different configurations of its constituent parts (aṅgabhadra).
Through mutual non-obstruction, whether enclosed or open, various types of houses arise whose number is not known;
for that which is connected by four wings, with a central hall and a veranda, is indeed such [a house]. ||39-40||
We shall now describe the names of the other single-beat (ekabhadrā) meters of the houses;
those who know the art of prosody declare that these single-light (ekalaghu) meters are [distinguished] according to their sequential numerical divisions in the metrical expansion (prastāra). 41.

The Prāgāyata, Prāgvilagna, Jaya, Saṃyamanapriya, Pratīcya, Prāsavinyāsa, Subhadra, and Kalahottara—these eight are the single-bhadra (ekabhadrā) pavilions; now we shall describe the double-bhadra (dvibhadrā) ones. 42–43.
According to the prescribed rule, here the directions proceed from east to north in order;
just as the eastern [direction] is first, so too the south and others follow.
Īraṃ, Sunītha, and Āgneya are the [eastern] continents, while Susaṃyama is the western one.
Ardharca, Aiṣama, Vyākośa, Nairṛta, Vṛṣabha, Vinam;
Kāvya, Vipāsamānīra, Kānta, Saubha, Vipaścima; Gavaya, Śrīvaha, Śliṣṭa, Gaṇa, Bhīma, Ayogama. (45–46)
Varta, Cala, Śaṭha, and Krānta—this is the group of twenty-eight known as the Dvibhadras; hereafter follow the Tribhadras:
Aindra, Viloma, Āyāma, Vadha, Ekākṣa, and Antika.
Prakāśa, Paitra, Māyasta, Bhadra, Prānta, Prasādhaka;
Kṣama, Vighāta, Āyāta, Kānta, Citra, Dvimandira;
Sudakṣiṇa, Bhaya, Śliṣṭa, Pramoda, Vyāyata, and Viyat. ||48-49||
The Āpya, Sunāga, Nāgendra, Mīrita, Śobhana, Ghana, Śastottara, Kapha, Karṇa, Kruṣṭa, Krānta, and Kramāgata are declared in sequence.
Dviśasta is said to be Dvibhaya; Cakra, Malayam, and Āyata [follow].
The forest, the burden, that which is called Sugāra, the abode, and Vīra;
likewise Vyāyāma, Āyuta, and after that Vyāhṛta;
Durgama, that known as Kṣobha, Kṛtrima, and Kṣobhaṇa. ||51-52||
And the names Cāru, Ruci, and Abhidhāna are fixed; how so? In sequence:
the Ṣaṭbhadra, Pañcabhadra, Tribhadra, and after that the Caturbhadra;
then the Kṛta, Arcāyana, Pauṣṇa, Udgata, Miśra, and Utsuka.
Vighna, Vipakṣa, Āhūta, Rucaka, Vardhana, Pṛthu, Kalaha, Chalamāyāsya, Trinābha, Svastika, Sthira, Śarala,
Dviguṇa, Nādya, Citra, Bhrānta, and Vidhāraṇa. (54–55)
Sādhāraṇa, Nata, Tryaṃśa, Ṛṣabha, Roga, Viśeṣaṇa, Pratīcya,
Trisama, Svaira, Supratīka, Nala, Kṣapa,
Vyāpta, Ākrīḍana, Vyartha, Īśāna, Sukha, and Avyaya. ||56–57||
Māgadha, Kṣipra, Āgastya, Eka, Ojas, Dvigata,
Liha, Parka, Viloma, Uddaṇḍa, Muṇḍa, Mātaṅga,
Ākhila, Kharva, Pināka, Udyanta, Viśikha, Prasabha, and Rajas. ||58||
Curuka, saphala, vāma, vardhana, dhāvana, saha, caya,
sevya, kala, and tīrṇa— these are the seventy *caturbhadra* [combinations].
Now, the fifty-six *pañcabhadra* combinations are stated in sequence.
Kānala, Lolupa, Jihma, Pragāla, Sālina, Jinam,
Sujaya, Vijaya, Yāma, Jaya, Jñāta, Japa, Tapa, Jama, Vara,
Cara, Vaira, Viśiṣa, Suprabha, and Prabha. ||61||
Pratīkṣam, kṣamiṇam, yuktam, śāntam, traitam, vinodanam;
(62) sandoham, vipradoham, ca, vidrutam, satatam, tatam;
vyākulam, līnam, ālīnam, vicitram, lambanam, kharām. (63)
The crest, the wise one, Caitra, the attached, the state of prosperity, the triple-pointed,
the clever, the attained, the well-situated, the ill-situated, the stationary;
the wheel, the crooked, the light, the gain, the contact, the root, the imperishable.
Understand that there are twenty-eight other *ṣaḍbhadra* [constellations]:
Kinnara, Kaustubha, Harmya, Dhārmika, Niṣadha, Vasu, Sāṭika, Vāmana, Gaura, Asthira, Kramiṇa, and Khala. ||65-66||
Vivara, Vāliśa, Dhauma, Tripuṣṭa, Mandira, Bhava, Aśoka,
Bhāsvara, Auṣya, Lātavya, Susvana, Makha,
Vājinetra, Bhrama, Ghoṣa, and Saptabhadra— beyond these [are the others].
Bhāṇḍīra, Vaisaha, Prastha, Pratāna, Vāsula, Kaṭa,
Lakṣmīvāsa, and Sugandhānta— these are the eight [types] by name;
and another is the Sarvatobhadra, which consists of eight Bhadras.
Having thus described the four-sided house, we shall now speak of its auspicious and inauspicious qualities.
A clockwise orientation is auspicious, while a counter-clockwise one is the opposite.
In cases of doubt, one should determine what is good or bad by observing which aspect is more prevalent.
Likewise, one should calculate eight *ekabhadra*s, seven *saptabhadra*s in succession,
twenty *dvibhadra*s joined with eight, twenty *ṣaḍbhadra*s, fifty-six *tribhadra*s, and five *pañcabhadra*s. (71–72)
There are seventy houses with four *bhadras* and one house with eight *bhadras*;
thus, the total aggregate of houses is two hundred and fifty-six.
According to the previously mentioned rule regarding *bhadras*, the construction of four-winged (*catuḥśāla*) and other types of houses is performed.

A *mūṣā* (a wall-opening) occurs in those four-winged houses (*catuśśāla*) built against a wall; when these openings are situated along the longitudinal axis (*anuvaṃśa*), they are called *svastika*, while if they face outward, they are called *parāṅmukha*. Furthermore, when two such openings are positioned at the front facing each other, they are known as *avakosima*.
It should not be made facing north;
it must be made with its neck facing east. Likewise, when the structure is to be expanded, it should be made with its neck facing east, so that the opening of the well becomes like a mouth.

In the Nandyāvarta house, all [the channels] should be of the Nandyāvarta type; two should be long and curved (staru) in the right crucible (mūṣā), while the two in the left should be straight (avakosima).
In the Rucaka house, the two should be curved (staru) in the crucible, while the two in the straight one should be of the avakosima type.
In a house that is auspicious on all sides (*sarvatobhadra*), there are crucibles (*mūṣā*) carrying [the fire] through all the doors;
indeed, one crucible should be at the beginning, for that house is elongated toward the east.
With the second [crucible], it is joined toward the east, and immediately after that, with the third.
By circling the houses clockwise with each single mouse-track, there shall be victory and so forth; thus they are described in sequence. Now, their respective fruits are stated:
wealth, the destruction of wealth, victory, and constant misfortune.
Joy, agitation, auspiciousness, and strife follow in sequence;
where the first two [notes] are in the *mūrcchanās*, that is proclaimed as *īra*.
Where the first and the third [are in the *mūrcchanās*], they know that house to be *sunīta*.
In the Āgneya [Purāṇa], the second and third [pādas] are present; in the first and fourth islands, the second and fourth likewise; in the Susaṃyama [Purāṇa], the third and fourth;
in the half-verse, the first and fifth; and in the second Bhava [Purāṇa], the second and fifth.
In Vyākośa, the third and fifth [tithis] are auspicious; in Nairṛta, known as Dviśara, the first and sixth;
likewise in Vṛṣabha, the first and sixth, and also the second and sixth;
and in Kāvya, the third and sixth; and in Vipāśa, known as Abdhirasa (64), the same.
In Ānīra, the fifth and sixth [syllables] are long; in Kānta, the first is long along with the seventh.
In Saubha, the second and seventh are long; in Vipaścit, the third and seventh are long.
In Gavaya, the seventh and fourth are long; in Śrīvaha, the fifth and seventh are long.
The sixth and seventh [tithis] are conjoined when the group is "Pūrva"; likewise, the eighth is conjoined with the second in "Bhīma"; and in "Ayoga," both the third and the eighth are joined.
In "Varta," the fourth and the eighth are joined; and in "Cala," the fifth and the eighth are joined.
"The sixth and eighth [are auspicious] when the Sun has entered Cancer, as are the seventh and eighth;

thus, twenty-eight [asterisms] here are declared to be 'twice-auspicious' (dvibhadra) for householders. Now we shall describe those that are 'thrice-auspicious' (tribhadra); among them, the asterism of Indra (Jyeṣṭhā) increases prosperity."

A house that has its entrance on the south-west and is provided with the first three *ūṣās* is called *viloma*; it increases the prosperity of Śūdras, provided its entrance faces the west and is formed by the first, second, and fourth [of those *ūṣās*]. (91)
In the *sarvatomukha* (all-facing) type of *āyāma*, the first, third, and fourth [lines] should be used;
in the *vadha* (multiplication) type, the second, third, and fourth should be used, and the entrance should be in the northern direction.
Where the first and fifth are doubled, that is declared to be the *ekākṣa* (single-eyed) type.
Where there are two and five [lines] on the first day, that is declared to be the *gṛhamantika* (near-the-house) [type].
Where there are two, three, and five [lines], it is *prakāśa* (manifest), which brings about all prosperity.
Where there is one [line] on the first day, and four and five [lines] follow, that is called *paitra* (pertaining to the ancestors).
Where the fifth, second, and fourth [syllables] are heavy, that is called Āyata.
The wise say that where the third, fourth, and fifth are heavy, it is Bhadra;
and where the first, second, and sixth are heavy, that is termed Prānta.
The first, third, and sixth [lines] should be in the house of the accomplisher (prasādhaka);
that [house] shall have doors on all sides and likewise accomplish all aims.
The second, third, and sixth [lines] are in the house named Kṣama.
In its western direction is the door that brings prosperity to the Śūdra class.
The sixth, fourth, and first [houses] belong to the house called Vighāta;
when the sixth, second, and fourth are in it, that house faces south.
That which is joined with six, four, and three is beautiful and a accomplisher of all aims;
that which is joined with six, five, and so on is variegated and faces the southern direction.
That house in which the second, fifth, and sixth [notes] are found is the "double-house" (dvimandira).
Where the third, fifth, and sixth [syllables] are long, they call that *sudakṣiṇa*.
Where the fourth, fifth, and sixth [syllables] are short, that does not produce growth (*vṛddhi*).
Where the first, second, and seventh [syllables] are short, that is designated as *śliṣṭa*.
They desire this southern-facing house to be auspicious for men and the bestower of all goals.
The first, third, and seventh [measures] are proclaimed to bring joy;
where there are two, three, or seven [of these], that dwelling is known as "extended" (vyāyata).
Where the first, fourth, and seventh [lines] are equal, that is the *vyoma* [house].
Reaching the second, fourth, and seventh [lines] as equal, it would be the *dakṣiṇāmukha*.
By means of the third, fourth, and seventh [lines], however, the house is celebrated as the *sunāga*.
And that [crucible] which faces south or west bestows wealth, grain, and happiness.
O Lord of Nagas, the seventh and fifth [lines] from the east are designated as the crucible (mūṣā).
The crucible is said to face south when it consists of two, five, or seven [lines].

A house adorned with three, five, or seven *mūṣās* will be beautiful. Where the fourth, fifth, and seventh [lines] are present, that is a solid [structure]. The first, sixth, and seventh are remembered as auspicious when located in the northern part of the house.
The second, seventh, and sixth [houses] from that which is called Yama (the Sun) are known as Kapha;
this is the Vāruṇa door, and it is beneficial for the twice-born.
The western door is Karṇa, joined with the third, sixth, and seventh [houses].
The fourth, seventh, and sixth [notes] are called *mūṣā* in the *kruṣṭa* [jāti].
That which is joined with the seventh, fifth, and sixth [notes] is the *krānta* [jāti], which bestows fame.
The first, eighth, and second [notes] are declared to be *mūṣā* in the *kramāgata* [jāti].
The first, the eighth, and the third [houses] are remembered as being doubled when they fall upon a house;
where the eighth is on the third and second, that is declared to be "Dvibhaya" (twice-frightening).
Where the first, the eighth, and the fourth [are doubled], that is designated as "Cakra."
Where the fourth, eighth, and second [notes] occur, they know that as Malaya;
where the fourth, eighth, and third [notes] occur, that is called Āyata;
and where the first, eighth, and fifth [notes] occur, that is remembered as Vana. ||113-114||
If the second, fifth, and likewise the eighth [lines] are the crucible (mūṣā), that is called Bhāra;
it is auspicious when facing north, otherwise it causes obstacles.
However, with the third, fifth, and eighth [lines], it is proclaimed as Sugāra.
That house where the eighth, fourth, and fifth [notes] are present is likewise [described];
that in which the first, eighth, and sixth are found is here celebrated as *vīra*.
In the house named *vyāyāma*, the sixth, eighth, and second [notes] reside. (116–117)
An arrangement with the sixth, eighth, and third *mūṣās* is said to be ten thousand (*āyuta*).
Where the sixth, eighth, and fourth occur, they know that as *vyāhṛta*.
An arrangement with the sixth, eighth, and fifth is considered difficult to traverse and productive of disease.
When conjoined with the first, eighth, and seventh [notes], it is called *kṣobha*.
When conjoined with two sevens and an eighth, it is known as the artificial *gṛha*.
However, by means of three sevens and an eighth, there occurs *kṣobhaṇa* through the *mūṣās*.
That which is endowed with four, seven, and eight [syllables] is called Cārurucya;
that joined with seven, five, and eight is known as Dhruva.
How is it that one joined with six, seven, and eight bestows the accomplishment of all aims?
Thus have been declared the "Three Auspicious" (tribhadra) [combinations], as well as those which are praised among them;
these should always be employed by wise men for the castes.
Where the first four crucibles are used, that is designated as "Kṛta. (122–123)
The house should have double the dimensions of the previous one and its entrance facing west, not otherwise;
that house in which the first three and the fifth [lines] constitute the arcāyana shall possess all auspicious qualities and have its door facing west.

That house in which the first, second, fourth, and likewise the fifth [syllables] are [long], is the Pauṣṇa type with a southern entrance, which brings all prosperity to men. That house in which the first three as well as the first [syllable] are [long] is the Udgata type. ||125-126||
This is recommended with the western or the southern entrance;
where there are two or more up to four [entrances], that mixed type increases joy.
For Kṣatriyas and others, its eastern or southern entrance is praised.
That [mandala] in which the first three, as well as the sixth, are the *mūṣās* is called *utsuka*.
It is auspicious with its western door and brings victory to the Brahmins and other castes.
That [mandala] wherein the first, second, fourth, and sixth are the *mūṣās*— ||128–129||
Facing south or west is auspicious; the one named Vighna increases the prosperity of the family.
That [house] is auspicious in which the first, third, fourth, and sixth [syllables] are present.
The abode named Vipakṣa has its door facing west.

A house in which the second, third, and sixth lines (mūṣās) are auspicious is called *āhūta*; it has its door facing south or west. That house in which the first, second, fifth, and sixth lines are auspicious [is called *pratihūta*]. ||131-132||
The one named Rucaka has its eastern and southern doors and grants all desires;
where there are one, three, five, and sixty-one [units], that is the Vardhamānaka.
It has eastern, western, and northern doors and bestows prosperity upon the four castes.
That house in which there are two, three, five, and six cells is known as Pṛthu, having its entrance on the east and south. That one in which the first, fourth, fifth,
and sixth cells exist is known as Kalabha.

A dwelling endowed with all excellent qualities and having its door facing north is praised; however, if it has doors on the second, fourth, fifth, or sixth [floor], it is called deceptive. Its southern or western face is also recommended.
That [house] in which there are four pillars and three doors and so forth is called Āyāsya;
those who know it declare this to be inauspicious and the lowest of dwellings.
That house in which there are the first three and the seventh types of mūṣās is likewise [inauspicious]. ||137-138||
A temple with three naves and a northern entrance, endowed with all auspicious qualities, is praised;
that which possesses [entrances] on the first, second, fourth, and seventh [pillars] is known as the *svastika*.
An entrance facing east, west, or north is also recommended for all four castes.
A house in which the first, fourth,
and seventh [lines] are the crucibles (mūṣā) is said here to be "stable" (sthira), and its door is on the south.
Where the second, third, and seventh are [the crucibles], they know that to be "straight" (sarala).
That house shall have its western door and be free from all defects; it is called "Twofold" (dviguṇa) where the first, second, fifth, and likewise the seventh [lines] are doubled,
and its door may be as desired.
That [naming] in which the first, third, fifth,
and also the seventh [syllables] are not long is excellent for all embodied beings;
the second, third, fifth, and seventh syllables should be short in the name.
Where that palace named Citra stands— possessing wonderful gates adorned with variegated qualities,
where the first, fourth, fifth, and likewise the seventh [notes] are present—
that is called Bhrānta; its eastern and northern gates bring about prosperity.
Where the second, fourth, fifth, and likewise the seventh [notes] are present, that is the Vidhāraṇa house, which increases all desires.
Where the third, fourth, fifth, and likewise the seventh [notes] are present... [146-147]
They call that "common" (sādhāraṇa), which brings happiness through all its gates;
where the first, second, sixth, and seventh [syllables] are bowed (short), it is so.
Likewise, in a three-part [meter], the first, second, sixth, and seventh [syllables] should be short.
The second, third, sixth, and seventh [notes], O Sage;
likewise, the first, fourth, sixth, and seventh should be used in the case of disease.
That [melody] wherein the second, fourth, sixth, and seventh [notes] occur is [the one for] that [condition].
The house named Viśoṣaṇa faces the south and north;
it is that house where the third, fourth, sixth, and seventh [asterisms] are located,
with its desired door facing west, which grants all desires.
That house where the first, fifth, sixth, and seventh [notes] are indeed equal in measure (trisama) bestows abundant prosperity and is endowed with all virtues;
likewise, that house where the second, fifth, sixth, and seventh [notes] [are so]. || 152–153 ||
Therefore, they say that a house built here according to one's own preference brings wealth, grain, and happiness.
The third, fifth, sixth, and seventh [auspicious] asterisms are the northern door;
or it may be the western door, where it is well-proportioned and brings prosperity.
With the four [lines] beginning with the fourth, Nala faces the northern direction.
With the first, second, third, and eighth, there is destruction, causing all diseases and fear.
When pervaded, the first, second, fourth, and likewise the eighth [are significant].
In the Ākrīḍa [mandala], the first, third, and fourth [lines] should be [drawn], and likewise the eighth;
for the purpose of the two [deities], the second, third, and fifth lines should be drawn in sequence, and the eighth should likewise be a *mūṣā* (enclosure).
In the one called Īśāna, the first, second, third, and fifth [lines] should be [drawn], and likewise the eighth.
That [arrangement] in which the eighth, third, and fifth [notes] are in the front (east) is designated as "Sukha" (Ease).
That [Sukha] arrangement, when facing east or north, leads to prosperity; otherwise, it leads to loss.
Where the eighth, second, and third, or the eighth, second, and fifth [notes] are located, that is considered here to be "Avyaya" (Imperishable).
Those learned in the science of architecture (vāstuvidyā) have declared that its door may be as one desires;
however, that [site] where the eighth, fourth, fifth, and ninth [asterisms] from Pūrva-phalgunī are located is indeed Magadha.
Wise men praise this [site] as having doors facing the east, north, west, or south.
Where the second, fourth, fifth, and likewise the eighth are the crucibles (mūṣās), that is called "thrown" (kṣipta);
it is desired as a door for happiness according to one's wish.
In the case of the western-facing Āgastya [mudrā], the third, fifth, eighth, and fourth [are the crucibles]. 161–162.
Where the second, third, sixth, and eighth [houses] are odd-numbered, that is called *ekoja*.
Where the third, fourth, sixth, and eighth [houses] are present, that house is called *dvigata*.
That in which the second, third, sixth, and eighth [houses] are also present is called *liha*.
Where the first, fourth, eighth, and sixth [notes] are present, that is called *parka*.
A house named *viloma* consists of the sixth, eighth, second, and fourth;
one consisting of the sixth, eighth, second, and fourth is celebrated as *uddaṇḍa*.
In that [system] called Muṇḍa, the first, eighth, sixth, and fifth [tithis] are [the days of practice];
in that named Mātaṅga, they are the second, fifth, eighth, and sixth;
and in that named Askhala, they are the third, fifth, eighth, and sixth.
When the third, fourth, and fifth, as well as the eighth, are in the asterism named Kharva;
or when the first, second, seventh, and eighth are in Pināka;
or where the third, seventh, and eighth are preceded by the first—these are called Udyantam. (167–168)
A house in which the second, third, fifth, and eighth [lines] are [occupied by the moon] is called Viśikha;
likewise, in Prasabha, the first, fourth, seventh, and eighth [lines] should be so.
In Raja, the second, fourth, seventh, and likewise the eighth [lines] are the Mūṣās.
They know that configuration as *rucaka* where the third, seventh, eighth, and fourth [lines] are present;
its door faces east or west, and it bestows great prosperity upon Śūdras.
The *mūṣā* configuration consists of the seventh, first, and eighth [lines], and the fifth is also included along with the *saphala*.
On the left side, the crucibles should be known as having two, five, seven, and likewise eight [fingers].
That in which there are three, five, seven, and eight [fingers] is the *vardhamānaka* (ascending) type;
those who know it say that this specifically brings about prosperity for the Vaiśyas.
That in which there are four, five, eight, and seven [verses] is called *dhāvana*.
That in which there are seven, eight, six, and six [verses], beginning with the seventh, is called *saha*.
The piling (*caya*) is performed with *mūṣā* bricks consisting of two, seven, six, and eight [verses].
That [day] in which the sixth, eighth, and two seventh [tithis] occur is said to be "sevyam" (to be resorted to);
where the fourth, eighth, sixth, and seventh [tithis] occur, that is "kalam";
when the sixth, eighth, fifth, and seventh [tithis] have passed, it is "sarvakāmade. (175)
That in which the first five [syllables] occur is declared to be *kānala*, which grants all desires (176).
That in which there are one, two, three, four, and sixty [syllables] is known as *lolupa*.
That in which the first three, as well as five and sixty [syllables] occur, is called *jihma* (177).
In the *pragāla*, the fifth, sixth, fourth, first, second, third, fourth, fifth, and sixth [syllables] should be long; this is called the *sālinī* meter.
Where there are two, three, four, five, and six [long syllables], that is called the *jina* meter.
In the *Sujaya* [yoga], there should be one, two, three, or four [units] joined with the seventh;
in that called *Vijaya*, there should be five, seven, two, or three preceding [units].
Where there are one, two, four, five, and seven, that is the name of the watch (*yāma*). (179–180)
Where there are one, three, four, five, or seven [syllables], that is known as *japa*.
Where there are two, three, four, five, or seven [syllables], it is designated as *mūṣā*.
Furthermore, where there are the first three, as well as the sixth and seventh, that is *japa*.
They know *tapa* by means of the first, second, fourth, sixth, and seventh [syllables].
For *jaya*, the sixth, third, fourth, and seventh [syllables] are considered to be preceded by the first;
likewise, for that which is named *vara*, the second, third, fourth, sixth, and seventh [syllables are used]. (182–183)
That [direction] is the one where the first two [Tithis] are joined with the fifth, sixth, and seventh;
at a Caitya, the seventh would be the sixth, and the first would be the third.
For Viśiras, the second, third, and fifth [Tithis] occur, as do the sixth and the seventh.
In Suprabha, the fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh [tithis] from the beginning occur;
in Prabhākhyā, there are the second, fourth, fifth, and sixth, as well as the seventh;
and in Pratīkṣaka, there are the third, fourth, fifth, and seventh, as well as the sixth.

That [yoga] in which the first four [tithis] are present along with the eighth is indeed "Kṣamiṇa. Likewise, in the yoga named "Yukta," there are the seven preceding [tithis] as well as the second, third, fifth, and eighth. In "Śānta," the second, fourth, fifth, and likewise the eighth should be present from the beginning.
In the *Vinoda* [chapter] of the work titled *Traita*, the first, third, fourth, fifth,
and eighth [verses] are included;
likewise, in the *Sandoha*, there are the second, third, fifth, fourth, and eighth, as well as the eighth, sixth, and the three beginning with the first.
They know that to be *vipradhoka* where there is the first, second, fourth, sixth, and eighth [syllables];
and they know that to be *vidruta* wherein the sixth, eighth, third, fourth, and first [syllables] occur.
That wherein the second, third, fourth, eighth, and sixth [syllables] occur is considered *satata*.
In the *atatanāman* [rhythm], the first, second, fifth, sixth, and likewise the eighth [syllables] are heavy;
in the *vyākula*, the first, third, fifth, sixth, and likewise the eighth are heavy;
and in that known as *līna*, the second, third, fifth, fourth, and sixth are to be understood [as heavy].
The fourth, first, fifth, sixth, and likewise the eighth [mudrās] are for the *ālīna* [state];
the second, fourth, fifth, sixth, and similarly the eighth are for the *vicitra* [state].
The first four together with the eighth are the *mūṣā* [mudrās] in that which is called *lambana*.

The first three [syllables], as well as the eighth and the seventh, should likewise be short (khara) in the Śekhara meter. In the Vibudha meter, the eighth, the fourth, the third, the first, and the seventh [syllables] are short. (194–195)
In the [yoga] called Caitra, the second, eighth, fourth, seventh, and third [tithis] are auspicious;
likewise, in the one called Vyāsakta, the first, second, fifth, and seventh, as well as the eighth;
and in the one named Sampat, the first, third, fifth, seventh, and eighth.
They know that *pada* to be where there are two, three, eight, five, and seven [syllables].
Likewise, in the *triśikha* meter, the fourth, first, fifth, sixth, and seventh [syllables] are short;
and in the *catura* meter, the second, fifth, eighth, fourth, and seventh [syllables] are short. ||197-198||
The third, seventh, eighth, fourth, and fifth [houses] are called "terminal" (prānta).
The first, second, seventh, sixth, and eighth are [called] "well-situated" (susthita) in the Susthita yoga.
Where the sixth, first, fourth, and likewise the seventh are situated, that is the Duḥsthita yoga.
It is recorded that during the stationing [of the moon], the eighth, the two seventh days, and also the sixty-third day occur;
in the retrograde motion (vakra), the sixth, eighth, fourth, seventh, and so forth are proclaimed,
while in the retrograde motion specifically, the second, seventh, sixth, eighth, and fourth days occur.
The eighth, third, and seventh, as well as the fourth and sixth, are proclaimed [as favorable] for gain (*lābha*).
Similarly, the fifth, seventh, and sixth, as well as the first and eighth, are [favorable] for gain.
The second, fifth, seventh, and eighth, along with the sixth, are designated as *saṃparka* (contact).
The sixty-third, fifty-third, sixth, and seventh [verses] belong to the name "Root" (Mūla), as does the eighth;
while the eighth, seventh, sixth, fifth, and fourth belong to that which is called "Imperishable" (Avyaya).
Where the six molds begin with the eastern direction, that house is named Kinnara.
Where the first, fifth, and seventh [syllables] are long together with the seventh, they know that as the *kaustubha* meter.
In the meter named *harmya*, the first, second, third, fourth, sixth, and seventh [syllables] are long.
In the *dhārmika* meter, the seventh, fifth, and sixth [syllables], as well as those preceded by the second, third, and [first], are long.
In the Niṣadha [meter], there are two, four, five, six, and so on, with the seventh likewise;
where there are three, four, five, six, seven, and so on, that is Vasu.
In the Sāṭīka [meter], there are three, four, five, two, and sixty, and likewise the eighth.
They know that when the first, fifth, and seventh [syllables] are short, it is called *vāmana*;
when the first, second, third, fourth, sixth, and eighth are short, it is named *gaura*;
and when the first, second, third, sixth, eighth, and fifth are short, it is designated as *asthira*.
In the *kramin* [formation], the third, fourth, fifth, sixth, eighth, and likewise the first [notes] are used.
In the *khala*, the first, eighth, sixth, third, and fourth [notes] are used, joined with the fifth.
In the *vivara*, the third, fourth, fifth, second, sixth, and likewise the eighth [notes] should be employed.
In the one called Bāliśa, the first, second, third, fourth, seventh, and eighth [tithis] are auspicious;
in the one named Dhauma, the first, eighth, second, third, seventh, and fifth [are auspicious];
and in Tripuṣṭa, the second, fourth, fifth, seventh, first, and likewise the eighth [are auspicious].
In the temple, the [days] are the third, fourth, fifth, seventh, and so on, as well as the eighth;
likewise, the second, third, fourth, fifth, eighth, and seventh.
In the Aśoka [shrine], they are the second, third, sixth, seventh, and eighth, together with the preceding one.
In the *Bhāsvara* [tattva], there are sixty-two [deities] beginning with the seventh and joined with the eighth;
in the one named *Auṣya*, there are three [beginning with] the seventh, the eighth, the sixth, and those beginning with the fourth;
in the *Lātavya*, there are the second, third, fourth, eighth, and sixth, as well as the seventh.
In the Susvana sacrifice, the second, seventh, eighth, sixth, fifth, and first days are prescribed;
likewise, in the Makha sacrifice, the third, fifth, eighth, sixth, seventh, and first days;
and in the one named Vājapeya, the second, third, seventh, eighth, sixth, and fifth days.
In the *netra* [tāla], the second, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, and likewise the eighth [beats] occur;
in the *bhrama*, the second, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, and likewise the eighth [beats] occur;
and in the *ghoṣa*, the third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, and likewise the eighth [beats] occur.
If there are one, two, three, four, five, six, or seven [units],
then they call that dwelling Bhāṇḍīra;
likewise, where there are one, two, three, four, five, six, or eight [units].
Those learned in the science of architecture call such a house "vaiśasa.
If there are one, two, three, four, five, seven, or eight mouse-holes in a house, one should know it by the name "prastha. (220)
The first, second, third, fourth, sixth, seventh, and likewise the eighth [houses] are the positions;
that in which the crucible (mūṣā) is located is here called the "extension" (pratāna), the residence. A house built with crucibles excluding the fourth house is called vāsula.
A dwelling should be understood as *kaṭa* when it has eight openings, excluding the third;
one with eight openings, excluding the second, is declared to be *lakṣmīvān*;
and one with eight openings, excluding the first, is called *sarvabhadra*. ||223||
Thus have been described the dwellings beginning with the *ekabhadra* up to the *aṣṭabhadra* house.
He who knows these various types of four-winged (*catuśśāla*) houses shall receive honor in the world.

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Rules for Four-Winged Houses," in the *Vāstuśāstra* composed by the Great King of Kings, the illustrious Bhojadeva, also known as the *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*.
Now begins the twentieth chapter, titled "The Results of Low and High [Elevations], etc.
In a house, the terms "front" (*agratas*) and "rear" (*pṛṣṭhatas*) are determined by the door;
that side where the door is located is the front, and the opposite side is declared to be the rear. ||1||
If the width (dra) is excessive due to an increase in length (āyāma) and breadth (vyāsa),
whether it be on the left or the right, or in front or behind,
that house which is excessive in width destroys the wealth; and that which is excessive in length destroys the family.
If the ground is higher on the left side and lower on the right, the worship will be greater than the height [of the structure], and the progeny will be more extensive than the width;
however, such a site possesses many defects and leads to the destruction of sons and grandsons.
If the ground is sloping toward the south and elevated on the left,
then even that which is performed with great effort will yield little fruit for the patron.
The ground should be sloping toward the west and more elevated in the front.
Where that house which grants all desires exists among all castes;
yet, if it is low in front and high at the back,
that mansion will quickly lead to the master's loss of passion and misfortune.

In this context, the house is said to be of four kinds: with a canopy (sacchatra), with side-chambers (sakakṣa), likewise with a circumambulatory path (saparikrama), and with radiance (saprabha). Furthermore, [the types] are:
with water on the exterior (bāhyodaka), with a canopy, and with water on both sides (ubhayodaka).
One should know that a house with dew is one that has a circumambulatory path (parikrama).
Even if it has only a single portico (alinda) at the front, the back, or the side, it shall possess radiance; however, the characteristics [of these types] are distinct from one another.
A single portico should be constructed either at the front or on the right;
at the front it leads to royal favor, and on the right it increases wealth.
However, one should not construct a single portico on the left or at the back.
