If it is on the left, it leads to the destruction of wealth; if behind, the householder dies. If there are two porticos (alindas) on both sides of the house, one should know that the head of the household will gain wealth upon entering it.
He who has two *alinda*s both in front and likewise behind,
that householder obtains wealth, grain, and good fortune.
Or he who has a *halaka* and an *alinda* at the entrance or on the right side—
Through the king's favor, its owner prospers with wealth and grain.
(15) If the plowshare and the furrow are made on the left side and at the front, one should know that there will be fear of royal punishment and his wife will perish. (16)
If the Halakālinda is made on the right and on the west,
then there will be even greater prosperity and supreme good fortune.
If the Halakālinda is made behind and on the left, [the same results follow].
In that case, there will be the death of a wife and also misfortune.
Now we shall describe, in due order, the results of an *alinda* (porch) constructed behind, to the left, in front, or to the right. ||18-19||
If it falls behind, it leads to the destruction of one's wife; on the right, to the acquisition of wealth;
in front, to the favor of the king; and on the left, it causes the destruction of one's property. When a building site has been completed and thoroughly purified on all sides, [it is auspicious].
That shall be auspicious for the master and bring glory to the architect;
his earned wealth increases, and he attains growth through royal prosperity.
His virtue and desire flourish, as do his fame, longevity, renown, and strength.
There, one would perceive houses of many kinds with three wings, where people were constantly sporting, where prosperity was ever-present,
which were perpetually filled with the joy of dance, instrumental music, and song, and free from all affliction. (23) There, one would observe dwellings of various types with three halls.
Among all the types, those abandoned by Yama and the West are censurable:
in one there is the death of the master, and in the other the loss of wealth.
Those abandoned by the East and the North are auspicious; and their names are according to their types. ||24-25||
In sequence, there should be the [squares] named Hiraṇyanābha, Sukṣetra, Cullī, and Pakṣaghna, excluding those in the north, east, south, and west; their application,
such as the Alinda and Malindavyūha, is according to one's desire.
Now, the two-winged houses (dviśālā) are described in sequence as six.
One should designate the two-winged houses at the corners of the directions, and those on the other corners of those;
one should recognize these six as being joined together facing one another.
In the south and west, there is the accomplishment of one's goals; here, the success of one's aims is attained.
In the south and east, where Yama and the Sun reside, there is always fear of death. In the east and north, however, there is the staff (daṇḍa); there, punishment shall always prevail.
In the east and south, however, there is the site known as Vāta; that which follows it is Kalaha.
When facing north and south, it is a two-winged site called Kāca;
in that case, there will be discord with kinsmen, so one should never construct such a house.
One should designate the *cullīvāstu* (the hearth-site) in the orientation facing east or west;
there, a terrible loss of wealth occurs, so one should never allow this to be done.
A four-winged house (*catuśśāla*) may be joined with a three-winged house situated at the edge along the perimeter wall.
To the east, among the seven-hall structures, there is that which is known as Maṇic-chanda;
others likewise speak of three more: Prānta, Pradakṣiṇa, and Apara-paridhāna, along with Sapakṣa. ||33-34||
"Two *śālās* sharing a single wall is called a 'house-conjunction' (*gṛhasaṃghaṭṭa*).
One should not construct such a thing, for it always brings about the faults of imprisonment and death.
(35) Thus has been declared the result of the high and low portions of a house.
In this [science], even the *alindaphala* (the result of the porch) is both inauspicious and auspicious;
whatever marks belong to houses of two or three *śālas*, those too are correctly included here as arising generally from the combination of both. (36)

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Characteristics and Results of Houses with Low or High Roofs, Verandas, and Courtyards; the Results of Auspicious Vāstus; and Large and Triple-Hall Houses," in the *Vāstuśāstra* composed by the Great King of Kings, Śrī Bhojadeva, also known as the *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*.
Now begins the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Seventy-two Triple-Hall Houses.
Now we shall describe the seventy-two triple-hall houses in their proper order.
The characteristics of the various types of *abhighāna* (anvil) have been described individually and in their entirety.
Among them, four principal ones are mentioned by name:
Hiraṇyanābha, Sukṣetra, Cullī, and Pakṣaghna.
The excellent *hiraṇyanābha* [configuration] becomes inferior if it lacks the *uttaraśālā*;
however, when combined with the *pūrvaśālā*, it bestows wealth upon the master. A *sukṣetra* endowed with these characteristics grants prosperity and growth to the lord.
A house lacking a fire-pit (cullī) in the south causes the loss of grain;
one lacking it in the west brings about the destruction of wealth, creates enmity, and leads to the ruin of the family.
These defects are remedied by the addition of an alinda (porch) through the application of a small extension.
Through the application of crucibles (mūṣāyoga), there are eighteen distinct varieties:
Jāmbūnada, Hiraṇya, Rukma, Hemasaṃjñita, Kanaka, Kāñcana, Svarṇa, and Suvarṇa; beyond these [are the others].
Santāpasaṃjña, Sāra, and likewise that called Amīkara;
Tapana, Tāpanīya, and also Śātakumbha;
Hiraṇyanābha, Kalyāṇa, Bhūṣaṇa, and Bhūtibhūṣaṇa.
These eighteen varieties of the Hiraṇyanābha [sandalwood] are as follows:
Nāga, Sūryaprabha, Mattavāraṇaka,
the fourth called Kesarī, Vāsava, and Indrameva.
Harihaṃsa, Sārasāṇḍa, Kuñjara, Toyada, Meghamālābhidhāna, Dhārāsāra, Mahodara,
another named Kardama, Sukṣetra, and likewise Prakara. ||10-11||
They say that other [types] follow from the "good field" (sukṣetra) and are full of grain;
now I shall describe the varieties of the *cullī*, the first of which is the *bhujaṅgama*.
These are the one called *nirjīva*, the *vihaṅga*, the *nakula*, and the one named *pannaga*.
Śatacchidra, Sarpa, Kopa-saṃjña, Bhagaṃdara,
Udvejanākhya, Sannyāsa, Nistoṣa, Karuṇānana, Vāraṇa, Dāraṇa, Cullī, Kakuda, and likewise Kandara. ||13-14||
Thus, we have described eighteen types of houses among the various varieties of *cullī* (stoves/furnaces).
Now, we shall state the names of houses associated with the *pakṣaghna* (wing-breaker) configuration:
Rākṣasa, Dhvāntasaṃhāra, Devāri, and Suradāruṇa.
Ghoṣaṇa, Vyāghraśārdūla, Śoṣaṇa, Viśoṣaṇa, Mattada, Nirānanda, Śākuna,
Vighnanirghṛṇe, Ripusaṃhada, Pakṣaghna, Sutaghna, and Vairipūraṇa. ||16–17||
Thus, eighteen varieties of *pakṣaghna* have been described in their proper order.
Among the varieties of *hiraṇyanābha*, the *jāmbūnada* is the most auspicious;
it is characterized by the first four crucibles (*mūṣā*) mentioned in succession. (18)

That [arrangement] in which the first, second, third, and fifth [syllables] are long is called *hiraṇya*, which is auspicious. That in which the fifth, first, second, and fourth [syllables] are long is *rukma*; its house is the giver of gold. That in which the first, third, fourth, and fifth [syllables] are long is designated as *hema*.
With the second, third, fourth, and fifth [syllables], it is *kanaka*, which brings gold;
with the first, second, third, and sixth, it is *kāñcana*, which bestows gold.
With the first, second, fourth, and sixth, it is *svarṇa*, for the increase of gold.
That which consists of gold in the first, third, fourth, and sixth [verses] is "Suvarṇada" (Gold-Giver).
That which consists of gold in the second, third, fourth, and sixth [verses] is "Santāpa" (Heat), which brings about the pacification of suffering.
Where there is gold in the first, second, fifth, and sixth [verses], that is the "Uttamasāra" (Supreme Essence).
With sixty-three and so forth up to five [parts], it is the excellent *cāmīkara*;
with two, three, six, and five, the palace named *tapana* is formed.
With six, four, and so forth up to five, it is declared to be *tāpanīya*.
The Śātakumbha house is formed by two, six, five, and four [parts];
the Hiraṇyanābha is said to be formed by three, four, five, and six;
and the Kalyāṇa is declared to be formed by the first [one], three, four, five, and six.
That which consists of six, five, two, three, and four [syllables] is known as Bhūṣaṇa;
that which consists of one, two, three, four, five, and six [syllables] is Bhūtabhūṣaṇa.
Now, we shall state the definitions of the various types of Sukṣetra.
That [mandala] where the first, second, third, and fourth [lines] are present is called the Nāga temple.
That where the first, second, third, and fifth [lines] are present is said to be Sūryaprabha.
That where the first, second, fourth, and fifth [lines] are present is Mattavāraṇa.
Where the first, third, fourth, and fifth [notes] occur, that they know as Kesarī;
where the fifth, fourth, second, and [first], it is called Vāsava. Where the sixth, first, third, and second [notes] occur, it is declared to be Indramandira.
That which is designated as *hari* is described by means of the first, second, fourth, and sixth [syllables].

The dwelling designated as *haṃsa* is established by means of the first, third, fourth, and sixth [syllables]. That which is known by the name *sārasa* consists of the sixth, second, third, and fourth [syllables]. ||31-32||
In this system, one describes a *kuñjara* house by means of the first, second, fifth, and sixth [lines];
a *toyada* house is to be recognized by the first, third, fifth, and sixth;
and a *meghamāla* house is declared by the third, sixth, fifth, and second.
A house with four, five, six, and so forth [cells] is called Dhārāsāra;
that with two, four, five, and sixty is known as Mahodara;
and that named Kardama, consisting of six, five, three, and four, brings victory.
A field with six, five, four, three, or two [lines] at the beginning shall be a fertile field that bestows wealth.
With two, three, six, five, or four [lines], it becomes a *prakara* that grants prosperity.
And with these first six [configurations], it should be known as a granary that fills one with grain.
These eighteen varieties of excellent fields and houses have been proclaimed.
A *bhujaṅgama* house is formed by the first, second, third, and fourth *mūṣās*;
a *nirjīva* house is formed by the first, fifth, third, and second [mūṣās]. ||37-38||
In this world, one identifies a bird by means of the first, second, fifth, and fourth [notes] being carried forward;
one knows a mongoose by means of the fifth, first, third, and fourth [notes] in the mūṣā [scale].
A serpent would exist by name through the fifth, second, third, and fourth [notes].
With the first, third, and second [lines] having one hundred openings, it becomes the *gṛha* (house) [meter].
With the first, fourth, sixth, and second [lines], it is called *sarpa* (serpent).
With the first, third, sixth, and fourth [lines], it is designated as *kopa* (anger).

A house formed by the sixth, fourth, third, and second [lines] results in fistula-in-ano (bhagandara). That which is formed by the first, second, fifth, and sixth [lines] is declared to be "distressing" (udvejana). A house formed by the first, fifth, third, and sixth [lines] is the lowest type of dwelling (sannyāsa).
By the second, third, sixth, and fifth [syllables], however, it is called *nistoya*.
By the fourth and so on, up to the fifth and sixth, it is called *karuṇānana*. By the second, fourth, fifth, and sixth, it is called *vāraṇa-mukhavāraṇa*.
With three, four, five, or six [units], there is "Splitting," which is the auspicious Vidāraṇa;
with three, four, five, or six [units] starting from the hearth (cullyā), there is the destruction of wealth. With six, five, two, three, or four [units], the mansion is named Kakuda.
A *kandara* (cave) consists of six, four, five, three, two, or one [verses]; it is the lowest type of house.
Now, eighteen varieties based on the *pakṣaghna* (wing-breaker) are described.
Among them, the first is called *rākṣasa*, consisting of two, three, or four [verses]. 46–47.
The "Mass of Darkness" (dhvāntasaṃghāta) is proclaimed by the first, fifth, second, and third [syllables];
the "Enemy of the Gods" (devārī) is declared by the first, fifth, second, and fourth [syllables].
The "Devadāruṇa" is to be known by the first, third, fifth, and fourth [syllables].
The proclamation with the fifth, third, second, and fourth [notes] is the "Proclamation of Suffering" (duḥkhaghoṣaṇa).
That which is proclaimed with the sixth, first, second, and third [notes] is called the "Tiger" (vyāghra).
With the first, second, fourth, and sixth [notes], the dwelling place would be the "Leopard" (śārdūla). ||49-50||
One should know that the drying of the son occurs by means of the first, third, fourth, and sixth [syllables],
while the drying of all [the elements] is understood through the sixth, fourth, second, and third.
By means of the first, second, fifth, and sixth, one knows the temple named Mattada.
The one called Nirānanda is said to be formed by the first, third, fifth, and sixth [syllables].
Śākuna by name arises from the fifth, sixth, second, and third.
Vighna is formed by the first, fourth, fifth, and sixth; Vighnavardhana is likewise.
They say that [a yoga] with the second, fourth, fifth, and sixth [houses] from the ascendant causes mercilessness and brings about unhappiness;
with the third, fourth, fifth, and sixth [houses], it destroys enemies;
and with the sixth, fifth, fourth, and third [houses], it destroys one's faction and causes the loss of sons.
With six, five, two, three, and four [syllables], there are the *sutaghna* and *sutasūdana* [houses].
Where six, five, two, three, and four [syllables] begin, that is the *vairipūraṇa*.
Thus, the following houses of the *pakṣaghna* are eighteen in sequence.
In houses with three wings (triśāla), there are four types beginning with the first; the *mūṣā* type is on the exterior and not in the interior.
In the second [type] among those beginning with the *vinā*, there is the *pañcabhadra* triśāla.
Having set aside the sequence from the exterior, the rule for the triśāla has been declared.

Thus, these varieties of the four types beginning with Hiraṇyanābha and Adiniketana have been taught in their entirety as seventy-two, each arranged with eighteen subdivisions. Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Seventy-Two Triśāla Plans," in the *Vāstuśāstra* known by the alternative name *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*, composed by the Great King of Kings, the illustrious Bhojadeva.
Now begins the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Two-Hall Houses.
There are fifty-two types of two-hall houses, both auspicious and inauspicious;
we shall now describe their characteristics in due order. (1)
Siddhārtha, Yamasūrya, the one called Daṇḍa, the one named Vāta,
Cullī, and Kāca— these are indeed the six principal types of Dviśālā (two-winged) houses,
which are divided into many varieties through the application of minor expansions.

By means of the sequence of piercing the crucible, and by the sequence of differentiation and non-differentiation; likewise, through the concealment of the instruments, via the pathways of the *vīthī* and *kālinda*;
by the arrangement of the frontal neck and so forth, and by the reversal of the *dvaiśālya* and other measures.
We shall describe these in brief according to their occurrence,
by way of their execution and their failure to be executed, and by name;
[we shall describe] both the inauspicious and the auspicious according to their meter, their qualities, and their form.
For the benefit of kings, as well as for those of the various castes and those bearing religious marks,
a house in which there are two halls— one for an elephant and one for a buffalo—
should be known as "Siddhārtha"; it brings about the attainment of wealth.
A *mahiṣī* and a *gavī* together produce the *yamasūryaka* configuration, which brings death;
a *chagalī* and a *gavī* in the *śālā* house form the *daṇḍa*, which causes fear of punishment;
and a *kareṇu* joined with a *chagalī* forms the *vāta*, which causes agitation.
A hearth made with a buffalo and a goat causes distress and is a thief of wealth.
A window made with a female elephant and a cow destroys friendship and affection.
One should not construct a single-arched or archless window in houses with two halls.
By the transposition of the *kāca* and *cullī* meters, as well as by all three [types of] *sarva*,
the first four [meters] are divided into eleven varieties each according to the application of the *laghu-prastāra* method;
thus, the temples (mandiras) are designated by name in eleven ways each.
The other two are each divided into four types, with two varieties of placement for each.
Due to the various distinctions among these crucibles (mūṣā), they serve as the causes for external and internal extraction.
Of these, the first is Vasudhara, and after that is Siddhārthaka.
Kalyāṇaka, Śāśvata, Śiva, Kāmaprada, Strīda, Śānta, Niṣkalaṅka, Dhanādhīśa, Kubera,
and Siddhārtha— these eleven [names] follow in sequence.
Saṃhāra, Yamasūrya, Kāla, Vaivasvata, Yama, Karāla,
Vikarāla, Kabandha, Mṛtaka, Śava,
and likewise Mahiṣa— these are the manifestations of Yamasūrya’s abode. ||15-16||
Pracaṇḍa, Caṇḍa, Daṇḍa, Uddaṇḍa, Kāṇḍakoṭara,
Vigraha, Nigraha, Dhūmra, Nirdhūma, and Dantidāruṇa—
these eleven are the divisions of Daṇḍa, which bestow the fear of punishment.
Marut, pavana, vāta, anila, and prabhañjana;
ghanāri, ambuda-vidhvaṃsin, pralaya, kalaha, kali, and kalicullī—these are the varieties of wind that cause agitation. ||18-19||
Disease, the hearth-fire, ashes, the fourfold division of the hearth,
the deception of glass, glass itself, the destroyer of the family, and the adversary—
these fifty-two varieties of the *dviśālā* (two-hall) house have been proclaimed.
Now we shall describe their individual characteristics separately.
When the first and second channels flow through the two nostrils while bestowing wealth,
that house is called "Vasudhārā" (Stream of Wealth), and it brings about the fulfillment of all purposes.

Where the first and third [lines] flow toward the Siddhārthaka, that indeed is free from all calamities; it brings about success and fulfills desired aims. Flowing toward the Mūṣa in the second and third [lines], it brings about auspiciousness and prosperity.
The supreme, eternal, and auspicious house is one that carries [the seed-syllables] from the first to the fourth;
it bestows happiness through the second and fourth when they carry [the syllables], and it becomes a granter of desires and a fulfiller of every thought through the third and fourth. ||24-25||
With the first three [mantras] beginning with the first, it bestows women upon the Lord;
with the first, second, and fourth, it is peaceful and bestows peace;
with the first, third, and fourth, it is stainless and brings about prosperity.
With the second, third, and fourth [lines], one [obtains] Dhaneśa, the increaser of wealth;
with the first four lines respectively, one obtains Kubera, the maker of the increase of riches.
Regarding the various divisions of Yama and Sūrya, we shall now describe their marks and results.
The first and second tubes together indicate destruction and the ruin of one's master;
the first and third indicate a house that brings death, known as the "Sun of Yama.
Carrying the second and third tubes indicates Time (Kāla) and the destruction of women.
The first *turya* [of the *vaivasvata*] brings disease;
the second *turya* leads to the abode of Yama, where the master beholds Yama;
the third and fourth [combined] bring about the terrible destruction of the master’s life. (30–31)
With the first three [syllables], there is the destruction of one's master, characterized by deformity;
with the first, second, and fourth, there is a headless trunk (kabandha) that destroys the master;
with the first, third, and fourth, there is a killer of the master, which is the abode of death.
The syllable *śaba* with the second, third, and fourth vowels brings death to the master.
They know the buffalo [mantra] consisting of the first four vowels to be a killer of the master.
Among the divisions of the staff-mantras (*daṇḍabheda*), *pracaṇḍa* is formed with the first vowel and the second.
One should first understand the house [of the Moon]: it brings fear of the king to the master.
From the first and third [houses] being fierce (caṇḍa), there is fear of severe punishment (caṇḍadaṇḍa).
From the second and third being a staff (daṇḍa), there is terrible royal punishment.
The *uddaṇḍa* [mudrā], formed by the second and fourth fingers, causes fear of punishment for the master.
The *kāṇḍa* [mudrā], formed by the second and fourth fingers, causes division like a reed. The *koṭara* [mudrā], formed by the third and fourth fingers, brings about conflict with the master.
One who employs the first, second, and third [lines] brings about war through killing and imprisonment;
one who employs the first, second, and fourth [lines] brings about subjugation accompanied by conflict;
and one who employs the first, third, and fourth [lines] brings about smoke-colored [misfortune] that steals all wealth.
With the second, third, and fourth [lines], it is smokeless and causes the destruction of wealth.
With each of the first four [lines], it is as fierce as an elephant and takes away one's fortune.
With the first two lines, it is like a furnace within houses during the various types of winds.
There, for those who dwell [in that house], there will always be strife known as "Marut";
the wind [wind-planet] characterized by the third and subsequent [houses] causes agitation.
That which is called "Vāta" [wind-planet], [characterized] by the second and third [houses], always causes torment.
From the first and fourth [syllables], there arises wind characterized by distress, displacement, and activity;
from the second and fourth, there is *prabhañjana* (the shatterer), which causes grief and torment;
and from the third and fourth, there is *ghanāri* (the enemy of clouds), which causes agitation.

By the first [line] together with the second and third, there is disease and the destruction of one's purpose. By the first, second, and fourth, there is ruin that causes mental anguish. By the first, second, and fourth, there is a quarrel that brings about strife.
With the second, third, and fourth [lines], Kali causes torment;
with the first four lines, it is the "Kali-hearth" (kalicullī), which steals wealth.
With the first and second lines, it is the "disease-hearth" (rogacullī), which brings grief among the various types of hearths.

If the second and third [syllables] are [short], the hearth (cullī) causes the destruction of wealth; if the third and fourth are [short], the dwelling is named Vasughna-Anala. If the first and fourth are [short], it is always called Bhasman, which destroys the master's wealth.
If the fire flows through the eastern side of the crucibles while the crucibles themselves face north,
there will always be a deception known as *chala*, which causes humiliation among one's circle of kinsmen.
Then, the house named Kāñca brings joy to virtuous people;
however, if the flow occurs through the two southern channels, it will be a "Kula-ha" [house] that causes the destruction of three lineages.
If the flow occurs through the western side of the northern and southern channels, [the same result follows].
The house named Virodha causes opposition with everyone in the world.
Thus, fifty-two types of Dviśālā houses have been described in brief.
These have been illustrated according to the different types of underground channels (mūṣā) and the resulting differences in their effects.
"Thus, the houses with two wings have now been correctly described; hereafter, the single-winged houses are set forth.

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Two-Winged Houses," in the *Vāstuśāstra* composed by the Great King of Kings, the illustrious Bhojadeva, also known as the *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*.
Now begins the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Characteristics, Results, and so forth, of Single-Winged Houses."
Now we shall describe the characteristics of single-hall houses, both those that are auspicious and those that are censurable, in due order and according to the rules. First,
one should duly arrange the four heavy syllables (gurus) at the beginning.
From these very [elements] arise the sixteen varieties of houses (veśman).
One should place a light (laghu) below a heavy (guru), with the preceding [element] as above;
thereafter, one should fill it with heavies until all [positions] are light.
The wise man should provide verandas (alindas) on all small spaces;
he should arrange these starting from the front of the house with a counter-clockwise rotation (savyāvarta).
Due to the various combinations of these verandas, there are distinct types of houses.
From this point forward, the names and their respective qualities and defects will be described in sequence:
Dhruva, Dhanya, Jaya, Nanda, Khara, Kānta, Manorama, Sumukha, Durmukha, Krūra, Supakṣa, Dhanada, and Kṣaya. (5–6)
In the Ākranda, Vipula, Vijaya, and Uttama-mūla constellations, one attains victory;
in Dhruva, there is constant success; in Dhanya, there shall be the arrival of grain;
in Jaya, one conquers enemies; and in Nanda, all prosperities abound.
Indeed, she brings a house free from harshness and deceit, and she obtains beauty and prosperity.
Longevity, health, sovereignty, as well as the abundance of wealth—
these are proclaimed as the delights of the mind for the master of the house.
In Sumukha, there is honor and sovereignty; in Durmukha, there is constant strife.
In Krūra, there is fear of cruel diseases; in Supakṣa, it brings about the increase of one's lineage.
In Dhanada, a man obtains gold, jewels, and cattle.
It brings about destruction, total ruin, lamentation for the home, and the death of kinsmen.
(11) If, however, O fortunate lady, a second *mukhālinda* is employed, there will be health, great renown, victory, and all forms of prosperity. (12)
That house, possessing a beautiful name here, brings good fortune to its master;
it is well-joined with a second [entrance] called Nanda by means of a side-porch (mukhālinda).
Known as Śrīdhara, prosperity shall eternally dwell within it.
If a second *alinda* (veranda) is also placed at the mouth of the beloved [house],
that excellent mansion becomes joyful for its master and brings him prosperity,
provided that another *alinda* is set upon the face of the *sumukha* (the first veranda). ||14-15||
If that house is increasing in size and increases the fortune of its owner,
yet is cruel and joined with a second entrance or porch,
one should know it to be formidable; the master of such a house perishes.
Furthermore, if joined with a second *alinda* on the side of the giver of wealth (*dhanada*), that house would have a beautiful center (*sunābha*); in such a case, one obtains cattle and sons.
If another *alinda* is constructed in front of the *ākranda* [hall], [the same result follows]. ||17-18||

The wise declare that house to be censured as being known by the name "Crow" (dhvāṅkṣa) if the construction of a second porch is at the front of the Vijaya [entrance]. However, if that occurs, the house is renowned as "Prosperous" (samṛddha) and belongs to those of meritorious deeds.
Having understood the division of the halls for these sixteen previously mentioned houses beginning with Dhruva, one should arrange six wooden beams (ṣaḍdāru) across them;
furthermore, there shall be sixteen other variations, along with their names in successive order.
Sundara, Varada, Bhadra, Pramoda, Vimukha, Śiva,
Sarvalābha, Viśāla, Vilakṣa, Aśubha, Dhvaja,
Uddyota, Bhīṣaṇa, Śūnya, Ajita, and Kulanandana.
One should determine the virtues and defects of these houses by their names,
since these names have been declared according to their true meaning without prolixity. From these very names, sixteen other types of houses may also be derived.
For the sake of the six wooden beams required for the construction of the hall,
he [sought] a swan that was well-marked, gentle, victorious, auspicious,
and supreme; beautiful, well-provided, secure, bringing security, virtuous, and a bull among men.
Ucchanna, Vyayamāna, Ānanda, and Sunanda are thus proclaimed.
One should examine their merits and defects according to their literal meanings;
furthermore, one should install the six wooden beams (ṣaḍdāru) situated transversely within the hall.
Setting aside the piercing of their vital points,
we shall briefly describe, in due order and by their actual names, these sixteen other varieties of these very dwellings.
The adorned, the ornament, the lover, the full, the sky;
the meritorious, the well-filled, the jar, the destitute, the empty, the desired; the auspicious, the saluted, the wretched, the powerful, and that which grants all desires. ||29-30||
By means of six wooden back-panels situated within the hall,
sixteen other varieties of houses are also specified:
Prabhava, Bhāvika, Krīḍa, Tilaka, Krīḍana, and Sukha.
Yaśoda, Kumuda, Kāla, Bhāsura, Sarvabhūṣaṇa, Vasudhāra, Dhanahara, Kupita, Vittavṛddhida, and Kulodaya are to be known; their virtues and defects are as previously described. ||32-33||
Regarding the sixteen types of houses described here immediately above,
one should provide each of them with an *alinda* (veranda) on all four sides.
We shall now describe, according to the rules, the various forms that arise from their subdivisions.
Cūḍāmaṇi, Prabhadra, Kṣema, Śekhara, Adbhuta, Vikāśa, Bhūtida, Hṛṣṭa, Virodha, Kālapāśaka,
Nirāmaya, Suśāla, Raudra, Mogha, and Manoratha. ||35-36||
One should identify the dwelling called Subhadra by its designations;
it consists of one hundred and four single-hall houses.
This has been described according to their configurations and names in due order.
The female elephant, the buffalo, the cow, and the goat, respectively;
by doubling each of these, we shall state the names of the houses beginning with "two":
Dvihaṃsaka, Dvicakrāhva, and another, Dvisārasa. ||38-39||
The house of the elephant and so forth is known by the wise as "two-cuckoo" (dvikokila) in sequence;
the first three are for the increase of life-span, cattle, and grain respectively. However, the "two-cuckoo" house would lead to the destruction of these very things.
Thus, single-storey houses have been described according to their various types— such as *alinda*, *ṣaḍdāruka*, *apavaraka*, and *āvaraṇa*—
along with their designations, characteristics, and results, beginning with those named after the faces of elephants.
In this manner, the other types born in pairs [should be understood] by means of their halls (śālās).

Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Characteristics and Results of Single-Hall Structures, and the Characteristics and Results of the Dvihaṃsaka and Others," in the *Vāstuśāstra* known by the alternative name *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*, composed by the Great King of Kings, the illustrious Bhojadeva.
Now begins the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Measurement of Doors, Pedestals, Walls, and so forth."
Attached to the eaves of the houses, with pavilions situated in between,
there should be fifteen threshing floors with spacious courtyards.
[One should worship] Īśvara, Vṛṣabha, Candra, Roga, Pāpa, and Bhayaprada.
One should diligently recognize these houses known as *halaka* by their names: Nandana, Khādaka, Dhvāṅkṣa, Vikṛta, Vilaya, Kṣaya, Yāmya, Viparīta, and Bhadraka. ||2-3||
One should assign the names "one," "two," "three," and "four" respectively to the consonants *ha*, *la*, *ka*, and *na* located in the directions of Agni (SE), Rakṣas (SW), Vāyu (NW), and Īśāna (NE).
By this sequential application, the various meters arise.
Therein, by the first [measure], the house named Īśvara should be built;
it is endowed with all auspicious characteristics and bestows the fruit of all prosperity.
By the second, however, is the Vṛṣabha [house], which increases one's sons and wife.
If the first and second ploughs in the house are endowed with all auspicious marks, they bring prosperity to men; however,
where the northwest plough is located, it brings disease and increases illness.
If there is a plowshare (halaka) in the first or third house,
that is sinful by name and causes all manner of evil;
from the two corners mentioned for the father's diseases, it brings fear, disease, and death.

One should designate the Nandana house in the directions of the fathers (north), diseases (east), and fire (south-east); it is proclaimed to be pleasant, wealth-bestowing, and peaceful. In the northeast, by the fourth [square], is the Khādaka, the devouring house.

When the first hall (śālā) is in the Lāṅgala configuration and the other is in the Īśāna direction, that Vāstu is named Dhvāṅkṣa; it is prescribed for the poor. If the second and fourth halls are in the Lāṅgala configuration, [the result is as follows].
When the first, second, and fourth houses from the Lagna are deformed (vikṛta), inhabited by deformed beings (vikṛtāvāsa), or when there is exile (pravāsa) for the family members,
that house is always subject to dissolution and loss, and it causes the destruction of wealth.

Furthermore, when the plow is in the northwest and again in the northeast, it will always cause destruction; Guha should be present among the plows. If the sheds for Agni, Vāyu, and Maheśāna are located at the plow, [it brings success].

One should never perform [the plowing] in the southern direction, for it brings death to men; likewise, the plow should not be turned back in the north, southwest, northeast, or at the corners of the house,
as such a reversal causes disease and destruction for men.
Wherein four ploughs are situated facing clockwise—what is that site called, O Bhadra, which brings about all prosperity?
[Tell me] the height and width of the doors of houses, as well as the height of their foundations. ||17-18||
The height of the pedestal, the width of the wall,
as well as the wooden framework prescribed for house construction, the arrangement of the single hall, and their respective names— [all these have been explained]. (19)
We shall now explain that, exactly as it is and in proper sequence:
the collection of sixteen, another of twenty, one of twenty-four, and likewise one of twenty-eight. (20–21)
Including the other [group] of thirty-two, these are considered the five classes of leaders.
The width of the wall is prescribed to be one-fourth of the hall.
Regarding the walls in the groups of sixteen and so forth, up to five, the characteristics of the walls have been stated.
Where there may be pain to the vital points (marmas) caused by walls, pillars, beams, and so forth, one should effect a reduction or an increase there, avoiding injury to those vital points;
the wise man should act with this in mind regarding the intended dimensions of the structure. ||23-24||
One should construct a small vestibule (alindaka) for a house situated on inferior ground;
this should be made upon a field that has been leveled and made perfectly square,
with a raised platform (pīṭha) above, half as high as the floor level.
When the pedestal (pīṭha) has been fixed, one should add one finger-breadth for every cubit of the width of the site;
this increase, along with seventy [units], should be joined together.
Thus the heights of the doors are declared for the five aforementioned classes.
The width [of the door] is half its height, diminished by one-eighth;
the width of the fillet (paṭṭa) is desired to be one-quarter of the width of the door.
The thickness above the base of the altar (vedi) is half its width, plus a half.
The wise man should ensure an increasing expansion upward according to the branches. The width and thickness of the altar (vedī) should be made equal to those of the two branches.
At the base of the pillar, its width should be one-fourth of the width of the doorway.
The fillet (paṭṭa) at the top, reduced by one-tenth, is equal in measure to the pillar;
the tip of the fillet is prescribed to be one-third of the height of the pillar's capital. The projection (hīra) at the top should be four times the length of the pillar's capital.
There, one should produce other bands according to the width and thickness;
those learned in the scriptures know that the measurement of the *tantraka* (the central band) should be half the height [of the main structure] and project out by half that height. ||32-33||
One should reduce the materials of this [structure] by one-fourth part of the tip of the cloth (paṭṭakoṭi), according to the division of higher and lower.
That house which faces east has its door joined with the Māhendra [direction].
If there is a female elephant and a house, that dwelling is known as Bhadra. O Bhadra, it brings prosperity to its master and increases his fame and strength;
while living in a house called Bhadra, one's undertakings succeed.
The house facing south has Gṛhakṣata at its door;
its hall is Mahiṣī, and that house is Nandapīṭhaka.
The Nandapīṭha house is remembered as constantly bestowing joy upon men.

Endowed with all the qualities of prosperity and increasing wealth and grain, the house facing the west and having its door named after the flower (Kusuma) is such that the cow-stall is likewise called Gāvī; the wise know this as Saurabha. ||38-39||
For householders dwelling in the Saurabha [quarter], there is perpetual joy;
agriculture and trade become fruitful, and sons remain obedient.
The sacrificial fire-chamber (dhiṣṇya) has its door facing north and is joined with the Bhallāṭa [deity].
The hall shall be goat-shaped, and it is called Puṣkara.
One born in the Puṣkara yoga is virtuous, eternally contented, affectionate toward friends and good people, fortunate, and endowed with many sons and wealth. ||41-42||
One should employ Bhadra, Nandapīṭha, Saurabha, and likewise Puṣkara in the first half of the first group. All the layouts beginning with Sarvabhadrā that have been proclaimed [should be used].
Those five [deities] have arisen from the five celestial palaces (vimānas) in groups of five.
The measurement of the door, the pedestal, the sanctuaries, and the wall has been declared in due order;
likewise, the wooden ornaments and all the characteristics of a dwelling whose structural defects have been completely eliminated.

Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Vāstus Deficient in Doors, Pedestals, Walls, Measurements, and Timber," in the *Vāstuśāstra* composed by the Great King of Kings, the illustrious Bhojadeva, also known as the *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*.
Now begins the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Enumeration of All Houses.
Hereafter, the characteristics of five-hall houses (*pañcaśālā*) are described.
In number, these amount to one thousand and twenty-four,
due to the arrangement of ten types of heavy syllables and their prosodic expansion;
such are the varieties of five-hall houses according to the division of light syllables.
A five-winged house (pañcaśāla) arises from the combination of two or three wings;
alternatively, it may arise from the combination of four wings or one wing.
This type of residence is recommended for members of all four castes.
From the *hiraṇyanābha* and other [colors],
eight types of houses for the castes may be produced here through the combination with *siddhārtha* and others.
Through the combination of *hiraṇyanābha* with *siddhārtha*, a house is formed.
By the wind of this very [deity], the peak of Hemakūṭa becomes golden;
and by the conjunction with Siddhārtha, it brings prosperity to Sukṣetra.
By Yamasūrya, his very abode becomes a great treasure-store.
The fire of the *cullī* (the hearth) is always produced as ignited by the *yama-sūrya* (the twin suns).
Through its conjunction with the *daṇḍa*, it becomes known as *citrabhānu*.
One should always indicate the fault of the *pakṣaghna* (the wing-killer) by means of the *daṇḍa*.
It is said to be free from obstacles only when there is no contact with the wind that strikes the side;
however, the conjunction of a fire-hearth and so forth is not recommended in houses with three wings and the like.
Because they are merely looking at one another, their specific distinctions have not been mentioned here.
In a four-winged (catuḥśāla) residence, there are variations consisting of those joined with one wing [and others]. We shall describe twenty variations for five-winged (pañcaśāla) residences;
when the Ajā wing occurs in the Sarvatobhadra residence, [these arise].
They call that house with five halls "Sudarśana";
by the addition of a female elephant, it is called "Surūpa.
By the addition of a buffalo it is "Sundara," and by the addition of a cow it is "Śobhana."
Through the sequential application of these halls to a growing structure,
there arise the houses known as Sunābha, Suprabha, Yogya, and Vinoda.
In the case of the Nandyāvarta plan as well, they are produced in exactly the same way through the arrangement of the halls.
Sukhada, Nandana, Nanda, Puṇḍarīka, and the Mandira [mandala] belong respectively to Rucaka and those beginning with Aja through their application;
by name, they are Bhadra, Rucira, Rociṣṇu, Praharṣaṇa, and [the last].
By this same method, four types of houses may also be formed in the *svastika* pattern:
Ghoṣa, Sughoṣaṇa, Nandighoṣa, and Śrīpadma.
There are twenty [varieties] starting from the *sarvatobhadra*, according to their structural configurations.
The five-fold (pañcaśālā) types suitable for kings have been described;
together with the eight previously mentioned, there are twenty-eight types of houses.
Now, the sequence of the divisions of the *mūṣā* (architectural layout) for these five-fold houses is being told.
Among them, there is one Vibhadra; those with one Bhadra are said to be ten in number.
Furthermore, they declare that there are forty-five Dvibhadrās.
As for the Tribhadrās, there are two hundred and twenty, plus two sets of ten more [making two hundred and forty].
There are two hundred and fifty-two houses of the *caturbhadra* type;
those of the *pañcabhadra* type are one hundred and ten; those of the *ṣaḍbhadra* type are two hundred and twenty;
and those of the *saptabhadra* type are one hundred and twenty.
There are forty-five houses of the eight-bhadra type;
there should be ten of the nine-bhadra type, as well as one of the ten-bhadra type.
Thus, there would be one thousand and twenty-four [houses].
We have described the construction of houses with five wings according to their various measurements.
Now, we shall state the characteristics and the enumeration of houses with six wings,
as well as the arrangement of houses with one, two, three, and four wings in relation to one another.
Through the combination of two-winged, one-winged, and three-winged [layouts], a six-winged mansion is produced; its variations, however, number sixteen.
Furthermore, through the combination of the *pakṣaghna* and *vātaya* with a single-winged house— ||25-26||
There may be a house named Paṅkajāṅkura, an excellent six-hall structure;
and by joining it with a single-hall building called Hiraṇyanābha or Siddhārtha,
the auspicious Śrīgṛha house is formed.

From the conjunction of the *ekaśāla* with *sukṣetra* and *yamasūrya*, a house named *dhaneśvara* arises for the increase of wealth. From the conjunction of the *daṇḍa*-named *cullyoḥ* and the *ekaśāla* house, [the same occurs]. ||28-29||
The house may possess abundant gold and have a golden luster;
one should understand that there are twelve other types of dwellings according to this same method.
Among these very varieties, there are auspicious ones for all social classes.

From two equal three-winged (triśāla) houses, four six-winged (ṣaṭśāla) houses arise; from the combination of two two-winged (dviśāla) and four four-winged (catuḥśāla) houses, another four [six-winged houses] arise.
When there is a conjunction of houses with four wings according to the Siddhārtha [proportion], [another type is formed]. ||31-32||
Then that house would be a six-winged (ṣaṭśāla) structure, auspicious and bringing joy to the three worlds;
when joined with the Yamasūrya configuration, it is called a collection of delights.
A four-winged (catuḥśāla) house provided with a staff (daṇḍa) shall be known by name as "Giver of Happiness" (sukhada).
And by means of the Vāta [arrangement], the Śrīpada type shall be joined with four halls (catuḥśāla).
There are twenty-four others through different combinations of six halls;
among these, five types of four-halled structures are suitable for kings.
By the combination of two of these, we describe six types of halls:
when the *siddhārtha* and *sarvatobhadra* are joined, there is the *śrīpura* house;
when the *sarvatobhadra* and *yamasūrya* are joined, there is the *śrīvāsa*.
When the Daṇḍa [configuration] is joined with the Sarvatobhadra, it becomes the Śrībhūṣaṇa house. They know that when the Vāta [configuration] is joined with the Sarvatobhadra, it is the Śrībhājana.
When the Siddhārtha is joined with the Vardhamāna, it becomes the Bhūtimaṇḍana.
When the Yama-sūrya is conjoined with that very same [element], it is the vessel of prosperity (bhūti-bhājana);
in the one called Daṇḍa, it is the measure of prosperity (bhūti-māna), and in the one called Vāta, it is the ornament of prosperity (bhūti-bhūṣaṇa).
Through the yoga of Nandyāvarta, there is the tetrad beginning with Siddhārtha.

Śrīmukha, Śrīdhara, Śrīmṛcchīdhara, and [the fourth] are born from the combination of the four [starting with] Siddhārtha and the Rucaka [arrangement]. Likewise, Śriyākāra, Śriyovāsa, Śrīyāna, and Śrīmukha arise from the same. ||40-41||
From the combination of the four beginning with Siddhārtha and the Svastika,
there arise the types known as Dhanapāla, Dhana, Anantadhana, and Dhanaprada. Thus, by means of the royal palace configuration, there are twenty houses.

The twenty-four [types] mentioned previously, plus four, make forty-four; we designate these as the *ekabhadraka* and so forth, according to the process of casting in a crucible (*mūṣā*). By means of various divisions, one [type] is formed by the crucibles, while the *abhadraka* consists of twelve types through a single [division].
By two [methods], sixty-six are indicated; by twenty, two hundred and three;
by four expanded [arrays], there would be five hundred minus five.
There are five hundred and seventy-two five-bhadra [arrays].
The six *bhadra* [type] houses are said to number nine hundred and twenty-four.
One should know that the seven *bhadra* [type] houses are in number like the five *bhadra* [type].
For the eight *bhadra* [type] houses, there are four hundred and ninety-five.
They know there are two hundred palaces with twenty-nine bhadras;
sixty-six with ten bhadras;
likewise, twelve numbered with eleven bhadras; and one known as having twelve bhadras.
Thus, there are four thousand six hundred and ninety-six houses with six wings;
now we shall describe those with seven wings.
A pair of three-winged houses is joined with one single-winged house. ||49-50||
When there are seven halls, then by the number twelve,
the one-hall and two-hall [structures] are joined with the four-hall;
when that occurs, another seven-hall residence is produced.

A house with one wing (saikaśāla) or four wings (catuḥśāla), when joined with the yamasūrya configuration, will then be free of division and shall bestow prosperity. Likewise, it bestows prosperity through the vāta configuration and shall likewise be a bestower of prosperity through the daṇḍa configuration.
In the same manner, Śrīmāla is produced by Siddhārthaka;
there may be four houses of three bays (śāla) suitable for kings from the five [types],
while seven houses of three bays arise from the combination of one-bay and two-bay structures.
The Sarvatobhadra layout is appropriate when the house is for the purpose of attaining success; likewise, a single-winged (ekaśāla) house may arise as Śrīpada or Sarvatobhadra.
Of these, the Sarvatobhadra belongs to the house, while the Yamasūrya and Ekaśāla belong to the individual.
By the application of yoga, a house named Śrīphala brings prosperity;
when it is joined with a single-winged (ekaśāla) structure and two daṇḍas in the Sarvatobhadra configuration,
then that mansion is named Śrīsthala and becomes an abode of fortune.
If two winds meet in a single-winged house, it is called the Sarvatobhadra;
this house is known as Śrītanu, the abode of Lakṣmī.
When a single-winged house is joined with Siddhārtha and Vardhamāna, it is likewise auspicious. ||58-59||
At that time, there shall be an excellent mansion named Śrīparvata;
through the conjunction of Yama and Sūrya, with their single halls increasing,
there shall be a house named Śrīvardhana, which brings about the increase of prosperity.
When there is both a *daṇḍa* and a *vardhamāna*, together with a single hall (*ekaśāla*), then it becomes the excellent residence named Śrīsaṅgama.
When a single hall called *vāta* is joined with a *vardhamāna*, [it is likewise]. ||61-62||
At that time, there shall be a palace worthy of a king named Śrīpraṣaṅga,
provided with a single hall for the accomplishment of goals and adorned with the Nandyāvarta design.
There shall also be a palace named Śrībhāra, frequented by kings.

Through the application of the *nandyāvarta* plan for the *yama*, *sūrya*, and *ekaśāla* types, a palace that brings happiness to kings is known as *śrībhāra*. A palace with one wing (*ekaśāla*) and the *nandyāvarta* and *daṇḍa* plans is called *śrīśaila*.
Through the application of yoga, a king’s excellent seven-hall residence brings about enjoyment;
through the application of a single hall, there may be the Nandyāvarta and Vāta types.
A palace named Śrīkhaṇḍa shall bring prosperity to rulers.

Through the conjunction of Siddhārtha with Ekaśāla and Rucaka, there arises a residence named Śrīṣaṇḍa, which is suitable for kings. Through the conjunction of Rucaka alone with Yama and Sūrya and Ekaśāla, [there arises another]. ||67-68||
Śrīnidhāna and Śrīkuṇḍa are [varieties] of that [type] with one *daṇḍa* and one *śāla*.
That which is joined with *vāta*, one *śāla*, and *rucakas* is called Śrīnābha;
such a mansion for rulers of the earth shall be a bestower of prosperity.

When the *siddhārtha* and *svastika* are joined with the *ekaśāla*, then that house will be dear to Fortune (*śrī*) and constantly beloved by prosperity. When the *svastika* is joined with the *yamasūrya* and the *ekaśāla*... [70-71]
Then, when there is a combination of the Daṇḍa and Svastika [plans] with a single hall (ekaśāla), they call that abode "Śrīkānta," which is beneficial for kings;
by name it is the Śrīmat residence, and it brings about victory.
When the combination of the *vāta* and *svastika* forms enters into a single hall (*ekaśāla*),
they call that the "Śrīpradatta" residence for kings.
Because each of these has two variations, this [category] becomes forty.
Thus, there would be forty-eight varieties here when a three-winged mansion is joined with a four-winged one; even then, it would be seven-winged. In brief, this is fourfold.
If five royal houses meet at one [central] point, then there shall be the *triśāla* (three-winged) house; likewise, the *saptaśāla* (seven-winged) house has twenty varieties.
By means of the *hiraṇyanābha* (golden-navel) arrangement, the *sarvatobhadra* (auspicious on all sides) mansion is formed.
The Śrīvatsa mark produces a home that brings benefit to kings;
the Śrīvṛkṣa mark occurs when an auspicious field is joined with the Sarvatobhadra.
Furthermore, when that same [field] is joined with the Cullī, the one named Śrīpāla arises.
When the *pakṣaghna* is joined with the *sarvatobhadra*, it is called *śrīkaṇṭha*.
When the *hiraṇyanābha* is joined with the *vardhamāna*, it becomes *śrīvāsa*.
However, when the *sukṣetra* is mixed with the *vardhamāna*, it is *śrīnivāsa*.
They know that a house adorned with prosperity is one where a *vardhamāna* [arch] and a *cullyā* [chimney] are present;
when a *pakṣaghna* [gable] comes into conjunction with a *vardhamāna*,
then that best of dwellings is born as the one named *śrīmaṇḍana*.
When there is a conjunction with the Nandyāvarta at the birth [of the asterism] of Hiraṇyanābha,
there shall be a house named Śrīkula, the family abode of Śrī.
When it is joined with the Nandyāvarta in a favorable field (sukṣetra), there shall be Śrīgokula.
When the *nandyāvarta* and the hearth (*cullyā*) are joined, there arises the auspicious *sthāvara* house;
when the *nandyāvarta* and the *pakṣaghna* are joined, the *kumbha* is produced.
When the *hiraṇyanābha* and the *rucaka* are joined, there is the auspicious *samudgaka*.
In a good field (sukṣetra) joined with the one called Rucaka, there arises the name Śrīnanda;
in a hearth (cullī) joined with Rucaka, the name Śrīhrada is produced;
and in a Pakṣaghna joined with Rucaka, the name Śrīdhara occurs. ||85-86||
In a Svastika [layout] joined with Hiraṇyanābha, it is called Śrīkaraṇḍaka;
in that same [layout] joined with Sukṣetra, it is known as Śrībhāṇḍāgāra. When joined with Cullī, it becomes Śrīnilaya, which is dear to kings.

When the Svastika is joined with the Pakṣaghna, it is then known as Śrīniketana, the palace of a king. Thus have been described the seven types of halls (saptaśālā) according to their names, characteristics, and combinations. ||88-89||
All these [auspicious signs] belong to universal monarchs (sārvabhauma), kings, and even ministers;
they serve to increase the wealth, fame, and victory of the virtuous.
Furthermore, there are various types of houses distinguished by the carrying of one or more jars [of water].
We shall now state the enumeration of these seven types of halls (saptashala) in their proper order.
That house where even a single mouse does not run about should be known as the *vibhadra*, and there are fourteen such *ekabhadra* houses. 91–92.
Ninety-one *dvibhadra* houses are proclaimed;
three hundred and sixty-four *tribhadra* mansions;
and one thousand and one *caturbhadra* dwellings.
Of your Pañcabhadras there are two thousand two hundred;
of the Ṣaḍbhadras, three thousand, and three houses;
and thirty-two hundred of the Catustriṃśadbhadras and seven hundred of the Saptabhadras. ||94-95||
For houses with eight auspicious features (aṣṭabhadra), there are as many varieties as the number six; for those with nine auspicious features (navabhadra), there are two thousand and two;
and for those with ten auspicious features (daśabhadra), one thousand and one is declared.
Likewise, for those with eleven auspicious features (ekādaśabhadra), there are three hundred and sixty-four;
for twelve auspicious features (dvādaśabhadra), there would be ninety-one houses;
and here, houses with thirteen auspicious features (trayodaśabhadra) shall be fourteen. ||97-98||
Indeed, that which consists of fourteen auspicious [rooms] is but a single dwelling;
thus, among these seven-hall houses, there are sixteen thousand,
twenty-nine hundred, and eighty-four [thousand].
Now we shall describe buildings with eight halls (aṣṭaśālā).
Briefly stated, one [type] consists of two sets of four-hall units (catuḥśālā) joined together;
the others, such as the Sarvabhadra and so forth, consist of ten types formed by the combination of two [sets]. 100–101.
One should divide the square field into twenty-nine parts;
with two parts there shall be the *mūṣā*, and with four parts the hall (*śālā*).
One should construct a courtyard and a pond in its center using five parts.
And there, on that site, there should be four mounds (mūṣās) facing each direction.
Among them, the seven-hall (saptaśāla) temple has rice-grains (śālayaḥ); the six-hall (ṣaṭśāla) is devoid of two;
the five-hall (pañcaśāla) is devoid of three; and this eight-hall (aṣṭaśāla) exists in some places.
When two equal triple-winged structures (triśāla) are joined with a double-winged structure (dviśāla),
then eight types of eight-winged houses (aṣṭaśālā) are described; now,
the arrangement of these eight-winged houses according to the method of casting in a mold (mūṣāvyūḍhi) is being told.

In that regard, the number [of types] distinguished by their excellence (bhadra) is as follows: those designated as "carrying the mouse" (avahanmūṣa) consist of sixteen single-excellence (ekabhadrā) types; they know there to be one hundred double-excellence (dvibhadrā) types;
and twenty-six times five hundred—that is, one thousand three hundred—should be understood as the triple-excellence (tribhadrā) types. 106–107.

One should correctly understand that there are eighteen hundred and twenty-four "four-fold auspicious" (caturbhadra) houses, five thousand four hundred and sixty-eight "five-fold auspicious" (pañcabhadra) houses. 108. One should properly contemplate those dwellings.
They declare that there are eight thousand and eight [houses] known as Ṣaḍbhadra;
one should know that there are eleven thousand, four hundred,
and forty-four houses known as Saptabhadra.
Those expert in the science of architecture (vāstuvidyā) state that there are exactly twelve thousand eight hundred and seventy [types] of the eight auspicious (aṣṭabhadra) [buildings].
Likewise, there are eleven thousand four hundred [others].
The number of houses with nine auspicious features (navabhadrāṇi) is forty-one;
those with ten auspicious features (daśabhadrāṇi) are eight thousand plus eight;
and the count for those with eleven auspicious features (ekādaśabhadrāṇi) is the same as that for the five-auspicious ones.
There would be one thousand eight hundred and twenty mansions;
such is the number of dwellings for those with twelve auspicious features (dvādaśabhadrāḥ).
For those with thirteen auspicious features (trayodaśabhadrāḥ), there would be five hundred and sixty.
There may be one hundred and twenty mansions with fourteen auspicious features (bhadrās), and likewise sixteen with fifteen auspicious features; indeed,
only one type of house is to be known as having sixteen auspicious features.
Sixty-five thousand, five hundred and thirty-six,
is the total number of eight-hall houses when calculated together;
this results from the combination of two identical four-hall types in brief.
From the combination of each of the nine *śāla* types with four others,
and from the mutual union of pairs among the principal ones such as the *Sarvatobhadra*,
there are forty other [varieties] arising from the addition of one *śāla* at a time. (118–119)
By means of three equal triple-unions, another fourfold arrangement of houses with nine halls has been described by the ancients.
This configuration of houses consisting of nine halls has thus been explained.

Now, the number of those [houses] is stated according to the distinction between the carrying and non-carrying crucibles (mūṣā): there would be one house with a non-carrying crucible; with one carrying crucible, eighteen;
and with two, there would be one hundred and fifty-three houses. ||121-122||
With three [units], there would be eight hundred and sixteen houses;
with four of those, it would be three thousand and sixty;
and with five, it would be eight hundred and eighty-five.
By means of the flowing [channels], the houses here are produced from the crucibles;
one should designate eighteen thousand, five hundred, and sixty-four houses by means of the six crucibles. 124–125.
They know there to be thirty-one thousand houses, together with eight hundred and twenty-four, along with seven crucibles. There are forty-three thousand dwellings.
They know that with eight crucibles there are seven hundred and fifty-eight [units],
and with nine crucibles there are forty-eight thousand, six hundred and twenty [units]. ||127-128||
Forty-three thousand, one hundred fifty-eight [atoms] from ten crucibles;
thirty-one thousand, eight hundred twenty-four [atoms]. 129.
The sages have declared that there are eleven types of crucibles (mūṣā) for houses; thus,
for twelve crucibles, eighteen thousand five hundred and sixty-four temples are produced.
There are eight thousand and five hundred [houses];
there would be thirteen *mūṣās* and sixty-eight dwellings. There would be fourteen *mūṣās* and three thousand sixty-three.
With fifteen crucibles (mūṣās), there are likewise one hundred and sixty-eight [units] of *dhāman*;
with sixteen crucibles, there would be one hundred and fifty-three;
and with seventeen crucibles, there are clearly eighteen houses (*veśma*). ||133-134||
Those who know the science understand that one house consists of eighteen *mūṣās*.
There are two hundred and sixty-two thousand nine hundred and forty houses with nine halls (*navaśālā*). (135)
Briefly stated, by the combination of two identical four-winged [houses], there is one;
and by the combination of one two-winged house with four ten-winged houses, there is another, arising from the mutual union of the primary types such as the Sarvatobhadra. ||136-137||
And from the combination of one or two broad [bays], there are likewise another forty;
when there are three equal triple-bays joined with a single bay,
that is then another common type consisting of four ten-bays.
When [the temples] are equal and joined with the Sarvabhadra and other types,
then another twenty-fold arrangement of ten-hall temples arises;
among those, one carries a single *mūṣa* (projection), and by means of that one *mūṣa*, there are twenty.
By two [verses] flowing together, there would be one hundred and ninety;
by three, certainly eleven hundred and forty;
and by four, there would be eight hundred and four thousand.
Forty houses arise along with five;
likewise, fifteen thousand and five hundred, together with four, arise from the crucibles. ||142-143||
Thirty-eight thousand,
seven hundred and sixty houses are produced by this calculation;
there would be seven thousand and seventy-seven houses.
There would be another five hundred and twenty;
one hundred and twenty-five thousand, nine hundred and seventy more are produced. (145–146)
One hundred and sixty-seven thousand nine hundred and sixty [coins] result from the circulation of nine crucibles.
One hundred and eighty-four thousand [coins] and [the remaining] hundreds... [147]
Likewise, there would be seven [hundred] increased by ten, and fifty-six;
one hundred thousand, sixty-seven thousand, and nine hundred increased by eleven—thus one should specify the number of dwellings. (148–149)
One hundred thousand, twenty-five thousand, twelve hundred, nine hundred, and seventy;
by this count, there are seventy-seven thousand dwellings. (150)
With thirteen [units], it is said to be five hundred and twenty;
with fourteen, there would be thirty-eight thousand seven hundred and sixty dwellings. ||151-152||
It may be fifteen thousand and five hundred [yojanas] in extent;
there are fifteen crucibles (mūṣās) and four palaces.
There are likewise four thousand and eight hundred [yojanas].
Likewise, there are sixteen *mūṣās*, forty-five thousand,
seventeen hundred, and forty houses in total by calculation. (154–155)
One hundred increased by ninety is said to be one hundred and eighty;
with nineteen [additional], there are twenty houses of the mice.
By carrying even a single house, it becomes the support for twenty mice.

The total number of ten-hall (daśaśālā) units, calculated according to the distribution of the different types of crucibles, is one prayuta, four ayutas, eight thousand, five hundred, and sixty-seven houses;
this is the single count for the ten-hall units. ||157-158||
One should describe houses beginning with the four-winged type up to those with ten wings as being quadrupled in each direction by means of an *alinda* (veranda).
From the mutual conjunction of houses having one, two, three, or four wings, [other types arise].
Thus have houses ending with ten halls been described in detail. Now,
beginning from the four-hall house up to the ten-hall house,
we shall state the total number of all these types combined.
By way of the different types of crucibles (mūṣā), there would be thirteen hundred thousand houses,
as well as ninety-eight thousand and sixteen houses; furthermore,
these are distinguished by the various shapes of the crucibles.
Since millions of variations arise [from these], they have not been stated here.
Thus, the houses with four halls (catuḥśāla) and so forth, up to those with ten halls (daśaśāla), have been described;
and their total number, resulting from the mutual combinations of the various types of halls, has been correctly declared.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Enumeration of All Houses," in the *Vāstuśāstra* composed by the Great Emperor Śrī Bhojadeva, also known as the *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*.
Now begins the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Āya and Other [Factors].
We shall now describe the sequence for the procedure of laying the foundation lines (*sūtrapāta*).
One should perform that [rite] on an auspicious day during a favorable month and the bright fortnight.
In Caitra, the husband becomes overwhelmed by grief; in Vaiśākha, he is endowed with wealth;
in Jyeṣṭha, the householder perishes; and in Śuci (Āṣāḍha), his livestock perish.
In Śrāvaṇa there shall be an increase of wealth; in Nabhasya one should not dwell at home;
in the month of Āśvina there will be quarrels, and in Kārttika servants perish.
In Mārgaśīrṣa there is the acquisition of wealth, and in Sahasya there is the fulfillment of desires.
In the month of Māgha there is indeed danger from fire, while in Phālguna there is unsurpassed prosperity.
The second, fifth, seventh, ninth, eleventh, and thirteenth lunar days are the principal ones; these dates bring about auspiciousness.
The strength of the moon and stars, as well as the favorability of the lord [of the day], is praised;
for this rite known as the "laying of the thread" is to be performed in the construction of a palace,
in the settlement of a city, and at the commencement of a house.
In the laying of a foundation, and in the raising of doorposts and pillars, one should indeed take heed during the bright fortnight and at an auspicious *lagna*. When the Sun is situated in Virgo,
Libra, or Scorpio, the house should face the direction of Varuṇa (the west).
One should not perform it, for it would be void and there would be no prosperity for the lord;
nor should one do so when the sun is situated in the sign of Sagittarius (Mṛga) with its face turned southward,
for that would be fruitless and cause the king's punishment, death, and other such evils.
One should not perform [the rite] facing east when the sun is situated in Pisces, Taurus, or Aries,
for that destroys wealth and causes strife, meanness, and affliction from kings and thieves. Nor should one face north when the sun is in Gemini or Leo, nor even when it is in Cancer.
For that indeed brings poverty; one should instead grant the status of a foot-servant.
Now we shall declare the income, expenditure, and the portions of the lunar mansions (nakṣatras) for houses.
According to the measurement of the house, one should properly determine the strength and weakness of the positions for the builder.
In a city or a town and so forth, measurement is prescribed by means of rods;
in the absence of those, it should be done by cubits for the sake of correctly purifying the income.
Where the measurement of a field is in *hasta*s, there the income is dependent on the *hasta*.

If a field cannot be obtained, it should be taken right there; in this case, it should be measured by finger-breadths (aṅgula). If a field measured by finger-breadths is unavailable, it should be taken according to the size of the field, using either quarters (pāda) or barley-corns (yava). 15.
In houses, the measurement may be made either by the hand of the craftsman or by the hand of the owner;
however, in the sanctuaries of the deities, it must be measured solely by the hand of the craftsman.
One should multiply the length by the width and then divide the product by eight.
Whatever remains of that [calculation], one should know it as the "flag" (dhvaja) and so forth, as seen in the scriptures:
the flag, smoke, lion, dog, bull, donkey, elephant, and crow—these are designated in the directions starting from the east, proceeding clockwise. (18)
Facing one another and moving at their own will as they please, these are declared by the ancient teachers to be the bringers of increase in prosperity;
bulls, lions, and elephants are recommended for palaces, cities, and dwellings. ||19-20||
With the banner (dhvaja), there is gain of wealth; with smoke (dhūma), distress; with the lord of beasts (mṛgādhipa), enjoyment;
with the dog (śvan), strife; with the bull (vṛṣa), wealth and grain; with the donkey (khara), the blemish of a wife;
with the elephant (gaja), auspicious things are seen; but with the crow (dhvāṅkṣa), death is certain.

One should place an elephant in the position of the bull, and a lion in the positions of both the bull and the elephant. One should not place a bull elsewhere; however, the banner (dhvaja) is praised in all positions.
A lion brings auspiciousness, especially for a Brāhmaṇa.
An elephant is prescribed for a Kṣatriya, a bull is recommended for a Vaiśya,
and for a Śūdra, only a banner is always recommended as a provider of wealth.
Thus, all these sources of income for householders and others have been proclaimed.
One should place a lion on the seat, and a banner upon the sunshades;
likewise, among all the insignia such as chowries, fans, and the like, one should depict either a lion or an elephant on the weapons, the chariots, and the armor. (25–26)
A wise man should employ an elephant for the saddles of noble horses and men, as well as for bulls; he should employ an elephant for vessels used for holding wealth and for beds;
and indeed, he should employ an elephant for carriages and for riding mounts.

One should offer the banner upon palaces, images, liṅgas, pedestals, pavilions, and altars; also in sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) and upon the implements of the deity. The rite for the pavilion of the marriage altar should be performed as for a house.
One should give a bull at the kitchen, at a water-cistern or reservoir,
at the cooking pot and the eating vessel, and at the granary where food is stored;
likewise, one should give it in the house and among the household utensils.
One should place a bull in an elephant stable, or indeed an elephant itself;
a bull in horse stables, and in cow stables and herds.
One should carefully avoid placing a lion in stables for elephants, horses, or bulls.
For those of low status, the donkey, the crow, the smoke, and the dog bring auspiciousness.
Smoke is praised for those who live by fire, and the crow is beneficial for renunciants (saṃnyāsins).
For one's own group, for outcastes (śvapākas), and for one's own household, the donkey is auspicious.
In the houses of actors, dancers, and courtesans, a donkey is auspicious.
(34) Likewise, for potters, washermen, and others who live by means of donkeys, one should calculate the result for the site of their houses and so forth by dividing it by eight. (35)
One should divide the remainder by three; when the asterism is divided by eight, it is the expenditure (vyaya).
Expenditure is considered to be of three kinds: Piśāca, Rākṣasa, and Yakṣa.
It becomes long [in duration] according to the sequence of its being equal, greater, or less.
Having added the expenditure to the area of the field and the letters of the house-name, one should divide that by three; whatever remains there shall be the *navāṃśaka*.
Just as a mantra consisting of four parts is principal, so too is the *navāṃśaka* principal in the ascendant. ||37-38||
Likewise, regarding houses and so forth, three divisions (aṃśakas) are declared to be primary:
Indra, Yama, and Rāja;
these three divisions are to be understood as yielding fruits corresponding to their own names. (39)
One should count from the natal asterism (nakṣatra) of the master until the asterism of the house;
when that total is divided by nine, the remainder is proclaimed as the lunar mansion (tārā).
These are: birth (janma), prosperity (sampat), adversity (vipat), security (kṣema), sin (pāpa), accomplishment (sādhaka), and destruction (naidhanī).
They say that *maitrī* and *paramamaitrī* are equal in their results;
one should avoid the third, seventh, and fifth lunar mansions from the natal asterism of the master.
Furthermore, the first, second, and eighth lunar mansions are considered mediocre in this context.

Likewise, even when the asterism is unfavorable and the moon has entered the eighth house, the Tārā of sixty-four removes the sins of men. There are three groups of asterisms known as those of the gods, the Rākṣasas, and mortals. ||43-44||
The house belonging to the same group as the husband’s nakṣatra is auspicious.
Mṛga, Aśvinī, Revatī, Svātī, Anurādhā, Puṣya,
Punarvasu, Hasta, and Śravaṇa— this is the ninefold group known as divine (deva).
Viśākhā, Kṛttikā, Āśleṣā, Nairṛta (Mūla), Vāruṇa (Śatabhiṣaj), Maghā, Citrā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Dhaniṣṭhā constitute the ninefold Rākṣasa group.
Ārdrā, Bharaṇī, Rohiṇī, the three Pūrvas, and likewise the three Uttarās [constitute the other groups]. ||46-47||

Thus, this group of nine constellations is to be known among the human class. That house which possesses equality of planetary strength, auspicious stars, small income and expenditure, and favorable divisions (aṃśaka) bestows auspicious results upon its master.

Income and expenditure, the source [of the house], the stars, the divisions of the houses, and the name of the house—these six are the factors (karaṇas) to be considered for a house. A house is auspicious with three auspicious factors, and inauspicious with two or one. ||49-50||
With the first four Karaṇas being auspicious, the house becomes exceedingly auspicious;

it should not have equal income and expenditure, nor no expenditure at all, nor excessive expenditure. One should not construct a house with a second portion that has an incompatible birth-sign (yoni).
One should abandon from afar a house whose name is identical to that of one's husband. Furthermore,
the seventh and first, the third and eleventh,
as well as the fourth and tenth houses should always be made into one's own residence.
The six-square, the triangle, and likewise the double-twelve (the twenty-fourth) should be avoided.
In the six-square, death, wretchedness, and separation shall occur in the house.
For those dwelling in the triangle, suffering and widowhood are produced.

Twice twelve (twenty-four) [signifies] the loss of sons, grandsons, teachers, kinsmen, and wealth. When the area of the field is divided by eight and the remainder is divided by twenty-three, that remainder is the lifespan; when this is divided by five, death occurs. ||55-56||
Having measured the dimensions in length and breadth— including the arms, the six wooden supports, and the assembly hall at the front—
one should divide it; thus the site (vāstu), being perfectly measured, is purified on all sides.
That shall be auspicious for the master and bring glory to the architect.
When the site is thus honored, it flourishes with women, cattle, and men;
it increases in fame, longevity, wealth, grain, and with great festivals of joy.
Meru, Khaṇḍameru, Patākā, Sūcikā,
Uddiṣṭa, and Naṣṭa— these six meters are proclaimed here.
One should arrange squares increasing by one, beginning from one, according to one's own desire.
Starting from the first [cell], its increase should be equal on both sides;
the number [of cells] exceeds that of Meru by one, and its shape is like that of a shallow bowl (śarāva).
In the first cell there is the number one, and this continues until the end on both sides.
One should place the sum separately in the middle of the two rows situated above;
in that [middle cell], the number of desired permutations will be found in the final row.
One should likewise place the Khaṇḍameru on one side.
There too, with the compartments increased, the figures are as before and the result is likewise.
Now, another Khaṇḍameru is formed by making the compartments there in the desired number,
decreasing them by one in the left-hand division and decreasing them downward.
One should place the numbers beginning with one and increasing by one in the first row;
in the other rows, one should arrange zeros up to the end, and in the first cells of those [other rows],
one should place each of those [numbers] one by one.
In the second [row], one should arrange in the third and subsequent cells, in due order,
the other results arising from diagonal combinations and those produced by vertical and horizontal conjunctions;
one should calculate the result arising from a diagonal combination for each single cell.
One should draw squares horizontally according to a desired number increased by one;
within them, one should place the numbers starting from one, each increasing twofold,
with one less than that on the back and one doubled at the front.

One should not exceed the highest number; this is called the *patākā* (banner) method of calculation. The number of the *vinesṭa* (vineṣṭa) and so forth is the count; then, by means of those [numbers] starting from one, the numbers are placed in the houses (*gṛha*).
The numbers established by the *alinda* (verandas) and so forth shall be the calculated totals. ||70-71||

One should write each [syllable] in its respective desired places, starting from the one with the vowel *e* (ai) and proceeding further; except for the last one, one should join each subsequent [syllable] with the preceding ones.
Likewise, beginning from the last, one should proceed in reverse order through the syllables ending in *a*.

In cases such as the *alinda* and others, wherever there may be a number, they know that to be a *sūcī*. One should place the indicated number where it is indicated; it should occur as the indicated [number].
One should split it when joined with a *rūpa*, but one should split it when joined with a *nāma*.
In the process of breaking down the light syllables (laghu-svarūpa), when one and a half [units] remain, a heavy syllable (guru) is placed;

this continues until the desired number of feet is reached, and the light syllables constitute the beginning of the alcove (alindaka). Having thus established the meter as specified, two [units] are placed at the end of that light syllable.
One should place one [unit] for the heavy syllables (*guru*), and then double it twice [for each subsequent heavy syllable].
Conversely, in the place of a light syllable (*laghu*), one should take one from the doubled [value] of the heavy syllable.
One should make that [result] equal in number to the digit in the first position; in the case of the "lost" (*naṣṭa*) method, this shall be the house (*gṛha*).

One should place a single number in the first cell and then assign them upwards with an increment of one for as many rows as desired. One should write the desired numbers starting from one in successive order; at the corner, one should place zeros. Whatever number arises from the sum of the figures located at the corner, one should place that in the cells in due order.
