O auspicious one, those [lines] in the middle which have the indicated number as their mark are the rat-holes resulting from the contact with the ear. (79) Now, when the numbers beginning with one have been doubled up to the desired number of rat-holes and applied in sequence, one should know that the dwelling has a total count produced by adding one to the sum of the marks of the rat-holes and the exit-path made in the indicated house. (80)

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Results of Income, Expenditure, Lunar Mansions, and Zodiac Signs, as well as their Combinations, Asterisms, Numerical Values, Origins, and Metres," in the *Vāstuśāstra* composed by the Great King of Kings, the illustrious Bhojadeva, also known as the *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*.
Now begins the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Eight Types of Assembly Halls" (*Sabhāṣṭaka*).
The assembly halls are thus described as being of four types: Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, and Pūrṇā.
Likewise, Dakṣā and Pravarā, and Vidurā is considered the eighth.
When the field has been made square and then divided into six parts,
there shall be four squares in the middle, while the boundary and the veranda are each one part.
The first is called the *alindaka*; similarly, there is one named *pratisara*;
and the third is called the *prāggrīva*. These may extend outwards from the central field in all four directions, or they may be projected in only a single direction.
Then the halls (sabhās) shall be Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, and Pūrṇā in sequence.
When the site has been divided into six parts, one should establish the corner wall;
there, the fifth hall shall be named Bhāvitā, provided with a front porch (prāggrīvā).
One should place these thirty-six pillars within all five [types of] halls.
One should specify that the pillars connected to the front neck (prāggrīva) are distinct from these.
The sixth, called Dakṣā, is surrounded on all sides by a third veranda (alinda).
This seventh assembly hall, Pravarā, is proclaimed as being provided with gates. The eighth assembly hall, Vidurā, is joined with a gate at the front neck.
Thus has the characteristic of these eight assembly halls been fully described.
Thus, these characteristics of the eight types of assembly halls have been declared according to the distinctions of the porticos (ālinda) arising from the cardinal directions,
as well as the corresponding conjunctions of doors and porticos.
"When this is known, the application of sites for kings shall take place.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Eight Assemblies," in the *Vāstuśāstra* composed by the great king of kings, Śrī Bhojadeva, also known as the *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*.
Now begins the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Dimensions and Materials of Houses."
We shall now describe those things which are to be accepted and those which are to be abandoned here, as well as the measurements for household articles.
The width of the door should be equal to the number of cubits that constitute the width of the house, measured in finger-breadths (aṅgulas).
The height should be joined with seven [units], and the width should be half of that. One should fashion the door of the house according to this sequence, starting from the smallest;
for those of medium size, one should exclude a twelfth part by means of the rule of three.
Thus, the height [of all] is [one unit], and the width of all is half of that. For the best [type of] buildings, one should make the height reduced by one-eighth.
One should make the smallest [type] joined with finger-breadths (aṅgula) in width.
The height of the sixty-four doorways should be half their width;
their height in cubits should be equal to their width, or else fifty-six hundred and five finger-breadths (aṅgulas), while the width should be half that height. ||5-6||
Alternatively, the height of the door may be three-quarters of the height of the house;
its width, however, should be half of that—this is another rule. One should insert [the measurement] into finger-breadths equal to the number of cubits in the height of the door.
The width of the door-lintel (pedyā) should be four parts;
one should make it one and a quarter, or one and a half, or with an additional third part, or double, but never more.
When done in this way, the width of the door-lintel will be clearly established.
With one and a half times the thickness of the base (pedyā), the thickness of the ambara should be made;
the width of the udumbara should be one and a half times the width of the base.
The auspicious width of the branch (śākhā) should be equal to the thickness of the base.
The extension of the *rūpa-śākhā* (form-branch) is also [determined] by this same [measure] plus one and a half units.
The *khalva-śākhā* (hole-branch) is prescribed as being half the width of the *pedyā* (pedestal),
or it may be equal to the *rūpa-śākhā*, or one and a half units on the outer circle.
In temples, the projection of the *bhāra-śākhā* (the supporting beam) should be equal to three-quarters, two-thirds, or half of the width;
the first *śākhā* shall be the goddess, and the second is called Nandinī.
The third branch is named Sundarī, and the fourth shall be Priyānanā;
the fifth branch is called Bhadrā—these five are praised in the house.
Any branches in excess of these at the door of the house are not auspicious.
The height of the floor is praised as being one-sixteenth of the width and measuring four cubits; this is the rule for those who understand the construction of dwellings.
In the largest [type of house], it should be seven cubits, and in the middling, it should measure six cubits.
In the smallest [size], the rise should likewise be made five cubits;
in the largest, the hall should be seventeen cubits wide;
in the medium, ten cubits, and in the smallest, five cubits.
For the purpose of the *udumbara*, one should cause an abundance [of ornaments] and the placement of the *tala* (pedestal) to be made;
the cloth-strip (*paṭṭa*) for the enclosure of the vestibule (*alinda*) should be equal to the *tala*-placement.
The pinnacle of the pillar (*stambhakoṭi*) is prescribed to be one-fourth of the width of the door.
Then, one should construct its guardian with an eleventh part, increased by an eighth part, or again with a third part; likewise,
one should make nine pillars, excluding an eighth part, or otherwise twelve.
Then, with parts equal to half of its own [total] and combined with half a part,
the base for supporting the pillar (pratipādanā) shall be eight parts below;
the projection onto the ground shall be half the width of the base of the pillar.
The projection of the *masūraka* should be made with half of that measure.
The height of the *utkālaka* is auspiciously equal to the mass of the pillar;
its mass, like that of the *kumbhikā* and the *utkāla*, is measured at one-eighth of the width.
The length of the first leaves is prescribed as one and a quarter times the previously mentioned pillar-section;
for the remaining [leaves], it is reduced by one-quarter.
Each subsequent leaf is diminished by one-quarter from the height of the tongue (rasanā).
The girdle, resembling a thorn, should be made one and a half parts high;
or else, the shank may be one and a quarter parts high, while the remainder is as previously described.
In this manner, the lotus pillar (padmaka-stambha) shall be constructed with its constituent forms joined according to the proper method.
Alternatively, it should be made octagonal by means of the circumferential lines of the pillar;
having set aside a height equal to its width, one should divide it into parts. According to the measurement for cutting the octagon, one should extend the outer lines slightly outward.
One should fashion the corners in the middle portion, adorned with leafy scrolls (pallavikā).
The ghaṭikā should be embellished with flower garlands and leafy scrolls;
the section for the cut-out (chedabhāga) should be made even and devoid of any external parts.
This pillar is proclaimed by the name Ghaṭapallavaka;
when constructed for houses, it shall lead to the welfare of the owner.
Alternatively, Kubera should be fashioned [as the deity], endowed with the ritual of sixteen facets.
Above, it is covered with foliage, and its shank is square;
Śrīdhara should be circular, and his design is like that of Kubera.
Thus, the four pillars of houses are described with their characteristics.
The width of the base (talapada) should be made one and a quarter times the width of the pillar's root;
its thickness should be three-quarters [of that].
In width it should be equal to the pillar, and in thickness it should be measured by the [width of the] base.
The height of the neck (hīra) should be three times the width of the pillar's top.
One should divide the width of the neck into seven parts;
one part beyond that should be the projection, and one part should be the desired recess.
Below that, with a three-pronged [mark] suspended by one-third [of its length],
one should draw two half-moons on both sides.
Then, having made a depression (khalva), the middle part extends downward for two parts.
One should fashion a beautiful three-pronged [structure], then a *tumbikā* and a *lambikā*;
furthermore, another prong situated between the two in two parts,
and a hanging *tumbikā* adorned with various kinds of leaves.
Its opposite shore should be adorned with lotus petals;
the pedestal (pedra) should be equal in width and height to the cloth-strip (talapaṭṭa).
On the shore, it should be one-third the width of the cloth-strip, with a projection equal to half the thickness of the cloth-strip.

The beam (tulā) should be made equal in length to the top of the pillar, and its width and thickness should correspond to that. The width of the *piṇḍas* (blocks) for the *jayantīs* (smaller beams) should be half of that;
the *sandhipālas* (connecting joints) should be made three-quarters the size of those, or according to one's preference.
One should have the cloth strips on the side-posts made three-quarters as long;
the cloth strips on the balance-beam should be three-quarters [of that], and the *jayantikā* strips half of that.
The width of the *pratimoka* (the binding) should be made half the length of the beam.
The neck [of the structure] should be above the cloth-band (paṭṭa) and adorned with sculpted work (rūpakarman).
A turret (niryūha) in the form of a railing, lattice-work, or similar design is highly praised; it should be provided with a parasol and connected to a courtyard pond (aṅgaṇavāpikā). ||44-45||
One should fashion broad pillar-panels there, each with a base;
the beam-blocks should be made level and joined with very firm bindings. The floor should be made beautiful, provided with a pedestal and a lattice-work.
On each successive level, that [measurement] should be reduced by one-twelfth.
Drainage channels should be constructed on all sides, with their intake at the base and their outlet at the top.
There should be a protective railing (daṇḍacchādya) for the houses, and it should be known to be of four kinds.
Likewise, there are the types known as Bhūta, Tilaka, Maṇḍala, and Kumuda. Regarding those roof-coverings, the height is also fourfold.
The supporting beam (daṇḍaka) should be made with a length equal to one-fourth of the site's width.
Half of that is the length of the fist (muṣṭikā), and the overhang (lambanā) is one-third of the staff (daṇḍa).
The roof-covering (chādyaka) of houses should be made square, level, beautiful, sweet, very firm, and dense; it is highly honored by the name Bhūta.
When its eighteenth part is greater in height, it is called Udaya-tilaka; that is recommended for house-building work. If it is higher than the first two, it is Maṇḍala; with three, it is Kumuda.
That which stands without a wall and is to be covered should be adorned with lines like the moon;
the wall may be endowed with qualities and colors, or consist of a dense mass. That which is to be covered therein is known as the *avadhāraṇa*. ||53-54||
One should avoid houses that have the shapes of a lion’s ear, a pigeon’s wing, a bell-ear, or half a wing; likewise, one should avoid those shaped like a banner, an umbrella, a youth, or a flagstaff.
One should also avoid houses with rows of wings, banners, lion’s ears, youths, bells, or those resembling a battle or a curved leaf.
One who desires auspiciousness should not construct houses with half-panels nor with mismatched leaves.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Dimensions of House Materials," in the *Vāstuśāstra* composed by the Great King of Kings, Śrī Bhojadeva, also known as the *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*.
Now begins the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Beds and Seats."
Now we shall describe the characteristics of beds and seats,
by which the thorough discernment of the auspicious and inauspicious is properly produced.
When the moon is in the Puṣya asterism, during the Muhūrta called Mūtra, on an auspicious day—
Having properly worshipped the deities, one should undertake the commencement of the rite.
In that regard, the following trees are praised: sandalwood, *tiniśa*, *arjuna*, *tinduka*, *sāla*, *śāka*, *śirīṣa*, *āsana*, and *dhanvana*.
Haridru, devadāru, syandana, uka, padmaka,
śrīparṇī, dadhiparṇa, śiṃśapā, and whatever other auspicious trees there are—
those trees which are not desired for house-building work are likewise censured here.
A bed should be made by the wise, covered with gold, silver, or ivory, or even covered with brass; likewise,
when wood previously cut is intended for the purpose of beds and seats.
When beginning that [rite], one should observe auspicious signs:
curds, unbroken grains, a full water-pot, jewels, or flowers;
fragrant substances, garments, and the like; as well as fish and a pair of horses.
Having observed other auspicious signs, such as an intoxicated elephant, one should direct an auspicious rite.
A finger-breadth (aṅgula) is declared to consist of eight husked barley grains;
a bed measuring one hundred and eight of those [finger-breadths] is the largest for kings.
The middle bed for kings should be one hundred and four cubits;
that which is declared to be one hundred cubits is said to bring victory to monarchs. For a prince, it should be ninety cubits, and for a minister, that same length minus six.
The length of the bed for the Lord of the Army should be less by twelve units, and that of the domestic priest less by eighteen.
One should determine the width of all beds as half their length,
or else increased by one-eighth or one-sixth of their own measurement.
For Brahmins, a bed seventy finger-breadths in length is recommended;
for those of the remaining castes, it should be reduced by two finger-breadths each.
The thickness of the best lotus-fiber mattress should be three finger-breadths.
The thickness of the central shaft (madhya-daṇḍa) should be two and a half finger-breadths, and that of the smallest shaft (kanīyasa-daṇḍa) should be two finger-breadths.
One should make the thickness of the Ishana-shaft equal to an utpala (the measure of one finger-breadth).
Its width should be one and a half, one and a quarter, or one and a third of an utpala.
The height of the bedstead, including its frame, is prescribed to be half of its width.
Its base should rise from the middle, with two or four parts omitted [from the sides].
The thickness at the center is desired to be half of the width at the middle.
Some authorities maintain that it should be reduced by one-third, while others desire it to be reduced by one-quarter.
In terms of thickness, it should be equal to a lotus flower at the bottom of the head;
in the middle it is one-quarter greater, and at the base it is one-half greater—such is the gradual increase.
Alternatively, its [the base's] width may be increased by one-sixth at the middle or by one-third at the bottom;
that cavity (kuṣya) should have three parts of an utpala at the root and half of that at the top.
Its width should be made equal to its height, or increased by two aṅgulas.
Adorned with leaves, buds, and leaf-cups as mouthfuls, one should arrange the limbs of the bed all around with their tips pointing toward the right;
all the feet [of the bed] should have their tips pointing upward for the sake of the master's prosperity. ||20-21||
A bed made from a single, excellent substance is best; one made from mixed substances is not praised. They commend a bed of a single piece of wood, while a bed of two pieces brings danger.
However, if it is constructed from three pieces of wood, the death of the master is certain.
Since it arises upon the bed, one should therefore avoid it.
A piece of wood whose base is joined with its tip, which is turned to the left, or which is censured;
or where the base is pierced by the base, or where two pieces of wood are joined at their tips—these are dreadful. ||23-24||

A wound in the center causes death; in one-third of the body, it brings about disease; in one-fourth, it brings distress; and when located on the head, it causes loss of wealth. When the limbs are free from defects, as in the case of a reclining posture, no evil dream is seen.
One should not make a bed or a seat with knots or hollows; therefore,
a seat and a bed free from knots and hollows are said to bring many sons and to be the means for achieving dharma, kama, and artha.
When it moves upon mounting, it likewise trembles while lying down;
these two [defects] respectively bring about travel to foreign lands and quarrels.
Therefore, one should make it well-joined, flawless, and radiant with color.
The master builder, for the sake of increasing the husband's desire, [should construct] one that is firm and stable;

the "enclosure" (niṣkuṭa), the "boar-eyed" (koladṛk), the "boar-eyed" (kroḍanayana), the "vatsanābha," the "black" (kālakam), and the "binding" (bandhakam)— this is declared to be the summary of the types of openings.
They desire a nest that is hollow in the middle like a jar, with a narrow opening and a small interior,
the size of a mung bean or a flat bean;
it should be one and a half finger-joints long, discolored, and irregular.
Regarding this, the great sages say that the eye in the center is the "hole" (chidra).
When it is split, measured by a joint (parva), and spiraling to the left, it is the "vatsanābhaka.
That which has a black luster is the "kālaka," while that which is completely split apart is the "bandhaka."
A hole that resembles the color of wood brings no auspiciousness;
in the Niṣkuṭa mark there is loss of wealth, and in the Kolalocana, the ruin of the family.
In the Kroḍanayana there is fear of weapons, and in the Vatsanābha, disease and danger.
It is not auspicious when [the wood] is from the *kāla* tree, from one called *bandhaka*, or pierced by insects. Wood that has many knots everywhere brings all manner of undesirable results.
A seat fashioned from the types of wood prescribed for the purpose of a bed is recommended.
The honor consisting of the pleasure of being seated is ordained for one who is praiseworthy;
it should be prepared by Puṣkara with the hand of the cook, starting from a circumference of four finger-breadths and extending up to nine finger-breadths in width.
The staff (daṇḍa) should be made four times the width of the bowl (puṣkara).
The flat board (phalaka) should be half the size of the bowl, and its base (bhūlaka) should be equal to that.
It should be thick by one-fourth of the width of the staff and bowl.

The depth of the pit within the lotus-pond should be determined by the required capacity; its purpose is to be constructed from highly esteemed, solid heartwood. Furthermore, it serves for the serving of food and as a support for the cooking vessels.
A smooth *kaṅkatika* (comb) should be made from excellent, soft wood.
It should begin at a length of eight finger-breadths and extend up to twelve finger-breadths;
its width should be one and a half finger-breadths, and its thickness should be one-fourth of its length. ||41-42||
And its thickness in the middle should be one-eighth of its width; on one side, its tusks should be thick and broad,
while on the other side they should be dense, slender, and sharp at the tips.
Leaving aside one-third in the middle, the ivory [sections] are in the two parts.
When those are divided by three, one should avoid whatever remains as a remainder.
That which is made of elephant ivory is the best, as is that produced from the śākhoṭa tree.
The middle [type] is made from the remaining wood, while the inferior is made from wood lacking core substance;
it may be decorated in the center with figures such as the svastika.
It is used for removing lice and the like, as well as for combing the hair.
When sandals are to be made with a length exceeding that of the foot by one finger-breadth,
they should be divided into five parts; three parts should be placed at the front and two parts at the back, and in this manner their construction is prescribed.
The height should be three finger-breadths, and the width should follow the measurement of the foot;
in the middle space between the toes and the big toe, two pegs—made of wood, ivory, horn, or other materials—should be fashioned, adorned with fish and other such designs. (49)
Elephant tusks, *śrīkhaṇḍa*, *śrīparṇī*, and *meṣaśṛṅgikā* (50),
as well as *śāka*, milky trees, and *cirabilva*, are recommended for sandals. Herein lies the description of beds and seats.
Having thoroughly understood the auspicious and inauspicious signs manifested by the ladle,
the hair-comb, and the sandals,
a wise man who knows all this attains honor in the world. (51)

Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Beds and Seats," in the *Vāstuśāstra* composed by the Emperor of Emperors, the illustrious Bhojadeva, also known as the *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*.
Now begins the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Royal Palace.
The largest [palace] should be one hundred and eight cubits, and the medium one ninety cubits.
A royal palace measuring seventy cubits is recommended as the minimum;
one desiring great prosperity should not construct it smaller than that.
When the ground has been made level and divided into ten parts, [the first part is for the entrance]. ||2||
A wall occupying half a share (bhāga) is recommended, resting upon the primary corner;
in the center, there should be a square (catuṣka) consisting of one share, provided with four pillars.
Outside of that, an alinda (veranda) should be constructed, surrounded by twelve pillars.
The second *alindaka* should be endowed with twenty pillars;
then the third *alindaka* shall have twenty-eight pillars,
and the fourth is proclaimed to have thirty-six pillars.
Thus, one hundred pillars in the center are prescribed by the wise for the conquest of the earth;
its doors are four, each arising with five branches. Its four projections are all said to be divided [symmetrically].
In all directions, O auspicious one, the bhadra projection must be constructed in this manner. With half of the middle wall, there shall be a wall on each of the three bhadras.
On each bhadra, there should be twenty-eight pillars.
"May there be auspiciousness for the face," so it was said by the vedikās and mattavāraṇas.
The ground from the rise of the field-division (kṣetrabhāga) onwards is the interval between the earth and the fruit of the non-earth (ābhūmi).
One should fashion its pedestal (pīṭha) with half the height of the initial ground.
Having divided [the height] into nine parts, the *kumbhikā* (pitcher) should be made with one part;
the pillar (*stambha*) should be made with four parts plus one-eighth;
it should be provided with a base (*pāda*), and likewise, the *utkalaka* (neck-ring) should be made with one part.
The *hīragrahaṇaka* should be made with a portion reduced by one-quarter;
the *paṭṭa* should consist of one and a quarter parts and be provided with a *stambhaka*.
The *jayantīs* should be half the size of the *paṭṭa*; this is the sequence for each successive level on the ground.
On other levels, half of the calculated rise is reduced.
The ninth floor, however, should be covered with a measurement of five parts;
that which is below the pedestal (vedikā) is to be covered with a measurement of three and a half parts. ||13-14||
It should be provided with a neck (kaṇṭha) such that the pedestal (vedikā) is covered by it;
at its neck, one and a half parts should be placed in the middle.
The width of the pedestal should be made there to be six and a half parts.
Upon the pedestal (vedikā), the bell (ghaṇṭā) measures fourteen and a half parts;
the neck (kaṇṭha) is two and a quarter parts, while the band (paṭṭa) is five parts.
Then, the second [band] is four parts and the third is three parts.
The temple pinnacle (sadmaśīrṣa) should be given according to beauty and taste;
the dome (kalaśa) should be made equal to the portion of the site up to the top of the spire (cūlikā). The intermediate spaces and the floors should be [determined] by half the height of the ground.
The pedestal (pīṭha) for it should be made very beautiful according to what is auspicious.
Its khuragharaṇḍikā should be made with two and a half parts;
the shaft (jaṅghā) should be four parts, and after that, one should apply the covering (chādya).
Two parts less one-quarter are proclaimed as the *chādyapiṇḍa* (the covering mass).
Its projection (*nirgama*) is one-fourth part, and above that is the one called *haṃsa*.
Then, one-quarter less a part should be made, and from there the second *chādya* (covering).
One should design the *jaṅghā* (the lower portion) of the palace using four stories;
then, upon the top of the fourth story, one should place the *muṇḍā* (the dome).
The remaining stories, however, should be constructed by means of successive, momentary insertions.
The altar (vedikā) should be as previously described, provided with a bell and a water-pot (kalaśa);
it should be constructed with pure lines, and all the [pedestal] sections (muṇḍas) should be made according to their respective proportions.
Having divided the "half-rise" (ardhodaya) into three parts, one should further divide the third part into ten.
Vāmana, Cātapatra, Kubera, Bhramarāvalī,
Haṃsapṛṣṭha, Mahābhogin, Nārada, Śambuka, Jaya, and Ananta as the tenth— these are [the attendants] by the power of the Creator. (25–26)
The architects must construct it for the sake of establishing the profile of the spire (muṇḍarekhā),
adorning it with side-altars (vedikā), lattices (jāla), and intoxicated elephants (mattavāraṇa),
provided with balconies (vitardī) and gate-towers (niryūha), and embellished with moon-chambers (candraśālā). ||27||
One should construct the Pṛthivījaya temple, which is rich in ritual action and highly variegated.
Those great palaces that are to be built should be made with the Samodaya style; however, smaller ones may be made with the Ardhodaya style. This is the sequence for temples such as the Avākoṇa.

The elevation from the eight levels of the ground is commensurate with the extent of the site; for it is said that upon your destruction, the palace shall be the only remaining ornament. In those [palaces], many clusters are provided, among which courtyards are given.
On the first, second,
or even the third line, the enclosures are prescribed there.
This elevation of the ground should be made in a field divided into ten parts.
In the case of a division that is deficient or excessive, the work should be carried out according to the proportion.
Now, the characteristics of the *muktakoṇa* (the released corner) as they follow from the ritual procedure are stated:
when the field has been made square and marked with twelve divisions.
In the center of this [structure], there is a four-part division adorned with four doors (34).
Beyond that, an *alinda* (veranda) consisting of one part is supported by twelve pillars;
likewise, the second *alinda* is also supported by twenty pillars (35).
The third [alinda] should consist of twenty-eight dhara-s;
the fourth alinda should be constructed with thirty-six dhara-s;
and the fifth should be joined with forty-four dhara-s.
One should fashion the *gitti* (the neck) at half a part, having left aside one and a half parts;
then one should make three parts for the front neck (*prāggrīva*) in both length and width. One should design the *bhadra* (the frontal projection) as one part in both its width and its projection.

From that [central part], a portion has projected outward; indeed, there is another auspicious *bhadra* in the middle. This same rule applies to the width of the projection in all directions. Each *bhadra* is provided with fifty-four pillars.
In its center, there should be one hundred and forty-four pillars;
O Bhadra, there should also be two hundred and sixteen additional pillars.
Thus, for all these types of temples, there shall be three hundred and sixty pillars.
Just as in the case of Pṛthvījaya, here too the remaining construction is desired;
on top of the third level, courtyards (prāṅgaṇas) should be made for all the exits— this specific detail is proclaimed here.
Now, for that known as Sarvatobhadra and also named Śatrumardana,
this same procedure should be followed for the accomplishment of the circular lines (muṇḍarekhā).
In the center of the Śrīvatsa as well, there should be a pillar and so forth, like the [design] with released corners.

Having set aside one-and-a-half parts, the *karṇaprāggrīva* of this [structure] shall extend across three parts and project outward by one part (*bhaga*). Its *bhadra* should also be made with an extension equal to its width in parts.
Like the *muktakoṇa*, its central bay (*madhyabhadra*) is also constructed;
this is the rule for all directions, while the remainder is as before.
For each bay (*pratibhadra*), there are thirty firm and auspicious supports (*dharā*). ||46-47||
This hundred-and-twenty-fold [plan] of all the foundations has been proclaimed here;
thus, for all the pillars, there are two hundred and sixty-four.
Now we shall describe the characteristics of that which is known as the Sarvatobhadra.
When the site has been made square and divided into fourteen parts, its central four-part area (catuṣka) shall consist of one part;
it is adorned with four pillars, and the first portico (alindaka) shall be provided with twelve pillars. ||49-50||
The second porch (alindaka) should be joined with twenty pillars;
the third porch should likewise have twenty-eight pillars;
and the fourth porch should be adorned with thirty-six supports (dharas).
The fifth [type] should be adorned with forty-four supports (dhara);
the sixth has fifty-two supports. All of these are its constituent parts.
A wall that is very firm and solid on all sides is praised as being half a part (bhāgārdha).

Having set aside one and a half parts, the width of the three parts shall constitute the *karṇa* (corner) and the *prāggrīvaka* (front projection); the *nirgama* (projection) shall be one part. The *bhadra* (central projection) of this [temple] should also be made with a width and projection of one part.
In the middle, a *bhadra* (projection) should be fashioned, extending out by two parts.
In the middle of this [central hall] as well, there should be a *bhadra* with an extent of three parts;
its projection should be one part, and it should extend inward by one part from within that.
O Bhadra, one should design another [type] endowed with the proportions of the parts;
this very rule for the design of the Bhadra has been declared for all directions.
In its center, one hundred and ninety-six pillars are to be constructed.
O auspicious one, in all these [types], there shall be one hundred and sixty [pillars] by way of an equal distribution according to the number of pillars;
thus, for all the pillars, there are three hundred and fifty-six.
However, the shank of this [image] named Śatrumardana should be measured at three bhūmikās; now the characteristic of its face is described:
the middle part should be equal to the earth-victory (pṛthvījaya), and the wall (bhitti) should likewise be of that same measure.
Having set aside half a part,
one should construct the *bhadra* in the middle of that, measuring one part in length and width and extending across three parts;
this *bhadra* itself should be made with a projection of three parts.
On both sides, the *bhadra* should be one part in length and width;
its projection should be one part, with a width of three parts.
Beyond that, the central *bhadra* should likewise be one part in both length and width.
This sequence should be applied in all directions for its successful accomplishment. Furthermore, after the *ūrdhvapṛthvīja*, another [structure] should be made,
namely the *pratibhadra*, provided with forty-four pillars.
In its center, one should construct two hundred very firm and auspicious pillars;
thus, it shall consist of two hundred and seventy-six pillars.
Furthermore, for all five of these [structures], eight hundred cubits is the supreme measurement.
One desiring prosperity should construct the palace according to its height and width [as specified].
In the *Pṛthivījaya*, the measurements for the middle and lowest classes have been proclaimed;
now, another set of five types of houses for the king’s pleasure is described.
The first is Kṣoṇīvibhūṣaṇa, the supreme Pṛthivītilaka,
another is Pratāpavardhana, and after that Śrīnivāsa;
the fifth is proclaimed as Lakṣmīvilāsa.
When the site has been made quadrangular and divided into ten parts,
a central hall (catuṣka) four parts wide and supported by four pillars should be constructed;
outside of that, there should be a veranda one part wide, and at its end, [rooms] three parts long.
The *karṇaprāsādakas* (corner pavilions) should be constructed with a width of three *bhāgas*;

in their center, there is a wall consisting of six wooden beams (*ṣaḍdāruka*) measuring half a *bhāga*. Outside of that, on the *bhadra* (central projection), it extends by one *bhāga* and is one *bhāga* in width.
Joined with three front projections (prāggrīvas), encircled by a one-part (bhāgika) Ālinda,
and surrounded by a wall of half a part, this four-celled (catuṣka) temple shall be a captivating ornament of the earth. ||73-74||
When the field has been made square and divided into twelve parts,
there should be a central hall occupying four parts, and two outer verandas, each occupying one part.
One should then install temples in the nine compartments at the corners.
And a six-beamed structure (ṣaḍdāruka) should be constructed, resting within those [pillars].
Then, a wall measuring half a part should be made on the outside of all [the bays]. In the central bay (bhadra), it should extend for one part and project out by one part in the four directions.
It is prescribed that it should have four corners and be surrounded by an *alinda* (veranda).
Three *bhadras* (projections) should be made for this, each with an extent and projection of one *bhāga*. It is further prescribed that it should be surrounded by a wall measuring half a *bhāga*.
In its two broad ears, two auspicious [projections] emerge, each measuring one part;
such is described as the Prāsāda known as Bhuvanatilaka.
When the square site is divided into twelve parts... ||79-80||
In the center, a four-sided structure with four pillars is prescribed, measuring one part on each side;
outside of that, there is an *alinda* (veranda) of one part, and a second [structure] also of one part.
One should then arrange nine-celled temples at the corners.

And a *ṣaḍdāruka* (six-wood) structure should be made, resting within them. Then, a wall measuring half a share should be constructed on the outside of all [the parts]. On the *bhadra*, extending for one share, there is a *bhadra* projection supported by four pillars. ||82-83||
The square [central hall] is surrounded on both sides by two *alinda*s occupying one-quarter [of the width];
the *bhadra* protrudes outward from that by three parts,
and one should construct a *pratibhadra* of one part on each side symmetrically.
The wall surrounding the *bhadra* on the outside should be half a share;
this procedure is to be applied likewise in all four directions.
This temple is celebrated by the name Vilāsastabaka. ||85-86||
When it has two *karṇaprāggrīvaka*s and two *śālāprāggrīvaka*s,
it is then celebrated as the *kīrttipatāka*.
When this same [temple] is provided with a pedestal (*pīṭha*) and surrounded on all sides by eight detached halls (*nirmuktaśālā*), [it becomes the *kīrttipatāka*].

When these very [elements] are given in a structure where the halls are interconnected, it is known as the Prāsādasundara, which is endowed with corner pavilions (karṇaprāsāda) and joined by corners devoid of halls;
it is then the ornament of the world. ||88-89||
These have been declared as the talacchandas (ground-plans), along with the enclosures for the legs and so forth;
whatever measurements of the ground and other details there may be, they should be like those of the Pṛthvījaya [temple].
Now, the characteristics of the temple known as Kṣoṇībhūṣaṇa are being described.
In a square measuring fifty-five cubits, divided into eight parts, each part is known as a *catuṣka*.
Its veranda (*alinda*), provided with four pillars, measures one part. || 91-92 ||
The first [type] is joined with twelve pillars, and the second with twenty;
the third, which has an *alindaka* (porch), possesses twenty-eight,
and it is constructed by leaving one and a half parts out of the half-part of the wall.
The *bhadra* should be five parts wide and project out by one part;
another *bhadra* in the middle of that should also be made three parts wide and project out by one part.
It should be constructed with one part extended and one part projecting out;
this rule must be applied in all directions for its successful completion.
It should be joined with sixty-four central pillars made of solid wood.
Each *pratibhadra* should be constructed with eighteen pillars;
thus, there shall be one hundred and thirty-six pillars here on all sides.
This [temple] should be made with four gates, increasing fame, fortune, and renown. ||97-98||
Now the characteristics of the Pṛthivītilaka temple are described:
on a site measuring forty cubits, divided into fifty-six parts,
there should be a central square consisting of one part, adorned with four pillars.
The *alinda* (veranda) also consists of one part and is provided with twelve pillars;
the second [section] consists of twenty [parts], and its wall should be one-quarter [of the total].
At the corner, there should be a pavilion (*prāsādaka*) consisting of three parts, projecting and extending in length.
Two *bhadras* should be made for this [central shrine], with a width extending one *bhāga* outward;
between the two corner shrines (*karṇaprāsāda*), it should be five *bhāgas* wide. A *bhadra* should also be made from the middle of that [central shrine], extending one *bhāga* outward.
It is three parts wide and one part projected outward;
likewise for the *bhadra*, another [part] is projected forward by one part from the middle.
There should be thirty-six pillars within, eight on each *bhadra*, and two hundred [pillars] in total.
Now, therefore, we shall describe the characteristics of Śrīnivāsa;
its center is proclaimed to be like a tilaka-mark upon the earth.
Having set aside one-quarter part, it is three parts in width.
O auspicious one, one should fashion its front porch (bhadra) extending out by one part.
Furthermore, that which is situated in the middle [of the structure] is made with a width extending out by two parts, and it is constructed very firmly, provided with ten pillars. 106–107.
O auspicious one, this same arrangement should be applied in all directions;
thus, the total number of pillars for this [temple] becomes seventy-six.
Now, the characteristic mark of Pratāpavardhana is being described.
At the mark of twenty-five cubits, marked with three and a half parts,
there is a central quadrangle formed by four parts on each side;
its portico is one part wide and is provided with twelve pillars.
Its wall should have a plinth (pādikā), and one should fashion a *bhadra* for it;
its projection and width should be one share, and it should be adorned with four pillars.
This rule should be applied in all directions for its successful accomplishment.
This [temple] should be provided with thirty-two pillars, both externally and internally.
For all types of temples, there is a calculation of sixty-four [pillars].
Now, the correct characteristics of the Lakṣmīvilāsa [temple] are being described.
One should design it like that of the middle [type], Pratāpavardhana;
this is declared to be equal to Pratāpavardhana in every respect.
However, one should have its side-bhadras (pārśvabhadras) made exactly like those of the bhadra type.
There are also *bhadras* at the corners and likewise on both sides;
the projection (*nirgama*) of these parts is considered a specific feature distinct from this [standard].
The middle of the *bhadra* has ten pillars, while the center [of the temple] has sixteen supports (*dharas*).
This [mandala] should have four gates according to one's desire, situated within a moment [of time].
Another gate should be fashioned, beautifully adorned in its own place.
The ornament of the earth (the mandala) should be constructed with six and a half levels (bhūmis).
With seven and a half [units] of land, it shall be known as Pṛthvītilaka;
with five and a half units of land, it shall be Śrīnivāsa;
and with four and a half units, it is prescribed as Lakṣmīvilāsa. ||118-119||
The structure known as Pratāpavardhana is constructed with three and a half [units];
it serves for kings as palaces for world-conquest and the like, as well as for pleasure residences and ornaments for the earth. (120)
Now the measurement of the door for those [temples] such as Pṛthvījaya, which were described as being for the residence and recreation of kings, is stated:
that which is forty-five parts wide, plus three cubits. ||121-122||
That is declared to be the height of the door; its width is half of that.
For the pillars, a base (piṇḍa) equal to one-third of their own height is recommended.
It should be twenty-seven [units] plus a quarter, along with four cubits.
The ground for the residential portion of royal palaces shall be the first [type].
When the height of the ground is divided into nine parts, four such parts shall be the projection of the overhang;
two parts shall be the width, and three-quarters of a part shall be the height. ||124-125||
Likewise, the antarāvaṇī should be made, extending beyond the height of the covering;
it is praised when its thickness is half of the mass of the diamond-holding [section].
Its width is recorded as being three-quarters of its own thickness.
The emergence of the *madalā* is equal to the *antarāvaṇika*.
Likewise, from its own emergence, its height should be one and a quarter [units].
A quarter of nine parts of the height of the base is desired as its mass (*piṇḍa*). ||127-128||
The width of the *madala* (pedestal) is three parts less than the height of the base;
the width of the pillar at the root of the *lumā* (fillet) is declared to be half [the height].
Its width at the top is one-third of that, and at the base it should be increased by two-eighths (one-fourth).
Tumbinī, Lambinī, Helā, Śāntā, Kolā, Manoramā, and Ādhmātā—these are declared by the wise to be the seven *lumās*. Among them, Sā is straight; Lambinī is said to reach the ear. ||130-131||
In the interval, five others are proclaimed to be placed in succession;
one should fix a firm and auspicious *madalā* upon the pillar to support the roof-covering.
Furthermore, in the absence of a pillar, the wise man should install it even upon a wall or a wooden beam.

Seven, five, or three *lumās* are prescribed for the *mallacchādya*. These should be placed in the corners; others, distinct from these, should be made straight and even. In some cases, on the *karṇa* of the *chādya*, they should be fashioned as ornaments with the faces of sea-monsters (*makara*).
Those [pillars] as well, provided with Vidyādharas and in some cases with elephant-trunk motifs,
should have their height divided into three parts;
there, one should make two parts [of the base] and the remaining parts [the shaft] each measuring three and a half units.
There, the throne-seat (rājitāsana) should be made with a portion of three-quarters. Then, a pedestal (vedī) provided with a plinth (sāṅghri) is prescribed with one-quarter of that;
here, the seat-slab (āsanapaṭṭaka) should be made equal to half the portion of the gabled chamber (kūṭāgāra). ||136-137||
That desired width shall be the height of the *mattavāraṇa* (the elephant-enclosure);
its projection should be made at one-third of its own height.
It should be adorned with *rūpaka* figures, *karaṇas*, and beautiful pillars.
Its beautiful railings and other features were also covered with decorative plates;
it was made firm with iron rods and bolts.
These fifteen royal residences, beginning with Pṛthvījaya, have been described.
The king is pleased with him who knows their measurement along with its defining characteristics.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Royal Palace," in the *Vāstuśāstra* composed by the great emperor, the illustrious Bhojadeva, also known as the *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*.
Now begins the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Construction of Machines."
This machine of the three worlds, with its hundreds of revolving discs of the sun and moon, has an imperceptible center.
May he who, having fashioned all the elements as the seed-syllables,
perpetually sets them in motion— victory over the god of love— protect you.
Now we shall explain the chapter on the yantras exactly as they follow in the sequence.
That which is the sole cause here for dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa; that which,
having restrained beings who act by their own will along their own paths,
leads them toward this [goal]— that is celebrated as the "yantra."
Since the elements, having proceeded by their own inherent nature through their own volition, govern that which has been created, it is known as a "machine" (yantra).
Its seed is fourfold: earth, water, fire, and air.
And because they serve as the substratum, they are also useful for victory.
The charioteer has been declared by the experts to be distinct [from the warrior], yet they do not understand this correctly;
by nature, the earthly one (the king) is the charioteer, and therein the action should take place.
Therefore, because it possesses the nature of earth (*pārthivatva*), this [fire] is never distinct from it;
for if its state of being produced from fire (*agnijatva*) is postulated on the basis of its being a substance (*dravyatva*),
then no contradiction with fire itself arises for it.
Due to its fragrance, its heat, and its opposition [to cold], the earth-nature prevails by force.
The self alone is the seed of all, yet each of the others is likewise a seed;
thus, through their mutual intermixture, many further varieties arise among them.
One [type of carriage] should be self-propelled, another likewise should be driven once and left;
another is to be driven from within, while yet another is to be driven from nearby.
Here, the self-propelled is superior, and the other three are inferior.
Among them, they praise that which is distant yet invisible, as well as that which is situated nearby;
they praise that which has arisen and is invisible, and that which, though one, is effective among many;
and they praise other such things as well, because they cause wonder in men.
One's own movement is in the painting, while another is dependent on the carrier;
both of these are seen in the case of an insect clinging to a water-wheel.
Thus, by virtue of these two movements, one may imagine a manifold variety for oneself.
Since invisibility and variety are praised in the case of machines, there may be another [type] to be impelled from within;
this, however, is the second, the intermediate one, through the combination of two, three, or more, and by the union of all four. ||14-15||
Because of the relationship between part and whole among all beings, their number exceeds calculation;
he who understands this correctly becomes a man beloved by women, kings, the wise, and the learned. (16)
What gain, fame, honor, renown, respect, and wealth does that man not obtain who knows this in its true essence?
It is the sole abode of delights and the supreme state of wonder. (17–18)
The abode of Rati is a singular source of wonder,
because one perceives therein the true forms, gestures, and other attributes of the deities and others.
They are pleased by this, and such pleasure is proclaimed as the dharma of the ancients.
From the satisfaction of the king, wealth arises; in wealth, desire is established. Through the accumulation of wealth, its fulfillment occurs, and from this, liberation is not difficult to attain.
[The earth] is nourished by earthly seeds and by those born of water.
That very [body] is produced from fiery elements, from those born of wind,
and likewise from watery seeds, as well as from those of fire, wind, earth, and water.
(22) It is composed of elements born of fire, those born of wind, those of earth, and those of water.
The wind [is the seed] for the winds, and likewise for the waters and the earth;
even in that which is born of fire, there may be a seed, and that too is in the fire.
It becomes the seed of the earthly elements and also for the restraint of the watery ones.
Thus, all the seed-measures (bījas) for everything have been proclaimed,
as well as the wall-construction lines, the pressing of the load and the spheres,
the suspension, the hanging-frames, and various kinds of wheels.
Iron, copper, silver, and tin are used in the crushing of substances;
likewise, wood, leather, and cloth are employed according to their respective natures.
Furthermore, there are the urdaka, the knife, the staff, the wheel, and the drill-bit.
Śṛṅgāvalī, nārāca, and svabīja are known as the seeds of fire; likewise, tāpa, uttejana, stobha, and kṣobha arising from contact with water are said to be the seeds of fire for an earthen vessel. 28.
Thus they describe the primary seeds of fire.

A stream, a mass of water, and likewise the swirling of water—these and others like them are declared to be the water-born [ornaments] of the arms. Just as there is height, so too is there abundance and density. ||29-30||
The state of ascending extremely upward arises from its own seed and its own sequence;
it is born from the nature of the vital air (marut) and is seized by firm grāhakas.
It is produced by means of the *dṛti* and so forth, by the *vījanā* and so forth, and by the "elephant-ear" [posture] and so forth.
When this [substance] is churned and strained, it becomes the seed for that which arises from the earth.
Wood, sustenance, and iron exist in the watery realm;
let that which is earthly be otherwise as well—whether horizontal, upward, or downward. ||32-33||
In water-born yantras, one's own seed-syllable is used;
that which was previously described as beginning with heat (tāpa) and so forth shall be produced from fire in the water-born [yantra].
It is gathered, bestowed, filled, and repelled.
In water-born machines, it attains the state of being a seed of air (marud-bīja);
in fire-born ones, such as earth, copper, iron, gold, and so forth, those expert in seeds declare that the seed therein is of the nature of earth (pārthiva) during its extraction. //35-36//
Fire becomes the seed of fire, and water likewise becomes water;
through the aforementioned elements beginning with earth, the wind attains the state of being a seed.
It is both the recipient and the progenitor, as well as the impeller and the grasper.
That which is gathered is born of the earth, while the seed arises from the winds.
Impelling, striking, transformation, and likewise whirling—these are held to be the seeds for water-born things arising from the winds. (38–39)
Whatever effects are proclaimed to arise from fire when it is gathered, heated, and so forth, those very same effects occur through the winds:
being impelled, gathered, and generated by the wind. (40)

Thus it becomes the seed of the self; in this same way, one should conceive of the others. Here, one element is predominant while another is deficient, and yet another is even more deficient, through such various conceptualizations. ||41-42||
There are many different varieties of these; who could describe them in their entirety?
The earth is inactive, whereas activity exists partially in it and is innate in the remaining three [elements].
Therefore, for the most part, that [activity] is produced in the earth alone with effort.
The arrangement [of the letters] occurs according to the form of the object to be accomplished;
therefore, the shape of the yantras cannot be determined [by that alone].
Furthermore, the proper conjunction of the seed-syllables (bīja), their firm cohesion, and their smoothness are also required. ||44–45||
Absence of definition, lack of conclusion, triviality, deficiency of sound;
when sound is the object to be proven, its excess, lack of firmness, lack of depth, and in all the modes of leading [the argument], lack of cohesion and faltering movement. ||46||
Acting according to the desired purpose, following the *laya* and *tāla*,
being half-visible at the intended time, again the concealment of perfection, lack of vulgarity, conformity to that nature, firmness, and likewise smoothness. ||47-48||
Durability over a long period is also considered one of the qualities of a machine.
One [machine] may move many others, while another is moved by many.
Being well-joined and being imperceptible are the supreme qualities of machines.
Now, we shall duly describe the various operations of the machines,
neither in excessive detail nor in too brief a manner;
for one operation is to be accomplished by one means, while another requires a different time.
Sound belongs to some [element], and elevation, as well as color and touch, belong to others;
however, actions are proclaimed to be infinite according to the requirements of their effects.
[These include movement] across, upwards, downwards, backwards, forwards, and also to the sides.
Going, fleeing, and falling—these are the varieties arising from action. Time is divided in many ways by its subdivisions such as muhūrta and kāṣṭhā.
Sound is manifold, providing pleasure, creating delight, and likewise being terrifying.
The height of the water may be [measured] at some places, and it is also commended on the ground;
likewise, there should be song, dance, and instrumental music, as well as the drum,
the flute, the lute, the bronze cymbals, the *tṛmilā*, and the *karaṭā*.

Whatever else is manifested here, such as musical instruments and the like, all of that arises from the machine by the power of the creative imagination (kalpanā). As for dance, there is the dramatic performance (nāṭaka), the refined dance (ukṣa), the tāṇḍava, and the lāsya. ||56-57||
The royal road and the local dialect— all these are accomplished through the machine;
likewise, even those behaviors that follow one's birth and those which are contrary to one's birth—
all of them are successfully achieved through the proper application of the machine.
The movement of land-dwellers occurs in the sky, and the arrival of sky-dwellers occurs on the earth;
likewise, through the construction of machines, the various desired activities of mortals come to pass, just as they do for those who touch the ground. ||59-60||
Just as the Asuras were conquered by the gods, just as the ocean was churned,
and just as the Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu was slain by Nṛsiṃha;
[therein are described] the running, the elephant-fights, and the capture of elephants.
There were various kinds of amusements and houses with diverse foundations;
there were wonderful swings and likewise pleasure-houses, as well as variegated tents and servants who carried them themselves. ||62-63||
Assemblies of various forms, both real and illusory, are thus fashioned;
other such things as these are accomplished through the power of imagination from the mechanical device.
Having established five stages, the bed remains situated in the first stage.
Moving through other [positions] every watch, it proceeds to the fifth.
Such various [motions], when properly executed by means of the mechanism, result in the teeth revolving in a bowl in three hundred turns in succession. (65–66)
In the midst of that, a female figurine (putrikā) fashioned [therein] should awaken each channel (nāḍī).
There is the vision of fire in the water, and the emergence of water from the midst of fire.
Though non-substantial, it possesses substantiality; and though substantial, it is otherwise.
By his exhalation he ascends to the sky, and by his inhalation he comes to the earth.
His bed lies in the midst of the Ocean of Milk, supported below by the Serpent King;
and the sphere of the sun and other celestial bodies has been established by him to revolve clockwise.

Wandering day and night, it displays the movement of the planets; a man who has been transformed into the form of a charioteer within the forms of elephants and other creatures wanders for a period of time and,
at the end of that duration, destroys his food.
A little girl fashioned as a lamp-bearer offers [the oil] whenever it is exhausted.
Dancing around the lamp clockwise to the rhythm of the beat, she drinks continuously as much water as is poured [upon her]. ||71-72||
An elephant fashioned by a machine does not appear to move;
parrots and other birds are likewise constructed to follow the rhythm of the tāla repeatedly,
causing wonder among the people as they dance and recite.
Whether it be a doll, a lordly elephant, a horse, or even a monkey,
dancing with its turns and movements to the rhythm of the *tāla* steals the mind;
by whichever path the field is held, by that same path its water flows.
Just as one goes and returns again from a pit, so too do they move among lotus ponds;
some remain on rafts, while others run about according to their inclinations.
They bestow gifts, fight, and go forth without weariness or obstruction.
They dance, sing, and likewise play flutes and other instruments;
moreover, whatever divine or human gestures there are, they perform those very ones here through the mastery of the breath restrained and released by means of mechanical contrivances. ||77-78||
Whatever else is difficult to accomplish is achieved through these mechanical devices.
The construction of these devices has not been described here for the sake of secrecy, nor due to ignorance;
rather, this reason should be understood: that if they were made manifest, they would not yield their intended results.
The seed-syllables (bījas) for these yantras have been stated here, but not their construction.
Therefore, once these have been made manifest, there will be neither loss of purpose nor lack of curiosity;
for in truth, everything has been explained here by the recitation of the seed-syllables.
The functions of machines, exactly as they are, should be inferred by the wise through their own intellect;
moreover, those machines which have been observed and described here should be understood from this instruction, for they are to be rejoiced in. 82.
All of this has been conceived by us entirely through our own intellect.
Furthermore, we shall state hereafter that which was taught by the ancients:
they declare that the seed (bīja) in this yantra is of four kinds.
[It is] established by space, fire, earth, and wind, each in its proper place.

For each [element] individually, there would be many varieties through their divisions; yet, when mixed with qualities, this [world] transcends all calculation. What else could be more wondrous than this in the world?
What else could bring satisfaction, or what indeed could be a source of wonder?
What else could be a temple for fame, or another abode of desire?
What could be more meritorious than this, or what better for quelling distress?
(85) These combinations of seeds, when applied by master builders, produce results that grant exceeding joy.
Due to delusion, one might think there is no other [artist], yet the wheel fashioned from wood, the swing, and so forth—this is the fifth [category].

(86) Tradition, skill along with instruction, study of the treatises, application to the work of architecture, and intelligence—whosoever possesses this pure collection of factors knows how to create such variegated machines in this world. (87)
Those who know this fivefold form endowed with various qualities, which falls within the scope of the science of machines (yantra-śāstra),
or those who properly apply it here in its entirety— their fame covers both heaven and earth.
(88) [The wheel] is measured by a finger-breadth, raised by a quarter-finger, having two rims, and being thin and circular.

That [instrument] should be made of solid copper, straight, with a central cavity, and its joints well-fitted. When placed inside wooden birds, it produces a soft sound as it vibrates by the force of the air emerging from within; this becomes a source of wonder for those who hear it. ||89-90||
Having fashioned it with two well-joined halves so as to have a perforation within, resembling a drum (muraja),
and having its middle cavity gripped by a pair of earrings, that soft [substance] should be placed therein. Then,
when this has been cast into the interior of the previously mentioned apparatus according to the prescribed method, it comes to rest upon the surface of the bed.

Then, from that movement, she produces a sound that heightens the delight in the passion of amorous play. As she emits distinct cries upon being placed beneath the bed, the pride of those with eyes like young fawns departs, as if out of fear.
Moreover, for these women who possess intense love,
the amorous sports increase more and more in their maturity as they proceed around their beloved.
[The instruments include] the ḍamaru, the mṛdaṅga, the flute, the conch, the lute, and the kāhalā.

All these musical instruments, such as the ḍamaru and the ṭiviḷe, produce sounds that are exceedingly sweet, intense, and wonderful; this is entirely the manifestation of the wind that has been obstructed and then released by the Creator. 94.
Having fashioned a great bird out of light wood with a body firmly joined together,
one should place a liquid-container within its belly and a receptacle for fire beneath it, well-filled.
A man mounted upon it would, by the wind forcefully expelled from the movement of its pair of wings, [ascend].
Having its interior filled with mercury, it moves far through the sky by its power, performing wonders; 96.
In this very manner, a swift wooden chariot, resembling a celestial palace, moves along;
one should duly place within it four sturdy jars filled with mercury. 97.
By means of the quality produced from that jar heated by a slow fire applied to an iron lid,
it instantly attains the state of an ornament for the sky through its power, like a thunderbolt from a cloud roaring with heat.
Then, having fashioned an iron machine with rounded joints and filled its interior with mercury, [he acted].
Placing the heated *siṃhanāda* drum upon a high spot, he beats it;
such is the vast and throbbing majesty of this Narasiṃha, before whom these herds of elephants, though shedding rut-fluid, [stand submissive].
Even upon repeatedly hearing a deep and terrifying roar,
they flee in haste out of fear, casting aside even the goad;
their eyes, necks, bellies, hands, forearms, thighs, and the branches of their arms [are all agitated].
One should join together that entire body, which has holes, piece by piece at its joints;
having made it wooden, it should be bound with leather and concealed by the method of using pins,
having fashioned the form of either a man or a young woman, exceedingly beautiful.
With threads joined by iron pins according to the prescribed method, inserted into every joint and opening, one effects the movement, extension, contraction, and other actions of the neck;
as well as the grasping of the hand, the offering of betel, the pouring of water, and so forth. (103) [The measurement and other details follow.]
He performs such acts as looking into mirrors, playing the lute, and so forth;

likewise, he carries out other similar deeds that inspire wonder, by means of the method expanded from his own intellect, through the power of the wheel of qualities drawn forth and released. 104–105.
Having fashioned a wooden figure of a man and placed it upright at the door of the dwelling with a staff held in its hand, one blocks the path for those who wish to enter.
Whether that [staff] be held in the hand like a sword, or like a mallet, or even like a spear— [if it be so placed].

It forcibly slays thieves who enter at night when its mouth is closed at the gate. Those weapons such as the *cāpa* and *śataghnī*, those such as the camel-necked (*uṣṭragrīva*) for the protection of the fortress, and those such as the *krīḍā* for the amusement of kings—all these should exist through the application of the various qualities [of the rampart]. (107–108)
Now we shall describe the water-machine (vāriyantra) which follows from the present context;
they know its movement to be fourfold, for the sake of sport and for the accomplishment of tasks.
Water flows downwards from a place situated above, such as a trough or a reservoir.
Where there is a water-lifting machine for the purpose of gardens and the like,
it is called "Equal-Descent" (ucchāyasama-pāta), wherein the upper tube releases the qualities of the water reservoir,
while the lower tube [receives] it. ||110-111||
Where, having fallen from a height, the water reaches a corresponding height upon falling,
and then, through the connection with a porous pillar, moves sideways and rises upward;
and where, having fallen from a height, the water then moves sideways and rises higher and higher.
By means of the "pierced pillar" (sacchidra-stambha) technique, that [water] shall reach a height equal to its fall.

Whether in a pond, a well, or a constructed long tank and so forth, wherever it causes the water to rise upward according to the prescribed method, that is here called "height" (ucchraya). ||113-114||
That he drinks the water contained in his vessel, which has the form of a wooden elephant,
is declared to be the majesty of this [elephant], whose height is equal to that [of the mountain].
Water brought from the regions of the celestial caves by a low-lying path over a great distance—
That wonderful water-pavilion here creates [its effect] through its equal height and width;
it may be a single shower-house called *pravarṣaṇa*, or a second one, or a *prāṇāla* submerged in water, or likewise another known as *nandyāvarta*. ||116-117||
This is not intended for ordinary people; it is suitable for kings.
This divine abode, which bestows contentment and nourishment, is a sanctuary of auspiciousness. Having taken recourse to some beautiful spot near a reservoir of water— ||118||

The pipe should be made twice or three times the height of the water-wheel; it should be capable of carrying away the water, smooth on the inside, and solid without gaps on the outside. When the water has been discharged from it, the house should be built during an auspicious moment.
It was provided with all kinds of medicinal herbs and filled with jars of gold;
it was adorned with various fragrant garlands and resounded with the humming of bees.
It was further furnished with wonderful pillars made of jewels or fashioned from gold.
Sometimes made from silver, or perhaps from deodar wood,
or from sandalwood, or from the excellent trees beginning with *sāla*—
whether numbering one hundred, thirty-two, or even sixteen. ||122-123||
Alternatively, it should be constructed with twenty-four pillars endowed with four [features], or with twelve,
or even with four that are most beautiful and well-adorned;
[the temple] should be decorated with various lattice-windows and highly variegated porticos at the front.
It was surrounded by altars and made delightful by pigeon-cots;
it was beautiful with charming carved statues and adorned with various mechanical birds,
as well as with pairs of monkeys and numerous groups of *jambhakas*.
Delightful with Vidyādharas, Siddhas, Bhujaṅgas, Kinnaras, and Cāraṇas;
its regions adorned by dancing peacocks of supreme beauty;
covered with various Kalpa-trees and clusters of variegated creepers and shrubs. 127.
Charming with rows of cuckoos, bees, and swarms of geese;
in its center, it possesses well-joined and fixed channels through which all the flowing streams pass;
provided with a central perforated tube, it is beautiful in its various forms. (128–129)
Having thoroughly applied a very firm coating with "vajralepa" and other substances around the well-joined tips of the tubes, which are supported by pillars, scales, and walls,
[one should apply a mixture] blended with the powders of lac, resin, and the horn of a ram.

A diamond-paste (vajralepa) thoroughly saturated with linseed oil and karañja oil serves as a means for firmly binding joints; it should be applied there twice or occasionally once. Furthermore, a plaster made from hemp fibers, śleṣmātaka, beeswax, and oils may also be used. ||131-132||
Then, having surrounded it on all sides with revolving water using an elevating machine,
the master builder should display to the king that which is joined with various descending movements;
within this [machine], he should depict pairs of elephants engaged in water-sports on all sides.
With eyes closed out of fear of the spray tossed by each other's trunks, they imitate the rainy season;
and seeing this, the elephant, full of joy, should discharge water like rut-fluid from his trunk, which acts as a hand for his fierce gaze. || 134-135 ||
There, a certain woman was creating a stream of water with her pair of breasts;
another was shedding drops of water like tears of joy through her eyelashes; and yet another bore a stream that seemed to have issued forth from the river-like navel-lake.
A woman should sprinkle [the king] as if with the rays from her fingernails.
By performing many such various, natural, and delightful gestures that cause agitation, the master builder should produce wonder in the king. (137-138)
In its center, a lion-throne fashioned from stainless gold and jewels should be prepared;
there the king, the lord of the earth, the divine Śrīpati, should sit.
At times, his joy increased by auspicious songs, he might bathe upon this throne.
Attended by those skilled in instrumental music and dance like the Lord of the Gods,
the king [remained] in this cool fountain-house with its clearly flowing streams, amidst the intense exhaustion of thick summer heat. ||140||
Beholding various waterworks, he would dwell in happiness; could this mortal not indeed be the Lord of the Gods residing upon the earth?
(141) One should construct another house, as before, provided with eight groups of clouds.
Then, by means of showers of falling rain, it receives the name "Pravarṣaṇa. In this rite, men wearing divine ornaments should be employed against each [of the directions]:
three handsome men according to the rule, or four, or seven, who are very firm. ||142-143||
Then, having fashioned those men with a mechanical device of equal height— or one that is a quarter less—
and provided them with mouths and tubes, he should fill them with pure water. Thereupon, he should seal all the apertures through which the water might enter the men.
Then he should release all the water-channels of the limbs;
men release their water along with the mouths and conduits by unblocking the doors, discharging it at will in various falls like a painter [creating diverse patterns]. (145–146)
In this manner, he may at will pour forth water from these clouds— either all at once, or with an interval of two [days], or with an interval of three— most wonderfully and in great abundance.
This is the first ancestral abode of various forms belonging to the Lord of Rati.
It is the dwelling place of variegated colors and the sole imitation of the clouds.
In the summer heat, for whom does the cooling of the sun’s scorching rays by the falling streams of milk not become an exceedingly great source of joy to the eyes?
(148) Now, [it may be supported] by one pillar, or four, or eight, or even twelve.
Or one may construct here a charming two-storeyed house using sixteen [pillars];
it should be square, endowed with four *bhadras*, joined with all walls,
provided with *īlīs* and gateways, and fashioned in the shape of a *puṣpaka*.
Above that, situated in the center, a firm courtyard pool (prāṅgaṇavāpī) should be constructed;
in its middle, a pericarp (karṇikā) adorned with lotus petals should be made.
In all four corners of it, beautiful wooden pillars (dārudārikā) should be erected.
With their eyes fixed upon the central lotus, adorned with ornaments and full of amorous passion,
they [should remain] while the lord of the earth is seated upon the lotus according to the previously described application of the yantra;
thereafter, the courtyard pond should be filled with pure water from golden jars (bhṛṅgāra).
Having filled that pond with water contained within its inner lining,
[the image] certainly rises up on all sides, surpassing even the best perfumes,
through all its complete, variegated, and beautiful forms carved upon the face-cloth. (154)
It releases water through its limbs— the nose, mouth, ears, eyes, and so forth;
this most wonderful fountain-house, known as a *praṇālā*,
maintains its presence upon the courtyard ground of that ornament of kings.
The master builder likewise accomplishes this with his clever intellect;
thus, both of these are highly venerable among those of perfected wisdom.
A beautiful, very firm, and profoundly deep square pond should be constructed.
Then, her inner chamber should be made with its joints plastered;
it should have an entrance and exit established by means of a subterranean tunnel, with the door placed below, and the upper part covered by beautiful rain-spouts. 157–158.
Then, according to the method taught in the Citra-adhyāya, it should be adorned with variegated patterns;
its middle portion should be fashioned to resemble the garment of the Lord of Waters (Varuṇa),
with lotus stalks emerging upwards, produced from the patta-kanda.
Then, one should fill with water for sprinkling the entire area up to the edge of the stainless lotus— which has been illuminated by the rays of the sun situated within its central pericarp—
having properly constructed a beautiful abode according to this very method. ||160-161||
Its side-galleries, archways, and gates were fashioned with various forms and ingenious designs;
it was made beautiful by long halls extending in all four directions,
and it was adorned even with artificial fish, crocodiles, and birds born of the water.
One should have a lotus-filled pond constructed through the employment of skilled artisans.

There, the chief men among the neighboring vassals, having obtained shelter by means of the king's command, and the envoys arrived from foreign kingdoms, should remain stationed here in secret. ||163-164||
Then, having witnessed the water-sports performed according to the rules in the manner previously described,
the delighted king should ascend the couch.
While the king is seated there, surrounded by his attendants—
Surrounded on all sides by courtesans in a place where the light was submerged beneath the water.
Just as the joy of the Lord of Serpents becomes boundless and filled with delight in his subterranean abode,
so too [is the joy] in the previously mentioned pond, constructed in its center with four pillars. 166.
Then one should have a *laṭabha* pavilion constructed, adorned with pearls and coral;
having filled the area around the pond with flowers, one should make it very firm and beautiful on all sides with inner walls featuring *svastika* patterns and excellent exits. ||167-168||

Within that palace, the king enjoys himself happily in the pleasure-pond, playing with his playful companions by means of diving and surfacing: submerged in one place and seen again in another, they strike him with water and then vanish. (170–171)
Then, standing at the edge of the pond, she bowed low with shame, covering the weight of her breasts with her sprout-like hand.
Here, a fortunate man gazes upon his beloved woman, whose garment is tightly clinging to her as she is released from the obstruction of the water;
we shall now properly describe the construction of wooden carriages, swings, and other such devices.
That which is proclaimed as the fifth, the activity of rotating the mechanical device (yantra), consists of these five swings (dolaka):
Vāsanta, Madananivāsa, Vasantatilaka, Vibhramaka, and Tripura; these five are thus described. (173–174)
One should dig four pillars that are straight, very firm, equal in intervals,
and resting on well-polished pedestals, aligned with a single cord;
these should be erected according to the dimensions of the site in the direction prescribed for the temple, having a length of eight cubits.
A delightful underground chamber should be constructed with a depth of half that [measurement].

Within its interior floor, a pillar should be made, resting upon a base of iron; it should be equipped with a rotating mechanism, provided with a pedestal, and covered by supporting beams (*tulā*) that enclose it. ||176-177||
Having firmly established upon the pedestal a well-proportioned *kumbhikā* (dome-base),

one should then enclose it with eight auspicious pillars rising to the height of a bow (*dhanus*). Thereafter, one may construct the height of the floor above it according to one's own desire, ensuring it is perfectly straight.
One should place a pillar-capital (stambhaśīrṣa) joined with a cloth-band above the wrapping;
up to the point of the diamond-joint (hīragraha), the elephant-head (gajaśīrṣikā) should be fashioned—firmly constructed with effort and pleasing to the mind, according to its beauty. ||179-180||
Upon the cloth, a four-sided platform should be made according to the desired measurement of the site;

upon that, a floor-base (talabandha) with a very firm foundation should be constructed. Then, twelve pillars, beautiful and properly erected, should be placed on the site according to the rules. ||181||
The ground situated at the corner of the Rūpavatī should be made larger;
a circular path (bhrama) should be constructed in its center, established upon the central pillar.
Then, according to the measurement of the site, one should cover it with cloths (paṭṭas). ||182-183||
And likewise, upon the tips of the chariot-riders' crests,
one should place five rotating wheels above the fruit-shaped pinnacle and upon the central pillar.
Above that, for the sake of beauty, a tiered platform in the shape of a flower should be constructed.
Supported by a central pillar and adorned with a vase-shaped finial at its summit, there is a revolving platform beneath the pillar upon which the stage floor rotates rapidly;
it is equipped with a chariot and a bee-hive mechanism that turns one another via a wheel-contrivance. ||185–186||

The king, who brings a festival for the eyes, performs in the abode of the gods that which is celebrated as the "Vasantarathikā-bhrama"— a dance characterized by an exceeding grace produced by the whirling of noble women mounted upon it.
In the spring season, he indeed becomes the abode of stainless fame.
