Then, having erected a single firm pillar devoid of underground chambers and the like, a floor four cubits high should be constructed above it. 187–188.
In the center, one should provide a bee-design; all else here should be executed as previously described.
One should also fashion the *puṣpaka* on the pillar, slightly loosened and surmounted by a *kalaśa*.
Above that, a neck (*grīvā*) provided with four seats (*āsana*) should be constructed.
Two bell-pillars, exceedingly strong, should be constructed there along with the main pillar.
Thus, while the hidden person remains within the interior space of the *puṣpaka* platform,
he should properly and gradually set in motion the collection of rotating machine-wheels.
Meanwhile, those fawn-eyed women remained there upon the chariot-seats in the Puṣpaka;
all of them wandered about, their eyes fixed with curiosity upon the abode of Kāma.
Then, he began to fix four very firm pillars at the corners of the rafters.
They should be arranged upon well-joined pedestals, equidistant from one another according to the dimensions of the site. Above them, a floor should be constructed joined with lattice-work.
There, four chariot-paths (rathikās) arise, situated in the cardinal directions as before.
Above that, a half-floor should be constructed with well-jointed wooden joints;
it should be provided with a central turret, adorned with figures, and equipped with a *mattavāraṇa* (elephant-ornament).
From the spring [quarter], the outer line should consist of various types of architectural work.
Having beheld the Vasantatilaka temple of the gods, which is delightful with the whirling of all its chariot-warriors on wheels set in motion by the friction of one another's mechanical levers;
One approaches [the subject] as if it were an ornament, yet one does not fall into astonishment.

Having first prepared the stage for the purpose of mastering other treatises, the ground should be made four-cornered, beautiful in form, endowed with the four excellences, and well-ordered. (195–196)
O auspicious lady, bees should be placed in restraint at every corner;
above that on the ground, eight-seated bees should be made.
Pure lines should be drawn, and others should be decorated both inside and out.
Then, other stages should be constructed situated in the middle of the pedestals (pīṭha).
By means of wheels placed in the center of the pedestal and joined to one another by spokes,
all the bees, together with their offspring, whirl about with speed in the revolution.
He who, while seated on a swing,
performed such exceedingly wonderful amorous dalliances among the abodes of the gods that he surpassed even the most skilled courtesans.
His fame, ever-surging, brings joy to the lord of the earth; it does not even find room within the three worlds.
Then, having made the sacrificial field square and divided it into eight parts:
O auspicious one, with the remaining parts, one should fashion a square upon that [base].
Its height should be twice that, according to the number of divisions of its tiers.
Among those, the first tier should be four parts in height.
There, the tiers (bhūmikā) above one another are successively reduced by eight, six, and four parts;
thus, they become three [tiers] joined with half-parts.
The bell (ghaṇṭā) should be made square in body and its height equal to the remaining portion.
The two [upper] floors, consisting of three and four [parts], should have a width increased by six and four parts respectively.
On the first floor there should be a courtyard (raṅga), and on the second floor there should likewise be corner galleries (rathikā).
There should also be auspicious, well-proportioned balconies (bhadra) and delightful swings (dolā).
On the third floor, chariot-pavilions (rathikās) should be constructed, which are exceedingly beautiful in the auspicious (bhadra) sections;
furthermore, seats should be placed in the corners, and a circular walkway (bhrama) should also be made in the half-vāstuka sections.
In that [structure], there should be a swing-chariot pavilion, four seats, and a circular walkway with eight seats.
That which is the single position of the young woman here is said to be the *āsana*;
all other [positions] assume a rotation facing toward that [central] rotation.
Where these *āsanas* exist, that is called *bhrama* (the whirl) here, and it is considered superior. 207–208.
Above and below the sacrificial post (yaṣṭi), one should join a single wheel for rotation;
likewise, one should fix small wheels upon the seats here.
Firm pegs should be made, attached to the circumference of the small wheels' spokes.
All [the spokes] should be of equal intervals and very light, attached to a wheel-hub. A small wheel at the tip of the charioteer’s banner-pole should be made, joined with spokes that rotate;
four staffs should be provided, equipped with two wheels set crosswise upon the sword.
Above the second level, one should place the mechanisms between the third level;
these machines are fixedly attached to the revolving shafts of the chariot.
[212] The support-shafts of the seats are joined to the wheels of the chariot.
Below, one should fashion four equal intervals for the enclosures (parivartaka).
Then, within the interior of the swing of the second floor, one should fix two poles at equal intervals;
likewise, one should place them upon a single wheel joined [to the structure] between the southern and northern wheels.
Similarly, one should place four staffs from below, joined at their upper ends to the corner-rathikas and the wheel;
these two-wheeled [staffs] are then to be fixed to the other two wheels.
At the two outer wheels, they are joined to the corner-rathikas and the wheel.
The central pillar should be placed within a swing-frame, with successive cross-beams extending horizontally.
One should construct the door in the eastern part of the *bhadra* section, adorned below with steps;
then, one should install the deity’s swing on the western side of the inner sanctum (*garbha*).

Having correctly understood the mutual rotation like a whirling wheel and its liberation according to the prescribed method, one should employ that which moves swiftly or moves slowly as required. Thus, the path of rotation has been clearly described by us in brief.
In the same manner, it should also be properly constructed for the purpose of causing [the image] to move;
it should be fashioned from firm and smooth materials such as pillars and other substances, with well-joined joints, and supported by long primary pillars. ||219–220||

One should properly construct Tripura, surrounded on all sides by turrets (tilakas) and provided with lion-ears (siṃhakarṇas), made variegated in form by various paintings. It should be equipped with previously designed machines fashioned by the intellect; for one who thoroughly understands this chapter on machines (yantrādhyāya).

He attains his desired objectives accompanied by fame, and he is honored daily by the lords of the earth. This entire circle of twelve kings revolves at will around this crest-jewel of monarchs, its existence dependent upon the pillar of his arm.
That illustrious king, the sole delight of the world, quickly composed this chapter on machines along with the various arrays of machines devised by his own intellect.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Chapter on Machines," in the *Vāstuśāstra*— also known as the *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*— composed by the great emperor, the illustrious Bhojadeva.
Now begins the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Elephant Stable.
We shall now describe the characteristics of elephant stables. Having made the site square and divided it into eight parts: ||1||

In the center, one should construct a space for the elephant with a width of two parts. The sections should be arranged like those of a palace, in the order of superior, middling, and inferior. Outside of that, there should be a veranda (alinda) one part wide, and another [veranda] outside of that as well.
The wall should consist of one part, situated outside the second portico (alinda).
At the location of its door, both kūrpara-angles should be constructed;
a *karṇaprāsādikā* should be made, resting upon the second portico.
One should construct two windows on each of the three walls;
when the hall has its gable-end facing east at the front, it is called Subhadra.
When this same hall has its wings and gable-end at the entrance, [it is called Yamala].
Then, a hall named Nandinī should be constructed for the increase of the world.
When there are two "fore-necks" (prāggrīva) on its two sides,
it is proclaimed as the third type, named Subhogadā.

When another [hall] is placed upon the back of this very one with its front facing east, it is called the Bhadrikā hall; it bestows nourishment upon elephants. The fifth is square and is honored by the name Varṣaṇī.
The sixth [type of hall] is likewise deficient in a front porch, an inner courtyard, and a turret;
it is a "destructive" hall that robs one of grain, wealth, and life.
Therefore, one should avoid this one and construct the others for the accomplishment of all goals.

"A hall renowned here as *pramārikā* would lead to the destruction of life, crops, and wealth; therefore, one should not construct it. However, those [other halls] as described should be built for the increase of life and riches.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Elephant Stable," in the *Vāstuśāstra* known by the alternative name *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*, composed by the Great King of Kings, Śrī Bhojadeva.
Now begins the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Horse-Stable.
Herein, the characteristics of the horse-stable are declared in detail:
it should be constructed on the site designated as Gandharva within the layout of one's own dwelling.
Alternatively, the place for the horses' residence at the site known as Puṣpadanta is proclaimed to be one hundred *aratnis* in length;
that which is eighty *aratnis* long is middling, and sixty *aratnis* is the lowest.
The place for the horses should be made on a spacious, secluded, beautiful, and clean stretch of land;
it should be level, quadrangular, auspicious,
and situated in a location that is easy to traverse.
One should perform that [rite] on ground free from low-lying thickets, trees, stumps, shrines, temples, and dwellings, as well as free from anthills and gravel; it should be secluded,
devoid of hidden obstacles, and sloping toward the east or the north.
Having observed that the site must be prepared in such a manner, those who are well-composed,
on an auspicious day approved by the Brahmins,
should examine the divisions of the ground and bring trees that are beautiful. ||6-7||
One should avoid trees that have grown in cremation grounds, in temples, or in other forbidden places; having brought auspicious trees near the husband's house, [one should plant them]. 8.90–91ab.

Then one should examine the ground—whether it be praiseworthy or delightful. A stable for horses should not be constructed on a funeral pyre site, an anthill, in a village, a grain field, or a threshing floor, nor in monasteries. ||9-10||
There will be suffering for the master regarding the village, grain, and threshing floors;
by building a house in a cremation ground, one should predict death for men. A site established upon a playground or an anthill will lead to misfortune.

A house built with trees that serve as shrines (caitya) causes constant distress and brings about the ruin of ascetics; it generates divine calamities, causes the destruction of women, and inspires fear of malevolent spirits. ||12-13||
A dwelling constructed for a master with thorny trees becomes a source of grief;
built upon ground that is cracked or elevated, it brings about ruin;
and a house built on ground that is sloping causes hunger and fear.
Therefore, for the sake of the horse’s prosperity, its stable should be constructed on excellent ground—auspicious, beautiful, square, pleasing to the mind, and auspicious;
such a dwelling brings about well-being. (15–16)
Just as the horses of the master pass on his left side when he goes out,
the architect should construct the stables for the horses accordingly;
and that [stable] should be situated to the south of the area of the inner apartments.
Just as their neighing at the time of entry is auspicious when directed toward the south,
so should the stables for the horses be constructed for the benefit of the master;
its entrance should be made facing either the east or the north, and it should be provided with an ornamental archway (toraṇa).
It was joined with a porch at the front, consisting of four halls that were spacious;
it was ten cubits in height and eight cubits in width,
beautified by ivory pegs, and provided with half-walls in the front.
Or, on the back wall, one should arrange the stations there;
they should face either eastward or northward,
measuring one cubit in length and three cubits in width.
One should have them made tall, with their upper portions elevated and square; one should prepare the ground within them so that it is high at the front and easy to traverse.
In the middle of the line, however, there should be a space of one cubit on all sides.
And it was covered with firm wooden planks that were smooth, closely fitted, and made from dhātaki, arjuna, punnāga, kakubha, and other such trees;
they were eight finger-breadths in height and one and a half cubits in width. ||24-25||

The place for fodder should be provided with flawless, solid, and well-fastened wooden beams on both sides, free from insects, according to the opinion of physicians, and it should be beautifully strewn with auspicious bundles of straw.

It should be three *kiṣkus* high, well-composed in a secluded spot. One should construct a food-storage pit measuring two cubits in size, well-smeared, free from foul odors, and equal in both width and height. (27–28)
At various places, three very firm spikes shaped like crowns (kapiśīrṣaka) should be prepared;
two should be placed in front for the purpose of restraining the five limbs,
and one should be securely arranged behind for the purpose of binding.
Leaving aside the four corners of the hall, which measure four cubits in extent,
one should place all the ritual materials (guru-gaṇas) in these locations.
There, one should perform the bali offering, the fire sacrifice (homa), the recitation of auspicious prayers (svastivācana), and the chanting (japa).
In summer, the ground there should be well-swept and sprinkled with water;
in the rainy season, it should be free from mud and water; and in the winter, it should be pleasantly enclosed.
Horses should stay there without fearing excessive crowding.
They should be arranged so that they do not touch one another and are free from all obstructions.
One should prepare a place for the fire in the south-eastern direction and place a water-pot slightly toward the eastern quarter.
In the northeastern direction (brāhmī), a place for fodder should be prepared;
and in the northwest (vāyavī) direction, a place for the mortar should be prepared.
Ladders, kusha grass mats, and wells should be made, covered with wooden planks.
Shovels, hoes, balls of clay, fermented gruel, and likewise horse-shoes; hair-seizers, horns, and even axes;
as well as lamps—these are for the use of horses and cattle. (36–37)
In the southwest (Nairṛta) direction, there should be a collection of articles for easy movement;
for the purpose of protection against fire-related calamities,
a wise person should keep nearby items useful for breaking bonds, such as water, lamps, and so forth.
And one should prepare various vessels with the desire to remove [the afflictions], such as:
a hand-held stone, a lamp, a ladle, a hoe, sandals, various colorful baskets, and many kinds of enema bags. ||39-40||
One should diligently arrange other such items as well;
vessels supported by pillars in front are prescribed for the armor and other equipment.
One should station the horse in a house facing the east, in the western direction.
In the eastern quarter, or even in the region of Mitra and Varuṇa, many [beings] exist; by that [quarter], they attain prosperity.
For that direction is proclaimed as worthy of worship and worthy of praise.
In rites of fire-offerings (homa), pacification (śāntika), and charity, as well as in other supreme religious acts,
the eastern quarter— presided over by Śakra himself—
is praised; for in that direction, the sun rises in its natural course.
He follows behind the horses in due order toward the west.
Those who desire auspiciousness should perform the bathing, the perfuming, the worship, and other supreme rites for the horses while they face the east. (45–46)
When this is done, there is an increase in the king's power over the land, his allies, and his fame; therefore, the eastern direction is praised.
That place shall become one that bestows prosperity upon the master through the first morsel of food.
In a hall facing south, there is a place that grants desired objects for horses,
prepared in the position of the Fire-god;
that direction is presided over by Agni, and Agni is the very soul of horses.
There, the horse may become old and a great consumer of fodder;
yet, even in a dwelling facing north, horses obtain auspiciousness.
For horses situated thus, the sun remains to their right.
Having circumambulated them clockwise, he rises and departs;
then, having stationed the horse to his left, they proceed facing north.
The moon and the sun rejoice [at this], and thus one should bind the horses.
The king obtains victory, success, sons, and long life;
the horses become free from disease and increase his progeny.
One should cause them to face south, but not when they are armored for battle, nor when they are leading the way.
For purposes other than ancestral rites (pitṛkārya), the southern direction is indeed to be avoided.
This is because all the departed spirits (pretas) are established in this very direction;
the sun rises from the left and sets toward the south.
And when Soma is in the Pṛṣṭha [nakṣatra], horses afflicted by the gods suffer from various disorders caused by the planets; overwhelmed by enemies,
they are tormented by fear and diseases and do not wish to eat their fodder.
They cause defeat, dissatisfaction, and misfortune for their master;
therefore, one should never under any circumstances tether horses facing south or those that have been tied up facing west. ||57-58||
The sun rises from behind and sets in front;
therefore, there can be no victory for a lord who follows behind it,
because he follows Śakra and acts contrary to the course of the sun.
Diseases that swiftly destroy their bodies arise within them;
because of these, they brood, tremble, and fall into terror at the sight of water;
they take no pleasure in fodder and utterly abandon their patience.
If the horses are bound facing the southeast (āgneyī) direction,
then they suffer from various diseases arising from blood and bile (raktapitta),
and they bring about the master's imprisonment, death, or consumption of the heart.
Furthermore, there will be fear for the horses caused by fire and burning;
there will be defeat for the master, obstacles, and even danger to his life, if the mounts are bound facing the southwest (Nairṛti) direction. (63–64)
Then they take no pleasure in eating, drinking, or food;
as they repeatedly tear up the earth with their hooves,
they neigh many times upon seeing humans, birds, and beasts.
And standing all around the Nairṛtī direction, they cause their limbs to whirl;
in whatever way these enraged Rākṣasas act, they bring about their destruction.
Or, if through ignorance the horses are driven toward the Vāyavyā direction, they are bound.
Then they will be afflicted daily by wind-related diseases;
the body of the lord will become unsteady, and there will be distress for those who depend on horses.
There will be death among men, and fear arising from famine.
Horses tied facing the northeast perish;
this should be declared for those tied facing the rising sun.
When horses are tied while resorting to the direction of Brahmā (the east), [they are bound]. 69–70.
Those who dwell there are bound by celestial planets and afflictions born of their own thoughts;
the performance of funeral rites and offerings to the gods does not bring victory to their lord.
Furthermore, the horses born there result in the suffering of the twice-born.
Furthermore, it is not recommended to place a horse in a stall along the length of the beam;
for that would lead to indigestion for its master and to the destruction of the horses.
Therefore, one should always keep the horses in an auspicious location.
The sick should not be kept for even a moment in the presence of the healthy,
because diseases may afflict even the healthy through contact with those who are ill.
To the east of the stable for horses, an infirmary should be constructed.
To his left, one should arrange all the necessary provisions;
for the sake of the horses' medicine, one should also set down containers,
as well as antidotes, medicinal herbs, oils, wicks, and salts.
Near the medicinal storehouse, one should construct a house for funeral offerings (ariṣṭa),
as well as a residence for the sick and a stable for horses;
that too must be made very secure, like the previously described buildings.
These four houses should be constructed as interconnected,
with walls made firm by a plastering of lime, and provided with front porches and lofty gateways;
all four should be made spacious and easy of access.
One should protect the horses stationed in such dwellings as these.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Horse Stable," in the *Vāstuśāstra* composed by the Great King of Kings, the illustrious Bhojadeva, also known by the name *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*.
Now begins the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "That Which Should Not Be Used and That Which Should Be Used."
In the dwellings of kings, army commanders, and even those of the [four] orders; or in the courtyards of houses, in assembly halls, and in temples;
or upon beds, seats, and vehicles, and in vessels and ornaments—
Regarding umbrellas, banners, flags, and all types of implements—
those which are not to be employed and those which are to be employed—
they shall now be explained in detail for the benefit of embodied beings.
We shall first describe here those [mantras] which are exclusively unfit for use in the dwellings of the aforementioned kings and others;
in those [dwellings], not even a single deity should be invoked.
The Daityas, the planets, the stars, the Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and Rākṣasas;
the Piśācas, the Pitṛs, the Pretas, the Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and Uragas;
the Cāraṇas, the hosts of Bhūtas, as well as their women and sons—[all these were present].
The doorkeepers, the female doorkeepers, and those who hold authority over them;
their weapons and all the hosts of Apsarases;
as well as those initiated for sacrifice, those observing vows, heretics, atheists, and those tormented by hunger—[all these were struck down].
Those afflicted by disease, bondage, weapons, fire, oil, blood, mud, or dust;
those suffering from colic, fever, and other such ailments; and other men of this kind, including those intoxicated, insane, dull-witted, impotent, naked, blind, deaf, and so forth. || 8-9 ||
Swinging on swings and the capturing of elephants are not approved;
battles between gods and asuras, and conflicts among kings, are likewise forbidden.
Fights between living beings, violent crushings, and hunting are not praised.
The sentiments of fury, dejection, wonder, terror, disgust, and compassion—excluding the comic and the erotic—should not be directed toward living beings.
[One should also avoid depicting] elephants, horses, chariots, vehicles, celestial palaces, and temples. ||11-12||
The houses and forests were ablaze with fierce fires;
the trees were devoid of flowers and fruit, their habitats defiled by the presence of birds;
they were stunted with only one or two branches, rough, broken, withered, and full of hollows.

The kadamba, śālmalī, śelu, tārakṣa, āraluka, and others, as well as those trees that are pungent and thorny, are not accepted because they are the abodes of spirits. Among birds, vultures, owls, pigeons, hawks, and crows [are likewise excluded]. ||14-15||
The heron, as well as those birds that roam at night, are not praised;
nor are elephants, horses, buffaloes, camels, cats, donkeys, and monkeys;
[nor] the lion, the tiger, the hyena, the boar, the deer, and the jackal. (16)

Likewise, those who roam the forests, carnivorous beasts and birds—these should not be made [as attendants] in the house, nor those who dwell in mountains and wilds. By making these, the teacher is deprived of his wealth. (17–18)
The master of the house encounters terrible disease, calamity, and even imprisonment; wherever he may be, he suffers loss of wealth and defeat,
and quickly meets with exile, bondage, ruin, or death.
Thus have been described the things that are not recommended for householders in their homes.
Hereafter, those things which are to be employed there will be told.
Whatever devotion one may have toward a particular object, and whichever be one's family deity (kuladevatā), [that should be honored]. 21.
By constructing them according to the measurements prescribed for the hand, one incurs no fault.
On both sides of that door, two well-adorned door-keepers (pratīhārau) should be fashioned,
their hands busily holding staffs of cane, and equipped with sheaths for swords as their attire.
Endowed with beauty and youth, adorned with various garments and ornaments,
Dhātrī, Vāmanikā, and Kubjā were surrounded by their female companions,
On both sides of the door, charming female door-keepers (pratīhāryaḥ) should be fashioned,
as well as corresponding treasures marked with the brilliant signs of the conch and the lotus,
carrying heaps of jewels, pearls, and gold emerging from their mouths. ||25||
Or she may stand upon a lotus, holding a full vase, adorned with jewels and garments;
[she is characterized] by curved [limbs] standing upwards, filled with flowers, fruits, and sprouts, and by a full vase, a goad, an umbrella, a śrīvṛkṣa tree, a mirror, and a chowrie. ||26-27||
At the entrance, the eight auspicious symbols (aṣṭamaṅgala) should be fashioned with garlands of conch shells and fish;
situated in the center of the door-mandala, the goddess Śrī should be depicted being bathed by the finest elephants,
seated upon a lotus throne, holding a lotus in her hand, and beautifully adorned.
A bull, or a cow with its calf, adorned with an umbrella, garlands, and ornaments;
[the mountain was also graced] with various kinds of fruits and foods offered for sustenance, and with various flowers and fruits, and with bending śāla trees standing in all directions. ||29-30||
Variegated leaf-patterns should be painted on the outer and inner walls,
featuring swans, kāraṇḍava ducks, and cakravāka birds resting upon lotus leaves,
along with young boys playing with graceful arms.

The women, intent on amorous play, are settled in the dwelling place, adorned with various ornaments and garments; the hero, however, by chance, has a pale complexion and wears only a few beautiful decorations. (32-33)
With their slightly slender limbs,

they should be made eager for amorous dalliance by the *campaka*, *aśoka*, *punnāga*, mango, and *tilaka* trees, which possess spreading branches and thickets and tremble with their reddish shoots. (34)
The garden grounds should be adorned with trees provided with shade, flowers, and fruit, as well as others, resounding with the warbling of cuckoos and bees;
and the seasons should be represented, decorated with their respective characteristic signs such as fruits and flowers. ||35-36||
Adorned with delightful distinctions and birds appropriate for the season,
their girdles were formed by kadamba, kurara, krauñca, haṃsa, and sārasa birds;
they were further embellished by groves of cane and ketakī trees growing along their banks.
The ponds were covered with lotus groves and fish submerged within the water;
and on the lower portions of the house walls, there were paintings of long ponds, along with fruits, edible sugarcane, and vessels of precious gems and gold. (38–39)
Drinking halls should be depicted with lotus leaves arranged [as seats] and filled with blue lotuses;
likewise, joyful women skilled in dance and song, holding various musical instruments in their hands,
should be painted in the places for spectacles and musical performances.
Cakoras, parrots, and mainas should be kept in cages;
likewise, delighted cuckoos, peacocks, and cocks—these are the creatures that have been prescribed for being maintained in the house. ||41-42||
All of those are commended even among all types of implements;
likewise, persons born of divine origins are praised, whereas those who are censured,
as well as those who cry out in distress, are not recommended for use on couches, beds, seats, and the like.
Those which have been mentioned here previously and those which are to be employed [now],
these are recommended for use in the inner apartments, in assemblies, and in temples;
as well as in narratives, tales, and the like, concerning divine and human matters.

Those auspicious [signs] have been declared as many as they are for paintings and other such works; thus it has been stated what is not to be employed and what is to be employed by means of the intellect in houses,
beds, rooms, temples, and so forth.
He who constructs according to what has been stated and avoids that which is censured becomes worthy of honor by kings and artisans.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Unfit and the Fit," in the *Vāstuśāstra* composed by the Great King of Kings, Śrī Bhojadeva, also known as the *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*.
Now begins the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Installation of the Stone. Now we shall describe here the procedure for the installation of the stone according to the scriptures:
at the northern solstice, during the auspicious bright fortnight, on a favorable day. ||1||

On a day when the planets are stable and the astrological configurations (karaṇa) are auspicious, one should perform the laying of the foundation stone during the asterisms of Tiṣya, Aśvinī, Rohiṇī, the three Uttaras,
Revatī, Śravaṇa, and Hasta.
One should undertake the construction of a dwelling when there is the rising of a stable zodiac sign aspected by benefics and friends,
when there are auspicious omens, favorable portents, and the recitation of blessings for a holy day,
and when joy has arisen in the mind. ||3-4||
Noble by nature, learned in the scriptures, pure, bathed, and composed,
the master builder (sthapati), having performed the rites of worship to the gods, should commence his work on a site that is full,
level, symmetrical, and faultless.
A wise man should examine the first layer of stone for auspicious signs:
[the presence of] jars, goads, banners, umbrellas, fish, chowries, and archways;
as well as dūrvā grass, nāgaphala fruits, turbans, flowers, svastikas, and sacrificial altars. ||6-7||
Adorned with *nandyāvarta* designs, yak-tail fans, tortoises, lotuses, and moons,
as well as excellent thunderbolt-patterned enclosures, they are conducive to success in one's undertakings.
They may be long, short, small, uneven, lustrous, inflated, or unexamined.
A footprint that is confused in direction, lacking limbs, containing bone or charcoal,
mixed with gravel, fragmented, burnt by overcooking, cracked, or black brings fear of calamity;
however, footprints of men, cattle, and horses lead to prosperity and well-being.
One should avoid stones touched by the feet of carnivorous animals or birds.
These four types of stones are Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, and Pūrṇā;
likewise, they are known as Vāsiṣṭhī, Kāśyapī, Bhārgavī, and Āṅgirasī.
There, in the northeastern direction of the site or dwelling,
or in the southwest, one should prepare a square altar, level and covered with flowers, measuring the size of an ox-hide, and provided with fragrant jars.
In the southeast, one should first install the stone of Nandā in due order,
[using] roots that are not out of season, free from defects, along with lotuses, water-lilies, and sprouts;
and with all medicinal herbs, gold and other materials, as well as vessels made of gold, silver, or clay.
One should also consecrate her with copper jars using mantras;
one should perform the consecration with waters from sacred fords and springs, containing gems, unbroken rice, and lotuses, fragrant and accompanied by the proclamation of an auspicious day.
The water of great rivers originating from the Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Revā, Sarasvatī, and others is praised, as is that produced at auspicious bathing-places (tīrthas);
likewise, so too is water born from mountains, forests, ponds, and divine abodes.
One should bring water for the purpose of consecration as it may be obtained;
and with this mantra, one should perform the consecration over them:
"Golden-hued, purifying, pure, and destroyers of evil. (18–19)
"May the peaceful, glorious waters, dripping with honey, purify you. Then,
having bathed the stone with water purified by mantras,
the master mason should anoint it with auspicious fragrant paste.
Having strewn it with fragrant powder of Himalayan sandalwood,
one should quickly cover her with parched grain, garlands of flowers,
incense, floral offerings, curd, meat, unbroken rice, and other such items. ||21-22||

One should worship the goddess Iṣṭakā with abundant pairs of garments. Then, at the southwest corner of the dwelling, one should honor an equal number of pure and wise Brāhmaṇas who are stationed there with sacrificial fees and fruits.

Amidst the sounds of the syllable *oṃ*, the word *svasti*, the proclamation of *puṇyāha*, and the resonance of songs and musical instruments, the performer— with his hair standing on end from joy— should offer salutations to them,
and then present the sacrificial offering (*bali*) to Vāstoṣpati and to the elemental spirits (*bhūta*).
One should fashion other secondary stones (upaśilā) separately for those four;
two should bear the marks of a wall and a svastika, and likewise one marked with the śrīvatsa.
In the case of the full [altar], there should be one nandyāvarta mark, respectively.
One should first establish Nandā beneath the southeast corner of the site;
then, in sequence, the others—Bhadrā and the rest—in the other three corners.
These are the installation mantras for all four of them.
These four rivers, which reveal eternal beginnings and were sung by the sages,
were consecrated by the noble Vedas with the power of the primordial Boar;
first, I shall establish Nandā, the daughter of Vasiṣṭha.
On an auspicious day at a favorable moment, you were placed within Nanda’s household.
May you bring about long life for its provider and the highest prosperity here;
you are auspicious and beneficial in every way, O blessed one—may all that is auspicious be ordained for you.
May prosperity attend the two beloved sons of Kaśyapa, the householder;
may victory be the lot of the lord of this great-souled home.
May his fame sprout here upon the earth as long as the moon and sun endure.

"When the full moon is placed upon the site of the dwelling, this master of the house becomes one whose desires are fulfilled; thus, with the recitation of mantras and auspicious blessings, one should perform the rite of laying the foundation. (33-34)
With those wonderful, gold-colored bricks,
the city was built so as to incline toward the northeast— blessed indeed— and not toward the southwest;
they were used for the construction of altars, temples, walls, and the city itself.
On the canopy, in the arrangement of the altar-mound, in the temple of the Four-faced One (Brahmā),
on the altars for the rites of pacification, and during the installation of the images,
one should install the stones in due order according to the sacrificial injunctions. ||36-37||

With the *Sāman* chants characterized by the *triṣṭubh*, *jagatī*, and *anuṣṭubh* meters, along with the great vows (*mahāvrata*), and following the sequence of the *gāyatrī*, *uṣṇih*, *anuṣṭubh*, and *bṛhatī*,
he should pile all four layers; thereafter, he should cease.
Having understood the measurement of the wall and the fourfold arrangement of the citi,
one should thus complete the initial rite, from the smallest up to the highest.
First, those [bricks] are established on the ground, well-positioned and level.

One must not cause it to shake; if it shakes, there will be great danger for the master of the house. One should know that trembling brings fear, whereas their steadiness brings supreme auspiciousness to both the architect and the master of the house. (41)
If there is movement toward the east-south (Agni), there is great danger for the master of the house;
in the south-west (Nairṛti), the destruction of the wife; in the direction of the Wind (Vāyu), emptiness and fear;
and in the north-east (Īśāna), there is danger from the teacher—even if there is improper conduct, that [danger] shall arise.
Having established [the image] in this manner first, one should not move even the pillars, nor should one lift them up or push them; for the procedure for these two is the same.
Therefore, being fully concentrated, one should first perform the installation correctly.
Just as one is a master of stones, so too is he in every respect a master of pillars, gates, walls, halls, cities, and dwellings;
since the rule for these is measured by that [same standard], he should be honored therein. ||45-46||
Thus has this procedure for the laying of the foundation stone been duly taught by us here.
When this is performed, houses, temples, and other structures reach completion without any obstacle.

Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Laying of the Foundation Stone," in the *Vāstuśāstra* known as the *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*, composed by the great king of kings, the illustrious Bhojadeva.
Now begins the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Ritual for Offering the Bali Sacrifice.
Now we shall describe the sequence of the ritual for the form of the bali offering,
by which the gods, together with Maheśvara, become pleased when worshipped.
One should prepare a mandala for the Vāstu deity in the center with cow dung;
there, one should place a water-pot (kalaśa) containing flowers and gold. Then, the deities of the Vāstu should be assigned according to their respective positions.
Afterwards, one should present the arghya with various kinds of excellent garlands.
One should worship Viśvakarman with garlands, incense, and ointments;
being well-composed, one should honor him with many kinds of edible foods and fruits.
One should worship Śikhin again with clarified butter, milk, and curd;
one should worship Parjanya with grains such as śāli rice, wheat, and mung beans.
One should worship Jayanta with mangoes, grapes, dates, and the like.
One should worship the Lord of the Thirty-three with *mālatī* and *mallikā* flowers,
as well as with red flowers, incense, and anointments of red sandalwood.
Thereafter, one should worship Sūrya, the Lord of the World and the Eye of the Universe.
One should worship the god whose name is Truth with jambīras, bījapūras, nāraṅgas, and yellow fruits; by that, he is pleased.
All those led by the Rākṣasas are pleased by fish and meat.
He is greatly satisfied by white coconuts as offerings;
one should worship the deity named Nabhah with the application of perfumes and incense.
Māruta is satisfied by fragrant white flowers. ||9-10||
One should devotedly offer kṛsara mixed with honey to Pūṣan;
and one should worship Vitatha with other auspicious offerings, avoiding liquor and meat. Thus honored, Vivasvat, the great sage, attains satisfaction.
With flowers and those possessing blossoms, Gṛhakṣata attains satisfaction. With excellent offerings consisting of fish and meat, Yama is always pleased.
A wise man should worship the Gandharvas with incense made of Punnāga and Agaru.
One should gratify Bhṛṅgarāja with foods mixed with deer meat;
one should worship the god Mṛga with royal jambu fruits and bilva fruits, along with milk-rice mixed with honey, meats, and excellent cooked rice. 14.
One should worship the ancestors with substances fragrant with camphor and containing aromatic woods,
along with flowers, modakas, parched grain, and meat-mixtures.
One should diligently worship Dvārika, the cause of obstacles.

One should always worship Sugrīva with unprecedented, beautiful fragrances, incenses, and unsurpassed garlands, as well as with flowers of the thorny jasmine (kaṇṭakajātī). One should also offer him betel leaves with flowers, various foods, curd, cooked rice, and milk-rice (pāyasa).
One should worship the god Puṣpadanta, who is endowed with fame and heroism;
one should always worship Vainateya with the flesh of boars and other such animals;
and one should honor the great being Varuṇa with incense and sandalwood.
One should satisfy Rāhu with meats and various kinds of food;
Śanaiścara attains satisfaction through the offering of blood.
Through meat, Kṣaya, the lord of diseases, shall attain satisfaction.
One should worship the serpent who causes fear to all the worlds with offerings of fat.
A person should constantly worship Vāsuki by offering milk.
One should worship the divine Lord Viśvakarman as before.
A wise person should worship Bhallāṭa with offerings of white flowers;
one should worship Soma everywhere with food mixed with curd.
A man should constantly worship Kubera with the offering of incense.

One should worship Aditi with gold and also with lotuses; one should likewise honor the bull with garlands of arka and mandāra flowers. The worship of other gods as well should be performed with incense and perfumes.
A wise person should always perform these rites with all kinds of flowers and fruits; thus,
all these offerings have been prescribed for the sake of pacification,
during the purification and plowing of the ground, and in the preparation of images.
On an auspicious day for entering a beautiful house, on festive occasions,
during the establishment of a military camp, the founding of a city or village,
and the construction of temples or royal palaces— ||27||
One who desires to undertake another construction-related task should, being purified, offer the aforementioned oblations to the gods;
by performing this rite, he shall become a recipient of his desired goals. ||28||

Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Ritual for Offering Oblations," in the *Vāstuśāstra* composed by the great emperor, the illustrious Bhojadeva, also known as the *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*.
Now begins the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Planting of the Pegs and the Laying of the Lines.
One should employ those woods appropriate for the various castes for the purpose of the ritual pegs.
Now I shall describe them for the sake of spiritual welfare, fame, and benefit: Khadira, Udumbara, Aśvattha, Śāla, Śāka,
Dhava, Arjuna, Añjana, Kadara, Aśoka, Tiniśa, and Aruṇacandana.
For the rite of driving in stakes, trees with masculine names—such as the śirīṣa, sarja, nyagrodha, and bamboo—are recommended; those with feminine names are censured.
The aśvattha and the khadira are these two that bring about prosperity for Brahmins.
Poles made from red sandalwood and bamboo are honored for the Kṣatriyas.
Śāka and Khadira are beneficial for the Sāmantas;
poles made from Śāla and Śirīṣa are proclaimed as auspicious for the Vaiśyas.
For a Śūdra, [trees] originating from the Tiniśa, Dhava, and Arjuna are recommended;
for the dwellings of Vaiśyas and for rites intended to bring good fortune, those born of the Aśoka tree should be used.
The Nyagrodha is for the abode of merchants, and the Udumbara is for the work of leveling the ground.
In the houses of the chief ministers and the veterinarians, the sacrificial stakes (kīla) should be made of Sarja and Arjuna wood.
For Brāhmaṇas, they may be made from trees belonging to all castes; for Kṣatriyas, from trees born of three castes;
for Vaiśyas, from those mentioned for two castes; and for Śūdras, according to their own natural order.
One who desires prosperity should not perform the rite with the nails reversed;
now, the specific measurements for the kīlas are declared individually.
Kīlas thirty-two finger-breadths long bring auspiciousness to Brahmins.
Furthermore, for Kṣatriyas, they should measure twenty-eight finger-breadths;
for Vaiśyas, those measuring twenty-four finger-breadths bestow auspiciousness;
and for the Śūdra caste, stakes of twenty finger-breadths and so on are beneficial.
All of these, with a circumference of six finger-breadths, bring auspiciousness; for the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas, they are four-sided, eight-sided,
and six-sided respectively, while for the Śūdra, it is six-sided according to the nature of his disposition.
For the Brahmins and the other castes, [the girdles] should be made of darbha grass, muñja grass, wool, or cotton, respectively.
The cord should be firm, well-twisted, and have a thickness equal to half a joint.
However, if one's own prescribed material is unavailable, a wise man may use any one of the others mentioned.
Others, however, may take up the cord according to their own preference.

Having thus gathered the necessary materials on an auspicious day during the bright fortnight, the master of the house— pure, having bathed, and wearing white garments— as well as the architect, [should proceed].
One should determine the locations for the deities based on the signs of the householders.
The domestic deities should be fashioned from flowers and unbroken grains (akṣata).
First, one should examine the sites for the stakes (śaṅku) on all sides.
In all of those [rites], worship must be performed according to the prescribed rules.
Having sprinkled the center of the house and having prepared the site for Brahmā,
one should construct a well-characterized altar (vedi) smeared with cow dung.
It should be square with four doors and well-established with unbroken grains (akṣata).
In its center, a pitcher should be installed—either made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay; if the preceding material is unavailable, each subsequent one may be used.
That tree, whose roots are not of the wrong season, being unblemished, filled with water, and well-adorned—
filled within with gems, jewels, corals, gold,
and silver— should be installed, accompanied by unbroken rice grains, flowers, fruits, and seeds.
Having smeared it all over with white sandalwood paste,
one should place a sprout of a milk-tree upon it;
then, one should fumigate the four directions with fragrant incense.
One should wrap it all around with a new, white cloth;
for Brahmā, who exists in the form of the jar, resides in the middle of the Vasus.
A wise man should then place the stakes on the northern side of the jar.
One should examine the eight stakes and install them according to the prescribed rule.
Having smeared them with white sandalwood paste, one should adorn them with white flowers;
they should be anointed with lac-dye and well-perfumed with fragrant incense.
One should wrap it with a three-colored thread made of wool;
one should smear the base parts with honey, clarified butter, curd, and milk.
One should worship the axe, the thread, the wedge, and all other items on every side.
Then, having arranged the ritual implements there with incense, flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), and so forth; thereafter,
in the north-eastern portion of the site (vāstu), upon a spot smeared with cow dung belonging to the deity Saptārcis (Fire), he should take his place upon a bed of kuśa grass.
The domestic priest should perform the fire-ritual as well as the propitiatory rite;
the astrologer, being pure, bathed, having performed his ablutions, and composed in mind,
should correctly determine the auspicious moment (lagna) by means of a gnomon or its corresponding ghaṭikās.
One should thus determine the night-lagna by means of the constellations situated at the meridian, the setting point, or the rising point, if one desires success for oneself;
and one should honor the domestic priest with worship that brings satisfaction. ||31-32||
Since Brahmā becomes honored when he is worshipped,
therefore worship should be performed according to the rules for the anniversary of his passing. Since Bṛhaspati becomes honored when the anniversary is worshipped, [one should perform it].
Thereafter, one should worship the architect (sthapati) with the desire to please Tvaṣṭṛ,
for the work— whether auspicious or inauspicious— is dependent upon him.
Having smeared them with white sandalwood paste and honored them with white flowers, [one should proceed].
One should honor them with unwashed, new garments and finger-rings;
and those who serve as attendants, one should honor according to one's ability.
One should satisfy them with gifts of gold, clothing, and the like, or by pleasing words.
One should act with diligence so that they may be well-disposed.
Then, having sipped water (ācamana), the wise architect should perform the rite of offering (balikarma);
at the laying of the foundation lines, he should perform the offering to all beings (sārvabhautika).
In the absence of that [offering], a bali-offering should be performed; that which is to be done is now described.
One should prepare sacrificial oblations (carus) separately—white, red, yellow, and black—consisting of milk-rice, rice-and-pulse porridge, milk, flat beans, and white boiled rice.
One should offer to the deities curds mixed with parched grain, meat, sweetmeats, clarified butter, and rice combined with curds;
and one should worship the god Agni with sesame seeds together with clarified butter.
Then one should offer milk-rice with curd at the station of Brahmā;
thereafter, in due order, one should present the bali-offering to the deities. Having performed the rite of bali according to the rule, one should have the Brahmins recite the benedictions.

One should honor those of one’s own Vedic branch who are pure and wise with gifts and fruits. Then, amidst the sounds of songs and musical instruments accompanied by the utterances of "Oṃ," "Svasti," and "Puṇyāha," the master, together with the Brahmins, should perform a circumambulation of it.
Having first caused unbroken grains to be placed in the jar by the most excellent of the twice-born,
the pure master-builder, clothed in unwashed garments, should then proceed to the southeast while auspicious benedictions are being recited, and take his seat upon a throne.
Having sat down facing east and holding a wooden stake (śaṅku) with his right hand,
the hero should then take it up with his left hand and, having placed it upon the ground,
strike it with an axe while reciting the mantras. ||46-47||
"May the Nāgas and likewise the World-Protectors enter its base;
may they establish themselves in this house, and may it become a source of long life and strength.
One should then strike eight firm blows upon the head of the kīla.
Then, while the stake is being struck, one should observe the omens:
[the sight of] cows, Brahmins, chariots, elephants, maidens, excellent royal women, as well as the sound of conchs, drums, flutes, and singing. ||49-50||
If, when this [object] is being struck, the master manifests therein,
then he constantly attains happiness and increases in peace and sovereignty. To ward off a strike, a sneeze, or a mishap, there is the use of a thread and a peg.
The sight of any heretics whatsoever does not bring happiness.
Having observed auspicious omens, one should then drive in the ritual stake (śaṅku).
When the stake being struck enters the earth slowly and steadily, [it is successful]. 52–53.
In that case, there will be success in one's undertakings and a home furnished with jewels; however,
when the ritual peg (kīlaka) does not sink even while being struck,
there will be no success in one's undertakings there, and one should observe it as an unfavorable omen.
If, even with a single blow, the wedge does not enter the earth,
then one should not build a dwelling there, nor should one enjoy what has been prepared;
one should strike with a piece of iron or a stone, and never with wood under any circumstances.
If a stake struck with wood causes a fire-hazard;
if it is struck with stone, then it brings about disease.
A stake inclined toward the east (Aindrī) brings about wealth and honor.
If the kila is tilted toward the southeast, there will be great danger from fire;
in the southern direction, death for kings, and in the direction of the Rākṣasas (the southwest), fear of demons;
in the western direction, loss of wealth, and in the northwest, fear of disease. ||58-59||
One who is gentle, having obtained the favor of the king through his gentle conduct,
attains supreme prosperity when Kīlaka and Kūrcaka arise for him; he increases in wealth and grain along with the lineage of sons and grandsons in his home.
When, despite being struck with effort, even a single peg should break,
one should know that there will be the destruction of either his wife or his eldest son;
if the peg should snap, the death of the master occurs.
When the wedge falls from the hand, then there shall be a downfall for the architect;
and he who has let it fall from his hand shall suffer a fracture of the jaw when it slips from his grasp.
If, while being struck with ease, the wedge does not remain firmly fixed, [the same result follows].
Then, one should again offer him eight further blows;
furthermore, one should perform a ceremonial sprinkling with offerings of garlands, perfumes, and incense.
Having briefly reflected upon this highly meritorious Sāman, [one should proceed].
The wise man should recite the Traiśoka hymn until the consecration of the sacrificial stake (śaṅku).
Then, having gone toward the southwestern direction (nairṛtī āśā), he should fix the stake there.
He should perform its proper sprinkling with the Ūrṇāyava Sāman.
Then, having gone toward the direction of the wind (the northwest), one should fix a stake there;
one should perform its consecration with the *mahāratna-sāman*.
Then, having gone toward the northeastern direction, one should fix a stake in that [direction].
One should perform its consecration with the *bhāga* and *sāman* chants as previously described;
thereafter, one should tie a cord around the left [arm] with a double twist,
extending it clockwise according to the prescribed procedure for the placement of the *śaṅku*.
When the cord being spun releases even slightly from the peg, one should know that it portends the death of a son; if it breaks, it forebodes the death of the owner himself.
Therefore, one must exert effort while the cord is being drawn out. ||70-71||
There is no fault in cutting away the nourishment of even all four arms;
having stretched out the thread, the wise one should distribute the previously prepared *carus* according to this procedure in their respective places.
At the locations of the spikes, white and other oblations (carus) should be offered in sequence.
One should recite this mantra with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya-mantra) toward the intermediate direction of the southeast,
and likewise for all the Maruts and for human beings.
I offer them an oblation consecrated by mantra;
likewise, taking up a blood-oblation and facing the southwest,
[I offer it] to the Lord of the Southwest and to those Rākṣasas who dwell in the southwest.
I offer to them an excellent oblation of blood and rice.
Having taken a black oblation and gone toward the direction of the Wind, [one should say]:
"Salutations to you, the King of Nagas, and to those others who depend upon him. (76-77)
I offer to them an excellent oblation of black rice;
having set aside the oblation of turmeric, I take refuge in the northeastern direction (aiśānī), saying:
"Obeisance to all the Rudras and those others who have taken refuge in them."
"I offer to them an excellent oblation of turmeric and curd.
In this manner, one should duly present all these offerings;
thereafter, one should consecrate the auspicious water in the jar with a divine chant of conciliation.
One should perform the sprinkling of the site with the Vāmadevya hymn; thus have the trees for Brahmins and the others been described in connection with the fixing of the pegs.
The fruit yielded by the peg and the various signs here are clearly stated in many ways.
Likewise, according to the Sūtra, the ritual for the offering (bali) should be performed in each direction with mantras,
as prescribed by rule upon the stakes for the satisfaction of the thirty-three gods.

Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Laying of the Stakes and the Sūtras," in the *Vāstuśāstra* known by the alternative name *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*, composed by the Great King of Kings, the illustrious Bhojadeva.
Now begins the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Matrix of the Layout of the Dwelling Site.
We shall now describe the matrix of the layout of the dwelling site,
for the purpose of habitation by those who properly subsist upon all types of occupations.
Quadrangular, even, oblique, long, and circular;
shaped like a conch, a cart-axle, a vulva, a mirror, a thunderbolt, and a neck-ring;
with a severed ear, a distorted ear, resembling a conch-shell, and like a razor.
It has the appearance of a spearhead, the back of a tortoise, or a scorpion; it is shaped like a fan, a shallow bowl, or a svastika; it resembles a mṛdaṅga drum or a paṇava drum;
it is free of gravel, resembles a headless torso (kabandha), or has the shape of a grain of barley in its center.
The *utsaṅga*, which resembles the teeth of a king; likewise, that which is like an axe (*paraśu*);
the *visrāvita*, the *śvabhra*, the *pralamba*, and the *vivāhika*;
the *trikuṣṭa*, the *pañcakuṣṭa*, and another called *paricchinna*.
The Diksvastika, the Śrīvṛkṣa,
the Vardhamāna, the Eṇīpada, and the Narapada— these forty fields have been briefly described; now their application is prescribed.
In a square and level [encampment], the king should reside; in one shaped like a bed, the domestic priests;
in a long one, the princes and the commander-in-chief; in one that is circular and elongated, he should dwell.
All those seeking comfort should reside in one shaped like a conch shell.

The inner apartments and the residence are situated in the *sama* (even) configuration; merchants are in the shape of a cart (*śakaṭa*); courtesans are in the shape of the vulva (*bhaga*); goldsmiths are in the shape of a mirror (*darpaṇa*);
and people who are city guildsmen are in the shape of a diamond (*vajra*). ||9-10||
Those desiring sons should dwell in a field shaped like a conch shell.
Elephant-drivers should dwell in a field with a severed ear, and hunters in one with a distorted ear.
Those who see only one eye should dwell in a field resembling a conch, and teachers of the Gaṇas in one resembling a razor.

The superintendent of religious observances [should sit] at the mouth of the Śakti; the garland-makers on the back of the tortoise; the tailors and horse-keepers in the portion of the seat; the fansmiths in the portion resembling a fan;
the carpenters in the portion resembling a shallow bowl; and the bards and panegyrists in the Svastika portion. ||12-13||
Those resembling a *paṇava* drum or a *mṛdaṅga* drum are players of flutes, trumpets, and other instruments;

those resembling a pebble are chariot-warriors; and those resembling a headless trunk (*kabandha*) are, moreover, low-caste dog-cookers (*śvapāka*). Those resembling barley are those who live by grain.
In the lap [of this field] are the ascetics, the elephant-riders at Rājadantaka;
in the field resembling an axe are the prison guards; in the field that exudes [liquor] are the liquor-makers; and in the field resembling a pit are the laborers. (15–16)
In Yugala, the barbers shall dwell, along with those who perform their own marriages and those who guard the treasury.
In Trikuṣṭha and Pañcakuṣṭha, those who live by fire (blacksmiths) shall reside. All those who subsist on measurement shall live in places completely enclosed on all sides.
In the Diksvastika [plan], one should construct shrines (caityas) and dwellings on all sides.
One should cause trees resembling the Śrīvṛkṣa and sacrificial enclosures (yajñavāṭa) to be made;
these very same things one should also fashion at the mouth of the Vardhamāna-shaped [plan].
In a place called Eṇīpada, courtesans [thrive], and in a place resembling Narapada, thieves;
thus have been described the auspicious dwelling places for those who subsist by all kinds of occupations.
These [places] are intended as dwelling sites for people who live by their work.
Having carefully considered the prescribed shapes of the sites,
which architect would not be honored on this earth who constructs their dwellings according to the rules? (21)

Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Matrix of the Layout of the Site" (*vāstusaṃsthānamātṛkā*), in the *Vāstuśāstra* composed by the great king of kings, the illustrious Bhojadeva, also known as the *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*.
Now begins the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Qualities and Defects of Doors" (*dvāraguṇadoṣa*).
Thus have the houses for all those who live by their craft been described.
Henceforth, the dwellings for those of the various castes and for householders shall be described as follows: 1.
In the quarters of Bhallāṭa, Dhanada, Caraka, or Pṛthivīdhara, the house of a Brāhmaṇa should have its excellent door facing the northeast (Māhendra). 2.
For a Kṣatriya, an auspicious residence should be constructed in the Māhendra, Ārka, Satya, or Āryaka quarters, with its door facing the Gṛhakṣata (southwest) direction;
or likewise in the Yāmya, Vaivasvata, Gāndharva, or Gṛhakṣata quarters.
The auspicious residence of a Vaiśya should have its door in the Puṣpa direction;
or it may be in Vāruṇa, Pauṣpada, Maitra, or Āsura.
The excellent residence of a Śūdra should have its door in the Bhallāṭa direction.
For Brahmins, a house site facing east or facing south shall always increase in wealth,
grain, sons, and grandsons.
A house site facing south or facing west [is likewise auspicious].
For a Kṣatriya, wealth, grain, and prowess increase here.
A western door for the site and a house facing north—
therein a Vaiśya prospers with riches, grain, sons, cattle, and so forth.
The site for the house should have its door facing north, and the house itself should likewise face east;
thus, the livelihood of a Śūdra prospers with wealth and grain.
Even in a single hall, four [types of] rooms are prescribed.
The various types of door-sites (niveśa) are now described, both auspicious and inauspicious:
the Utsaṅga, the Hīnabāhu, the Pūrṇabāhu, and the fourth is proclaimed as the Pratyakṣāgra. ||10-11||
When the two entrances of the dwelling site and the house are positioned such that they form a "lap" (utsaṅga),
it bestows good fortune, the increase of progeny, wealth, grain, and victory. Where, upon entering, the dwelling site is to the left, that house becomes auspicious.
A dwelling with its left arm deficient is censured by those who contemplate the site;
one living in such a place will have little wealth, few friends, and few kinsmen, and will be constantly overcome by women and afflicted by various diseases. ||13-14||
That house which lies to the right of the entrance to the site (vāstu) should be known as *pūrṇabāhuka* because of its clockwise entry;
therein one finds sons, grandsons, wealth, grain, and happiness.
Men who dwell constantly on a firm foundation always attain prosperity.
When the door of the site (vāstu) is situated facing the back of the house,
it is manifestly censurable, like an entrance that turns to the left.
A Brāhmaṇa should dwell in the Mukhya [tīrtha], a Kṣatriya in the Dvināman;
a Vaiśya should dwell in the Vitatha, and a Śūdra in the Sugrīvanāman. These indeed are the specific [residences] for all the social classes in their respective order.

The locations for the site and the placement of the gates have been described along with the dwellings. Now, the construction of houses for the various castes—Śūdras, Vaiśyas, Kṣatriyas, and kings desiring victory—is described in ascending order. ||19-20||
One should construct a house for Śūdras of three and a half stories for their prosperity;
that which exceeds this brings about the destruction of the family.
For a Vaiśya, one should increase the house to four and a half stories.

In that case, excessive measurement leads to the depletion of his wealth and kin. One should construct the house of a Kṣatriya as having a maximum of five and a half stories; for prosperity and the increase of power, anything beyond that results in its destruction.
But the dwelling of the Brahmin was seven-and-a-half stories high;
it was exceedingly lofty for the purpose of Vedic study, proper conduct, and enjoyment, yet it was terrifying.
Those lords of the earth who sacrifice with the Rājasūya and other rites [reside there].
One should cause an excellent residence for them to have seven and a half stories (seven and a half *talas*).
For that king who is a performer of many sacrifices and a sovereign over kings,
one should likewise provide a residence with seven and a half stories.
That twice-born man who has performed the Vājapeya sacrifice with a concentrated mind,
or he who has gifted ten million cows— he too shall be honored there during that spring season,
as designated by its proper measure. Thus spoke the king and the others.
They attain supreme prosperity, but in the opposite case, they meet with decline.
A house, including its pedestal and floor, is proclaimed according to measurement;
for a Śūdra, the maximum is twenty cubits by the common hand.
A height of forty-two cubits is praised for a Kṣatriya, sixty for a preeminent Brāhmaṇa,
eighty for a chief of the twice-born, and one hundred cubits for a lord of the earth.
Beyond this, no greater vertical measurement for men is said to be recommended.
For the gods, dānavas, daityas, piśācas, uragas, and rākṣasas;
for the siddhas, gandharvas, and yakṣas, [the construction] should be made even higher than this.
For a śūdra, however, no house is permitted below the level of the ground.
The house of a Vaiśya should be built no lower than half a story;
the palace of a Kṣatriya should not be built lower than two stories. The residence of a Brāhmaṇa may be up to two and a half stories, and that of a king (Kṣatriya) up to three stories.

A house built by some unskilled artisan in any way with inferior proportions leads to the destruction of the master's prosperity and results in the opposite of praiseworthy character and other virtues, especially when there is fear of the Lord [or the King]. (34) I shall now declare the merits and defects of doors in all types of dwellings.
It should be well-situated, quadrangular, beautiful, and joined with its own appropriate materials.
It should be straight in its own cardinal direction, neither too short nor too high;
it should not be small, nor crooked, nor uneven, nor protruding outward.
That which is neither distended nor emaciated in the middle, not receding into the inner cavities,
neither dispersed nor contracted— that is the door that bestows supernatural powers (ṛddhi).
It is located at the twelfth part of the foot, proceeding clockwise from the center of the foot.
A [gate] that has been established attains growth, and it brings prosperity to the entrance.

[This applies when it is obstructed by] a carriage road, a crossroads, a triangular junction, a pond, a well, a water-jar, a wall, a corner, a tree, a pillar, a house, a chariot, and so forth. ||38-39||
A house door that has been pierced does not lead to auspiciousness.

One should ensure that the door is properly aligned with the door; one should never cause a single entrance to enter through another door. One should never allow [the ritual thread] to enter the sacrificial bed (vedī) through any other opening.

A wise man should cause [the guest] to enter through the main gate, but never by any means through the side door, nor through the stairs, nor through the windows. He should never allow one who has entered by an outer or inner door to proceed further.
For that which has been prescribed would always result in many evils for those whose houses possess arches, gate-towers,
gates, or watchtowers; one should cause these to enter the ears of the primary doors of such houses.
A door should be made for a door on the successive levels;
it should be made following the clockwise direction (pradakṣiṇa), and never otherwise.
One should make the entrance on the successive levels follow the clockwise direction.
One should not perform the mounting of the door by going counter-clockwise (apasavya).
On whichever wall it was previously made, one should construct [the next] above that;
likewise, on another wall, that door should be arranged so as to be clockwise (pradakṣiṇa).
One should not place a door in the middle of the house, nor indeed in the middle of a *pada*;
it is not desired in a *sthūla*, nor in a *pada*, nor where a vein (*sirā*) intersects. In a mansion, substances situated in their own parts and extending crosswise [are considered auspicious].
The piercing of a vital point (marmavedha) or the piercing of a doorway (dvāravedha) does not cause defect anywhere.
However, the shadows of Yavanas, watchtowers, or the city deities' temples must not fall upon the door of a house; nor should the rays of the moon or the sun enter it. 49–50.

Neither by a rampart, nor by a wall, nor again by a parapet, are the vulnerable points of the gates ever rendered invisible. If the gate is too high, there is danger from the king; if it is too low, there is danger from thieves.
If the *kubja* [type of house] extends outward, there will be affliction to the family and humiliation;
if it is bloated (*ādhmāta*), there is extreme poverty; if its middle is slender, there is the ruin of men;
if it is pierced by a road, there will be disease; and if by a crossroads (*catvara*), death. ||52-53||
If pierced by a śṛṅgāṭaka, widowhood arises for daughters;
if pierced by a large pond or a well, there shall be danger from dysentery. From a corner (koṇa) it gives fear of death, and from trees there will be fear of disease.
Through a pillar the master dies; through a whirlpool wealth does not remain.
(55) Through a drainage channel there is great suffering, great fear, and great strife;
therefore, with every effort, one should avoid piercing the door. (56)
That site which has [openings] in front and behind, and at both doors and both walls,
wherein the two [houses] resting on a single path are separated from one another—
that site is called "divided body" (bhinnadeha), and it brings about divided ownership.
Therein, no growth occurs for anything that has been established.
A door made on the belly-side of the house brings fear of all diseases;
however, an eastern door dedicated to Mahendra is praised as granting all desires. 58–59.
Gṛhakṣata is ordained for the south, bringing auspiciousness;
or else, Gandharva should be placed there for the sake of welfare. Puṣpadanta, which brings victory, is praised when used with the fifth [digit].
The northern door facing the Bhallāṭa deity is auspicious for the master of the house.
Whether it be in that [plan] of eighty-one squares or even in one of four-square units,
we shall describe the results starting from the southeast for those doors located in the cardinal directions.
Fear of fire, birth as a woman, wealth, being beloved by the king,
anger, falsehood in men, cruelty— these follow in sequence as before;
even a daughter leads to a low state in the next life, while eating [certain things] brings about the prosperity of sons.
One born when the moon is in the *raudra* asterism is ungrateful and lacks livelihood; one in *yāmya* robs the strength of his sons.

Suffering for children, the increase of enemies, failure to obtain wealth or sons, yet the attainment of wealth and sons through offspring, the acquisition of wealth, and cruelty—fear and loss of wealth are said to follow in sequence for those facing other [asterisms]. (64–65)

In the directions starting from the southwest (Nairṛta), there is bondage, loss of wealth, increase of enemies, and the foremost attainment of wealth and sons, as well as an abundance of virtues; likewise, the acquisition of sons and wealth through the enemy's son, and faults arising from women—
these qualities and defects situated at the gates have been described exactly as they are.
Having recognized them, one who is most excellent among those skilled in the arts and sciences attains honor in the world.
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Qualities and Defects of Doors," in the *Vāstuśāstra*—also known as the *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*—composed by the Great Emperor Śrī Bhojadeva.
Now begins the fortieth chapter, titled "The Measurement of the Pedestal" (*Pīṭhamāna*).
Now the measurement of the pedestal (pīṭha) for gods and humans is described:
the smallest pedestal shall be one part, the middle one one and a half parts, and the best one shall be two parts;
this is the height of the pedestal.
It should be the most excellent for Maheśvara, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā;
that [same form] should not be made for other deities by the wise.
The seat of the Lord should be constructed by the discerning according to their respective desires.
In whatever place Brahmā and Viṣṇu are to be installed, Īśvara should be made present everywhere; no fault is found therein.
However, for the other deities, their pedestal and portion should be raised high.
By whichever specific proportion the measurement of the site (vāstu) is prescribed for a particular [structure],
by that same proportion the height of the pedestal (pīṭha) is prescribed.
And the pedestals for human dwellings are [determined] by means of the divine pedestals.
One should make them equal; the gods, when installed above, bestow prosperity.
In the center of the city, however, the excellent house of Brahmā should be constructed;
it should be made four-faced so that he may behold that city.
It is superior to all other dwellings and even to the royal palace itself (8).
Even though the royal palace is superior, it is praised as being better than the abodes of other gods,
because the king is the most excellent among the five guardians of the world (9).
Thus, these seats for the gods have been described in their entirety.
Now we shall describe the seats for the four castes, in order beginning with the Brahmin.
A seat thirty-six finger-breadths in height is recommended for a Brahmin.
For the other castes, however, it should be short by four finger-breadths.
A Brahmin may use the seats and houses of all four castes;
a Kṣatriya, those of three; a Vaiśya, those of two; and a Śūdra, his own, according to the sequence.
Thus the master architect should determine the distribution of the sacred seats (pīṭhas),
desiring the welfare of the patron and the prosperity of the king; for when the deities are established according to the correct proportions, they indeed become worthy of worship.
This measure of the sacred seats (pīṭhas) has been declared, as well as that which is fixed for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the other gods dwelling here in heaven.
Therefore, all that has been declared regarding the Brāhmaṇas and the other castes should be applied by architects who desire prosperity, according to what is appropriate for each.
Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Measurement of the Pedestal," in the *Vāstuśāstra* known as the *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*, composed by the Great King of Kings, Śrī Bhojadeva.
Now begins the forty-first chapter, titled "The Method of Piling.
Now, the merits and defects of the piling (cayana) are described here:
a piling that is well-proportioned, level, beautiful, and symmetrical is auspicious. (1)
It should be unconfused, free from doubt, indestructible, and not torn out;
unsurpassed, not twisted, not crooked, and not pressed down;
with even joints, straight, and likewise internal.
Well-rounded, well-jointed, well-established, well-knit, and straight—
these are the twenty qualities of a [well-made] chariot.
By the opposite of these, there are likewise twenty defects.
When they dig toward the southern wall facing outward,
one should know there will be fear of disease and predict the rod of death.
When they dig toward the western wall facing outward, [the same applies].
Then one should know there will be loss of wealth, and there will be fear from thieves.
But when it probes the northern wall facing outward,
it will bring calamity to either the builder or the owner.
When an architect builds a wall facing east and opening outward,
the wise should predict that there will be fear of royal punishment;
one should declare this same result if the wall falls or is shattered.
If one's right ear should throb outwardly toward the east,
there will be a terrible fear of fire and danger to the master of the house.
When the right ear throbs outwardly toward the southwest, [the same consequences follow].
There will be strife and calamity there, and there is danger to one's wife.
But when the Bahirmukha [wind] blows toward the northwestern corner,
danger arises there for one's livestock, vehicles, and sons.
When the left ear protrudes outward,

there arises doubt among teachers regarding the matter, as well as concerning bulls and the like. If it becomes large on all four limbs while one is performing the piling [of the altar], [it portends success].
It should have a shape like the pericarp of a lotus or the form of a jasmine flower;
for there, the income would not be such as the expenditure would be. Due to the fault of that accumulation, the household, being depleted, flees.
If, for one who is gathering [the signs], there arises an excessive contraction therein, that is designated as "Brahman"; in that case, there will be fear of the king.
If it is expanded among the outer [limbs] and contracted in the middle, [that is likewise noted]. ||15-16||
That which is described as having a slender middle is known therein to bring fear of hunger;
if it is elevated at the ears and diminished in the middle,
one should know that by the name "nirṇata," and there shall be fear of thieves.
If the ears are deficient at the edges yet elevated in the middle,
it should be known as "elevated like a tortoise," which brings fear from all defects;
in the case of ears that are unevenly elevated, one should predict the loss of wealth.
One should know that there is an abundance of food and drink when [the bricks] are equal and when the prescribed rites are performed.
Thus have these merits and defects of the piling (cayana) been proclaimed.
Therefore, one should employ the rite of piling with every effort.
Having leveled it with water, one should carefully apply the means for correct determination;
for there is no other way to reach a certain conclusion regarding that area than by this method.
Therefore, one should first diligently take a circular mark with water.
Then, once the cord has been well-beaten, the wise man should proceed as follows:
having made a cord twice the length of the measurement of the field, he should then, at its two ends,
[mark] a point according to a measurement of three-quarters of that field.
One should place two stakes, reaching to the interior of the field, at the corners;
having fixed them, one should join their ends.
When the line has been drawn, it should measure three-quarters of the field.
The measurement should be made by the "serpent-gait" (bhujagatyā) according to the desired proportions;
