one should mark the signs, for that shall be the ear (karṇa), and thus one should rectify any defects. One should not provide excessive covering, nor should one break the bricks there.
Standing at an uneven spot, one should cut those [lines] with an axe and make them even.
Just as the thread should not be touched, so should the wise man examine it. One should fix one's gaze upon the wall at its beginning, middle, and end.
When the entire surface has been traversed and the ground has been uncovered,
then the wise practitioner should not remain in one place, but move about in succession.
This is the uncovering of the coverings, if he desires his own success.
In each of those places, one should apply this if it is beneficial for the pierced area;
for otherwise, it would become difficult to bear, therefore one should avoid that.
A skillful practitioner should place the arm level above and at the side.
"The lattice-work (caya) that is cut all around and honored upon the walls—
therefore, one should always exert effort in the work of lattice-making.
Thus, the lattice-work was executed by the artisans according to rule, as described in the spoken instructions.
"In this world, fame shall spread abroad, and even for the master of the house, there shall be abundant wealth.

(33) Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Rule for the Piling [of Bricks]," in the *Vāstuśāstra* composed by the Great King of Kings, the illustrious Bhojadeva, also known as the *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*.
Now begins the forty-second chapter, titled "The Rule for the Rite of Pacification" (*Śāntikarmavidhi*).
Now we shall explain the procedure for the rite of pacification (śāntikarma):
having duly worshipped the guardians of the quarters and offered oblations,
the wise practitioner should bathe the pericarp with water-pots containing gold, in the proper sequence.
Anointed with all kinds of perfumes and adorned with garlands of flowers,
dressed in fine garments and smeared with honey at its base,
one should plant it in the ground for the purpose of pacifying all defects.

The architect, being self-restrained and pure, and knowing the ritual procedure, should have the best of Brahmins recite blessings and perform the auspicious *puṇyāha* ceremony; he should then install all the *karṇikās*, including the honey-pitcher, the *ariṣṭa*, and the moss.
By this rite, one should cause the work of the four castes to be performed.
Wherever a *karṇikā* has been planted and is then uprooted and replanted,
that house will not be completed, and the owner perishes therein.
If wood that has been driven in is cut or struck again,
there will be a total loss of wealth, grain, and the master himself in this matter.
If wood pressed by a creeper is driven into the ground at the entrance, [the same result follows].
There is a terrible fear of venomous serpents, characterized by portents during that upheaval.
When [the deity] arises, the pericarp must be protected from the assault of all beings;
for in a new undertaking, wild animals, beasts of prey, and reptiles are ill-omened.
One should declare these defects when they ascend the pericarp:
if crows alight upon a garland that has been worn and then discarded,
there will be a journey abroad for the householder, and his food and drink will diminish.
If it is found on a peacock, the king shall take that house after five years have passed.
If it is on the head of an elephant, disease arises; if on cuckoos, after two years;
and if on ravens, a very great danger arises after three years.
If it be a parrot, there will be quarrels and the like, and the household shall not prosper.
In the case of a cock, one should know there is danger from fire, or great fear arising from the king.
In the case of a maina, however, there is misconduct on the part of the women as well as the master of the house.
If [the house] is seized by a serpent-like obstacle, it does not reach completion. If a *kuliṅga* bird appears, the man and woman become doers of evil;
if a *pārāvata* pigeon appears, the man and woman become violators of their teacher’s bed.
If it is a cat, the family is tormented by diseases along with their servants;
or fire, water, or an elephant destroys that house.
These results from wild birds will occur within a year after the sighting.
Death occurs for young men, and the loss of wealth comes from attachment to honey. Seeing an owl in a bad dream likewise portends the death of children.
If the bird is startled, terrified, or hidden away, the king shall seize the empty house.
But when smoke is seen ahead, or even if it enters the ears,
the fire quickly burns [the house], or lightning strikes the dwelling.
Where a vulture alights, one should consider that place touched by the feet of the twice-born (birds).
Having ploughed it with hundreds of ploughs, one should then sow the seeds;
cows should be milked there, and rites for pacification should be performed.
When the clouds have rained abundantly, one should again construct a temple there.
In whichever parts of the house there may be a store of honey,
one should order the destruction of that part, as well as the removal of any danger to the female messenger.
For that reason, one should cause crowns to be placed upon the tips of the crests.
O gentle one, one should protect [the seed] on all sides until it has been sown;
however, once it is hidden by birds, nothing is praised [as auspicious].
Therefore, one should guard it with great effort against the portents previously described.
Now, the propitiatory fire-offering (śānti-homa) for the timber of houses that have collapsed is described.
If the Indra-kīla, the Mahākūṭa, the Pṛṣṭhavaṃśa, or the two Uttara-dhara pillars collapse,
or if the Alinda-pādas or the Pragrahas collapse, these calamities kill the master of the house.
The *tulā* and the *sthapatya*, the *kūṭa*, the *vedikā*, and the *karṇapālikā*; the *netra* and the *kapotapāli*, the *hanapraviṣṭa*, and the *kuṭumbinī*;
the *ambagrāḥ*, the *pakṣivaṃśas*, the *mallakas*, and the *sakumārakas*. ||26-27||
The watchtowers, the moats, and the young maidens stationed there,
as well as the crossbars and the side-panels of the gates— these calamities strike down their own kin.
A superior man destroys one who is joined with him, while an inferior man destroys one who is beneath him.
The Sthauṇya planets or the Pratimoka may destroy desired possessions;
the Udadhi planet may harm one’s sister or attendants.
For men, [the effects] occur through substances with masculine names, and for women, through those with feminine names. ||29-30||
Damage caused by neuter objects always results in the destruction of wealth;
a fissure in the ground portends the ruin of women, while a breach in the wall foretells the destruction of the house.
A wooden pin or a crack along a joint brings misfortune through the loss of friends.
In a new house, fresh timber— whether being worked, already finished, being fitted, or already joined— that has stood for less than a year,
breaks, cracks, or splits apart, leading to the destruction of the body.
Having dedicated the house to a Brāhmaṇa and having marked another with jewels,
one should cover it with new cloths and have it rebuilt.
When [the house] is burnt, broken, shaken, collapsed, or struck by lightning, [it must be reconstructed].
When [the house] has grown, cracked, or settled, it is prescribed that pacificatory rites be performed with all kinds of medicinal herbs;
having offered various oblations and caused the Brahmins to pronounce blessings,
if the pillar is broken, one's fame is destroyed.
There, one should worship the Moon and the Sun; then the sin is pacified.
Having brought a tree of that same kind, one should have her [the image] made anew upon it.
When this is done, she shall become happy, and her fame and lifespan will be secure.
The bowl of one who breaks it has his manliness destroyed.
One should perform an expiation for an inauspicious constellation appearing during a meal;
having brought wood of that same kind, one should fashion a replacement bowl.
By acting thus, he shall become happy and his strength will increase;
however, by fracturing the spinal column, a householder may incur bondage.
In that case, one should worship the Rājarāja and perform the appropriate expiation.
Having performed that, one becomes happy and prospers in every respect.
Brāhmaṇas should be invoked with blessings of well-being, accompanied by sacrificial fees and unbroken grains.
He who breaks the pillar is consecrated as the eldest son.
One should worship Pṛthvīdhara there and likewise perform the expiation;
having brought back a tree of that same kind, one should cause it to be planted again.
By doing this, one becomes happy and also prospers with sons.
If the head of the family is divided, he who is the eldest of the lineage prospers.
There, one should worship the ancestors and the gods, and likewise perform an act of atonement.
By doing so, one becomes happy, and the ancestors are likewise pleased.
If the pillar of one's house breaks, his son will suffer;
in that case, one should worship the gods and perform the appropriate expiation.
Having brought a tree of that same kind, one should have the pillar reconstructed from it.
Having acted thus, he becomes happy and prospers through his sons.
Where the subordinate ministers suffer, there the chief minister perishes;
in such a case, one should sacrifice to Vāsava and perform the appropriate expiatory rite.
Having brought such a tree, one should have it used as a pretext;
when this is done, there will be happiness and [the king's power] increases through his ministers.
But he whose body suffers, his servant is destroyed.
One should worship the Yakṣa deity there and likewise perform an expiatory rite (prāyaścitta).
Having brought wood of that same kind, one should have an image fashioned from it.
When this is done, he shall become happy and even increase in prosperity through his servants.
If the scale trembles for one whose wife trembles,
he should sacrifice to the Earth and perform the appropriate expiation;
having brought such a tree, he should place his well-adorned wife upon it.
Then, observing other rites, a wise man should have them performed;
having clothed her well-adorned like a bride in new garments,
he should have the Brahmins recite auspicious blessings and then cause her to proceed toward him.
Having acted thus, one becomes happy and always increases in wealth; however,
when the central pillar within the pericarp-arches breaks,
the owner of that house encounters suffering during that portentous sign.
Having brought there a wise and highly learned architect,
one should offer oblations to whichever deity is determined by the division of the site,
and one should cause an expiation to be performed for that deity.
Having acted thus, one becomes happy and prospers in every respect;
however, wherever the yoke causes distress, there shall be suffering for the cattle.
One should worship Īśāna in that case and perform an expiation.
Having brought such a tree, one should have a yoke fashioned from it.
When this is done, his happiness arises as well as the increase of his cattle.
Or, if in the case of two balances or two carts, the foot of one breaks, [the same result follows].
In that case, there will be a loss of life; one should worship Baladeva.
Having performed an expiation, one should then have [the rite] performed for him again.
By doing so, the head of the household becomes happy through that propitiatory rite.
If the Mahendra portion of a door-component is damaged during the construction of a new house,
one should worship the god Indra there and likewise perform the expiation.
If the Gṛhakṣata portion of a door-component is damaged, one should worship Yama there.
One should worship Varuṇa there at the side of the door of Puṣpadanta;
for if Bhallāṭa, who is at the side of the door, is harmed during the new construction,
one should worship the god Soma there and perform an expiation.
By performing this rite of pacification (śāntika), the householder becomes happy.
If the top of the central pillar (sthūṇārāja) is crooked toward the south,
the body will suffer there steadily for every year.
If it is behind, there will be long-lasting grief; if to the north, loss of wealth;
if to the east, punishment by the king; therefore, that which is straight (aligned with the front) is recommended.
For those [trees] belonging to the body or the house, four parts are destroyed.
The scales, the backbone, and the upper garment upon the supporting cloth—
on these one should place the aforementioned powerful substances and likewise perform the expiatory rite.
Thus, it shall become auspicious, propitious, and a cause for the increase of prosperity, progeny, and strength.
Having thus recognized all these signs associated with the home and having observed all the auspicious omens,
one should perform the pacification rites as described individually.
One attains fame, happiness, wealth, and long life.

Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Procedure for Peace-Rites," in the *Vāstuśāstra*—also known as the *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*—composed by the great king of kings, the illustrious Bhojadeva.
Now begins the forty-third chapter, titled "The Consequences of a Broken Door."
Whatever has been stated here regarding new construction work should be understood to apply to sacrifices,
houses, villages, cities, capitals, and likewise to towns;
as well as to the layout, shape, measurement, and the expansion or contraction of the arms.
One who is discerning should recognize that it is indeed one and the same everywhere.
One should point out the marks of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) in the work of carpentry;
one should recognize the falling [of the tree] by the fall itself, and the carving by the act of carving.
One should predict the raising of a sacrificial post by the rising of logs of wood;
a breakage is indicated by a breakage, and a successful completion by a successful completion.
Whatever in a new construction is smooth, fragrant, and pleasing to the sight—
One should point out that as a destination for humans, it is auspicious.
Whether it be a city, a village, or a house, if it is lusterless and full of hardship,
it will indeed possess such characteristics.
One should predict that in that house there will be delusion, disease, and grief— [a place] harsh like a ruined site, as if it were a new construction.
And when it is crowded with people yet appears as if devoid of luster, one should likewise foretell misfortune.
A householder living there for six months will not die; of this there is no doubt.
That which is empty yet appears as if not empty—whether it be a house or a city—should be designated as wealth endowed with all desirable qualities.
If the eastern part of the city is beautiful and pleasing to behold,
there will be a beloved wife, mental composure, wealth, and grain for the king.
(10) If the southeastern part of the city is beautiful and pleasing to behold...
Then the king attains great fame and abundant gold.
When the southern part of the city is beautiful,
there will be the acquisition of a commander-in-chief for the king, as well as abundant wealth and grain.
When the eastern, southern, and western portions of the city are delightful,
then the king’s wealth prospers and his subjects increase.
By means of the delightful western portion of the city, the monarch [attains success].
Abounding in sons, kinsmen, and grain, he attains supreme prosperity.
Furthermore, O lord of men, in a delightful western-northern quarter,
the king attains ever-increasing growth through his servants, sons, and vehicles.
If the northern part of the city is delightful,
the lord of men conquers all his enemies, and the domestic priest prospers.
If the north-eastern part of the city is pleasant to behold, [the same results follow].
In such a case, one should predict that the king will quickly attain supreme bliss.
If any portion of a completed city or similar structure is not pleasing to the mind, one should predict the decline of that very portion. ||17-18||
If the door-panel at the city gate of a new [city] should break upon being closed,
one should predict the destruction of a woman, whether her name is actually "Woman" or otherwise.
This applies to temples, city gates, ramparts, and watchtowers as well.
In elephant stables, horse stables, or likewise in chariot sheds,
in storehouses, or in armories— if any auspicious or inauspicious omen should be observed,
one should predict its result for the king.

Where the upper beam breaks, there the king perishes; likewise in the case of the breaking of a bolt, an ant-hill, or a key during a new construction. These [omens] occurring in a village, the village then perishes.
If, in the construction of houses for householders, any part of the country's [architectural] layout rises up in a double measure,
or if it breaks or bends,
or if it cracks or splits, the death of the householder is certain. (23–24)
Regarding all omens, whether auspicious or inauspicious,
their result for a house under construction should be understood as occurring after one year;
at the end of that full year, one should designate it as "ancient."
Where a gourd jar breaks when the new construction work is finished,
the most excellent woman there perishes within six months;
likewise, the house of such a person also perishes.
If the backbone of one who is engaged in new work breaks, he will certainly destroy his servants, slaves, and those he trusts; the householder dies there, and the household perishes after a year.
And here, the servants perish, especially when [the hair] is being torn out.
When the *lūmā* sections are split, one should predict the death of a daughter;
when the *muṇḍaka* sections are destroyed, his friend perishes.
If the *anupūrva* [auspicious marks] are broken, the death of sons is certain;
if the *muṇḍagodhā* [the ring-finger] is in distress, his mother perishes.
But upon the breaking of the *nāgapāśaka* [the thumb], the death of servants occurs.
If the door-panel is damaged, there is the death of a brother; if the bolt, the killing of a wife.
If the side of the bolt is destroyed, the death of a son will occur.
But if the door-fastening is destroyed, it will swiftly bring about the ruin of the family.
If the pillar of Indra, which is firm, breaks from its very root,
one should predict the ruin of that person’s family, along with their sons and herd of cattle. If the archway (toraṇa) breaks, his wealth perishes.
One should ascertain from the gods that the death of the master of the house will occur.
If [the central pillar] in the middle of the site is destroyed, the one who has grown old through misconduct perishes;
likewise, wherever the staircase breaks when the new construction is completed.
His servants, cattle, and gold perish;
his altar is shattered, and his wife perishes.
His window shall be destroyed, as shall even his firm pillar of cloth.
If the elephant-trunk beam, the horse-beam, or the pigeon-hole beam breaks, or if the *sthapanī* plank breaks, one should then predict the death of a woman. Furthermore,
if the *viṭaṅka* or the *tulā* should somehow break, [the same result follows].
If a pillar of the hall should perish, his wife will die;
if the capital of the pillar should fall off, or if even a firm pillar should crack,
or if the wooden bracket should break, there will be the death of the master.
But if there is a break in the flow of the river of the lineage, there will be the destruction of the elders of the family.
O sons, when the surface of the sky of the household is severed and destroyed, the members of the family perish within six months; of this there is no doubt. ||41-42||
When the courtyard of the palace is destroyed and the roof-ridges are broken,
the wife of that householder will undoubtedly meet her destruction. Or, if a palace that has collapsed or dissolved is further shattered, [the same fate awaits].
If the *pralīna* [defect] occurs, there will be the death of a servant; if the *vilīna* [defect] occurs, there is loss of wealth.
When the *miśra* [defect] occurs in a ruined temple, all prosperities perish;
one should predict either death or the disease of leprosy in that case.
In those places where collapse or bending is proclaimed,
or where affliction or obstruction occurs, their results have also been declared.
If they appear glossy, they are endowed with firmness.
One should then predict wealth, longevity, and joy for those previously mentioned.
If the pillar within the pericarp or the base of the hall is deficient,
the master of the house undoubtedly encounters suffering.
Having carefully deliberated upon the relative strength and weakness [of the omens], the wise and tireless man,

by pointing out the strength [of his own side], obtains power, wealth, long life, and likewise fame. Thus, having deliberated upon the relative strength and weakness indicated by such primary omens, the intelligent man [proceeds].
The knower of the science who clearly prescribes [the layout] in this matter enjoys fame, wealth, and riches.
Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Results of Door-Construction," in the *Vāstuśāstra*—also known as the *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*—composed by the Great Emperor, the illustrious Bhojadeva.
Now begins the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Architect."
We shall now describe architecture as it follows in this sequence, by knowing which the merits and defects of architects are understood:
the treatise, practical work, wisdom, and character combined with action. ||1||

A man should be devoted to the treatises on the meaning [of the sciences] that are endowed with both the definitions and the things to be defined. Likewise, he should master the science of bodily marks (sāmudra), arithmetic, astrology, prosody,
the knowledge of veins, as well as the arts (śilpa) and the rules for the construction of mechanical devices (yantra).

A wise person should know these constituent parts of the science of architecture; having ascended according to the treatises, he should observe their defining characteristics. One should establish the knowledge of architecture through well-known examples found in the scriptures.
He who, by means of the well-determined vital points (marmas) and piercing points (vedhas) of the site along with its channels and beams,
further knows all the guardians of the site’s doors according to the scriptures—
he alone is a true architect; whereas he who would act as an architect without understanding the scripture [is not].
That king who kills [beings] out of false knowledge, who is full of egoism, and who has not exerted himself in the sacred scriptures, must himself be slain by the king like death itself;
such a person wanders upon the surface of the earth as untimely death for the world.
But he who knows only the scriptures and is not firmly established in actions,
becomes bewildered at the time of performance, like a coward beholding a battle;
he who knows only ritual action does not comprehend the true meaning of the scriptures.
Like one who is sightless, he would be led helplessly along the paths by another.
The site of the ritual act, its location, measurement, and dimension;
the field, the caste, and the rites—these are the fourteen [topics] including the ploughing and the drawing of lines.
One who knows the four types of joint-cuttings within the seven circular cuts—
joined perfectly by the union of joints, arranged in upper and lower layers,
and provided with external lines— and who understands this pure [structure], is a knower of the craft.
Even a master builder (sthapati) who is capable in the performance of the sacred rites will, without wisdom,
be like an elephant deprived of its rut, even while performing other tasks;
for he who possesses ready wit is likewise a master builder when struck by adversity.

Strengthened by wisdom, he shall not be deluded at the time of action. Having boarded the boat of wisdom, the wise man shall cross over the ocean of worldly existence— that which is unknowable, difficult to perceive, of hidden meaning, and vast in extent.
One who possesses knowledge, is eloquent, and is even established in ritual actions— though endowed with such qualities, he is not superior if he is devoid of good character.
[This is so] because of anger, hatred, greed, delusion, and likewise passion.
Otherwise, one falls into inconceivability due to the lack of discernment regarding those of immoral conduct.
(17) One who possesses virtue is honored in the world; one who possesses virtue is esteemed by the virtuous.
One who possesses virtue is fit for all undertakings; one who possesses virtue is pleasant to behold. (18)
The master builder should always exert the greatest effort in the foundation of the site;
from that, works succeed and produce auspicious results.
Likewise, the eightfold work should always be understood by the master builder. (19)
Painting, the various types of writing,
woodwork, as well as the crafting of stone, perfected gold, and other such arts—
endowed with these qualities, the master builder (sthapati) attains honor. ||20-21||

The architect of pure intellect who understands this fourfold architecture through its eight constituent parts attains honor in the assembly of craftsmen, achieves supreme status, and enjoys a long life.

(22) Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Architect," in the *Vāstuśāstra* composed by the Great King of Kings, the illustrious Bhojadeva, also known as the *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*.
The forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Eight Limbs":
Architecture has been declared to be fourfold for the successful accomplishment of the principles of the site (vāstu);
we shall now describe that very same subject as endowed with its eight limbs.
Among these, the first limb is declared to be the conceptualization of the Vāstu-puruṣa;
the second consists of the layout of the city, the construction of the gates,
the division of the streets, and the placement of the walls and watchtowers.
The layout of the main streets and the locations for their divisions;
the palace as the third; the hoisting of the banner as the fourth;
and the king’s residence along with the distribution of other sites as the fifth.
The division of the four castes, the division of the house, and the sixth [topic];
the seventh is declared to be the measurement of the sacrificer’s hall;
as well as the dimensions of the sacrificial altar and the ritual procedure for the *koṭihoma*.
The eighth [topic] is the layout of the royal camp and the construction of fortifications.
He who knows these eight branches is the best of architects here;
he obtains fame and honor, and is revered by kings.
If one employs as a master builder a man who is ignorant of the treatises and unskilled in the craft, his building site will not succeed; even if it were completed, it would bring misfortune.
Therefore, that man who knows both the craft and the treatise—[he alone is fit].
He who knows even these eight branches shall become the royal architect (sthapati).
The branches have been previously mentioned in detail according to the Vāstuśāstra;
among them, that which pertains to palaces (prāsādika) we shall explain in detail hereafter.
Now we shall describe the seventh limb, which is employed in sacrifices:
once the city has been established and the abodes of the gods have been previously prepared,
one should measure out the ground for the sake of sacrifice in the south-eastern direction.
One should establish a residence there, square on all sides;
it should be constructed with a length of eighteen cubits and a width of [the same],
and its eastern gate should be established by the wise in the station of the Sun.
To the west of that, there should be a hut for the patron;
sixteen cubits in length and breadth, it is praised when facing the east. At the door of the patron’s hut, the deity who has been mentioned [should be worshipped].
From that point onward, one should construct the *prāgvaṃśa* hall to the east.
That [hall] should be situated in the middle of the altar; this is the measurement for the altar recommended by the wise. Thirty-six *prakramas* should be made from east to west.
In the central portion of the thirty-one bays, one should arrange eighteen;
there shall be twenty-four prakramas in the location of the head.
There, the head of the Puruṣa is established within the Prāgvaṃśa hall.
Therefore, the space between the eastern and western [altars] should be known as that which is honored in all sacrifices.
A space for the altar (vedyantara) must be made by which the cart passes;
from there, the northern altar (uttaravedī) is to be prepared to the north.
Indeed, the sacrificial ground (homaceṣṭa) here is made with a length and width of two cubits;
its orientation toward the southeast is recommended for the sacrificer.
It should always be made hip-high or even navel-high.
If performed with more than that, famine and drought arise.
This sacrificial rite has been described; now the Koṭihoma shall be explained. It should be performed within the city, in the quarter of the Fire-god (Agni). ||21-22||

In that place, a *koṭihoma* should always be performed in the city; likewise, a *lakṣahoma* should be performed, whether as a regular or occasional rite. However, if due to the nature of the ground a suitable location can never be found, [the following should be done].
One should establish the place for the oblation from all sides, starting from the station of Brahmā,
having taken recourse to the northeast direction, with Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas,
who know the reality of the preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa), and who are always devoted to the six duties.
The king shall be victorious when accompanied by Brahmins who are ever devoted to peace;
no calamities arise, nor does prosperity abandon his city.
There is no fear of drought, and abundance is always present.
The sacrificial limb (yājñikamaṅga), however, has been described as more praiseworthy than all other limbs.

Everything must be understood by the master builder (sthapati) in consultation with Brahmins who know the truth. One should measure the sacrificial ground using the eighty-one-square grid (ekāśītipada). ||27-28||
Now we shall describe the eighth limb, the encampment of the camp;
for when the king is about to set out from his station on an expedition,
one who knows the truth should inspect the layout of the camp.
Or a master builder who knows the rules of the science of architecture (Arthaśāstra) should design it.
The camp may be square, circular, or sometimes oval; it may also be rectangular, or in some cases, irregularly shaped. ||30-31||
According to the requirements of the terrain, one should construct a camp with a great main road on both sides; furthermore, one should diligently provide four gates for the camp.
The road for the army should be half as wide as the measurement of a city road.
O Lord of Men, the residence for ministers should be established in the Mitra quarter, or in the Pṛthvidhara,
or in the Āryama, or in the Vaivasvata quarter;
it should be situated to the west of the royal palace.
To the north of the royal priest and to the east of the commander of the forces,
he should station the harem and likewise the treasury. As the king enters the palace, he should station the horses to his right.
And on the left side, one should station the elephants; thus one should encamp the army.
One should cause a moat to be made around that royal palace, measuring three, four, or even five cubits in width. ||36-37||
The wise should divide the camp into sixty-four sections;
the layout of the camp has been described, and now the construction of fortifications is being told.
Six types of forts are said to exist for kings who desire victory.

A water-fortress, a mud-fortress, a forest-fortress, a mountain-fortress, and likewise a hill-fortress— these great fortresses should be constructed by kings. Among all types of fortresses, the hill-fortress is praised as the best.
The division of the locations for the [nine] forts has been proclaimed by the one named Aḍola;
however, in the center, the unconfined place of Brahmā is ordained.
Beginning from the place of Brahmā, five palaces are recorded.
The main road shall be three cubits wide, while the remaining roads are prescribed as two cubits wide.
A narrow path for difficult terrain should be provided all around the fort.
The gate should be constructed according to the dimensions of the road and should not be excessively high.
The affliction caused by enemy armies will be equalized, and that fortress shall always remain well-protected;
the location of the lord of the fort should be situated all around Brahmā,
or in the directions of Vaivasvata, Aryaman, Maitra, or Pṛthvīdhara.
Just as that place was previously described in the past, so it remains even in this difficult situation.
For these heroes are auspicious, faultless, and esteemed by the protector of the earth;
they are experts in the rules of the science of archery, skilled in weapons, and have mastered the scriptures.
Beautiful and numerous excellent women should be stationed in the fort;
he should also settle the harem, the treasury, and the princes there. Thus has this summary of the construction of a fort been declared.
Thus, the essence of the eightfold science of architecture has been clearly stated by us in brief;
by knowing which, one crosses the ocean of architectural science without effort, like a skilled artisan.

Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Eightfold [Architecture]," in the *Vāstuśāstra*—also known as the *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*—composed by the Great Emperor, the illustrious Bhojadeva.
Now begins the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Pacification of the Collapse of Arches and Other Portents.
If the archway of a deity or of kings—whether ancient or new, or already built or half-finished—should collapse; (1)
It may break, or burn, or bend, or become stuck;
or it may ever be struck by fire, lightning, water, and the like.
In that regard, we shall explain the defects as well as the means for pacifying those defects.
The entire gateway might fall upon his head in some way;
[this applies] to kings, army commanders, gatekeepers, and domestic priests,
as well as to the principal horses and elephants, and to the brahmins and the citizens.
In that regard, one should recognize the fear of death and also predict famine;
therefore, for the sake of achieving pacification, the wise man should perform this rite together with the officiating priests,
Brahmins, the steadfast master of the site, and the family chaplains.

At night, one should perform the fire-oblation and the bali-offering in the four directions of the city— at the crossroads, the market squares, the junctions of three roads, and in the palace of the king. In these places,
the Brahmins and others should prepare an altar strewn with unbroken grains (akṣata).
One should perform there a fire-oblation (homa) for pacification as well as an offering (bali), [using] jars, substances, fragrances, and white garlands and garments;
in this way, one shall pacify everything whatsoever that has arisen from evil.
If the archway (toraṇa) is broken, one should predict the ruin of the kingdom.
To pacify this, one should perform the previously mentioned rite.
If only that single archway of the city were to burn, [the same applies].
Then one should predict fear of fire for the kingdom and the city, both internally and externally; O Brahmin, one should employ this rite.
Or, if it is bent, decayed, or broken, one should indicate suffering from disease.
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) and the bali-offering, as well as the re-consecration of the archway. If the archway is broken by wind or lightning,
diseases will prevail, along with afflictions to the family and the loss of wealth.
One should perform a rite of pacification; thus it will become peaceful.
When this has been done first, the wise man should subsequently perform the consecration again.
He should fashion [the image] once more, making it superior to its previous construction of limbs.
It was firmly bound and well-concealed, endowed with strong timber;
rich in various forms and craftsmanship, it was well-proportioned and beautiful to behold, neither crooked nor bent, and thus even more excellent than before. ||15-16||
But once [the bird] has been dispatched, one should then have the Brahmins recite pacifying prayers (śānti),
whether [the building] is old or new, or whether it was constructed by oneself or caused to be built by another;
this applies if a pigeon enters either a palace or even a private house.
In that regard, faults arise, as well as rites for pacification.
There is Kālamūrti, the dove, and the basket that is the root of sin;
the vile bird, the base one, the black-walker, and the Vihiṅgama.
It has been declared by the sages rich in asceticism to be of four kinds:
the white, the variegated-necked, the multicolored, and the black.
If a white-colored pigeon should ever enter anyone's house—
Fame, the wealth of knowledge, and merit quickly go to ruin.
Illnesses constantly increase, and suffering for children arises.
Citrakaṇṭha takes away one's wife, while Vicitraka destroys all sons.
When the pigeon has entered, all accomplishments vanish, the dark-bodied one becomes enraged and destroys the lineage;
all diseases increase, as do calamities and misfortunes,
and various forms of bondage arise.
Therefore, becoming diligent in effort, one should perform the rite of expiation (prāyaścitta).
Having bathed, with a self purified at the three times of day, fasting, with senses subdued,
devoted to the worship and honoring of the gods, constantly intent on giving gifts, and pure— ||24-25||
Eating primarily barley-rice, constantly devoted to the fire-sacrifice (homa),
intent upon his guru and the Brahmins, and likewise wearing white garlands and garments,
a householder who has a wife should observe this vow.
In the Śvetaka it is five nights, and in the Citrakaṇṭha it is ten;
in the Citra it is fifteen days, and in the Kṛṣṇa it is twenty days.
One established in the vow must perform the delightful fire-ritual (agnikārya). ||27–28||
Having obtained as much as available, one should cut his body,
including the skin, into eight hundred pieces;
these auspicious portions should be soaked in ghee and mixed with honey and parched grain.
When the fire-rite has been performed with unbroken grains (akṣata) under the name of the five Varuṇas,
the knower of mantras should then offer meat as the sacrificial oblation (havya).
Once the raw flesh has been offered, he should then offer milk, curd, honey, and clarified butter.

One should worship all the planets and then cause the Brahmins to recite benedictions. One should bestow upon the Brahmins one-quarter of one's wealth for a white horse; half of one's wealth for a horse with a variegated neck; and three-quarters for a horse that is entirely variegated.
O Kṛṣṇe, one must perform the renunciation of all wealth before a Brāhmaṇa;
in this way, peace shall prevail in the home, bringing about the destruction of all defects.
One attains great prosperity, and the acquisition of wealth arises.
Through sons and grandsons, he attains infinite prosperity; self-restrained, he shall obtain a long life.
Having performed this, he is liberated from all sins, just as the cool-rayed moon is freed from the clouds in autumn.

Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Peace-Rites for the Breaking of Arches and the Entry of Doves," in the *Vāstuśāstra* composed by the great emperor Śrī Bhojadeva, also known as the *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*.

Now begins the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Altar. We shall fully describe those four altars which were previously declared by Brahmā, according to their names, forms, and measurements.
The first [altar] should be square, the second is called Sabhadrā,
the third is named Śrīdharī, and the fourth is known as Padminī.
These are used at the time of sacrifice, at marriage, and for the installation of deities.
In all lustration ceremonies (nīrājana), in the constant fire-oblation (vahni-homa),
in the consecration of a king, and in the erection of Indra’s banner—
these [musical instruments] are suitable for kings, as well as for the other castes in their proper order.
The quadrangular altar (vedi) which measures nine cubits on all sides is proclaimed as the Sarvabhadrā;
the Śrīdharī is to be known as seven cubits in measurement.
The lotus (nalinī) is prescribed here by those learned in the treatises as being six cubits [in size].
It should be made square, perfectly square on all sides;
it is the Sarvatobhadra, adorned with auspicious designs in the four directions.
Śrīdharī should also be understood as being joined with twenty corners;
and Nalinī should be known as possessing the configuration of a lotus. These [temples] should be made such that their height is one-third of their respective width.
One should construct long [altars] with those bricks accompanied by mantras;
at the time of sacrifice, they are remembered as being square, while for marriage they are known as "Śrīdharī.
For the installation of deities, one should arrange the altar as "Sarvabhadrā."
In the Nīrājana ceremony, in the fire-ritual, as well as in the consecration of a king,
on the altar, in the Padmāvatī rite, and likewise in the raising of Indra’s banner,
the altar should be made four-faced with staircases on all four sides.
It was provided with door-panels, adorned with a crescent moon,
equipped with four pillars, and beautified by four water-pots made of gold, silver, copper, and likewise of clay. ||12-13||
In each corner, the height of the altars should be made according to the measurement of the pillars and the nature of the roofing, adorned with beautiful monkeys placed at every corner;
[the roof] may consist of one, two, or even three layers of *sāmalasārika* tiles.
Having anointed the bases of the pillars with molasses, honey, and ghee—
or having anointed them with fine rice-milk (paramānna)— one should set them down in their proper places.
Then, having worshipped the deities, one should cause the Brahmins to pronounce blessings.
That artisan in whose mind the fourfold characteristics of the altar (vedikā) as described here exist in their entirety attains honor on earth and gains the favor of the sovereign of the land.
Prosperity shines for him in the assembly of architects, and his bright fame resounds.

Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Altar" (Vedīlakṣaṇa), in the *Vāstuśāstra*—also known as the *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*—composed by the Great King of Kings, the illustrious Bhojadeva.
Now begins the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of House Defects" (Gṛhadoṣanirūpaṇa).
Henceforth, the construction of houses and other structures that are improperly elevated will be described,
because it has been stated that [a building] should be perfectly level in one place; otherwise,
there would be flooding in the directions of the Rakshasas, Varuna, Yama, Marut, and Agni.
If the earth is submerged at its center, it brings about disease, poverty, and death.

If it is submerged by fire, there is fear of fire; if submerged on the south, it leads to death. If submerged on the west, it causes illness; if submerged on the north, it results in the loss of grain and wealth.
If the wind blows over the floating earth, it leads to quarrels, exile, and disease;
however, if the earth floats in the middle [of the water], it results in total destruction.
If the earth is covered with husks, bones, hair, insects, cow-hide, shells, ashes, or saline soil, [it portends disaster].
One should avoid a house with broken pottery or charcoal, as well as one inhabited by wicked beings or ignoble people.
A house built in Caitra brings grief; in Jyeṣṭha, it bestows death;
in Āṣāḍha, it causes the loss of cattle; and one built in Bhādrapada becomes empty.
In Āśvina, it leads to quarrels; in Kārttika, to the loss of servants;
and in Māgha, it would lead to danger from fire—one should not have [the house] constructed during these months.
[Furthermore, it should not be built] on the site of a fire or behind the backbone (the central ridge).
One should first apply the stakes and other elements at the corners of the city palaces.
A site (vāstu) that is confused regarding the east and west directions causes the destruction of women;
one that is confused regarding the north does not reach completion and destroys everything.
That which is confused regarding the southern direction leads to death;
therefore, one should construct a palace or a temple in the city within the eastern site.
One should abandon that which is twisted, unstable, wandering, or lacking its measuring cord.
That which emerges from the mouth and is curved is proclaimed as *valita*.
That which emerges from the back is *calita*, while that which is confused in direction is called *bhrānta*.
*Visūtra* is that which is devoid of the ear; we shall now explain their respective results.
If it moves when bent, there will be displacement; if it moves when straightened, there will be conflict.
Moving in a circle leads to the destruction of women, while moving like a thread with many loops brings about many enemies.
[A path] bordering on a heap of mouse droppings or an anthill, or one that is crooked like a serpent, is likewise inauspicious.
Land that is cut, split, or has a missing corner is not auspicious for a dwelling site. Land containing a heap of mouse droppings destroys wealth; land with an anthill kills the son.
A site with a missing corner causes ear disease, while one that is cut leads to ruin.
The uneven ground causes division, and the crooked [ground] produces crookedness of mind.
A house whose length from the front entrance is one and a quarter, or one and one-third, or one and a half, or even double [the width], yields undesirable results.
A house that has two wings, three wings, or even four wings, yet is devoid of a *mūṣā* (a connecting passage), yields undesirable results. Likewise,
if it lacks an *alinda* (veranda) in front, behind, or on the sides, it is likewise inauspicious.
A hall in one's own house is not praised, but one in a temple is indeed praised.
A dwelling whose door is situated on the back side is called "devouring";
such a house leads to mutual discord between the two householders.
A house with a protruding thorn, one lacking a foot, one with uneven joints, and one heavy at the top—
this is declared to be the fourfold defect of the vital points (marmas) of dwellings.
Whichever limb of the site of the building a path runs through, [that is its specific defect].
One should point out that a particular limb of that site has been cut off by him.
A site with a severed limb is deficient; it causes fear and brings about all manner of evils.
The limb of its owner is thereby broken, and otherwise, the piercing of that site is fruitless.
If the path passes through the middle of two houses,
it will certainly incur the defects prescribed for piercing a door. And when the path goes along both sides of the two houses, [the same applies].
Then that piercing of the path would cause grief and torment.
The utsaṅga, the pūrṇabāhu, and likewise the hīnabāhu—these four types of entrances are said to be for direct perception. ||24-25||

Where the door of the dwelling faces directly toward the site, it is called *utasaṅga*; if it is to the right, it is *pūrṇabāhu*. If it is to the left, it is *hīnabāhu*; and if it is behind the site, it is *pratyakṣa*.
This fourth entrance of the site has been described by the wise.
In the entrance known as Utsaṅga, there shall be loss of progeny for the householder;
there will be a depletion of his wealth and grain, and death will certainly occur. ||27-28||
For a householder living in that dwelling site where Pūrṇabāhu resides, sons, grandsons, wealth, grain, and happiness are constantly present.
In the site of Hīnabāhu, the householder has few friends and very few kinsmen.
One who possesses little wealth may be defeated, or he may be tormented by women and ailments.
However, in whichever house entry toward the west is prescribed,
for the men dwelling therein, a certain loss of wealth shall occur.
When the fire-places are not properly situated, it is known as "the breach of the hall" (śālābheda);
one dwelling there encounters death, suffering, and disease.
[This applies when] the northern and southern halls, as well as those extending east and west, are misaligned.
Alternatively, a door that is positioned otherwise causes slaughter and imprisonment. One should cause the bees to enter the frames but must not break open the hive;
for when the hives are broken by the bees, the householders perish.
Where there is a division of the hall either at the back or on the sides,
the householder will certainly suffer the loss of wealth and grain. Where the hall faces west, that house is known as "Vikokila."
The lifespan and the four-footed livestock, as well as the grain of those dwelling there, perish. For one who has breached the boundary markers of a temple, a palace, or a house,
prosperity becomes unstable and their residence shall not endure for long.
The Moon (Candrā) in the womb (Garbha) should be known as causing all defects;
it leads to destruction without a crucible (mūṣā), and the window (gavākṣaka) leads to the cessation of desire (kāma).
When the cheek, the belly, the back, or the armpit is pierced, [the result is as stated].
At that time, a pair of unbearable swellings arises for the husband;
from the womb, two goiters appear on both sides, located in the armpits and on the walls of the ears.
One should identify the right and left sides of the belly, and the back situated behind.
If the door established [in its proper place] is obstructed, urinary stones arise for the householder;
but if that door is opened, no misfortune arises for him.
However, one should never obstruct the eastern door, even by a ninth part.

If the ears are obstructed, there is the affliction of urinary stones; if the channels are severed, there is an inability to bend. Where the severed parts are piled up and the windows for looking out are blocked, there shall be no birth, and even if one occurs, it perishes.
When the wall being built inclines outward toward the south,
one should know that there will be fear of disease as well as fear of punishment from the king.
But when the western wall extends outward at its front, [the same result follows].
Then one should know there will be loss of wealth and fear from thieves.
But when the northern wall being built extends outward,
there will then be great calamity for both the householder and the builder.
When the top of the eastern wall being built extends outside,
then for the householder there will be severe fear of punishment from the king. When the southeast corner being built extends outside, [the same result follows].
In that case, there would be incomparable fear of fire and doubt regarding the master.
When [the breath] goes out through the right and rear ears,
there will be strife and affliction therein, and there is danger for the wife.
If the northern or western corner of the altar being constructed should go outside,
there will be misfortune for the son, the vehicle, and the servants.
When the northeastern corner goes outside the dwelling, [the same result follows].
At that time, there would be a depletion of cattle, bulls, and elders.
(51) That house whose four walls protrude outward while being built is here called a "mandira" in the shape of a jasmine flower. (52)
In such a house, there is neither income nor expenditure as great as that which occurs when,
emaciated by her very fault, her husband flees; indeed,
the house is diminished even as it is being built on all sides.
That which is contracted should be known as such; in that case, there will be fear of the king.
That which is contracted at the ends and expanded in the middle, having the shape and configuration of a mṛdaṅga drum—in that case, there will be fear of disease.
A house that is wide at the front and back but narrow in the middle is designated as "mṛdumadhya" (soft-middle); in such a place, fear of hunger arises.
A house with uneven and protruding corners causes the loss of wealth.
One should also indicate the previously mentioned results for the ears as being like those for the walls.
A door must never be made in the middle for human dwellings;
if a door is made in the middle, the destruction of the family occurs there.
A door pierced by another door leads to an inauspicious rebirth;
it brings contact with undesirable objects and the destruction of wealth and grain.
When a new door is joined with an old one, it seeks out another master.
A door that is slanted downward, pierced by a royal staff, or condemned is inauspicious. A door made of new material joined with old, or of substances that cause strife,
or one arising from mixed species of materials, is not auspicious for either a door or a house.
Whatever substance has been consecrated and established in the locations of a house,
its movement causes instability for the master of the house.
One should not employ a substance removed from one site for use at another site.

There shall be no worship in the palace, nor shall the householder dwell in the house. When a residence is constructed with wealth consumed by the gods, the master does not dwell there; even if he dwells there, he perishes.
The shadow of a tree arising from the sun and the shadow of a banner are censured;
by crossing over these doorways, they cause hunger, disease, and strife.
The shadow of the pinnacle of a palace is likewise proclaimed to be the shadow of a banner.
The third, fifth, and seventh lunar mansions (tārās) are not auspicious for the master’s house.
A door that is uneven, jagged, facing [the entrance], situated at the back,
or opening to the left is not auspicious when it is positioned directly in front of the house.

If it is in a low place, the husband will be dominated by his wife; if in a high place, he will live among wicked people. If it is in front, there will be suffering for one's children; if behind, the wives will be fickle.
If it is on the left, there will be loss of wealth; if at the door, it occurs before the master.
Therefore, wise men should not construct a door of such a form [as previously described].
Tusks, scales, pillars, walls, crucibles,
and windows should not be placed in the middle of a door, nor should these be situated unevenly.

That which is recounted in the Itihāsas and Purāṇas as a representation of past events is not desired if it is censured when in the home; however, that same thing is praised in the temples of the gods. Those stories which are like Indra’s net and those which are composed falsely [are likewise condemned].
One should not place in one's dwellings anything that is terrifying.
A door that opens by itself brings about expulsion;
it either steals wealth, causes enmity with kinsmen, or provokes strife.
A door that is closed by oneself causes much suffering;
it is noisy, creates fear, is cold to the feet, and may cause a miscarriage.
One should not place an object with its face downward, nor facing west or south.
If the tips [of the pillars] face west, there is affliction; if they face south, however, it is emptiness.
One should not construct the pillars, the door, or the walls in a reversed manner;
by the reversal of these, many faults would arise for men. ||75-76||
According to the root sūtra, [the structure] should be built upon the ground;
whatever houses are built higher and higher cause distress.
Whatever moments (kṣaṇas) there may be on the lower floor, one should have an equal number on the upper floors.
One should not perform [the ritual] by omitting the subsequent [elements] as they are prescribed.
(78) In that place where the hall is low and the porch is higher, death occurs there, along with constant grief and fears. (79)
One should construct the doors on the upper floors in accordance with the main door;
otherwise, they will bring about fear.
A door that is too high causes hunger and fear, while one that is crooked leads to the destruction of the family.
If [the door] is pierced excessively, it causes suffering; if it is pierced at the very edge, it leads to total ruin.

If the outer leaf is pierced, there is exile; if it is pierced in the direction of the quarters, there is fear of bandits. If the root-door is pierced by another door, it brings about destruction. (81–82)
If pierced by a crossroads or a carriage road, there is exile and hatred born of servants;
if pierced by a tree, there is loss of wealth and harm to children.
If pierced by mud, there will be grief; if it leaks water, there is expenditure.
If it is pierced by a well, epilepsy occurs; by a deity, destruction;
by a pillar, the corruption of women; and by Brahmā, the ruin of the lineage.
If the door is higher than the measuring line, fear arises from the king.
From the *māna* [line] comes misfortune; from the *hīna* [line], there is fear of thieves.
From the *śvabhra-viddha* [line], there are diseases and the depletion of wealth.
From the *devadhvaja* [line], there will be imprisonment and the fearful loss of sovereignty.

The fear of a derangement of the humors (sannipāta) is equal to that of a well; the appearance of the [astrological] figure is seen as such. Heartache arises from the potter’s wheel, while poverty results from the water.
Disease comes from the peak of the sickle, and the loss of a son from the oven.
By a broken mortar one becomes afflicted with gravel; by a stone, one suffers from urinary stones (aśmarī).
By a water-jar, one becomes ill-fated; by ashes, one is seized by hemorrhoids (arśas).
Poverty comes upon the head of the householder if the door is pierced by a shadow.
By [seeing] land, chariots, or anthills, there will be travel to a foreign land.
[The face] is emaciated, deformed, very high, formidable, flaccid, broad, crooked, wide, upturned, like the point of a spear, and has a short belly. ||90-91||
A door that is tilted toward its own base, short, with deficient corners,
or with its face bent downward, and which has deviated from the path of the side-lines, is not auspicious;
it brings about terrible ruin and the destruction of the master's prosperity.
Therefore, one should always avoid quarreling while living there.
One should not make the outer gate higher than the inner gate, nor should it be too narrow;
for a gate that is either too high or too wide does not lead to auspiciousness.
If the joint of the cloth (paṭṭasandhi) should somehow be located in the middle of the door,
then there will be the destruction of the builder and the total ruin of his lineage.
If the scales (tulā) or the counter-scales (atula) are made obliquely at the door, [the same calamity follows].

Then poverty, disease, and suffering afflict the master. (96) If such women enter the household through successive generations, there arises a deficiency of wealth and longevity, as well as ill health. (97)
That balance named Lalāṭī is placed upon the Udumbara tree;
it brings about either the disgrace or the death of maidens.
If, when placed upon the belly of the northern beam, it is level with the forehead, [the maiden is pure].
Even that forehead-mark made with *tulā* would cause the destruction of the family.
When applied with a mass of *tulā*, it should be known as a substitute for the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*);
it brings misfortune to one who lives there and causes unhappiness to the household. ||99-100||
If even a single balance-beam should somehow be pierced through the middle,
then the excellent body [of the balance] would break and the wealth would be lost.
(101) No breach of the wall should be made by any of the tips of the beams.
One who has placed his foot upon the station of Brahmā (the head) will cause the destruction of his lineage by means of a burden-band.

(102) If a treaty is made between two parties—whether they are unequal or equal—by means of a burden-band, then the eldest son born from that treaty, as well as the maker of the treaty itself, shall perish. (103)
One should never eat or sleep with the grain-mark facing downward;
for one who eats thus there will be loss of wealth, and for one who sleeps thus, great disease.
If it is placed sideways, there will be destruction and diseases, and from a Rakshasa there is fear.
Death occurs for one who has a bedstead placed upon a wall-peg in the bedroom (105).
One should avoid having eaves, bird-cages, bells, banners, umbrellas, and putto-shaped figures, as well as lion-ears and pigeon-holes, constructed in houses (106).
One should not place an Indra-kīla, a Śukra, a Tumbī, or a half-bamboo beam in a house, because such things, when so situated, bring about all manner of evils.
That which is produced too quickly or after a very long time, that which is made of inferior materials, or that which is poorly supported— [these are likewise to be avoided].
A house that lacks a stable foundation collapses in five ways.
Just as a man with a body that is excessively stout or short is deformed and weak, so too is a dwelling by means of its material substance. (108–109)
Wood that is decayed, worm-eaten, mixed with other materials, inferior, crooked,
fallen from its natural position, fierce, pointed, curved at the corners, pierced at the joints, having a small base,
a narrow middle, a thick root, or split in the belly— such wood [is unfit].
One should avoid trees that have split roots, those shaped like the back of a tortoise, and those that are devoid of branches.
One should avoid trees that have been felled by elephants, horses, fire, water, or wind, as well as those that are the dwellings of many birds or frequented by crows and owls. 111–112.
One should avoid those born from honey-vessels, piśācas, serpents, or wicked beings; those growing on shrines or in cremation grounds;
those born at crossroads, in groups of three, or at the confluence of great rivers and on roads;
those born in temples; and those that are withered at the top or have wounded leaves.
One should avoid trees entwined with creepers, those full of hollows, cavities, and knots, as well as thorny trees, and those falling toward the southern or western directions;
specifically, the wood-apple, fig, holy fig, śirīṣa, banyan, and campaka trees. (114-115)
One should avoid trees such as the kovidāra, dhava, ariṣṭa, śleṣmātaka, and vibhītaka; furthermore, one should abandon trees that bear seven-leaved leaves, milky sap, or fruit (116),
as well as places where vital points (marmans) are afflicted by doors or walls.
One should predict poverty or the ruin of the family for the householder there [at that time].
By pillars, the master perishes; by scales, the death of a wife is certain.
By the *saṅgrahas*, there will be the destruction of kinsmen; by the *jayantīs*, the death of a daughter-in-law.

If the bodies [of the figures] are situated at the vital points (marmasthāna), the master’s body is afflicted; if they are at the joints (sandhi) as gatekeepers, one should predict a separation from friends. Through the pegs (nāgadanta) there is affliction of the house; through the serpent-nooses (nāgapāśa), the loss of wealth.
One should declare the destruction of servants through *kāpicchaka* trees situated at vital points (*marmasthita*).
Furthermore, six types of wooden structures, as well as windows and lookout points, when located at vital points, produce great danger. (120–121)
When the door is pressed down by pillars, or by the middle sections of the doors, or by beams, or by nāgapāśakas,
or by windows, or by nāgadantas,
diseases increase, there is loss of wealth, and the destruction of the family. (122)
There will be fear of royal punishment and suffering for one's offspring. Furthermore, if the six wooden beams are pierced in their centers or at the middle of the door by nails, wood-splinters,
and the like, one should predict this very same result.
A bedstead that is pierced by wooden pegs,
pillars, or windows brings fear of weapons from one's husband or even from thieves. A door constructed in the middle of a house causes the destruction of wealth and the treasury.
A wife might incite a quarrel with her husband or corrupt his character;
even by provoking him at a vital point with wealth increased by one [unit], the destruction of the householder’s entire property or his death would certainly occur. (126–127)
If the doors, pillars, scales, and verandas are constructed with the aforementioned defects,
and even the structural cords and wall-brackets are missing, that house becomes a void.
This occurs when the sites for buildings lack the prescribed divisions and proportions.
In cases involving Yakṣas, Mothers (Mātṛs), or ritual actions [of malevolent spirits], death from disease occurs without a doubt.
One should not allow trees that are pungent, thorny, foul-smelling, or inhabited by Guhyakas and the like to stand near cities, palaces, or dwellings.
Where the jujube tree, the plantain, the pomegranate,
and the citron grow within a house, that house does not sprout [with progeny].
Wealth destroys wealth, and lineage destroys lineage from its very extent.

One should perform worship that is superior in height, and provide a lineage [of offerings] that is superior in extent, by means of pillars, structural members, walls, bands, capitals, and likewise houses;
as well as by windows, arches, and so forth, by canopies, and by bulbous finials. ||132-133||
Through the destruction, falling, or loss of diamond-studded branches,
door-frames, joints, bolts, thresholds, and new lattices,
misfortune certainly befalls the householder. (134)
Disease, poverty, suffering, affliction, and destitution arise [from these defects].

[A banner] that is excessively covered, has a hole in its interior, is twisted, or vomited [of its color], which is deficient in the middle, has lost its thread, is pierced by a thorn, or is heavy at the top—[these are defective]. 135–136.

Its veranda was ruined in its splendor, and the floor of the hall was uneven; it was pierced here and there by various objects, divided by broken steps, its upper walls were deficient, and its pillars and walls were destroyed. ||137||
A house with broken walls, one from which the rafters have been removed, one lacking its foundation, one devoid of people,
or one that is dilapidated, brings about undesirable results for the master. Therefore, having avoided these defects, one should construct a house that brings auspiciousness.
Since such a house would bring harm to both the owner and the builder,
these defects must always be understood by vigilant artisans and avoided by those who desire auspicious renown.

Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of House Defects," in the *Vāstuśāstra* (Treatise on Architecture) composed by the Great King of Kings, Śrī Bhojadeva, also known as the *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*.
Now begins the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Temples such as the Rucaka.
We shall describe the origin and development of those temples which are considered appropriate for the gods, kings, and especially for the members of the [four] castes.
In ancient times, Brahmā created five celestial chariots for the enemies of the asuras—
glorious and vast, wandering through the paths of the sky.
Among them were the Vairāja, the Kailāsa, the Puṣpaka, and the one named Maṇika.

The Lord of the Universe [granted] golden palaces variegated with jewels for the Lord of Wealth who holds a spear, for the wielder of the noose, and for the Lord of the Gods; and the fifth was Triviṣṭapa, each in due order. ||3-4||

He likewise fashioned many other [images] of the Sun and other deities for their specific distinction, according to the forms previously described for each respective divinity; and he also constructed palaces of similar form using stone, unbaked brick, and other materials.
He fashioned [these] for the purpose of adorning the cities:
the Vairāja should be square, the one named Kailāsa should be circular, and the Puṣpaka aerial chariot should have the shape of a long rectangle. ||6-7||
The water-jar (maṇika) is circular and elongated, while the triple-altar (triviṣṭapa) should have eight corners;
the Lord created various other types of these, including the glorious ones.
Those specific varieties which were previously ordained there by the Lotus-born One [are to be followed].
We shall describe all of them according to their names, shapes, and dimensions:
Rucaka, Citrakūṭa, the third Siṃhapañjara, Bhadra, Śrīkūṭa, Uṣṇīṣa, Śālākṣa, and Gajayūthapa. ||9-10||
Nandyāvarta, Avataṃsa, Svastika, Kṣitibhūṣaṇa, Bhūjaya, Vijaya, Nandin, Śrītaru, Pramadāpriya,
Vyāmiśra, Hastijātīya, Kubera, and Vasudhādhara. ||11||
The Sarvabhadra, the one called Vimāna, and the Muktakoṇa by name—
these twenty-four have been briefly described as square. Now we shall describe other palaces that are circular.
Valaya, Dundubhi, Prānta, Padma, Kānta, Caturmukha, the one called Māṇḍūka, Kūrma, Tālīgṛha, and Ulūpika—
thus the ten palaces have been briefly described according to their forms.
Those which are square and elongated are also described by name:
Bhava, Viśāla, Sāmmukhya, Prabhava, Śibirāgṛha, Mukhaśāla, Dviśāla, Gṛharāja, Amala, and Vibhu. (15–16)
Thus, these ten types of square and rectangular [buildings] have been described. Now, we shall describe the circular and rectangular palaces by their names:
Āmoda, Raitika, Tuṅga, Cāru, Bhūti, and Niṣevaka.
Sadāniṣedha, Siṃha, Suprabha, and Locanotsava—these ten temples are declared to be long and rectangular by name. Now I shall briefly state the names of those that are octagonal. ||18-19||
Vajraka, Nandana, Śaṅku, Mekhala, Vāmana, Laya, Mahāpadma, Haṃsa, Vyomacandra, and Dayāv—
these ten types of temples are said to have eight bases.

Thus there are sixty-four types; their characteristics are now described. According to their configuration, dimensions, and arrangement, as well as by the number of pillars and other features, their specific varieties will be explained individually in due order. ||21-22||
The largest portion should be four cubits, the next three and a half cubits,
and the smallest should be measured at three cubits;
thus they are divided into large, medium, and small portions.
All temples exist according to the sequence of superior, middling, and inferior [dimensions].
When the site has been made square and divided into four parts,
one should construct the pedestal (pīṭha), raised by one part, which provides support and stability for the structure.

Likewise, a haṃsapṛṣṭhī should be placed upon it on all sides; it should be one cubit high, circular, and adorned with water-issuing ornaments. Then, within that pedestal, its length and width should be two parts.
The Rucaka temple should be constructed with a height of three parts;
its roof (saṃchā) should be one and a half parts, and the other [section] should also be one and a half parts.
With that, there should be three roofs together with a neck (kaṇṭha), and by means of that, it becomes a Sāmalasāraka.
Its door should be one part in height and half a part in width;

it should be provided with a pediment (prāgrīva) and surrounded by fourteen [parts]. It should be beautiful with a mansion (saudha) and a porch (ālindaka), and equipped with an upper roof-covering (ūrdhvacchādya) and a recess (upakarṣa).
When it is constructed here, surrounded by twenty-two pillars,
adorned with a fore-neck (prāgrīva) and embellished with an *alinda* measuring one part,
the temple in its central region is celebrated as the Rucaka type. ||30-31||

The *rucaka* [type of chariot] is adorned with various colorful, forward-pointing ear-ornaments (*karṇaprāgrīvaka*), and is surrounded by two forward-pointing structures on each of its four sides, along with two windows (*gavākṣa*) on every side. ||32||
Encircled by a row of pigeons and adorned with the excellence of its gates,
that palace was then called Citrakūṭa. (33) [Citrakūṭa]
Furthermore, when this very [structure] is built with six pillars and is devoid of a front porch (prāgrīvaka),
it becomes a lattice-like form;
that auspicious temple is then called a *siṃhapañjara*.
The Siṃhapañjara (Lion’s Cage):
when two of its [corners] have their *rīvikās* at the ears,
and it stands with its movement situated in the *alindaka*, then it is proclaimed as the Bhadra.
It should be auspicious, with four prominent peaks on the four cardinal directions;
having four gates both outside and inside, it is known by the name Śrīkūṭa.
Śrīkūṭa:
If this very [temple] has six wooden beams (ṣaḍdāruka) and a front door, and its central core consists of pillars, then it is designated as Uṣṇīṣa. (37)
The *uṣṇīṣa* (pedestal) is four parts wide and six parts in length;
this is declared to be the auspicious pedestal for a hall-house, including its projection from the hall.
To the west of its center,

one should construct the inner sanctum (garbhabhavana), measuring two parts in length and breadth, and adorned with a portico (alindaka). In front of it, a boundary wall (sīmā) should be made, extending for two parts.
One part shall be wide and adorned with four pillars;
in front of that, another boundary should be made, six parts in length,
extending crosswise, one part in width, and beautified by two entrances.
This is the hall-house (śālāgṛha), surrounded by twenty-two pillars,
featuring auspicious front porches, altars, lattices, wings, and stairs;
it is called a "hall."
On a site where the width measures five parts and the length eight parts of the area,
one should construct a pedestal on both sides, made of stone and provided with stairs;
in the rear portion from the center of this, one should establish the temple of the deity.
It should be square, well-proportioned, with its length, height, and width divided [into parts];
its middle section should have a width of three-quarters of a part and a height of one and a half parts.
Its face should be constructed in the center, adorned on both sides.

The boundary line that has emerged [from the center] should be divided into two parts, three parts, and so forth, as appropriate. At its front, there should be a square structure with four pillars, one part in width;
another boundary line should likewise be made five parts in length across.
In this [mandala], thirty-two pillars should be erected in total.
The outer enclosure surrounding the inner sanctum (garbha) shall have an extent of one part.
Thus, it should be adorned with altars, lattices, forms, and so forth.
And this palace, which is like the leader of a herd of elephants, rises high on the outside. On a square field divided into six parts on all sides, [the palace stands].
The inner sanctum (garbha) should be made two parts; the door should be one part in height.
The width of the door should be half a part. Furthermore, one should make the height of the palace four parts and cover it like the Citrakūṭa style.
Outside of that, there should be two-part halls with verandas;
enclosed by outer walls, they should be auspicious and four parts long.
There should be two windows each, and six pillars for every hall.
Or it may be constructed by righteous builders supported by four pillars.
This Nandyāvarta [temple] would thus consist of four front-projections (prāgrīva);
endowed with eastern and western doors, the temple possesses auspicious characteristics.
The Nandyāvarta [mandala]: In a field with a width of six parts and a length divided into ten parts, one should establish the chamber of the deity in the middle of the rear portion of it. 55.
The square should be laid out on all sides with four divisions; its door should be made one and a half parts in height and three-quarters of a part in width,
adorned with lion faces.
The boundary for that [hall] should be made equal to the Devakoṣṭha, provided with sixteen pillars rising two parts in height;
it is surrounded on all sides by walls belonging to the Devakoṣṭha boundary. ||57-58||
The *alinda* (porch) should be made with one share and adorned with lattice windows;
at the front and sides of the boundary walls, it should be provided externally with six wooden supports.
The *prāgrīvas* (front projections) should be made with two shares and surrounded by an *alinda* of one share.
All [the pillars] are supported by two pairs of pillars and adorned with rows on their sides.
The *alinda* (porch) should be constructed with four pillars at the front of the *prāgrīvaka* (antechamber);
this is known as the *avataṃsaka*, endowed with all auspicious characteristics.
The temple has been correctly described.
An ear-ornament.
The Svastika is now described:
having made the site square and divided it into six parts,
one should construct the temple in the center, measuring two parts in both length and width.
Its door-jamb is half a part in width and one part in height. The inner sanctum has four pillars, and the veranda outside is one part wide;
it should have twelve pillars, and there is another veranda of one part. ||63-64||
It should be constructed all around, joined with twenty pillars;
the front portion, however, is covered by a projection (cayāvṛta) and provided with eight supporting columns.
Leaving one part on each side, the two corners are extended by one part.
With its projections and recesses divided into parts, and with windows on three sides,
this palace known as the Svastika is described as having variegated characteristics. (67) [The Svastika.]
Now, the temple possessing auspicious characteristics is described:
when the square plot is divided into six parts on all sides,
the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) in the center should have a length and width of two parts each.
It should be provided with pillars that are two parts in height, clearly defined and possessing the proper characteristics.
One should join beautiful archways (toraṇas) to the four directions at the outer projections of the base of the sanctum.
Equal in measure to the pillars of the inner sanctum, or perhaps two such pillars,
they were raised up and joined with finials (kalaśas) shaped like the solar disc,
and further adorned in many ways with foliage and various arrangements of leaves and other ornaments.
Furthermore, its face should be adorned with the mouths of sea-monsters (makara) upon the crown;
one should place two makara-ornaments as fillers between the two pillars,
joined together and facing one another at the mouths of the two makaras.
The procedure for all four archways has been described by me;
another [portion], the *alinda*, is proclaimed to be one part on the outer side.
At the edge of the *alinda*, there should be shrines (*dhārmikāyatana*) measuring one part each.
They should be wrapped around the outer wall, facing one another. On the ground that lies outside the walls of the righteous abodes,
there should be six wooden beams, each raised by the measure of one share.
One should adorn those [walls] with directional circles (dikcakra) provided with steps and projecting eaves (prāgrīvaka). Furthermore, from the second part of the western wall,
one should place a divine chamber (devakoṣṭha) in the middle, extending across two parts.
One should also construct a door-socket (dvārapāśa) for it, rising to one-eighth of the [total] height;
likewise, its width should be half a part. Thus has this ornament of the earth, the Prāsāda temple, been correctly described, endowed with all its characteristic features.
One should divide a square plot of ground into twelve parts;
