in the center, one should construct the inner sanctum (garbha) consisting of four pillars, occupying two parts. Outside of that, the veranda (alinda), possessing twelve pillars, should occupy one part.
One should construct a toraṇa arch from the two pillars situated in the middle of the western side.
The porch (alinda) should be one part in size, enclosed by a wall of one part;
in the east, there should be a six-beamed structure in the center, with a length equal to the measurement of the interior chamber (garbha).
The third part shall be a portico (alinda) enclosed by a wall;
furthermore, it should extend for four parts, and thereon should be the "six-wood" structure (ṣaḍdāruka).
One should construct a front porch (prāgrīva) with a width of one part and a length of two parts.
In front, it is supported by pillars and surrounded by a collection of parts situated within the divisions;
as it is described for the eastern direction, so it is for the northern and the southern as well.
But in the western direction, furthermore, it is outside of the second *alindaka*.
One should construct the divine chamber (devakoṣṭha) with its length and width measuring two parts;
it should be beautiful, provided with wings and doors, and adorned with door-sockets (pāśa).
From that, there should be an alinda measuring one part, surrounded on the outside by a wall.
It may be covered with a screen on the outside or adorned with lattice windows;
because it conquers the earth, it is called Pṛthivījaya or Bhūjaya.
When both [sides] of the Pṛthvījaya are at the corners, with their tips reaching the ears and each measuring one part, then it should be known as Vijaya.
This is Vijaya.
When this [structure] is raised all around, excluding the outer veranda (bāhyālinda), it is then joined by corner pavilions (karṇaprāsādaka) situated upon the middle veranda and the palace (saudha);
thereafter, the inner portions of the first veranda are raised even higher than that. ||89-90||
When both [the subject and object] are concealed by the two veils, then it is called "Nanda"; thus, Nanda.
When the site has been made square and divided into ten parts, there shall be a square central chamber for the deity occupying two parts.
Its door-frame should be made one part in height and half a part in width. ||91-92||
There may be an outer porch (*alindaka*) consisting of twelve parts extending from the divine chamber (*devakoṣṭha*);
it should be understood as being one part wide, and the other [part] is joined with a wall.
This [porch] is provided with two-part *prāgrīva*s that project by one part.
Likewise, there should be a third vestibule (alinda) surrounded on all sides by walls,
adorned with four pillars having projecting fronts (prāgrīvaka) and entryways;
the outer wall should consist of one part, while the other [inner wall] should be equal to the supporting pillars.
Thus, this palace named Śrītaru has been fully described. This is Śrītaru.
On the walls of the second portico of this very pillar-interior (stambhagarbha),
six wooden beams (ṣaḍdārūṇi) should be constructed according to the established form;
two double-fronted (prāgrīvaka) structures should be made outside the third portico.
And those two [pillars] are separated by two [spaces], extending out from all sides.
Thus, it is surrounded on all sides by five parts of pillars, including two [main ones],
with four pillars provided with entrances and exits.
This palace is renowned by the name Pramadāpriya. 99.
Pramadāpriya.
When its fore-neck (prāgrīvaka) has the same extent and width as its [main] portion,
and two transverse wings (śāle) are placed in front of the broken vestibule (bhinnālinda), that is the auspicious Mukha [plan].
When it is joined with corner-palaces (karṇaprāsādaka) in the position of the second vestibule, [it is likewise auspicious].
Thus, this temple is proclaimed as having a mixed designation; it is the Mixed [type].
And when the wall of this *vijaya* is joined with *karṇa-lāṅgalaka*s, it is then called the *hastijātīya* type. (102) [This concludes] the *hastijātīya*.

When conquering the earth, if there are boundary-foreheads (sīmāprāgrīva) on the grounds, they should have two parts on both sides; likewise, in the case of transverse halls (tiryakśālāmukha), [the measurement applies]. In the rear hall of the porch (alinda), the entire hall is auspicious for all to behold.
Likewise, in this case, the Ṣaḍdāruka [hall] should be four parts long;
everything else is as before, and Kubera shall be its presiding deity.
Kubera.
Another temple is described here as Dharādhara;
it was erected by Kubera’s son, adorned with corner-towers (karṇa-prāsādas), provided with a central door, and is known as the glorious Dharādhara. ||105-106||
The upholder of the earth.
That which has Citrakūṭa at its front and, from there, extends toward all directions with the splendor of a mountain,
is called the *sarvatobhadra*.
This is the *sarvatobhadra* [type of temple].
When there are two *karṇaprāgrīvakas* and also two *śālāprāgrīvakas*, then this [temple] is called the auspicious *vimāna*. (108) This is the *vimāna* type.
When a vimāna is released from its pedestal and surrounded on all sides by halls (śālās),
and when it is joined with one another through the connection of these halls, it is then established as a vimāna;
it is endowed with corner pavilions (karṇaprāsādaka) and joined with corners that are devoid of halls.
That palace, with its corners released, would be exceedingly beautiful;
this is the *muktakoṇa* (released-corner) style.
The square palaces have already been described individually by their own specific characteristics;
now those that are circular are being described by their respective attributes. Among them, first is the one shaped like a ring, which is called Valaya.
When the field has been rotated all around and divided into four parts,
one should construct an auspicious pedestal (*pīṭha*) with a landing (*sārohaṇa*), rising to a height of one and a half parts;
it should be encircled by elephant-heads and by a *makara* emerging from the water.
A temple should be constructed there, provided with an outer section;
its width should be three-quarters [of the main hall], adorned with a door whose height is double [the width].
Its veranda should have eight pillars, and this constitutes the outer enclosure.
The *vṛttacchādya*, the *siṃhakarṇa*, as well as the *jālakarūpa* and the *bhūlavaya*. ||115||
It may be *prāgrīvaka* if it is bent by the height of a pillar; that is called *dundubhi*. When those three are at the edge, it is so designated.
This very same [posture], with four auspicious *prāgrīvakas*, is the *padma*.
When it is constructed with four pillars at its rear,
with a circular central chamber and walls situated on both sides,
that circular-shaped temple is renowned as the *Kānta*. ||117-118||
Wherein there are four doorways and a porch belonging to the veranda itself,
the second part, measuring one-eighth [of the whole], should consist of twenty-four pillars;
and the *prāgrīvaka* (antechamber) is provided with two pillars each.

Where there are four [entrances], that is declared here to be the four-faced temple (prāsāda). When it has only one entrance, it is the Prāgrīva, surrounded by an alinda; likewise, there is another single type called Prāgrīva situated in front of it.
This excellent Vṛtta-prāsāda is known as Māṇḍūka; when its front-projections (prāgrīvaka) are arranged in the cardinal and intermediate directions,
this Prāsāda then becomes the invincible one named Kūrma.
When, in each of the directions, four *prāgrīvakas* surrounded by *alindas* are constructed with eight pillars each, like the limbs of a tortoise;
and other *prāgrīvakas* are placed transversely at their front. (123–124)
When [the measurement] occurs in the middle portion of that which is provided with sixteen pillars, one should know that the defects are to be identified; [this is] the foremost green-necked [type].
Thus have the circular temples been fully described according to their names and characteristics.
Now we shall describe the rectangular palaces here.
On a site that is eight parts long and four parts wide, the pedestal (pīṭha) is desired to be two parts, one and a half parts, and one part [respectively]. 126–127.
Leaving out the western portion, the divine chamber (devakoṣṭha) shall occupy two parts;
one should establish the boundary within it by means of eight pillars at its front.
Outside this divine chamber, together with its boundary, there shall be an Ālindaka occupying one part.

It is joined with twenty supporting pillars and encircled by a lattice-work on the altar-platform. At its front is a prāgrīvaka (front porch), adorned with a pair of pillars, covered with two layers of roofing, glorious, and embellished with lion-ear (siṃhakarṇa) ornaments. ||129-130||
This palace named Bhava is now described as being extensive;
when it increases both in its exit and in its boundary line,
then there should be two *valabhīs* on the two sides, and it would be known by the name Viśāla.
When there is a wall in the womb of Viśāla on three sides,
and two windows each facing one another, then it is Sāmmukhya;
when its vestibules face the three directions and its inner chamber is elongated, then it is Prāgrīva.
Having abandoned the two *valabhya*s, two *prāgrīvaka*s are prescribed;
likewise, by omitting one part from each of the *karṇa*s, there shall then be the *prabhava*.
When both *prāgrīvaka*s are at the mouth of this very [structure], [it is so].

When there are two more on each side and two in front of the neck, and there are walls at the corners, then it is a *śibirāgṛha*. When a hall (*śālā*) of double the width of its [the main hall’s] face is added to its very front, [it becomes a *śibirāgṛha*]. ||135–136||
In length, there are six parts; two of these are for the neck-protrusions (prāgrīva) at the front. On both sides of those walls, there should be two windows (gavākṣaka) each.
At the boundary, there should be twelve pillars, and then the front hall (mukhaśālā) comes into being.
The *alinda* (veranda) should be made as a partitioned section on the exterior of the *viśāla* itself;
it is surrounded by walls with windows in the areas of the front-projections (*prāgrīva*), and when it is constructed with six pillars at the front, it is joined together. ||138-139||
Then a palace renowned as "Dviśāla" (double-winged) arises;
when all its pillars are arranged on every side,
it then becomes a "Gṛharāja" (king of houses), with two front porches on both sides.

When there is an *ālinda* for the entire [structure], another part should be extended by one share (*bhāga*). The two *valabhīs* (pinnacles) should be at the ends of the boundary, extending out by one share.
The remaining wall is prescribed to be adorned with lattice windows (*gavākṣa*). ||141-142||
And when there is a ṣaḍdāruka in the front, then it shall be named Amala.
In a field that is eleven units long and six parts wide,
one should leave two parts at the back and then place the chamber for the deity (devakoṣṭha).
Leaving aside one part at the front, one should establish a boundary consisting of four parts.
Then there are eight pillars; the portico consists of twenty pillars per part.
Another [structure] has a surrounding portico of one part and possesses twenty-eight pillars.

Three front porches (prāgrīva) should be constructed, each consisting of two pillars and arising from the central cell; likewise, there should be two *valabhī* roofs at the boundary, with two porches in the middle between them.
Furthermore, there should be two other porches in front, each with two pillars, adorned with a pedestal (*vedikā*) and a lattice (*jāla*).
Richly adorned with the form of a lattice-work railing and beautified by lion-ears,
this temple named Vibhu was described as the delight of its master.
Thus, these ten temples, which are square and elongated, have been fully explained.
We shall now describe other palaces that are square and elongated, according to their ninefold architectural characteristics.
The width of the inner sanctum (garbha) is two *bhānas*, and its horizontal length is double that.
In the center, the door is raised by one part and its width is half of that;
it is joined with four pillars at the front boundary of the door, measuring two parts in length and width, and rising to the same height. ||150-151||
One should enclose that boundary, together with the interior chamber, with another partition;
there, a wall with windows should be constructed on all four sides.
Indeed, this temple, provided with six wooden supports, is called Bhava.
When this very [structure] has four projections at its four faces and is provided with six wooden beams, it is then called *viśāla*;
it is known as *sāmmukhya* when there are six pillars at each face on the exterior.
When this very [line] is situated at the ear, joined with two pillars,
and extends outward from the front of the neck, then it is the origin of the boundary.
When it is situated in front of that same [boundary], joined with two pillars—
Then the Śibirāgṛha would have its prāgrīva [portico] extending out from the [main] section (bhāga).
When there is a hall at the front of a large layout, and when there are halls on both sides and three prāgrīvas, [it is a different type]. 156–157.
When each projecting portion is joined with a pair of pillars,
that temple should then be known by the name Mukhaśāla (Front Hall).
When there are fourteen pillars for the front hall of the Mukhaśālā, [it is designated as such].
The *prāgrīva* (fore-neck) is of two kinds; at the front, it should then be twice as broad.
At that time, the wall becomes the palace, the king of houses.
Its length should be equal to the interior chamber (*garbha*), and its width at the front and back should be one part.
Where there are four parts of four units each at the front neck and two on each side,
and these are of two types [in height] and equal to the width of the inner sanctum (garbha),
that temple is called Amala, possessing auspicious characteristics.
When this very [structure] has two pillars each at the front and the back,
it is then called the tenth sovereign temple, the Prāgrīva.
We shall now describe ten other circular and oblong temples.
One should then construct a square measuring one-eighth of the length and width of the face; from that, one should fashion it as oval-shaped, both externally and internally.
Then, the inner sanctum (garbha) should be one-fourth of that on all sides, located at its western part.
One should establish a boundary in front of it, two parts in width,
measuring three parts and separated by one part,
joined by eight very firm and beautiful pillars. ||165-166||
One should construct a *devakoṣṭhaka* surrounded by an *alinda* and enclosed by a boundary wall,
with a porch (*prāgrīva*) at the front provided with sixteen pillars;
this, when covered with two layers of roofing, is celebrated as the *āmoda*.

Among those with circular bases, the first type of palace is beneficial for the master. When its two front necks are symmetrical and joined at their parts, and it has four stone pillars, it is called the "Elevated" (tuṅga) palace, characterized by its two circular forms. ||168-169||

When the boundary wall is adorned with windows and there is one circular *prāgrīva* while the others are otherwise, it is then called the *cāru* (beautiful) type. Two *prāgrīvas*, each as wide as one part, should be constructed in the middle of the boundary.
In the three [sections] designated as "Southern," three [arches] should be made with a length equal to their width;
these should be sloping forward and measured by the inner chamber (*garbhakoṣṭha*).
This temple, possessing auspicious characteristics, is called *Bhūti*. ||171-172||
The face should be four parts long and as much wide; then one should construct a square courtyard (kṣetravṛtta), and in its center, the inner sanctum (garbhaveśma).
That [sanctum] should be four parts long and two parts wide.
Outside of that, there is an alinda (veranda) provided with twelve pillars;
its width is two parts, and the prāgrīva (front porch) projects by one part. This temple is known as the Niṣedha by the ancients. ||174-175||
If there should be a prohibition of this [type of structure], provided that it has a portico (prāgrīvaka) in front,
is enclosed by four walls, and is surrounded by an *alinda* or an eight-fold (*aṣṭadhara*) veranda;
or if this very same [structure] is encircled by a partial *aṃśaka* or an *alinda*.
Excluding three parts of the front face and being enclosed by a wall,
when there are two *karṇaprāgṛīvas* and a *prāgṛīva* at the front,
and there is a special arrangement provided with twenty-two supports; ||177-178||
Then, provided with beautiful windows, it is proclaimed as the Siṃha (Lion) plan;
it is twelve parts in length and six parts in width.
Then, having set aside two parts from the rear, it is two parts in both length and width.
A divine treasury (devakoṣṭha) is to be constructed; its door should be raised by one part.
At the edge of the boundary, it should have an interval, be twice as wide [as the door], and four times as long.
Its inner sanctum (garbha) should indeed have eight pillars, while the outer area has sixteen pillars.
In front of that [main hall], there should be an *alinda* (porch) and also a circular *prāgrīvaka* (projection).
One should fashion circular *sīmā-prāgrīvakas*, *ālindakas*, and *koṣṭhas*.
On both sides, there should be two *prāgrīvakas* equal to the boundary (*sīmā*), extending out by one part.
The two pillars should be known as being joined by pairs and circular in shape.
All of this should be fashioned and encircled by a lotus-patterned band (alinda).
This [pillar] is praised when it possesses twenty-four parts and is divided into one share.
One should construct three front-projections (prāgrīva) for the interior chamber, each joined with two pillars;
thus is described this auspicious and radiant temple, Suprabha. Those front-projections mentioned here have a width of two parts.
If there are eight squares, joined by two pillars each,
and the remaining space forms a wall adorned with lattice windows,
then this should be known as the tenth temple, the Delight of the Eyes (Locanotsava). ||186-187||
Now we shall describe the eight-sided palaces along with their characteristics.
When the site is divided into four parts and further made octagonal,
the inner sanctum (garbhakoṣṭha) shall occupy two parts, and the portico (alinda) one part.
In the lotus-pedestal of the eight pillars, there should be a front projection (prāgrīva) in front of it;
covered with two layers, this glorious temple shall be the Vajraka.
When its boundary in front is square and supported by four pillars...
It may have twenty-four pillars, and another porch consisting of one part;
this is known as the Nandana, with three *śaṅku* projections at the front.
Its wall should be constructed by the wise on a site endowed with eight corners.

Furthermore, two dwarf (vāmana) windows are considered for each of the three directions. When this very [hall] extends for three parts from the boundary section at its front, is two parts in width, and has a depth of two parts, it is supported by eight pillars. ||192-193||
When the *prāgrīva* and *makhalā* are surrounded by the *alinda*,
and when the *prāgrīvas* are surrounded by the wall-area (*bhittikṣetra*) of that very [structure],
then it is joined with six *dharas* by means of six *alindas*; that is the *laya*.
When the area has been divided into eight parts and made octagonal on all sides,
one should construct a beautiful chamber for the deity measuring two parts,
adorned with four doors and surrounded by a portico (ālinda) measuring one part. ||195-196||
Then there are eight pillars for the *alinda* (veranda) and another [set] for the *vidhāṭavyā*;
furthermore, the *alindaka* should have twenty-four pillars and consist of one *bhāga*.
Likewise, the third [section] is of that same kind, as are the *prāgrīvas* (porches) in the four directions.

This Mahāpadma palace belongs to Brahmā and Śaṅkara. A second [structure] is within its very portico (alindaka), with projections (prāgrīva) on all four sides. Enclosed by such a portico, this is proclaimed as the Haṃsa [palace].

When its *prāgrīva* is covered by an *ālinda* and there are two *karṇas* and two *prāgrīvakas*, it is then known as the *vyoma*. When the *valabhis* are like those of the *haṃsa* at the positions of the *prāgrīvas*, [it is the *haṃsa*].
Enclosed by four pillars and provided with a veranda on all four sides,
the auspicious palace named Candrodya is then produced;
thus, these sixty-four palaces have been described.
Thus, it is declared that among the celestial abodes, this [city] consists of seventy-four wooden palaces, accompanied here by four main residences.
"This [architectural form], which produces joy and is as bright as a crescent moon,
is well known to craftsmen as the 'Wish-fulfilling Cow' (Kāmadhenu).

Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Sixty-four Temples beginning with Rucaka," in the *Vāstuśāstra*— also known as the *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*— composed by the Great King of Kings, Śrī Bhojadeva.
Now begins the fiftieth chapter, titled "The Auspicious and Inauspicious Characteristics of Temples. We shall now describe the characteristics of temples—
both those that are auspicious and those that are inauspicious— that exist upon this circle of the earth.
Those which are even, with equal ears, equal pillars, and equal hooves;
neither too tall nor too short, and not wavering from the proper length of their ears;
unconfused in their distinct divisions and well-established in their proportions.
Provided with upper and lower galleries and surrounded by moats,
they were situated in distinct locations, covered by canopies of their own prescribed dimensions,
well-proportioned, excellently constructed, and fashioned from beautiful, flawless materials. ||3-4||
They were divided into equal portions and provided with uniform verandas;
they were surrounded by those of their own kind and not defiled by others of different kinds;
they were unmixed [in caste] and well-situated in body and configuration.
Temples that are purely of one type and pure in their proportions grant auspiciousness to men.
They should have very firm foundation-pilasters, being strong from the base to the summit;
they should not have inverted arrangements and should possess well-knit joints of the building materials.
Adorned with ornaments renowned among the celestial beings,
these palaces are ever auspicious and increase the merit of worship and consecration.
Both the builder and the one who commissions them shall attain supreme prosperity.
We shall also describe the inferior palaces by their unfavorable characteristics:
those that are uneven or deficient in corners bring about suffering, bondage, and fear;
those with pillars or columns that are uneven are causes of death for the master.

If [the proportions] are too high, there will be fear of the king; if they are short, the army is crushed. Palaces that are deficient in the measurement of their length (from corner to corner) become terrifying.
Those devoid of proper division are known to bring the fear of poverty.
With missing corner-stones (karṇapādīs), they cause distress to men;
with obscured, crowded, or deficient [parts], they are known to bring about the destruction of the lineage.
When poorly divided, ill-situated, and joined with defective materials, they are likewise harmful.
They bestow disease, affliction, and death in due order.
Through uneven, deficient, or lacking bricks, there is danger from illness;
through those that are surrounded or defiled by other species, there is defeat.
Those which have been overturned, those mixed with others, or those whose frames are joined with others—these do not bring joy to the maker, the one who caused them to be made, nor even to oneself;
they are weak at their base and have joints in the seat that have come apart. ||15-16||
Those palaces are short-lived and bring about fear;
when they are joined by [mouldings] placed above and below, they should be known as causing disease.
Palaces endowed with improper instructions and ornaments do not bring happiness.
Those who desire fame and victory over beings should have [temples] constructed endowed with auspicious marks;
however, other types of excellent palaces (prāsāda) should be avoided by those desiring splendor, glory, prosperity, victory, and the like.

Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "The Auspicious and Inauspicious Characteristics of Palaces," in the *Vāstuśāstra* known by the alternative name *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*, composed by the Great King of Kings, the illustrious Bhojadeva.
Now begins the fifty-first chapter, titled "The Assignment of the Sites.
When the palace has been thus constructed for the king, or when it has been planned upon the ground,
his attendants should construct palaces along the perimeter if desired.
Then, for the sake of the prosperity of all of them, their arrangement according to the directions, their locations, and their measurements are here described in sequence:
[the measurements] of the kings are, respectively, one thousand, eight hundred, and six hundred bows.
It has been stated that the measurement of the site (āyatana) is threefold, according to the distinction of "excellent" and so forth.
Likewise, the field (kṣetra) of the site itself is square on all sides;
there, those devoted to it, being affectionate toward their master, should construct it in three ways.
And those who are esteemed by him, born of noble family and wishing him well—
[the measurements] for those born later in succession should be reduced by one-twelfth respectively.
He should place them to his left at a distance double their height.
O King, the one learned in the scriptures should construct the palaces for all the king’s wives in the south-western direction, making them ten parts less [than the king’s];
he should have them built in the western direction, reduced by an eighth part.
The divine altars for the sisters should be established with cords according to the prescribed rule,
extending from the north-east up to the north-west in nine successive divisions.
Therein are the palaces for the minister, the commander-in-chief, the door-keeper, and the priest.
The residence of the Queen Mother, situated in the eastern portion of these [buildings],
should be made one-eleventh part smaller;
it is for the king’s use and extends from the northeast (Īśāna) corner up to the Indra quarter, equal in size to the dwellings of the gods.

The dwellings for the sisters, the maternal uncles, and the princes should be established in due order; likewise, in the south-eastern quarter, the residence for the foremost of the twice-born must be provided,
or else the palace for the family priest should be constructed in that same place.
To the south of the king’s palace, they should construct [temples] reduced by one-eighth in size respectively for the vassals,
elephant-riders, warriors, and the common people;
one should assign these abodes to them according to their respective shares.
Out of a desire for their welfare, one should not cause these [beams] to pierce vital points (marmavedha), nor those situated at the piercing of doorways, nor those separated by their own positions—
namely, by vestibules (alinda), inner chambers (garbhakoṣṭha), boundary pillars (sīmāstambha), or latticed windows (gavākṣaka). ||14||
One should not construct [a temple] with doorways, materials, surfaces, or heights that are disproportionate; nor should it have front-protruding necks (prāggrīva) or lion-ears (siṃhakarṇaka).
A structure that is symmetrical in form and adorned with ornaments is righteous (dharmya), whereas one that is ill-proportioned does not bring prosperity.

If there is an excess [of that], there will be oppression by the king and the destruction of the lineage. A wise man should not cause a residence for the protector of the earth to be built with any material superior to that of the palace, nor should he place it outside the perimeter wall.
In terms of configuration, measurement, breadth, or height,
it is auspicious when it is slightly smaller than the previously mentioned proportions.
Each successive layer should be twice as large as the one covering it, and the space between each is auspicious.
And one should make that [palace] highly enjoyable with many interior chambers,
granaries, dining halls, and storehouses for utensils and equipment;
it should be completed with halls for stone-cutters and artisans, while filling up the remainder [of the space].

One should have all [the buildings] constructed as praiseworthy, of auspicious form, and pleasing to the mind. Generally, the lords of men should arrange their own residences and other houses for everyone according to the layout of the sanctuary itself. ||21-22||
"If there is otherwise, there is great fault; if it is the reverse, there is the destruction of the lineage.
Thus, by means of the conjunctions with the aforementioned divisions of directions and so forth, the divine abodes of whatever king [are constructed], they become [efficacious].
With his prowess constantly rising and ever-increasing,
he shall rule for a long time over the earth conquered by his own arm.
Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, titled "The Layout of the Temple Site," in the *Vāstuśāstra* known also as the *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*, composed by the great emperor, the illustrious Bhojadeva.
Now begins the fifty-second chapter, titled "The Class of Palaces.
Since the descent [of these structures], the layout of dwellings, and the ritual for the site (vāstu) originate from this,
we shall therefore describe that most excellent progenitor of the assembly in its entirety.

We shall describe the sequence of lineages, castes, and orders, as well as those with long and short lifespans; their physical constitution, and both their defining characteristics and the objects of definition.
Among these, they declare the Vairāja to be the first, comprising both the auspicious and the inauspicious.
Therefore, the characteristics of that aforementioned celestial vehicle (vimāna) are now described;
specifically, the arrangement of the form of the Vairāja [palace] in its entirety.
One should divide an equal square field into eighty parts.
One should construct an auspicious sanctum (garbhagṛha) joined with eight parts;
the boundary, provided with the interior chambers (garbhakoṣṭha), consists of fifty-two divisions.
All these thirty-two divine chambers are separated by single intervals.
Then, from that external location, with twelve pillars made of gold and jewels, adorned with white silk cloths,
and with canopies and ornaments inlaid with white decorations, [the ground] was supported by those firm columns through twelve acts of agitation.
With various lattices made of crystal and platforms of emerald,
with side-chambers, half-domes, and niches for rows of swans and pigeons,
and with a bell suspended above the inner sanctum at its edge.
That which was created by the Lord of the World is called the primordial Vairāja. From that, the first type of house-design known as Svastika is born;
from that, too, arise the Catuḥśāla, the Triśāla, and the Hiraṇyauka.
The *siddhārthaka* has two halls, while the *kumbhaka* has one hall;
furthermore, there are the *sṛṣṭa*, *vimāna*, *vara*, *vīra*, and *caturmukha* [types],
respectively for the *gaṇas*, the deities, and Skanda.
These other twelve palaces, endowed with auspicious characteristics, were produced:
Svastika, Śrītaru, and thirdly Kṣitibhūṣaṇa; Bhūjaya, Vijaya, Bhadra, Śrīkūṭa, and those known as Uṣṇīṣa. ||12-13||
The Nandyāvarta, the Vimāna, the Sarvatobhadra,
and the Vimuktakoṇaprāsāda— these are born from the Vairāja.
In this manner, each one arose sequentially from each [of the preceding].
From the Svastika, the Rucaka is to be known; from the Śrītara, the Hiṃpañjara;
from the Kṣmābhūṣaṇa, the Taśālā; from the Bhūjaya, the Gayūthapa; from the Vijaya, the Avataṃsa; and from the Bhadra, the Nandī emerges. ||15-16||
From Śrīkūṭa comes the one named Citrakūṭa; from Uṣṇīṣa, Pramadāpriya; from Nandikāvarta, Vyāmiśra; from Vimāna, Hastijāvaka;
from Sarvatobhadra, Kubera; and from Muktakoṇa, Harādhara.
And those born from these [elements] are called "lesser" (kanīyāṃsaḥ) by name;
they are the subdivisions of those [elements], to be recognized by their own various respective forms.
Among them, the former [beings] are [constituted] by the superior portions, and the middling ones likewise by the middling portions.
One should construct the palaces for the younger [deities] with smaller [proportions];
from that, palaces joined with other spires came into being.
Among them, the first is the *rucaka* and the second is the *vardhamānaka*.
The third is the Avataṃsa, while the fourth is called the Bhadra.
The fifth is the Sarvatobhadra, and the sixth is the Muktakoṇaka.
These eight—the Meru and Mandara—are to be known as the most excellent of peaks (śikhara).
The auspicious abodes of the gods are declared to be square;
all these, born of the lineage of Brahmā, are to be established.
The most excellent palaces are those produced from the family of Vairāja.

From these others were also born sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons—belonging to their own lineages, well-provided with attendants, devoid of rival lineages, endowed with auspicious marks, and possessed of splendor by one desiring prosperity; these are to be established. ||24-25||

The Nandakas and Vardhanas indeed bestow the fruits of all desires; they are crowded with joyful and well-nourished people, and they increase through worship and consecration. (26) For if these should become deficient, they are defiled by another lineage.
They would cause constant agitation among men, the loss of wealth, the destruction of the family, suffering for their masters, and whatever else is reprehensible;
therefore, these [Brahmins] must not be defiled by other castes. ||27-28||
Thus has been proclaimed the origin of those born of Vairāja; this lineage of Vairāja-born beings, reaching up to the celestial abodes,
has thus been described here in brief as possessing auspicious fortune.
"Thus, [a temple] made [according to these rules] brings about joy, fame, wealth, and grain;
however, one of a different kind results only in misfortune for the builder.

Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "The Classes of Temples," in the *Vāstuśāstra* known by the alternative name *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*, composed by the great king of kings, the illustrious Bhojadeva.

Now begins the fifty-third chapter, titled "The Door of Inferior Sites. Hereafter, we shall describe the measurement of the doors of inferior sites, as well as their width, height including the roof, and the rules for the breadth of the materials used.
Regarding those supportless palaces described as being elongated horizontally,
one should divide the inner sanctum (garbhavāsa) into four parts.
One should construct the door with half a part [in height] and extend its width by half a part.
The width of the pedestal (pedyā) should be one-quarter of the width of the door;
its thickness (piṇḍa) should be half of that width, and the udumbara (lintel) should be equal to that.
From the base upwards, the udumbara should extend by half [the thickness], and the branches (śākhā) should be determined according to their breadth.
The pedestal-piṇḍa (pedyāpiṇḍa) should be made of four types according to its measurement;
however, the branch (śākhā) and the pedestal-piṇḍa are prescribed by their width.
The form-branch (rūpaśākhā) should have a width that is one and a half times the width of the branch.
Indeed, half of the *pedyā* mass is prescribed for the *khalva* branch.
The *tunga-śākhā*s should be made equal in form to the *rūpa-śākhā*s, but in terms of width;
and whatever other branches are fashioned, they are placed on the exterior of the *tunga*.
All of these should be made with an extension of more than one-eighth [of the width];
whatever the total number resulting from the sum of the length and width of the door,
that shall be the measure of the height of the plinth (talodaya), which is equal for both the inner sanctum (garbha) and the pavilion (maṇḍapa).
If a certain pavilion is deficient in order to create a distinct floor level,
then the height of that floor in the pavilion should be equal to the height of the door;
this measurement of the floor is prescribed for smaller palaces.
In the case of the *jyeṣṭha* (largest) type, it exceeds by one-sixth; in the *madhya* (middle) type, it exceeds by one-eighth.
This rule for the strength of the foundation, with equal steps, is prescribed for the temple (*prāsāda*).
It should not be applied below, nor above the *udumbara* (the capital).
The *tulā* (balance-beam) is [placed] upon the *kumbhikā*, the *bharaṇa*, the *paṭṭa*, the *jayantī*, the *śīrṣaka*, and the *āyaphalaka*.
Regarding this, it has been stated: "One should not construct anything more than what was first mentioned here, nor less.

Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "The Door of the Lowest Class of Buildings," in the *Vāstuśāstra* composed by the Great King of Kings, the illustrious Bhojadeva, also known as the *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*.

Now begins the fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Measurement of the Door of the Palace" and so forth. We shall now describe, in due order, the height, width, thickness, and circumference of palaces according to their constituent materials.
The gate of the palace is desired to have a height equal to one part of the palace's total elevation; it may be raised to two parts, or even to one and a half parts.
Furthermore, its width is desired to be half of its respective height.

The width [of the base] is one-fourth of a part, and the thickness of the *pedyā* is half of that. The branch (*śākhā*) is, according to measurement, as thick as the *pedyā* and as wide. One should fashion the northern components (*uttarāṅga*) so that they are equal to the *pedyā* and the branch.
The form-branch (rūpaśākhā) is prescribed with a width equal to one-and-a-quarter parts;
above that, the pedestal-base (pīṭhabandha) should be made endowed with form-branches. Below the circle, it should be made circular and continuous with leaf-patterns.
The *bharaṇa* (neck-piece), adorned with ornaments, should have a width double that of the pillar;
it should be made very beautiful, resembling the form of a branch.
Above, extending all around for a measure of one-eighth [of the total height], it should be square.
Above that, the height of the *bharaṇa* (neck) should be three-quarters of the total height;
below it, the *kapota* (eaves) is prescribed, and its interior is the *śīrṣagarbha*.
Alternatively, it may have the leaf-patterns of a chariot-temple, projecting out by half of its own elevation.
Above that, one should fashion a leaf-shaped canopy (ucchālayapatraka).
A chariot-path (rathikā) should be constructed for both of those elevations;
its ornamentation, consisting of flowers and other such elements, should have a height measuring one and a half units.
Or it may be adorned on all sides with figures as they appear beautiful and with small pillars;
from there, the pinnacle (kūṭa) should be one-third less than the height of the neck (kaṇṭaka),
and it should be decorated with lion-wheels or elephant trunks.
The *kapota* (dove-niche) and other features should be fashioned within the space between the two forms of the pillars.
All these elements should be made in odd numbers by the wise.
Therefore, a circular [structure] should be fashioned on the outside on all sides.
That [branch] is prescribed by measure to be equal to the final branch.
Upon that twelve-branch [structure], the lotus-petals of fame are to be made;
these are the branches of speech, elevated to match its width.
Below that, the girdle should be half [the height] of the neck;
likewise, the space below should be equal to one and a half neck-units.
One should make the leaf-patterns [occupy] two parts, and the shank (jaṅghā) below that should consist of three parts. ||15-16||
The secondary branches (aśākhā) are indeed prescribed according to the measure of the primary cluster (pedyāpiṇḍa);
the external arrangement of branches is proclaimed to be equal to the primary cluster.
By this sequence, the minor branches should be fashioned according to one's desire.
The door-frames should by no means be made wider than nine [units];
whether for exit or entry, they are provided with a width equal to that of the gateway,
or half of it, according to the rule for the frames.
The *udumbara* [pedestal] should be equal in measure to half a *peyāpiṇḍa*;

the placement of the base (*tala*) should be half of that, and the ground and the *aṅga* should be equal to that. The lion-faces [should be made] according to the measurement of the *udumbara* pedestal.
The *piṇḍa* (block) of the *paṭṭa* (fillet) may be one-quarter less than, equal to, or greater than the *udumbara*;
it is threefold in width and exceeds the pillar in height. The pillar is equal to one-fourth of a *bhāga*, and the *prapīḍita* (projection) is one-twelfth. ||21-22||
It should be made in two parts, endowed with the characteristics of form;
this [pillar] consists of sixty-four varieties, manifested through a diversity of forms.
It is as wide as the thickness of the pillar, and its mass is reduced by one-quarter.
It is desired that the width be three times the length; the *dhīra* and *agrahaṇa* [mouldings] are prescribed [at the base].
The *kumbhika*, *utkāla*, and *ka* [mouldings] are always to be included within the measurement of the pillar.
One should fashion the upper fillet (*paṭṭa*) so that it is equal to the lower fillet (*talapaṭṭa*).
Its base (tīra) is made with one-third of that height;

one should fashion a fillet (paṭṭa) or similar element slightly protruding according to what is beautiful. Above this, it should be adorned as is fitting with a neck-mold (kaṇṭhaka) and a seat (āsana).
With small chariots of various forms, and gabled pavilions with arched gateways;
on the verandas, in the halls, in the courtyards, or upon the roof-terraces—there were diverse canopies with elevated surfaces. ||27–28||
One should fashion them according to their characteristics as is appropriate.
We shall now describe the hollows (lūmāḥ) made by means of wooden moulds (phalakavartībhiḥ),
as well as the various types of elevations that arise in all architectural structures.

Tumbinī, Lambinī, Helā, Śāntā, Kolā, Manoramā, and Ādhmātā—these seven are declared by name to be the *lumas*. [They are to be placed] upon a beautiful and auspicious ground, once the field has been made square. ||30-31||
Having made the cord equal to the field, one should divide it from corner to corner;
one should lay down the central cords situated between those two,
and furthermore, one should place other cords in the middle.
Having drawn a circle in the center, a gourd-like shape resembling a lotus should be fashioned. There, one should proceed with the field by dividing the circle into parts;
along each thread, one should draw the lump-shaped *luma* with a thread.
In all the intervals between the *lūmās*,
it is proclaimed by Vaikaṭya that between those two [intervals], at the root of the *lūmā*, there is the *vikarkara*;
it may be double or triple [the size], and from there one should draw the *valinī*.
The rising [of the gnomon] here should be performed using half the diameter in that mandala.
From the point of intersection of the horizontal lines and from the top of the gnomon (tumbikā), the vertical line is established.
The rising of the horizontal line and the interval between it and the gnomon are likewise determined.
In the previous sūtra, one should fashion straight thorns at the tips of the *luma* lines;
one should certainly establish the target (*lakṣa*) at the outer positions and at the ends.
Having taken the target, one should mark the upper sūtras along the lower sūtra.
At the end of the thorn-mark at the rising point, one should likewise continuously apply the subsequent cord for the folds (*luma*), the *akhala* sections,
the width of the lumps (*piṇḍa*), the folds (*valī*), and the expansion of the *kṣobhaṇa*. (39–40)
That which has a hollow at the ear and is blown open is proclaimed as *ādhmātā*.
Another, when cut, is *pravartitā*; the *manoramā* is slightly smaller than that. The third is called *kolā*, and the fourth is proclaimed as *śāntā*.
The fifth is named Helā, the sixth is Lambinī by name, and the seventh is Tumbinī;
these emerge from the thread of Māga.
With these, one should construct the kola and the canopy, a festival for the eyes. (42-43)
Kolāvila, Hastitālu, Aṣṭapatra, Śarāvakam,
Nāgavīthīvitāna, Puṣpaka, Bhramarāvalī,
Haṃsapakṣa, Karāla, Vikaṭa, and Śaṅkhakuṭṭima.
Śaṅkhanābhi, Sapuṣpa,
Śuktivṛttaka, Mandāra, Kumuda, Padma, Vikāsa, Garuḍaprabha, Purohata, Purāroha, and likewise Vidyunmandāraka. ||45-46||
These canopies are twenty-five in number;
we shall now describe their forms and construction.
They may be square on all sides, or rectangular.
When a field has been made into a plot, that [area] is called a *tatkoṭi* by means of a single side.
When a field is square, in all the locations of its diagonals,
through the construction of squares, there is the construction of squares.
Valinī is of a formidable form; its previous occurrences are likewise below.
That which is the circular revolution in the middle is supreme;
there, other lūmās are fashioned, where five tumbikās are well-positioned and well-concealed. 50.
At the end of the path, below the thread, that shall be a festival for the eyes.
[51] In a square field divided into eight parts, one should draw a circle in the middle two parts using a gourd-seed. [52]
There, at the end of the circle, one should draw sixteen circles along the thread;
those threads which are straight, one should designate as the *lūmās*,
and those remaining threads, one should designate as the *valīs*.
One should fashion a circle upon the *tumbinī*; this is called the *gajatāluka*.
On the eight-petaled [lotus], one should divide the field into sixty-four parts;
the petals are placed in the positions of the *lūmās*, and they are likewise divided within by the intermediate spaces.

One should place gourd vessels within all the sections; there should be a circular shallow bowl (śarāva), and its arrangement should be supported by pillars. Alternatively, whether it be square or circular, it should be divided into three parts.
One should fix the "elephant-binding" (nāgabandha) at the intersection of the offering-line and the measuring-thread.
This is called the canopy (vitāna), which a person who desires to construct makes by means of stalks extending upwards and across, placed without any gaps. 57–58.
That which is filled with flower garlands is called the glorious Puṣpaka;
that which is strewn with Aśoka sprouts and has a curved connection is called Bhramarāvalī, provided it is arranged in a square formation. (59)
When the *ādhmātā* reaches the ear and rests in the position of the *tumbikā*,
and where the *tumbinī* is in the middle, that is called the *haṃsapakṣa*.
When the *manoramā* is joined to this very *pakṣa*, [it is likewise so designated].
The *tumbinī* is declared to be formidable (*karāla*) among the opposing types;
the *kolā lumā* occurs in the *vikaṭa* type, while the *śaṅkha* is proclaimed as *śāntā*.
A thread equal in size to the navel of a conch-shell proceeds from the *tumbikā*.
In all the positions for the *luma*, it should be provided with a single line;
this is called the "conch-naveled" (*śaṅkhanābhi*) canopy, which is the most excellent.
In the position for the *luma* of this very [canopy], there is a gourd-shaped element (*tumbikā*) surrounded by lotuses.

They know that which is adorned with circles (valaya) and possesses flowers to be the Śukti [mandala]; one should have it made in a field of circular or oblong shape. In a circular field, the mandala becomes circular through the work of the circles.
In a square field of equal area, that which is reduced by half and then further halved,
resulting in circular, agitated, and broken lines, is called the *mandāraka* pattern;
while the *kumuda* pattern is like that of a water-lily, formed here by the projection of the *luma* from the middle.
In the *padmaka* [hand-gesture], the middle finger is bent downwards; in the *vikāsa*, it is curved at the middle joint.
In the *garuḍa* [gesture], the *garuḍa* [finger] is in the middle, adorned with serpent ornaments.
That which was previously directed downwards, having gone down, becomes upward-pointing once again.
Having gone downward to the base of the city-ascendant (purāroha), and upward from there, and again downward from that;
filled with various agitations, it should be rotated repeatedly at the end.
With eight spokes in the middle, it becomes the lightning-mandāraka.
Now we shall describe the measurement of height for palaces and covered structures.
One should fashion the ridge-pole (vaṃśa) above at half the width of the covering.
This is declared to be the "Half-Rise" (Ardhodaya); the next is known by the name Āvantya.
The emergence of the Vāmana [style] occurs when one-third of the width is covered.
One should divide the space between the Vāmana and the Āvantya into nine parts;
these eight [styles] are known as the emergences starting from the Vāmana, increasing by one part each.
Vātapatra, Kaubera, the one named Śamana, as well as Avalī,
Haṃsapṛṣṭha, Mahābhogin, Nārada, Śambuka, Vāmana, and Āvantya—
these ten were the first among them.
Now, the rising of the covered (chādyāna) and circular (vṛtta) [eclipses] is being described.
Having made [the diameter] equal to the base-line (tala-sūtra), one should divide it into twelve parts for the rising.
Starting from the sixth part, there shall be seven risings, each increasing by one part.
Kuberaśekhara, Candra, Nāga, Cāturgaṇādhipa,
Mukhya, Accha, and Subhadra are recorded as the seven *udayas* in the *vṛtta* [meter].
Having formed the *trikarkarapada*, one should then write upon the back of the *lumā*.
The procedure for drawing the covering [mandala] should be performed when the area has increased by half a part.
When the area has been increased by half a part and provided with the sequence of the ground-lines (talasūtra),
one should again draw the first line (lūmā) continuously according to the sequence of six.
Just as the *ṛkṣā* [measure] follows immediately after the *advihasta*, so too does the *lumā*;
that *lumā* is increased by three parts less one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*).
And immediately following that is the *lakṣmī*, which is increased by three full finger-breadths.
The next [line] is six [units] minus one-third; the following is ten [units] minus one-third;
another would be fourteen [units]; then it increases by half-fingers;
but the seventh, situated at the corner, increases by twenty fingers.
By this sequence, the measures for the increase and decrease of the lunar mansions (luma) should be calculated through proportion according to the area of the eclipsed region (chādyakṣetra).
[The results are] Kubera, Vallarī, Candra, Pannaga, and Gaṇanāyaka.
"O Subhadrā, these [measures] beginning with the 'Mugdha' constitute half of the work for the crescent moon (candralekhā).
For these, four types of gaṇḍikā-cuts are proclaimed:
upward, horizontal, three-quarters, and likewise half of three-quarters. ||84-85||
Having made the width of the *chādyaka* (the covering) equal to its projection,
one should divide the field into six parts equally according to its width and length.
Therein, one should first cut out the *gaṇḍikā* (the corner-piece) by means of the measurement of the upper part.
In that [process], one should cause a pendant (lambaka) to be given according to the measurement of the cut;
below the joint (gaṇḍikā), one should fashion the thorns (kaṇṭakāni). Having understood the depressions and elevations, one should mark three points. ||87-88||
In the womb, likewise above, and at the edge is the third; from the middle of those two,
wherever the thread remains and touches the three points,
one should extend that thread from there and rotate the karkaṭa.
In this manner, the positioning above the middle of the bamboo tube is established.
With a cord of equal length held above,
one should rotate the karkaṭa at the point where it hangs from the edge for the sake of its successful completion.
First, one should fashion the plank as divided by two parts at the corner;
this is called the *lumā-pārṣṇi*.
One should then divide the remaining *lumā* into four long parts.
Beyond the four elements, its function is to be performed as a circular flow (vṛttavartana).
At the time of half-rising, its height is one unit and its width is measured at two parts;
its rising is prescribed to be half a part both at the base and at the top.
Then, in the lower field, having taken a thread as a guide according to its width—
just as it is in a field of equal width, resting upon one and a half parts of that [width]—
one should take a third part of the tip of the *luma* and that which is situated between those two.
The wise one, having fixed the cord there, should rotate the compass;
according to the requirement of each successive square of the divisions, the drawing of the circle must be performed duly upon all four corners.
Or else, on three-fifths of the field of the base-line (mūlālū),
or at half the width, one should draw two circles on the back of the lumā such that they intersect; having drawn it thus, one should perform the remainder as previously described.
From the base of the *lumā*, at four parts equal to one-seventh of the field’s width,
one should draw two circles on the back of the *lumā* with a radius equal to half the width,
so that they intersect; having drawn them thus, one should perform the remaining work in six parts.
Alternatively, one may divide the field itself into nine parts starting from the base;
then, at half the width, one should draw two lines across the back of the base.
Thereafter, with the remaining six parts, one should proceed as before.
For the smallest of the palaces, the projection should be made at half a part;
for the larger ones, the projection is made with parts of the *chādyaka* itself. As for those palaces situated between them, their [projection] should be according to the proportions of the site.
The emergence of the eclipsed body should be calculated by the learned through proportionate calculation.
The minimum emergence of the eclipsed body is one-third of its emergence, while the maximum is half of it. That difference should be divided by six.
The other five are known as "increasing by parts" (bhāgottara), and seven are considered to be "rising" (udaya).
Now we shall describe the characteristics of the *siṃhakarṇa* [bandha]:
it consists of the covering, the rising, and the rising again; one should divide that into ten parts. ||105-106||
The width of its base shall consist of sixteen parts of those same units;
having set aside four parts from the top, one should fix the ritual stake (śaṅku). Once the field has been made square, starting from the corner stake, one should proceed along the diagonal.

Then, one should draw a circle and subsequently fix a gnomon (śaṅku) upright. From the upper point [of the gnomon], at a distance of one part, it should be placed; then, at a distance of four parts, one should draw another circle produced by a compass set to two parts less one-third.
Immediately above that, the neck should be made as a single unit;
within the womb, there should be two horizontal divisions between the tips of the two horns.
In the middle, three horizontal divisions should be made by the wise between the tips of the two ears.
Above the neck, there should be one part for the crest (śikhā).
The tip of the crest should be made above [the neck] and joined with the interior;
likewise, the tip of the crest should hang downward by half a part from above.
The tip of the ear should extend to one part, and the tip of the shoulder likewise;
the base of the two ear-sections should meet at the region of the shoulder.
From the center of the previous circle, the svastika should have a width and length of two parts.
In this manner, one should place the upper portion of the peg above the lower thread.
Once the portion has been placed, one should complete everything from the previous circle onwards in its entirety;
all that was previously described up to the svastika should be performed exactly as before.
Above the bottom line, it is equal to the interior [of the temple] by four parts;
likewise, by two parts each on both sides, it extends horizontally;
and similarly, above the bottom line, it is equal to the interior by one part.
With four parts on each side,
one should draw semicircles joined at a single corner as before;
and the prongs should be single, joined with half-svastikas at their necks.
Arising from an external circle outside the line of the palm,
with the heel clearly entering three finger-widths [into the ground],
this is declared to be the *siṃhakarṇa* (lion’s ear) posture, known as the "charming triple-fold. (119)
When the rise is divided into ten parts as before, the fillet (vali) shall be one and a half parts wide in a corner that is fourteen parts wide;
when it is ten parts high as before, it shall be thirteen parts wide. ||120-121||

Kṣetra, Ekavali by name, and another called Siṃhakarṇa— these three, endowed with beauty, should be made with triangular enclosures. Thus has been declared the measurement and arrangement of the doors of the palaces.
In this [treatise], the canopies for the pillars and their *luma* ornaments are clearly described;
the elevation of the circular covering (*vṛttacchādyocchriti*) is stated, as are the *luma* ornaments of the covering's configuration.
Seven types have been declared, and another well-known variety is the measurement of the *siṃhakarṇa*.

Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Measurement of the Prāsāda-Door, Pillar-Placement, Vitāna, Lūmā, Vṛtta-chādyalūmā, and Siṃhakarṇa," in the *Vāstuśāstra* composed by the Great King of Kings, the illustrious Bhojadeva, also known as the *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*.
Now begins the fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Sixteen Prāsādas beginning with Meru. Herein are the specific characteristics of the sixteen types of temples.
We shall explain, in due order, the superior, middling, and inferior [types].
How and by what means they are divided, and how they are prescribed for the past and the future— as much as their measure may be, so shall it be described for each.
Meru, Prāsādarāja, Kailāsa— the beloved of Hara— as well as Sarvatobhadra, Vimāna, Chada, Nandana, Svastika,
Muktakoṇa, Śrīvatsa, and that known as Haṃsa.
The *rucaka*, *vardhamāna*, *garuḍa*, *gaja*,
*mṛgarāja*, *padma*, and *valabhī*— these are recorded as such;
they are neither less than thirty-three nor more than fifty.
Those who know the ancient lore state that the number of cubits for Meru is as follows:
having divided the site into ten parts, one should make the peak two parts;
having made the middle six parts, the projection is given there.
The space for the water-course should be made with a sixteenth part of the [total] portion.
The width of its inner sanctum (garbha) should be made with sixteen parts;
the wall of the temple should be one part thick, and the interval between them should be one part wide.
The outer wall (bāhyabhitti) should be one pada; this is how it was traditionally taught at that time.
The arrangement of the altar-bench (vedikābandha) consists of two padas, while the plinth (jaṅghā) rises to five padas.
The inner fillet (mekhalā) and the decorative leaf-pattern (antarapatraka) are each half a pada.
The height of the spire (śṛṅga) shall be three parts, and the height of the pinnacle (śikhara) nine parts.
Those who know this should construct sixteen storeys (bhūmikā) for this pinnacle.
It is expanded by six parts at the shoulder (skandha), and the maṇḍaka is one part in height.
The neck (grīvā) should be made with its height equal to the width at the base of the spire (śikhara);
one should draw the bamboo-receptacle (veṇukośa) using a cord six times that length.
Furthermore, for the bhadra projections, one should make their height twice their width.
One should construct the *kumbha* (dome) with one part in all types of temples.
Thus, for one desiring their own welfare, this Meru-like temple should be made with four peaks and adorned with four gates. 13–14.
Whatever merit one might obtain by giving Mount Meru made entirely of gold,
one would obtain even more by constructing that same mountain out of bricks and stone. (15) [Mount Meru]

On a square plot measuring twenty-seven cubits, one should divide it into ten parts; that shall be the Kailāsa [temple], which increases merit. The inner sanctum (garbha) occupies the central Brahma-cell, while the remainder constitutes the walls and the surrounding enclosure.
The *bhadra* should be one-fourth [of the width], and the root-ears (*mūlakarṇa*) should be three parts each.
The *jaṅghā* (lower wall) is seven parts in height, and the *mekhalā* (waistband) is half a part.
The *antarapatra* (inner leaf) should be one part, and the *aṇḍaka* (egg-shaped capital) is one part in height.
The portion at the front of the neck is ten units high, and the pinnacle (śikhara) rises [from there].
In this structure known as Kailāsa, the shoulder (skandha) has a width of five and a half parts;
having placed a cord upon the inner leaf (antarapatra), it should be struck well.
With that [cord] tripled, one should draw a beautiful bamboo sheath;
it should be eight units in height, glorious, and adorned with a flower-cluster.
One desiring prosperity should make its height double that.
Its work consists of six stages, auspicious and projecting out by half a part;
its molding is like a lion’s ear, and its completion is achieved with the central pillar.
This is specifically called Kailāsa, the beloved of Hara.
Kailāsa.
Now the Sarvatobhadra temple is described.
It should be twenty-six cubits at most in measurement.
The belly and the outer boundary are indeed the enclosing walls that create darkness.
The height of the legs and the two ears are recorded as being like those of Mount Meru;
likewise, the Bhadra [shrine] should be constructed with its widths extending out by half a share.
The *rathika* (pediment) is one-fourth [of the width], and then [the next part] is two and a half parts;
the mutual arrangement of these parts is prescribed as being part by part.
The spire (*śikhara*) should be made six parts wide and seven parts high.
The width of the trunk at its base should be six or ten parts.

The neck should be half a part in height, and the *daṇḍaka* (the upper portion) should be one part in height. The carving should be joined so that it follows the line of the original base measurement. ||27-28||
Its line should be drawn in such a way that it accomplishes all forms of supreme welfare;
one should adorn the peaks of this Meru with "lion-ears" (siṃhakarṇas).
One should cause a cluster of blossoms (mañjarī) to be fashioned everywhere, resembling the tip of a lotus bud.
It brings victory, prosperity, fame, renown, and all desired fruits;
it produces auspiciousness in every respect—this is the Sarvatobhadra, which has been composed as "auspicious on all sides.
Sarvatobhadra.
When the site has been made square and divided into one hundred parts,
the wise man should divide the temple (vimāna), which brings about prosperity, nourishment, and happiness;
he should construct it with four *bhadras*, as well as with *karṇas* and *prāggrīvakas*.
This [temple] may consist of five stories or perhaps three;
the largest should be thirty cubits, the middle one twenty-five,
and the smallest twenty-one or sixteen cubits.
One [type of vimāna] is pure by birth (jātiśuddha), while another is indeed made of *mañjarī* flowers;
the other is the mixed (*miśraka*) type. Thus, the enumeration of vimānas is declared to be threefold.
The best is that constructed from *miśraka*, and it is fashioned by Kaulāśa Bhadra.
The middle [type] should be pure in its proportions, while the smallest is provided with a *mañjarī* (flower-cluster).
The *bhadra* (frontal projection) is proclaimed to have an extent of five parts.
The width of the *karṇa* (corner), *prāggrīva* (foreneck), and *vistāra* (overall breadth) should be made equal to one part.
Half a part should be made for the *kṣobhaṇa* (the base), and the *talipa* (the pedestal) should be between that and the *tajha*;
it should be provided with hidden ears if one desires it to be endowed with auspicious characteristics.
Therefore, one should cause the *niṣkaṃśa* of the *bhadra* (the front projection) to be made with one part.
A wise architect should construct the *bhadra* as one-fourth of the *miśraka*.
The *jaṅghā* (lower story), together with the *khura* (pedestal) and *piṇḍaka* (plinth), should be five parts in height.
The *rathikā* (upper story) should be made two parts, and the floor space should be four parts.
The third stage is held to be reduced by one-half of the second half;
the fourth, however, is reduced by three parts, while the fifth is reduced by half. Whatever rise there is for a stage, one should construct the pinnacle (kūṭa) at half of that measure. ||40-41||
One should construct the *kumbhikā* with half [of that measure], provided with a *ucchālaka*;
the pedestal (*vedikā*) rising above it should be five parts high.
The bell (*ghaṇṭā*) should be made with a width of six parts and a height of two parts.
Thereafter, one should divide the height of the bell into three parts;
one should then fashion the neck, the throat, and the egg [bulb] as being one part each.
The region of the neck should be one part, and the height of the staff [daṇḍikā] should likewise be one part.
The height of the pitcher (kalaśa) should be made with two parts, [measuring] half a ghaṇṭā;
likewise, everything such as the Sūrasena and other features should be executed as before.
One should adorn the auspicious [structure] here with beautiful lion-ears (siṃhakarṇas).
One should draw the lotus bud with a cord five vyāmas long. This shall consist of three creeper-lines; one should fashion it with those creepers.
The Miśraka [style] is formed by mixing the constituent parts, while the Śuddha [style] is endowed with the ground-plan (bhūmikā).
The Vimāna [mandala] of Nandana shall have a boundary constructed of thirty-two cubits; indeed,
it consists of sixty-four squares through a division of eight by eight.

Its central chamber (garbha) shall consist of four parts; the remainder shall be the wall and the dark space (andhakārikā). The *bhadra* should be made equal to the central chamber, and its projection should extend upward from that.
Furthermore, there should be two chariot-projections (*ratha*) on the sides, extending everywhere along the diagonal lines of the ears (*karṇasūtra*).
The shank is five parts high, and the girdle (mekhalā) is measured at one part.
This ground (bhūmi) shall consist of six tiers, each being one-twelfth of a part.
The configuration of the lines, shoulders, egg-shapes (aṇḍaka), and so forth, is identical to that of the Kailāsa [temple].
This Nandana delights [the heart] and destroys calamities when it is prosperous;
thus it is called Nandana. In a square field measuring twenty-five cubits, ||52||
Then one should lay out the lines, extending as far as the mouth of the ritual site;
thereafter, with a cord marking half the boundary, one should correctly draw a perfect circle.
Then, one should divide that [circle] into twenty-eight parts according to the required measure.
One should construct [the chariots] half the size of the hall, aligned with the directional lines. Of these, three chariots (ratha) should be made for each [hall], situated in the middle;
others should be made as half-chariots (ardharatha), positioned at the corners of the hall.
The shank is six parts in height; the girdles are half a part each;
the inner leaf (antarapatra) shall be one part, and the raised circular molding (udvṛttamaṇḍaka) one part;
the central beam (jīvā) is half a part in height, with a width of four parts.
The height of the pinnacle (śikhara) is desired to be eleven parts;
for all types of Latina [temples], it is indeed twice that measure.
The cord (sūtra) from the shoulder (skandha) onwards is twice the width, and it is also sixfold. ||57-58||
Having drawn out the cord, one should draw the lotus bud;
that [mandala] measuring twenty-five cubits is the largest, sixteen is the medium,
and twelve cubits is the smallest, according to the wise.
This [measurement] for the eldest is the number of shares; the middle one is half of that;
and the youngest is half of the middle one’s share.
The shank of the eldest is proclaimed to be six shares in measure.
It should be seven parts high at the middle and the small [end];
this rule regarding the area has been declared for all types of *latina* temples.
This is known as the *Svastika*, which bestows well-being and prosperity upon men.
The Svastika.
Now we shall describe the subtle [form] of the Muktakoṇa; it is of three kinds:
sixteen, twelve, and eight cubits in measurement for the other [types].

The largest [Prāsāda] consists of sixteen parts, the medium one twelve, and the smallest is said to consist of eight; this is the Prāsāda with released corners (muktakoṇaka). This very same difference applies between the Muktakoṇa and the Svastika types.
In that [temple], the svastika is circular, while another is remembered as being square.
The pillar-shaft (jaṅghā) should be five parts in height, and the chariot-porch (rathikā) should be two parts.
The second floor (bhūmikā) of that [structure] should be made with four parts.
The stages (bhūmikās) of that [structure] should be executed by taking half of half [of the total height].
Having divided the womb (garbha) into nine parts, it should consist of thirteen [parts];
the first [stage], the jaṅghā, should be forty-seven and a quarter [parts], and the first [section] should be one ṣaṇḍikā.

The Mukta-koṇa [mandala]: having divided the width into ten parts, one should draw the middle [line] as six parts. The two corners are two parts each; the middle [space] should again be divided into four. 69.
Similarly, two parts in the middle, or one part each on the left and right, should be made;
the projection of the chariot (rathanirgama) should be fashioned with a number of finger-breadths (aṅgula).
It is adorned with prominent frontal necks (prāggrīva), well-proportioned pillars, and excellent architectural workmanship.
Thus endowed with these qualities, the Śrīvatsa bestows happiness.
A space of two, three, or even four finger-breadths should be made as the interval for the Śrīvatsa and the Nandana.
The Śrīvatsa [is described]: when divided into ten parts in width, the mañjarī should consist of six parts;
its root and ears are each two parts, like those of the Sarvatobhadra.
One should fashion another water-line for the Śrīvatsa;
this is correctly proclaimed as the Haṃsa, which bestows auspiciousness and is endowed with the proper characteristics. 74. [The Haṃsa].
The *rucaka* [temple] should likewise be devoid of an inner water-course (*udakāntara*).
Its walls shall be one-fourth [of the total width], and the sanctum (*garbha*) is considered to be half the width. (75) — *Rucaka*.

When the field has been made square, one should divide it into ten squares; there, one should construct the one called Ardhāmāna by proceeding with circular turns. And the Bhadra should be four parts wide on all sides.
With each single part, the left and right chariots [should be formed];

the two ears shall have a width of two parts, and the projection (nirgama) shall be by finger-breadths (karāṅgula). This increasing [structure], when employed in construction, shall increase fame and fortune.
Whether it be the *racaka*, the *vardhamāna*, the *śrīvatsa*, or the *haṃsa*—
whichever one among these pleases [the patron], the wise man should place that upon Garuḍa.
Its two wings should be made to extend out by half the measure of the temple (*prāsāda*).
One should also cause the nose of the Garuḍa to have three chambers (trigarbhā). [Thus ends the section on] Garuḍa.
One should divide the auspicious temple on a field of sixty-four squares.
With a cord measuring half the field, one should draw a circle at the back.
Its shank consists of four parts, and its girdle is half a part.
This [pedestal] is sun-shaped in front and elephant-shaped at the back.

The elephant has sixty-four squares; the lion has sixty-four squares; the *bhadra* consists of four parts; the two corner-roots (*mūlakarṇa*) consist of two parts each; and the inner chamber (*garbha*) consists of sixteen squares. (83)
The leg (jaṅghā) shall be half the width; the girdle (mekhalā) shall be one square (padikā).
Each of its chariot-mouldings (rathikā) shall be three parts in height.
Its lines, neck, egg-shaped member (aṇḍaka), and so forth, shall be like those of the Sarvatobhadra [temple].
A temple with lion-entrances (siṃhākrānta) and likewise with auspicious (bhadra) features is called a Siṃha; this Siṃha temple brings prosperity to those of valorous and upright character. 85. Siṃha.
The number of petals for the lotus should be sixteen or twelve;
it should be made circular, and its cord should be according to the method for the svastika.
All chariots are recorded as being beautiful in the shape of lotus petals.
One should create a water-enclosure for the sake of prosperity, as in the case of Nandana;
this is the characteristic of measurement previously described for the Padmaka and Svastika [gardens]. ||88||
A wise person should mark everything with that very [measure],
according to the division of the base in the *svastika* and other [postures],
as well as the division of the trunk according to the division of the center of the lines. (89)
A cross-shaped mark (svastika) should be fashioned auspiciously at the height of the *śukanāsa* (gargoyle).
That [mark] should be established for the prosperity of temples by means of seven parts;
in the case of a *vimāna* temple, it should be made by the wise one as being reduced by three parts of the base (*dharā*).
Kailāsa, Turaṃśona, Vidhena, Śukanāsikā, Sarvatobhadra, and the one called Siṃha— these are specifically for the Meru class [of temples]. However,
the wise practitioner should fashion the śukanāsā (front porch) without six parts.

The supporting structure (sandhāra) is proclaimed to be as high as the palace (prāsāda); the inner sanctum (garbha) is half the width [of the base], and the walls are made from whatever remains. The height of the rise of the beams (tula) within the sanctum is equal to the height of the lower story (jaṅghā) of the palace. ||93-94||
The wall should be equal to the interior space; in the supporting arches, there should be the emergence of the beam (tula).
This should be constructed again with its width, or perhaps slightly elevated.
One should then draw the root-line divided into ten parts.
Having established the *garbha-sūtra*, one should fashion the *siṃhakarṇa* (lion’s ear).
With a cord measuring one and a half parts, one should draw the middle [section];
the chest is equal to two parts, while the head is one part in height.

Half [of that] is its height; the height of the wings is two parts. One should indicate the curvature at the boundary of the chest by means of a cord. Both types of lion-work (siṃhakarma) are recorded as being ninefold and tenfold respectively.
The first [region] is one-sixth wide and five parts in height from the base;
the second is Sūrasena, which has the same height and width as itself;
and Siṃhakarṇa is three times as wide as its height, extending one and a half units beyond the base. ||99-100||
One should cause the *kāmalas*, *mallakas*, and other [ornaments] to be fashioned from *siṃhakarṇa* wood.
Indeed, all of these are ornaments for every kind of temple;
one should install each in the place where it is appropriate.
In the construction of a Valabhī [temple], one should draw a horizontal line across the width and divide it into seven parts.
One should then fashion five parts for the front face, and with that same unit of measurement,
design the mekhalā, the antarapatta, the jambha, and the kumbhaka.

One should make it five parts high, and likewise raise the pinnacle (śikhara). Those very celestial palaces (vimānas) which are celebrated in the path of the gods are renowned as "temples" (prāsādas) by virtue of their stationary nature.
Kailāsa is for Maheśvara, while that named Garuḍa is for Viṣṇu;
a lotus is to be made for Prajāpati, and an elephant for Gaṇanātha. Indeed, it is traditionally held that these [vehicles] are not intended to be assigned to other deities. ||105–106||
That which is Triviṣṭapa is the abode of all the gods; however,
those other palaces that are remembered as being of various forms belong to all the gods without distinction.
On the ground, the base should be constructed with a width equal to the height of the temple;

its height is declared to be auspicious when it is one-ninth of the inner sanctum (garbha). Furthermore, it is traditionally held that the height of the pavilion (maṇḍapa) should be half of a sixth part or a fifth part [of the temple's dimensions].
The *karṇaprāsādakas* (corner pavilions) should be constructed from one-third of the main temple;
they should be made facing east and west, or facing south and north, respectively,
in the directions of Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, and Kubera.
One should place a valabhī (pavilion) in each of these four directions;
it should be as wide as the interior of the sanctum and two-thirds as long as its front.
Thus, in the outer enclosure, the pillar-base (jaṅghā) is according to the measurement of the temple.
Having stretched a thread across the interior of the pavilion from east to west,
the guru’s chamber should then be constructed, provided with windows and pillars. The pavilion should always be made twice the width of the temple.
The jagatī surrounding the pavilion should be twice as wide as the pavilion itself on the outside.
Corner pavilions (karṇaprāsādaka) should be constructed at half the size of the main pavilion, or even smaller;
one should arrange the placement of the valabhīs at one and a half times their [the corner pavilions'] size.
By this sequential arrangement, it is well-enclosed from the outside to the inside;
for just as a king shines with armlets, bracelets, and earrings, so does this sovereign palace shine with its own ornaments. (116)
For one who is worthy of honor and exceedingly gentle, this brings forth prosperity, fame, and victory.
A temple consecrated according to this rite shall always bring benefit to men.
One should install Āditya in the east and Kumāra in the southeast.

To the south, one should place the elephant-faced [Gaṇeśa] along with the Mother-goddesses; above the south, Gaurī in the western quarter, and Caṇḍikā in the north-western quarter. Likewise, Viṣṇu in the direction of Kubera (the north) and Maheśvara in the north-eastern quarter.
Now the sequence for the other deities is also described.
There, one should place Īśāna, the leader of the world, in the northeastern direction, and Vāsava, the slayer of the Dānavas, in the eastern direction as well. 120–121.
One should install Vaiśvānara in the southeast, Dharmarāja in the south,
Nirṛti in the southwest, Pracetas in the west,
Vāyu in the northwestern quarter, and Kubera in the north.
