For these eight high-souled ones are proclaimed as the guardians of the world;
established each in their own respective places—in fortresses, coastal strongholds, villages, and cities—they protect the entire universe. (123–124)
Arranged in this sequence, they shall bring happiness to the people.
One should fashion the door where there is no obstruction to the deities;
according to the dimensions of the temple, the door shall be auspicious.
Now, therefore, the measurement of the doors is correctly described in sequence.
For the best, middling, and smallest types, the material associated with the pillars shall be sixteen *aṅgulas* for the doors in the temple. 126–127.
In a two-cubit [image], that [measurement] should be doubled; in a three-cubit [image], two cubits is auspicious;
for a four-cubit [image], sixty-four finger-breadths (aṅgulas) are recommended.
Beyond this, an increase of three finger-breadths per cubit is desired.
One should apply finger-breadths equal to the height of the door;
the width [of the base] should be half of that, and in the *dhruvaka* (pedestal) it should be four finger-breadths.
Its breadth is double that, and the mass of the pillar is indeed that same measure.

The pillar is properly constructed with a width ranging from one, two, three, four, five, six, or seven parts of the door's width. The boundary pillar should be made according to measurement with a width of four parts.
Likewise, due to the abundance of the pillar, two parts out of four parts [of the height] should be made there with a reduction;
the height of the capital (hīra) should be elevated, and the height of the fillet (paṭṭa) should be made with three parts. ||132-133||
The width of the *nīsyātavya* (the part to be cast out) should be one part, and it should be fashioned with a third part of a *bhāga*.
In the *paṭṭahasta*, an extension of two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) is to be provided;
its width is praised as being equal to that of the pillar.
Beyond that, there should be an additional finger-breadth on each side of the cloth-strip;
thus, the width of the cloth-strip should be made by dividing [the total] into four parts. One part is desired for the height of the support for the balance-beam. ||135-136||
From the height of the tulādhāraṇaka, divided into four parts,
one part is set aside and its mass (piṇḍa) is prescribed. It should be slightly less in measure at the base of the shaft (meḍhi), and one should place it there at the bottom of the crossbeam (śalā).
The width of the *jayantī* and the *piṇḍa* should each be two parts, equal to the width of the base (*mūla*).
Thus, by way of summary, the description of the marks for the *hīra*, *graha*, and so forth has been given.
The *kumbhikā* should have a width exceeding five parts of the pillar’s width.
One should make the height of the *kumbha* (pitcher) one and a half times the width of the pillar, O Garga;
or alternatively, it may sometimes be twice the width of the pillar's neck (*karṇa*) or twice the height of the pillar's top.
The height of the *agrakumbha* (top pitcher) should be three-quarters of the width of the pillar.

Whether from the width of the pillar or from the corner, or else regarding the mass at the frontal pitcher (agrakumbhaka), we shall explain its divisions so that it may be properly joined according to the pitcher. Here, the mass is divided into three parts; with one part, the figurine (puttalī) is made.
One should draw a lotus for that central [mandala] using four [units].
When the height is divided into five parts, there is a turning by three;
one should perform the turning slightly, and indeed should not act otherwise.
Having given the thread for the turning of the *kumbha* and *kumbhaka*, it should be well-stretched;
it should be equal to the stalk of a lotus and must not be devoid of rows [of ornaments].
When the height is divided into nine parts, the *vīragaṇḍa* is one part.
The *paṭṭikaṭṭikā* should be made with each single part;
the *dhvaja*, *saṃchāka*, and *kāla* should be made measuring two parts.
One should divide the *talakumbhaka-piṇḍa* into five parts.
With one part, there should be a lotus; with one part, one should draw a pitcher (kalaśa).
With two parts, one should draw a jar (kumbha), and with one part, a band (paṭṭikā). A circular ornament (varta) should be made, as much as is necessary for its beauty.
This sequence of the pitcher (kumbha) has been declared as established within the pillar-base (stambhapāda).
The mass (piṇḍa) of the base-slab (talapaṭṭa), however, should be equal to the slab of divisions (bhāgapaṭṭa). Indeed, in all these materials, perfect beauty is intended.
One should apply even a fraction of an inch more or less than this in the measurements.
One should recollect everything— the height and width of the door, as well as the arrangement of the materials—
exactly as previously specified.
The second [branch] is prescribed by means of the total [measurement] from the root-branch;
it is fashioned together with the pedestal, and then that branch, along with its form, is praised as being equal to half [the height].
One should fashion the outer branch so that it is equal to half of the root-branches.
The seventh and ninth [projections] belong to the upper fifth branch;
they should be of the same form— neither less nor more—
and the projection for all of them should be made equal to half their width.
One should fashion the waves extending from the expansion of the branches.
The height of the *udumbara* (the capital) is equal to half the total mass of the *dhruva* branches.
One should fashion the lion-faces using the mass of the *udumbara*.
Half of that should be the joint (vilasandhi), and the ground (bhūmi) should be equal to that;
the beam (paṭṭa) should be level with the placement of the base (tala) and situated as previously established for the mass (piṇḍa).
It should be adorned with various gabled forms (kūṭākāra) and beautiful decorative works (rūpakarma). ||156-157||
Just as a cook prepares the throat [of a dish] as desired with various leaf-herbs and pungent,
sharp, and other flavors according to their respective tastes,
so too the master builder (sthapati), having carefully examined [the requirements], should perform all actions accordingly. 158.
Whatever has been stated and whatever has not been stated— all that clearly,
having reflected upon what is appropriate, one should practice according to what is beautiful.
Beginning with Meru, these sixteen principal temples have thus been described in due order.
In brief, [this concludes] the characteristics of the *jagatī* (pedestal/base) on the ground, as well as the measurement of the wood related to the doors and so forth.

Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Sixteen Temples beginning with Meru, the Characteristics of the *Jagatī*, and the Proportions of Doors and so forth," in the *Vāstuśāstra* composed by the Great Emperor Śrī Bhojadeva, also known as the *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*.
Now begins the fifty-sixth chapter, concerning the sixty-four temples beginning with Rucaka.
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the sixty-four types of palaces, beginning with the Rucaka, along with their names and characteristics in due order. Following that,
the five types of celestial mansions (vimānas) which were previously mentioned shall be explained.
All twenty-five palaces bore that same form;
they were adorned with pinnacles of various shapes and single *aṇḍas*,
while some were provided with three *aṇḍas* and others were endowed with five *aṇḍas*.
These palaces, which grant all desires, should be known as being slightly different from one another;
made of gold and silver, they are always dear to the gods.
They are exquisitely adorned with ornaments such as gems, pearls, and corals.

Through brass, copper, bronze, and other such materials, these worlds of the Piśācas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas come into being; they move about at will according to their desires. Furthermore, those in the netherworld (Pātāla) are likewise described as being made of stone and crystal.
In the world of mortals, these [images] made of brick, wood,
or stone bring joy and bestow happiness upon both the maker and the one who causes them to be made.
We shall describe these, endowed with their characteristic marks, according to the prescribed rule.
For the sake of adorning the ancient [temples], they bestow enjoyment and liberation upon men:
the Rucaka, Bhadra, Kūṭa, Haṃsa, Haṃsodbhava, Pratihaṃsa, Nanda, Nandyāvarta, and Dharādhara. ||8-9||
Vardhamāna, Adrikūṭa, Śrīvatsa, Trikūṭaka, Muktakoṇa, Gaja, Garuḍa, Siṃha, Bhava,
Vibhava, Padma, and likewise Mālādhara. ||10||
Vajraka, Svastika, Śaṅku, Malaya, and Makaradhvaja—
these twenty-five temples have been declared by name.
We shall now describe their architectural construction according to the prescribed rule.
Among these, eighteen are proclaimed to be square (caturaśra), namely Rucaka, Bhava, and Vibhava; or else, Bhava and Vibhava may be square and elongated.
Padma and Mālādhara are declared to be circular (vṛtta).
Then there are the *malaya* and the one called *makara*; these two are circular and elongated.
The *vajraka*, the *svastika*, and the *śaṅku*—these three have eight corners.
These are indeed declared to be the *lalita* (graceful) types; now we shall describe the others, the mixed ones.
Subhadra, Yokita, and Sarvatobhadra;
another known as Siṃhakesarin, and the mountain Citrakūṭa;
Tilaka, Svatilaka, and likewise Sarvāṅgasundara.
The nine mixed types have been described; now those that are effective for practitioners are being told:
Kesari, Sarvatobhadra, Nandana, Nandiśālaka, Nandīśa, the one called Mandira, Śrīvṛkṣa, and Amṛtodbhava. (17–18)
Himavān, Hemakūṭa, Kailāsa, Pṛthivījaya,
Indranīla, Mahānīla, Bhūdharas,
Ratnakūṭaka, Vaiḍūrya, Padmarāga, Vajraka, and Mukuṭotkaṭa.
Airāvata, the royal swan, Garuḍa, and likewise the bull;
Meru, the king of palaces— for that indeed is the abode of the gods—
we shall now describe their conjunctions and supports according to the prescribed rule.
Latā, Tripuṣkara, Pañcavaktra, Caturmukha, and Navātmaka— these are known as the five Nirgūḍha temples. The first temple, which is called Kesarī, should be constructed with five aṇḍakas.
That which is to be constructed as the Sarvatobhadra consists of nine cells (aṇḍakas).
That which is named Nandana shall consist of thirteen cells.
And that which is declared to be the Nandiśāla shall consist of seventeen cells.
Nandīśa is surrounded by twenty-one *aṇḍakas*;
a wise man should have Mandara constructed with twenty-five *aṇḍakas*.
Among these, the Śrīvṛkṣa is praised for having twenty-nine *aṇḍakas*.
The Amṛtodbhava palace should indeed consist of thirty-three aṇḍakas;
Himavān is constructed with thirty-seven aṇḍakas;
Hemakūṭa should have thirty-one, and [Meru] consists of forty aṇḍakas.
That which is known by the name Kailāsa consists of forty-five *aṇḍas*;
Pṛthivījaya consists of forty-nine *aṇḍakas*.
And that which is called Indranīla consists of five hundred *aṇḍakas*.
The Mahānīla temple is joined with fifty-seven aṇḍakas;
the Bhūdhara temple is endowed with sixty-one aṇḍakas;
and the Ratnakūṭa, joined with sixty-five aṇḍakas, is highly praised.
A Vaidūrya [temple] endowed with auspicious characteristics should be made with sixty-nine eggs;
a Padmarāga is prescribed as being joined with seventy-three eggs;
and a temple named Vijaya consists of seventy-seven eggs.
One endowed with eighty-one eggs should be fashioned as the *mukuṭotkaṭa*;
Airāvata is proclaimed to have eighty-five eggs,
while the *rājahaṃsa* is praised when it is joined with eighty-nine eggs.
A palace is formed by ninety-seven *aṇḍakas*, and the bull (*vṛṣabha*) by [ninety-eight];
Meru, the king of palaces, is said to consist of one hundred and one *aṇḍakas*.
[This applies] to Hari, Hiraṇyagarbha, and Bhāskara.

This Meru must be constructed by a Kṣatriya, and not by any other inhabitant of heaven. Of this Meru, the king of palaces and the abode of the gods, the Kṣatriya alone is the builder; for a Vaiśya, there would be a master-builder (sthapati).
While this is being done on Mount Meru, even both [the architect and the king] rejoice,
provided the Kṣatriya architect is one who knows the rules of the science of architecture (vāstuśāstra). However, if he is not, then his truthfulness, purity, and valor truly perish.
Even when the Brahmin Īśvara was the builder of the Meru temple, there was suffering for both the maker and the one who caused it to be made, yet his worship was not of such a kind;
he was a Brāhmaṇa architect, highly skilled in the science of architecture (vāstu-śāstra). ||38-39||
Even if he is wealthy, he should engage in the business of trade;
for among all Brahmins, he is designated as a builder and a master craftsman.
All the deities residing therein [in his house] will somehow bring about his prosperity.

Even if he is an expert in the rules of the science of architecture (vāstuśāstra), if the king who is the patron or the Kṣatriya who is the builder acts otherwise, then Mount Meru itself would be [the result];
there would be the ruin of his kingdom, and his subjects would flee in the ten directions.

If the worship of Meru is performed there by a Kṣatriya, a lord of men, acting as the architect (sthapati), then that Kṣatriya shall also attain the imperishable state. And whatever the measurement of each [pillar], and whatever the authority of the Karṇa [pillar]...
And this is correctly described for all types of palaces:
when the site has been made square and divided into four parts, the wall shall be one part on all sides, and the remainder shall be the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha). ||44-45||
In front of that, moreover, the eastern neck (prāggrīva) should be made, emerging from two parts;
it should be one-third in width and adorned with pillars.
The leg (jaṅghā) should be two parts in height, equal to one part of the height of the pedestal (pīṭha).
The leaf should be half a part less [than that], and the varaṇḍikā should be one-quarter [of a part].
The height of the śikhara is recorded as four parts and a quarter. One should draw the lotus-bud (padmakośa) using a cord three times [the diameter].
One should divide the space between the shoulders and the chest into three parts:
the neck should be one-half part, the *āmalasāraka* (the collarbone) one part, and the lotus-head (*padmaśīrṣa*) is traditionally said to be half a part. One part [remains for the rest].
Thus addressed, this one named Rucaka is [called] Rucaka.
Now, the one called Bhadra-kākhya is described:
Bhadra-kā.
One should cause a water-interval to be made between the two *bhadra* projections;
then one should recognize it as a *haṃsa*, a palace, or a temple for the deities. 52.
*Haṃsa*.
When, like a swan, one should leave a gap at the end of the auspicious [pattern],
then it is proclaimed as the temple named Haṃsodbhava.
(53) Haṃsodbhava.
When there is likewise a water-interval between the Rathānta and Karṇa [pillars],
then this beautiful temple is called Pratihaṃsa.
(54) Pratihaṃsa.
The front necks of the *rucaka* [type of temple], expanded according to their respective dimensions and extending outward by the measurement of the *bhadra*,
are then called *nanda*. (55) *Nanda*.
If Nanda is adorned with projections (prāggrīva) according to the measurement of the Bhadra,
they should emerge on all sides according to the measurement of the divisions and be square.
The projection should be made at the front, decorated with two pillars.
Then the Nandyāvarta temple is proclaimed, which brings about victory.
[Regarding] the Nandyāvarta:
when one makes a water-issuance at the end of the bhadra in the Nandyāvarta [plan], [it is so called].
Then the Dharādhara [mandala] is to be known; it is a temple, the best in the world.
When the square field has been divided tenfold on all sides, [the Dharādhara is formed].
The *karṇa* (corner) should be made with two parts; one should divide the remainder into seven parts.
With three parts, the middle *rathaka* (chariot-piece) is prescribed for it;
with two parts each, the left and right *rathakas* are formed.
Its projection should be one-third of its width;
this is declared to be the *vardhamāna* (ascending) type.
This is the *vardhamāna*.
Now, the Girikūṭa is described. ||61|| One should join the Bhadrastha with the middle thread of the Vardhamāna;
one should lay down four threads from the two tips of that corner-thread. ||62||
O Bhadra, from those born of him shall come Sthakarṇa, Citrakūṭaka,
and Girikūṭa.
If there should be a body of water between the ears and the edge of the chariot,
then for the *vardhamāna* [diagram], the *śrīvatsa* will be auspicious.
This is the *śrīvatsa*.
When it has been placed in the form and configuration of a mountain peak,
one should join the ears (karṇas) to all its counter-chariots (pratirathas),
following the path of the ears according to the two lines produced by the counter-chariots as before. ||64-65||
At that very time, the temple of the deity should be a palace known as Trikūṭa;
it is Trikūṭa,
situated in the configuration of Trikūṭa itself, with the Bhadra and Karṇa parts set apart.
In the *svarūpabhadra* configuration, a *muktakoṇa* (open corner) is produced.
A *muktakoṇa* [is formed] when the field is four parts wide and five parts long. 67.
The wall should be made with one part, and the remainder shall be the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha).
With a cord equal to half the dimension of this [sanctum], one should draw a circle behind it.
In front of it is Śūrasena, and behind it is the form of an elephant.
This palace is prescribed for the one named Gaja, the lord of the Gaṇas. [Thus ends] Gaja.
One should place Garuḍa in the position of Vardhamāna.
Its two wings are to be fashioned extending out by half the length of the temple (prāsāda).
On the two wings, one should divide its ten parts for the *vardhamāna* ornament;
the chariots (*ratha*) should be made pure in their proportions, and Garuḍa should be placed on the sides.
Regarding the Garuḍa [temple]: one should apply the two ears at the position of the Vardhamāna as before;
the chariot-base (rathikā) should be made with two parts, and the remainder should be fashioned as the Bhadra.
The pedestal (pīṭha) of this [temple] should be five parts of its shank-height, and half of that for its base;
the two inner leaves (antarapatra) should be one part each, along with water-channels (āpa) of half a part.
Likewise, the height of the spire (śikhara) should be raised by nine parts, which constitute three parts of the total height.
Kumbha and Amalasāra have come and gone from this lion. 74.
The Lion.
On a field made square and divided into four sections,
one should fashion its chariot-paths according to the measurement of the boundary's width;
these paths extend outwards from each side by one-quarter [of that measure], in sequence in all directions.
Furthermore, one should construct its neck-projections (*prāggrīva*) in all four directions, each twice as wide as the [main] part and extending outward by a sixth part of a *pada*.
Its inner sanctum (*garbha*) should be made four parts in length and two parts in width.
The height of the *jaṅghā* (the lower wall) and the pedestal (*pīṭha*) should be as they are in the *Bhadra* [type];
this temple, known as *Bhava*, is the abode for a triad of deities. (78) *Bhava*.
When one makes the chariots of the Bhava itself have water-exits and adopts another type of double-bend, that is the temple named Vibhava; it possesses three characteristic marks. ||79|| Triliṅgaḥ ||
When the square field has been divided eightfold on all sides,
one should sequentially lay down the lines for the central womb (garbha), the diagonal lines (karṇa),
and all the directional lines (dik-sūtra); [the measurements shall be] half a boundary-line and one full square (pada).

One-eighteenth part of the *pada* is used for that [circle]; by means of its connection, one should draw the circle. The inner sanctum (*garbha*) shall be half the width, and its walls shall be half of that.
By means of a thread extending outside that circle, one should divide it into sixteen parts.
One should fashion chariot-paths within the directional threads and the corner-threads;
the chariot-paths should be made as two parts, adorned with intervening water-channels.
One should arrange the intervening water-channel for this [area] like that of the Śrīvatsa.
It should likewise be applied to the height of the shank, the pedestal, and the pinnacle;
that is to be known as the forehead-support (bhālādhāra), which is equal both externally and internally. This is the garland-support (mālādhara).
In the location of Mālādhara, one should establish a field situated as before;
there, one should place a lotus separated by water,
and likewise construct projections in front with a width equal to half the span of the ear.
Having the appearance and form of lotus petals, pure by birth, and possessing the [auspicious] marks—
this is Padma.

In a square field that is divided into six parts both in length and in width, the inner sanctum (garbha) shall be two parts wide and four parts long; the cord (sūtra) measuring the width of the sanctum shall be provided with a quarter-part for the pedestal (pada).
One should rotate a semicircle by means of that [compass] to the south and to the north,
following that circle both in front and behind with a measuring line for the width of the boundary, increased by one-quarter of a square.
This square field shall be divided into twelve parts.
The width of the *bhadra* is two parts, while the width of the *bhadrās* is one part each. Between the *rathas*, the *bhadrās* are extended by one part.
And here, one should act like Mālādhara regarding the water-interval;
the temple named Malaya should be made circular and elongated. 92. (Malaya)
If one should arrange charioteers at the very ears of the Malay [temple],
separated by the interior water [courtyard] and projecting by one-sixth of the footprint;
and whatever may be the height of the pedestal, the pillar-shaft, and the pinnacle here—
When joined with a single mātrā, it is perceived by you as the *latinā* [line].
(94) Where, due to the reduction of half [the length] at the corners of triangles and squares, an octagon arises, that too is called *nara*. (95)
One should divide the octagon into four parts;
therein, a wall one part thick should be constructed, and from that, the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) shall consist of two parts.
Around its recesses (rathikās), an exit for water should be provided.
The temple named Vajraka is said to possess auspicious characteristics.
||97|| Vajraka.
In the layout of the Vajraka [temple], excluding the interior space for water,
when divided into forty parts, the chariot-paths (rathikās) shall consist of three parts each.
In the eight directions, its corner-projections (karṇas) shall consist of two parts each.
This [mudrā], whose ears are equal to lotus petals, is declared to be the Svastika. ||99|| [The Svastika]

Regarding the chariots previously shown in the layout of the Vajraka [mandala], one should construct each of them with four square units (aṃśaka). The central part, extending from the chariot-body (rathakośa), should consist of two units.
This temple named Śaṅku is specified as having eight corners. (101) Śaṅku.
Sixteen are declared to be square, two are square and oblong; two each are circular and circular-oblong, and three are octagonal. These twenty-five are known as the graceful (lalita) temples.
Now we shall describe the characteristics of the mixed types in their proper order.
When there is a *bhadra* configuration in the *bhadra* position, it is known by the name Subhadra; such an elephant is distinguished by its prominent ear-lobes (*karṇakūṭa*). (103–104)
When the previously mentioned Bhadra-śṛṅga becomes a Kesari,
it is then called by the name Sarvatobhadra, as described in the section on the Latā. Having abandoned the Bhadra-śṛṅga, one should construct the Siṃha in that very same place.
In the mixed configuration, that mixed form of those two becomes the Siṃhakesarī.
One should place a kūṭa in the position of the Śrīvatsa on the Bhadra;
by that same method, it is adorned with pratiśṛṅgas at the corners.
Together with seventeen pitchers, a lotus, a bell, and pure [ornaments],
that [structure] is called Trikūṭa, endowed with variegated peaks; when it occurs at the ear, the auspicious spot, the foundation, the full [part], or the summit.
Then, with seventeen *aṇḍakas*, that mountain-shaper [the temple] shall be formed.
One should place a *kūṭa* on the ear in the very position of the Śrīvatsa;
when there is a *bhadra* and a *śṛṅga* on the *bhadra*, it is then called a *tilaka*.

O auspicious lady, just as it is on the ear, so too should it be on the peak of Citrakūṭa; and likewise, that which is on the head should be beautiful in every limb. When a peak is placed upon all the subsidiary peaks, [it is truly complete].

That [temple] is to be known as Miśraka, while the one named Śrī is the Antika; each Antika is situated close to another. All [the temples] should be covered with domes (kūṭa), and all should have four faces.
The Miśrakas have many peaks, while others are designated as Kuṭīs.
This has been declared here as the characteristic of the nine mixed [mandalas]. Now, we shall clearly state the common characteristic.
When a square field has been divided into eight parts, ||114||

In its center, there should be a womb-chamber (garbha) occupying two parts, which serves as the abode of the deity. One should establish the inner wall in one part and construct the supporting beam (kārikā) in one part.
Furthermore, for the sake of its completion, the outer wall should be made in one part. ||115-116||
On its corners, two-part chariot-pavilions (rathikās) should be constructed;
the remainder should be made into a bhadra, adorned with water-channels. This procedure should apply to all directions, with [the projections] extending out by one part.
The leg (jaṅghā) should be four parts high, and the karaka should be half of that. One should fashion the varaṇḍī and the antarapatra with one part each.
The rathikā should have an interval of one part and be three and a half parts high.
The pinnacle (śikhara) should be one-sixth at the base, and its height should be equal to the remaining portions.
Having divided that height into three parts, one should draw the bamboo-receptacle (veṇukośa).
Then, one should divide the space between the shoulder-receptacle (skandhakośa) and that [pinnacle] into four parts.
One should fashion the lotus-head and the neck with one and a half parts;
one should make the kalaśa and the āmalasāraka with one part each;
and above that, one should fashion the bījapūraka with half a part.
The palace named Kaisarī was beloved by all its inhabitants on every side;
it was Kaisarī.
Having made the ground portion square and level, the wise architect should construct the temple (prāsāda) here with a base (jagatī) twice its width;
he should fashion the pedestal (pīṭha) of the jagatī so that it is half as high as the temple.
Having established [the structure] upon the pedestal, one should then divide the temple;
when the measurement in cubits is such that it forms a Sarvatobhadra configuration,
the largest [temple] is declared to be thirty-seven and a half cubits.
The middle [type] of temple should consist of twenty-seven [parts] increased by a kalā;
the smallest temple is declared to consist of fifteen [parts]. When these follow the ground-plan (talacchanda), they likewise follow that same progression in their upward extension.
Thus, the superior, middling, and inferior [proportions] are correctly described.
When the site has been made square and divided into one hundred root-parts (mūla),
one should place the womb-chamber (garbha) in its center, consisting of four sets of squares (pada).
The inner wall (garbhabhitti) shall be one-quarter [of the width], and the dark chamber (andhakārikā) shall be the same;
likewise, the outer wall (bāhyabhitti) shall be two parts for the ten-faced [Rāvaṇa].
The space for water (jalāntara) shall be one-sixteenth part of the measure of each individual color-section.
The remaining portion of the *bhadra* should be made to extend out by half the depth of the sanctum (*garbha*).
One should cause half a part to project on the side and likewise perform the outward extension.
The width of the *bhadra* should be the remainder, and it should likewise be five parts in length.
Its pedestal (pīṭha) should be made twice the height of that [base];
likewise, one should fashion its shank (jaṅghā) at double that height.
The girdle (mekhalā) should be half a part, and the fillet (antapatraka) one part.
In that [structure], the first tier (rathikā) should be made three parts high;
the second tier should be one and a half parts high.
The space between each successive tier of both [the inner and outer walls] should be made one part.
One should make the spire (śikhara) six parts wide and seven parts high;
thus the wise man should construct it with eight levels (bhūmi).
The chariots (ratha) and counter-chariots (pratiratha) are likewise separated by the outlets for water.

One should draw a lotus bud with four separate threads; the cluster of blossoms should be made graceful, shaped like the petals of a blue lotus. The neck [of the bud] should occupy one half-part, and the calyx [malasāraka] should be formed.
The wise [architect] should fashion the lotus-head (padmaśīrṣa) according to the measurement of the neck;
with one and a half parts, there is the dome (kumbhaka) above the lotus, which is called the Sarvatobhadra—the crest of various lines. 138–139.
Having constructed a beautiful abode for the gods in the Sarvatobhadra style,
one attains the supreme world in heaven, where one may speak according to one's own will. (140) [The Sarvatobhadra]

When the square field has been divided into ten parts, the womb (garbha) is one square; the dark band (andhakārikā) is half of that. The shank (jaṅghā), the shoulder (skandha), the ear (karṇa), and whatever constitutes its auspicious part (bhadra) [are likewise determined].
O Vatsa, everything [of the] Sarvatobhadra [mandala] should be arranged in the four directions.
One should surround all its auspicious parts with walls; furthermore, one should place a *vardhamāna* upon each and every auspicious part.
The emergence of the pinnacle (śikhara) should be five and a half parts;
one should cause rathikās shaped like crows to be made here on all sides.
One should make the base of the pinnacle six parts wide and its height greater than that.
One should employ these [elements] here in the Sarvatobhadra configuration;
the neck, the amalasaraka, and the dome (kumbha) should likewise be formed. This temple of the deity is to be made known by the name Nandana. ||145-146||
When this is performed, the Lord rejoices and burns away all misdeeds; he is the one who causes delight.
Then, having divided the site into twelve parts for the devotee and made it square,
the wise architect should construct the inner sanctum (garbha) along with the wall, consisting of seven units; the expert should make the wall one-quarter of a unit thick within the sanctum.
The outer wall should be likewise, and the dark chamber (andhakārikā) should also be likewise;
so too the height of the pedestal (pīṭha), the leg (jaṅghā), and the chariot-arches (rathikā) at the corners.
In the Sarvatobhadra type, one should join the corner-arches (mūlakarṇa) in the shape of a crow's beak.
One should place another chariot on each of the two wings.
Likewise, one should position four chariots at each corner. The remaining width of the *bhadra* should project out by half its own width.
One should adorn it with lion-ear (siṃhakarṇa) ornaments rising to half the width of the bhadra;
there, one should place the pinnacle (śikhara), which is eight parts in width.
With a cord four times [the height], one should draw the bamboo-receptacle (veṇukośa).
One should divide the space between the shoulder and the neck into three parts:
one part for the height of the neck, half a part for the amalasaraka (the smooth neck-base), half a part for the lotus-head, and one part is prescribed for the kalaśa (the pinnacle). ||153-154||
Three chariot-pedestals (rathikās) are proclaimed to be three pādas in height;
this is known as the Nandiśāla, which has the form of a Sarvatobhadra. 155.
Nandiśāla.
In the configuration of the Nandiśāla, when it is established in that form,
one should enclose all its auspicious parts with walls. In each and every auspicious part, one should place a Vardhamāna.
Likewise, the height of the auspicious pinnacle (bhadra-śikhara) should be five and a half parts.
One should fashion the height of the pedestal (pīṭha), the shaft (jaṅghā), and the height of its pinnacle as being equal in form to the Nandiśāla. ||157-158||
This temple, which increases joy, must be constructed for all the gods;
it is Nandivardhana.

One should fashion the Nandivardhana configuration as described previously. Between both ears, where the two chariot-riders (rathika) are situated, a pinnacle (śikhara) endowed with the proper characteristics should be constructed above them.
This [pedestal] is six parts wide and six and a half parts high;
one should draw the bamboo-receptacle (veṇukośa) with a cord four times [the height].
The neck and the amalasaraka shall be the support for the pitcher (kumbhaka).
It should be constructed in the form of the Sarvatobhadra; this is the certain conclusion.
This temple, known as Mandira, is a palace that adorns the earth.
Mandira.
In the layout of the Nandivardhana, situated according to that form, there are eight chariot-paths (rathikā) along the diagonal lines and the corner-lines;
these chariot-paths should also be twice as long as they are wide. ||163-164||
Its width shall be six parts, and one should fashion the remainder as the pinnacle (śikhara).
Its height should be made seven and a half parts;
the width of the shoulder (skandha) is six parts, and its neck (grīvā) is two parts.
The line, the *āmalasāra* (myrobalan), and the pitcher that is here present—O child, this is the *sarvatobhadra*; this is declared to be the *śrīvṛkṣa*.
[This is the *śrīvṛkṣa*.]
When the site has been made square and divided into fourteen parts,
one should construct rathikās (chariot-paths) with a width of two parts;
these should be separated by water-channels and joined at the corner-angles.
The remainder is the width of the *bhadra*, and its projection is half of that;
having divided this *sarvatobhadra* into *bhadras* on each side,
one should place it in the four directions, endowed with the aforementioned qualities.
Its inner sanctum (garbha) should be constructed with a width of one and a half parts;
the wall in the middle of the sanctum should be of that same measure, and its outer wall likewise; the remainder should be used for the circumambulatory path (bhramaṇa). ||170-171||
The pedestal (pīṭha) should be one-sixth of the height of the shank; its [upper] ledge (varaṇḍī) should be half of that.
One should fashion the leaf-pattern (patra) in the space between them with a single part (bhāga).
The chariot-base (rathikā), twelve parts in width, should be joined one above the other.
There should be three tiers upon each corner in successive order.
The first tier for the chariot-riders should be three parts high;
the others above it should be reduced by one-quarter [of a part] each.
One should cause its pinnacle (śikhara) to be made in the shape of a bird, eight parts wide and nine and a half parts high;
this temple, known as Vimāna, is celebrated as being born from the nectar of immortality.
The Vimāna [style]: one should divide the Himavat [type] into two parts, each measuring seven [units] in length and breadth.
Therein, one should place four chariot-paths (rathikās), situated at every corner (karṇa).
All [the tiers] should be made with a width of two parts, one above the other.
Its first floor should be three parts in height, while the subsequent floors should be reduced by one-quarter [of the height] each in succession. ||177-178||
One should cause a pinnacle (śikhara) endowed with the qualities of the Nandiśāla style to be constructed here;
in its center, one should fashion the "Sarvatobhadra" [pediment] and the tiers (bhūmikās).
Its *rathikā* (recessed projection) shall consist of two parts, and it shall be raised three parts in height.
One should have the second story constructed according to the measurement of the ground.
The height of the spire (śikhara) should be made equal to one and a quarter times its width.
Furthermore, the pillar-base (jaṅghā) and the pedestal (pīṭha) here should be like those of the Amṛtodbhava type. ||180-181||
This Himavat, the best in the world, is pure by birth;
[he is] Himavat.
When it is situated in the configuration of Himācala and established in that form, one should apply the *vardhamāna* (ascending) style to all its auspicious parts;
it should have an extent of six parts and project out by half of that. ||182-183||
The height of its pinnacle (śikhara) should be seven and a half parts;
one should decorate the pillar at the front of the pinnacle with lion-ears (siṃhakarṇa).
One should perform all the construction for this [temple] according to the previous method using the cardinal lines.
Its height of the shank, its ear, and whatever constitutes its pinnacle—all this should be made like the Himavat by one who understands;
this palace is renowned throughout the three worlds as Hemakūṭa. ||185-186||
This Hemakūṭa, the abode of the three forms [of the Divine], must be made; it is not for anyone else.

One should construct a palace with a shape equal to that of the Himavat mountain. In its center, one should fashion the structure known as the Sarvatobhadra; however, the placement of a Vardhamāna within its middle must be avoided.
Then, one should apply the *khaṇḍarekhā* (segmented lines) at all the designated places;
subsequently, one should adorn the *bhadra* with *siṃhakarṇas* (lion-ears) having a height equal to the diameter.
Furthermore, the spire (*śikhara*) above that should be avoided by the wise.
Two *rathika* mouldings should be made,
each two units high with an additional one-quarter unit; and above those, a square-shaped *śikhara* (spire) should be fashioned, its height being five and a half units relative to its width.
In all the directional sūtras, one should arrange the ritual action in this manner:
the outer line and the base (jaṅghā) are known to be like the Himavat mountain. This [structure] is celebrated as Kailāsa and should be fashioned for the wielder of the trident (Śūlapāṇi).
Kailāsa.
When this very [structure] is raised up with lion-ears (siṃhakarṇaka), two beautiful chariot-pavilions (rathika) are placed there on each side;
the remaining width of the pinnacle (śikhara) is five parts in height. ||193–194||
And in the auspicious projections at the front, they extend out by one part each;
in width, they are four parts—this is the rule for all directions.
Furthermore, an outer line resembling a celestial chariot (vimāna) is prescribed for it.
Endowed with these qualities, that temple was named Pṛthivījaya.
[This occurs] when the square field is divided on all sides by sixteen parts.

The interior (garbha) shall consist of eight parts; in its center, the inner wall (bhitti) shall occupy two parts. The circular passage (bhramaṇa) and the outer wall are likewise declared to be of equal measure.
At the corners, chariot-pavilions (rathikā) should be constructed, adorned with water-channels.
Other carriage-roads (rathikās) should be of equal length and width;
likewise, the third carriage-road should be similar. The Bhadra type is four paces long and extends out by half its width, causing agitation from the Vardhamāna.
One should construct the intermediate leaf of the *varaṇḍī* with one and a half parts.
Indeed, the successive parts above should be diminished for the sake of gradual beauty.
Between the two *rathikās* on the *bhadra*, a *siṃhakarṇa* is prescribed.
The height of this [structure] is proclaimed to be five parts;
on its two sides, there are charioteers situated upon lion-ears (siṃhakarṇas).
Above those two, the spire (śikhara) shall be six parts in width.
This [pedestal] should be made one-third higher, or even more;
upon its two sides, above that [pedestal], one should place a lion on the *rathika* (the molding). This is the rule for all directions as well. ||203-204||
Then, at the base of the pillar, the pinnacle (śikhara) should be made with a width of ten units and a height of eleven units, beautiful due to its gradual tapering. Then,
one should draw the bamboo-receptacle (veṇukośa) using a cord four times the [base] length.
One should divide this [height] into three parts according to the previously mentioned *sātarambha* proportion.
The neck (*grīvā*) should be half a part in height; the *daṇḍaka* should be one part elevated;
the lotus-head (*padmaśīrṣa*) likewise by half a part; and the pinnacle (*kalaśa*) should have a height of one part.
This is declared to be the Indra-nīla, which is the abode of the gods;
it is so called when its uppermost peak is fashioned otherwise [than the standard form]. (208) Indra-nīla.
And for this [temple], a fourth, exceedingly beautiful chariot (rathikā) is provided;
it is devoid of one quarter according to the previously mentioned rule.
The width of the pinnacle (śikhara) is eight parts, and its height is nine parts.
The remainder is prescribed as being like sapphire;
this palace, the abode of the gods, is declared to be Mahānīla.
Thus ends the section on Mahānīla.
In the location of the sapphire (indranīla), one should place the Sarvatobhadra pinnacle on all sides along the directional lines;
this rule is prescribed for all directions. ||211-212||
One should avoid the placement [of ornaments] on the *bhadra* of the *vardhamāna* temple;
one should instead adorn its *bhadra* with lion-ears (*siṃhakarṇa*) that are as wide as they are high. One should fashion everything for this [temple] so that it resembles the *mahānīla*.
The Bhūdhara temple, resembling Indra’s palace in appearance, is prescribed for the Lord of the Gods (Indra); it should by no means be constructed for others.
This is the Bhūdhara.
When the configuration of the Bhūdharapīṭha has been established in its proper form, O auspicious lady, the wise man should then install the Vardhamāna-pīṭha;
it should have a width measuring four parts and a height of four and a half parts. ||215-216||
This temple of Śrīpati is known as Ratnakūṭa.
On a square field divided into twenty parts, [the plan is laid out]. (217) Ratnakūṭa.
One should construct five chariot-paths (rathikās) extending from the corners, with a width of one module;
above those, again five, and then one above that.
The first storey of this [temple] should be made three modules in height.
The subsequent stages are progressively devoid of pedestals.
Above those two chariot-like structures situated between the auspicious ears,
one should construct a pinnacle (śikhara) with a width of ten units and a height of ten and a half units.
Following the proportions of the base and the ear, whatever pinnacle (śikhara) may be there,
its width should be twelve [units] and its height thirteen.
One should adorn the bhadra with beautiful leaves and charming lion-ears (siṃhakarṇa).
One should draw the sheath of the cane with a cord measuring five vyāmas. One should divide the space between the shoulder and the sheath into three parts;
likewise, one should fashion the lotus-head and the neck with one and a half parts.
One should construct the *kumbha* and the *āmalasāraka* with one part each;
the *jaṅghā* should be nine parts high, with a *kharapiṇḍikā* half that height;
and one should make the *varaṇḍī* and the *antarapatra* with two parts.
This palace of the enemy of the Dānavas is declared to be made of lapis lazuli (vaidūrya). O auspicious lady, when this very [palace] has a *vardhamānaka* pinnacle, it is called *vaiḍūrya*.
In the same way, there would be a *padmarāga* [gem]; this [object] should not be considered a *padmarāga* because of its being a *padmarāga*. 226.
*Padmarāga*.
In the *padmarāga* type, one should avoid the *bhadra* projections;
in the two flanks of the *bhadra*, one should provide two *rathikās*.
One should adorn the *bhadras* with *vyāsa* and *ucchraya* proportions and with *siṃhakarṇas*.
Whatever else belongs to it, all that would be like a ruby.
This is declared to be the *vajraka* [diamond], which is to be employed by the enemy of Tripura.
The *vajraka*.

O auspicious one, for the Vajraka [temple] alone, as before, when situated upon a chariot-base (rathikā), one should install a pinnacle there with a width of six parts and a height of seven parts; this is the rule for all directions. ||229-230||
This temple, the abode of the gods, is called Mukutojjvala;
it is resplendent with crowns.
But when, O auspicious lady, in place of this very [shape], a *vardhamāna* is constructed on all four sides— excluding the *siṃhakarṇa*—
with the third [section] standing upright, it has seven in height and six in width. ||231-232||
This temple, the abode of the gods, is to be fashioned as Airāvata;
[thus it is] Airāvata.
When the temple is situated in the Airāvata configuration as previously described,
if the *vardhamāna* is omitted from above and a lion is placed [therein],
one should avoid the four spires in all directions. ||233-234||

One should establish the womb-chamber (garbha) with a width equal to the extent of the site; the *bhadra* should be four parts long and divided by its projection. One should employ three *bhadras*, encircled by the thickness of the wall.

The height of the door should be half the width; the elevation [of the structure] should be one and a half times that. Arches (gavākṣas) should be made there so that the door may be cleared. In the center, a four-sided pavilion (catuṣkikā) should be constructed, measuring two parts in both length and width.
This palace, praised by Brahmā and the other gods,
is a royal swan.
In the third configuration of the Rājahaṃsa, above the chariot-pavilion (rathika),
when the pinnacle (āraśikhara) is seven units in height and six units in width,
then it is named Garuḍa, which is dear to the one whose banner is Garuḍa. ||238-239||
Likewise, for the builder of a palace that is entirely [of this nature],
Garuḍa [is the presiding deity].

Leaving aside two parts from the base and the pinnacle of this very [structure], the *rathikās* (chariot-projections) are made; when it is complete, above that, the *mūlamañjarī* (root-cluster) is made when the height is twelve [parts] and the width is ten parts.
Then there shall be one named Vṛṣabha, beloved of the bull-bannered Lord Śiva.
He is Vṛṣabha.
One should fashion the largest Meru with a width of six and a half cubits; for the medium one, the measurement in cubits shall be twenty-two;
and for the smallest, the number of cubits is said to be thirty-one.
When the site has been made square and divided into twenty parts,
the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha), together with its wall, shall measure half the width [of the total].
The thickness of the wall of the sanctum is prescribed to be one part in measurement.
The other wall should likewise be two and a half parts, serving as the dark chamber (andhakārikā).
A wise architect should make the rathikā two parts on each corner;
the rathas in the bhadra should be four parts, projecting by half of that [width].
At the two corners of the *bhadra*, there should be a water-interval (*jalāntara*) equal to one-eighth [of the width];
likewise, chariot-pavilions (*rathikā*) should be constructed on both sides of the *bhadrās*.
And for all these chariot-pavilions, the *svabhadra* should be half the width [of the pavilion].
Just as the Bhadra-śṛṅga is made as a single unit, so should all [the others] be constructed.
One should place the Vardhamāna at all the cardinal lines;
the pillar (jaṅghā) is eight parts in height, and the mass of the hoof (khurapiṇḍa) is half of that.

Those which are situated on the inner leaf of the wall and project out by two parts are the first chariot-projections (*rathikās*); they are three units high. The upper floors should be diminished successively by one-quarter of a unit.
In the cardinal lines that possess the ears, the ritual procedure is prescribed as before.
The spire (śikhara) has a width of ten parts and a height of twelve parts;
one should draw the bamboo-receptacle (veṇukośa) with a cord four times [the length of the base]. ||251-252||
One should divide the space between the shoulder-knots into three parts;
the neck and the lotus-head should each be half of that part in height. The *āmālasāra* should be one part, and the *kalaśa* likewise one part.
This palace is said to be Mount Meru, surrounded by its seven peaks. The merit gained from circumambulating that [Meru] is equal to the merit of circumambulating the Mountain of Gold (Sumeru);
however, when this [palace] made of stone bricks is constructed, the merit is even greater than that.
Meru.
In the position of the Nandiśāla, when it is established in that form,
a second chariot (rathikā) should be made, extending out by two parts. The remainder is the width of the Bhadra, which is half its own width protruding outward.
The length and width [of the hall] shall be eight parts, projecting outwards by half its own width.
Furthermore, there should be a hall in front with a length and width of eight parts;
in the center of that hall, the sanctum (garbha) should be two parts in both length and width.
Its inner wall (garbhabhitti) shall extend out by one part;
likewise, the outer wall (bāhyabhitti) shall be equal to that, as shall the enclosing wall (andhakārikā).
Its chariot-path (rathikā) shall consist of two parts and be adorned with water-channels (salila).

The remaining width of the Bhadra [section] shall be one part as the projection (nirgama). One should construct the height of the girdle (gaṅgha) and the pedestal (pīṭha) according to the Nandisāra [standard].
There, the chariot-arches (rathikās) should be made three parts high at the corners (karṇa). ||260–261||
One should make the width six parts and the spire seven parts high;
its *sāmalasārikā* line should be fashioned like that of a lion.
One should also apply these same qualities to the two sides of this [structure].
This palace, known as the *latā*, should be constructed for the enemy of the Dānavas (Viṣṇu).
This is the *latā* type.
When the front part is placed behind [the rear],
it then becomes the temple known as Tripuṣkara, a celestial abode for the thirty gods.
This is the one called Tripuṣkara.
When the lion of Nandiśāla appears in all directions,
then that five-faced one of the Lotus-born [Brahmā] must be fashioned.
(265) The Five-Faced One.
And when no central womb (garbha) is provided for the five-faced [mandala],
the external lines and so forth are arranged in all directions as before.
A four-pillared structure should be made, and in its center, a square pavilion (catuṣkikā).
One should place a canopy above it, with an ornament in its center.
Hara, Hiraṇyagarbha, Hari, and likewise Dinakara—these are to be installed upon the four faces; this [procedure] does not apply to others.
Four-faced.
In a field measuring sixty-four cubits, one should employ twenty-one units of measurement;
the inner sanctum (garbha), together with its wall, is prescribed as seven parts. The wall of the sanctum shall be one part, and the dark chamber (andhakārikā) likewise one part.
One should divide the width of the ear (the wall) into ten parts;
six of these parts shall constitute the inner sanctum (garbha) together with its wall.
The outer wall shall consist of one part, and the dark chamber (andhakārikā) shall likewise be one part.
The width of the ears should be two parts, adorned with an interval of water;
the remaining width of the *bhadra* should extend out by one-fourth. One should cause agitation in half a part, and the interval of water should be half of that.
One should know that they are adorned above with intoxicated elephants and pillars;
one chariot-track [unit] is three parts, while the other is two and a half parts;
the mutual projection between them is prescribed as one part each.
The remaining width of the peak is six and a half [units], and its height is the same;
one should draw the bamboo-receptacle (veṇukośa) using separate lines tripled [in length].
One should divide the space between the shoulder-receptacle (skandhakośa) and that [peak] into four parts.
The height of the neck should be one and a half parts; the *āmalasāraka* (neck-ring) should be one part.
Likewise, the *padmaśīrṣa* (lotus-head) is one part, and the *kalaśa* (dome) is measured at one part. One should cause the *bījapūraka* (finial) to be made with a height of half a part.
The wise should perform these actions in all types of pavilions (karṇas).
One should construct a balcony (valabhī) on the outer portion of the lines marking the directions;
its projection should be five parts, with one part cast out transversely.
Its womb (garbha) shall consist of two parts, and it shall rise three parts in height at the center.
The wall (bhitti) shall be half a part, and the inner chamber (andhakārikā) shall be equal to that.
At its front, one should construct [the structure] provided with six wooden beams (ṣaḍdāruka).

One should join each individual chariot-moulding (rathikā), measuring one and a half parts, to the corners. The remainder shall be the width of the *bhadra* (front porch), and its projection shall be one part.
Thus, the *bhadra* division shall be provided with two pillars.
Between the *valabha* and the *āvarta*, one should construct a space one part wide;
there, one should create an inner water-chamber adorned with the gateways of the Gaṇas.
The *jaṅghā* (the wall) should be nine parts high, and its *pīṭha* (pedestal/base) half of that.
One should fashion the inner leaf of the girdle (mekhalā) measuring two parts;
the chariot-moulding (rathikā) shall be two parts, and then [the next element] one and a half parts.
The remainder is the width of the spire (śikhara), and the height of the spire is five parts.
One should construct two *sarvatobhadra* grids one above the other [285].
One should place two *sarvatobhadra*s on each and every corner;
one should arrange the procedure in this manner across all the directional lines [286].
The height of the pinnacle (śikhara) should be half of its width;
[this is determined] by a cord of five [units] across.
One should divide the space between the bamboo-receptacles (veṇukośa) of this [pinnacle] into three parts.
The neck and the lotus-head (padmaśīrṣa) should each consist of one part; these two together [make up] two parts.
The pitcher (kalaśa) and the amalasaraka should each be made with one part.
This temple, the abode of the gods, is thus described as having six parts.
It consists of nine aspects.
One should install [the deity] in the northeast, Puruṣottama in the southeast,
Brahmā in the region of the wind (northwest), and Divākara in the southwest. Śiva is to be established in the central womb, and Purandara also in the east.
This is the law: Varuṇa is in the west and Soma in the north.
One who is endowed with power should diligently cause a palace to be built in the vicinity of the ancient sanctuary; one must not at all oppress that original site.
In whatever location one should situate a palace, whether it be superior or inferior, we shall describe those rites pertaining thereto.
One must not construct [the site] facing directly forward, nor should it be deficient or excessive.

If the Vedic divisions (vedabhāgas) are situated on both sides of that [central axis], the temple (prāsāda) would be extremely censurable. A piercing (vedha) on either side of each other is called "deficient" (hīna).
One should predict death when there is a piercing in the deficient [alignment] without the Vedic divisions, and loss when it is merely deficient.
Hara, Hiraṇyagarbha, Hari, and likewise Dinakara—
these gods are said to be mutually antagonistic.
One should not place these [images] on the right side of those residing in the city.

To the left, one should not place the temples of other deities, nor in inferior dwellings. One should not construct the abode of others to the right of these [deities], whether it be inferior or superior, if one desires prosperity for oneself. (297–298)
To the north of those [shrines], if one should indeed construct a temple,
one should have another temple built at a distance of thirty-six [units] according to the measurement of the site of the palace,
avoiding the piercing of vital points (marman).
Whether in front, behind, or on both sides,
one should apply the four great vital points (mahāmarmāṇi) with diligent effort;
during all these intervals, one must not allow even a single substance to be given away.

At that time, one should avoid the piercing of the junctions (*vedha-marma*). If, out of delusion, a single substance is offered during the interval of a moment, there will be suffering for both the agent and the instrument; such an offering is not [true] worship.

Therefore, with every effort, both the master builder and the craftsman should diligently avoid the vital points (marmas) in the vicinity of the temple. Now, one who desires to construct a temple free from such vital points— ||303-304||

Therefore, he should always ensure a great distinction regarding the palace; moreover, a superior palace should be constructed, adorned with fruits and flowers. Whoever should have a temple for the deity built endowed with these characteristics [shall attain great merit].
One obtains wealth and grain, and rejoices in happiness alone.
Hara, Hiraṇyagarbha, Hari, and also Dinakara—
these are declared to be the gods who are honored even by the gods themselves.
They should be fashioned individually, yet endowed with a single uniform form:
eight-armed, four-faced, adorned with earrings, radiant with a crown,
equipped with necklaces and armlets, and beautified by a garland of jewels.
The Sun-god, lotus in hand, should be depicted with a sage standing before him;
and the god Madhusūdana, bearing the conch and discus, should be on his left,
adorned with neck-ornaments and a resplendent crown upon his head.
Brahmā should be depicted on the western side, with a large circular belly,
holding a water-pot (kuṇḍikā) and a rosary (akṣasūtra), and adorned with a tuft of hair (kūrca).
Here, twenty-five graceful Prāsāda and Rucaka-type temples are to be placed as before.
Following those, an equal number of *sandhārakas* (sustainers) beginning with *kesarimukha* are proclaimed;
likewise, nine are called *miśra*, and five are mentioned under the name *nigūḍha*.
This total is known to be sixty-four, and it should be understood as leading to prosperity (*sampad*).

Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Sixty-four Temples beginning with Rucaka," in the *Vāstuśāstra* composed by the great king of kings, the illustrious Bhojadeva, also known as the *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*.
Now begins the fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Twenty [Temples] beginning with Meru.
Next, we shall describe other [temples] in brief, according to their subtle characteristics.
Here, fifty excellent palaces were built, beginning with Śrīdhara. They are:
Śrīdhara, Hemakūṭa, Subhadra, Ripukeśarī, Puṣpa, Vijayabhadra, Śrīnivāsa, and Sudarśana.
For these are dear to the Blessed Lady, as is Kusumaśekhara;
and this beautiful celestial palace is beloved by Lord Śambhu.
Also Nandyāvarta, Pūrṇa, Siddhārtha, and Śirivardhana.
Trailokyabhūṣaṇa, Padma—the beloved of Brahmā;
Pakṣabāhu, Viśāla, and another, Kamalodbhava;
and the one known as Haṃsadhvaja: these are the palaces dear to Brahmā. ||4-5||
The temple of the Enemy of Madhu (Viṣṇu) has Lakṣmīdhara as its eye; it consists of the Vastatā [plan] and is like the Mahāvajra. Another is the Ratitanu, and likewise another is the Siddhakāma.
There is also the one known as Pañcacāmara, and indeed the one called Nandighoṣa.
Anukīrṇa, Suprabha, Surānanda, and Harṣaṇa;
Durdhara, Durjaya, Trikūṭa, Navaśekhara, Puṇḍarīka, Sunābha, Mahendra, and Śikhiśekhara. ||7-8||

Varāṭha, Sumukha, and Śuddha—these are said to be the forty; however, ten are declared to be mixed due to the mutual differentiation of their functions. Nanda by name should be known, and likewise another, Mahāghoṣa.
And there is another palace named Vṛddhirāma, as well as Vasundhara;
then Mudgaka, Bṛhacchāla, and likewise Sudhādhara;
the one called Saṃvara, which resembles a parrot, and Sarvāṅgasundara. ||10-11||
Thus, fifty types of palaces have been described in their proper order.
Now we shall describe the Śrīdhara temple, which fulfills all desires, is beloved by all the gods, and is the supreme cause of merit. 12.12-13ab.
When the field has been made square and divided into twenty-four parts,
one should join the corner-ridges (karṇaśṛṅga) at all twelve corners;
the width of each one should be specified as four parts.
And here, this [structure] is prescribed as having two parts (dvipada) with a projection (niṣka);
the *karṇibhadra* elements consist of two shares, and the projection (*nirgama*) is half a share. The *karṇa* should be placed at the position of a *karṇa*, and its width is half a *pada*.
The central part submerged in water should be made ten parts;
the projection (nirgama) should be three parts, aligned with the same horizontal line. The outer wall should be two parts, and the inner dark chamber (andhakārikā) should also be two parts. ||17||
The root (kanda) shall consist of one hundred squares, and its interior (garbha) twenty-six parts.
The ear-root (karṇakanda) consists of two squares, and each limb (pratyaṅga) is recorded as being one square.
It extends outward by half a part and is situated in the four directions.

A hall consisting of four bays (catuṣpada) should be constructed, extending out by one part; it should be situated between the outer wall and the base (kanda), both internally and externally. The space between these two should be made five parts wide.
One should create an intermediate space, and that *śṛṅga* should have four parts (*catuṣpada*).
Its division should be exactly like that of the outer *śṛṅga*.
Furthermore, between the wall and the *kanda*, six wooden beams (*ṣaḍdāruka*) should be constructed by the wise.
One should construct a beautiful pavilion in front, adorned with archways on the four sides and endowed with all auspicious characteristics;
its height here should be measured by fifty parts.
Among these, twenty are to be employed for the emergence of the *tula* [pedestal].
In their midst, the binding of the altar (*vedībandha*) is prescribed with six parts.
There, within that altar-binding divided ninefold, equal squares are formed.
The *kumbha* there consists of four parts, while the *masūraka* consists of two parts;
the *antarapatra* should be one part, and the *mekhalā* is recorded as being two parts.
The *jaṅghā* should be raised by ten parts, namely those which are the root portions.
The girdle (mekhalā) is said to consist of two parts, with an inner leaf (antarapatraka) occupying two shares;
below the upper wing and above the base-band (talapaṭṭa),
sixteen parts are to be fashioned, wherein this work of worship (vārcana) should be performed.
One part shall be for the stream of forms (rūpadhārā), and Senaka [shall be] one and a half parts each.
The altar (vedī) is three parts in height, and the seat-slab (āsana-paṭṭaka) is two [parts].
The upward gaze (avalokana) with the crescent moon above should be made with one part.

The pillars above the seat are prescribed to be five and a half padas in height. The *ucchālaka* (the capital) should be made with one part, and the *śīrṣa* (the head-piece) should be one and a half padas high.
The *paṭṭa* (the fillet) should have a height of two padas, and the width of the *chādyaka* (the covering) should be three padas.

The support (ālambana) should be half of that, or it may be made according to what is aesthetically pleasing; the upward curvature of the petal may also be fashioned out of sequence. At the corners, a pinnacle (kūṭa) should be constructed with various elaborate artistic efforts.
Their width should be one-fourth [of the total] and their height one-sixth. The corners (karṇas) are provided with bells, and the measurement for the pinnacles (kūṭas) is prescribed;
there, one should construct them one by one above that according to the sequence of death (mṛtyukrama).
And their equality should be maintained both in width and in height;
there should be four [ornaments] on each ear, thus making sixteen in total for all [the ears].
The measurement of the width of the *siṃhakarṇa* (lion-ear) should be one-eighth [of the whole].
Its height shall likewise be one-sixth [of its width], and it is adorned with chariot-riders (rathikas).
Equipped with triple doors, it is named Śūrasena;
it should be constructed with lion-ears (siṃhakarṇas) and is suitable for all ritual activities. ||36-37||
After the emergence of Siṃhakarṇa, there should be the Uromañjarikā;
it shall be one-eighth of the width and one-ninth of the height.
Adorned with five creepers, this Mañjarī shall be most beautiful.
The neck (grīvā) shall be three-quarters of a part (pādonabhāga), and the pillar-base (aṇḍaka) shall be one part in height.
The moon-ornament (candrikā) shall be half a part, and the pinnacle (kalaśa) shall be one part.
Above that, there shall be a second tier (kūṭa), and likewise the uromañjarikā.
Twelve parts wide and one and a half parts high shall be the base;
the neck shall be one part, and the dome (aṇḍaka) one and a half parts.
The capital (kapardin) shall be half a part, and the pinnacle (kalaśa) two parts.
Thus there are eight *uraḥśikhara* peaks, making fourteen in total.
Above the second *kūṭaka*, the root-cluster (*mūlamañjarī*) should be constructed;
it is sixteen parts in width and eighteen *padas* in height.
Indeed, for all [temples], the height of the *skandha* (pedestal) should be as previously stated for the hundred-vastu type;
the neck (*grīvā*) should be one and a half parts, and the *daṇḍaka* (neck-base) should be provided with two parts.
All the *aṇḍakas* (domes) should be made resembling the fruit of the *kaṅkatī* tree.
A pair of Caṇḍikās, made of Sāmalasāra wood, should be fashioned two pādas high.
Above that, there should be a round pitcher (kalaśa) three pādas in height,
adorned with arches, crocodiles, and leaf-patterns complete with tips and varālakas.
One should fashion Śrīdhara as being strewn with elephant-heads, adorned by a multitude of lower lips,
and decorated with all ornaments; indeed,
that man who causes Śrīdhara to be made, even for the sake of fame, [attains great merit].
In this very world he obtains happiness, and in the next, O Lord, you shall attain it. Having enjoyed worldly pleasures, the man is led to heaven and to the supreme state;
liberated from all sins, he will become peaceful—of this there is no doubt. ||48-49||
Śrīdhara.
Now we shall describe Hemakūṭa, which is endowed with auspicious characteristics;
it is the abode of all the Vidyādharas and the refuge of the wielder of the Pināka bow (Śiva).
In a square field divided into twenty-six parts:
In that [structure], there should be six-pada ears; the halls (śālās) are twelve parts wide and project outwards by three parts on all four sides.
Furthermore, they are eight parts long, with a projection of three pādas.
This same rule applies to all directions for the four pillars and four sides.
The space between the corner halls (karṇaśālā) should be made one square (pada) in width;
it enters [the interior] by one square, and that itself constitutes the water-interval (jalāntara) here.

The corner (koṇa) should be one pada at the ear (karṇa), and the secondary limb (pratyaṅga) should be one pada in width; it should project by half a part (ardhabhāga) and be symmetrical and beautiful. In the Bhadra type, the chariot-base (rathikā) measures two padas and projects by half a pada.
The wise man should thus measure the four corners;
the width of the outer wall is proclaimed to be three padas.
The inner sanctum (garbha) shall consist of sixty-four padas, and its wall shall be three padas.
The three-fold part shall be the measurement of the ear (karṇa), joined with a water-channel (vārimārga).
Half a pada shall be the water-channel, and its entrance shall be one pada.
The hall (śālā) shall be eight padas in width and project out by half a part (bhāga).
O auspicious one, it should extend for four parts and project out by half a part;
such is the placement of the base on the Hemakūṭa due to the determination of the divided sections.
One should construct a large pavilion at its front, honored for its excellent qualities.
Above Hemakūṭa, it should be double [the height] with an additional one-sixteenth part.
Its base below is seven parts in height;
by one part there is a plinth (khuraka), while in the middle of the two aforementioned [sections], there is none.
Henceforth, we shall again describe the measurement of the pedestal (pāda) in due order.
In the construction of the altar-base (vedībandha), one should make it very beautiful, rising to seven parts.
Half of that is for the dome (kumbhaka), half is for the neck (grīvā), and by one part is the height of the pitcher (kalaśa).
A leaf-pattern is fashioned between the foot and the pillar as it appears beautiful.
Furthermore, the very beautiful *kapotālī* is said to be one and a half *pada*s in height.
The *jaṅghā* (shaft) should be made ten parts in height and endowed with excellent characteristics.
Above this, the *bharaṇa* should be fashioned with a height of two units;
on the leaf-patterned band between the *mekhalā*s, however, they are prescribed at three units.
Below the *mekhalā*, but likewise above the *khuraka*, [the same applies].
They declare that nineteen parts [make up] the subsequent [measure];
the measure of its action is stated separately in the middle.
The Rājāsena should have two feet, and the Vedā [should have] four feet.
The design of the *āsana-paṭṭa* (the seat-slab) should be determined according to its proportional measurements;
it should be made with two and a half parts, and above that, the crescent moon (*candrāvalokana*) should be fashioned.
One should join pillars measuring one-eighth [of the total] with half of the *āsana-paṭṭa*.
On the head of each supporting pillar, a pedestal (padaka) is prescribed;
it should consist of two parts, with a half-strip (ardhapatta), beautifully adorned by a covering (chādyaka).
Therein, the width of the covering is proclaimed to be three parts.
This measurement has been fully described for the four sides of the *alinda* (veranda).
Now we shall describe, in due order, that which is above the inner panel (*antarapatra*).
In a six-part division, the width of the corner is one part, and the corner-cluster (*karṇamañjarī*) consists of seven parts.
One should make the neck half a unit (pada) and the egg-shaped dome (aṇḍaka) one unit.
The moonstone (candrikā) should be half a part (aṃśa), and the height of the pitcher (kalaśa) should be one part.
Its "hair" (roma) and flower-cluster (mañjarī) should be made with a width of four units.
On the neck-egg (grīvāṇḍaka), a dome (kumbhaka) should be fashioned with half a part;
furthermore, a lion’s ear (siṃhakarṇa) should be made with two parts in the middle of that very [neck].
Thus, the five-egg [ornaments] are prescribed for the ears on the golden peaks (hemakūṭa).
One should make it eight parts in width and six parts in height;
that delightful *siṃhakarṇa* (lion-ear) should be situated above the *alinda* (porch).
On the *siṃhakarṇa*, occupying two parts, one should construct [a structure] twelve parts in width.
One should construct the *uromañjarikā* [pediment] with a height of thirteen parts;
the shoulder (*skandha*) is seven parts wide, and the neck (*grīvā*) is one part high.
The dome (*aṇḍaka*) is half a part, and the *candrīkā* is known to be half a part.
One should fashion the Ākāśaliṅga, which is two-pada and very beautiful.
Its width at the base of the stalk (mūlamañjarī) is measured at twenty parts;
its height is twenty-one parts, and the shoulder (skandha) is twelve parts.
The [stūpa] should be made with five tiers so that it becomes beautiful;
there, the first tier is prescribed as five parts.
Each subsequent tier is prescribed to be progressively smaller by half a part.
The height of the shoulder (skandha) should be established as one unit;
having divided this into ten parts, one should fashion five exceedingly beautiful creepers.
On the corners of Hemakūṭa, there are Nara-kinnaras in every limb.
I think that the *tilaka* pinnacles should be constructed without intervals;
O Golden One, such a cluster (*mañjarī*) should be fashioned emerging from the pinnacle.
The neck (*grīvā*) is said to be one and a half units [in height] and eight parts in width.
The dome (aṇḍaka) should be two padas in height and eleven padas in length.
The staff (daṇḍikā) should be seven parts in height and nine parts in width.
The pinnacle (kalaśa) should be made three padas in both width and height. ||84-85||
The man who constructs such a delightful Hemakūṭa mountain sports in heaven for as long as the sport of the wielder of the Pināka bow continues. (86) [Hemakūṭa]
Now we shall describe the temple known as Subhadra, which is exceedingly auspicious. It is called "Subhadra" because it is endowed with every kind of excellence (bhadra).
When the site has been made square and divided into fourteen parts: ||87||

The inner sanctum (garbha) consists of sixteen parts, while Skanda is six parts in width. The wall (bhitti) shall be twenty parts; therein, the projections (karṇas) are drawn equal to the bulb-base (kanda), and the other subsidiary limbs (pratyaṅgas) are each one part in width.
Two parts constitute the width of the central section, which extends two paces outward on both sides;
the width of the lake is two parts, with projections extending from the occupied paces.
The outer wall should be two paces wide, beautifully adorned.
The ear [projection] is four paces long, and its auspicious [inner] portion is two parts.
Its outward extension should be half a part; thus it is beautiful.
At the corners of the ear, there are one-pada projections in all directions which are highly ornamental. ||91-92||
The concealed width should be made measuring five padas together;
therein, an exit of two padas is prescribed in all directions.
One should construct a water-channel between the two karṇabhadras.
The entrance has been described according to the measurement of the footprint;
now its vertical measurement is duly stated:
a very beautiful royal throne (rājapīṭha) should be constructed with half a part. 94–95.
The upper portion shall be the pedestal (khurakapīṭha), measuring four parts.
The height of the dome (kumbhaka) is two parts, and the moonstone (somasūra) is three-quarters of a part.
The interval between them is half a part, the leaf-pattern (patra) is one part, and the moldings (mekhalā) are three-quarters of a part.
The shank is six parts high; the neck-band (grāsapaṭṭikā) is one part. The girdle (mekhalā), the inner leaf (antarapatra), and the foot (padaka) are each remembered as being one part.
From the lower band (paṭṭa) up to the upper hoof (khura), there is an interval of eleven parts.
The king’s seat is declared to be one *pada* in height, which is not very beautiful;
when it is more than half a *pada* higher, the elevation of the pedestal (*vedikā*) should be two *padas*.
Half a *pada* should be made for the seat, and two parts for the moon-viewing (*candrāvalokana*).
Above the seat-cloth, the pillar is provided with five squares;
it is provided with five squares.
The *bharaṇa* and the *stambhaśīrṣa* (capital) should be raised by one *pada*;
one should construct the *paṭṭaka* (fillet) covered by a *chādyaka* (roofing) using one *pada*.
The width of the *praśchādya* (overhanging eaves) stands on two *padas*, while its projection is one *pada*.
Above the inner leaf (antarapattraka), the width shall be as it stands [in the model].
(102) On the four-cornered ears (karṇas), those small ears (padikas) which are situated on the ears—on them, pinnacles (śikharakas) should be made, one pada in both width and height. (103)
The kalaśa (pitcher) and the neck should likewise be raised by one and a half padas;
the lion-ear (siṃhakarṇa), however, is equal in both width and height, measuring two padas.
Below that, the śikhara (spire) should be fashioned with a triple-pada karṇamañjarī (ear-ornament).
Above that, it should have three parts, and the width of the shoulder should be two parts.
The kalaśa and aṇḍaka, together with the neck, should be made with one and a half parts.
The ears should be fashioned like those of a lion-prasāda, possessing auspicious characteristics. ||105-106||
They are as wide as the base measurement and stand upon the concealed [base];
the second and third [sections] are likewise elevated above that.
Above the kalaśa situated at the corner, the root-cluster (mūlamañjarī) should be fashioned.
Its width is ten parts, its height twelve parts.
It is adorned with five creepers and various artistic works;
its shoulder is known to be six parts, and its neck four parts. ||108-109||
It is described in detail as being one-quarter less than a pada in height;
the *aṇḍaka* is one-sixth of the height of the base (*pāda*) in width;
the *candrīkā* is three-quarters of a part, and the *kalaśa* consists of two parts.
Those who cause a temple known as Subhadra to be built, endowed with auspicious characteristics—
for them there shall be welfare for thousands of millions of kalpas in the presence of Śiva.
Subhadra.
This temple, known as Ripukeśarin, is proclaimed to destroy all sins and is celebrated throughout the three worlds.
It is constructed on a square site divided into twenty parts. ||112-113||
The outer wall should be two pādas [in thickness], and the middle wall should be of the same measure.
A circumambulatory path (bhramaṇī) should be made two pādas wide, extending in all directions.
The inner sanctum (garbha) should be eight units in width, and the corner (karṇa) should be one and a half parts of the base (kanda).
One should make the *bhadra* four parts long and project one part outward;
this is designated as the *rathaka*, which is to be constructed on all four sides.
On both flanks, two *pratirathas* should be made, each measuring one and a half parts in length.
Emerging by half a pad from various [positions],
the Karṇabhadra has a width of four parts and a length of two pads (117).
It emerges by half a pad and is situated at the outer ear.
The space between the ear and the *tilaka* [ornament] should be made one *pada* wide, extending from the foot [of the column].
The width of the *tilaka* should be two parts, and its projection should be one *pada*. ||118-119||
The *tilakas* should be well-proportioned and situated at the corners of the *bhadra*;
the *bhadra* shall consist of eight parts and project three *padās*.
This should be constructed in all four directions, adorned with pillars.
Now we shall describe the vertical measurement, which brings ease to each individual panel (pratipatra).
The vertical dimension should be made double [the width] plus two kalās;
in the middle, the emergence of the base (talodaya) should be formed with nineteen parts. ||121-122||
From among these, very beautiful altar-bases (vedībandha) are to be fashioned.
A *kumbhaka* consists of two padas, while a *kalaśa* shall consist of one and a half padas.
