The inner leaf-pattern (*antarapatra*) of the girdle (*mekhalā*) should be made with a height of one and a half padas.
The shank is nine parts in height, and the decorative band (rūpapaṭṭikā) is two parts.
One should provide two parts for the inner leaf of the girdle;
the middle part should be sixteen parts, and this applies to the hoof-base (khuraka) as well.
One should construct the royal army (rājasenā), the altar (vedī), and likewise the seat-cloth (āsanapaṭṭaka) with five units (pañcapada) according to the vertical measurement.
One should make the moon-view (candrāvalokana) two units (dvipada) in measurement.

Above the seat-slab (āsana-paṭṭa), the pillar (stambha) should be seven parts in height. The entablature (bharaṇa) and the capital (stambha-śīrṣa) together should measure two parts according to the vertical measurement.
The mass of the fillet (paṭṭa-piṇḍa) should be two parts, and the width of the covering (chādya) should be three parts.
Now, that which is above the inner leaf (antarapattram) is being described:

the four-footed [portion] consisting of the ear-ornament (karṇaśṛṅga), in terms of its length and height—[measuring] one part for the neck and the egg-shaped ornament (aṇḍaka), and half a candrikā for the [remaining] portion. ||129||
The kalaśa should be made with half that portion; of this there is no doubt.
Above this, a second karṇamañjarī should be fashioned.
The neck (grīvā) should have a height and width of three padas, and the egg-shaped kalaśa (aṇḍakalaśa) should be one pada.
In the Bhadra-karṇa type, the width at the base is known to be two parts;
its height is three parts, and above that, there should be a second [section].
Its height is known to be two and a half parts, and its width is two parts.

Likewise, one should fashion two lion-ears (*siṃhakarṇa*) measuring seven parts in height and eight parts in width, according to the rules of excellent proportions. Above the second *tilaka*, a breast-ornament (*uro-mañjarikā*) should be made. ||133–134||
It should be half a part in width at its base and nine parts in height;
the width of its shoulder (skandha) should be four and a half parts.
The neck (grīvā) should be half a part in height, with the central core (sāra) extending down for one part from the base.
The *candrikā* occupies half a part (*bhāga*), and the pitcher (*kalaśa*) rises for one part.
Above that, there should be the second [element], the root-cluster (*mūlamañjarī*) of the corner-ornament (*karṇaśṛṅga*), which is twelve parts in width and one part more in height. ||136–137||
The shoulder (skandha) is said to be seven parts; the neck is raised by one part.
The height of the dome (aṇḍa) is two parts, and its width is seven parts.
The moon-motif (candra) is one part, and the pinnacle (kalaśa) is two parts.
One should not employ any other work here than the task of digging a tank;
for those who desire victory as well as abundant enjoyments and the destruction of all sins, the *Ripukeśarī* [fortress] should be constructed. 140.
Ripukeśarī:
Now we shall describe the palace named Preṣaka, which was formerly constructed by Viśvakarman for the sake of the Giver of Wealth (Kubera). 141.
When the field has been made square and divided into fourteen parts, one should divide it such that four corners are formed by three units each; by means of that [measurement],
the lines for the corners, the non-corners, and the interior are made equal.
Having applied red threads, the two tips of those [threads] are prescribed.
Then, one should draw out four corners situated in the cardinal directions by means of the thread; thus, the other four corners are likewise fully established. Indeed, everything is complete.

In this manner, one should fashion eight petal-like projections (karṇas) that are circular; at the end of these projections, there should be a water-gutter (jalāntara) with an entrance and width of one part. The main hall (śālā) should be six parts in length, and its projection (nirgama) should be three parts.
The outer wall should be two units [in thickness], and the expansion of the *kanda* (pedestal-base) should be six units.
One should rotate the thread situated within the core of the *kanda* like a spindle; from that, a perfectly circular, well-proportioned, and beautiful form arises. ||146-147||
In the center of that, one should fashion a bulb (kanda) with sixteen petals;
that which remains between the wall and the bulb shall be the dhamantikā.
The placement of the pedestal for the flower (puṣpaka) should have the form of five flowers.
Now, its upper part is described, preceded by the measurement [of the base].
Above that, there should be twenty-nine squares in sequence as before;
outside of this, the pedestal (pīṭhabandha) should be constructed with three squares.
The *jayo-kumbha* should be one and a quarter parts; the *masūraka* should be three-quarters of a part.
The *antarapatra* should be half a part, and the *kapotālī* is equal to that.
The *mālā*, *vidyādharī*, and *kāyā* are adorned with flower-hands.
The tulodaya (the rising of the base) should have a height of twelve padas.
In its center, a vedībandha (altar-base) should be constructed occupying one-third [of the height].
One should fashion the khuraka (plinth) with half a pada and the kumbhaka (pitcher) with one bhāga.
The *masūraka* is half a *pada*, and the girdle (*mekhalā*) is one *pada* in measure;
the shank (*jaṅghā*) is declared to be six parts high in the Puṣpaka [temple], adorned with *varāla* birds, crocodiles, and also flowers and *vidyādharas*. 154.
Its ears are made equal to the subtle ears, and its shank is likewise prescribed.
One part is for the base (bharaṇa), one part for the fillet (paṭṭikā), and the inner leaf-pattern of the girdle (mekhalāntarapatra) is raised by one part. ||155-156||

The head of the upper cloth-band (paṭṭa) above the horizontal cloth-band should be fashioned with eleven parts, adorned with ears (karṇa). The royal section (rājasena) shall consist of one part, and the height of the altar (vedikā) shall be two parts.
The seat-slab (āsana-paṭṭa) should be raised by half a part;
it should provide a moon-like view and be one part high, suspended by three parts.
Above the seat, one should construct an auspicious pillar measuring five parts. ||158-159||
The *hīragrahaṇaka* head consists of two parts and one and a half parts;
the *gulāpaṭṭa* is one part, and the *mallaka* and so forth are two parts.
That [structure] should hang down by one part, being well-finished and very beautiful.
Above this, a fillet (chedapaṭṭikā) should be made.
Above this, by one unit, on the inner covering of the pigeon-hole (kapotālī),
it should be six units wide and five units high.
One should construct the Śūrasena [arch] with a central archway and side-arches,
adorned with peacocks, parrots, crocodiles, boars, elephants, and trunks;
it is filled with such figures and situated above the *alida* (pediment).
One should construct a corner with a flower-pinnacle (*puṣpakūṭa*), uninterrupted by the work of flowers. It should have four levels, each successively lower than the one before.
The first level should be the highest, and each subsequent one lower than the last.

The width of the first corner-protrusion (koṇakūṭa) is recorded as three padas; for the others, however, it should be reduced successively by one pada each. One should join them to one another from the outside, adding a portion (aṃśa) to each.
In the middle, a creeper should be made, six parts in width;
at the shoulder, one should fashion a central cluster with a width of two parts.
Taking a cord sixfold [in length], one should draw the line of the creeper.
Then one should fashion the drawing, perfectly pure and beautiful in its proportions:
the height of the pedestal (vedikā) is one part; the width of the shoulder (skandha) is six parts;
the neck (grīvā) is one part; and the amalasaraka is two parts.
The *padmaśīrṣaka* (lotus-head) should be fashioned resembling a large lotus.

The two [elements], the *candrīkā* and the lotus-leaf-like [portion], are elevated from the base. The *kalaśa* (pitcher) should consist of three parts, resembling the bud of a night-blooming jasmine (*jātīkunda*). ||170–171||

We shall describe the characteristics of Vijayabhadra and Subhadra;
this [Vijayabhadra] is dear to the Six-faced One (Kārttikeya) and bestows great merit.
When a square field has been divided into twenty-eight parts, [the following occurs].
One should construct an eight-padded Karṇabhadraka, or for him, a four-padded one.
This is the rule: it should extend out by one pad from all corners;
an internal water-channel should be made, measured in pads and elongated in length.
The auspicious [shrine] should be made ten parts in length and three parts projected [at the front].
A front pavilion (mukhamaṇḍapa) should be constructed facing the entrance.
The outer wall should be three parts, and the inner partition (andhakārikā) should also be three parts.
In the center, the measurement of the palace (prāsāda) should be made as sixteen parts.
The corner (karṇa) consists of four parts at the base (kanda), while the bhadra for these [other elements] consists of two parts.
Indeed, those [projections] resting on the base and corners should extend out by one part.
The middle part shall consist of six padas, and its projection shall be two padas;

that which lies between the two corner-halls (karṇaśālā) is prescribed [as such]. The wall of the foundation (kandabhitti) shall be two padas, and the inner sanctum (garbha) shall consist of twelve parts.
The upper measurement (ūrdhvamāna) here is said to be double [the height] plus two kalās.

At the end of the twenty-fourth part, from the middle of the height of the balance (tulocchrāya), whatever upper measurement has been described—such as the neck, the egg-base (aṇḍa), and so forth—is situated outside of that. ||180-181||
The work should be as high as the rising of the balance-beam (tulodaya), and the base of the altar (vedībandha) should consist of seven parts.
The pitcher (kumbhaka) should be three parts, the cord (sūtra) one and a half parts, and the masūraka one part.
The inner petal (antarapatra) should be one part, and the girdle (mekhalā) one and a half parts.
The shank [of the column] consists of twelve parts;
the neck-band (galapaṭṭikā) is two parts, the blind-moulding (andhārikā) is half a part, and the cornice (varaṇḍikā) is one and a half parts.
The inner leaf (antarapatra) should be one part, richly adorned with decorative work (rūpakarma). ||183-184||
Between the upper and lower bands, there are twenty-one parts.
From the middle of this, the *rājasenaka* should be made two parts wide.
The altar (*vedī*) is said to be four parts, and the seat-band (*āsana-paṭṭaka*) one part.
With one and a half padas, the moon-viewing [pediment] (candrāvalokana) should be made.
The pillar is nine parts in height and is fully adorned with leaf-patterns;
the base (bharaṇa) is one part, and the capital (śīrṣaka) is two parts.
The *ucchālaka* consists of two parts; the *hāragrahaṇa* is one part;
the height of the *paṭṭa* is two parts; and the external width is four parts.
Above that, the support (*ālambana*) is two parts, followed by the *rūpaka* and the *paṭṭikās*.
And that [spire] should consist of three parts, well-joined and beautifully decorated.
(189) The width of the pinnacles at each corner should be two padas;
the height, including the neck, the egg-shaped dome, and the pitcher, should be three parts. (190)
In the middle, there should be a four-pada *karmādu* with a *mañjarikā*;
its height is six padas, and the neck and egg (*aṇḍa*) are two padas high. The height of the pitcher (*kalaśa*) should be one part; thus is the construction of the corner (*karṇa*).
The *karṇa* (ear) and the *piṇḍikā* (pedestal/base) should be fashioned in the auspicious region (*bhadra-deśa*) and likewise elevated.
The *siṃhakarṇa* (lion-ear), well-adorned, should be made with seven parts.
Likewise, on both ears and the two peaks, and above them in the four directions— ||192–193||
From the base up to the *uromañjarikā*, there are fifteen [parts];
its bulbous root (*kanda*) consists of eight parts, and the neck (*grīvā*) is elevated by one part.
The circular base (*maṇḍaka*) should be made of two parts, and the *candrikā* is raised by one part.

The pitchers (kalaśas) should have three parts; between them, the central cluster (mañjarī) should be joined with five talas and endowed with the caraṭa-projection. The root-cluster (mūlamañjarī) should be made twenty parts in width.
The shoulder (skandha) should have a height of twenty-two parts and be divided into twelve sections.
The middle creeper (latā) should be filled with rasa, sena, karma, and rūpa.
The neck (grīvā) should be made with a height of one and a half padas, and the maṇḍaka [of the head] should be two padas.
One should fashion Caṇḍikā with one part and the pitcher (kalaśa) with four parts.
This temple, possessing auspicious characteristics, has twenty-nine pillars;
its pedestal is said to be six parts, and its conduct is according to the previous ritual rules.
Health and the birth of sons shall belong to those who achieve victory;
for those who perform this [rite] with devotion, the Six-faced One (Kārttikeya) is pleased.
— Vijayabhadra.
Now the temple known as Śrīnivāsa is correctly described. It is constructed for the sake of complete satisfaction; there, Jayaśrī resides.
[201] When the square site has been divided into eighteen squares, [The text continues with the architectural layout.]
The *andhārikā* and the wall each consist of two squares respectively.
The beautiful *garbha* of Śrīnivāsa should be made with six squares.
In the *kanda*, the ears (*karṇa*) should be two squares, and the water-interval (*salilāntara*) should be one square.

The Bhadra type should be made with four feet, each foot protruding by one unit; the ears should be three units long and joined with two-unit Bhadra sections. In the Bhadra type, the ears at the fourth position should have one unit protruding.
The corners should be made extending for half a square (pada). A cloud (ambudhara) should be fashioned with one square, according to its projection and width;
the *bhadra* should have a width of six squares and a projection of two squares.

Within the space between the *nīra* (water-course), *tilakas* should be made, two parts in width and extending out by one *pada*, adorned with beautiful craftsmanship. Now, we shall describe the vertical measurements for the *Śrīnivāsa* temple in due order.
The height of the *khuraka* on the pedestal is desired to be three-quarters of a *pada*;
one should make the height of the *jāḍyakumbha* by one and a quarter parts, the *antarapatra* by one part, and the *mekhalā* by one part. ||208-209||
In the Śrīnivāsa [temple], the height of the pedestal (pīṭha) shall be four parts;
the plinth (khuraka) of the altar-base (vedībandha) is raised by half a part;
the pitcher (kumbhaka) is one and a half parts, and the [maṇḍa] is half of that.
The wing of the eight-peaked [structure] is three parts of one part; between each peak of the eight-peaked [structure],
there is an interval of water.
The mutual projection of the horns is recommended by one part;
the auspicious [central part] is ten parts in length, with a projection of one-fourth part.
Thus has this *talacchandas* been described, O beautiful goddess;
now we shall explain the *ūrdhvamāna* according to its divisions and in their proper order.
Starting from the pedestal (pīṭha), the width should be doubled for the height;
one should likewise decorate the sub-pedestal (upapīṭha) with a height of one part.
The height of the door is one and a half padas less a quarter-pada;
the elevation of the jaḍyakumbha is prescribed as one and a half bhāgas.
On the northern petal of the *kalaśa*, it should be raised by one and a half units;
above this, a *grāsapaṭṭikā* (lip-band) should be made measuring half a unit.
The āyapīṭha is said to be the foundation of the entire structure;
the khuraka is half a pada, and the kumbhapūraka occupies one and a half parts.
One part should be made for the pitcher, which is perfectly round and exceedingly beautiful;
one and a quarter parts should be made for the inner leaf-pattern of the girdle.
The shank should be raised by six parts; the grāsapattikā (moulding) should be half a part;
the karṇa (corner) should be one part, and the kuṇapa should be half a part. One should fashion the hīraka (diamond-shaped ornament) with one part so that beauty is produced.
One should fashion the inner leaf of the girdle with one and a half parts;
from the top, between the two feet, it should measure twelve and a half parts.
In the middle of that, the royal belt with its cloth-strip should be one and a half parts.
Two parts shall be for the pedestal (vedikā), half a part for the seat-slab (āsanapaṭṭaka),
one part for the moon-light niche (candrāvaloka), and a pillar shall be placed upon the top of the seat.
One should establish the base as five parts; then the entablature (bharaṇa) shall be one part.
The height of the capital (śīrṣaka) shall be one part, and its length double that.
One should make the height of the *paṭṭa* one and a half parts;
its outer form is two and a half parts, shaped like a messenger's staff (*dūtāvala*) and carved.
Two parts above the screen should be made for the decorative molding;
it should be made shining with beautiful, well-proportioned ornaments.
Within the intermediate petals of the girdle,
however, the second girdle should be made by the wise with two parts, endowed with the same proportions.
Beyond the kūṭas, one should construct all other structures joined with functional elements;
within each of the kūṭas, one should include a lion and a pitcher.
The *uro-mañjarikā* occurs in those very places in their respective order:
at the ends of the three sets of eight *aṇḍakas*, there should be four [sections] of six *aṇḍakas* each;
having made two [sections] of four *aṇḍakas*, the wise know this to be the *karṇa*.
The nine pits are equal in width, measuring two and a half padas each;
likewise, each one is a height of two and a half padas.
Thus, each individual pit shall be constructed with a bamboo staff of one pada.
Siṃhakarṇa is six units in height; O auspicious lady, it is the width of the float (plava), and the second is Anudanta, adorned with beautiful craftsmanship.
The third part should be made into a beautiful lion-ear;
the width of the root-cluster (mūlamañjarī) shall be fourteen units.
When the height is seventeen parts, it should be like the calyx of a lotus with its mother-parts.
The shoulder is said to be eight padas wide, and the neck is one and a half padas in height.
The height of the bulbous base (*caṇḍaka*) is two parts, and it is raised by half a part for the *candrī*;
they say the *kalaśa* (dome) is three parts; this is the origin of the *mātuliṅga* [type of stūpa].
In the center of the root-cluster, however, one should fashion three peaks—
well-lined, very pleasing, and adorned with all regional ornaments.
In this [structure], there should be two hundred and fifty-six small cells (aṇḍakas);
thus has this excellent temple been described according to the measurement of its cells.
In the middle [world-system], there are seven hundred and sixty-nine;
furthermore, they say that the smallest [world-systems] consist of one hundred and one eggs.
O Surasundara, one should construct such a celestial palace, beautiful as the gods, which has the appearance of mandāra flowers.
He, beautiful as a celestial maiden, is honored in the world of the Sun for a hundred yugas of Brahmā.
Now we shall describe the Nandyāvarta temple, which brings about the prosperity of kings.
Adorned by charming Naga maidens and beloved by the lords of the earth,
[this was done] when the field had been made square and divided tenfold.
Having taken these two lines from the center of the Brahma-line, one should draw the square; its interior and exterior shall be equal.
The inner wall should be one part, the ambulatory (bhramantikā) should be one part,
and the outer wall should be one part, excluding five squares.
One should make a division at the base (kanda); then, the flower-crests (puṣpaśekharaka) should be fashioned, and the circular ears (karṇa) should be placed on the outside with two squares (dvipadā).
And those svastika-shaped figures should be fashioned according to the body;
there are four rathika-kandakas at the corners and a set of four at the ears.
One should fashion the *bhadra* extending five parts with a projection of one and a half parts; this *bhadra* should fall at the end of the fifth part.
The remaining auspicious portion should be made three parts wide;
it is extended by half a part, and likewise has an entrance of one part.
In this matter, the wise should determine the measurement of the space between the waters;
it should be auspicious, following the *talacchanda* style, or the *nandyāvarta*, according to the sequence.
Now we shall describe the measurement of the upper portion, starting with the Nandyāvarta in its proper sequence:
the pedestal above it should have a height of two and a half parts.
In the middle of the rising span of the *tula*, there should be a base of eight parts;
likewise, within that rising span, the construction of the altar (*vedībandha*) should occupy two parts.
The *kumbhakośa* should consist of one part, joined with a *mekhalā* and a *kalaśa*;
the *jaṅghā* should be four parts, and the *bharaṇa* should be one part.
One should fashion the inner leaf of the girdle with one part; the royal band should be one-quarter [of that], and it should be circular from the cloth-strip.
The altar (vedī) should have a height of eight padas, and the seat (āsana) should be one-quarter of a pada;
one should make the slope (nata) half a pada, and the [pedestal] one pada, consisting of five folds.
The pillar should be three-quarters of a pada in height, adorned with foliage,
and its capital should be fashioned for the reception of diamonds, rising to the height of one bhāga.
One should fashion a fillet one part in height and a covering two parts in length;
above that, one should make a molding-strip for beautiful craftsmanship.
The Siṃhakarṇa [pediment] should be three parts in height and four parts in length;
it should be adorned according to its own aesthetic essence, and it should not be made overly ornate.
The two horns should be two padas in width and two and a half bhāgas in height;
above these, there should be another horn with similar height and breadth.
Furthermore, the secondary members (pratyaṅga) and the pinnacles (kūṭa) on the wings (vaṅga) should have a height of one and a half parts.
The second is Siṃhakarṇa; it should be upon the head of Siṃhakarṇa.
Then the third [element] should be the śṛṅga (peak), and the fourth is above that;
the root-cluster (mūlamañjarī) situated on the corner-ridge (karṇakūṭa) has a width of six parts.
The height of the trunk should be seven parts, and the height of the head should likewise be [seven parts];
the cluster of hair at the top should be situated midway from the base of the trunk.
Its width is four parts and its height is six;
it is joined with a pitcher and a dome (aṇḍaka), and there is a mañjarī within the corner (karṇa).
With twenty-one lines of strokes, there is the auspicious Nandyāvarta design;
those who have this unsurpassed Nandyāvarta fashioned with devotion [attain great merit].
Having ascended a beautiful celestial chariot, they go to the world of Śakra.
This is the Nandyāvarta [arrangement].
Now we shall describe the Prāsāda, which fulfills all desires.
The field, which was made quadrangular and divided into ten parts by the Kinnaras, Yakṣas, humans, and Pitṛs who had paid their respects, was beloved by them.
The interior (garbha) should be two parts in width, while the wall (bhitti) should be one part;
the kandabhadra should also be two parts, and its projection (nirgama) should be half a part.
In all directions, the *bhramantikā* is two *padas* wide;
the outer wall is one *pada*, and the width of the *karṇa* (corner) is two *padas*.
In the future, four parts are to be projected from the corner wall;
its auspicious and very beautiful [front] portion is to be made two-parted.
The *parṇa* (leaf) is a square foot with its wings extending half a part;
the interval between the waters is half a part, equal in both length and projection.
One-fourth of this structure shall be the inner chamber (garbha) and one part shall be the wall;
one should cause a *valabhī* to be constructed for those who desire fame, as well as for women, wealth, cattle, and longevity.
One should cause a door to be made in the eastern direction in this four-chambered temple;
now we shall describe the vertical measurement of this temple.
The pedestal (pīṭha) should be made of two parts, and the base-molding (vedībandha) likewise of two parts;
the shaft (jaṅghā) consists of four parts and is adorned with sculpted figures.
Two steps should be made, including the umbrella;
the height of those [steps] joined with the pitcher and the egg-shaped ornament should be three steps according to the wise.
The *valabhī* (pinnacle) should be constructed according to the measurement of all the ear-ornaments (*karṇaśṛṅga*),
elevated four units in height, and provided with bells and a water-pot finial (*kalaśa*).
One should construct three *mallacchādya* (canopies) above the *karṇaśṛṅga* (corner pinnacle),
each individually one part in height and joined with an *antarapatra* (intermediate panel).
The bell should be made with one part, and the auspicious pitcher-base (kalaśāṇḍaka) with two parts;
the wise man should cause the cord to fall upon the ear at the base of the pitcher.
A canopy for the wrestler should be fashioned, marked with a single thread;
he who, full of devotion, constructs this very temple shall possess a full lifespan.
The man who desires the seven [worlds] is honored in all the world;
he is fulfilled.
Now we shall explain the Siddhārtha [mantra], which accomplishes the attainment of all desires and purposes.
Desires are fulfilled for the one who performs the rite both in this world and in the next,
when a square and level field is divided into ten parts.
One should construct a six-pada interior sanctum and a four-pada [hall] for it;
with one pada, the beautiful [veranda], and with one pada, the outer wall.
The wise should construct the two ears with two padas each and the hall (śālā) with six padas;
above that, one should fashion the ear-projections (karṇa-śṛṅga) according to what is aesthetically pleasing.
One should construct its exit with three steps and four-sided platforms in the four directions;
one should provide it with four doors, both in the middle and on the outside.
The height of the *unnata* (the raised portion) should be one-twentieth of the measurement;
the pedestal-base (*pīṭhabandha*) should consist of three parts, with its external height being double [that].
The altar construction should be made beautiful with two and a half parts;
the girdle (mekhalā) should be at the height of one and a half kumbhas, with equal projections.
The shank should be made beautiful with a height of four and a half parts;
one should fashion the lower fillet and the middle leaf with one part.
The girdle (mekhalā) should be one part, up to an interval of seven parts;
with two parts, one should construct the Rājasena and the altar (vedi) along with its pedestal (āsana).
The pillar shall be three parts [of the height]; the capital (hīraka) shall be half a part less than that;
the pillar-head (stambhaśīrṣa) shall be half a part; and the height of the fillet (paṭṭa) shall be one part.
The *sūryacchādya* (sun-shield) shall consist of two parts, the *lambana* (pendant) one part,
and the height of the finial (*śṛṅga*) three parts, together with the dome (*kalaśa*) and the egg-shaped ornament (*aṇḍaka*).
The lion-ear (siṃhakarṇa) should be four parts in height and six parts in width;
above the two horns, one should fashion a beautiful root-cluster (mūlamañjarī).
The base (skandha) should be known as eight parts wide and nine parts high;
it consists of five sections (pada), while the neck (grīvā) is half a part in height.
The egg-shaped portion (aṇḍaka) should be one part; above that, the crescent moon (candrīkā) is one part.
The pitcher (kalaśa), being circular and equal in width, is two parts.
O auspicious lady, here the varāṭakas should be fashioned like those on the Hemakūṭa mountain;
whoever makes them or causes them to be made shall attain all perfections and the fulfillment of every desire.
He shall attain all desires and be eternal in the world of Śiva; his purpose is accomplished.
Now, Śaṅkhavardhana, the destroyer of all sins, is being described.
It is the abode of all the gods and the beloved palace of the mountains;
it is purified by the diagonal measurement within the womb on a square and level field.
Thereafter, one should cause it to be marked in all the corners;
the inner sanctum (garbha) should be half the width, and the remainder shall constitute the enclosure (bhartiva).
One should cause it to be twice as high above [the base], divided into twenty parts;
the emergence of the balance-beam (tulodaya) shall consist of eight parts, and the cluster (mañjarī) twelve parts.
One should fashion the *kumbhaka* and the *kalaśa* with two [parts each], and the *kapotālī*.
The *jaṅghā* should be five parts in height; in its middle is the *grāsapaṭṭikā*.
One should have the inner leaf of the girdle made with one part;
the wise man should have the *vartaka-mañjarī* made with half a part.
One should construct conch-shaped and dome-shaped structures in detail,
according to the measurements appropriate for this site divided into one hundred plots.
The shoulder and the neck should be raised by half a bhaga;
the *candrī* together with the head should be made one and a half padas high.
In the Śaṅkhavardhana [stūpa], the height of the dome (kalaśa) should be made two pādas;
it should have a core and a covering, with its number [of parts] being that of the circular canopy (vartavitānaka).
He who performs the Śaṅkhavardhana rite enjoys the earth for a long time,
and the goddess Lakṣmī, whose garment is water, shall remain perpetually under his control.
Śaṅkhavardhana.
We proclaim him as the ornament of the three worlds, saluted even by the gods;
the refuge of all deities and the destroyer of evil.
The smallest [measure] should be thirty cubits, the middle one thirty-three, and the largest fifty cubits; thus it is threefold according to the number of cubits.
In a square and equal field, one should prepare thirty divisions;
the womb (garbha) should be ten parts long, and the bulb (kanda) seven times that doubled.
One should fashion a four-footed base, auspicious and consisting of two parts;
then one should construct a six-footed hall extending out by one part.
It is blind on one side and has two and a half bays; here, the walls consist of two bays.
There should be a single pinnacle in the middle, four paces in width.
In the interior of the middle of the pinnacle, there should be a structure of six wooden beams.
The second beautiful [section] consists of two parts, and the outer wall is two parts.
The two ear-lobes (karṇaśṛṅga) should be made four units (padas) in width;
the hall (śālā) measures twelve parts, and its projection (nirgama) is three units.
Its eight ears and horns are like the fruit of the durjana tree;
it has four feet and protrudes from the portion of its two horns.
Its auspicious *bhadra* on two feet, and its exit should likewise be on two feet;
with half a foot between both horns, it is the *pakṣabhadra*.
Half a pada is the water-channel, and its projection is equal to one pada;
now we shall describe the vertical measurement, which is raised by a sixtieth part.
Then follows the twenty-five-fold cluster of the rising of the scales;
that increase of the true measure of the king is prescribed in these divisions.
In the middle of the tulodaya, there is an altar (vedī) rising five padas;
one should fashion the pitcher (kumbhaka) as half of that, and likewise the girdle (mekhalā) of the vase.
The shank consists of eleven parts; the diamond (hīraka) is three parts.
The girdle (mekhalā) is two parts, and likewise the second [girdle] is also two parts along with the star (tārakā).
Above the surface slab, with sixteen squares,
the Rājasena should be one and a half parts, and the altar (vedī) should be made two parts.
Half a *pada* is the seat; one and a half *padas* is the gaze of the moon;
seven *padas* is the pillar; and three and a half parts is the length of the necklace.
The head (śīrṣa) should have a height of one and a half padas; the wing (pakṣa) should be two padas;
one should make the covering (chādyaka) three padas, hanging down by one part (bhāga).

The two parts, however, should be for the cutting and removal of the feet; or else, let there be two strips (paṭṭikā). Above that, one should fashion a cluster (mañjarī) adorned according to the Drāviḍa style.
The corner-pinnacle should rise seven units in height, equipped with bells, a vase, and a small dome;
one should construct the second story above this using that same measurement.
One should construct six squares by aligning ear with ear;
one should make two [squares] in the sixth section and four sections of six [squares each].
Thus, in brief, there should be forty ear-lobes;
twelve parts in width and nine parts in height.
In the first stage, one should know it as being endowed with the action of the *drā* and *viḍābha*;
the eight-egg [structure] is ten parts in both height and width.
One should know that the second, the Bhadra-krama, is adorned with ritual action;
its width, according to the Mūla-mañjarī, is measured at twenty-two parts.
The height is twenty-three [units], and the shoulders are thirteen;
the neck is two padas high, and the maṇḍaka is elevated by three padas.
The *karpara* measures two parts and the height of the *kalaśa* four parts;
in this [structure], twelve *nūramañjarikās* are prescribed for temples and the like.
It should be understood that the number of eggs is considered to be seventy-three;
having fashioned this ornament of the three worlds, it brings joy to the thirty gods.
That man, the ornament of the three worlds, shall dwell in the abode of the thirty gods for as long as the end of the eon.
Now we shall describe the temple named Padma, which is dear to the Aśvins.
When the field has been made square and divided into seven parts,
one should leave three parts in the middle and mark two [points] at the corners.
It should be two, two, and eight cubits, and sixteen at the rear;
the inner sanctum (garbha) should be half the width, and likewise, the exterior should be half the width.
Now we shall describe the vertical measurement of the one named Padma in due order:
its height is twice its width, divided into twenty parts.
On this [pedestal], the altar (vedī), the pillar-shaft (jaṅghā), as well as the garland (mālā) and the flower-cluster (mañjarī),
along with the neck (grīvā), the egg (aṇḍa), and the pitcher (kalaśa), should be fashioned according to the method of the conch-increase (śaṅkhavardhana).
By him who caused the temple named Padma, beloved of the ten [directions], to be built,
his own self has been rescued from the great ocean of the mire of sin.
The one named Padma.
Now we shall describe the Pakṣabāhu temple, which delights the lineage,
removes all diseases, is meritorious, and brings auspiciousness to all the world.
When the site has been made square and divided into twelve parts,
one should construct the inner sanctum (garbha) with a length of eight parts, and the wall (bhitti) should consist of two parts.
One should make the *karṇa* (corner) two units with half a unit as the water-interval;
each secondary member (*pratyaṅga*) is one and a half units, and that hall is indeed four-footed.
Emerging from both sides by half a part each,
the two arms on the wings should be made separately, measuring eight parts in their width.
The interior of those two [shrines] shall be four paces, and the width of the walls shall be two paces;
the *bhadra* (front projection) shall be one-fourth [of the width], and the corner shall likewise be two parts.
Now we shall describe the vertical measurement, which is divided into twenty-four parts:
the band of the pedestal (vedikābandha) consists of three parts, and the elevation of the shaft (jaṅghā) is five parts.
Two parts should be made for the vase (kalaśa), and two parts for the moon-stalk (candrikāṇḍaka).
In the middle, a cluster (mañjarī) should be fashioned, and bells should be attached on both sides.

He by whom the arm-guard (pakṣabāhu) is fashioned with three cavities (trigarbha) and adorned with ritual markings (karmabhūṣita) shall possess the prowess of the Three-eyed One (Trinetra) and become a leader of a fourfold army.
Pakṣabāhu.
I shall fully describe Viśāla, which is endowed with vast qualities,
beloved by the son of the Kṛttikās, and honored by the Gaṇas and Kinnaras.
One should make a tenth part for the field; the central cluster consists of six parts, and the walls should be made one part each, revolving accordingly around it.
The ear should consist of two parts and be joined by a water-path;
one should fashion a *tilaka* (ornamental mark) with one square, protruding by half a part.
Its porticoes, measuring one-fourth of its length and breadth, are recommended;
likewise, a central chamber with four pillars and four doors is praised.
The height above ground is prescribed as twice the width;
one should construct the binding of the altar-platform measuring one and a half parts.
A wise man should make the height of the leg (jaṅghā) with four and a half parts;
he should cause the garland and the inner petal to be made with one part each.
The horn divided into two parts is joined with a pitcher-shaped finial (kalaśāṇḍaka);
the other horn, measuring half of that, is prescribed to be of the same dimension.
The shank should be six parts wide, and the inner part seven parts;
the width of the shoulder should be six parts, which is one-tenth of that [inner] width.
The elevation of the neck should be made equal to half a square;
the height of the bulb (aṇḍaka) is one part, and the crescent (candrīkā) is half a part.
One should construct a two-footed pitcher (kalaśa) with perfectly aligned lines and great beauty;
thus, this extensive temple shall consist of seventeen eggs (aṇḍakas).
Whoever performs this shall become a lord of the Nāgas in this world;
he obtains many desires and, at the end of the body, the supreme state.
Viśāla.
Now we shall describe the lotus-born temple, beloved of Lakṣmī,
where Skanda resides together with the Siddhas and Gandharvas.
Having made a square and level field on the ground, and having drawn a circle within it, it should be divided into thirty-two parts in all directions and intermediate points.
Then one should divide each [section] into two parts, making one petal-band from each;
the corner should be fashioned with sixteen [parts], having a form resembling a lotus.
When the boundary is divided by five, the interior (garbha) shall consist of three parts;
one should fashion the lotus pedestal (padmapīṭha) below the āsamatta [moulding].
Having doubled [the measurement] upwards, one should divide it by twenty-two;
thus there shall be a portion for the emergence of the *tula*, and the *mañjarī* shall consist of twelve parts.
The pedestal, the shaft, and the garland should be as in the Śaṅkhavardhana style;
above that, there should be lotus-crests, elevated like lotus petals.
Five stages should be made, each succeeding one less by a quarter;
its pedestal should be fashioned like a blossoming hundred-petaled lotus.
The neck is three-quarters of a part, and the pedestal (padamaṇḍaka) is one-and-a-quarter parts;
the moonstone (candrikā) is one part, having the form of a blossoming lotus.
One should fashion a two-footed water-pot adorned with lotus petals and sprouts;
if this is made in the eastern quarter, there shall be health for the one born from the lotus.
Longevity, prosperity, increase, and sons shall result from the number of retreats;
thus says Kamalodbhava.
Now we shall describe the Haṃsadhvaja [mandala], adorned with the sport of swans.
Frequented by hosts of gods and beloved of the Lotus-born One,
this field was divided tenfold, beginning from the station of Brahmā.
Taking three parts from each side, one should fashion a circle;
thus should the interior (garbha) of the *chādya* be constructed with the *jagatālū* bricks.
The wall on the exterior should be two padas wide; the *karṇa* (corner) should be made two parts wide;
the *bhadra* (frontal projection) should be five padas wide; and the water-interval (*udakāntara*) should be half a pada.
Two parts should be the auspicious projection, provided with two pillars;
in the middle, one should construct a covering, twice as wide as the height of the opening for air.
One should construct the archway with its full extent, elevated at four points, adorned with crocodiles and sea-monsters; likewise, there should be *likkā* ornaments upon the pillars.
The wise man should first measure the pavilion according to the prescribed proportions;
now we shall describe the vertical measurement: the cord should consist of twenty parts.
The girdles, altars, and pillars should be designed like the Śaṅkhavardhana;
the ear-ornaments and chariots should be made three units high and provided with finials.
A four-stepped pedestal with five tiers, joined by a series of rings,
should be fashioned together with a pinnacle-pot, equal in both its width and its height.
One should fashion the root-cluster (mūlamañjarī) with two parts for the blind corner (kāṇa) and the horn (śṛṅga), making it one-eighth of the total height;
it is elevated by nine parts and enclosed by five stories (pañcabhauma).
The first stage consists of two lines and is comparable to the activity at Hemakūṭa;
the others should be made with one line, half a line, and so on, decreasing respectively.
Upon changing the ground-level, it should be made with great jewels;
the height of the pedestal should be one part, while the base should consist of a hundred plots.
One should fashion two feet with a height equal to the neck and the testicles;
on the testicles, a rounded curvature should be made resembling the fruit of the *kaṅkatī*.
If one part is of the *candrikā* meter and two parts are of the *cet*—
by him has the *haṃsadhvaja* been created, which is dear to the lotus-born [Brahmā].
At the end of the body, he who possesses the swan-banner goes by various vehicles to the destination of the Vasus.
Now we shall speak of Lakṣmīdhara, by performing which a man attains victory.
One obtains sovereignty, long life, honor,
and the powers of the qualities when the sacrificial field has been made square and divided into sixteen squares.
A six-petaled lotus should be constructed with a bulb (kanda) and four lines for the interior;
in all four directions, there should be a circular border consisting of three parts.
The outer wall should consist of two parts and be auspiciously constructed on all four sides;
there should be one pinnacle on each corner and two pinnacles situated in the middle.
Those ten peaks should be doubled in width, making them two parts;
and six halls should be constructed in all three auspicious directions.
With four parts toward the south and projecting two parts [toward the front], this ground-plan (talacchanda) is prescribed; such a pavilion (maṇḍapa) should be situated in front.
The height of this palace should be double its width;
here, the rise of the *tula* (pedestal) should be one-thirteenth of that measure.
Above that, there should be twenty padas for the altar-base (vedībandha) and three padas for the neck (grīvā);
the shank (jaṅghā) shall be six padas in height, and the entablature (bharaṇa) shall consist of one part.
The three divisions [of the base] form the two girdles; the pinnacle and the pitcher should be fashioned with three parts each in height, along with four lion-ears.
One should fashion ten prongs and a bell for the sale;
the root-cluster (mūlamañjarī) has a width of fourteen parts and five branches.
The height of the neck is seventeen parts and two padas;
the egg-shaped dome (aṇḍaka) should be made with two padas, and the skull-bowl (karpara) with one part.
One who constructs on the surface of the earth a temple named Lakṣmīdhara, beautiful and with a three-tiered pinnacle (kalaśa) at its summit, [attains great merit].
He dissolves into that imperishable state, the ultimate reality; of this there is no doubt.
— Lakṣmīdhara.
Now we shall speak of the Great Vajra, which is auspicious and removes all evil.
One should cause a palace to be built where the Lord of the Gods is well-pleased;
the smallest should be eight cubits in measure, and the middling twelve.
The best [measurement] is said to be sixteen [units];
thus, by the number of cubits, having drawn a circular field with a cord according to its own width.
Having marked the corners, one should divide [the area] into thirty-six parts;
here, the pericarp petals should be made in a number of twelve.
Between the two pericarp sections, the pillar should be circular;
it should be fashioned in the shape of a hundred-petaled lotus, with two parts measured for the top.
Below the girdle, it should be like that arising from a lotus;
one should cause the peaks to be fashioned among those [spokes] within the center of the pericarp.
One should draw a very beautiful design above the pericarp;
five grounds should be made, arranged in sequence and extending in length.
The neck should be half a part in height and four parts in width;
the egg (aṇḍaka), together with its shell (karpara), should be made with one and a half parts.
The pitcher (kalaśa) consists of two parts, along with horns and ears adorned with sprouts;
he who constructs such a great vajra-pedestal becomes an ornament of the city.
Contented in heaven, that Mahāvajra, together with his wife, delights with hosts of apsarases.
Now we shall describe the most beautiful temple, the body of Rati.
It is the palace of Kāmadeva, crowded with throngs of Apsarases;
it is situated upon a field divided into eight equal parts, which are perfectly symmetrical and level.
The *karṇakūṭa* should consist of two bays (*dvipada*) and be provided with a water-channel;
its width and length are equal, each being one-fourth of the *alinda*.
The outer wall should consist of one part; one should arrange the remaining space as the inner sanctum (garbha).
In the center, a four-pillared pavilion (catuṣkikā) should be constructed, wherein the pillars are most beautiful.
They were endowed with many-colored, three-faced hands,
all of which held sprouts, serpent-bonds, and *sālabhañjikā* (statuesque) figures.
There, a *khellikrā* (a type of decorative arch) should be fashioned, emerging from the mouths of sea-monsters (*makara*).
On the exterior, there are four vestibules (*alinda*), with a foundation consisting of two pillars.
The first temple should be constructed in a manner consistent with its purpose and endowed with ritual efficacy;
the second temple should be built free from external sectarian marks.
The remaining ritual actions should be performed in the same manner as they were in the first [enclosure];
however, in the third [enclosure], a four-legged platform with four pillars must be constructed.
The *khelikās* and *toraṇas* are placed [there], as are the *varālakas* facing forward;
there are the *kuṭakas* on the front of the pillars, and the *siṃhakarṇas* in the middle.
One should fashion three successive layers to be covered by the middle lattice, each half a *vya* in width and one part in height, joined with beautiful inner petals.
One should fashion the bell with its consort, having an upper part made of pure essence;
the moon-stone (candrikā) should be one-quarter of a part, and the height of the pitcher (kalaśa) should be two parts.
He who constructs such a temple, beloved of Rati, shall please Kandarpa and become a possessor of merit among men; he is as if the very embodiment of Rati.
Now we shall describe the Siddhikāma [mandala], adorned by the Pramathas,
wherein a man, having performed the rite, obtains wealth, sons, and a wife.
When the site has been made square and divided into four parts,
one should make the inner sanctum (garbha) two parts and the wall one part for the sake of beauty.
The wise man should construct the *bhadra* with a width of two parts, projecting one part outward, and a *karṇa* of one part in every direction.
Above this, one should make it double [the height], divided into six parts;
on one part, there is the binding of the altar (vedikā), and the plinth (jaṅghā) is raised by one and a half parts.
The interval between the waistband and the navel is considered to be one-quarter less than a *pada*;
the height of the thigh should be four and three-quarter *padas*.
The neck is three parts wide and one-quarter of a part in height;
they say the maṇḍaka is half a part, and Caṇḍikā is one-quarter of a part.
The height of the pitcher (kalaśa) is considered equal to half of that portion;
these are the second [elements], consisting of five constituents, according to the thread of qualities.
He who performs this rite for the sake of attaining siddhi is liberated from all sins;
all his desires, whatever they may be that reside in his mind, are fulfilled. This is the seeker of siddhi.
Now we declare: he who devoutly causes this five-chowrie palace to be built rejoices in heaven for a long time.
In a square field divided into twelve parts on all sides,
the inner sanctum (garbha) shall occupy four parts, and one should construct the wall with one part.
The *andhārikā* (blind wall) shall have two parts, while the outer wall shall consist of one part;
within those [spaces], four-pillared pavilions (*catuṣkikā*) should be constructed, projecting out by three parts.
When the height is stated as double [the width], it should be provided with a bell and a finial (aṇḍaka);
by this measurement, the rise of the balance (tulodaya) should be made in ten parts.
The arrangement of the pedestal (vedikā) shall have three parts; the shaft (jaṅghā) should be six parts;
and one should fashion the girdle (mekhalā), the inner leaf (antarapatra), and [the other elements] with one part each.
Above the three parts, the pinnacle, the dome, and the finial (aṇḍaka) should be made;
twenty peaks should be fashioned along with the walls and all the pavilions.
Below the pinnacle, one should construct a beautiful *mallacchādya* (pavilion);
in this manner, one should cause *mallacchādya*s to be made in all the quadrangles.
The central principal temple should be constructed with five types of roof-coverings;
the height of the ghaṭikās is desired to be one and a quarter padas.
The neck and the base of the bell should be made with one and a half parts;
the *āmalasārī* should be three-quarters of a part, and the *baṇḍikā* likewise.
A two-legged pitcher should be fashioned, endowed with seed-syllables and vowels;
having surrounded it with five bells, one should place upon it a celestial chariot with five chowries.
O Originator, the world, having passed beyond all its vastness, attains the state of the Five Chauris.
Now we shall speak of Nandighoṣa, which destroys the fear of adversaries.
Whoever should perform this with devotion shall become free from old age and death.
On a square and level field, divided into four parts, [one should proceed].
One should make the Bhadra twice as wide and project it by one part;
in this case, no wall should certainly be constructed in any direction whatsoever.
One should perform the inspection of the sacrificial altar and the moon by means of the Rājasena [formula];
this sequence applies to all directions, excluding the four intermediate quarters.
The first tier should be made with a height equal to its width;
and the pillars should be divided according to the proportions that will be described.
The royal seat (rājasena) should be made with one part, the altar (vedi) with two parts,
the moon-shaped area (candrālōka) with one part, and the cushioned seat (āsanapaṭṭaka) with half a part.
The height of the pillar-base (stambha) shall be three parts, and from that, the capital (śīrṣaka) shall be one part;
the height of the fillet (paṭṭa) shall be one part, and there shall be twenty-four supports (dharā).
The second floor should be constructed with various assemblies and shoots, with faces of artisans performing beautiful work, and provided with sixteen pillars.
In this manner, the ritual action is prescribed even on the second ground;
on the third, it is joined with four pillars, and on the fourth, it is fourfold.
He by whom the sound of joy has been produced becomes supreme splendor;
having cast off the body through the exhaustion of karma, he attains the highest state.
The sound of joy.
We shall now describe the palace, carved with the figures of Manus, vast and swift,
which was formerly fashioned by the Self-Existent One (Svayambhū) himself after careful deliberation with his intellect.
On a site six parts wide, one should construct a circle in the center within a womb-space of four parts, using nine lines for the circular boundary.

Eight chariot-riders should be stationed in the field, either in the cardinal or the intermediate directions; now we shall describe the vertical measurement, which is double [the horizontal] and augmented by two paces.
The covering should be constructed up to one and a half times that [measurement];
one should fashion eight and a half parts above the rising of the beam (tulā).
The beautiful binding of the altar (vedībandha) should be made with one and a half parts;
then, the height of the plinth (jaṅghā) should be made with two and a half parts.
One should fashion a pleasing diamond of half a part, provided with a chisel;
and one should have it made upon the inner leaf of the girdle with a single part.
Then the height of the pinnacle (śṛṅga) should be made measuring two and a half parts;
one should draw a circle at the top of the middle of all the pinnacles.
Its width should be six parts and its height six parts;
the *mañjarī* should be made to the same proportion as that which was prescribed for the [main] body.
One should have this temple constructed with three or five stories, adorned with various ornaments;
its neck (grīvā) should be one-quarter of a bhāga in width and twice that in length.
One should make the *pada* deficient by one quarter; from this, the *daṇḍaka* arises according to the human tradition.
By means of a quarter of the *candrikā* portion, the skillful one forms the *pādona* [meter].
He who even mentally performs such a mental recitation (manukīrtana) of the temple shall attain the abode of Śambhu and the status of a leader of the Gaṇas.
Overwhelmed by pride.
Now we shall describe the palace named Suprabha,
which, by its radiance, eclipses the splendor of others, just as the sun does.
When the site has been made square and divided into twelve parts,
one should construct the womb-chamber (garbha) occupying four squares, its width being equal to its length.
The bulbous base (kanda) should be half the height of the temple (prāsāda), and the auspicious neck-base (kandabhadraka) should be two padas;
the circular path (bhramantī) extending in all four directions should also be beautiful and two padas wide.
The outer wall is one pada; the width of the corner is two padas;
the central *bhadra* is four padas, projecting outward by three padas.
With its shafts, it should again be made into a four-cornered structure with two feet;
the wise man should construct two Atibhadras on the sides of the Solā.
With one foot, one should push out the filling from both sides;
one should lead the *pādika* between the *pārśvabhadra* and the *karṇa*.
One should decorate it with lattices so that light appears in the center;
in this manner, one should perform this in all directions in due order.
One should construct a pavilion in front according to the rules for the portion of the temple;
in all four directions, flower-clusters (mañjarīs) should be placed in their proper order.
The height of the base, the shanks, and the neck should be as previously described;
the height [of the plinth] should be twice the width of the base plus two kalās.
The *tulodaya* (the rising of the base) consists of ten parts; the *mañjarī* (the cluster) consists of sixteen parts.
The height of the *vedībandha* (the altar-base moulding) is measured at two and a half parts.
The lower leg (jaṅghā) should be five parts in height; the fillet (hīra) should be one part in elevation;
and the intermediate band (mekhalāntarapatraka) should be made with one and a half parts.
The height of the ear-ornament (karṇaśṛṅga) should be one-third of the interior of the pitcher (kalaśa);
furthermore, the Diṅmañjarī should be made four units (catuṣpada) in width.
The five parts [of the base] are to be determined by the *udaya* according to their proportions; the neck is one-quarter of a *pada*, and the *kalaśa* (dome) shall be half a *pada*.
The width of the root-foliage (mūlamañjarī) should be made ten parts;
the neck (grīvā) should have a height of three parts, and its base one part.
The *aṇḍaka* (egg-shaped pinnacle) is one and a half parts; the height of the *kalaśa* (dome) is two parts.
From the base to the top of the *skandha*, this [measurement] constitutes six-tenths. This is the final [dimension].
The width of the root-fillet (mūlamañjarī) should be made one-tenth [of the total];
this temple, possessing auspicious characteristics, should be constructed with nine sections (navāṇḍaka).
The devoted person who constructs this radiant temple shall sport in heaven and,
at the end of the body, attain liberation.
Possessing auspicious marks.
Now we shall describe the exceedingly beautiful Surānanda temple:
one should divide the square site into ten equal parts.
The width of the inner sanctum should be six parts, the extent of the wall two parts,
the water-trough (jalāśraya) should be made with one and a half parts, and [the door] with half a part.
One should construct the Pratyaṅgasthānaka with a circular portion including the surrounding area;
the halls, auspicious in form, should be made with three paces on all four sides.
On both sides of the hall, a water-channel one half-pada wide should be constructed;
moreover, a mutual recess of one part each is prescribed.
The height should be determined by the wise as being twice the width;
the womb-covering (garbhacchādya) consists of eight squares, and the cluster (mañjarī) consists of twelve parts.
The construction of the altar-base (vedībandha) is prescribed as one-quarter of the width of the site;
above that, the shaft (jaṅghā) consists of four parts, and the cornice-band (grāsapaṭṭikā) is half a part.
The intermediate petals of the girdle should be fashioned with a height of one *pada*;
the corners of the *draviḍakūṭa* consist of circular pillars and *varāṭaka* beads.
There should be twenty-four [parts] for the middle arches;
the width of the shoulder is six parts, and the neck is one part.
The head (śiras) should be known as one and a half parts, and the moon-ornament (candrīkā) as one part;
the pinnacle (kalaśa), adorned with foliage, should be made with a height of two parts.
The Mothers grant boons to him who brings joy to the gods;
indeed, they carry away his wine and his unavoidable untimely death.
Surānanda.
Now I shall describe Harṣa, which brings joy to all the worlds;
where Śrī dwells eternally, and which is the abode of Viśvakarman.
When the field has been made square and divided into eighteen squares,
the corner-portions (karṇabhāga) should be established in each corner by means of three [squares] each.
One should construct a two-footed *karṇabhadra* protruding by one part,
making it a water-channel and entering it evenly from the watchtower.
One-third of this [measurement] should be the projection for each individual limb;
one should arrange the work on each limb by means of the altar (vedi) and the moon-like window (candrāvaloka).
A wise man should construct the middle portion with four squares and its auspicious (bhadra) front portion with two squares, each extending outward by one square.
The *valabhīs* (pediments) should occupy two parts on all four sides, corresponding to the width of the opening;
the central core (*garbha*) is prescribed to be made with four parts for the *valabhīs*.
The outer wall shall be two pādas thick, and the circumambulatory path (bhramantikā) likewise two pādas;
the shoulder (skandha) shall consist of ten parts, and the inner sanctum (garbha) of thirty-six pādas.
Its height should be forty paces,
and one should provide it with a beautiful covering consisting of sixteen parts.
The altar-base (vedībandha) shall consist of five parts, and the shaft (jaṅghā) shall be eight parts;
the wise man should construct the hall (śālā) and the inner leaf (antarapatra) from three parts each.
Above, an inner leaf (panel) should be constructed in due order;
the covering of the *valabhī* (pinnacle) by the wise should be one-fifth of the height.
The elevation of the section should be made with *śṛṅga* and *siṃhakarṇa* ornaments;
the *karṇamañjarī* should be constructed with three units according to the *vardhamāna* proportion.
Above the three squares, there should be the pitcher and the egg by one part;
the root-cluster (mūlamañjarī) should be made sixteen squares in width.
Its upper portion consists of twenty parts, and the shoulder is nine units in length;
the neck should be made one and a half units, and from that, the *maṇḍaka* (the head) is two units.
Where the *harṣaṇa* [pitch] is produced from one part of the *candra* and three parts of the *kalaśa*, that region prospers with happiness.
There shall be security for cows and Brahmins, and the king shall have his desires fulfilled;
he is a source of joy.
Now we shall describe the Durdhara palace, which possesses auspicious characteristics.
In a square field divided into twenty-four parts,
the *karṇas* (diagonals) should be made six squares each, and the *pratiratha* should be two.
A hall of eight squares should be constructed, with its exit consisting of four squares;
it extends two squares outward on all sides and is adorned with ears.
The outer wall should be two padas, the dark space (andhakārikā) four parts,
the wall of the base (kandabhitti) two padas, and the inner sanctum (garbha) eight padas in length.
The root-hall (kandaśālā) is six paces [in length], and the root-ears (kandakarṇa) are three paces;
the height is twice the width, plus two paces.
The height of the *tulā* is twenty units, the *śikhara* is thirty *pada*s;
the *kumbha* is two and a half *bhāga*s, and the height of the *kalaśa* is one *bhāga*.
The interval between the petals shall be half a part, and the fillet (mekhalā) one part;
the pedestal (jaṅghā) shall be ten parts in height, and the diamond-pattern (hīraka) shall be one part.
Then, two girdles should be made using four parts each:
one below the upper fillet and one above the lower fillet.
The interval between these two [the base and the neck] should consist of sixteen parts;
the binding of the altar (vedikābandha) is two parts, and the body of the altar (vedīkāyā) is four parts.
The pedestal (āsana) should be one part, the pillar (stambha) five parts,
the base (bharaṇa) one part, and the capital (śīrṣaka) one part in height.
The fillet (paṭṭa) has a height of two parts, and the covering (chādya) is three parts in length;
there are four root-fillet ornaments (mūlabharaṇa), and the corner-bhadras constitute the neck-ornament (ṇika).
There are ten ears and two horns on this [altar], four in each direction;
the neck consists of the *bhaga* and the *saṃtāna*, and the height of the horns is three steps.
The ear-ornaments consist of six parts; they are raised by seven parts. The neck is half a part, and the height of the egg-shaped finial (aṇḍaka) shall be one part.
The Siṃhakarṇa should be made three units high and four units wide;
its height in the middle of the Bhadra should be half a unit less than its width.
The width of the root-bud (mūlamañjarī) shall be sixteen padas;
its height shall be eighteen padas, and the neck shall be one and a half padas in height.
The *aṇḍaka* should be made with two parts, and the *candrīkā* with one part raised;
one should know that the *kalaśa* consists of three parts and is endowed with all auspicious characteristics.
A temple built with seventeen eggs shall be difficult to sustain;
he who constructs such a difficult-to-sustain structure here on earth shall attain power through his share.
In due time, union with Śiva is proclaimed for the one who is difficult to restrain.
Now we shall describe the Durjaya temple, which crushes its enemies.
Having performed which, one becomes invincible in the world and sports upon the earth;
[this is done] when the field has been made square and divided into five parts.
One should construct the womb (garbha) with nine squares; the wall should consist of sixteen parts.
The corner-rathika (bhadraka) is one part, and the central chariot (ratha) is two parts.
This is the rule for its exit in the four directions:
one should make a water-channel between the two auspicious ears (bhadra-kaṇas), measuring one and a quarter padas.
The height above [the plinth] should be established as ten parts;
the base of the altar (vedibandha) is one and a quarter parts, while the shank and the shoulder are each joined with a quarter part.
On the inner leaf of the girdle, one should fashion [the ornament] with half a pada;
the pinnacle (śikhara) shall be six and a half parts in height.
The width of the shoulder [of the altar] should be three pādas; the lines should be shaped like lotus petals;
and five layers should be made, each successively smaller in measurement.
The first [section] consists of one and a half parts; the next is reduced by one-quarter part in sequence.
The shoulder (skandha) should be three-quarters of a part, and the neck (grīvā) half a part.
The egg-shaped dome (aṇḍaka) should be one part, and the bowl-shaped capital (karpara) half a part;
the pitcher (kalaśa), perfectly round and very beautiful, should have a height of one part.
In whatever city or town Durjaya is installed,
there shall be neither famine nor fear caused by disease.
Difficult to conquer.
We speak of Trikūṭa, which is resorted to by the thirty-three gods beginning with Brahmā;
by it one obtains the fruit of a thousand sacrifices and attains liberation.
One should construct a square field equal in area to that which is to be established, according to the desired measurement;
then, one should divide each of its sides into four parts.
The wise one should make the middle auspicious part two parts, the corner-wing (karṇapakṣikā) one part, the inner sanctum (garbha) half [of that], and the three walls half [of the sanctum].
Having divided the width into five parts, one should make the height double that;
the construction of the altar-base (vedibandha) should be made with a height of one and a quarter parts.
Its height should be made two parts, including the shanks and the feet;
one should fashion the lower leaf of the girdle with half a part.
The stalk of the pillar should be fashioned according to the previously mentioned method, divided into five parts up to the end of the *mañjarī*, which itself consists of six parts.
The neck is one-quarter of a part, and the dome (aṇḍaka) is half a part;
the moon-motif (candrīkā) is one-quarter of a part, and the pinnacle (kalaśa) is one part in height.
He who causes a three-peaked temple to be built, which is dear to Brahmā, Īśāna, and Hari, becomes a perfected being (siddha) and goes to their city; of this there is no doubt.
Trikūṭa.
Now we shall describe the nine-peaked temple (Prāsāda). One should divide the square field into nineteen parts by its side-lengths.
The ears should be made four parts; of these, the *bhadra* is two parts.
It projects by half a part, and the water-channel is... [as follows].
That [hall] should be made by the wise to extend for nine parts;
the hall should measure one part from the corner-line toward each individual limb.
The chariot should be made with three parts, and there should be four clusters of blossoms;
the wall should consist of four parts, and the inner sanctum (garbha) should be eleven parts.
From forty padas upwards up to the shoulder and the entire top,
the emergence of the *tula* is by sixteen [padas], and the *mañjarī* is by three times eight.
The base of the altar (vedibandha) shall be four parts, and the shank (jaṅghā) shall be eight parts;
by one part there is the supporting member (bharaṇa), and by three parts the girdle (mekhalā) and the intermediate leaf (antarapatraka).
The Karṇamañjarī should be made five units in height;
the neck portion should consist of one unit, and the staff (daṇḍaka) likewise should be one unit.
The crescent moon above is one part, and likewise the pinnacle (kalaśa) is one part;
they know the hall (śālā) to be one and a quarter parts in width, along with the cluster of blossoms (mañjarī).
The neck is one-quarter part, with a half-aṇḍaka (half-egg) of one-quarter;
from one part comes the candrikā, and the emergence of the kalaśa (dome) is by two parts.
The width of the root-cluster (mūlamañjarī) should be made as fifteen parts;
likewise, its height is seventeen parts, and the extent of the trunk (skandha) is nine parts.
The neck occupies one-half part, and the maṇḍaka is two and a half parts;
the vaṇḍikā is one and a half parts, and the emergence of the kalaśa is three parts.
Thus, he who causes this temple with its nine peaks to be built enjoys the earth together with its nine divisions.
The Nine-Peaked [Mountain].
Now we shall speak of the Puṇḍarīka, the supreme increaser of glory;
when this is performed, one's fame becomes firm for as long as the earth endures.
One should divide a level, square plot of ground into five parts;
one should designate three parts for the inner sanctum (garbha) and one part for its wall (bhitti).
Its third part should be auspicious, extending outwards from the portion of the sādhana;
in that auspicious part, there should be a circle in the cardinal directions with four chariot-paths.
With one part [of the width] it is a chariot-shaped structure; this is declared to be the *mūlacchanda*.
Its height should be twice [the width], consisting of ten parts.
One should know that the *ucchālaka* (the upper molding) is one part, while the *mekhalā* (the girdle) is half a part;
one should not construct a *vedibandha* (pedestal), and the *jaṅghā* (shaft) shall consist of two and a half parts.
The girdle (mekhalā) should be made with half that portion and consist of intervening leaf-patterns;
the height of the cluster of blossoms (mañjarī) should be five and a half units.
The width of the shoulder should be three parts; the neck should be one part and so forth;
the dome (aṇḍaka) should be half a part, and the moon-ornament (candrīkā) one-quarter of a part.
The pitcher (kalaśa) should be made with its height equal to one part and endowed with auspicious characteristics;
in the middle, by means of the root-cluster (mūlamañjarī), there is the three-part auspicious cluster (bhadramañjarī).
The neck is three and a half units in height and one unit in projection;
the dome (aṇḍaka) is three parts, and the pinnacle (kalaśa) is one part in height.
This Puṇḍarīka, which increases auspiciousness, should be made with five eggs.
[Puṇḍarīka]
Now we shall speak of Sunābha, who is saluted by gods and dānavas.
One should divide a square field of four sides, which is beloved by the world-protectors, praiseworthy, and endowed with excellent characteristics, into seventeen parts.
The corners should extend for five parts, and the inner sanctum (garbha) should be made with three squares;
between both corners, there should be an interval of seven parts.
From the distraction [of the center], one should mark the interval between the two ears;
the entry of the portion should be half a portion, and the width at the water's edge should be half a portion.
The outer wall should be two padas wide, and the ambulatory (bhramantikā) three padas;
in the center, extending over five parts, should be the principal temple (prāsādanāyaka).
Its central bay (garbha) shall be three padas, and the wall (bhitti) is prescribed as one part (bhāga).
The corner-bhadra (karṇabhadra) shall be three padas and project out by one part.
One should establish four corners measuring one foot;
the corner is prescribed to be divided into the same proportions as the bulbous root (kanda).
Five embryos (garbhas) should be fashioned, arranged with equal and identical proportions;
their height, excluding the neck and the egg-base (aṇḍaka), should be double [the width].
The junction of the Vedas (the *bandha*) consists of three quarters, and the shank (*jaṅghā*) should consist of seven quarters;
the two girdles (*mekhalā*) should be made by the wise with three quarters each.
Above the outer *chanda*, a *karṇamañjarī* should be made;
there are six *ṣaṭpada* *karṇamañjarīs*, and a two-footed *kalaśāṇḍaka*.
The root-cluster (mūlamañjarī) should be made twelve units long and seven units wide;
its neck (grīvā) should be thirteen units in height and one unit in elevation.
The *aṇḍaka* is two parts in height; the *candrikā* is one part in height;
and the *kalaśa*, circular and possessing auspicious characteristics, is three parts in height.
As long as the earth, as long as the ocean, as long as the moon and the sun endure,
so long shall these divine beings remain, as long as the preceptor of the gods and the gods themselves exist.
Having beautiful navels.
We shall now describe the Māhendra temple, an ornament of the earth,
frequented by yakṣas, gandharvas, and the highly resplendent lords of serpents.
A wise man should divide the Māhendra [temple] into fifteen parts;
he should make the inner sanctum nine parts in length and the wall three parts thick.
The width of this hall is renowned among experts as three padas;
on both sides of the hall, wise men should construct two chariot-pavilions (rathas) measuring one and a half padas each.
An inner space for water should be made within the chariot-shed;
the width of the chariot's front is five aratnis, and the width of the house-work is half a pada.
The individual parts, including the side and the half-side, should be equal to the interval between the waters; and a measurement of two sides should be made at each of the four corners.
The exit for these [channels] should be arranged for one another by means of their respective portions;
however, the vertical measurement should be made double the extent of the boundary.
The *tulodaya* should be one-tenth [of the height], and the *mañjarī* twenty parts;
the wise man should fashion the *vedibandha* with two and a half parts.
The height of the two shanks should be four and a half parts;
one part should be used for the *bharaṇa* (torus), which should be adorned with leaf-patterns.
Above that, a girdle (mekhalā) should be made, two parts in height;
above that, a beautiful cluster (mañjarī) should be fashioned in due order.
The base is nine parts in length, the neck is one part in height,
the dome (aṇḍaka) is two parts in elevation, and the candrikā is one part in height.
One should fashion a two-footed pitcher such that its width and height are equal;
seven lines should be drawn there, and we shall describe their family-like forms.
In the middle of the creeper, there is the ear, the fillet, and the sixfold sequence;
on each minor limb, there are the tilakas, the kūṭas, the pañcālas, the ardhās, and the dvipakṣakas.
In the corners of the Mahendra temple, counterfeit cowries should be placed;
by making such a Mahendra, one becomes a king and shall dwell in the world of Indra.
Mahendra.
Now we shall describe the temple known as Varāṭa, which possesses auspicious characteristics,
is beloved by the lords of the Kinnaras, and is exceedingly dear to the Nāgas.
One should divide an even, square field into ten parts;
one should make the inner sanctum with six parts and the wall with two parts.
One should make the width of the two ears equal to the width of the four corners;
the width of the water-enclosure (udakāntara) should enter by half a part.
The space between the two water-paths should be five parts long, O Bhadra;
the projection of that Bhadra should be made equal to half its width.
One should fashion an excellent circle in the center using eight and a quarter parts;
when combined with the path of the water-line, this is declared to be the *talacchanda* (floor-plan).
Its height above [the base] should be double its width;
the height of the *tūla* (pedestal) is eight parts, and there are twelve steps above it.
O auspicious one, the pedestal (pīṭhaka) should be made with a height of three padas;
one should cause the height of the altar-base (vedibandha) to be half of that [height] divided by two.
One should make the shank four parts high, the diamond (hīraka) half a part,
and the inner leaf of the girdle one part high.
The pinnacle (śṛṅga) should be three units in height, as should the neck (grīvā) and the pitcher-egg (kalaśāṇḍaka);
above that, the auspicious urormañjarī should be six units in height and five units in width.
The neck should be made with half a part, and the dome (aṇḍaka) with one part;
the base-bud (mūlamañjarī) is eight parts in width and raised by one part for the pitcher (kalaśa).
Its height should be made nine parts of the measurement;
the shoulder should be five parts, and the neck should be one part less than a quarter-part.

In the Varāṭaka type of temple, the *candrikā* should be one and a quarter times the measure of a foot (*padam*), and the *kalaśa* (dome) should be half a foot in height; thus, the total height of the *prāsāda* should be two and a half feet.
The devoted man who causes a temple to be built with cowries goes by various celestial vehicles and attains imperishable heaven.
A cowrie shell.
Now, the characteristic of the Sumukha [mandala] is described as it has fully arrived;
when a square is divided into nineteen parts, [the following occurs].
In that [mandala], the central womb-chamber (garbha) consists of eleven parts, the walls consist of four parts each,
the corner is two parts, and the water-interval (jalāntara) there is one-quarter of a part.
Its entrance is half a part, and its width is four parts;
thus the *bhadra* is prescribed as extending out by half a part.
Between the two Karṇabhadras, at a distance of one and three-quarter parts,
three Pratirathas should be made, joined together by water-channels.
Their mutual emergence consists of half a share and another half a share;
its height above [the base] shall be double, increased by two kalās.
Its rising point of Libra (tulodaya) should be established by five parts;
above that, there should be a cluster (mañjarī) consisting of twenty-five divisions.
The construction of its altar-base (vedībandha) should be made from four and a half parts;
the shaft (jaṅghā) with eight and a half parts, while the cornice (varaṇḍī) is two parts.
The cluster (mañjarī) of this [tree] should be fashioned as before, joined with nine creepers;
the width of its trunk is to be one-eleventh part of that.
One should draw the bamboo-receptacle with a cord of fourfold length;
its *pratiratha* and *drā* are prescribed to be situated near the corners.
Nine tiers (bhūmikās) are to be constructed; the remaining work is to be done as in the case of Mahendra.
Its neck (grīvā) is prescribed to be one and three-quarter parts.
