One should fashion the auspicious shaft (daṇḍaka) measuring two and a half parts;
Caṇḍikā is one and a half parts, and the pitcher (kalaśa) consists of three parts.
Thus has this temple named Sumukha been correctly described;
he who causes it to be built with devotion attains all his desires.
Having enjoyed abundant pleasures here, one attains the eternal state.
The Sumukha Palace.
We shall now describe those four-faced [forms] of Śrīdhara and the others that have been mentioned.
Now, because the gods cannot turn back,
that form of Vijayabhadra which exists through its perfect characteristics has thus become established.
A temple named Vijaya, dear to the deities, should be constructed;
furthermore, there are the Karṇa, Kesari, and Sarvatobhadra types.
It should be placed upon chariots endowed with all auspicious marks;
above it, a beautiful floral cluster (mañjarī) should be fashioned.
One should make its width one unit greater than its height;
the shoulder should be made six units wide, and the neck should be one unit in height.
The egg-shaped [mandala] is one and a half parts, and the moon is also equal to that;
in the very center of that, one should fashion the *āmalasāraka*.
Above that, one should fashion a pitcher (kalaśa) with a height of two and a half parts,
and its cluster (mañjarī) should be made of ivory and cowries.
Nor have they taken refuge [in her] in birth after birth—
Nanda.
Now, another palace called Mahāghoṣa is described.
Established in the form and configuration of Nandighoṣa,
one should bestow auspicious qualities upon all its makers.
O auspicious lady, a four-pillared pavilion should be constructed with a width of two parts and no projection;
the inner wall shall consist of one part, and the remainder is known as the sanctum.
One should place the spires upon the ears; this is the first stage.
The second stage, however, should be performed without the arrangement of walls.
One should arrange the moon-shaped altar (vedīcandrāvaloka) facing the four directions;
one should also construct a third floor supported by four pillars.
The wise should construct a covering for it with awnings above;
let him who builds this most excellent palace cause the sound of joy to resound.
The prosperity desired by him does not perish even within his lineage;
this is the Great Proclamation.
The palace is indeed in the Miśraka [courtyard], where the increase and coloring are prescribed.
The configuration of the female organ is said to be the same as this [male organ],
except for the exclusion of the "embryo-tuber" (garbhakanda) and its enclosure by sixteen pillars.
Its middle portion is to be fashioned like that of Śrīnivāsa, and the remainder likewise;
it should be adorned with eight chest-bells and horse-stalls.
One should fashion for him auspicious ornaments endowed with every kind of decoration;
he is beautiful, being provided with all those varieties that belong to the earth.
Rāma is praised as the builder of this temple for as long as the moon, sun, and stars shall endure, provided there is an increase of twenty-one kalaśas.
Meanwhile, Vṛddhirauma sports like Indra in heaven with hosts of apsarases.
In the location of Āma, there would be a temple for Vṛddhi, known as Vasundhara.
Setting aside the outer walls, the inner wall (garbhabhitti) is constructed;
it takes the form of a pedestal (vedikā), is adorned with auspicious arches (toraṇa), and possesses the nature of time and other attributes.
The Prāsāda temple, endowed with these various divisions, shall be known as Vasundhara;
he who causes this to be built with devotion undoubtedly dwells [in that realm].
Even the abode of Mahādeva, which is difficult even for the gods to attain,
was reached by Vasundhara.
Now we shall describe the temple named Mudga.
When the site has been made square and divided into six parts,
one should construct a wall one part thick and its central core (garbha) as circular.
The *bhadra* consists of four feet and two feet in its projection;
the *svastika* and those of equal form are known as the four *rathika* types.
All the ears should be fashioned, surrounded by six facets;
the shank, the altar, and the pedestal there are like the forms of fame.
One should construct the corner-ridges (karṇakūṭa) with a width of one part and a height of two parts, adorned with leaf-patterns and sea-monsters.
The Bhadra [temple] should have a width of four padas and a height of five parts;
one should construct the neck, the dome, and the kalaśa with two and a half padas.
One should draw the base of the central cluster with a width of six units;
its height, including the neck and the pinnacle, should consist of ten parts.
One should compose this *Mañjarī* for the sake of my fame, just as it has been composed;
whoever, out of devotion, should cause this temple to be built—
The Kinnarīs sing of his stainless fame in heaven;
[this is] the Mudgaprāsāda.
Now, this great hall, the abode of the gods.
One should establish this [mandala] as it stands within the lotus-born configuration,
using the diagonal line for the cardinal lines, just as in the case of a chariot.
At the edge of the ear and in its middle, one should provide an interval of water;
it should be as wide as one-quarter of a pada, with a projection of half a pada.
The six parts, beginning with the *karṇa*, should be shaped according to the six types of amṛtaliṅgas:
the pedestal (*pīṭha*), the altar (*vedī*), the shaft (*jaṅghā*), the girdle (*mekhalā*), the inner leaf (*antarapatraka*), and [the rest].
The work should be performed in many ways, as in the case of the Lotus-born;
one should fashion the pinnacle that is to be made.
Just as it was described in the Puṣpaka that the earth was strewn with great crocodiles, sea-monsters, and demons who had swallowed elephants, so shall it be seen here.
One should construct the insertion of the six wooden beams at the center of the measurement of the upper pedestal as well as that of the covering.
It was adorned with beautiful *sālabhañjā* statues at the archways of the *ruṣṭika* gate,
enriched by royal armies on the platforms, and its pavilions were visible from afar.
The *mlalla* roof-covering, adorned with lion-ears (*siṃhakarṇa*), should be constructed with a pillar-like capital (*sastambhaśīrṣa*) and decorated with cloth-patterned bands (*paṭṭaraṅga*).
One should construct the pinnacle of the ear (karṇakūṭa), which is three parts in height and two parts in width, adorned with various excellent lion-figures and other diverse ornaments.
Along with the neck and the dome (aṇḍaka), and provided with a pitcher (kalaśa) on the cornice (varaṇḍī),
there should be fifty-six separate pillars here.
They should be adorned with three *uromañjarikā* ornaments;
at the edge of the ear, the line of the base should be one-seventh of the width.
Its height should be made eight and a half parts;
likewise, four *uro-mañjarikās* should be fashioned in each intermediate direction.
The first line of the chest should be adorned with twelve egg-shaped ornaments (aṇḍakas),
the next with fourteen, and the third with sixteen parts.
The fourth [line] is proclaimed as being endowed with eighteen squares;
the root-line (mūlarekhā) is prescribed as being joined with thirty-six squares.
The neck should be three-quarters of a *pada*, and the *maṇḍaka* (pedestal) should be one and a quarter *padas*.
That *candrīkā* (the fillet) is equal in height to a *lavalī* fruit, and it is raised by one *pada*.
One should know that the *dvipada* consists of a beautiful, symmetrical pitcher (*kalaśa*); its upper half should be fashioned as a lotus bud.
On a floor of various colors, seventeen pillars were drawn,
fashioned with diverse arrangements and many structural variations.
Adorned with various wondrous works and auspicious marks everywhere,
they were equipped with moon-chambers and the like, as well as with archways and beautiful fly-whisks.
Likewise, with unbroken mouthfuls remaining in the form of dense masses,
there were serpents with flickering tongues and crocodiles joined with their own prey.
Adorned by the faces of elephants swarming with swarms of bees blinded by rut,
and graced by throngs of Vidyādhara women arrayed for the commencement of their play.
It was surrounded by the beautiful women of the gods, by Kinnaras with lutes in their hands,
and by throngs of Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Yakṣas standing on all sides.
I shall emerge with divine apsarases, with rows of celestial chariots,
and with those intent on playing in beautiful swings made of refined gold.
It was adorned on all sides by clusters of nāga maidens,
with such grounds extending everywhere without interruption.
The Meru, the leader of the palaces, should be adorned and constructed;
the largest Meru should be made with twice as many small towers (aṇḍakas) as the medium-sized one.
The placement of the eggs is said to be such that the smallest is placed with half of the middle one;
one should place the largest among the large ones and the middle among the middle ones.
In the lower realms, the linga is of the lowest kind; likewise in other abodes.
But for Meru, even though it is threefold, the linga is supreme and bestows prosperity.
That king who causes a divine Mount Meru, equal to Meru itself, to be constructed, [commits] an offense committed by one who acts otherwise than prescribed.
He attains supreme liberation, that of Sadāśiva—
just as one who circumambulates the golden Meru partakes in the abundance of its fruits.
One who constructs this [shrine] out of stone, brick, or wood partakes in the abundance of its fruit; [it is like] Mount Meru.
Now, the characteristics of the Mandara palace are described.
In the field made quadrangular and divided into sections, which bestows accomplishment and is praised for its merit even by the gods; |||
The inner sanctum (garbha) should be made of four parts; the wall should have an extent of one part;
the blind wall (andhārikā) should be one part, and the outer wall should likewise be one part.
In the corners, chariot-paths (rathikās) measuring two squares should be made;
four pavilions (maṇḍapas) measuring thirty-six squares should be constructed.
Porches with four pillars should be constructed on all four sides;
they should extend outwards by one part and possess auspicious characteristics in every respect.
The wise should make its height twice its width;
the piercing of the ears is everywhere understood to be the limit of the width.
One should properly determine the original measurement for the palace;
the pedestal should be made with a height of two units, extending outward from the front of the sage’s [measurement].
The temple should be adorned with lotuses and lions;
the *khuraka* (pedestal) should be made half the height of the foot [of the column], excluding the *prāsāda* (the upper portion).
The very beautiful altar-binding (vedībandha) should be made with two and a half parts;
the pillar-shaft (jaṅghā) is four parts in height, and the decorative band (rūpapaṭṭikā) is half a part.
The inner leaf of the girdle should be made one square unit high;
the prongs at the ear should be two squares long according to the measurement.
Their height is three parts; together with the neck, the egg-shaped dome (aṇḍa), and the pinnacle (kalaśa), a base-line (mūlarekhā) must be established above the corner-ridge (karṇakūṭa).
It is praised when it is nine parts in height and eight parts in width;
having divided the width into ten parts, the width of the shoulder (skandha) is made with six of those parts.
The five creepers should be fashioned as they have been described for the Śrīvatsa;
one may construct it with five stories or even seven stories.
The neck (grīvā) should be three-quarters of a part, together with a one-pada maṇḍaka;
the candrikā should be made as one pada, and the kalaśa should have a rise of two padas.
One should make it three-fold in height and three-fold in width, leaving out one part there;
one should fashion the śukanāsa (the frontal projection) extending from it, adorned with the position of a lion.
Just as a man adorned with golden ornaments shines resplendent,
so too does this king of palaces gleam with its variegated paintings.
Having divided the *mañjarī* into ten parts, one should fashion the decorative beauty of the work;
the width of the *bhadra* shall be six parts, and its projection shall be one part.
One should place two share-measuring chariot-parts there, with their emergence from the shares;
one should also set down ears measuring two shares in the intermediate directions.
Four halls should be constructed, joined with beautiful gables;
those eight [halls] should have water-filled intervals and be provided with double the number of flower-clusters.
On the peak, at its midpoint, the first floor should be made with a height of two parts;
the subsequent floors above should be reduced successively by one-quarter of a part.
The neck should be raised by half a part, and the maṇḍaka (the base) should have a height of one part;
the kalaśa (the pinnacle) should be made with one part, endowed with all auspicious characteristics.
The construction of the altar (vedībandha) should be made with half the width [of the mandala] and should be level;
one should draw the central line using a cord six times [the length of the altar].
The wise one should draw the second [line] with a cord five times [the length],
and with a cord three and a half times [the length], he should draw the line.
Adorned everywhere with various clusters of blossoms,
the auspicious Mandara palace should be constructed according to these proportions.
Having constructed an excellent palace shaped like Mount Mandara,
one attains supreme happiness in this world and an auspicious state in the hereafter.
Mandara.
Now let us describe Kailāsa, which is frequented by all the gods,
inhabited by the foremost of the Pramathas, and is a palace that increases merit.
When the square-shaped site has been divided into one hundred parts,
the hall should be made with a width of six parts and a projection of one part.
One should make them three parts of a *kalā*, joined with the interior of water;
starting from the station of Brahmā, they are equal for two quarters.
Having rotated it to form a circle, one should fashion the inner core (garbha) and its constituent parts;
likewise, the wall (bhitti) should be constructed all around with a thickness of half a part.
The outer wall should be divided into sections and adorned with auspicious motifs;
however, one should provide darkness everywhere within the interior spaces.
Wise men should construct porches (alindakas) occupying one-fourth of the area on three sides;
they should project out by two parts from all sides and possess auspicious characteristics.
A fourth enclosure should be constructed, provided with two pillars;
at its entrance, however, a pavilion adorned with rows of pillars should be made.
Now we shall describe the measurement of Kailāsa as it exists:
its pedestal (pīṭha) should be made with two parts (padas), adorned by the Gaṇas.
The *khuraka* should be made with half the measure of the *pada*;
above that, the height of the temple (*prāsāda*) is known to be double [the height of the *khuraka*].
The *kumbhaka* (retention) should be performed with one part, excluding the equal portion;
however, the *masūraka* is prescribed with three-quarters of a part.
The work on the floor should be done with a quarter-unit (pāda), and then the intermediate panel (antarapatraka) with half a unit (ardhapada);
it should be adorned with a moon-chamber (candraśālā) using half a unit for the girdle (mekhalā).
The shank above that should be made with four and a half padas;
one should fashion the inner leaf of the girdle with one pada.
One should construct the ear-ornament (karṇaśṛṅga) with three parts, including the entire dome (śāṇḍaka);
above that, the pinnacles (kūṭas) should be two units in height.
There should be an insertion of these aforementioned [syllables] by means of word-parts;
having divided the expansion of the *kūṭa* into four parts, [one places them] in two word-units.
One should cause the lion-strides (siṃhakrānta) to be made with three parts;
one should make the width of the root-cluster (mūlamañjarī) equal to six parts.
One should determine its height on Kailāsa as seven parts;
the height of the maṇḍaka should be half a part, making it one part.
One should make Caṇḍikā with half a part and the kalaśa with one and a half parts;
and its śikhara should be made according to what has been prescribed for the svastika.
It is appropriate that it be adorned with the eight stages as its flower-clusters,
and one should further embellish its auspicious parts with various lion-ears.
The expansion of the *skandha* should be performed; therein, one should establish four squares using a drawing-line that is three times [the length of] the [original] cord.
Thus— whosoever constructs a Kailāsa,
he shall obtain here prosperity endowed with happiness and good fortune.
Having attained various desires, as well as fame and health,
and having enjoyed pleasures on Kailāsa for as long as desired until the end of the kalpa;
One attains the state of Śarva— peaceful, eternal, and free from disease—
at Kailāsa.
Now we shall describe Triviṣṭapa, the palace beloved by the immortals.
It is frequented by yakṣas, gandharvas, siddhas, vidyādharas, and others;
it is a field made square and divided into twenty parts.
The hall (śālā) should be six parts in width and four parts in projection;
there shall be one hundred and seventy-two chambers (koṣṭhaka), consisting of four parts.
Thus it arises together with the auspicious ones situated in the three directions;
one should construct eight inner sanctuaries (garbhagṛha) in these very directions.
In the corner, there are sixteen parts; in the middle of that, four square parts;
and the wall consists of twelve parts—this is the determination for the inner sanctums (garbhas).
The central lord of the temple should be made with sixty-four squares;
one should fashion the inner sanctum (garbha) for it in the center using sixteen squares.
Outside of that, a wall twice as wide [as the door] should be constructed;
it should revolve twenty-four times and extend five paces in length.
One should likewise construct gables on all four sections divided into two parts; each subsidiary member, including the corner halls and the spaces between the gables, shall measure two padas.
And that [mandala] is indicated as having two feet on the water-path, with half a foot [in between];
one should construct pavilions in all four directions using twelve feet.
One should construct for the palace [entrances] adorned with the splendor of artistic work;
one should provide four doors for the interior of the main palace.
In the *Digbhadrā* [mandala], one should likewise fashion the internal water-channels within the cognizable area according to the path of the lines, even on the minor limbs and the two sides.
One should construct the outer wall measuring one part;
having divided [the area] in this manner, one should construct the front mandapa.
The height above the plinth is thirty [units], and there the pedestal is four units high;
the middle part of the temple's shaft is likewise raised to that same height.
Therefore, the height of the spire (śikhara) should be twice the width in terms of padas;
and in its center, one should construct the base of the dome (tulodaya) as sixteen parts.
In the middle of the tulodaya, one should fashion two altars (vedībandha) together with the pañcakā;
the shaft (jaṅghā) should consist of eight parts, and in its center, a seat-slab (āsanapaṭṭikā).
An inner leaf should also be made for these, raised three finger-breadths high;
now the measurement for the top of the base of the balance is stated.
In four-footed animals, the ears are one unit; the protuberance (kūṭa) is five units in height;
the neck is three-quarters of a unit; and likewise, the scrotum is three-quarters of a unit.
One should fashion the height of the moon-stone (candrikā) and the pitcher (kalaśa) with one-sixth [of the total];
on each minor limb (pratyaṅga), there are three parts for the decorative marks (tilaka), joined with bells and pitchers.
In the center, however, there should be a lofty gable-peak (*valabhīśṛṅga*) measuring seven paces;
above the *tilakas*, there should be a *mañjarikā* of ten [paces].
In its width, the upper portion should consist of twelve parts;
the width of the shoulder-band and so forth, as well as the neck, should be three-quarters of a part.
The dome (aṇḍaka) is one and a half parts, and the moon-motif (candrikā) is one part in height;
the height of the pitcher (kalaśa) is two parts, and the citron (bījapūraka) is likewise.
The width of the root-cluster (mūlamañjarī) should be made with sixteen squares;
its height is seventeen, and the trunk (skandha) is recorded as nine squares.
The excellent root-bud should be fashioned with seven layers;
its neck is one part, and the āmalasāraka is two parts.
One part should be for the moonstone (candrikā), and the height of the pitcher (kalaśa) should consist of three parts;
this [measurement] applies to those [architectural elements] previously mentioned as the root-creepers (mūlamañjarī) in temples.
In its construction, it should be of great proportions and adorned with beautiful workmanship;
it should be provided with outer walls on all four sides of the palace.
A wise person should construct a canopy for the wrestler, making it as beautiful as possible,
adorned on all sides with various lovely forms and auspicious characteristics.
One should adorn the façade with captivating lion-ear (siṃhakarṇa) ornaments,
provided with three pediments (valabhī) and four corner pinnacles (karṇakūṭa).
In this celestial palace, everything should be arranged according to what is most beautiful;
as for the vital points (marmas) that have been described on all sides within the hundred-square plot of the site-plan (vāstu).
Having carefully discarded those [old materials],
one should have this palace constructed here in the aforementioned form, as a celestial abode.
Having constructed a divine palace for Triviṣṭapa as an ornament for the city, one shall obtain fame and sovereignty in this world, and indeed infinity in the hereafter.
He shall dwell in Triviṣṭapa until the dissolution of all beings;
at the end of that, the human being attains absorption into the supreme reality.
Triviṣṭapa.
Now, the Perfect Palace, the Conqueror of the Earth,
which is worshipped by Kinnaras, Asuras, Yakṣas, and other foremost among the gods, is described.
When the site has been made quadrangular and divided into sections,
the hall shall consist of four parts and project out by one and a quarter parts.
Two ear-lobes (karṇaśṛṅga) should be made, each one square-unit (bhāga) in width,
projecting by three-quarters of a unit (pādonapada).
The inner sanctum (garbha) shall consist of four parts; the wall (bhitti) should be made of one part;
the circumambulatory path (bhramantikā) also one part; and the outer wall (bāhyabhitti) one part.
One should construct a quadrangular courtyard for this [mandala] in three directions using two parts;
in front, one should build a pavilion endowed with ritual splendor.
Having thus conceived the divisions according to their respective locations, the wise one should create a beauty of craftsmanship all around, like that of Mount Mandara.
The measurement for its upper portion is now described here:
below, there should be a nāga-pīṭha measuring two padas.
One should place a diamond in its center measuring one-quarter of a part;
its height should be twice its width, increased by half a part.
In the middle of the upper measurement (ūrdhvamāna), there should be the removal of six padas and so forth;
and in the center of that, a pedestal-band (vedībandha) measuring one and a half parts (sārdhabhāgika) should be constructed.
Then, the four legs joined with diamonds and the leaf-pattern within the girdle should be made measuring half a *bhāga*.
The vedikā and the rājaseraka should be made with two parts;
the wise one should fashion the candrāvaloka with one part.
One should fashion a seat-cloth (āsana-paṭṭaka) there with one-quarter of the module;
with two and a quarter modules, one should place the pillar above.
One should fashion the capital and the neck (stambha-śīrṣaka) with one half-part;
the fillet (paṭṭa) with one half-part; and the covering (chādya) with a length of one and a half parts.
Two fillets should be made, equal to half a part;
above the inner leaf, they should be arranged in order as follows.
The wise one should fashion the neck, the egg-base, and the kalaśa together with the candrikās;
the height of the ear-ridges (karṇaśṛṅgas) should be one and a half parts according to the measurement.
The wise should reconstruct the missing horns using the pillar-line;
one should construct five pinnacles (kūṭas) correctly on the first level.
One should construct three [terraces] on the ground; however, on the second and third [levels], one should make a pinnacle (kūṭaka), its height and width being equal according to measurement.
Thus, nine distinct kūṭas (pinnacles) should be placed upon each ear;
the elevation of the śukanāsa (fronton) should be made by the wise to be two and a half parts.
The eastern [section] may be Syāduromañjarī, situated above the Naṣṭaśṛṅga;
it should be three padas in width and three and a half bhāgas in height.
One should make the neck one and a quarter parts, along with the entire kalaśa;
above the second horn, there should be another uromañjarikā.
It should be made four parts wide and five padas high,
together with the shoulder, the descent, the neck, the candrikā, and the kalaśa.
The height of these, however, is prescribed as one and a half parts;
in this manner, one should construct eight breast-crests (uraḥśikhara) in the four directions.
Above the third ear-ornament (karṇaśṛṅga) there should be a root-cluster (mūlamañjarī);
it should be six units in height and five units in width.
The width of the shoulder should be three pādas in all four directions;
one should adorn the mañjarī with various types of kūṭas and nyāsas.
The neck should be raised by half a part and two and a half parts in width;
the height of the dome (aṇḍaka) should be one part less than three parts.
The *karpara* should be made with half that portion, and the *kalaśa* should rise one unit;
this [pedestal] should be provided with nine *śikhara*s on all sides.
The construction of the altar (vedībandha) should be performed everywhere according to the pattern of the hundred sites (śatavāstu);
by means of that same division, one should also fashion beautiful pitchers (kalaśas).
One should fashion mañjarīs resembling the tips of lotus petals everywhere;
herein there are forty-five egg-shaped ornaments (aṇḍakas).
That king who constructs such a temple as the Pṛthivījaya conquers the entire earth, having utterly routed his enemies.
Furthermore, whoever else should perform this devotion to the letters with a hundred-fold intensity,
even they shall obtain happiness and, finally at the end, the supreme state.
The conquest of the earth.
Hereafter, I shall describe the temple that is the ornament of the earth,
which is worshipped by all the immortals as well as by the hosts of apsarases.
When the field has been made square and divided into twelve parts,
there shall be five squares for the *bhadra* and three squares should be made for the corner.
The wise one should divide the interior (garbha) into sixteen parts;
the wall of the base (kandabhitti) should be made on all sides with twenty-six parts.
For this temple, a beautiful pedestal consisting of two units should be made;
there shall be a molding and an outer wall, and the projection of the *bhadra* shall be two units.
The intervening space between the water is the portion for the windows;
in the center of the bhadra projections, there are five beautiful and well-pleasing openings.
One should construct an outer veranda adorned with altars and lattices;
above that, one should erect a very beautiful canopy of garlands.
Now we shall describe the vertical measurement for the temple that adorns the earth:
one should fashion its *kṣuraka* (pedestal-base) as three units in height, joined with a *pīṭha* (plinth).
Its height from that point shall be twenty-five and a half padas;
in the middle of this, the rising of the balance (tulodaya) should be made with ten padas.
The line should consist of fifteen parts; the shoulder-head (skandha-śīrṣa) should be half a part.
The wise should construct the altar-base (vedī-bandha) as two and a half parts.
The shank should be one-sixth of the height; the auspicious *secharas* should occupy half a part (*bhāga*).
One should cause the *mekhalā*, the *antara*, and the *patra* to be made with one part each.
A four-legged stool (catuṣkikā) should be made five units wide and three units high;
above that, another step should be made two units [wide], and the next one unit higher.
Five levels should be constructed, each successively smaller than the one above;
the first level should be made by the wise with two and a half parts, while the windows should occupy three parts.
Three parts and a quarter are declared for the second [verse-quarter];
the third has three feet, and the following one is beyond that.
The fifth stage is thus described:
the neck consists of three and a half feet, and the frog-like part consists of one and a half feet.
One part should be like the moon, auspicious and resembling a lotus petal;
one should know that the vessel consists of three parts and is provided with a mātuliṅga.
Either Drāviḍa, Nāgara, or Vārāṭa style would be auspicious;
whichever one he desires to construct, he should fashion that particular form.
It was adorned with pillars of various kinds decorated with diverse ornaments,
and embellished with water-pots, lotus petals, and diamonds.
It was provided with moon-chambers fashioned with artificial crocodile-mouths,
and adorned with archways endowed with auspicious marks and joined by crocodile-shaped ornaments.
One should perform the delightful rite, as prescribed and according to one's means, adorned with various corners, diverse forms, and wonderful paintings.
Just as a virtuous king adorns the entire earth,
so too does this palace, an ornament of the ground, adorn the earth.
For as many particles of dust as there are in the materials used for the plaster,
for that many thousands of eons shall the maker dwell in the abode of Śiva.
The ornament of the earth.
Now the Saṃsthāna Sarvatobhadra is being described. One should divide a square field into ten squares.
In that regard, the interior space (garbha) should be of such a size as to reach the station of Brahmā;
both the wall and the station are each one [unit].
With six parts, it should be auspicious; the projection should extend out by one and a half parts.
One should make the *karṇa* two parts, provided with a *lamba-agra*.
The width of the waterway at each step was such that it would be auspicious for only one person to pass, adorned with beautiful pillars.
That object would bring joy and bestow wealth, grain, and happiness;
it is expanded by four parts and projects outward by half a part.
That which is auspicious is indeed in front of the auspicious one; they know that to be the outer belly (bāhyodara).
Its height is proclaimed to be twice its width.
One should make the *kumbhaka* one part; the *masūraka* half a part;
and then one should make the *antarapatraka* one-quarter of a part.
One should cause the height of the girdle (mekhalā) to be half [the height] of that;
the pillar-shaft (jaṅghā), four parts in height, should be provided with a spear and small bells.
The *pada* [ornament] is devoid of feet, with diamonds set in its positions;
it has leaf-patterns within its girdle and rises to a height equal to half a *pada*.
One should make it bent by one-third; at that point, there should be a moon-shaped ornament.
Above the seat-band, one should fashion a pillar two units high.
One should fashion the diamond-shaped head with one part;
the wise craftsman should make the cloth-pendant with one part.
The width of the covering for the two feet is [one unit], and the height of the *tulasvana* is half of that;
the belly, the outer boundary, and the walls are the *andhakārikā*.
The height of the shank and the height of the eaves should be as prescribed;
at the corners, chariot-arches (rathikās) should be constructed, extending for three padas and terminating in kalaśas.
A chariot path (rathikā) is proclaimed to have a height of two padas;
the height of the first lion-ear (siṃhakarṇa) is three padas.
The second [type] has two feet; from that very [base], there is an elevation.
There should be a mutual projection of the peaks by one part, increasing successively.
One should make the spire (śikhara) seven parts in height and six parts in width;
the neck (grīvā) should be half a part in height, and the dome (maṇḍaka) one part.
The *kalaśa* should be one and a half *padas* together with a quarter of a *candrikā*;
one should fashion the *mañjarīs* at the tips of the lotus petals so that they are equal in size everywhere.
Below, the auspicious pedestal (bhadrapīṭha) is beautiful with the Vāstu-foot;
he who constructs the Sarvatobhadra [mandala] endowed with all its characteristics [attains success].
Victory and glory arise for him— this is the Sarvatobhadra [arrangement].
Having given the celestial chariot, he then spoke the characteristics of the assembly hall.
In the field belonging to the beloved lord of heaven, frequented by hosts of Gandharvas, which had been made quadrangular and divided into a hundred parts;
A wise person should divide the vimāna, which brings about prosperity, nourishment, and happiness;
he should construct it with four auspicious bhadras, as well as karṇas and prāggrīvakas.
The inner sanctum (garbha) should be half the width; the walls shall be made from what remains. A temple of thirty [parts] is considered the largest, while one of twenty-five is the medium.
The minor [type], however, should be composed of sixteen or twenty-one [syllables];
one should be pure by birth, while the other should be adorned with clusters of blossoms.
The threefold nature of the Miśraka celestial palace has been proclaimed;
the supreme Miśraka is entirely composed of pure crystals like Mount Kailāsa.
The middling [type] is pure by birth but devoid of flower-clusters;
the inferior one is to be fashioned as adorned with flower-clusters.
The width of the ear and the neck-portion (prāggrīva) should be made equal to one square unit (bhāga);
the *kṣobhaṇā* should be made half a square unit, and whatever remains should be treated like the ear.
One should make the projection of the Bhadra with half a part;
the Prāggrīva of the Miśraka, however, is four parts in width.
In accordance with the Mūlasūtra, there are chariots with single-pada sides;
now the vertical measurement of the vimāna is described as it truly is.
The pedestal is said to be two pādas in height and adorned by kinnaras;
up to the shoulder, it is declared to consist of twenty-two parts.
The construction of the altar (vedībandha) should consist of two and a half parts;
here, one-fourth is for the covering, and the Kinnaras occupy half a part.
There should be an inner leaf-pattern at the end of the girdle and a single raised foot;
such forms should be on the shanks of the moving chariots.
In its center should be a star-shaped pedestal (starasekā), adorned with makara-heads and grāsa-motifs,
and beautified by arches (toraṇas) featuring bhallika-ornaments, lovely bells, chowries, and kinnaras.
Above the height of the balance, the first terrace is four parts;
on that terrace, it is elevated by one-fourth part.
The other [part] is one and a half parts in width and one and a half parts in thickness;
this is its first contraction, which should extend from the end of the pitcher (kalaśa) to the pedestal (pada).
The third [verse] should be made of three lines, with an extension of one-quarter of a line;
however, its contraction should be performed by the wise using half a line.
The fourth [line] should be made with three feet, together with the earth and the girdle;
it is graceful with clusters of blossoms and has the form of a blue lotus petal.
One should draw a cord five times the length of the boundary line up to the edge of the furrow;
the first entry into the ground shall measure one-fourth of the diameter.
Then, in the case of an increase by half [of the base], there are two other [measures]; the fourth, however, is equal to that.
The height of the pedestal (vedikā) is one-fifth of its width, measuring half a pada.
The neck should be three-quarters of a part, and the base-circle (bhaga-maṇḍala) one and a quarter parts;
it should have the form of a kaṅkatī fruit and the appearance of a mandāra flower.
One should construct a Vimāna with a neck like that of a moonstone, a pinnacle as high as a water-jar,
and a canopy endowed with all auspicious characteristics.
Whatever fruit may be obtained through hundreds of sacrifices, primarily the Aśvamedha, a human being attains that same fruit by means of a single Vibhāna.
The celestial palace.
Now we shall describe here the characteristics of the Nandana palace:
one should divide a site measuring twenty-two cubits into eight parts.
One should fashion its auspicious *bhadra* with a width of four parts;
its beautiful fore-projection (*prāgrīva*) should extend out by one part.
The two side-chariots of Mūlakaṇa should be made with feet [protrusions],
measuring six, three, or four aṅgulas.
One should create an interval for water, and therein a mañjarī is placed;
the interior (garbha) should consist of four parts, while the remainder is for the wall and the enclosing frame (andhakārikā).
The *kandabhadra* consists of two feet; from the foot of the *pada*, it extends outward. One should cause a pavilion named *sugrīva* to be constructed in front of it.
The height of the pedestal (bhadra-vedikā) should be half the width of the summit;
one should likewise fashion its lines according to what has been prescribed for Kailāsa.
The six stages and twelve eggs should be fashioned separately;
for this maker brings joy to the creator both in this world and in the next.
It was called Nandana by the wise; it is the most excellent of palaces, indeed a Nandana.
We describe the Svastika palace, which bestows well-being.
Worshipped by the hosts of gods and asuras, and by the Siddhas and great serpents of both sides,
this is the region of the *talacchanda* of the Eldest, the Middle, and the Youngest.
The correct measurement for the height is now properly described here:
in a square field measuring twenty-five cubits on each side.
One should first lay out the lines for the ear, extending horizontally and vertically;
then, having drawn a circle with certainty using a thread equal to half the perimeter.
Then, one should divide the circle all around with thirty-two lines; likewise, one should mark it with two hundred and fifty-eight points.
Then the wise one should draw three lines from the middle of the diagonal and the corner-line;
thus there shall be thirty-two divisions of equal measure.
One should construct eight halls, beginning with that of Indra and ending with that of Īśa;
and between these halls, one should fashion eight corners in due order.
One should repeatedly draw the thread from corner to corner, omitting two halls;
then, at the eight intermediate directions, one should bring the tips of the threads together like the petals of a lotus.
The corners and the chariot-paths (rathikās) likewise possess these auspicious characteristics;
the eight halls are square and extend for two parts.
The ear-ornaments are two-parted, auspicious, and resemble lotus petals;
its height is indeed twice the measurement from the top.
One should divide the remaining height by twenty; there, eight parts constitute the rise of the *tula*.
The wise man should fashion the *mañjarī* with the remainder, extending up to the base of the *skandha*.
One should determine the height of the pedestal (pīṭha) as one-fifth of its width;
the arrangement of the altar (vedikābandha) should consist of three units (tripada) and be provided with a beautiful coping (sueka).
One should make the jaṅghāṃśa support four parts in height;
one should cause the antarapatra within the mekhala to be made with one part.
A line twelve parts high should be made, as well as seven tiers;
the neck is half a part high and four parts in width.
The shoulder (skandha) should be made six parts in width, circular, and very beautiful;
one should draw the sheath (kośa) upon these [parts], with its own dimension being three times the width.
By that measurement of the cord by which the wall would be six parts wide,
the largest [temple] should be twenty-five cubits, and the next sixteen.
Furthermore, the Svastika should be known as the smallest [type], with twelve cubits;
for the largest, the height of the leg is declared to be six parts.
In the medium and inferior types, the height is respectively five and four parts;
when the svastika is thus constructed, it brings about the welfare of all the world.
And specifically, the svastika [mudrā] shall bring about the desired object for both kings and the performer.
Now we shall describe the Muktakoṇa temple; it is of three types.
In order, starting with the eldest, [the shares] are sixteen, twelve, and eight;
the eldest shall have ten parts, while the middlemost shall have fourteen.
The smallest [fire-altar] should consist of ten parts; its seat (sadas) is thus designated.
When the sacrificial ground has been made quadrangular and divided into eighteen squares, [the layout proceeds as follows].
Three hundred and twenty-four compartments should be laid out;
with thirty-six parts, one should construct the auspicious inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) in the center.
The outer wall, the blind wall, and the middle wall—
these three should each be two padas in measurement in width.
The hall is four parts in length and extends out by one part;
having fashioned this auspicious *bhadra* as an ornament of the hall, it measures two such units.
The wise man should make two additional side-panels on both sides,
and he should also provide water-channels in all eight directions.
Immediately following the intervening water, one should construct eight excellent chariot-pavilions, measuring two parts each, in the four cardinal directions.
In the corner, one should construct the *rathas* using two parts, measuring the same as the *āma* (shoulder);
having set aside the *rathas* in the corner, one should construct the remainder as prescribed.
This has been fully described as the medium [size]; now the smallest is being told:
when the field has been made square and divided into ten parts.
The hall should consist of four parts, projecting outward by one part;
and the side water-chambers should each measure one part.
In their midst, one should fashion a lotus-leaf-like ornament for the interior of the water,
positioned between the chariot-rims as prescribed.
One should perform the agitation (kṣobhaṇā) for half a portion, situated within the four corners;
one should fashion auspicious ears and frontal protuberances measuring one and a quarter portions.
This [proportion] is prescribed for water-tanks of small size;
it may also be employed for those of medium and large sizes, such as palaces.
This mukhakoṇa is thus described as being of three kinds in brief;
its height should be twice its width.
It should be fifteen [parts] high; its middle would be the tulodaya (the crowning fillet).
The vedibandha (base molding) consists of four parts, and the jaṅghā (shaft) consists of seven and a half [parts].
The leaf-pattern within the girdle and the half-diamond step;
the three steps, the ear-ornaments, the crest, the face, and the height ending with the vase.
And the Siṃhakarṇa should be made elevated in its own portion;
above it, the ear-peak (karṇaśṛṅga) and the root-cluster (mūlamañjarī) should be fashioned.
The detailed description with its faults follows: the height [of the base] shall be eighteen padas;
the circumference on all four sides shall be equal, and the *skandha* (the upper part) shall consist of nine parts.
In the city of Mañjarī, one should construct the neck with two parts and the Maṇḍaka with one part, rising as high as the nose of the mind.
The height of the pitcher (kalaśa) should be three parts, with Caṇḍikā occupying half a part;
this is the great-famed "Muktakoṇa" form which a certain man [should construct].
He has attained great happiness, liberated from all sins;
he is completely freed from all dualities and devoid of all impurities.
Completely liberated from all evil, he attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
he is one whose corners are released.
Now we shall describe the Śrīvatsa temple, which is worshipped by the gods.
When the square-shaped site has been divided into ten parts,
the inner sanctum (garbha) shall consist of six parts, and the wall should be made with two parts.
One should construct a three-pada chariot from each secondary limb measuring one and a half padas;
they say its ears measure two padas in all four intermediate directions.
Half a share is for the *kṣobhaṇā*; by throwing [the cord], half of that again is the interval of water;
the throw should be by half a *pada* from the outside of the measurement of the *pada*.
Two parts of it should extend outward, and one should place the *śukanāsa* (frontal ornament) there;
the width of the doorway should be made equal to one quarter of the total extent of the building site.
The wise should make [the height] twice the height and width of the door;
now we shall state the measurement of the Śrīvatsa as it has been taught.
The pedestal (pīṭha) should be equal to the base of the temple, and the cornice (khuraka) half of that;
from the pot-shaped member (kumbhaka) onwards, it should be made twice the width.
One should construct a long spire over them using twelve parts;
the height of the *tula* should be eight parts, and the altar (*vedī*) should be two and a half parts.
One should make the *kumbhaka* one *pāda* [in height], the *masūraka* three-quarters of a *pāda*,
and the inner leaf of the girdle (*mekhalāntarapatraka*) one-quarter of a *pāda*.
The shank should be four parts in height; the diamond (hīraka) should be half a part;
and one should fashion the inner leaf of the girdle (mekhalāntarapatra) with one part.
One should divide the shoulder, which is six parts wide, into ten squares;
the arrangement of the major and minor limbs at the shoulder is exactly as it is at the base.
The line on the shoulder, which is clearly visible on the exterior of the shoulder, should be divided into ten parts; thus one should divide the *rūḍha* (the raised portion).
There, the mass of petals should be divided into upper and lower portions;
one should fashion that external outline in the shape of those [petals] upon every limb.
One should rotate a thread having the measure of one *anul* and endowed with a third part;
there, by means of the western direction, the lines for the corners and the five [squares] should be drawn.
One should draw the chariot-line with a cord six times its width;
here there shall be seven grounds, the first of which is raised by two parts.
The second stage would be deficient by one-quarter of a quarter;
then, on the third stage, it would be deficient by two-quarters of a quarter.
The fourth [section] should consist of two quarters minus one and a half parts;
the fifth should be a quarter consisting of one and a half parts, forming the shoulder-head (skandhaśīrṣaka).
Thus, having mutually conquered the earth by a quarter-part,
one should divide the peak into three parts and set aside one part there.
The height of the śukanāsa (lion-face) should be equal to the remainder; it is presided over by a lion.
The neck is three-quarters of a part, and the egg-shaped dome (aṇḍa) is one and a quarter parts in height.
A line must be drawn; a mandala should be made neither too small nor too large. Two moon-marks (candrīkā) should be fashioned with a measurement of one and a quarter parts.
One should fashion it in the shape of a lotus petal, with an *āmalasāraka* in the center;
one should make a two-footed jar, excluding the *bījapūraka*.
He who causes a most beautiful temple marked with the Śrīvatsa to be built shall deliver a hundred generations of his lineage and go to Amarāvatī.
The Śrīvatsa mark.
Now we shall describe here the characteristics of the Haṃsa temple:
having made the site square, one should divide it into four parts.
The inner sanctum (garbha) shall consist of four parts, the wall (bhitti) twelve parts,
and one should then arrange the projections (bhadras) with two parts each.
It is recommended that they emerge from one-fourth of the womb;
and with a sixteenth part of that portion, one should make the intervals between them.
The pedestal, the arrangement of the railing, the shaft together with the girdle,
and the measurement of the upper portion should be executed according to what has been prescribed for the Svastika.
In the center, one should decorate the pedestal with lotus petals in the form of kinnaras, and above them,
with necklaces of serpents.
A wise man should construct this [temple] as three-storied or five-storied;
he should place the *nāgara*, *drāviḍa*, and *vesara* styles in each successive tier.
One should construct pinnacles corresponding to the levels, separated by one interval each;
and upon the chariot-mouldings (rathikā), one should fashion further chariot-mouldings according to the rules of the *vinyāna* architectural style.
The altar (vedī) should be half the width [of the base], and its neck (grīvā) should be half a square (padārdhikā).
The dome (aṇḍaka) should be made one square (padika), resembling the fruit of the kaṅkatī tree.
The pitcher for Caṇḍikā should be raised on a pedestal so that it shines like a swan perched upon the crest of Śiva.
Likewise, O best of the Bharatas, the palace known as Haṃsa shines resplendent in the center of the city;
whoever causes this palace named Haṃsa to be built [attains great merit].
The glorious swan shall dwell in heaven for as long as the fourteen Indras endure.
Now we shall describe the temple named Rucaka, the ornament of the city.
In the beginning, all things were fashioned by the Lotus-born [Brahmā] upon a field made square and divided into four squares.
One part shall be the wall (bhitti), its interior (garbha) two parts;
likewise the altar-base (vedībandha), the pillar-shaft (jaṅghā), the girdle (mekhalā), and the upper girdle (ūrdhvamekhalā).
One should fashion its *māna* (measurement) above and below like that of the *śrīvatsa*;
in the corners, pillars should be made, endowed with the syllables *hāi* and *hīi*.
In the center, however, a chariot-passage should be constructed, adorned with artistic craftsmanship;
this four-storied edifice must be built by you through your own skillful work.
A chariot-path (rathikā) is prescribed in the middle, extending across each level;
by him who has caused a rucaka-type temple to be built on an auspicious site.
By him a hundred lineages have been delivered, and likewise his own self has been uplifted—
Rucaka.
Now we shall speak of the Vardhamāna [stotra], which brings about dharma, health, and glory.
If one should cause [a temple] to be built, he shall possess eightfold sovereignty;
one should divide a square and level field into ten parts.
Then, with four parts, the central chariot should be made;
with one part each, the two chariots on the left and right.
The ears should be made with a quarter [of the width], avoiding the irregularities of the rules;
one should cause the projection of the *bhadra* there to be made with one part.
The projection of the side-chariots shall be half of the [main] portion;
the inner chamber (garbha) shall be half the width [of the hall], and the walls shall be made with whatever remains.
The upward measurement of this svastika should be as previously described;
this is called the vardhamāna, which increases fame and fortune.
Vardhamāna.
Now we shall describe here the characteristics of the Garuḍa temple;
this temple is always dear to the one whose banner is Garuḍa.
The field, measuring twenty-two squares along its length,
is further divided into ten parts from east to west.
The wise man should construct a temple in the center of that [site] measuring one hundred paces;
the thickness of the walls should be two paces, and the corner projections (karṇas) should also be two parts.
Having set aside the central portion of the palace on both sides,
one should leave two parts each at the front and at the rear.
With the remainder, the two bases (ṣaṭpadas) shall have a length and width of six [parts] each;
the inner sanctum (garbha) shall consist of sixteen parts, and the wall (bhitti) of these two shall be one part.
Among the rīvatsa, haṃsa, rucaka, and vardhamāna [arrangements], whichever one pleases [the practitioner], the wise man should fashion that single [form] of Garuḍa according to his own will.
His two wings should be fashioned extending to the left and right;
thus these three embryos are described in relation to Garuḍa.
Garuḍa.
Now we shall describe the characteristics of the elephant [temple].
Having divided the site into sixty-four squares, one should delineate the elephant.
Then, with a cord fixed at the boundary, one should draw a circle behind it;
one should make the womb with half of that—[forming] the shape of a line.
Now the vertical measurement of the elephant is clearly stated:
pillars as high as four pādas should be erected at the four corners.
This [measurement] for the *jaṅghā* has been specified; it should be between the hollows and the pillars.
The *mekhalā* should be equal in proportion to the two bands and the leaf-pattern.
In front there should be Śūrasena, and at the back the form of an elephant;
[this is] the elephant.
Now, the characteristics of the temple known as Siṃha are being described.
One should divide a square, level plot of land just as in the Nandana [plan]:
the inner sanctum (garbha) shall consist of four parts, while the wall (bhitti) shall be one part.
The *andhārikā* (blind wall) should be made with one part, and the outer wall with one part;
the *bhadra* (projection) should consist of four parts and extend out by one part.
The *karṇa* (corner) should be made two parts wide and provided with a water-course;
the pedestal (*pīṭha*) should be two parts high and occupied by lion figures.
One should fashion the *khuraka* with half a *pada* in the middle of the pedestal;
it should extend upwards from its width by double that amount plus one *kalā*.
One should construct the pedestal-band with two parts, its plinth with four parts,
and the fillet and the lower leaf with a rise of one part each.

The corner pinnacles (karṇaśṛṅga) should consist of three parts, together with the neck, the egg-shaped dome (aṇḍa), and the pitcher (kalaśa); the lion-ear (siṃhakarṇa), moreover, should be made four times the height [of the base].
In a palace known as the Lion, which is occupied by the form of a lion,
the root-cluster consists of six feet above the corner-pinnacle.
The height [of the neck] should be seven parts, adorned with five creepers;
however, the elevation of the neck itself should be made one foot less than a full foot.

The *aṇḍaka* (dome) should have a height equal to one *pāda*, and it should extend two units outward from the line; the height of the *candrakā* (moonstone) is proclaimed to be three-quarters of a *bhāga*.
One should have a two-footed water-pot made, joined with a citron fruit;
when one has it fashioned while still unbaked, that man will certainly become invincible.
In legal proceedings, in the royal court, in battle, and in the assembly of Śakra,
he is a lion.
Now we shall describe the Padmaka temple, which resembles a lotus.
He who causes this [altar] to be fashioned with corners attains all his desires;
[it should be made] on a quadrangular field, either in the cardinal or the intermediate directions.
One should lay down the lines individually and then fashion a circle;
between the two diagonal lines, however, is the Romaka square.
These thirty-two [parts] are said to be arranged with equal proportions;
furthermore, two parts are expanded as the ear-leaf ornaments (karṇapattras), which number sixteen.
The [inner] chambers should be like lotus petals and provided with water-channels;
the exterior should be free from confusion, and the walls should be constructed with the remainder of the space after allocating half for the boundary.
The lotus [mandala] has six, eight, and twelve spokes respectively for the Jyeṣṭhā and other [cakras];
its spokes (rathakās) should be thirty-two, sixteen, and eight respectively.
One should cause water-channels to be made for this [shrine] like those of the Śrīvatsa,
as well as a pedestal, a railing-band, and the moon-lights upon the neck and the crown.
One should fashion the egg, the pitcher, and the neck of this [stūpa] according to its height and width, following the proportions of a svastika.
Padma.
Now it is correctly stated that the temple Nandivardhana truly causes joy;
it delights its builder with children, wives, wealth, and so forth.
When the field has been made square, one should divide it into sixteen squares;
thus there will be two hundred and fifty-six divisions.
The inner sanctum (garbha) should be made one hundred units (padas), and the wall (bhitti) should extend for three units.
The measurement of the ear (karṇa) is three units, provided with a base-band (vavabandha).
One should divide the ear—extending along its length, broad at its base, and following the path of the water-channel—into five parts; of these, the *bhadra* portion consists of three parts.
Each part should be one share at the corner, and the projection of the *bhadra* should be half a share;
one should make each secondary limb (*pratyaṅga*) two squares, joined by a water-channel.
The projections on both sides shall extend by one and a half parts;
the width of the six-pillar hall (śālā) shall be six parts, and the portico (pratyaṅga) shall project out by one part.
One should properly construct the *bhadra* in front of that, measuring four paces in width;
its projection should be half a *bhāga*, and this same rule applies to all directions.
One should draw a circle from the center to the midpoint of the ear;
having first drawn that, one should extend the emergence of the limbs and sub-limbs according to its proportions.

One should construct the base (pada) as one and a half parts, supported by elephants, adorned with lotus petals, and provided with a girdle; the shank (jaṅghā) and the pitcher (kumbha) should be raised to a height of three-quarters of that.
The *kaṇaka* (fillet) is one-quarter of a module; the inner leaf (*antarapatraka*) is three-quarters of that;
the *grāsahāra* (moulding for the mouth) is half of that; and the *khuraka* (toe-moulding) is likewise half a module.
This height of the pedestal (pīṭha) is said to be equal to the plinth (khuraka);
its width should be double this, and it should extend downward from the upper portion. The emergence of the entablature (tulodaya) should be constructed with thirteen parts.
The spire, however, is one-twentieth [of the total height] and consists of four units.
One should fashion two parts less a quarter as the *kumbhaka*;
with one part the *kalaśa*, and with half [a part] the *antarapatraka*.
Its beautiful girdle should be made with a length equal to one-quarter of the base;
the height of the shank should be six parts, and the waist-band (grāsapaṭṭikā) should be half a part.
A diamond set in one part is prescribed for the ear;
and the leaf-pattern on the inner part of the girdle is raised by one and a half parts.
In the middle of the shank, however, rathakas and rathakās should be fashioned,
along with circular pillars, symmetrical grāsas, and muktāvarālaka ornaments.
The shank, however, should be made enclosed and adorned with wrestler-veils;
within the water-intervals, one should fashion auspicious forms using double-layered cloths.
One should construct [the base] above the rising of the tulā with these eight bhūs;
its shoulder (skandha) is one-eighth [of the height], and from the distance [of the base], it extends three paces.
The second is said to have three feet; the third is devoid of feet;
the fourth consists of two and a half parts; and the fifth is then one-quarter less.
The sixth [measure] should be made of two feet; then the seventh is three-quarters [of a foot];
the eighth, however, should be made as a *kṛti*, measured by one and a half parts.
There should be a mutual insertion of half a square for each one;
one should form the *kūṭas* in the corners, and the *tikas* and *lakas* in the secondary limbs.
O blessed lady, one should fashion various chariot-parts crowded with diverse carvings;
lines should also be drawn on both sides of the chariot.
Its pedestal (vedikā) should be made one part high;
the neck (grīvā) should be one part, and the dome (aṇḍaka) should have a height of two parts.
One should fashion the *sāmalasārī* and the *candrīkā*, each consisting of one and a half parts;
the *kalaśa* should be made with three parts, and outside of that, the *bījapūra*.
In front should be Śūrasena, and in the middle, one filled with beauty;
one should have this constructed so that it resembles the Miśraka celestial mansion.
The Nandivardhana palace is the ornament of this residence;
these twenty palaces,
beginning with Meru, are celebrated here as the most desired by all the inhabitants of heaven.
He who knows this according to its true nature shall become the foremost among the entire class of artisans and highly esteemed by kings.

Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Twenty [Plans] Beginning with Meru," in the *Vāstuśāstra* composed by the Great King of Kings, the Supreme Lord, the illustrious Bhojadeva, also known as the *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*.
Now begins the fifty-eighth chapter, titled "Praise of the Prāsādas":
The sixty-four types of *prāsādas* are now being described.
Those deities of the site (vāstudevas) who were previously granted by Brahmā to Viśvakarman and who reside at the vital points (marmas) must be worshipped as is appropriate;
their worship is prescribed for the temple, the pavilion, and the flagstaff.
Likewise, on seats, vehicles, and all types of implements,

as well as in palaces, pavilions, and pedestals, whatever is auspicious for the palace should be known as beneficial for those parts; conversely, that which is contrary to the architectural principles (vāstu) of the palace is considered detrimental.
Among them, eight are recorded for each of the thirty-three gods individually:
for Śambhu, Hari, Viriñca, the Lord of the Planets,
Caṇḍikā, Gaṇeśa, Śrī, and all the inhabitants of heaven.
The Vimāna, Sarvatobhadra, Gajapṛṣṭha, Padmaka, Pṛṣabha, Muktakoṇa, Nalina, and Drāviḍa—
these eight types of palaces are thus designated for the Destroyer of Tripura.
Garuḍa, Vardhamāna, Śaṅkhāvarta, Puṣpaka, Gṛharasa, Svastika, Rucaka, and Puṇḍravardhana—
these eight temples, the ornaments of the city, should be constructed for Janārdana.
Meru, Mandara, Kailāsa, the one called Haṃsa,
Bhadra, Uttuṅga, Miśraka, and Mālādhara as the eighth—
these eight palaces of Brahmā are said to be situated in the center of the city.
Gavaya, Citrakūṭa, Kiraṇa, Sarvasundara,
Śrīvatsa, Padmanābha, Vairāja, and Vṛtta—
these eight temples of the Sun, possessing auspicious characteristics, should be constructed. ||10-11||
Nandyāvarta, Calabha, Carṇadikhya, Siṃha, Vicitra, Yogapīṭha, Ghaṇṭānāda, and Patākina—
these eight temples of Caṇḍikā are to be constructed.
Guhārasaloka, Veṇubhadra, and Kuñjara;
likewise Harṣavijaya, Udakumbha, and Modaka—one should cause these eight auspicious temples of Vināyaka to be constructed. ||13-14||
Mahāpadma, Harmyānanala, Ujjayanta, and another known as Gandhamādana, as well as Śataśṛṅga,
Anavaṣka, and Suvibhrānta— these eight are proclaimed as the abodes of Lakṣmī.

One who is learned in the science of architecture (vāstu-śāstra) should construct temples for all the gods, beginning with the circular (vṛtta) and the oblong (vṛttāyata), followed by the one named Kiṅkiṇīlayanā, then the Paṭṭiśa, the one called Vibhava, and finally the eighth, the Cārāgaṇa. ||16-17||
Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, titled "Praise of the Prāsāda.
Now begins the fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Sixty-four Prāsādas, beginning with the Vimāna.
Next, we shall describe the Vimāna, the temple most beloved by Śambhu.
It is the ornament of all three realms— heaven, the netherworld, and the mortal world.
Among all dwellings, sites, and palaces,
this palace is the fundamental basis as well as the source of all architectural refinements.
In the case of a five-storied palace, the site-plan consists of eighty-one squares;
however, for other types of palaces, it is one hundred squares up to the corners.
In ancient times, Brahmā created these five-storied palaces before the Sun.
The auspicious [pillars] following the root and the ears have heights that are double [the width];
the projection of the remaining auspicious [pillar] consists of four divine auspicious [pillars],
serving as supports for the deities of space, and likewise in the intermediate directions.
The width of the vimāna is proclaimed to be ten parts;
the measurement of the inner sanctum (garbha) is five parts, and the wall is half of that. The front porch (prāggrīva) has a width equal to the wall and a length equal to the length of the sanctum.
Then, the width of the front neck (prāggrīva) should be disturbed [adjusted] by the fingers of the hand.
The width of the chariot (ratha) is one part, and the *karṇikā* is half a part.
That which has a width of five parts is proclaimed as the *bhadra*.
The emergence of its *bhūṇastova* is recorded as being one part;
the *kṣobhaṇa* of the water-path should be made with half a part.
One should measure the *karṇikā* and the water-path with a single straight line.
Now, the characteristics of the tiers (bhūmikās) and the pillars (stambhas) here are stated:
In every Buddhist temple, the shaft (skandha) is twice the width;
the height of the base (jaṅghā) shall be one-fifth of its own elevation.
The height of the *tilaka* should be made two parts;
one should measure the *śiroghaṇṭā* of the *tilaka* along a single cord.
One should fashion the hoof-mass (*khurapiṇḍī*) with one-third of the measurement of the *jaṅghā*.
One should measure the *khuraka* and the *vedibandha* with a level line.
One should fashion the *khurapiṇḍī* as one-third of the height of the *jaṅghā*;
one should align the *khuraka* and the *vedibandha* with a level line.
One should decorate the second floor with a lion-ear (*siṃhakarṇa*) ornament;
it is joined with a bell at the top and rises to a height of four parts.
Then follows the height of the third floor, which is reduced by one part equal to a *pada*.
The fourth storey should be made three and a half parts in height.
Between the *mañjarī* and the pillar, there should be a girdle with windows;
that which is the second storey is adorned with *siṃhakarṇa* (lion-ears). ||16-17||
Its door should be constructed provided with two panels;
on the earth, the third [level] should always have a door split by half.
It should be two feet high, and above that, there should be a vedī-mekhalā (altar-belt).
It should be adorned with lotus petals that are captivating to the sight.
(19) The pedestal (vedikā) should be made five parts in width and one part in height;
the neck (grīvā) should have a height of half a part, and the bell (ghaṇṭā) should be one part in height. (20)
The tip of the bell (ghaṇṭākoṭi) is prescribed to have a width of five parts;
one should measure the base (kumanda), the altar-binding (vedibandha), the top of the bell (ghaṇṭāgra),
and the height of the head (mastakodaya) with a single straight line across all five levels of the ground.
The entrances of the first [layer] from the earth shall be equal in number to the half-diameters in cubits;
those of the second are proclaimed to be two and a half finger-breadths;
that which results from the conjunction of these two should be indicated as belonging to the third.
Half of that [measurement] is for the fourth [tier], and the remainder is said to be for the fifth.
Above the altar (vedikā), one-third of its own base width is the extent of the creeper (latā) on the auspicious (bhadra) portion,
which is joined with the lattice-work (jālavartmana).
The altar (vedi) should be constructed with a width of one and a half [units];
it should extend from the boundary of the pillar to the cluster of blossoms (mañjarī) according to the measurement for prosperity.
On the portion of the altar, the projection of the hall (śālā-niṣkrāma) starts from the root corner (mūla-koṇa). ||25-26||
It should be adorned with various types of bases and lion-ear (siṃhakarṇa) ornaments;
one should draw its outline using a cord five times the width [of the structure].
One should have this graceful vimāna constructed for the God of Gods.
A celestial palace.
Now the *sarvatobhadra* configuration is described.
The belly, the outer boundary, the wall-enclosure, the height of the plinth, and the two ears should be made exactly like those of Mount Meru. (28–29)
In the same manner, O auspicious one, the width on all sides is six parts;
and on both sides, there are two parts each for the *rathika* and those known as the corners (*koṇa*).
The intermediate space (*udakāntara*) should be made with a width equal to a fist.
The height of the base (skandha) should be twenty parts, twice its width.
The pillar-shaft (jaṅghā) should always be made by the wise with a height of five parts.
The fillet (mekhalā) and the intermediate leaf-pattern (antarapatra) should each have a height of one and a half parts.
The pinnacle (śṛṅga) should have a height of three parts, including the neck (grīvā) and the amalasaraka;
one should place the upper floor within the interior of the base pinnacle.
One should divide the width of the second floor into ten parts.
Two parts for the width of the horns should be assigned to both sides.
By means of those [parts] belonging to the neck and the *amalasāra*, the position of the emergence of the horn is established.
The upper floor should be constructed with the interior of that horn.
One should again divide the width of that base into ten parts;
whatever remains should be designated as the measurement for the pinnacle (śikhara).
One may further divide it for the Vardhamāna or the Rucaka type, which is auspicious for the site.
O auspicious one, one should cause the *vallabhālabhi* to be made there in the middle of the *karṇa*.
One should divide the nine stories above the summit of the base (*bhūmikāśikhara*),
[measuring] from the central thread of the pedestal (*vedikā*) up to the upper story of the *karṇa*.
The ground, as well as the upper levels, shall have an extent of ten parts.
The withdrawal [of the structure] should continue up to the point of cutting, following the boundary of the base.
The neck occupies half the portion of the base, and the *nāmalasāraka* [is situated there].
And with half of the portion of the moon, the *kalaśa* (vase) should be formed;
this is the *sarvatobhadra* (all-auspicious).
Now, the configuration of the elephant and the palace is described.
One should divide the site-plan (vāstu) of the palace into sixty-four squares.
Then, with a thread marking the midpoint of the boundary, one should draw a circle behind it.
The shank [of the altar] shall measure five parts, and the girdle (mekhalā) one and a half parts.
In front, there should be the form of Sūrasena, and at the back, the shape of an elephant.
Having divided the boundary into eight parts, one should distribute them as in the Nandana layout.
O auspicious one, they know there should be two parts each for the two ears, making four in total;
the shank of the chariot-base (rathikā) should be separately [measured] as half the width.
A pinnacle (śṛṅga) three parts high is prescribed for the region of the ear.
The *valabhī* (roof-structure) resting in the middle is seven parts in height;

it has an auspicious form on all sides with features such as *rekhā*, *grīvā*, and *aṇḍaka*, and with *siṃhakarṇa* (lion-ears) on the *bhadra* projections—this is called the *garbha-prāsāda*. ||45-46||

It should be constructed on a *svastika* base by one who lacks the means to achieve it through wealth; all its parts should be like leaves. Furthermore, the width and the *jaṅghā* (shaft) should be as in the *latina* or *svastika* styles.
Like a lotus in the Nandana grove within the Śrīvatsa [lake] amidst the waters. ||48|| Padma.

Now we shall describe the Vṛṣabha type; it should be constructed with the aforementioned forms and measurements, possessing four auspicious features (caturbhadra), four doors, and having the shape of a celestial chariot (vimāna) with three peaks.
Its increase in size and its dimensions are determined by the height of its boundary walls and its pinnacles.
The *karṇaveda* and the *kapotālī* should be at the front of the *jaṅghā* and at the top;

the left and right [sides] should be made with urakas having a width of two and a half parts. The *bhadra* should be four parts, and the water-interval (*salilāntara*) should be half a part. ||50-51||
There shall be two pillars for that [temple] throughout all its internal sections;
there shall be one pillar in a vimāna, and two pillars in a vṛṣabha.
This distinction between the vimāna and the vṛṣa has been fully described.
The bull.
Now we shall describe the *muktakoṇa* (the "released-corner" plan): one should divide it into eight parts.
Both the left and right base-corners (*mūlakarṇa*) consist of two parts each;
the central pinnacle (*madhyaśṛṅga*) consists of four parts, as does the measurement of the belly (*jaṭhara*).
Between the two ears and the horns, one should leave a space of water;
on both sides, the two wheels should be full, and in the *bhadra* region, there should be a space of water.
The pillars (*jaṅghā*) should have a height equal to the width, along with the necks and the *āmalasāraka* [capitals].
It should be made like a Latin cross, with equal proportions on all sides.
(56) This is the *muktakoṇa* [cross].
Now we shall describe the Nalinī [river], its dimensions and characteristics;
upon it is the celestial abode of the divine offspring,
with its wall-width and length extending as far as the corners of the enclosure.
The peak that is in the middle region, as well as that which is between the ears and that which is in the corner of liberation—
these are the divisions according to the differentiation of the ritual action.
The wise maintain that these are located in the center of the square, at the ears, and at the peaks.

Next, we shall describe the *maṇika* (water-cistern). Its hall should emerge from the *liṅga*, and there should be a quadrangular courtyard (*catuṣkikā*) on all sides at the boundary of the half-porch (*alindaka*). 60.
This maṇika, intended for the sake of prosperity, nourishment, and happiness, is like a celestial chariot here;
it should have a tenfold division from the boundary of the site in every direction. [The divisions are:
the chariot-base, half the pericarp, the water-path, and then the auspicious portion (bhadra).

The base, the interior sanctum, and the height [of the structure] should be such that the bell is as wide as the top of the pillar. The height of the plinth (bhūmi) and the lower shaft (jaṅghā) should be equal, and the projection of the doorway should extend beyond the cornice (kapota).
Likewise, there should be lion-ears (siṃhakarṇa), pavilions (vimāna), and various decorative patterns on the pillars.
Then there were arches, garlands, and ornaments for it;
clusters of blossoms, beautiful in every way, shaped like the petals of blue lotuses.
Indeed, this other celestial chariot was the single source of origin for those two.
O auspicious one, this water-jar has been split asunder by mere separation.
Maṇika.
Now we shall describe the Garuḍa temple, which is most beautiful in every way.
One should first divide its field into ten parts.
Two parts should be made into chariot-paths (rathikās) extending out from the primary corner.

The auspicious [temple] should have a width of six parts, distinguished by wings, central beams, and so forth. An *alinda* (porch) should be constructed in the four directions with a projection equal to half the boundary.
However, the primary boundary should be made free from any intervening water.
The trunk (skandha) should be twice as high as the width of the base-line;
the plinth (jaṅghā), together with its intermediate leaf-pattern (antarapatra) and its base (kuṃ), should be one-third of the total height of the temple. 69. One should construct it thus.
The *jīraka* and the *vedibandha* should each be three parts in height.
One should cause the height of the *alimba*s to be made equal to half the height of the *śekhara*.
The wise architect should fashion the width of the *skandha* as six parts.
The neck (*grīvā*) shall occupy half a part in height; the *āmalasāraka* one part;
the *kumuda* half a part; and the *kumbha* shall consist of one part. This is the *garuḍa* [type].
Now it is said: one should divide that Vardhamāna into ten parts;
one should make the width of the two ears (karṇa) on the sides equal to one and three-quarter parts.
The left and right chariot-projections (rathaka) should have a width of one and a quarter parts each.
The *bhadra* (front porch) is proclaimed to be one-fourth [of the width] in its breadth.

One should fashion the height as double the breadth, extending up to the shoulder; this applies to the hoof-base (*khuraka*), the leg (*jaṅghā*), the flower-cluster (*mañjarī*), and the shoulder (*skandha*) as well. 74–75.
The measurement of the neck, the *mala*, the *sāraka*, and so forth, is like that of the *garuḍa* [style];
this is the *vardhamāna*.
Now the Śaṅkhāvarta [plan] with twenty-two cubits in length is described.
Its circumference at the base should be like that of a lotus;
the thickness of its walls and core should be one-quarter and nine-eighths [of the respective dimensions].
One should construct a porch (alinda) in front, adorned with lion-ears (siṃhakarṇa).

The pillar-base (jaṅghā) should be one-third of the height, and the altar (vedī) there should be one part. From the shoulder (āskandha) up to the binding of the altar, the height should be double the width.
And an inner leaf-pattern for the girdle is prescribed in the middle of the shank.
One should rotate [the compass] outward along a circular line on all sides using a thread from the ear;
thus, one should delineate the space between the ear and the direction-guardian using a circular thread.
One should fashion the remaining base-design (talacchanda) like that of a svastika; likewise,
one should construct the neck, the amalasaraka, the pinnacle (kalaśa), and the water-emanation (vārinirgama) according to the dimensions of the width and height of the svastika.
According to the limit of the trident, there should be a covering upon the cutting.
One should fashion a coiled form of that very same nature;
this is the "conch-spiral" (śaṅkhāvarta). ||82||

Now we shall describe the Puṣpaka; it should have a form resembling a celestial chariot (vimāna). It is of that same dimension, increases in size accordingly, consists of five elements, and is square. Its measurement is according to the vimāna standard, and its characteristics are those of the mañjarī.
