In this matter, the task must be performed by Mañjarī, and not by Puṣpaka, who is submerged in water.
Now we shall describe the king of houses: it should resemble Mount Kailāsa, surrounded on all sides by *viṭaṅkas*, projections, supports, and *niryūhas*;
it is adorned with a central *valabhī* (pavilion) and provided with windows and doors. ||85-86||
Extending to the pigeon-cots (kapota-stambha) and adorned with *śālābhañjī* brackets,
it should be surrounded on all sides by platforms (*vedikā*), sections of halls (*khaṇḍa-śālā*), and so forth;
it should be constructed and decorated with *mallaka*-canopies and *siṃhakarṇa* (lion-ear) ornaments.
The wise declare that the king of houses (gṛharāja) is measured by the division of the *alinda* [veranda].
Its configuration, both above and below, should be like that of Kailāsa;
such is the king of houses. ||88||
Now we shall describe its svastika, with its dimensions and characteristics as before.
A wise man should fashion all the latinas using that very same [measurement], so that the latinas, svastikas, and so forth, may be properly divided at the base. 89–90.

Likewise, one should fashion a line among these divisions of the *skandha*; thus endowed with these characteristics, the temple shall be named Svastika. Its own *sudhānāsa* (plinth) should be made one part in height.

The height of the *skandha* (the base structure) should be such that its width is twice as great. The *jaṅghā* (the pillar-shaft) should rise for one part, and the *mekhalā* (the belt-molding) should occupy one-eighth part.
The central hall (*madhyaśālā*) shall consist of two parts, measured according to the divisions of the foundational line (*mūlasūtra*). ||92-93||
The *karṇas* (corner projections) are likewise two parts each, while the waterway (*jalamārga*) is sixteen [parts].
There are eight *śālās* (halls) in this [structure], and eight *karṇas* on all sides. A wise architect should construct the *prāggrīva* (front porch) on the exterior.
The *kalaśa* (vase), the *caṇḍikā* (neck-base), and likewise the *āmalasāraka* (finial) at the top should have the same proportions as they do now;
this is the *svastika* [type]. ||95||
We shall now describe the *rucaka* [temple]; its division is tenfold.
The two ears (*karṇa*) measure two parts each, and the *bhadra* measures six parts. One should know that their projection (*vinirgama*) is one cubit in measurement. ||96-97||
One should construct water-channels in the Rucaka temple at certain places;
its height should be one-sixth of the remaining shoulder-width and twice its width.
The width of the pedestal (vedikā) on the shoulder is traditionally held to be one-sixth [of the total].
One should fashion the parts above the shank using one-third [of the total height] up to the emergence of the deity (surodaya).
The hoof and the kharaṇḍikā should be made with one-third of the shank's height;
likewise, the girdle and the intervening leaf-pattern should be made with one and a half parts.
With a cord three and a half times [the width], the front crab-mark (karkaṭanā) is formed;
with a cord four times the width of the base, the middle crab-marks are prescribed. Having divided the width of the shoulder into ten parts, one should fashion [the proportions] with those.
One should construct the *bhadra* with four [parts] and the ears (*karṇa*) with three by three [parts].
The ground-levels (*bhūmikā*) should be made as clear as one's own shadow, or they may consist of half the root portion.
The *āmalasāra* should be one part, and the *kumuda* should be half a part.
A wise architect should construct the *kumbha* (dome) with one part on the *rucaka* temple;
this is the common form for all temples of the gods.
(104) [This concludes the section on] the *rucaka*.
We shall now describe the Puṇḍravardhanaka temple, the favorite of Hari.
First, one should draw a circle everywhere that touches the boundary of the base; this should be constructed in all directions, joined with the corners of its halls. 105.
Whatever the measurement of the Svastika type may be, it should be doubled for the Puṇḍravardhana type.
Whatever the height and width of the Jaṅghodaka, Anta,
and Bhadra types have been stated for the Svastika, those same dimensions are to be understood as applicable to the Puṇḍravardhana.
Puṇḍravardhana.
Now it is said: one should divide Mount Meru there into ten parts;
one should establish its boundary and also the peak as a separate portion.
O Bhadra, in the measurement, the remainder is prescribed as a single portion.
The space between the water-channels should be made sixteen *pada*s.
The inner sanctum (*garbha*) is to be constructed with sixteen *pada*s, each measuring one *pada*.
Its walls, the *randhārikā* (inner partition), and the outer wall are thus prescribed.
The shank (jaṅghā) shall be six parts in height, and the girdle (mekhalā) one part;
the pinnacle (śṛṅga) shall have a height of three parts, and the spire (śikhara) shall be ten parts high.
This eleven-storeyed structure is to be constructed by those learned in the science of architecture (vāstuśāstra).
The shoulder (skandha) should have a width of four and a half parts, and the neck (grīvā) should be made with a height of half a part.
The dome (maṇḍaka) should have a height of one part,
the water-lily (kumuda) should be one and a quarter parts, and the height of the pitcher (kalaśa) should be one part.

The line for that [mandala] is proclaimed to be made with a cord of sixfold length. Whoever should cause this [mandala], resembling Mount Meru, to be constructed with stones or bricks, shall obtain great merit. (114)
Meru.
Now, the characteristic features of the Mandara palace are described. One should construct a *bhadra* projection extending from half the depth of the inner sanctum (*garbha*) on the Mandara;
it should be placed facing every direction, resembling Mount Meru. (115–116)
In the middle region, however, the *valabhī* (pinnacle) is raised above the summit; all other measurements here should be like those of Mount Meru. 117.
[This is] Mandara.
Next, we shall describe Kailāsa; one should divide it into ten parts.
Bhadra has a width of six parts and extends from the middle region.
Its two corners have a width of two parts each and are devoid of intervening water-channels.
The expansion of the *bhadra* should be made on all sides equal to half of the *garbha*.
In the middle, there should be a *lata-śikhara* (crested pinnacle) whose height is equal to half of the [main] *śikhara*.
This [pinnacle] should revolve around the walls, the *garbha*, the *bhrama*, as well as the *jaṅghā* and the *mekhalā*. 119–120.
One should fashion the width and height of the shoulders and the pinnacles (śṛṅga) in this [temple],
as well as the neck and the dome (aṇḍaka), like those of Mount Meru;
such is Kailāsa.
Now we shall describe the *haṃsaka* (swan) type; its division is like that of the *rucaka*.
Here, the distinction lies in the presence of an inner space (*jalāntara*); the remainder is as in the *bharucaka*.
This is the *haṃsa*.
We shall describe the characteristics of the Bhadra; one should divide it into ten parts.
The width of this Bhadra should be equal to the measurement of the interior of the womb (garbha).
The two chariot-fronts (rathaka) on the left and right should each have a width of two and a half parts.
One should cause the front neck (prāggrīva) to be made equal in length to half the interior (garbha);
the height of the front neck should be made equal to half the height of the pinnacle (śikhara).
One should place a gabled roof (valabhī) in its middle portion, provided with lion-ears (siṃhakarṇa).
With creeper-patterns, water-jets, and latticed windows on all four sides, it becomes the *bhadra*; the remainder here is as in the *rucaka* [plan]. 126.
*Bhadra*.
Now we shall describe the Tuṅga; for this is indeed the second Mandara type.

One should adorn it with lion-ears (siṃhakarṇas) and cause creepers to be fashioned above. Its height from the ground should be equal to the ground-level measurement, and likewise its pillars, paintings, and so forth.
Just as on Mount Meru, here in the center there are clusters [of deities] in every direction; they are lofty.
Now we shall describe the *miśraka* (mixed) type: it should possess the characteristics of measurement and configuration.
The base should be like a celestial chariot (*vimāna*), and in its center there should be a peak like Mount Kailāsa.
This is the *miśraka*.
Then, having made that [structure] in the shape of a garland, one should adorn it with windows;
whatever the measurement of the middle [section] may be, one should arrange it according to the first [section].
(130) This is the *gavaya* [type].
Now we shall describe Citrakūṭa; one should divide it into ten parts.
One should construct its neck protruding forward, measuring according to the dimensions of the interior (garbha).
The left and right ears should have a width of two and a half [parts] below that.
One should determine the height of the pillar-shaft (*jaṅghā*) to be one-third of the total height (*utsedha*).
One should place the pedestal for the base (*khurapiṇḍikā*) at one-third of the height of the shaft;
and there, the recessed fillet (*kapota*) and the decorative molding (*antarapatra*) should each be half a part.
Whatever the height of the pinnacle may be, one should measure it with thirteen units;
therein, one should proportionally determine the ground and its elevation.
One should construct the wall from pillars and architraves, and the friezes with decorative work.
One should assign that work by means of cutting the *kūṭas* (pinnacles) in every direction.
The floor-plan (*talacchanda*) is divided by an intermediate leaf (*antarapatra*);
above that, one should then place two *kūṭas* each on the left and right ears (*karṇas*).

In the middle of the hall, there should be four peaks on all sides; likewise, there should be terraces, lion-ears, and door-bolts for the gates. The height of the spires should be exactly as it was in the first [type].
Citrakūṭa.
The *kiraṇa* is said to be equal in measurement to the *padma*.
One should provide thirty-two *anārānas* in it, or sixteen;
there may be a variation in the halls due to the *karṇas*, while the rest remains as in the *mālādhara*.
A ray of light.
We describe it as beautiful in all its limbs through various types of architectural divisions,

supporting many creepers of diverse arts, endowed with numerous palaces, possessing a layout consistent with the principles of the *talacchanda* system, and characterized by many auspicious marks. (140)
In a most beautiful palace,
provided with arches, lion-ears, and various embellishments, whatever the dimensions may be here, one should know them all to be as they were in the beginning. ||141-142||
The most beautiful of all.
Now we shall describe the Śrīvatsa; one should divide it into ten parts.
Therein, the wise man should construct the hall with three parts.
The two chariot-projections (rathaka) on the left and right should have a width of one and a half parts each.

In this [plan], the corner projections (mūlakarṇas) are twice as wide as one part. Each bay (bhadra) protrudes from the temple by a measure of one cubit, or by two, three, or even four finger-breadths. ||144-145||
In the middle of the *bhalī*, however, clusters (*mañjarī*) resembling lotus petals should be fashioned;
the entire decorative work (*parikarma*) should extend from there, supported by the *rathikā* and the *karṇa*.
One should fill the area up to the end of the shoulder (*skandha*) with *āmali* and *candraśālā* elements.
The hoof-ball, the shank, the top of the pitcher, the summit, and so forth—
whatever [parts] there may be, they should be equal in measure to the *vardhamāna* [type].
This is the *nandyāvarta*.
We declare that it should be Valabhya, resembling the king of houses (gṛharāja).
It may be elongated or square, equal in measurement on one side;
however, if it is square, its height should be twice its width. ||148-149||
Furthermore, for the Ādhyatantra, the height of the structure is prescribed as one and a half times [the base];
its width is tenfold, and it is perfectly square on all sides. One should then divide it according to the measurement, resembling the previously described palace.
We shall describe its true form: it should be like the Śrīvatsa mark.
Alternatively, one may divide it according to the proportions of any single temple, such as the Vimāna, Rucaka, Vardhamāna, or other types of abodes. ||151-152||
The preparatory works for the foundation pillar, its width, height, and the girdle; the lion-ear, the chariot, the bell, as well as the pinnacle and the cluster at the top—
whatever [is required], that should be according to the measurement, just as it was in the original model.
The roof-ridges.
The true form and the measurement of Suparṇa are now described.
One should fashion the Sarvabhadra with a lion-like form divided [into parts];
the Bhadra is projected equally by four parts from the center.
The two parts are the base and the ears; the width of the *bhadra* is six parts;
the *jaṅghā* is five parts high, and its *mekhalā* is one part.
The height of the *kuravedī* is one-third of the base *jaṅghā*.
In the middle, however, two horns should be made on the left and right;
they should be two padas in height, divided toward all directions.
At the base and at the ears of the horns, the elevation should be three padas.
The *sevā* (pedestal) should also be four finger-breadths [in height],
and one should fashion the width of the *jālā* (lattice-work) in the *śrīvatsa* and *nandana* sections as follows:
the *skandha* (shoulder) should have a height double its width and a width of six parts.
The height of the leg (jaṅghā) is prescribed as one-third of the total height.
One should fashion the pedestal for the hoof (khurapiṇḍikā) as one-third of the leg's height.
One should provide the girdle (mekhalā), the inner leaf-pattern (antarapatra), and [the base] with a measure of one and a half parts.
The width of the shoulder should be divided into ten parts as before;
with a width of two and a half times that, the front *karkaṭanā* should be made. With a cord four times [the length], the middle *karkaṭanā* should be made.
The Śrīvatsa should occupy half the width [of the lotus] and its height; then there should be a Kumuda and a Kumbhaka.
In this [Kumbhaka], there should be an Āmalasāra, and it should be exactly as it was in the first [section].
This is the Śrīvatsa.
Now we shall describe Padmanābha, which is endowed with lotus-halls.
This second [type] is indeed Padmaka, auspicious and bearing a garland of lotuses;
all other measurements, however, are the same as those for Padma and Svastika.
Padmanābha.

Now I shall describe the Vairāja [style]; it is to be understood as being like a celestial chariot (vimāna). Its form consists of a pinnacle (*śikhara*), a height, and pillars with necks (*stambhagrīva*). It is likewise provided with assembly halls (*sabhā*), arches (*toraṇa*), gate-towers (*niryūha*), and "lion-ears" (*siṃhakarṇa*).
One should make it five-storied, with a common base and square in shape;
this Vairāja, resembling a celestial chariot (vimāna) in form, is thus described.
[Vairāja]
Now we shall describe the *vṛttaka* (circular) type: at the base it is proclaimed to be square;
then, at the base of the *jaṅghā* (shaft), it is circular with eight [sides] for three parts, and one-third of a part;
from the base, middle, and top, one should make it full in all directions. ||168-169||
The Bhadrakāra is in the auspicious [site], while the Caturaśraka is in the Vibhāga;
the Aṣṭāśri is shaped like a vajra, and the Vṛtta resembles a svastika.
Just as the emergence of the svastika occurs through the division of the root, so too does the latina [pattern].
Likewise, by virtue of its growth and its measure, this [vṛtta] also would be like the first one. (171) [This concludes the section on] the vṛttaka.
Now we shall describe the Nandyāvarta; one should divide it into ten parts.
One should fashion two ears on the sides, each having a width of three-quarters of a part.
One should design the *bhadra* with a width of four parts.
One should construct a chariot with a footpath between the corners of the hall;
the water-cistern chariot [should be] from the corner to the ends of the hall as desired.
The length of the six peaks should be such that a *valabhī* (pavilion) would be situated in their middle.
One should construct a water-channel from the root to the edge of the *śālākarṇa*;
otherwise, one should have it made somewhat like that of the *bhūsiṃha*.
This is the *suparṇa* [type]. ||175|| Suparṇa.
Now the measurement and the characteristics of the lion are described:
one should divide the extent of the field tenfold, equally on all sides.
The two parts for the left and right root-ears should be made.
The width of the Mūlabhadra is prescribed as six parts.
Its breadth should be made double the measurement of the height of the *skandha*.
The *jaṅghā* (lower wall) is five parts in height, and the *mekhalā* (moulding) is one and a half parts.
One should design the *khuraka* and the *vedibandha* using one-third of that [measurement];
the *śṛṅgas* (pinnacles) on the four sides should be three parts in height.
A wise man should adorn the middle with *valabhīs* (balconies), like the ears of a lion.
All other types of *pramāṇa* (measures) should be like the *sarvatobhadra*. [This concludes] the lion.
We shall now describe the *vicitrakūṭa*; one should divide it into ten parts.
In the case of the Mūlabhadra [temple], it should have two parts and its dimensions should be equal to those of the hand. One should construct a *valabhī* (pinnacled roof) in the middle of the hall;
one should place two *kūṭas* (pavilions) on all sides, joined to the *mūla* and *ka* [sections]. ||181-182||
This distinction has been fully described: the hall (śālā) should be devoid of a peak (kūṭa).
However, all other measurements are to be understood as being like those of the Citrakūṭa [temple]. 183. [End of] Citrakūṭa.
Now we shall describe the Yoga-pīṭha, which is like the supreme Triviṣṭapa;
one should divide the square on all sides into twenty parts. One should then construct squares with an extent of two parts each in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
One should construct two water-channels, one on the left and one on the right, each measuring one part.
Within these, the inner sanctum (garbha) should be three parts in width;
the plinth (jaṅghā), excluding the space for the pigeon-cornice (kapota), should be five parts in height.
One should construct the *khuraka* and the *vedibandha* with a height of three parts;
in width, it should be made double that height in all directions for this five-storied structure.
It should be adorned with lion-ears (*siṃhakarṇa*), chariots (*ratha*), bells, balconies (*bhramikā*), pillars, and arches (*toraṇa*).
Its construction is prescribed as being like that of the Puṣpaka;
this temple should be made with only a *sāndhāra* (enclosed) base by the wise.
It is a *yogapīṭha*.
Now we shall speak of the resonance of the bell; it should consist of five stages.
It should be made eight-cornered, and another, the Puṣpaka, by its configuration.
Bhairava, Bhadra, and Kālī should be established here, as well as the reciter.
The ringing of the bell.
Now we shall describe the *patākinam*, which is like a mass of clouds stirred by the wind;
it is Latin, having the form of a *latina*, and is divided in every direction.
One should fashion that for Caṇḍikā as a *rucaka* or a *vardhamānaka*.
I shall describe the *vṛkṣapatākina* [tree-bannered] formation, which is filled with trees possessing banners, just as follows: 192.
The *patākinaḥ*.
Now we shall describe the Guhādhara temple, which bestows prosperity, nourishment, and happiness.

When the site is divided into ten parts, the *bhadra* should be measured from the center of the sanctum (*garbha*). The projection of the *bhadra* should be made equal to half the measurement of the original sanctum.
The two ears, each consisting of one and a half parts, are placed on both sides.
A water-receptacle (jalādhā) should be made at the end of the root-ear on both sides.
In the middle of that doorway, however, one should install a pillar-gateway (stambhatoraṇa).
With a height twice its width, possessing four peaks and four faces, one should fashion it with a base, neck, girdle, and shanks like those of a lion; thus it shall become supported by a cave. 196.
The name of this palace was fashioned according to the distinction of its gates;
[it is called] Guhādhara.
Then we shall describe the *śālāka* (the hall); one should divide it into ten parts.

The two root-wings (*mūlakarṇau*) consist of two parts each, while the width of the central bay (*bhadra*) is six parts. The doors should be situated in the middle of the *bhadra*, equal in size to the main entrance.
Having four arms and four doors, this second type is indeed called Rucaka;
its name is proclaimed as Śālāka according to the measurement of its door,
while whatever other dimensions it may have would be like those of the Bhadraka.
Śālāka:
Now we shall speak of the *veṇuka* (the bamboo-pole), which should be square, even, and auspicious;
O noble one, one should not make it protrude beyond the measure of the umbrella itself for the sake of beauty. 201.
The height of the dome (kumbha) should be twice its width;

the pinnacle (śikhā) should be desired to be twice that measure, and the pillar-shaft (jaṅghā) is fashioned as one-third of that. The base-molding (khura-varaṇḍikā) should be made with a height equal to one-third of the shaft's elevation.
The *kapota* (dove-cornice) should be made with its inner leaf occupying one-sixteenth part [of the width].
One should draw the *veṇukośa* (bamboo-receptacle) using a cord reduced by one-fourth [the total width];
it should be made beautiful on all sides at the exit of the *kapota*.
On its front face, there should be lion-ears (siṃhakarṇas), excluding the candraśālas;
whatever its measurement may be, a bamboo-staff (veṇuka) is prescribed for it. (205) [The bamboo-staff.]
Now we shall describe the elephant, characterized by the marks of an elephant.
With half of the sūtra, one should draw a circle behind that [central] line.
The shank should be four parts, and the girdle (mekhalā) should be one and a half parts.
The wise man should make its back portion circular in shape.
In the halls, there should be "lion-ears" (siṃhakarṇas) on the sides, at the back, and at the front;
all these ears should also be filled with horns.
In the middle part, a Valabhī should be made, exceedingly beautiful; whatever its dimensions may be, it should be exactly as it was at the beginning. (209) [This concludes] the Kuñjara.
Now we shall describe the Harṣa temple, which is quadrangular and beautiful;
its height should be one and a half times its width, extending up to the top of the pinnacle.
One should construct a quadrangular covering form on all four sides.

The *śukanāsa* (frontal projection) is beautified by a well-executed finish; likewise, there is the elevation of the *jaṅghā*, the *mekhalā*, and the *surapiṇḍa*. The pinnacle of the bell, the *candraśālā* (dormer), and the *cchādyaka* (roof-covering) may be arranged according to one's preference.
One should establish another standard of measurement exactly as is pleasing to the mind;
this is the means of gladdening.
Now we shall describe the Vijaya temple, which is beautiful with its half-ornamentation.
One should divide it by means of the *vardhamāna* [measure];
one should place the projection of the *śukanāsa* (gargoyle) such that the height of the spire (*śikhara*) is reduced by one part. 213–214.
The two chariot-fronts on the left and right should have their tips and foremost points directed forward;
the bow should be drawn upward, full, and facing in all directions.
Both the Vijaya and the Vardhamāna [bows] are equal in measurement.
Because of the distinction of its vestibule (alinda), this [palace] is named Vijaya;
thus [ends the description of] Mahāpadma.
Now we shall describe the mansion (harmya) or palace (prāsāda); one should construct that as having a single story.
One should construct it of wood, square in shape, with cloth, beams, and walls;
it should have a covered walkway and a veranda on all sides,
topped above by a *tumbikā* and adorned with a cluster of lotuses.
One should adorn it with windows, lattices, altars, pillars, and arches; with gables, statues, and "lion-ears" (ornamental turrets). The width of this palace should be made equal to its height.
Harmyaḥ.
Now we shall fully describe the characteristics of Ujjayanta.
One should construct a temple here on ground measured according to the rules, adorned with a pavilion at the entrance;
it should have four doors and be provided with pavilions on all sides.
Every other means of knowledge for this [self] would be like that of a palace;
[this applies to] Ujjayanta.
Now we shall describe the characteristics of the Gandhamādana [temple].
The Gandhamādana palace should be constructed with the measurement of a *harmya*;
one should cause pavilions (*maṇḍapa*) to be built at its front and at its rear.

The lattice-work of the four-fold railings and other features on the left and right sides should be made according to the same proportions as those prescribed for the palace (harmya). This refers to Gandhamādana.
Now we shall describe the Śataśṛṅga [temple]; it should be equal to Triviṣṭapa. One should divide it into twenty parts and construct five [parts] for the base (bhauma).
The spires (kūṭas) should occupy two parts each, and there should be one hundred and one maṇḍas.
And on each successive level, there are peaks numbering one-tenth of the width of that level. Whatever its measurement may be, it should be like heaven (triviṣṭapa);
thus it is faultless.
Now we shall describe the *Vibhrānta* temple, which resembles the *Sarvatobhadra*.
One should construct it with supporting pillars and surrounded on all sides by pavilions (*maṇḍapa*).
One should provide lattice windows, altar-rings, and so forth, as well as four-sided porticos (*catuṣkikā*) in the cardinal directions.
Perplexed.
Now we shall describe the enchanting pavilion (maṇḍapa) as it should be:

that pavilion should have four doors in the cardinal directions, adorned with arches (toraṇas) and canopies; it should be provided with sacrificial altars, flower beds, water channels, and the like, as well as gateways, archways, and lattices.
It is completely filled with pitchers placed upon the surface of lion-thrones;

it has circular pillars covered by a *tulā* (beam), adorned externally with a roof-covering, and features lion, serpent, and elephant motifs on its panels, as well as arches supported by pillars at the entrance. ||230-231||
Furthermore, the measurement of the work is prescribed according to what is aesthetically pleasing,
so that it is captivating to the mind.
Regarding those two types—the circular and the elongated—we shall describe them; their form is like that of a conch shell.
In that [conch-like] form, the base is circular, the placement of the palm is square, and it consists of five parts.
From the top of the circular base, the circular portion rises as it appears most beautiful.
One should make another [type] with a long face, provided with a lion’s ear at the mouth;
[the other two types are] circular and circular-long.
We shall now describe the characteristics of a *caitya*: it should be provided with a dome (*śikhara*). Its shape and dimensions should be exactly as they are in the case of a circular [temple].
This is the *caitya*.
Now we shall describe the Kiṅkiṇīka, which has five domes and nine stories.
All these auspicious structures with circular domes should be fashioned with favorable characteristics; such is the Kiṅkiṇīka.
Now we shall describe the *layana* (temple-shrine); it arises from the excavation of rock.
It should be provided with ladders, ascending staircases, porticos, and windows;
with altars, circular ambulatories, and crowning cornices, as well as being joined with processional streets and gates. ||236-237||
The measurement for the neck-ornament (prāgrīva) of the carved [image] is as previously stated;
this is the sanctuary (layana).
Now we shall describe the *paṭṭiśa* banner, which originates from cloth:
it should be adorned with boars, web-footed birds, and clusters of altars; one desiring auspicious characteristics should provide it with a tortoise-back design. (238–239)
The sword.
That manifestation (vibhava) is said to be based on another [deity] such as Sūrya;
a wooden [image] should be joined with a wooden one, and that which arises from stone with one born of stone.
An earthen [image] should be made for an earthen [deity], and that which arises from a sacrificial altar (cayana) for one arising from a sacrificial altar.
In remote villages and market towns, it is constructed with wooden pillars.
It should be built by three righteous persons according to their means.
Wealth.
Now we shall describe the Tārāgaṇa [mandala]; it should take the form of a pavilion (maṇḍapa).

It is adorned with houses featuring cloth, rags, balances, and baskets, as well as swings, playful whirlpools, and dwellings made of cloth in various wonderful forms, along with bells, mirrors, and archways. ||242-243||
One should place here everything that is beautiful— such as banners, parasols, celestial chariots, and so forth, as well as tinkling bells;
this is the host of stars (tārāgaṇa).
By adding two more through specific combinations of eight-eighths,
these sixty-four types of palaces are formed;
these are declared to be the foremost among the vimānas.
"He who is born [under this asterism] shall be the foremost among the hosts of artisans.

(245) Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Sixty-Four Vimānas and Other Structures," in the *Vāstuśāstra*—also known as the *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*—composed by the Great King of Kings, Supreme Lord, the illustrious Bhojadeva.
Now begins the sixtieth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Thirty-Six Temples, beginning with the Śrīkūṭa."
Now we shall describe the twenty-six *prāsāda*s constructed in the Nāgara style.
Among them, the first is the *Sādhāra*; then follow the *Śrīkūṭa*, the *Śrīmukha*, the *Śrīdhara*, the *Badara*, and likewise the *Priyadarśana*.
Kulananda, Antarikṣa, Puṣpabhāsa, Viśālaka, Saṅkīrṇa,
Mahānanda, Nandyāvarta,
and another, Saubhāgya, Vibhaṅga, and immediately after that, Vibhava. ||2-3||
Then there are Bībhatsaka, Śrītuṅga, and another, Mānatuṅga;
then Rudrasaṃjña, and Bhavadvāhyodarastaca;
another is known as Niryūhodarasaṃjña, and from that, Samodara should be known.
Nandibhadra, Bhadra, Kośa, and Citrakūṭa after that; Vimala, Harṣaṇa, Bhadra, and Saṅkīrṇa immediately following;
then the one called Bhadra Viśāla and Bhadra Viṣkambha.
Ujjayanta by name, Sukha, Meru, Mandara, Kailāsa, Kumbhakākṣa, and Gṛharāja by name—
these thirty have been specified; their characteristics are now being described.
When the site has been made square and divided into twelve parts,
the wise man should divide the temple known as Śrīkūṭa, O beautiful one;
the largest shall be twenty cubits, and the medium fifteen.
The smallest [temple] is to be known as ten cubits in measurement;
the *bhadra* should have six parts of its width, and the ears (*karṇas*) should be made with two parts.
The *tilaka* should be made with one part, projecting out by one part.
Therefore, O Bhadra, it is prescribed that [the temple] shall emerge by one part.
The outer wall shall consist of one part, the *andhakārikā* (the dark space) two parts,
the inner wall of the womb-chamber one part, and the womb-chamber itself should be made four parts.
The lower part is designated as the *chanda* (base), and the upper part is called the *ūrdhvacchanda*.
The *jaṅghā* (shaft) should be half the width, and the *mekhalā* (girdle) should consist of one part.
The pinnacle (*śṛṅga*) should be three parts in height, and the second [pinnacle] should likewise be the same.
In the middle of the eastern pinnacle (pūrvaśṛṅga), that [ornament] should be fashioned by the wise. A tilaka measuring one and a half parts (sārdhabhāga) should be made, and another similar one;
above the second tilaka, it should be well-joined and endowed with beauty.
The *mañjarī* (flower-cluster) should be seven parts in height and six parts in width. The lower covering (*adhaśchādya*) of the *mañjarī* should be one part;
its width, however, should be divided into ten parts, and the remainder should be like the *śrīvatsa*.
The shoulder (skandha) is six parts in width, and the neck (grīvā) is half a part in height.
The dome (aṇḍaka) should be made one part, and the kumuda one and a half parts. The pinnacle (kalaśa), joined with a citron (bījapūraka), should be one and a half parts. ||17-18||
Above the second ear-ornament (karṇaśṛṅga) should be the root-cluster (mūlamañjarī),
rising to one-eighth of the height.
Its division into shoulders, neck, and so forth should be like that of the Śrīvatsa mark.
Thus has the Prāsāda known as Śrīkūṭasaṃkṣepa been fully described;
by constructing it, one rejoices in the celestial realm for three thousand divine ages.
This is the Śrīkūṭa.
Now, the measurement of the *lakṣma* is being described:
||21|| One should construct a pavilion here with dimensions equal to those of the palace; it should be square in length and width from the front. ||22||
The *bhadra* projections, the *karṇas*, and likewise the *tilakas* should be made;
in the middle, a square (*catuṣkikā*) should be constructed, equal in width to the *bhadra*. This [structure] is to be fashioned within the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*).
The elevation of the *jaṅghā-prāsāda* (the pillar-base) is prescribed to be equal to that of the *jaṅghā*.
The *mekhalā* (waist-band) is one part, as before.
The pillar is three parts in height, the pedestal (*vedī*) is one part, and the bell-capital (*ghaṇṭā*) is three parts. ||24-25||

The wise man should thus construct the pavilion for Śrīkūṭa, based on the sequence of five *yava*s for the *siṃhaka*, adorned with *siṃhakarṇa* ornaments, and excellently decorated with human figures and other limbs. ||26||
The pavilion of Śrīkūṭa is completed.
But when a beautiful vedikā (balustrade) is constructed on its very porch,
then that temple, known as Śrīmukha, shall bring happiness;
it is Śrīmukha.
When its lower corner (kūrpara) is square,
then it shall be the temple named Śrīdhara, a refuge for deities;
[this is] Śrīdhara.
But when its veranda is made devoid of the *bhadra* [projection],
O auspicious one, then that temple becomes the "Varada," bestowing boons and granting welfare.
It is called Varada.
When a single *bhadra* has been projected from this very [central bay],
then that palace becomes a *niryūha*, which is pleasing to behold—
pleasing to behold.
When the exit of this very [mandala] is fashioned as a *nandyāvarta*,
then it should be known as the *kulananda* temple, which brings about happiness;
[it is also called] *kulanandana*.
Thus ends the venerable group of six beginning with Kūṭa.
We shall now describe the intermediate [measurement]; its parts consist of twelve.
In the largest measurement, it is ten *karas* by twenty-six;
in the medium [measurement], the number of cubits is stated according to the medium measurement. (32–33)

The *bhadra* should extend five parts, and the ears (*karṇas*) should be made two parts wide. The width of the *tilakas* should be such that there is an interval between the *bhadra* and the ears. The projection (*nirgama*) of both the *bhadra* and the *tilaka* should be one and a half parts.
The *garbha* (inner sanctum) shall consist of sixteen parts; the width of the wall shall be one part.

The circumambulatory path (*pradakṣiṇā*) shall be two parts, and the outer wall shall be one part (*pada*). This has been described as the lower section (*adhaśchanda*); now we shall speak of the upper section (*ūrdhvataśchanda*).
The *jaṅghā* (pedestal) has a height of six parts, and the *mekhalā* (girdle) has a height of one part.
In the [remaining] height of three parts, the first *śikhara* (spire) is likewise [one part];
the second is equal to that, situated above the *tilaka*.
Below, the covering should consist of one part.
The spire (śikhara) should be made with a width equal to the interior (garbha), and its height should be six parts;
likewise, [the base] should be half the width of the interior.
Above the second peak is the root-cluster (mūlamañjarī) as previously described;
thus has the "Antarikṣa" been correctly explained,
because all the gods who dwell in celestial chariots (vaimānika) are fond of the intermediate space (antarikṣa).
The intermediate space.
In this very [plan], when it is made with eight parts, it is called the *alinda*;
then that temple, beautiful to behold, is to be known as the *puṣpābhāsa*.
This is the *puṣpābhāsa*.
Then, O auspicious one, his *malinda* is constructed;
from various palaces arises the beautiful *viśālaka*.
The *viśālaka*.
Then, O auspicious one, when it is joined with this [measure] and devoid of [the others],
it is proclaimed as the temple named Saṃkīrṇaka.
This is the Saṃkīrṇaka.
When the *nandikā* of the *saṃkīrṇaka* itself is made equal in parts by means of the exit (*nirgama*), then there arises the *mahānanda*.
This is *mahānanda*.
When the projection of the *nandikā* is equal to its width,
that temple is then known by the wise as the *Nandyāvarta*.
This is the *Nandyāvarta*.
The group of six concerning the intermediate space.
Now we shall describe the *saubhāgya* (the auspicious pavilion); it should consist of twelve bays (*pada*).
The best is twenty cubits, the middling is fifteen, and the smallest is thirteen;
thus, by measurement, the *saubhāgya* is of three kinds.
The *garbha* (central core) should consist of four parts; the *bhadra* (front projection) should be equal to that in width.
The *tilakas* (ornamental projections) should be half the size of the *bhadra*, and the ears (*karṇas*) should be made with two parts.
Two parts each should be assigned for the [side] projections, and likewise, there should be a single part for the outward extension of each.
One may provide for the exit of the auspicious [chambers] as a single share;
the inner wall of the womb-chamber shall be one share, the circumambulatory path (pradakṣiṇā) two shares,
the outer wall shall be one share, and the height of the plinth (jaṅghā) shall be six shares.
The girdle (mekhalā) is said to consist of one part; in its center there should be a pinnacle (śikhara).
Between the central dome (mallacchādya) and the pinnacle (śikhara), there should be a crest (śṛṅga).
That [crest] is one part in height, while the width of the flower-cluster (mañjarī) here is the same.
The wall of the inner sanctum (garbha) should be made equal [to the base], and its height should consist of seven parts.
Above the second pinnacle (śṛṅga), there should be a root-cluster (mūlamañjarī) as described previously;
the egg-base (aṇḍaka) and so forth should be as prescribed. This is proclaimed as the Saubhāgya [temple].
Fortunate.
When the *malindaka* is omitted from this very [layout],
then there shall be a most beautiful palace named *vibhaṅgaka*.
(54) The *vibhaṅgaka*.
O noble one, if this [brick] is removed from it, then again a most excellent palace named Vibhava arises. (55) Vibhava.
If the *nandikā* is made emerging from two parts,
then they call that the most excellent *prāsāda* known as *bībhatsa*. (56) *Bībhatsa*.
When the *nandikā* is equal in width to the projection (*nirgama*),
then that most excellent temple is to be known as the *śrītuṅga*. (57) [The *śrītuṅga*.]
But when an *alindaka* is constructed for this very [structure] and does not extend outward,
then the palace named Mānatuṅga arises. (58) [Mānatuṅga]
Now we shall describe the Sarvatobhadra; one should divide it tenfold.
The largest would be six times the smallest, which is ten cubits;
likewise, the middle-sized is proclaimed to be eighteen cubits.
The *karṇas* (corner projections) should be made two parts; the *alindas* (porches) should measure six *padas*.
The *bhadras* (central projections) should be four parts, with their outward extension being one part.
The inner sanctum wall (*garbha-bhitti*), the outer wall (*bahiḥ-bhitti*), and the *andhārī* (blind wall) should each be one *pada*.
The *garbha* (inner sanctum) is said to consist of sixteen squares; such is the description of the *chanda*.
The *jaṅghā* (plinth) should be half the width [of the garbha], and the *mekhalā* (waistband) one part.
One should first fashion the *śṛṅga* (spire), which is one and a half times its width in height.
The second peak there is small and situated in the middle of the eastern peak;
it is desired that six [units] be raised toward the south at the divine summit.
Likewise, the base summit should be made for the two upper peaks.
The wise one should divide the width of the *mañjarī* into ten parts;
the trunk (*skandha*) shall have a width of six parts, while the bow-shaped neck (*dhanurgrīvā*), the egg-shaped part (*aṇḍaka*), and so forth,
should be fashioned like the *śrīvatsa* according to the measurement of the parts of the *mañjarī*.
Or, adorned with the forms of five lions, it may be half the size of the *krama*. Thus has been described the *sarvatobhadra*, which brings about auspiciousness—
the *sarvatobhadra*.
When an auspicious *alinda* (veranda) is likewise constructed for this very [structure],
then it becomes the most excellent of palaces, known as the *bāhyodara*.
This is the *bāhyodara*.
If there is no *alinda* (veranda), but rather a single [projection] extending outward,
then that most excellent palace is called *niryūhodara*.
Thus ends the section on *niryūhodara*.
When there is no *bhadra* there, there should be an exit for the *nandikā*.
Then one should know the *bhadra-kośa*, the sixth and most excellent temple.
This is the *bhadra-kośa*.
The Sarvatobhadra is a sixfold [pattern]. Now we shall describe Citrakūṭa; one should worship it with eight squares.
One should extend it from eight squares up until there are twenty squares.

The width of the *karṇabhāgika* (corner sections) is the extent of the remaining *alinda*s (porticos). One should know that the *bhadra* (central projection) consists of four *padas* and extends out by one *bhāga*.
The *alinda* extends out by one *bhāga*, supported by a wall at every *pada*. ||71-72||
Its womb should consist of two parts; it is desired that the top and the base be level.
The dome (aṇḍaka) should be made with one part, and it should be gradually tapered in sequence.
Above the second pinnacle (śṛṅga), the root-cluster (mūlamañjarī) must be fashioned.
Rising seven parts as before, with a length of six parts;
one should construct such a temple as Citrakūṭa according to these proportions.
This is Citrakūṭa.
When Bhadrā, who has emerged from the cow-pen, becomes his very own,
then the palace named Vimala arises;
it is stainless.
But when its *alinda* is made inferior to this very [main hall], O Bhadra,
then that palace is known by the name Harṣaṇa.
This is the Harṣaṇa.
But when the elbow of this very [bhadra] is made to project by one part,
then, O Bhadra, an auspicious *saṃkīrṇa-bhadra* temple is produced.
This is the *saṃkīrṇa-bhadra*.
But when one part of this very *bhadra* has emerged,
then the temple is named *Bhadraviśālaka*.
It is called *Bhadraviśālaka*.
When this [temple] is constructed even without the *bhadra* [protrusion],
then the *bhadra-viṣkambha* temple shall be a bestower of good dreams.
This is the *bhadra-viṣkambha*.
The group of six beginning with Citrakūṭa.
On a square and level site divided by eight sets of eight [parts],
one should construct the most beautiful Ujjayanta temple;
one square shall be the corner, and the tilaka shall be of the same measure.
A wise man should construct the auspicious [temple] according to the measurement including the inner wall;
the outer wall shall be one part, the circumambulatory path (pradakṣiṇā) one part, and the inner wall one part;
and in the middle of the interior (garbha), there shall be four pādas.

The shank should be measured at five parts; there, the girdle (mekhalā) should be one part. The first horn (śṛṅga) with its base (aṇḍaka) should be made one part, and the second horn with its base should be half a part, equal to that, situated in the middle of the foot.
The *mallacchādya* (the coping covering) should be fashioned with a height of half a part;
the pinnacle (*śikhara*) should have a height equal to one module (*pada*), being the same as the thickness of the inner chamber wall (*garbhabhitti*).
A finial (*kalaśa*) should be made one part high, and the banner-staff (*dhvajaśaṅku*) should be of the same height.
One should make the base of this pinnacle six parts in width;
its height should be made one part greater by one who desires prosperity.
Above the *ṛtilaka* spire, the pinnacle should be one *pada* high.
One should cause the remaining portion, fifty [units] in width, to be fashioned like the Śrīvatsa.
Thus has the temple named Ujjayanta been correctly described;
this temple, characterized by auspicious marks, is to be constructed for every deity.
Ujjayanta.
Just as the palaces beginning with Vimala arose from Citrakūṭa, so too are the five beginning with Meru considered to have arisen from Ujjayanta:
Meru, Mandara, Kailāsa, and Kumbha. ||89-90||
These palaces, endowed with auspicious characteristics, are called "kings of houses. Here, one hundred and eight types of palaces have been described by the wise,
categorized as superior, middling, and inferior, as well as those with common foundations.
Among them, some are provided with *alinda* verandas, and some are encircled by *bhadra* projections.
Some palaces should be made identical in color, all of them being most beautiful;
indeed, all these must be constructed according to their established proportions.

The corners should not be made uneven, nor is a division of the sections (vargabheda) desired. Those [mandalas] proclaimed to be one cubit or two cubits in size belong to the Yakṣas, Nāgas, houses, and so forth, as well as to the Rākṣasas.
One should designate the smoke as threefold by means of its parts:
superior, middling, and inferior; this should be understood according to the measurement of its portions.
The superior is known to be three and a half cubits, while the middling is known to be three cubits. ||95-96||
The smallest [image] is prescribed as measuring two and a half cubits;
the largest is three cubits, while the other, the medium, is one cubit [in addition].
Half a cubit is proclaimed as the measurement for the portion of the smallest.

The largest portion should be two cubits (dvihasta), the middle one three-quarters of a cubit (pādona-kara), and the smallest half of the middle portion; such is the measurement of the portions in cubits. These thirty-six [varieties] are diverse.
The state of being a guest at Śrīkūṭaka and other such places arises from the wind.
The principal palaces here are divided into six groups,
including the pavilions.

Thus ends the sixtieth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Thirty-Six Palaces Beginning with Śrīkūṭa," in the *Vāstuśāstra* named *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*, composed by the Great King of Kings, the Supreme Lord, the illustrious Bhojadeva.

Now begins the sixty-first chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Five Pīṭhas. Now we shall describe the auspiciously characterized temples (prāsādas), which may consist of one floor up to twelve floors.
The pedestals (pīṭhas) are also described according to five characteristics;
among them, those with auspicious marks have five types of base designs (talacchandas).
Of these, the first pedestal is the most excellent, characterized by a foot-binding (pādabandhana).
The second is called Strībandha, and the third is Vedibandhana;
the fourth, the most excellent seat (pīṭha), is declared to be Pratikrama;
and the fifth seat is designated by the name Kṣurakabandhana. ||3-4||
These five pedestals have been described here in brief.
One should divide the height of the base-band (pādabandhana) into twenty parts:
the *khuraka* should consist of five parts, and the lotus-leaf ornament (*padmapatrikā*) two parts.
A *kaṇikā* (central circle) should be made one part; the *kumuda* (lotus petal) should be three parts.
The *kaṇṭha* (neck) should be one part, and the *kaṇa* (bud) two parts.
The *paṭṭikā* (band) should be one part, and the *padmapaṭṭikā* (lotus band) one part.
One should make the *kapota* (dove-cornice) three parts together with the nose (the *nāsikā*).
One part shall be the *cheda* (projection) on the pedestal known as the *pādabandha*.
The entry of the lotus-leaf (*padmapattrī*) from the *khuraka* (plinth) shall be two finger-breadths.
Its *grāsa* (projection) shall be six *aṅgulas*, and its *kumuda* (fillet) shall extend seven [units] outward;
the inward projection should likewise be as far as the *vicchedapaṭṭikā* (separation-band).
One should cause the *chedapaṭṭa* (cutting-band) to have a projection of six *aṅgulas*.
The entire framework should be constructed for both the *cheda* and the *kaṇika*.
From that, by way of its projection, the neck-band (*kaṇṭhapaṭṭikā*) shall be two finger-breadths wide.
Its lotus-leaf projection shall be three finger-breadths.
For the *kāpotta* [moulding], its [height] shall be three finger-breadths (12).
This is declared to be the *pādabandha*, consisting of the arrangement of the fillets (*paṭṭikā*) and the cuts made along equal lines; now the *śrībandha* is described. (13)
One should divide the measurement of the pedestal (pīṭha) into twenty-seven parts;
the *tīḍavarti* should be four parts, the lotus petal (*padmapatrikā*) two parts,
the pericarp (*kaṇikā*) one part, and the water lily (*kumuda*) three parts.
One should know one part as the *cheda*, and likewise one part for the *meḍa* and the *ratha*.
One part is for the *makara*, and one part for the *makarapaṭṭikā*.
One should know one part as the *cheda*, and likewise one part for the neck (*kaṇṭha*). ||15-16||
One part for the fillet (paṭṭikā), then one part for the altar (vedī);
one square unit (ekapada) should be made for the cut (cheda), and then the neck (kaṇṭha) should be two parts.
One part for the fillet, and [then] the lotus-leaf ornament (padmapatrikā).
One should fashion three parts consisting of a pigeon-shaped element joined with a tube;
one should also make a portion for the cut on the pedestal named Śrībandha.
This is declared to be Śrībandha; now the Vedībandha is described. ||18-19||
One should divide the width of the pedestal (pīṭha) by nineteen parts.
The inner chamber (nīḍa) occupies four parts, and the lotus petal (padmapatrikā) two parts. One should know that the pericarp (kaṇikā) is one part, and the lily (kumuda) likewise three parts.
The wise [architect] should fashion a one-unit (pada) cut; likewise, the meṇṭha should be one unit (tara). With one part, he should make the crocodile (makara) and the crocodile-band (makarapaṭṭikā);
the cut should be one unit, the neck one unit, and the lotus-leaf ornament one unit.
One should make the *bhāgikī* [moulding] and the *kumuda* should be three parts;
one should know the *cheda* to be one part, and from that, the *kaṇṭha* should be two parts.
One should make the *paṭṭikā* one part, and the [next] *paṭṭikā* one part.
Two parts shall be for the girth-band, while the covering should be a strip.
Thus is the stool described for each successive stage; now the binding of the razor is explained.
A wise man should divide the height of the stool into twenty parts. ||24-25||
The *nīravartī* shall consist of four parts—the *padmapatrikā*;
the *kaṇikā* shall be one part, and the *kumuda* beyond that shall be two parts. The *meḍa* and *akṣepa* shall each be one part, and the *makara* likewise one part. (26)
One part should be set aside for the makara-band;
then one should fashion the makara-pattern with a cut, followed by a neck of one part. One should know the band to be one part, and the lotus-leaf ornament likewise one part.

One should fashion the *kapota* (dove-cornice) with three parts, and then together with the nose (the *nāsikā*), a cut (*cheda*) of one part should be made; this is declared to be the *kṣurabandha*. That which was previously described as the "fivefold pedestal" (*pīṭhapañcaka*) has already been laid out by the measuring line (*sūtrita*).
Above the pedestal (pīṭha), the wise should recognize the excellent plinth (khuravaraṇḍikā).
There are other pedestals as well, manifold according to the differences in their characteristics;
among them, this pentad is proclaimed because of its excellence.
Now we shall describe the palaces (prāsāda) immediately following the ground plans (talacchanda).
In that regard, five palaces are proclaimed: Padma, Mahāpadma, Vardhamāna, as well as another, Svastika, and Sarvatobhadra.
Once the field has been made square, one should stretch the diagonal cord (karṇasūtra).
Then, having taken half of that diagonal, one should lead it out from the center by one eye’s measure (dṛk).
By dropping a cord from the tips of those two [lines], another square will be formed. ||33-34||
The wise one should construct the peak with two parts;
he should fashion the interior water-chamber in the shape of a boar’s snout.
Thus, in all peaks, an interior water-chamber is desired.

When the length has been divided into four parts by means of a cord, the inner sanctum (garbha) shall consist of two parts; by that [measure], the wall is said to be one part. Taking half of the sanctum and the corner-projections (karṇa), one should then mark the corners. ||36-37||
In the middle of the eight [petals] it should be thus, and likewise on the outside. In this manner, the *padmatalacchanda* should be laid out by the wise.
Now we shall explain the *mahāpadmatalacchanda*.

One should apply those [measurements] which were previously proclaimed as the *sampātas* established by the rules, within the cardinal and intermediate directions. Therein, one should cause half of the diagonal (*karṇa*) to be given, extending from the path constructed in the outer portion. ||39-40||
From the mark situated between the directions of Īśāna and Agni,
one should extend [the line] toward that which lies between Nairṛti and Yāmya;
from the midpoint between Nairṛti and Yāmya, one should extend toward the intermediate points of Vāyu and Ambu.
Between the directions of Vāyu (the northwest) and Āpaḥ (the west), and between the directions of Īśa (the northeast) and Soma (the north),
[one should place] the third [letter]— the interior of the *kūṭa*—
between the two *kūṭas*, resembling a boar's face.
This *talacchanda* known as Mahāpadma, honored by kings, has been described. Now, the *talacchanda* of the Vardhamāna [temple] is being declared.
First, one should divide the square field into fifteen parts.

The *kūṭa* shall consist of two parts, with an interval of water [between it and the next element]. (45) The *pañjara* shall consist of one and a half parts, with an interval of water. The *śālā* shall consist of four parts; and there shall be two types of *vidadhyā* within the *pañjara*. (46)
In these halls, the entrance for the water-channel shall be half a part;
it should be eight finger-breadths protruding outward and of auspicious appearance.
For the water-channel within the cage, the entrance shall be one-quarter of a part.
The entrance shall occupy half a part;
the space for water should be made equal to one-third of a part.
Immediately thereafter, one should construct the cage (pañjara) measuring one and a half parts.
One part is correctly described as the *talacchanda* (ground plan):
one should divide an equal square field into twenty-eight parts.
One should make the *kūṭa* (pinnacle) four parts, and the interval between the waters [the *salilāntara*] [should be likewise].
The *pañjara* (lattice-work) should likewise be three parts, and the intervening space for water two parts.
One should make the hall (*śālā*) six parts and the waterway two parts.
Again, the *pañjara* should be three parts, adorned with a moon-shaped *śālā*.
One should again divide it into two parts; the fourth part shall be the water-interval (salilāntara), and one should fashion the very beautiful chariot-pavilion (rathaka) as four parts.
In this manner, one should arrange [the layout] in all directions with equal divisions.
Then, in that field divided into four parts, one should construct the central core (garbha) occupying two parts.
In both the Svastika and Vardhamāna types, the walls are prescribed to be one part each;
this most enchanting ground-plan is called the Svastika.
Now the *talacchanda* known as *sarvatobhadra* is described.
Having made the site square, one should construct the central core (*garbha*) occupying two parts.
One should construct the pinnacle (*kūṭa*) occupying three parts and the water-channel (*jalamārga*) occupying two parts.
Then, one should make a pinnacle (kūṭa) occupying three parts, and the water-path two parts;
the hall (śālā) should be eight parts, and the water-path two parts;
furthermore, a pinnacle of three parts, and the space between waters two parts. ||57-58||
In the four directions, there should be fourteen chariot-paths (rathikās), each consisting of three parts.
When the square field has been divided into twenty-eight parts,
one should construct a kūṭa (pavilion) occupying three parts out of the fourfold division.
The walls should be made one part [in thickness], and likewise the inner sanctum (garbha) two parts;
thus is this Sarvatobhadra temple type prescribed according to its proportions.
These have been described as being without pillars (nirandhāra); now we shall describe those with pillars (sāndhāra). ||60-61||
One should divide the square-shaped field into twelve parts.
One-fourth of that shall be the inner sanctum (garbha), and the walls are prescribed to be one part each. Likewise, the foundation beam (andhārikā) is one part, and the outer walls are two parts.

Thus have these, beginning with Padma, which have the talacchanda as their base, been fully described. In this way, these five types of pedestals (pīṭhas) have been stated according to the names and characteristics of the temples (prāsādas).
"By understanding these five varieties of *talacchanda* (floor-plans) that have been proclaimed, one attains honor in the world.

Thus ends the sixty-first chapter, titled "The Fivefold Pedestal," in the architectural treatise (*Vāstuśāstra*) named *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*, composed by the Great King of Kings, the Supreme Lord, the illustrious Bhojadeva.
Now begins the sixty-second chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Drāviḍa Temple.
Next, we shall describe the vertical measurement starting from the base up to the pinnacle;
one should maintain this proportion for all [temples] according to the measurement of the *karṇa* (corner pillar).
Therein, the pedestal for a single-level [shrine] should be five cubits in width,
two finger-breadths [in thickness], and seven cubits in height;
the base should be two cubits in height and adorned with all ornaments.
The height is one and a half cubits, and its extent is the same up to the ceiling-beam (starāvadhi).
The garland-molding (mālā) is said to be two beams; the ceiling-beam (stara) is a *laśunaka*.
The support (bharaṇa) shall be one beam, and half of that support shall be two beams.
One should know that following the *kalaśa* [stage] is the *uttara*, accompanied by the *vārarā* and others;
one should then form the *kulaka* twice as wide, provided with lotus petals.
Furthermore, above that, one should again form a single *stara* consisting of the *vīragaṇḍā*.
The diamond-pattern (hīraka) is said to be two layers thick, and the cloth-strip (paṭṭa) is likewise;
the band (paṭṭikā) shall be one layer, while the spring-pattern (vasanta) is known to be two layers.
Above that, the spring-band (vasantapaṭṭikā) is prescribed to be one layer thick.
One should fashion a *kapota* (dove-cornice) provided with a nose-piece (*nāsikā*) consisting of three layers;

one should then make the interval between them a single layer, followed by that. One should likewise make a *makara* [projection] of the same measurement as the layer, as well as the *makara-paṭṭikā*.
One should again make a cut (cheda) and a layer (stara); then follows the binding of the altar (vedībandha) and a layer.
The neck (kaṇṭha) should be equal in measure to the layer, and then twice that for the layer. The fillet (paṭṭikā) is one layer, and likewise the lotus-fillet (ambujapaṭṭikā).
The height from the garland-base (mālā) to the end of the lotus-petal is said to be two cubits;
the height of the pinnacle (kūṭa) is proclaimed to be one and a half cubits.
Above that, it should be joined with a nose (nāsikā) and a lotus, and then there shall be a pitcher (kalaśa).
This measurement of a single-storied palace is proclaimed for a one-level structure.
||12|| One level.
Now, the characteristics of a two-storeyed palace are described:
it should be seven cubits in width and [seven] in height. Its division according to the measurement of the corner (karṇa) is now declared.
One should fashion the seed-syllable (bīja) as two cubits, and the shank (jaṅghā) as two and a half cubits.
This arrangement of the pinnacle (kūṭa) should be understood as consisting of equal parts;
furthermore, its second shank is to be made of one part.

The arrangement of the second kūṭa should consist of half a part; it should extend in all directions and, together with the neck (kaṇṭha), measure one part. Above that, the bell (ghaṇṭā) should be raised by one and a half parts.
The wise one should fashion [the pedestal] joined with a nose-lotus.
One should thus arrange the five types of pedestals previously mentioned—known by names such as *pādabandha* and so forth—in sequence, beginning from the base (*bhūmi*). 17–18.
Whatever may bring beauty to them should be executed by the wise architect;
above that, there should be a *jaṅghā* (plinth) adorned with garlands and the like.
There should likewise be an *bharaṇa* (frieze) and a *kalaśa* (pitcher), provided with door-panels and side-projections.
First, the *ucchāla* should be made according to the previous measurement, and then ten thousand *padmapatra*s;
furthermore, the *vīragaṇḍa* should be fashioned, and the *hīra* according to the previous sequence.
Above that, there should be a *paṭṭa* together with a *paṭṭikā*.
Above the *vasantavedī*, there is a fillet (*paṭṭikā*) upon that very [element];
then the *kapotaccheda* and the *meḍhakara*; then the *makarōṣṭhī* fillet, then the *bhedakaṇṭha*, and then a fillet.
The *vedīccheda*, the *kaṇṭha*, the *paṭṭikā*, and the *padmapaṭṭikā* [are to be made];

above that, one should fashion a *kūṭa* (pinnacle) that is variegated and provided with a *nāsikā* (nose-ornament). All of this is prescribed according to the previous measurement up to the end of the *cheda*. ||23-24||
Above that, moreover, is the shank, adorned with all ornaments;
then a garland, then garlic, then an archway, then a water-pot;
likewise a hero’s cheek-piece, an uchchāla, a leaf-pattern, and a hero’s cheek-piece.
Likewise, there is the *hīraka*, the *paṭṭikā*, and again the *vasantapaṭṭikā* (26).
Then the *kapotaccheda*, the *meḍha*, the *makara*, and its *paṭṭikā*;
the *cheda*, the *karapaṭṭikā*, the *vedīccheda*, and then the *kaṇṭhaka* (27).
A band, preceded by a lotus, should be fashioned;
then a cut should be made, provided with all ornaments.
Having thus cut it, it should be fashioned in such a way that beauty is produced.
Furthermore, a neck-piece should be provided, as well as a band and a lotus-band.
Then the neck should be fashioned, adorned with a garland of moons;
thereafter, the wise artisan should make a cut at the top.
Above that neck-band, another neck-band should be provided;
the projection of the bell from there should be seven finger-breadths.
Its width should be half a part, and its height half of that width.
In this way, the wise one should construct a two-storied palace. (32) [This concludes] the two-storied [palace].
Now, we shall describe the third palace, which has three stories;
its width is eleven cubits and its height fifteen cubits, with these [cubits] being increased by fourteen finger-breadths. (33)
This measurement for the ear-moulding (karṇa) of the ground-floor is beyond doubt.
One should first construct a pedestal (pīṭha) measuring two cubits there, as previously indicated;
the height of the shaft (jaṅghā) should be three parts, while the height of the capital (kūṭa) should be one part. ||34-35||
Then the third *jaṅghā* (pillar-shaft) should be two and a half parts;
then there is one part for the *kūṭaprasara* (the cornice-projection), adorned with a *candraśālā* (dormer-window).
Again, the third *jaṅghā* should be two parts in height.
Then follows the *akūṭaprastāra*, which is divided into parts and adorned with ornaments (37).
The division should be a *vedibandha*— possessing qualities, doors, and necks—
and this [structure] should be made as the fourteenth [unit], appropriately endowed with ornaments (38).
The bell-section (ghaṇṭāccheda) consists of two parts, each increased by two finger-breadths;
the eleventh tier (tarā), known as the Kuru, is prescribed above it.
Now, its division from the pedestal (pīṭha) upwards is described.
One cubit shall be the height of the base (jaṅghā), and the neck (grīvā) is said to be equal to that.
The garland-moulding (mālā) is declared to be two spans wide; then the garlic-moulding (laśuna) is one part, the fillet (bharaṇa) shall be one span, and the pitcher (kalaśa) is also equal to that.
Then, one should know that the *vīragaṇḍa* is joined with an *ucchāla* of two *tara*s;
then the *vīragaṇḍa* [is followed by] one *tara*,
[and then] a *hīraka* of two *tara*s, and a *vāsantapaṭṭikā* of six *tara*s.
Then one should have the *kapota* (dove-cornice) made with a nose [projection], three *stara*s in height;
the *cheda* (cutting) should be one *prastha* in measure, and the *meḍha* (phallus/pinnacle) should be of the same dimension.
One should make a *makara* (crocodile) of half a *stara*, and its fillet (*paṭṭikā*) should be half of that.
One should likewise make a *cheda* (projection), and then a neck (*kaṇṭha*) of one *tara*;
a *paṭṭikā* (band) and a *vedikā* (pedestal) are each prescribed as one *tara*. One should know the *cheda* to be half a *tara*, and the neck thereafter to be one and a half *taras*.
There should be a band (paṭṭikā) of one unit, and then a lotus (padma) of one unit;
in the remainder, the beautiful neck (kaṇṭha) should be fashioned by the wise.
Immediately after that, the second shank (jaṅghā) should be made of nine units.
And that [central part] should be constructed in the middle; above that, one should divide it.
From that, the *tara* (beam) becomes the hall (*śālā*), and half of the *tara* is the *laśuna*.
In the same way, the *bharaṇa* is to be understood according to the characteristics previously specified.
The *kalaśa* (pitcher) should likewise be provided with a *vīragaṇḍa*.
They know the *stara* (bedding) as being joined with a *padmapatraka* (lotus-leaf);
one should understand the *vīragaṇḍa* as the *stara*, and the *hīraka* (diamond/jewel) as half its portion.
One should likewise fashion the *paṭṭa* (fillet) with half the measure of the *stara* (course);
the *vasanta* (spring-course) should be one *stara*, and the *vāsantapaṭṭikā* (spring-fillet) should be one *stara*.
The wise man should make the *kapota* (dove-cornice) three *staras* in height, provided with a *nāsikā* (nose-ornament).
One should know that the *cheda* (cut) is half a *stara*; the *meḍha* (penis) is equal to that.
Then there is one *stara* for the *makara* (crocodile), and from that, a *paṭṭikā* (band) of half a *bhāga*.
The *cheda* shall be one *bhāga*, and above that, a *stara* for the *kaṇṭha* (neck).
A paṭṭikā and a vedikā are prescribed as a single layer;
one should make the cheda half a part (bhāga) and the kaṇṭhaka one and a half parts. One should make the paṭṭikā with one part, and likewise the lotus-leaf ornament.
Beyond that, one should fashion the *kūṭa* (the pinnacle) and the decorated nose;
the third leg should consist of two [parts] fashioned with four tiers (*stara*).
One tier is known as the *mālā*, and another tier they know as the *laśuna*.
One should construct a *bharaṇa* with one *stara*, and likewise a *kumbha* with one *stara*;
above that, there should be an *ucchāla* provided with a *vīragaṇḍa*.
One should make a *stara* elevated with a *vīragaṇḍa*.
Then the wise [architect] should fashion the *hīraka* with one part;
the *paṭṭi* should consist of one and a half parts, and the *stara* likewise half a *paṭṭikā*. The *vasanta* should be one *stara*, and the *vāsantapaṭṭikā* one *stara*. (58–59)
The *kapota* (dove-cornice) is two units in width; the *meṇḍhaka* (frog-moulding) is half a unit;
the *makara* (crocodile) should be made one unit; and the *paṭṭikā* (band) is half a unit.
The *bheda* (projection) is half a unit, and the *kaṇṭha* (neck) is proclaimed to be one full unit.
The three— the frieze (paṭṭikā), the railing (vedikā), and the neck (kaṇṭha)— should each be half a story (ardhastara) in height; the pedestal (pīṭhikā) should be made half a part (ardhabhāgika),
and above that, the lotus-leaf ornament (padmapatrikā) should be made with half a part.
Then the pinnacle (kūṭa) is fashioned, endowed with various characteristics;
there should be one layer (stara), and the neck (kaṇṭha) should likewise be so.
The fillet (paṭṭikā) should consist of one layer, and from that, the altar-base (vedī) should consist of two layers.
The *cheda* (cutting) should be one *stara* (unit), and the neck (*kaṇṭha*) should then be two *staras*.
For each [element] to be constructed, there should be one *stara*; the *paṭṭikā* (band) and the *padmapatrikā* (lotus-leaf ornament) [are likewise].
Beyond that, the bell (*ghaṇṭā*) should be made with a measurement of twenty *staras*.
The eleventh story shall be a dome (kumbha) for all [the stories] on every side.
This has been described as having three levels; now the four-level [stūpa] is being discussed.
(66) [End of the section on] the three-level [stūpa].
One should determine the field to be fifteen cubits in width;
its height, however, should be twenty-one cubits.
One should have a pedestal made two cubits high and the plinth (jaṅghā) three cubits in height.
The pinnacle (kūṭa) should be one and a half cubits and adorned with all ornaments.
The second leg should be made three cubits minus one foot;
above that, one should make another pinnacle measuring one and a quarter cubits.
Then the third leg should be made two and a half cubits;
thereafter, the kūṭaprastāra is prescribed to be one cubit.
Then the fourth leg should be made two and a half cubits.
Then, the kūṭaprastāra is prescribed as one cubit (hasta).
The fourth element, the jaṅghā, should be made two and a quarter cubits high;
the kūṭaprastāra is one cubit, and the vedībandha is likewise.
The bell should be made with a width equal to half its height and a height of three cubits;
the pitcher (kumbha), consisting of fourteen sections, is situated above all [the other parts].
This division is now described according to the number of fingers (sūcī) for each hand.
The pedestal (pīṭha) shall have a height of two cubits; this is called the "ornamentation of the shank" (jaṅghālaṅkṛti).
One-tenth [of the height] should be one "projection" (ucchāla), and from that, the "star" (stara) is twice as wide.
One should know the "heroic cheek" (vīragaṇḍa) to be one stara, and the "diamond" (hīraka) should be twice as wide.
The *paṭṭa* should be understood as being likewise; from that, the *paṭṭikā* is the height. The *vasanta* is two units wide—this is the *vāsantapaṭṭi*.
The *kapota* should be made three units wide, and a projection (*cheda*) of one unit is prescribed.
One should make the *meḍha* (the base) two *staras* wide; the *paṭṭikā* (fillet) of the neck should be made one *bhāga*.
Then, in the *tataccheda* (the carved section), there should be one *bhāga*.
Again, one should make the neck two *staras*, and from that, the *paṭṭikā* [should be one *bhāga*].
Likewise, there may be a lotus-leaf ornament, and from that, a bell with five tiers;
then one should place a pitcher (kumbha) endowed with the proper characteristics,
and then a second pillar for the shaft (jaṅghāstambha) measuring eight parts.
One should make the garland (mālā) two parts wide; then the garlic (laśuna) should be one part.
The base (bharaṇa) should be one part, and the pitcher (kalaśa) should be of that same measurement.
It should be joined with a hero-moulding (vīragaṇḍa), and the projection (ucchālaka) should be of the same dimension.
That [the *vīragaṇḍa*] should be known as two *stara*s in width; the *vīragaṇḍa* itself is one *stara*. One should know that the *hīraka* is two *stara*s, and the *padma* is likewise.
The *paṭṭikā* should be one *stara*, and the *vasanta* thereafter is two *stara*s.

One should construct the *vasantapaṭṭikā* as one part, and the *kapota* as three stories high. The *bheda* should be one part, the *meḍhaka* one story, the *makara* one story, and likewise the *makarapaṭṭikā*. ||83-84||
The neck (kaṇṭha) should be one *stara*, the fillet (*paṭṭikā*) one part and one *stara*, and the pedestal (*vedikā*) one *stara*;
one should fashion the cut-out (*cheda*) with half [the measure].
One should make the neck one and a half *staras* and the fillet one *stara*.
One should fashion the bell (ghaṇṭā) as four-tiered, dividing it into portions according to the proportionate lines (ābhājapatrikā).
It should be adorned with a neck (grīva) at the front; above that, one should fashion a pitcher (kumbha).
In the third [section], the pillar-shaft (jaṅghāstambha) consists of seven parts, with four [parts] for the base.

Then, for each successive layer (stara), there should be a garland (mālā), garlic (laśuna), a support (bharaṇa), a pitcher (kumbha), a pillar-base (kāṇḍaka), a protrusion (ucchāla), a cheek-piece (gaṇḍaka), and a diamond (hīra).
One should know that the lotus (padma) occupies one and a half layers, and likewise, the fillet (paṭṭikā) occupies half a part (ardhabhāga).
One part should be for the *vasanta* (spring), and one part for the *vāsantapaṭṭikā* (spring-band).
One should make the *kapota* (dove-cot) three courses (*stara*) high, and then the *cheda* (cutting) one course. Thereafter, one should construct the *meḍhaka* and the *mara*, each one course high.
The *paṭṭikā* (fillet) shall be half a *bhāga*, the *bheda* (projection) likewise half a *bhāga*;
the *kaṇṭha* (neck), the *vedi* (altar-base), and the *paṭṭikā*—these three [elements] shall each be one *stara* per layer.
The *cheda* (cut-out) shall be half a *stara*, and the *kaṇṭha* thereafter shall be one and a half *staras*.

A band (paṭṭikā) should be made at half a share, and the lotus-leaf ornament (padmapatrikā) should be of the same measure. The bell (ghaṇṭā) should consist of four shares and be provided with three-fold door-projections (guṇadvāra).
One should cause the pitcher (kumbha), situated above the bell, to be made twice as wide.
Thus, this third stage has been described; now the fourth is being told.

The *paṭṭarā* (pedestal) and the *jaṅghā* (shaft) should be fashioned together with great pillars (*mahāstambha*). Furthermore, there should be a garland (*mālā*), garlic (*laśuna*), as well as an ornament (*bharaṇa*) and a pitcher (*kumbha*).
The *ucchāla*, *gaṇḍaka*, and *hīra* are each [one] *prādeśa* [in measure].
The *pāḍa* shall be one and a half parts (*sārdhabhāga*), and from that, the *paṭṭikā* is half a *tara*. The *vasanta* shall be one *tara*, and its corresponding *paṭṭikā* is one *tara*. 95–96.
One should know the *kapota* to be two *stara*s in height, and the *cheda* to be half a *stara* from that;
likewise, the wise one should make the *meḍha* and the *makara* one *stara*.
They know the *paṭṭikā* called *makara* to have a *cheda* of one *stara*.
One *tara* shall be the neck (*kaṇṭha*), and half a *tara* the fillet (*paṭṭikā*).
Likewise, one should construct the altar-base (*vedikā*), and again half a *tara* for the cut (*cheda*).
The wise man should make the region of the neck consist of one and a half parts.
The band, however, should be designated as the liquor-mark and prescribed as one *stara*;
the bell should be made of two *staras* and adorned with triple-guṇa door-ornaments.
One should fashion a jar above it, measuring two *staras*, with the face of a lotus.
One part shall be the cut (cheda); from that, the neck (kaṇṭha) shall be two layers (staras).
The fillet (paṭṭikā) shall be one layer, while the pedestal (vedikā) shall be both [layers].
Again, there shall be a cut of one part; the neck is thus prescribed.
There should be one layer of wooden planks and likewise one layer of lotus-leaf patterns;
there shall be twenty layers, and the bell should have a width equal to half that of the inner sanctum (garbha). Beautiful moon-chambers (candraśālās) should be constructed on all four sides.

In this same manner, a wise man should fashion this bell for the *padma*, *mahāpadma*, *svastika*, *vardhamānaka*, and likewise for the *sarvatobhadra* designs. He should make the *kumbha* section elevated by means of fifteen tiers.
Thus, the *talacchanda* would indeed consist of four stages; however, it consists of four stages according to one's desire.
Now we shall describe the five-storeyed palace honored by kings. It should be constructed with a width of twenty-one cubits;
likewise, its height should be divided into two hundred and seventy-five cubits.
The pedestal (pīṭha) should be two parts, the shaft (jaṅghā) one and a half parts, and the capital (sārāmrā) three parts;
the wise architect should construct the kūṭaprastāra measuring one and a half cubits.
The second shaft should be made with a height of three cubits.
Furthermore, one should fashion the kūṭaprastāra to be one and a half cubits [in width];
the third jaṅghā should be made two and a quarter cubits [in height],
and the kūṭaprastāra is desired to have a height of one and a half cubits.
The shank of the fourth storey shall be two and a half cubits high;
the wise [architect] should construct the roof-plate according to the previous measurement.
On the fifth floor, one should make the shank two cubits high.
One should construct the *kūṭaprastāra* (roof-arrangement) just as it was previously described.
A wise man should also construct a *kapota* (dove-cot) with a height of two cubits;
the *mahāghaṇṭā* (great bell) is prescribed to have a height equal to one-fourth [of that].
Above that, on the five-storied palace,
one should fashion a pinnacle (kumbha) with nineteen tiers;
this configuration is to be made known by the name Sarvatobhadra.
One should distinguish it specifically from the division of the tiers (staras).
Then, the Śrībandha-pīṭha should be made with a height of two and a half cubits;
the shaft (jaṅghā), joined with pillars, should be made with fourteen tiers.

The garland (mālā) should be made twice the width of the star (stara); one should provide the garlic (laśuna) equal to the width of the star. One should make the pedestal (padma) endowed with two parts of the cheek (gaṇḍa), and the projection (ucchāla) should be made twice the width of the star; the portion for the iḍā is prescribed.
The diamond-pattern (hīraka) should be made two units thick, and the bands (paṭṭa) likewise;
the fillet (paṭṭikā) is one unit, and the spring-moulding (vasanta) is then two units;
