the spring-fillet (vasantapaṭṭikā) is one part, and the pigeon-eave (kapota) is then three units thick.

One should make the *cheda* one part, the *meṭhaka* the same as the *stara*, the *makara* one part, and the *carālapaṭṭikā* one part. One should make the *cheda* one part, and then the *kaṇṭha* one part. (120)

Then the wise one should make the neck one part, the *vākhyāpaṭṭikā* one part, and the pedestal (*vedī*) one part; then the cut (*cheda*) one part, the neck two layers (*staradvaya*), and then the neck [again]. ||121-122||
One should construct the *stara* (spreading) layer by layer, including the *paṭṭikā* and the *padmapaṭṭikā*.
In the *kūṭaprastāraka* (the pinnacle-spreading), one should fashion five makara-faces,
possessing diverse forms in all directions and endowed with every excellence.
Above the frieze, there should be a bell with five tiers,
adorned with various and most magnificent spires,
upon each of whose pinnacles auspicious marks are visible on all sides. ||124-125||

This temple is considered by artisans to be the Sarvatobhadra; following that, one should determine the cutting of the pillars according to the hanging cord. One should mark it on the ground with a thread equal to three times the height of the pillar.
The wise man should give two finger-breadths for the projection of the *meḍha*;
thereafter, the projection of the *makara* should be made five fingers long.
Then, one should mark out the band of the *meḍhaka* using a straight line.
The wise one should ensure that the entry of the cut is six finger-breadths;
as the entry is, so too should the cut be.
The projection of the band (paṭṭikā) should be made two finger-breadths.
An extension of six finger-breadths should be made from the railing;
the neck-band (kaṇṭhapaṭṭikā) should be projected by two finger-breadths;
then one should make the projection for the part called the lotus (padma) three finger-breadths.
Then, five finger-breadths shall be the emergence of the *yoni*;
here, a bell (*ghaṇṭā*) adorned with all ornaments should be fashioned.
From that, there should be a division, and above it, a base (*bhūmikā*) comes into being.
The shank of the second storey should consist of eight layers:
the *mālā* and so forth, a single *laśuna*, the *bharaṇa*, and likewise the *kalaśa*.
As the *mālā* is, so should the *ucchāla* and the *vīragaṇḍa* be as a layer (*stara*). ||133-134||
The wise architect should fashion the *ucchālaka* and the *hīraka* equal to the *paṭṭa*. The *paṭṭikā* should have a height of one part, as should the *vāsantaka*.
The *kapota* should have a height of three parts, and its projection should be reduced by one-third.
At half of the *cheda* (projection), there should be the *meḍha* and likewise the *paṭṭikā*.

Then, the wise one should fashion the *cheda*, the neck (*kaṇṭha*), and the *paṭṭikā* using half of the *mālā* (garland). Then, he should fashion the *cheda* itself [using the remaining portion]. ||136-137||
Furthermore, one should fashion the neck provided with diamonds;
the fillet should be preceded by a lotus, and the *kapotaka* should consist of three parts.
One should make a bell of four tiers, and likewise a *kumbha* above it consisting of two parts.
Again, there should be a division; one should fashion the shank with seven parts.
The *sītamāṭhā* should be provided, and the *mālocca* should be twice as wide.
The *laśuna*, *bharaṇa*, *kumbha*, and *gaṇḍa* should each be one part in width.
The *gaṇḍa* should be twice [the height of] the *ucchāla*, and likewise the *hīrapaṭṭa*;
there should be one layer of *paṭṭikā*, and for this, there is the *vasantapaṭṭikā*.
One should make the *pīṭha* ten times [the height of the *paṭṭikā*], with a *cheda* and two *eṇṭhas* at each layer.
One should fashion the *stara*, as well as the *makarapaṭṭikā*.
One should likewise fashion the *stara*, the *cheda*, the *kaṇṭha*, the *paṭṭikā*, and the *vedikā*;
then one should again make the *cheda* one part, and the *kaṇṭha* twice that.
There should be one course for the *paṭṭikā* and one course for the *vasantapaṭṭikā*.
The bell (*ghaṇṭā*) should consist of four courses and be adorned with a *prāggrīva*.
Above that, one should again fashion a *kumbha* (pitcher) measuring exactly half the height of the bell.
One should understand the *cheda* (cut) as one part; the *jaṅghā* (shank) is recorded as having seven parts.
The *mālā* (garland) should be made with two parts, and the *laśuna* (garlic) should be one part.
A wise man should fashion the *bharaṇa*, *kumbhaka*, and *gaṇḍa* like the *laśuna*.
The *ucchāla*, the *gaṇḍaka*, and the *hīrakānta* shall each consist of one part;
there shall be one and a half parts for the *paṭṭikā*, and the *stara* shall be half of that.
That [remaining] single part shall be the *paṭṭikā* known as the *vasantā*.
The wise craftsman should fashion the *kapota* (dove-cornice) with three layers (*tristara*) joined to the nose (*nāsā*).
He should effect the cut (*cheda*) by one part and have the molding (*maṇḍa*) made by one part;
in the *makara* (crocodile motif), he should provide a fillet (*paṭṭikā*), a cut, and layer after layer.
One should fashion the neck (kaṇṭha) as one part, and likewise the fillet (paṭṭikā) and the pedestal (vedikā).
One should again make a cut for one part, and from that, the neck should be two parts.
The fillet, preceded by a lotus, should be constructed layer by layer.
The wise [architect] should fashion the bell (ghaṇṭā) as one-fourth [of the height] above;
the pitcher (kumbha) above that should be half of that, and its cut (cheda) half of that again.
The shaft (jaṅghā) should be made six parts, and it should be well-fashioned with a mātrā-gaṇa.
One should fashion the *laśuna*, *bharaṇa*, *kumbha*, *gaṇḍa*, *ucchālavāḍaka*,
and the *hīraka* as separate one-part (*bhāga*) elements.
The *paṭṭa* should be one and a half parts, and the *paṭṭikā* should be half a part, with a height equal to that of the *tara*.
One part should be the *vasanta*, and the molding strip is called *vasantākhyā*.
One should make the *kapota* three units wide; the *cheda* should be one-third less than the *śaṅkha*.
The *maṇḍaka*, the *makara*, the molding strip, the *cheda*, and the *kaṇṭhaka* [are likewise arranged].
The neck (kaṇṭha), the fillet (paṭṭī), the pedestal (vedī), and the cut (cheda) should each be one square per layer.
The second neck should be two layers, and the fillet (paṭṭikā) should be one part. Likewise, the lotus-marked (padmajñā) fillet should be of the same height.
One should fashion the bell (ghaṇṭā) as four parts, and the dome (kumbha) as half of that [four parts]. The neck (cheda) should be one part, and the pillar-shaft (jaṅghā) half a part.
The garland-band (mālā) should be one part, and the onion-base (laśuna) one and a half parts.
In the same manner, one should perform the filling (bharaṇa) with a layer (stara) upon each pinnacle (ucchāla) of the pitcher;
one should provide a diamond (hīraka) of one part, and then a band (paṭṭa) of one and a half layers.
Then a fillet (paṭṭikā) of half a layer should be made, and then a spring (vasanta) of one layer.
One should make the *kapota* (dove-cornice) two *staras* high and the altar (*vedi*) likewise half a *stara*.
Just as the *cheda* (projection) is prescribed, so too are the *maṇḍa* and the *makara* (crocodile motif).
The *paṭṭikā* (fillet) should be made half a *stara*, and the *cheda* should also be half a *stara*.
The neck (kaṇṭha) and the fillet (paṭṭikā) should each be made two parts; the altar (vedī) should be made one part.
The recess (cheda) should be made one part, and another neck (kaṇṭha) three parts.
One should fashion a lotus-leaf fillet (padmapatrī) layer by layer.
Immediately thereafter, the movement of the *tuṅga* (the pinnacle) should be made in two parts.
The bell (*ghaṇṭā*) should be made thirty-three parts in height;
it should be joined with a *sarvatobhadra* motif and adorned with a *candraśālā* (dormer window).
One should fashion a lotus with three tiers, adorned with variegated petals;
above that, there should be a pitcher divided into fourteen parts.
The neck should be made of two parts, and the ear likewise.
Then, a *bījapūra* (citron) should be fashioned, joined with its reflection [of light] up to its midpoint.

A lotus, a wheel, or a trident should be placed there as appropriate, together with a very high *grāsa* (mouth-ornament) and adorned with sea-monsters (*makara*) and crocodiles (*meḍhaka*). ||166–167||
One should construct small pinnacle-rooms (*sottuṅgakūṭaka*) in this manner in the cardinal and intermediate directions;
on each successive level of the ground, a hall (*śālā*) with its supporting arches (*toraṇa*) must be provided.
In every corner, one should likewise fashion elephant-trunk-like projections (*karikyakara*).
One should construct the Sarvatobhadra [mandala], characterized by these features, with three peaks (kūṭas) and four internal water-channels (jalāntaras).
In this same manner, there are the Padma, Mahāpadma, Svastika, and Vardhamānaka [mandalas].
Beginning with these [mandalas] such as the Sarvatobhadra,
which consist of one level up to five levels, the common rites should be performed.
By means of these twenty divisions, the temples previously mentioned are established.
Beginning from the pedestal (pīṭha) and ending with the bell (ghaṇṭā), these five are endowed with their defining characteristics.
We shall now describe [the temple] starting from six stories up to twelve stories;
first, the five-storied [temple].
Now we shall describe the solitary six-storeyed [temple], which is thirty cubits [in length].
Its height is prescribed as forty-one cubits;
one should construct its pedestal (pīṭha) with a height of two and a half cubits.
The first *jaṅghā* (pillar-shaft) should be made four and a half cubits in height;
the wise say its *kūṭaprastāra* (roof-projection) should be one and a half cubits high.
The second *jaṅghā*, however, should be four cubits.
One should determine the height of the second kūṭa to be one and a half cubits;
the third bell (ghaṇṭā) shall be four cubits less by half a cubit [i.e., three and a half cubits].
One should again construct the expansion of the third kūṭa as before.
The fourth [element] should be the *jaṅghā* (the plinth), measuring three and a half cubits;
one should construct it above the *kūṭaprastāra* according to the previous measurement. The fifth [element] should be made with a height of three cubits for the *jaṅghā*.
Then one should construct a *kūṭaprastāraka* (roof-ridge structure) three and a half cubits in height;
the *jaṅghā* (pedestal/base) is prescribed as three and a sixth cubits, less a quarter-cubit.
As before, the *prastārakūṭa* and the *kapota* (dove-cot cornice) are three cubits in height.
Above that, there should be a bell five cubits in height;
above it, a very beautiful lotus six finger-breadths wide should be made. One should fashion the pitcher (kumbha) and its ornamentation with twenty-one parts.
This has been described as having six stages; it is also said to have seven stages.
[182] It has six stages.

It is declared to be thirty-five cubits in width and seven stories high; its height is fifty-one and a half cubits, and it is always raised one cubit from the ground. The pedestal is three cubits in height, and the pillar is five cubits high.
A roof-extension (kūṭaprastāra) of one and a half cubits in height is prescribed for it.
The construction of the altar-bench (vedikābandha) is two cubits, the height of the pillar-shaft (jaṅghā) is four cubits,
and the width of the roof-extension (kūṭaviprastāra) is desired to be one and a half cubits in height.
The altar (vedī) is one and a half cubits high, and the pillar-shaft (jaṅghā) is three and a half cubits;
the pinnacle (kūṭa) and the roof-extension (prastāra) are proclaimed to be one and a half cubits high.
The altar should be one and a quarter cubits, and the shaft should be three cubits plus a third.
The extension of the *kūṭa* (pinnacle) should be one and a half cubits in height;
the binding of the pedestal (*vedikābandha*) should be one cubit, while the portion for the pillar-shaft (*jaṅghā*) is two cubits.
The extension of the *kūṭa* is one and a quarter cubits, and the pedestal is one cubit.
The shank (jaṅghā) shall be one and three-quarter cubits; the pinnacle (kūṭa) shall be one cubit together with the base (pāda).
The altar (vedī) shall be one cubit in height, and the shank shall be one and a half cubits high.
The flat roof (prastāraka) of the pinnacle shall be one cubit, and the dove-cot (kapota) shall be three cubits.
With the lotus-capital and the bell, it shall measure five and a half cubits.
Thus has this seven-storied temple been described. Seven-storied.
Now we shall describe the eight-storied palace, which possesses auspicious characteristics.
One should calculate its width as forty cubits;
its height should be fifty-seven cubits, excluding thirty [from the total]. (191-192)
One should make the first floor nine cubits;
the second should be eight and a half; the third should be eight and a quarter cubits;
the fourth should be seven cubits, and the fifth should be six cubits.
Then the sixth [tier] shall be five cubits, while the seventh is four cubits;
(194) then the eighth shall be three cubits, and the binding of the altar-base two cubits;
one should make the bell four cubits; thus there shall be eight levels. (195)
It consists of eight stages.
Now it is said: a nine-storeyed palace [measured] by the hand-span should have a width of fifty-one [units] and a height of seventy-two.
Its corner measurement is stated [to be such that] its width and its height are equal.
The bell should be five cubits, and the base of the altar (vedibandha) half of that. One should make the ninth floor three and a half cubits;
the eighth [floor] four and a half, and the seventh five and a quarter.
The sixth [story] is six pādas less; the fifth is one pāda more;
the fourth is eight [pādas] less one pāda; and the third story is three hastas. Thus, the nine-storied temple is described in reverse order.
It consists of nine stages.

Now we shall describe the ten-storied palace (prāsāda). Its height is seventy-nine [parts], while its width is fifty-six and a quarter parts; we shall now explain it part by part according to the measurement of the corner (karna).
The body of the first stage is eleven cubits in height;
the second shall be ten and a half, while the third is ten cubits.
The fourth is eight and a half, and the fifth is seven and a half.
The sixth [altar] is said to have seven cubits; the seventh should be six cubits.
The eighth is to be known as five cubits, while the ninth has four cubits.
The tenth should be made three cubits; that altar [should be] two cubits plus a fraction.
Together with the measurement, there are four cubits;
thus has this arrangement for the Daśabhūmika [temple] been described.
This is the Daśabhūmika palace.
We shall describe the temple with its eleven storeys in brief:
it should be made sixty-five cubits wide and ninety-two cubits high;
such is the temple to be known by those learned in the scriptures according to the measurement of the ear.
The first stage of his [temple] shall be fourteen cubits;
the second twelve and a half, and the third eleven cubits high.
The fourth shall be nine and a half, and the fifth eight and a quarter. ||207-208||
The sixth [image] should be seven cubits; then the seventh is six cubits;
the eighth is five cubits; the ninth is four and a half cubits;
the tenth is four cubits; and the eleventh is three and a half cubits. (209)
The altar is two and one-quarter cubits, and the bell is four and a half cubits;
thus the eleven-storied temple has been correctly described.
It is an eleven-storied [temple].
We declare that it has twelve stories and is sixty-seven cubits in length;
its height shall be ninety-five cubits according to the measurement of the corner (karna).
Its first story is prescribed to be fourteen cubits. ||211-212||
The second [line] shall have eleven cubits; the third, ten and a half;
the fourth, ten cubits; the fifth, eight and a half;
the sixth, seven and a half cubits; and the seventh, seven cubits.
The eighth [altar] shall have six cubits; the ninth, however, shall have five cubits.
The tenth shall be four cubits, and the eleventh earth-altar (kṣiti) shall be three cubits.
The twelfth shall be two and a half cubits, and the binding of the altar-base (vedībandha) shall be two cubits.
The bell should be four cubits in height and adorned with all ornaments;
the wise artisan should fashion the pitcher (kumbha) according to the measurement of the pillar’s width.
The height of the neck (ucchāla) should be twice that of the pillar, and its circumference should be one and a half times the diameter of the pillar.
Thus, these twelve types of temples (prāsādas) have been correctly described.

Among them, one should arrange the lotus, great lotus, svastika, increasing (vardhamānaka), auspicious on all sides (sarvatobhadra), and creeper (latā) designs according to the base structure (talabandha). ||217-218||
One should begin with the single [central] line and the twelve-layered [structure];
the measurement above should be made common to those five,
consisting of twelve layers.
Those known by the name Drāviḍa were fashioned from the bases, the moldings, and the plinths.
Just as the principal palaces have been described,
so too is this [type] spoken of by those of little learning.
Thus ends the sixty-second chapter, titled "The Draviḍa Palaces," in the *Vāstuśāstra* named *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*, composed by the Great King of Kings, the Supreme Lord, the illustrious Bhojadeva.
Now begins the sixty-third chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Nāgara Temple Types beginning with Meru. Now we shall describe the Nāgara temples by their names and characteristics:
Meru, Mandara, Kailāsa, Kumbha, Mṛgarāja, and Gaja. (1)
The Vimānacchanda, the Caturaśra,
and another, the Aṣṭāśri, the Ṣoḍaśāśri, the Vartula,
the Sarvatobhadra, the Siṃhāsya, the Nandana, the Nandivardhana, the Haṃsaka, and the Vṛṣa.
Garuḍa, Padmaka, and Samudra—
these twenty are declared to be the [types of] temples for the Nāgas in brief.
A temple with one hundred mudrās has four doors and sixteen stories above ground.
Meru, filled with various peaks, is called a palace;
Mandara has twelve stories, and Kailāsa has nine floors.
It has many peaks, is variegated, possesses four gates, and is of great height.
The Vimānacchandaka is proclaimed to have eight storeys;
the Nandivardhana, joined with twenty eggs (aṇḍakas), has seven storeys;
and the Nandana palace should be made with six storeys and sixteen eggs.
The five-storied Sarvatobhadra temple, adorned with Bhadraśāla trees,
should be constructed with many pinnacles and numerous small domes (aṇḍakas). A Valabhicchandaka temple, shaped like a bull, should always be made for the deities.
The bull, however, is equal to its own height and is turned auspiciously in every direction;
it should be known as a mandala adorned with a single egg.
The lion is to be understood as having the form of a lion, and the elephant as having the form of an elephant. ||9-10||
The *kumbha* is shaped like a jar, likewise nine *bhūmikās* high, having the form of hollowed palms joined together (*añjalipuṭa*), and adorned with five egg-shaped domes (*aṇḍaka*).
It should be known as the *samudraka*, possessing sixteen facets on all sides. ||11||
On both sides there are moon-chambers, and it is two stories high in elevation.
Likewise, the lotus-like [temple] has eight corners and is three stories high;
that auspicious one is known to have sixteen corners and a variegated pinnacle.
The king of beasts is renowned as Candra, adorned with a moon;
he who is elevated upon the ground by means of his broad,
forward-reaching neck is called the elephant-prasāda, which possesses many moon-like domes.
The king of beasts was overturned; it was known by the name Garuḍa.
It was seven stories high, likewise provided with three moon-chambers (candraśālās), and it was surrounded on all sides by six corners (aśris). ||15-16||
Likewise, another [pillar] should be Garuda-shaped; in height, it may consist of ten stages (*bhūmika*).
A lotus-shaped pillar should have sixteen facets (*aśri*) and be two stages higher.
The *vāvṛkṣa* pillar, which has a breath-like appearance similar to a lotus, should be square.
The five-egg [temple] has a single story, while its womb-chamber (garbha) is four cubits;
this is the Vṛṣa [temple], and here it is not [the only one]. These temples described here have seven, five, or four stories, and they fulfill all desires. ||18-19||
The [other] equal [structures] should be known as those which have the same dimensions;
they should be made with variegated peaks and adorned with moon-chambers (candraśālā).
All of them should be provided with eastern projections (prāggrīva) and equipped with archways (toraṇa).
The [liṅgas] may be made of brick, wood, or stone, and should not be crowded with other materials.
The Meru-liṅga should be fifty cubits in height with nine projections;
the inner chambers (garbhas) should be twice the size of the liṅga, and the walls should be four cubits thick.
The *andhārikā* should be made six cubits on all sides;
the wise one should also construct the wall of the arms (*bāhābhitti*) for the *andhārikā*.
This Meru, endowed with all excellent qualities, is declared to be the common type.
Likewise, for other types of palaces (prāsāda), the inner core (garbha) is three times the size of the linga.

One should fashion the entire [structure], including the *andhārikā* (the blind wall/base), from the remainder left after setting aside the palace's core, dividing it into equal parts as before. ||24-25||

Those [sites] beginning with Meru and ending with Vimāna, which were previously proclaimed, are auspicious when cleansed for the installation of liṅgas; however, others bring fear. Those chief trees mentioned, ending with Nandivardhana, [are likewise auspicious].
These eight are considered auspicious for those of middling status, while others are known to bring suffering.
Those five which have been mentioned, beginning with Haṃsa and ending with Samudra,
are declared to be praiseworthy for the installation of Liṅgas.
The Mandara palace, however, has a body of forty [cubits];
the Vimāna and Uṣaroṣṭhita are likewise.
The Nandivardhana palace should be made with thirty-two cubits.
The *hastā* has thirty [units], as does the *sarvatobhadra*;
the *aṣṭāviṃśati* has twenty-eight [units] with eight [projections]; the *śrī* has sixteen [units] without three;
and there are also the circular (*vartula*), the lotus-shaped (*padmaka*), the white (*śveta*), and the *vimānacchanda*.
These [first] twelve are twelve cubits [in height]; the Gaja, Siṃha, Kumbha, and Valabhīcchanda should be made twenty cubits [in height].
These four should be equal in terms of their elevation and measurement.
Vāvṛkṣa, Mṛgarāja, and Vimānacchanda—
these should each be twelve cubits in measurement individually;
or Garuḍa may be ten cubits, and he is also recorded as being eight cubits.
Others maintain that one should construct the palaces according to these measurements;
those which are declared to be one cubit, two cubits, or three cubits in height should be dedicated to the yakṣas,
nāgas, grahas, and other such beings, as well as to the rākṣasas.
This is the rule for temples that has been briefly set forth.
Furthermore, we shall describe in detail the Vimāna known as Śuddhapuṣpaka:
when the site has been made square and divided into thirty-five parts. ||36-37||
The *rathikā* should be five parts, and the intervening water-space two parts;
one should construct the *kūṭa* as three parts and the *pañjara* adorned with a *prāggrīvaka*.
The second intervening water-space should likewise be two parts.
The water-interval, as before, shall be one-eleventh part of the *śāla*.
One should make the *pañjara* three parts and the water-interval two parts.
At the edge, there shall be a pinnacle (*kūṭa*) measuring five cubits; this is the rule for all directions.
This is the Nāgara style with a flat base (talacchanda) for the Śuddhapuṣpaka temple.
The pillar-shaft (jaṅghā), together with its pedestal (sapīṭhā), has a height equal to half the width of the site (kṣetra).
The second [section] is ten and a half cubits, and the third is nine cubits.
The fourth [terrace] should be eight cubits; the fifth, however, seven cubits.
The sixth terrace should be made with a measurement of six cubits for it;
the seventh is five cubits, and the eighth thereafter is four cubits.
A wise man should cause a variegated pedestal-band (vedikābandha) three cubits in length to be constructed;
this pedestal-band has a height that is double its width,
and above the shoulder (skandha) there should be a bell or a *vāmalasāraka*.
That [pedestal] should be made circular and auspicious, with the bell rising to half the height of the shoulder.
One should fashion the pitcher (kumbha) to be one-fourth the width of the bell.
This measurement is declared as the total proportion for the tiers (bhūmikās).
Now, each one is described specifically and in detail:
the ground-line (bhūmi) and the subsidiary line (aṅgikā) are to be established by means of measurement;
the hand (hasta) is the "khuraka" [measure], and the lotus-petal (padmapatrikā) consists of two parts. 47.
The *kaṇaka* should be one part, the *kumuda* three parts, and the *cheda* likewise;
the neck (*kaṇṭha*) is three parts, twice that [in height], and is adorned with *kiṅkiṇīs* and foliage.
A band (*paṭṭikā*) should be made half of that, and the *giripatrikā* equal to it.
In the middle of the enclosure consisting of three parts, there should be a cool terrace measuring half a part;
it should be aligned with the same plumb-line as the neck previously described.
Above that, the wise architect should fashion a single layer (starana).
Furthermore, the neck (kaṇṭha) should be provided, measuring two parts;
the fillet (paṭṭikā) is one layer, and the mountain-leaf ornament (giripatrikā) is equal to that. Then, the nose-like projection (vilakanāsikā) should be made fourfold or threefold.
Between the two pillars, one should cause the fivefold work to be performed; that should be made beautiful and endowed with what is called a *tilaka*.
Furthermore, a cut should be provided by the wise man according to the previous measurement.
The *jaṅghā* (shaft) shall have seven tiers, and above it, the *varaṇḍī* (cornice) shall have three tiers.
Below the *jaṅghā*, there should be a *kumbhaka* (pitcher) with three tiers.
Then, there should be a *mālā* (garland-cornice) joined with a bell (*ghaṇṭā*) and a *maṇḍapa* (pavilion), consisting of six *yaras*. ||54-55||
With half of that [measurement], garlic [should be made]; with one layer, the base (bharaṇa) should be formed.
Then, one should make the pitcher (kumbha) two layers thick, and the cheek (gaṇḍa) one layer from that.
One should make the neck (ucchāla) two layers thick, and then the hero-cheek (vīragaṇḍa) one layer.
The *paṭṭa* should be twice [the height of the base], and the *paṭṭikā* half of that;
the *giripatrī* is equal to that, and then the *varaṇḍī* is three times [the height of the base]. Above the pillar, a beautiful [member] should be fashioned with a height of one and a half parts.
Then there should be one *staraka*, then a *cheda*, then the neck (*kaṇṭha*) with three *starakas*;
the *paṭṭikā* should consist of one *staraka*, and the *giripatrikā* should be equal to that.
One should construct the *varaṇḍī* with three *starakas* combined with half a *prastara*.
Furthermore, the *cheda* and *stara* should be made; by that, the *kaṇṭha* is completed in its entirety.
The *giripatrī* is equal to that, and the *āmalasāraka* consists of three parts.
Then there are the *cheda*, the *kaṇṭha*, the *giripatrī*, and the *varaṇḍikā*.
One should perform [the measurement] again according to the previous measure in the event of a cut or a tremor.
Then, one should fashion the mountain-feather (giripattrī), the spread (stara), and the three parts of the sharp-edged [piece].
Then the wise man should again fashion the cut, the neck, the feather-piece, and then a single spread, followed by the cut.
One should construct the *varaṇḍī* (cornice) with three tiers, joined with half-stones.
One should fashion the *cheda*, the *kaṇṭha*, and the *pīṭha* as previously described, and likewise the other [parts] such as the *vāmalasārakaṇṭha*.
Then, one should fashion the *giripatrī* and the pedestal (*vedikā*) of two tiers, as before.
One should make a cut half of that size, and from there, the neck with two layers;
then one should fashion the beautiful *giripatrī* with one layer.
One should also fashion the *āmalasāraka* according to the measurement of a square.
One should fashion a lotus petal above its middle portion.

The pitcher (kumbha) should consist of four layers, and from that, the neck (kaṇṭha) should be one layer. Then the rim (karṇa) should be one layer, and the citron-shaped ornament (bījapūraka) two layers.
One should determine the width of the pinnacle (kūṭa) by dividing it into four parts; from that, one part should be made radiant.
A bud-like ornament (mañjarī), adorned with stars and crescents, should be fashioned using two parts.
Then, the architectural bond known as varaṇḍikā shall consist of one part each.
One should fashion the śukanāsā (gargoyle) with a width equal to that of the root-fillet (mūlamañjarī). Now, the measurement known as "two-and-a-half parts" is determined;
therein, the width should be made twice the height, or alternatively, according to the sequence of five parts.
Alternatively, this [pedestal] may be made with three parts: the *śūrasena*, the *kārya*, and the *śukanāsā*.
Having made the height threefold, the upper portion should be a *makara* (crocodile) joined with a pillar;
it should have a door with a decorative arch (*guṇadvāra*) and its base should be well-proportioned.
One should construct [the structure] joined with half-bricks on both sides.
There, a wise man should fashion either a central sanctum (garbha) or a pinnacle (kūṭa), which is auspicious.
On the second floor, however, the pedestal (pīṭha) should consist of seventeen layers.
The shank (jaṅghā) should extend up to the edge of the entablature (melānta), and a garland (mālā) should be made in four tiers;
the garlic (laśuna) is said to be two tiers, and the filling (bharaṇa) is desired as one tier.
The pitcher (kumbha) should be constructed in the same way, with its projection (ucchāla) provided with double [the height].
The *gaṇḍaka* should be one *stara*, and from that, the *paṭṭa* should be two *staras*.
The *paṭṭikā* should be made with half [of that], and likewise the *giripatrikā*.
The *varaṇḍī* should consist of three *sūras* and be adorned with *śūrasenas*.
One part shall be the *cheda* (projection), then two parts for the neck (*kaṇṭha*),
one part for the fillet (*paṭṭikā*), and equal to that, the *giripatrikā*.
One should make the pinnacle (*śikhara*) three parts, and the *cheda* for me one part.
One should make one *kaṇṭha*; the wise know the *pathikā* to be extensive.
One *staraka* shall be a *kaṇṭha*, and the *paṭṭikā* is equal to that.
A wise man should fashion the *giripatrī* with half a *bhāga*.
The varaṇḍikā should be three times as wide and joined with a half-pāda projection;
the wise architect should fashion the cheda and the neck according to the previous measurement. The paṭṭikā and the giripatrī are each prescribed to be one part [in height].
One should make the pinnacle twice [the height of the base], and likewise the cut (cheda) one part;
in this manner, one should fashion the neck (kaṇṭha) and the fillet (paṭṭikā).
The cornice (varaṇḍikā) should be two parts, provided with a water-spout (udakāra).
The *cheda*, the *kaṇṭha*, the *patrī*, the *girivartī*, and the *tribhāgikā*—
one should fashion these as before, according to the beauty [of the site], O Virihira... The fourth terrace (*bhūmikā*) should be constructed above, endowed with the proper characteristics.
The thirteenth tier is the pedestal (pīṭha), and the middle shank (madhyajaṅghā) is equal to it;
the garland (mālā) should consist of four tiers, and the garlic (laśuna) element is half of that.
The pitcher (kumbha) should be made equal to that, and the protrusion (ucchāla) should be two tiers.
One should make a *gaṇḍaka* half of that [width], and then a *paṭṭa* twice that;
a *paṭṭikā* and a *giripatrī* should be made, each one layer thick (*stara*).
A *varaṇḍī* should be made three layers thick; they know the *cheda* to be one layer thick.
One should make the neck twice [the width of the base], and the fillet (paṭṭikā) half of that;
the giripatrī should be equal to that, then two layers for the khirihira.
The cut (cheda), the neck, the fillet, and the giripatrī each consist of one part.
The *varaṇḍī* should be made twice as wide, and from that, the *cheda* should be one unit (*stara*).
The *kaṇṭha* and the *patrikā* are each one part; this is known as the *giripatrī*.
One should fashion the *vakāśi*, *khiri*, and *hira* first, and the *cheda* according to the previous sequence.
The nose, however, should be made twice as wide by the wise man.
(90) One should make a cut of one part; then the neck is two parts, the fillet is one part, and the *gītrikā* is equal to that. (91)
The bell (ghaṇṭā) is said to have seven tiers, while the lotus (padma) is said to have two tiers.
The pitcher (kalaśa) is twice that [in height]; one should perform the cutting (cheda) therein as previously described.
Above that shall be the fifth level, and the pedestal (pīṭha) shall have eleven tiers.
In that same manner, the *maṭṭā* should be the shank; then the *mālā* should be three stories high.
Below that, there should be a *laśuna* of one story, and the *bharaṇa* should consist of one story.
A wise man should construct the *kumbha* together with the *gaṇḍaka* as one and a half stories.
The *ucchāla* is said to be two *stara*s in width; the *gaṇḍa* is prescribed as one *stara*.
The *paṭṭa* should be two *stara*s, and the *paṭṭikā* half the width of the *paṭṭa*.
The *giripatrī* is equal to that, while the *varaṇḍikā* is three *stara*s wide.
One *stara* shall be the *cheda*, and the neck (*kaṇṭha*) shall be twice that;
the band (*paṭṭikā*) should be made half of that, and likewise the mountain-leaf (*giripatrikā*).
There should be two *staras* for the *virihira*, and one should perform the *cheda* as half of that.
In this manner, there should be the neck (kaṇṭha) and the fillet (paṭṭikā), as well as the giripatrikā;
it should have two layers (starau), and the tilanāsā should have a cut (cheda) one and a half cubits long.
One should make the neck twice that [length] and the fillet with one part (bhāga).
The mountain-leaf (giripatrī) should be equal to that; the bell (ghaṇṭā) should consist of five squares (pañcastarā).

One should make the lotus (padma) twice as large [as the bell]; the remainder is then according to the previous sequence. Then the sixth level shall be the ground (bhūmi), which is designated there as the pedestal (pīṭha). ||99-100||
The ground (bhūmi) should be two stara wide; then the aṅga, the tulā, and the khuraka [each] one [stara]; the cheda should be half of that; then the neck (kaṇṭha) should be two stara;
the paṭṭikā should be one bhāga, and the giripatrikā one bhāga.
One should make the *varaṇḍī* twice as wide [as the base], and one should prescribe its projection (*cheda*) to be half of that.
This pedestal (*pīṭha*) consists of twelve parts; the *jaṅghā* (shaft) is half of that, and the *māṭṭā* is half of that.
The *mālā* is said to be twice as wide [as the shaft], and the *laśuna* should be equal to that.
The *bharaṇa* should be one *tara*, while the *kalaśa* shall consist of two parts (*dvibhāga*).
The *ucchālaka* is equal to that, and the *gaṇḍa* is prescribed as one part.
One should make the *paṭṭa* twice the width of a *tara*, and the *paṭṭikā* with one part.
As before, there should be a *giripatrī* and a *varaṇḍikā* of one *stara*;
the *cheda* should be one *stara*, and the *kaṇṭha* from that point should be double that.
As before, there should be two *pattrikās*, and the *khirihira* should consist of two parts (*dvaṃśa*). ||105–106||
The *cheda*, the *kaṇṭha*, and the *paṭṭikā*—known as the *giripatrī*—are each one part (*bhāga*) in measure.
The *tilanāsā* should be two parts wide, while the *cheda* should be made one part.
Then the *kaṇṭha* should be two parts, and the *kaṇṭhapaṭṭikā* one part.
Thereafter, the *bhāgikī* and the *giripatrī* should be fashioned.
One should then make the *āmalasāraka* with five tiers reduced by one-third;
thereafter it should have three tiers—the remainder follows the previous sequence.
On the fifth stage, however, the pedestal (pīṭha) shall consist of twelve tiers;
the shaft (jaṅghā) shall have five tiers, and both the meḍha and the garland (mālā) shall each consist of two parts.
The garlic-moulding (laśuna) shall be half a tier, and the entablature (bharaṇa) shall be one tier.
The wise artisan should construct the *kumbha* together with the *gaṇḍa* as one *stara*.
The *ucchāla* should be made as two *staras*, and the *gaṇḍa* is prescribed as one part (*bhāga*).
The *paṭṭa* should be made as one and a half *staras*, while the *paṭṭikā* shall be one *stara*.
The *giripatrī* is equal to that; the *varaṇḍikā* is three times [the height of] the *tristarā*.
The *cheda* consists of a third part, and from the middle of the neck comes the *guṇa*. The two *pattrikās* consist of one part each; the *tilanāsikā* is three times [the height of] the *starā*.
This [pedestal] should be constructed with half-prastāra and then provided with a full prastāra;
one should divide the neck (kaṇṭha) into a part, and its height should be double that.
The two wings (pattrikā) are as before, while the bell (ghaṇṭā) has a height of four prastāras. ||114-115||
One should make the lotus twice as large; the remainder, however, is according to the previous sequence.
That which is the eighth stage (bhūmikā) should be fashioned with auspicious characteristics.
Thus, the twenty [mountains] beginning with Meru have been described.
One should construct these as the foremost palaces, extending up to eight stories;
such a person shall be worthy of worship in the assembly of artisans. ||117||

Thus ends the sixty-third chapter, titled "The Meru and Other [Temples] up to the Twenty," concerning Nāgara temples arising from the ground, in the *Vāstuśāstra* named *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*, composed by the Great King of Kings, the Supreme Lord, the illustrious Bhojadeva.
Now begins the sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Temples such as the Digbhadra.
Next, we shall describe this temple known as Vāra, according to its names and characteristics.
By their characteristics, among them are the *digbhadra*, the *śrīvatsa*, the *vardhamānaka*,
the *nandyāvarta* as the fourth, and the fifth is the *nandivardhana*;
likewise, there are the *vimāna*, the *padma*, and the one known as the *mahābhadra*.
The eleventh is named Śrīvardhamānaka, or alternatively Mahāpadma;
the twelfth is Pañcaśāla, and the thirteenth is Pṛthivījaya.
Among these, first of all, the Digbhadra is established in the month of Śrāvaṇa.
When the field has been made square and divided into nine parts,
the corner [pavilion] is two parts in width, and the two side-pavilions are known to be one part each.
The central hall should be made three parts wide, adorned with three *nāsikās*.
One should cause the mutual projection (viniṣkāsa) to be made with half a part;
likewise, between the corner-projections and the side-projections of the hall,
one should make the water-interval (salilāntara) with a sixteenth part.
The *sīmā* (the central core) is prescribed by dividing it into ten parts.
The six walls should consist of six parts and two parts [respectively].
Now we shall describe the *vardhamāna* (the increasing type), for its length is indeed double its width.
Two parts are to be known as the base of the pedestal (*vedikābandha*), and the pillar-shaft (*jaṅghā*) consists of four parts.
The *śāntāpatrā* and *kapotālī* [mouldings] are raised by one and a half parts.
The first storey (*bhūmikā*) should be made with a height of one and a half parts.
The second storey should be known as rising to three and a half parts;
the third should likewise be made, rising to two and a half parts.
The pinnacle (ucchālaka) and the pillar-shaft (jaṅghā) are prescribed for the storey-work.
The pinnacle (kūṭa) should be placed at half [the height], endowed with artistic beauty;
the bell (ghaṇṭā) should have a height of three parts and be provided with many facets.
One should place the pitcher (kalaśa) above, rising for two parts.
One should construct a circular pinnacle, joined with a citron (bījapūraka) and covered with sprouts,
rising to one-quarter of the height of the half-peak.
That man who causes this temple, known as Digbhadraka, to be built— ||13-14||
He too obtains the fruit of a hundred sacrifices; there is no doubt in this matter.
Now, the measurement of the temple known as Śrīvatsa is described:
when the ground has been made square and divided into fifteen parts.
Its height shall be three parts, and its width three parts less one.
Between the two *karṇaśālās*, both *pratirathas* should be made two parts wide; between those two, one should place the *mārga* at one and a half parts.
Having entered one part, the hall consists of three parts;
the exit should be by half a pad, while the inner sanctum (garbha) is nine parts.
The wall should be three parts; now its height is described.
The Śrīvatsa has now been described; the Vardhamānaka is being explained.
On a square field divided into parts, one should apply the cuts and so forth, ending with the mountain-patterns, according to the previous sequence. 19–20.
The altar (vedikā) is considered to be two or even three times [the width of the base];
the cut (cheda) should be one unit, and the neck (kaṇṭha) should be twice that.
One should have the fillet (paṭṭikā) and the "mountain-leaf" (giripatrī) made with half of that measure.
Then the bell should be ten *tara*s, or it may be the *vāmalasāraka*;
the lotus should be two *tara*s, and the pitcher (*kalaśa*) above that should be double that size.
Above that, the base (*bhūmikā*) should be constructed along with its pedestal (*pīṭha*), endowed with the proper characteristics.
The pedestal (pīṭha) should consist of fifteen layers (staras), and the shaft (jaṅghā) should likewise have that same number.
The garland (mālā) should be four layers, while the garlic (laśuna) should be two layers.
The neck-piece (bharaṇa) should be half of that [the mālā], and one should make the pitcher (kumbha) equal to that [the bharaṇa].
Its height should be double that, and the *gaṇḍa* should be a single tier.
One should make the *paṭṭa* twice as wide as this, and the *paṭṭikā* half of that.
The *giripatrikā* should be made according to the measurement of the *paṭṭikā*.
The *varaṇḍī* should be made three stories high and adorned with *śūrasena* ornaments;
beyond that, the *cheda* should be one story, and the *kaṇṭha* should be twice that height.
A *paṭṭikā* and a *giripatrī* should be constructed at every story.
Both [the *stara*] should be two units wide; the *cheda* should be one *stara*, and then the *stara* again.
Likewise for the neck (*kaṇṭha*), and similarly for the *paṭṭikā* and the *giripatrikā*.
The *varaṇḍikā* should be two *staras* wide; the remainder should be executed as before.
One should cut both stars into two parts, each with a width of one unit.
The *kaṇṭha*, the *patrikā*, and the *giripatrī* are as before.
The altar (*vedikā*) should be made twice as wide, provided with two half-units.
One should make the base (cheda) one *stara* and the neck (*kaṇṭha*) twice that;
one should have the leaf-pattern (*patrikā*) and the mountain-leaf (*giripatrī*) made with half of that measure.
With eight *staras*, there should be a bell (*ghaṇṭā*), or otherwise, an *āmalasāraka*.
The neck of this jar should be twice that [measurement];
the throat should be one *starā* (unit), and one should make the ear equal to that.
The *bījapūra* (bud) should be double; one should act in this same manner as before.
The *pratihāra* should be three parts, being one-seventeenth of the total;
the *pratiratha* should consist of two parts, and the *śālā* should be five parts.
Between the *śālā* and the *pratyaṅga*, there should be an interval of water measuring half a part.
The mutual projection (viniṣkāsa) shall be one foot less than the module (pada).
The inner chamber (garbha) shall consist of ten parts, and the wall (bhitti) shall be three and a half parts.
The molding of the pedestal (vedikābandha) shall be four parts, and the shaft (jaṅghā) shall be eight parts.
The first ground consists of five and a half [units] and is provided with a *kapotālī*;
the third level of this [structure] should be made with five [units], and the third [level] should also consist of four and a half units. (37–38)
The fourth stage is proclaimed by four parts and four words;
the bell should be made with three divisions, and the *kūṭa-bhaktyā* and so forth are as described previously.
The *śukanāsā* and so forth, as well as the *kumbha* and so forth, are declared to be as before.

This temple named Vardhamāna, characterized by auspicious marks, has been described. Now we shall describe the Nandyāvarta: when the site is divided into seventeen parts, one should construct the corners as four squares each and the penthouse (pañjara) as one and a half parts.

The hall shall consist of six parts, while the inner sanctum (garbha) shall be ten parts. The wall shall be three and a half parts; the height above that shall be double [the wall's thickness]. The altar (vedī) shall have a height of four parts, and the pillar-base (jaṅghā) shall rise eight parts.
The six-pada base should extend five padas for prosperity;
the third part, measuring four parts, should have its height increased by one pada.
There should be a pitcher (ghaṭa) at the shoulder [of the structure], and the kalaśa and other elements should be as before.
This temple, which grants all desires, is declared to be the Nandyāvarta.
Now, therefore, we shall fully describe the Nandivardhana temple:
on a square site marked with eighteen squares, [one should proceed].
The corner should have an extension of three padas, and each secondary limb (pratyaṅga) should be two padas.
The hall (śālā) is said to be four padas in extent and adorned with variegated work;
the mutual projection should be by the measure of three-quarters of a pada.

Between the corners and the side-wings, as well as between the halls and the side-wings, a water-gutter (salilāntara) should be made, extending one part in width everywhere. The inner sanctum (garbha) should consist of ten parts, and the wall (bhitti) of four parts.
Now we shall describe the vertical measurement; it is proclaimed to be double that [of the base].

Five parts are for the construction of the altar (vedībandha), and the shaft (jaṅghā) should consist of eight parts. The first storey (bhūmikā) should be made complete with a pigeon-cornice (kapotālī). 49–50.
The second [story] is likewise five parts and one-quarter;
the third floor of this [structure] consists of five parts.
The fourth floor should be known as four and a half parts.
A bell should be fashioned above it, raised three padas high.
Śukāghra, Śūrasena, and the decorative elements of the pillar-head (stambhikākūṭabhakti) should be provided;
its emergence of the pitcher (kalaśa) should be executed as before.
Whoever else should cause another temple, Nandivardhana, to be built, he becomes equal to the host of Nandins; of this there is no doubt.
Hereafter, we shall describe the Vimāna, which possesses auspicious characteristics.
When the field has been made square and divided into twenty squares,
the corners should be made five squares each, with a water-channel in the middle.
The pericarp (karṇikā) should be one and a half parts, and the water-channel between it should be half a part.
The *sālopa* should extend [outward] by one and a half parts;
the projection of the *karṇikā* is prescribed to be by half a part from the corner.
Its inner sanctum (*garbha*) should be constructed with a width of twelve parts.
The wall should be made with four parts, situated in all directions. Now we shall state its height measurement; it should be twice that [width].
There are five parts for the altar-base (vedībandha), and the shaft (jaṅghā) is nine parts in height. ||58-59||
The first floor should be constructed with six sections rising upwards;
one should fashion a *śatapatra* (hundred-petaled lotus) and a *kapotālī* (dove-cot cornice) in its center. The second floor of this [structure] should be made with five bays (*pada*).

On one half of this [structure] is the pillar-protrusion (stambhakocchāla), and the pinnacle (kūṭa) is situated on the other half. By means of mutual support, there are three other stories (bhūmikā) consisting of pillars,
pillar-heads (stambhikākūṭa), filling-blocks (bharana), Śūrasenas, and bells.
In this case, the wise man should perform the emergence of the *kalaśa* as previously described.
That bull among men who would cause this [temple] called a *vimāna* to be built with devotion obtains enjoyments in this world, as well as the granting of a true body in the hereafter.

Now, that which generates delight for the beloved of Padmā is called Padma. (64) When the field has been made square and divided into sixteen squares, the corners should be made four squares each, adorned with an inner water-channel. (65)
The penthouse (pañjara) is to be known as having two parts; within the womb (garbha), there are four corner-sections.
Each part shall consist of a sixteenth portion, and at its end is the water-interval.
The womb shall consist of nine parts, and the wall shall be three and a half parts.
Now we shall describe the vertical measurement; it should be twice that [of the base].
The second floor is known to be five parts in height.
Each of the two floors should be mutually reduced by half a part. ||67-68||
The *stambhikā*, *kūṭa*, *bharaṇa*, *śukāghra*, and *sūrasenaka* [elements],
as well as the *ghaṇṭā*, *kāra*, and *vistāra*, are to be arranged for this [temple] as before.
Whoever, endowed with devotion, should cause this *Padma-prāsāda* to be constructed—
Like the Lord of Śrī himself, he becomes the ornament of the earth.
Now we shall describe the exceedingly beautiful Mahābhadra temple:
on a square site marked with twenty-one divisions [71].
The corners are four parts, and the secondary members (pratyaṅga) are known to be two and a half parts.
The hall (śālā), situated in all directions, should be made five parts;
the water-interval (salilāntara) should be made with a width of three-quarters of a part.
The womb (garbha) consists of thirteen parts, and the walls consist of four parts each. Now we shall describe its height above [the base]: that should be double [the width].
The altar (vedī) has a height of four parts, and the pillar-shaft (jaṅghā) should be eight parts.
The first floor should be made with a height of seven parts;
in its center, it should have inner recesses and a row of pigeon-cots (kapotālī) occupying three parts.
The second floor of this [structure] is prescribed as being six and a half parts.
Then there are three other stages (bhūmikās) devoid of proportional divisions.
The bell (ghaṇṭā), together with the lotus-leaf (padmapatrikā), has a height of three parts.
[These include] the pillar-base (stambhikā), the pinnacle (kūṭa), the decorative molding (bharana), the parrot-beak (śukāghrā), and the śūrasenaka. ||76-77||
The kalaśa and the kumbha are not defective; these [other parts] are as before.
That devoted man who causes this Mahābhadra to be made here is served by celestial nymphs in heaven by the command of Madana.
Now, the characteristic of the Śrīvardhamāna [temple] is described.
(79) When the site has been made square and divided into twenty-four parts, the corners should be made with six parts each, and the halls should consist of nine parts each. (80)
The exit for the halls should be made here with two and a half bays;
one should create an opening for water there in the middle between the corner halls,
measuring one and a half parts in width and entering by one part.
The center should be established at the corner, with the interior space consisting of one part.
For a hall (śālā) constructed with nine parts, two are declared to be the western projections (pratyaṅgau),
having an extent of two parts and extending outwards by one part.
The inner sanctum (garbha) is fourteen paces [in width], and the wall is known to be five paces. Now we shall describe the vertical measurement; it should be twice that [of the horizontal].
The pedestal (vedikā) is six paces in height, and the pillar-shaft (jaṅghā) is eleven paces.
Its first floor should be seven units high;
the second floor is desired to be six and three-quarter units;
the third floor is produced with six and a quarter units. ||85-86||
The sixth part by a quarter [of the total] is known as the fourth storey;
for each successive storey, the entrance should be constructed with one part [of the width].
The height of the bell (ghaṇṭā) should be made with five parts plus a quarter.
Above that, there should be a pitcher (kalaśa) with a height of three parts.

The crow-beak (sukāghrā), the Sūrasena, the pillar-base (stambhikā), and the finial (kūṭa) divisions should be fashioned according to the previously mentioned method, adorned with various artistic works. ||88-89||
If a king should cause this temple of Śrī Vardhamāna to be built,
his fame, prosperity, and well-being shall increase more and more. Furthermore,
the abode of the lotus-born Brahmā is now celebrated.

In a field made square, with nineteen [units] at the end of twenty, the corners should be made four units; the secondary limbs (pratyaṅga) should also be equal to that. The beautiful transitions (parivartana) should be performed, each one adjacent to the other.
The hall (śālā) should be nine parts wide and project three parts;
the hall-laths (śālāla) should be made two parts, as should the bālamañjarī.
[These are placed] between the corner (karṇa) and the pratyaṅga, and likewise between the bāla and the pratyaṅga.
The internal water-chambers should be constructed in the middle of that measurement.

The inner sanctum (garbha) shall consist of seventeen parts, and the walls shall consist of six parts. Now we shall describe its vertical measurement; it should be twice that [horizontal measurement].
The altar (vedī) should have a height of six parts; the thirteen sections for the plinth (jaṅghā) should be made with a height of seven parts for the first storey (adibhūmikā).
The second [storey] should consist of six and a half parts, while the others are devoid of a one-part division.
The fifth [story] shall consist of four parts, and the others [the sixth through the ninth] shall each be half a part.
The entrance between the stories should be made with a pinnacle (kūṭa) and darbha-ornament;
half of the floor space should be provided, adorned with pillar ornaments.

Furthermore, one should adorn its summit with a pinnacle (*kūṭa*) that is half as high as the [main] body. The bell (*ghaṇṭā*) should have a height of five units and a width equal to the measurement of the interior (*garbha*).
One should fashion the excellent *sukāghrāya* (the "well-snouted" part) at the top just as described previously.
In this regard, the wise man should cause a temple named Mahāpadma to be constructed;
free from all dualities both in this world and the next, he enjoys supreme happiness.
Now, the five-hall temple is described according to its characteristics.
In a field made square, at the end of twenty-eight squares,
the lines resulting from its measurement are such that the corners are recorded as being five squares;
the secondary limbs (pratyaṅga) should be made three squares, protruding by two parts.

The hall (śālā) shall have an extent of eight padas and a projection of three padas. Between the corner and the secondary member (pratyaṅga), and likewise between the hall and the secondary member, it should be made one part wide and should enter into the water-interval (jalāntara).

The inner sanctum (garbha) shall consist of sixteen parts, and the walls likewise shall be six parts [in thickness]. Now we shall describe its vertical measurement; that should be double [the horizontal measurement]. A plinth (vedikābandha) should be constructed with a height of five and a half parts.
Its *jaṅghā* (lower wall) should be made there with eleven parts;
the floor-level (*bhūmikā*) should be constructed with a height of seven and a half parts.
A *kapotapālī* (dove-cot cornice) should be made for it, rising three parts in the middle.
This second tier may be according to the same measurement as the [first] ground;
the third with seven parts, and the fourth with six and a half.
The fifth should be made with six parts, and the bell five parts high.
In all the locations of the halls, a five-bell structure should be constructed;
joined with five youths, this is called the "Five Halls" (Pañcaśālā).
[Therein should be placed] Śuka, Āghrāsa, Sūrasena, and whatever else such as the water-pot (kalaśa) and so forth.
Therefore, as before, this task for the Pañcaśāla should be performed by the wise one.
For that fortunate person who causes this Pañcaśāla palace to be built on earth, incomparable happiness shall arise even within his lineage.
Now, therefore, we shall fully describe the Prāsāda temple known as Pṛthivījaya.
On a site divided into four by three lines and marked with twenty-eight squares,
the squares are thus defined.
The side-penetrations (bālapañjara) should be made with a width of two parts;

the hall (śālā) should have a width of six parts and a height of three parts. This applies between the corner and the secondary element (pratyaṅga), as well as between the hall and the secondary element. ||113-114||
In the intermediate space between the bays (kakṣā), a water-channel (salilāntara) one part wide should be constructed.
The inner chamber (garbha) should consist of ten parts, and its wall should be made six parts thick.
Here, the third [element] should be six parts; the others are raised by one part each.

Karna—there should be three bells, eight cubits in height; it should be adorned with pinnacles (kūṭas), and the crowning finial (śukāgra) and so forth should be made as before. Furthermore, one should cause these to be constructed at half the size of the temple (prāsāda).
A bell that is well-wrought, smooth, and adorned with bindings—
of the same kind as those prescribed for the pinnacles (kūṭa) of temples—
should be made for auspicious [structures] to ensure the complete success of the entire palace.
"O King, he who causes this Pṛthivījaya palace to be built enjoys the entire earth, garlanded by the seven oceans. Thus were the twelve [verses] spoken regarding the sacrificial pit.
Having recognized these as the foremost palaces, endowed with auspicious marks and known by the name *vāvāṭa*,
one obtains honor and dwells among kings. (120)

Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Vaṭoka Temple," in the architectural treatise on building construction named *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*, composed by the great king of kings, the supreme lord, the illustrious Bhojadeva.
Now begins the sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Bhūmija Temples.
We shall now describe, in due order, the characteristics of the Bhūmija Vimānas (temples).
Of those [elements] made square and those circular, as previously described,
for some there occurs an outward projection (*nirgama*) there according to the number of parts; for others, however, this [projection] is situated within the middle of the circle.
When the field has been made square and divided into ten parts, the characteristics of that [mountain] which is endowed with four terraces are now described.
There shall be four squares: Niṣadha and Malaya Mountain.
Among them, Mālyavat, Navamālin, and Niṣadha are mentioned.
Koṇa and Śambhūtara are two parts; Bhadra is half a part of Śambhu. It is declared that the width and length [of the temple] are five parts, while the Bhadra is five parts in width.
The projections of this Bhadra should be made with a portion less than a quarter [of the width].
Its *pallambikā* should be made with a quarter-portion in width.
The *karṇikā* should be made with one portion both in width and in projection.
And one should arrange the *pratibhadra* there, extending out by half a part.
The width of the *pratibhadra* shall be one and three-quarter parts;
the inner sanctum (*garbha*) shall be six parts, and its wall (*bhitti*) two parts.
The measurement for the height of the *talacchanda* has been stated; now the upper measurement is being described.
That [height] should be double the width, plus one-fourth more.
Its *vedībandha* (pedestal) should be two and a half parts in height.
One should divide those two parts and a half into four and a half [sub-divisions].
With two parts there shall be the *kumbha*; the *kalaśa* is recorded as being one part.
The interval is half a part, the *patra* is half a part, and the *kapotalī* is one part.
This construction of the altar-platform (vedikābandha) has been described as consisting of four and a half parts;
it should be provided with a plinth (jaṅghā) and a cornice (ucchālaka), and its height,
including the coping (varaṇḍikā), shall be three [parts].
Its second stage should be four and a half parts;
the *kumbha* and its *ucchālaka* should also be of that same measure. The third stage should be made four parts in height. ||13-14||
The fourth [section] consists of four parts from the base; the pitcher (kumbha) with its neck-protrusion (ucchālaka), as well as the height of the dome (kūṭa), are also as before.
The altar (vedī) should be one part, and the width of the shoulder (skandha) should be five and a half parts.
From the width of four times the half-kheta [of the hall], there is a hall on the ground floor said to be five parts in width;
the position of the entablature (skandha) is two parts in width. ||16–17||
The entrances of the various storeys should be constructed according to the lines,
extending from the base up to the neck of the bell-shaped pinnacle (ghaṇṭā).
The width of the temple should be five cubits for it to be beautiful.
The knower [of the proportions] should take half of the other portion of the hall according to its measurement;
one should divide that width which has been declared by six,
and with one part, there should be the entry of the neck all around.
One should conceive of the neck-circle as four parts in width.
One should divide the height of the bell (ghaṇṭā) into three parts;
from that, a wise man should fashion the lotus-head (padmaśīrṣa) measuring one part, starting from the height of the bell.
The kalaśa is two parts in height and one and a half parts in width.
The dyutāśikā should be three parts less than the śikhara;
thus, the Niṣadha temple is considered to have four stories with three parts [for each]. ||22-23||
One should adorn the Niṣadha palace for all the deities who are to be worshipped there.
Now we shall describe the characteristics of the Malaya mountain.
When the field has been made square and divided into twelve parts,
the diagonals (karṇas) should be made two parts each, aligned evenly with the water-channels.
The hall (śālā) should consist of five parts, while the pratīratha should be one and a half parts.
It should be constructed between the two ears of the hall (śālākarṇau), with a water-gutter (udakāntara) in between.
The projection (vinirgama) of the pratīratha should be half a part.
That division of the earth-element would be different—[as described] previously.
||27|| And those twelve parts which [are obtained] by dividing them by ten:
[one should apply them to] the inner wall, as well as the height of the plinth (jaṅghā) of the first storey. ||28||

One should cause the height of the altar-base (vedībandha) to be made according to the previous measurement. One should divide the middle portion, ending at the leaf-design (pallavikā), into ten parts by means of two śāla measures.
It should rise from the ground up to the previous shoulder (skandha).
It should be divided into twelve parts as described immediately above;
then, one should again divide that [height] by nineteen and a half. The height of the second storey shall then consist of those [resulting] parts. ||30-31||
The other three [measures] should be made in sequence, each reduced by one-quarter of a pada;
the height of the altar (vedikā) should be one part, and the hall (śālā) should be made in the Nāgara style.
Above the first level from the ground, the Śūrasenaka style of the garland (mālā) should be constructed.
As for those [pillars] at the corners and the pratirathas, they are five parts in height;
in their midst, with the pillar's elevation, the kūṭas are likewise raised.
They should be constructed with half [the height]; this same rule applies to other floors as well.

The expansion of the *skandha* (the base), the entry into the ground, and the height of the bell (*ghaṇṭā*) together with the pitcher (*kalaśa*) and the *śukanāsa* (gargoyle) shall be as previously described.
This temple, possessing auspicious characteristics, is said to be the Malayādri type.
All the gods are pleased with whoever causes this to be made;
for thousands of millions of years, he is honored in the heavenly world.
This is the Malaya Mountain Palace.
Now, the characteristics of the Mālyavat [temple] are described as they truly are:
[The base] should be divided by fifteen parts plus half; the ears (karṇas) should be made with two parts each, and the hall (śālā) should have an extension of five parts. 37–38.

The pair of pillars near the ears (karṇa) should be three-quarters [of the unit]; the pratīrathas should be three-quarters. On both sides of the hall (śālā), two pañjaras should be made, measuring one and a half parts each.
Separately from the hall and the pañjara, [the other elements] should be half a part.
The *pallavī* of the hall and its projection are each half a part;
those parts which have been stated as fifteen and a half—[these constitute] the inner sanctum (*garbha*), the width of the wall, and likewise the *khura-varaṇḍikā*. ||40-41||

From the base of the *jaṅghā* downwards, the first level (*kṣiti*) and the height of the lines (*rekhā*) are as before; it should be divided by [the number] increased by eight minus one quarter. The second floor (*bhūmikā*) shall have a height equal to five parts.
The other three stages (bhūmis) should be successively reduced by one-quarter of a pāda each.
The height of the pedestal (vedikā) should be made at one and a half parts by those who know the Vāstu-śāstra;
likewise, the line for the width of the shoulder (skandha), the bell (ghaṇṭā), and the pinnacle (kalaśa).
The arrangement of the stairs, the platforms, the turrets, and so forth,
as well as the height of the *śukanāsa* (the crow's-beak pinnacle), are all as described previously.
Thus is the palace named Mālyavān fully described.
For one who causes this to be made, all perfections arise;
his residence shall be in the world of Śiva, and he shall live for the duration of a kalpa.
Mālyavān.
Now the characteristic of that known as the Navamālika is described:
[47] When the site has been made square and divided into eighteen squares, the corners (karṇas) should be made two parts each, together with the water-paths (salilavartman). [48]

The hall (śālā) should consist of five parts; on both sides, there should be side-chambers (bālapañjara), each measuring one and a quarter parts, and these should be separated by a water-channel. Near the corners, there should be two pratiratha projections, each measuring two parts.
These two should be made with an interval of one water-course (udaka), and each should be one and a half parts in size.
These two belong to the *bālapañjaraka* and are situated between the *pratiratha* and the *pañjara*.
Alternatively, the *pratīratha* may be the *pañjara*, and likewise the *bālapañjaraka*.
Up to the *śālāpallavikā*, these [projections] should each extend out by half a part; as for the eighteen parts that have been mentioned,
one who knows the true principles of the site (*vāstu*) should divide them into ten sections.
The inner chamber, the wall, the height of the pedestal and the pillar-base,
the elevation of the first floor, and likewise the height of the pinnacle—
all this in this temple has been described by the wise as before. ||53-54||
The pinnacle (śikhara) shall consist of thirty-five parts less a quarter;
then the second storey (bhūmikā) should be made five parts high.
The remaining seven storeys, however, should each be reduced by a quarter of a part.
The height of the pedestal (vedikā) is one and three-quarter parts;
the width of the shoulder (skandha), the line (rekhā), the bell (ghaṇṭā), and likewise the pinnacle (kalaśa) [are as prescribed].
In the hall (śālā), there are the Śūrasenas, along with the arrangement of the pillars, the capitals (kūṭa), and so forth.
The height of the śukanāsa and its entry into the ground are as described previously.
Whoever should cause this Navamālika temple to be built with devotion,
the deities will be pleased with him and prosperity shall attend him.
The Navamālika [flower].
Now the types of trees suitable for palaces are described:
they are beloved by all the gods, born from the earth, ornaments of the city, the sole refuge of blessings, and heaps of glory. (59-60)
When they have arrived, they bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men;
among them, the first is named Kumuda, then Kamala, Kamalodbhava, Kiraṇa, Śataśṛṅga, and another, Niravadya. (61)
And the "Beautiful in Every Limb" (*sarvāṅgasundara*); these are the types of palaces.
Neither in detail nor in brief shall their characteristics now be proclaimed.
Among them, the first is said to be named *Kumuda*, which produces joy for all.
On a square site that is equal in width and length,
divided into ten parts, the inner sanctum (garbha) shall consist of three and six squares (nine).
There, with the remainder, one should construct four [elements].
Then, one should draw a circle there using the ear-line (karṇasūtra).
There shall be eight ears in the cardinal and intermediate directions, adorned with the intervals of water.
This [mandala] shall consist of ten squares extending to the edge of the ground on all sides.
The construction of the altar (vedībandha) should be performed with two squares of one and a half parts;
one should divide [the area] with four and a half squares.
The *kumbhaka* is two [squares].
The interval between [the pillars] is half a part, and the *kapotālī* (dove-cornice) is one part.

This is declared to be the *vedībandha* (pedestal-base). The height of the *jaṅghā* (shaft) should be four and a half parts; it is provided with a *talakumbhaka* (plinth-pitcher) and a *sopāna* (moulding). ||68-69||
On the first level, there should be a pinnacle (kūṭa) marked by three parts;
in the temple, one should divide the total height into fifteen parts.
There, the second level should be made five parts in height.
The height of the pinnacle (kūṭa) above [the third floor] should be equal to half the height of the pilasters (ucchālaka-stambha).
One should fashion the third floor with five parts less one-quarter;
one should construct the fourth floor with four and a half parts.
The construction of the corner pillars and so forth should be like that of the second floor.
A pedestal (vedikā) should be made six padas high, with a width equal to the thickness of the pillar.
One should draw the bamboo-receptacle (veṇukośa) using a cord six times [the length of the base].
The height of the bell should be made equal to one-fifth of the temple's height.
Then, one should divide that height of the bell into three parts;
with one part, one should fashion its neck, throat, and egg-shaped dome (aṇḍaka). ||74-75||
The width of the neck of the bell should be made with four parts out of the six parts into which the height of the bell has been divided.
One should fashion the lotus-head (padmaśīrṣaka) at the midpoint of the bell's height, using half of that height.

The height of the pitcher (kumbha) is equal to the height of the bell (ghaṇṭā), and its elevation is filled with the seed-vessel (bījapūra). The pinnacle (kalaśa) is remembered as being square, slightly curved, and elevated, with its width [equal to its height].
Whoever should cause this temple named Kumuda to be built out of devotion— ||77-78||
He rejoices in the auspicious abode of Śiva, the Lord of the World;
this is the Kumuda Palace.
Now, therefore, we shall fully describe the temple named Kamala.
When the site has been made square and divided into ten parts,
one should then draw a circle there using a cord equal to half the diagonal (karṇa).

One should construct four *bhadra* projections, each five parts in width, extending respectively toward the directions of Indra (East), Yama (South), Varuṇa (West), and Kubera (North). The width of the *pallavikā* [niche] should be one-quarter of a part.
The projections (nirgama) of the *bhadrās* should be made by one part outside the circle;
for each *pratibhadra* of the hall, it should project by half a *karṇikā*.
The width of the circle should be made three parts less a quarter.
The two *raśukas* should be twice as wide as they are long;
the two corners should be constructed by turning [the proportions] so that they extend beyond the water-line.
The inner sanctum (*garbha*) and the walls should be fashioned like those of the previously described temple.

Everything from the construction of the altar (vedībandha) up to the pinnacle (kumbha) for this [temple] is as before. From the first floor upwards, reaching as far as the second floor, Śūrasena should be constructed, excellently joined to the halls. 85–86.
The nyāsa-mantras for the kūṭas, pillars, and so forth are placed in the corners, pratirathas, and other parts.
The śālā should be five parts at its base and two parts above;
the height of the śukāghrā is three-quarters of the height of the śikhara.
That king who causes this palace named Kamala to be built shall become a sovereign over the victory of the Lord of Kamalā throughout the three worlds. This is the Kamala Palace.
Now, therefore, the temple Kamalodbhava is correctly described,
wherein the Lord himself, the eternal husband of Lakṣmī, finds rest.
When the site has been made square and divided into fourteen parts— ||89-90||
The arrangement of the auspicious five-fold [maṇḍala] should be as follows:
the *pratiratha* sections should be made with a length and width equal to two parts. The corners— ||91||
The emergence of the *pallavikā* should be made from the middle of the circle;
its division into halls (*śālā*) should be performed—
within the intermediate spaces, there should be water.
A wise man should determine that [measurement] to be either two or three finger-breadths;
he should divide the portions of this temple into ten squares.
The inner sanctum (garbha) should be constructed as before, and the walls likewise as before.
The plinth (khura) and the cornice (varaṇḍī) should be as previously described; the leg-base (jaṅghā), the pinnacle (kūṭa), and so forth, along with the ground-floor, should follow the same pattern.
The height of the spire (śikhara) should be as before, measuring twenty-one and a half [units].
Then one should divide [the area] into parts; the ground should be made as five parts of the second [unit].
Three remaining grounds should be made, each diminished by a quarter of a quarter. The altar (vedī) should be one part, and the entry into the ground should be made from here according to the lines.
The expansion of the meaning is as before, or there may be bells, pitchers, and so forth;
the pinnacle, pillars, and the like are as previously described, as is the height of the *śukanāsa* (the frontal pediment).
Whoever should cause this beautiful temple of the Lotus-born [Brahmā] to be built— //98-99//
That Lord of the entire world is born in every birth as the abode of the Lotus-born One.
Now we shall correctly explain, according to the traditional sequence, the characteristic of the radiating rays (kiraṇa).
When the field has been made square and divided—[as follows]—those fifteen parts which exist should again be divided by ten. 101.
In this case, the inner sanctum (garbha) should be constructed as before, and the walls likewise;
the plinth (khura) and the cornice (varaṇḍī) should be as previously described, and the height of the base-moulding (jaṅghākūṭa) should be the same.
The height of the spire (śikhara) should be as before, and one should divide that [height] by four parts less one.
The first stage there consists of twenty-four parts;
the second consists of five parts, while the other four stages are respectively reduced by one-quarter and one-half of those [parts]. (103–104)
Its vedikā (railing) should be made with a height of one and a quarter parts;
the height of the śukanāsa (gargoyle), the divisions of the pillars and kūṭas (pinnacles) of the hall,
the width of the pillar lines, and the bell, pitcher, and other elements should be as before.
O son of the Earth, the *kūṭas*, *drās*, and *viḍakas* should be prepared for each respective level.
This [rite] is to be performed for Hara, Hiraṇyagarbha, Hari, and likewise Dinakara; it is never to be performed for anyone else.
That king who should cause this temple named Kiraṇa to be built shall possess irresistible majesty upon the earth, like the thousand-rayed sun. (108) [The Kiraṇa Temple]
Now, the palace named Śaśaśṛṅga, which possesses auspicious characteristics, is described;
it is beloved by all the gods and especially by Śiva.
When the field has been made square, it measures nineteen units [on each side].
Then, one should fashion a circle here using the cord of the ear-measure (karṇārdhasūtra).
The ears (karṇas) should be made with two parts, and the hall (śālā) should consist of five parts. Its "hall-foliage" (śālāpallavikā) emerges from the middle of the circle.
Two *pratiratha* (side-entrances) should be made, each having twice the width and depth [of the *śālā*];
beyond the *vartanā*, there is circularity at the center of the corner-shrines (*koṇaśālā*).
Between the corners of the *śālā* and the *pratiratha*s, there should be a water-interval (*jalāntara*).
One should again divide those nineteen parts by ten.

The inner sanctum (garbha) is as before, and likewise the wall (bhitti), the plinth (khura), and the coping (varaṇḍikā). The height of the pillar-shaft (jaṅghā), the height of the base (bhū), and the elevation of the spire (śikhara) are as previously described.
Then, starting from the *meru* and extending to the edge of the terrace,
one should divide the height of the pinnacle by twenty-eight minus one— that is, by twenty-seven parts.
Of that [height], the second floor should be made five parts in height.
Five lines should be drawn on the ground, each one foot high;
an altar (vedī) should be constructed by the expert, rising one and a half parts.
The hall, its pillars, and the *śukanāsikā* (the gable-front) should be divided according to their respective proportions.
All this, beginning with the lines, shall be as before for the Śataśṛṅga temple. Whoever constructs this beautiful Śataśṛṅga temple,
his twenty-one lineages—
