Both the creator and the instigator of these worlds shall certainly be the two leaders of the Gaṇas for the enemy of Tripura;
[this is] the palace of Śataśṛṅga.
This is the definition of the faultless [measurement].
It is threefold: superior, middling, and inferior.
The superior is forty cubits long, while the middling shall be thirty cubits. ||120-121||
This is declared to be the smallest [mandala] when a square field is divided into twenty squares by its sides. Then,
one should fashion a circle here using two threads along the diagonals.
By those five [parts], a *śālāpallavī* should be constructed, circular in shape.
Furthermore, the division of the *śālās* for these two *śālās* shall be as before;
and in each corner, there are six-earned (*ṣaṭkarṇā*) [elements] measuring one part in length and breadth.
The account of the arrangement should be performed with water-intervals;
one should then divide those [sections] into ten parts by means of three divisions.
Having set aside the portions for the floor-levels, the remainder is for the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) and so forth.
That should be constructed as before, and likewise the height of the pinnacle;
furthermore, one should divide that [height] again into thirty-one and a half parts,
and the second storey should be made five pādas in height.
The remaining six types of ground plans (bhūmikā) are deficient by one-quarter of a pada;
here, the artisan should make the altar (vedī) three-quarters of a pada.
The arrangement of pillars, capitals, and so forth for the halls (śālā) belongs to the Śūrasenas.
The height of the parrot-beak, the bell, the pinnacle-pot, and so forth, are as described previously.
That wise person who causes this temple named Niravadya to be built attains the supreme abode, which is very difficult even for Brahmā and the other gods to reach. ||129-130||
A palace free from reproach.
Now we shall describe the beautiful Prasada temple, lovely in all its parts, the bestower of worldly enjoyment and liberation, and the ornament of the excellent enclosure wall.
When the square-shaped site has been divided into twenty-four parts: 131.
The *karṇas* (corner projections) should have a width of two parts, and the *śālā* (hall) should consist of five parts.
The *vṛttānta* (inner courtyard) should be made with *pallavis* (ornamental niches); the remaining [elements] in the halls are as before.
There should be three *pratirathas* (side-projections) in the middle between the corner-halls (*karṇa-śālā*).
Having turned back within the courtyard, the [passages] should have a length and width of two parts;
they should be located at the ends of the *śālākarna* and *pratiratha*, in the intervals between the water-channels.
Furthermore, twenty-three parts should be divided by the artisans.
The inner walls of the sanctum and so forth should be constructed as previously described, and the *varaṇḍikā* (the upper molding) should likewise be made.
The height of the *jaṅghā* (the plinth/base) and the successive stories, or the height of the spire (*śikhara*), should be determined as before;
one should divide that height of the spire into thirty-five parts.
Its second level should be five units high;
the remaining seven levels of his [temple] should be reduced by one-quarter of a unit each.
The height of the pedestal (vedikā) should be two parts, and the projection of the levels should be [one part].
Whatever remains of this [structure] must be executed according to the lines;
furthermore, the pillars, the pinnacle (kūṭa), and so forth, should be fashioned by one who knows that, just as before.
Whoever causes this temple to be built here, making it beautiful in all its limbs— ||138-139||
He obtains vast enjoyments with the beauties of heaven in the celestial realm;
he becomes a palace beautiful in every limb.
Now we shall describe the eight-hall [temples] among the classes of ground types:
||140|| Among them, the first is the Svastika, and another is known as the Vajrasvaritaka;
the third is the Harmyatalaka, and the fourth is the Udayācala. ||141||
And the fifth is proclaimed as Gandhamādana. Now, their specific characteristics are described:
on a field made square and equal in width and length— ||142||
By drawing a line from the corner to the midpoint of the side, one should draw a circle equal to it.
One should divide this circular field into sixfold eight squares;
eight halls are to be constructed, each four squares in width.
The *pallavī* is to be known by the rule for the *vṛtta* [meter]; next, the measurement of the *karṇikā* is stated.
A *vedibandha* (enclosure) should be constructed, rising two *bhāgas* in height.
One should divide that [measurement] into five parts; therein, the *kumbhaka* [is formed].
(146) The *masūraka* should be made with one part plus a quarter;
the subsequent petal with half a part, and from that, the *kapotālī* arises. (147)
The shank should be made from four parts, with one-quarter of that part added;
it is joined with the pedestal (tala), the pitcher (kumbha), and the neck (ucchālaka), and possesses auspicious characteristics.
The first ground should be made of two parts, complete with its coping (varaṇḍikā).
Having made the width ten units, the height should be twelve units by those same measures.
A wise person should construct the shoulder (skandha) there as six units;
one should draw the bamboo-receptacle (veṇukośa) using a cord of exactly sixfold [the required length]. ||149-150||
Having made the height equal to twelve parts,
the second earth (the second story) shall be made with two of those five parts;
then the other three earths (stories) should be made one-quarter of a part high each.
The womb (garbha) should be placed within the womb, and there should be an entry into the tiers (bhūmikās). Then the altar (vedikā) should be made, rising to one and a half parts;
the bell (ghaṇṭā) should be one and three-quarter parts, and one should divide that into three parts.
The *pada* should be the height of the neck (*kaṇṭha*), and the neck itself should be raised by one part. Upon it, a very beautiful egg-shaped dome (*aṇḍaka*) should be made, measuring one part.
One should construct the skull-like capital (*karpara*) with a height of one and a half parts, using *sāmalasāraka* wood.
The width of the bell (ghaṇṭā) should be made from four and a half parts out of the remaining four and a half parts [of the total height]. One should divide that [width] into six parts;
[the base] should be four parts in width from the bulb (kanda). ||155–156||
The height of the kalaśa (finial) is one and a half parts, and that of the śikhara (spire) is half of that;
the śukanāsā (front porch) is prescribed to be one-third of the śikhara's height.
It may be less than the width by one-eighth, measured according to the interior dimension.
Furthermore, Śūrasena is one and a quarter [units] in width;
above that, it is equal to the second floor.
Above the first floor, the three Śūrasenas are considered to be equal in width to the hall (śālā). ||158-159||
The hall and the eight Nāgarikas, adorned with the seizing of crocodiles—
blessed is he who would have this auspicious Svastika temple built; for him, in his subsequent birth, there shall be a vessel of well-being, prosperity, and fortune.
The Svastika Palace.

Hereafter, we shall describe the temple known as Vajrasvastika, which is endowed with the proper characteristics and is beloved by Śakra and the other gods. It should be situated in the center of a Svastika diagram that possesses the previously mentioned characteristics. 161–162.
"O auspicious lady, a sharp-pointed and very beautiful prong should be provided;
one should construct a pavilion in front, endowed with all the required characteristics.
Thus has this [mandala] correctly been described, known as the Vajrasvastika."
The fortunate person who would have this palace built, which grants all desires,
shall become an object of enjoyment for the celestial women and attain the station of Indra.
This is the Vajrasvastika Palace.
Now we shall describe the palace roof (harmyatala), the temple (prāsāda), the ornament of the earth:
When a field has been made square, with its width and length equal, one should draw a circle within it by dropping a cord at half the distance of the corner (karṇa). ||165-166||
One should then divide that circular plot into sixty-four squares;
within this, eight four-square halls (śālās) are to be constructed in detail.
The *pallavī* is formed by the circular line on the outside, and the *bhadra* and *karṇikā* are likewise defined.
Two ears (karṇas) should be constructed between each pair of halls;
they should have a length and width of one part and be adorned with an internal water-channel.
By means of mutual rotation, one should form sixteen corners.
In this manner, throughout all eight directions, the measurement should be accompanied by ritual acts;

the womb (garbha), the wall (bhitti), the altar (vedī), the pillar-base (jaṅghā), and the first floor (prathamabhūmikā) must be constructed according to the previously mentioned Svastika measurement by one who knows that system.
The height, which consists of twelve parts, is divided there by twenty;
that [measurement] here is to be made in twenty-eight ways for the ground-lines (*sūtrabhūmikā*).
The second [ground-line] is separately [divided] into five parts, minus one-quarter of a square (*pada*). ||171–172||
The other five levels should be two parts high and provided with altars (vedīs) on all sides;
one should fashion four *mañjarīs* made of *nāgara* and *karṇī* styles.
Furthermore, there are another four which are joined with *drauviḍa* craftsmanship.
The width of the *ghaṇṭā* (bell) should be equal to the width of the *skandha* (pedestal), as should the heights of the *vedikā* (railing) and the *kalaśa* (finial).

The *śūrasena*, *śukāghrā*, *stambhikā*, and the decorative motifs (*kūṭabhakti*) should be fashioned; furthermore, the lines (*rekhā*) of this temple must be executed by one who knows them, just as before. 174–175.
May both he who built this palace and he who caused it to be built attain a world where the arising of eternal bliss and happiness prevails. (176) [The Palace on the Roof-Terrace]
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the temple as the Mountain of Sunrise.
On an auspicious site made square, with its sides equal to its diagonals,
one should then draw a circle upon it using a cord half the length of the diagonal.
One should construct a circular field divided into eighty squares.
Eight halls should be fashioned, measuring four squares each, in the eastern directions.
The *pallavī* is formed by a circular line on the exterior, as are the *bhadra* and *karṇikā*.
Within the two halls, one should construct three corners each;
adorned with water-channels having a length and width of two parts,
twenty-four such corners are thus to be fashioned.
One should perform their mutual exchange in due order.

By this measurement of the *sāma*, one should design the interior chamber (*garbha*), the wall (*bhitti*), the altar (*vedikā*), the pillar-base (*jaṅghā*), the floor, and the pinnacle (*śikhara*) as previously described. ||181-182||
One should fashion eight clusters (mañjarīs) joined according to the Nāgara style,
endowed with Rudreśvara, and adorned with water-vessel supports (nīradhāra). There should also be bell-pinnacles (ghaṇṭākūṭa), lines (rekhā), pillars (stambhikā), and the Śūrasenaka style.
Equipped with a pinnacle (kalaśa) as wide as the shoulder of a parrot, one should construct the Eastern Mountain (Udayācala) according to the prescribed rules for the svastika;
its height, which is one-twelfth [of the base], is divided there into twenty parts. ||184-185||
It should be divided by thirty-five; therein is the foundation.
It should be made five parts high, and then the other seven levels [should be] one-quarter part high each. The altar (vedikā), however, is two parts high.
Endowed with all auspicious characteristics,
the man who, possessed of devotion, properly causes this temple to be built,
attains the eternal state that is difficult even for the gods to reach. ||187-188||
The palace of the mountain of sunrise.
Now, in accordance with the sequence, Gandhamādana is described.
On this mountain, which is rich in its own characteristics and dimensions,
one should prepare eight clusters on the eastern peak, joined with the actions of mercury and vitriol.
The pinnacles and finials should be fashioned, endowed with various artistic works.
In the appropriate places, there should be three lines for the hero's army—
[the base], as well as the *śukanāsa* (gargoyle), the bell, the shoulder, and the spire itself.
One should fashion the pinnacle, the pillar, and the dome as previously described.
That fortunate person who causes this temple, an ornament of the earth, to be built will undoubtedly become a glorious lord of the Vidyādharas. (192)
He enjoys various pleasures and is attended by celestial women;
this is the Gandhamādana Palace.
The twenty-five lines resulting from the various divisions of the *udaya* (rise) are described here according to tradition as belonging to the Latin, Nāgara, and Bhauma scripts.
For the Latin script, it is the *vāraṅga*; for the Nāgara, however, it is the *kūṭaka*.
For those built on the ground, the foundation should be established in front of the main hall (mathā).
The pinnacle should be equal in both width and diagonal; it may be of the lowest or highest grade.
Following this, [the measurement] of twenty-four parts should be applied. 195–196.
That many divisional lines (bhāgarekhās) are said to be auspicious,
beautiful, favorable, well-formed, and very pleasing;
likewise, they are pure, peaceful, Kāverī, and Sarasvatī.
Lokā, Karavīrā, Kumudā, and likewise Padminī;
Kanakā, Vikaṭā, Devaramyā, and likewise Ramaṇī; Vasundharā, Haṃsī, Viśākhā, and Nandinī. ||198-199||
Jayā, Vijayā, Sumukhā, and Priyānatā—
these are the lines enumerated, which are twenty-five in number.
These are the lines.
All these [temples] yield auspicious results for both the builder and the one who causes them to be built.
Thus has been described the square and the four-square [layout]; these seven types of earth-born [temples] are circular.

Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Chapter on Earth-Born Temples," in the *Vāstuśāstra* named *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*, composed by the Great King of Kings, the Supreme Lord, the illustrious Bhojadeva.
Now begins the sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Maṇḍapa.
Now we shall describe the eight types of maṇḍapas situated in relation to the temple.
One should first construct the temple, which must be pure in its proportions and endowed with excellent characteristics.
This [body] may be either covered or, in some cases, distinct;
it is "covered" when it is symmetrical and composed of four parts,
and it is declared "distinct" when it is divided by animal portions.
The *garbha* (central core) is praised when it is equal to the *garbha*; it should bring about the excellence of a well-fashioned vessel.
Thus, one should first lay out the pavilions (*maṇḍapa*) from the main house;
one should divide them according to what is known as the "hundred squares" (*śatapada*), distinguishing between the superior, middling, and inferior.
Among those, the pavilions (maṇḍapa) should be auspicious; one is named Nandana, and another is Mahendra, Vardhamāna, Svastika, Sarvabhadra,
and the eighth of these is proclaimed as Mahāpadma, the king of houses.
These have names corresponding to their actual nature; we shall now describe their characteristics.
A structure twice the length of the temple, or one and a quarter times its length, should be constructed in front of the divine sanctuary, otherwise it would be useless.
The width of the pavilion should be made equal to the height of the palace;
these [pavilions] should be provided with *śukanāsas* (gargoyle-like projections) and equipped with *alindas* (porches).
An *alinda* is that which extends out from all sides, measuring one part in width.
Sometimes, having emerged with half a part and being extended by one part,
a wise man should divide the auspicious [mandala] on all sides into nine parts;
the horns should consist of two parts each, joined together by water-intervals.
The measurement from the base to the top [of the structure] should be divided into parts.
On the corners, a chariot-arch (rathikā) should be made, projecting by one-quarter of a part.
It should extend out by one part and be four parts in width.
The Madhyabhadra [type of pedestal] should be constructed in all four directions.
One should not construct a pedestal for the temple-pedestal here in the pavilion;
on the floor-slab, there should be the Śokanāśa or the Yakṣitiraṅgikā.
One should place a palm-leaf mat beneath that pavilion;
in this manner, it should be made progressively lower and lower from front to front.
Alternatively, the architect who is most learned in the scriptures may provide it at an even level.
The entrance should be one-fourth the width of the hall and provided with six door-sockets;
the *agrabhadra* should be constructed, adorned with four pillars,
and likewise, there should be a *saṃsṛti* passage behind it in the Caitra pavilion.
The *saṃsṛti* should be like a parrot's nose, and the *pṛṣṭhabhadra* should be on the ground;
the remaining procedure for the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) should be performed in the same manner. It should be enclosed by walls on both sides.
One should construct the wall according to its proportion, adorned with windows;
and latticed windows should be made along with moon-viewing openings.
The width of the door in the pavilion should be the same as that of the palace door.
The upper door (ūrdhvadvāra) should be constructed with a measurement of one and a quarter, one and a third, or one and a half [parts],
without exceeding the proportions of the main door (mūladvāra). It should be provided with lattices, decorative railings, pigeon-holes, and ornamental elephant-protectors (mattavāraṇaka).
Lattice windows should be made with pillars fashioned from whorls;
the window-opening should be half the size of that, and the door-looker one-quarter less.
One should duly construct an auspicious quadrangular courtyard within the center of the hall.
In the *kṣobhā* [type], there is an outer line; one should avoid the *druma* [pattern] by means of the *kṣā* [measurement].
This is explained so that it may be according to the middle method of wooden construction (*dārukarma-vidhi*).
It is joined with equal *kṣaṇas*, equal pillars, and equal *ālindakas*.

With equal ears and possessing the arrangement of the sea-drums (samudra-vya-vidhāna), it should be constructed with six cross-beams; some should be made elongated at the front. The balance-beam (tulā) should be level, or else raised in the middle portion.
Those [arches] are dependent on the *tulā* and the six wooden beams (*ṣaḍdāruka*), or those [beams] are dependent on them;
some are joined with the movement of a churning-stick (*manthāna*) or a circular path (*alīgati*).
Alternatively, they should be made from the middle [of the structure], encircled by pillars and vestibules (*stambhālinda*).
It should be constructed with a great base, equal on both sides of the fourfold [structure].
The work of the elephant’s trunk should be executed using materials of progressively superior quality;
these various types should likewise be made from complete and unimpaired materials.
Whatever single ritual act a wise person may perform,
he should embellish it with intervals of time using *illī* flowers and arches (*toraṇa*). These should be joined with *vajra-bandha* knots and adorned with small bells and sprouts.
The pillars should be fashioned as being strewn with pearl necklaces and lotus petals, adorned with śālabhañjikās (statues of women), and decorated with the five types of ornaments;
they should also be provided with most wonderful neck-pieces, small chariots, and archways. ||30-31||
Adorned with various types of architectural forms and decorative works,
such [shrines] should be constructed, equal in size to the boundary wall and rising in proportion to it;
they should be placed in the front porticos, the verandas, in the central part, and on both sides.
The palm-prints are not prescribed so that the action may be performed according to one's desire.
Just as at the gate of a boundary one does not obstruct the entry of the wind, so too should the *addhvarikā* be made, situated upon the cloth. ||33-34||
O auspicious lady, a wise man should construct a six-doored pavilion there, resembling a row of peacocks, cranes, and pigeons, and possessing the majesty of an elephant in rut;
this should be done according to the measurements and procedures for the outer pavilion as well.
With pigeon-cots, parapets, and likewise with intermediate panels (antarapatraka), as well as with variegated corner-pavilions (karṇaprāsādaka), the work should be executed on the auspicious Maṇḍapa.
Of the height, ten parts should be distinguished by the wise, and one of these [parts] should be selected. ||36-37||

The height of the pavilion (maṇḍapa) should be one-third, or three-quarters, of the height of the pinnacle (śikhara); its measurement should be equal to the elevation of the śukanāsa. Alternatively, one may construct a palace (harmya) there, adorned with beautiful cornices (karṇa).
The characteristics of the auspicious pavilion.
In a field made square, one should divide the Nandana [courtyard].
The Bhadra [hall] should have a length of six parts and a width of four parts;
it extends by one part on each side, with pillars arranged at the front.
The Bhadrā situated within the corner should be known as five parts in length;
the wall should be one part in width and joined with the water-interval.
In this manner, the Nandana pavilion should always be constructed in all four directions.
Nandana.
The Mahendra [temple] has its base-chamber (talacchanda) with ears (karṇas) joined by ploughs (lāṅgalas).
It is one-fourth part wide on all sides and adorned with wooden carvings (dārukarma).
Its two-part peaks (śṛṅgas) should be made to ripple by means of water-filled recesses.
Extending for four parts, one part protrudes; one should provide a face on one side, free from the constraints of wooden craftsmanship.
This is Mahendra.
If Nandana is outside the Bhadra, it should be devoid of water-channels;
with a width of two parts and extending one part inward,
one should place it on both sides of the eastern neck (prāggrīva), situated above the height.
Or one may fashion it with a *votaya* handle; in that case, it becomes a *vardhamāna*.
(46) [The *vardhamāna*: The *vardhamāna* [is as follows].
On both sides of the Nandana, O auspicious lady, one should enclose it with walls and adorn it with lattice windows; one should not leave a gap for water.
This is declared to be the Svastika, endowed with all auspicious characteristics.
The Svastika.
Now, the characteristics of the *sarvatobhadra* [mandala] are correctly described:
if there are two ears and a ploughshare, each measuring two and a half parts in length, the arrangement of the wooden components among them should be executed accordingly. (48–49)
One should have a *bhadra* (projection) constructed, measuring one part in its width and six parts in its length,
consisting of two sets of six wooden beams, situated on the exterior;
this is the *sarvatobhadra*.
When the site has been made square, one should divide it by means of the eastern sections;
having left those out, one should place ploughs upon the diagonals in the middle,
situated at intervals of four parts and joined with six wooden pegs.

O Bhadra, one should construct four *bhadras* in the cardinal directions, extending out from the central portion. Then, from the length of that [central] part, one should make an *alindaka* (porch) on all sides outside;
furthermore, one should construct *pratibhadras*, each having a length of four parts.
With its exits and non-exits undivided and provided with pillars in all directions—
endowed with these characteristics, it is proclaimed as the Mahāpadma. (54) [The Mahāpadma].

On a field made square and adorned with four corners, one should construct it surrounded by porticos (alindas), with a front-projection (prāggrīva) situated at the entrance. Arches (gavākṣakas) and moon-windows (candrāvalokanas) should also be fashioned.
Likewise, it should have windows and illuminations, adorned with forms on all sides.
Indeed, the construction of a royal palace should thus be endowed with every beauty;
even a temple for the ancestors (atṛgoma) should be furnished with such characteristics.
The king of houses.

The best [measurement] for Śukanāsa should be from the base of Śukanāsa; the smallest may be determined according to one's desire. One should construct it equally on both sides, extending transversely and lengthwise.
Or else, with wide-reaching eyes, one should construct an incomparable temple and a pavilion outside;
in them, windows should be made as broad as the width of the doors, according to the previous proportions. ||59-60||
The height [of the door] should be equal to, one-quarter less than, or one-and-a-half times its width;
it should be provided with a lintel (brūma) of eight finger-breadths when the width of the door is divided into ten parts.
The width of the pavilion and the height of its pillars should be equal to the height of the door.
The width of the inner sanctum (garbha) of the pavilion (maṇḍapa) should be one-eighth, one-sixteenth,
or indeed one-half of the pavilion; this [measurement] for the inner sanctum of the pavilion should be executed according to one's capacity.
"He who dwells for hundreds of autumns in that abode of the gods, surrounded by throngs of Apsarases during the assembly of the deities.
Thus ends the sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Pavilion," in the *Vāstuśāstra* named *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*, composed by the Great King of Kings, the Supreme Lord, the illustrious Bhojadeva.
Now begins the sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Twenty-Seven Maṇḍapas.
Now the twenty-seven maṇḍapas are described. One should construct the smallest maṇḍapa there as twice the size of the temple (prāsāda).
In the case of the smallest temple, the middle [size] should be one and a quarter times [the base measurement];
in that same [temple], one should construct the smallest [size] according to the measure of one and a half [times].
For the middle [temple], [the sizes] are one and a quarter, one and a half, and one and a quarter [times].

In the case of the best [type of temple], the pavilions (maṇḍapa) may be one and a half, one and a quarter, or equal [to the width]; these are for the best and other [types]. In small temples, there may be many other pavilions that are one and a quarter, double, or one and a half times [the width], arising with intervals. 3–4.
Furthermore, if a suitable site cannot be obtained, one should employ all these [proportions] for all [structures].
One should take the length according to the length and the width likewise;
this measurement should be applied to the pavilion (maṇḍapa), the turret (valabhī), and the Garuḍa [pedestal] as well.
When the square-shaped field has been divided into ten parts,
the *bhadra* shall consist of four parts and the *pratibhadra* of two parts;
there shall be a projection of one part either at the front or at the back.
The projection of the *bhadra* shall be one part, or even one and a half parts;
it may also be one-third or one-fourth of the *prāsāda*.
Furthermore, the projection may be half, or one-sixth, or one-fifth [of the width].

The pavilions (maṇḍapa) should be made equal in measure to the palaces, or three-quarters of that measure, or even one-third less; they should be constructed with symmetrical sections. The *bhadra* projection at their front is declared to be equal to their own width. || 9-10 ||
The two ears (karṇas) should be known as occupying two parts each at their four corners;
together with the left and right portions, the bhadra measures six parts.
One should not, however, provide this [bhadra] on the front and back of the pratibhadra.
This pavilion, possessing sixty-four [pillars], shall be named Puṣpaka;
thus it is the Puṣpaka.
In the three directions, there are *pratibhadra* [bays], and at the entrance, the neck indeed faces east;
the *puṣpabhadraka*, *tistambha*, and *catuṣka* should be *suprabha*.
Thus, by passing beyond two pillars, we describe the twenty-fold pavilion (*maṇḍapa*).
Puṣpabhadra, Vrata, Amṛtanandana, Kausalya, Yudhiṣaṅkīrṇa, Gajabhadra, Jayāvaha,
Śrīvatsa, Vijaya, Vastukīrṇa, Śruti, and Jaya. ||14-15||
Yajñabhadraka, Viśāla, Suśliṣṭa, Śatrumardana, Bhāyaṃva, Dama, Mānava, and Mānabhadra;
Sugrīva is said to be Maṇḍapa, provided with auspicious four-footed animals.
It is provided with four ears consisting of three parts each, as previously described, and is joined with twenty-four pillars;
our residence has six other [pillars] due to the reduction of two pillars. ||17-18||
Sugrīva, Harṣa, Karṇikāra, Padārdhika, Siṃha, Sāgabhadra, and Sustatra as the seventh—
these are said to be the twenty-seven pavilions in brief. ||19||
These Miśrakas, possessing various forms and bearing the appearance of palaces,
should be understood as measuring two, three, or one cubit [in height];
they may be equal in size to the main palace, or increased by a third or a half.
A foot-pavilion (pādamaṇḍapa) is to be known as being at the tip of the double-pillar *śukanāsa*;
the walls of the pavilion are prescribed according to the measurement of the palace wall,
or they may be one-quarter or three-quarters [of that].

In some cases, one should construct sky-pavilions (ākāśamaṇḍapa) devoid of walls. This rule has been declared for [pavilions] with pillars; in those with supporting walls (sāndhāra), it is according to their own proportions. Whatever kind of temple there is, the pavilion in front of it should be of that same kind.
Those names which belong to the palaces (prāsāda) may also apply to the pavilions (maṇḍapa).
This distinction among pavilions is prescribed according to the specific type of building site (vāstu).
The location for the fifty-pavilion [temple] is half that of the Nīla [fortress], and the same applies to the dining hall.
O protector of men, for the sake of sacrifice, for the sake of the foremost ascetics, and for the sake of a monastery,
the expansion [of the site] should be made from ten cubits up to a limit of one hundred;
the measurement in number of cubits shall be according to the hand of the master of the house.
The first pavilion (nādyamaṇḍapa) should be constructed according to one's requirements and as conceived by one's own intellect, being either rectangular or square;
the largest measures one hundred and eight cubits, while the smallest is sixty-four cubits.

The smallest pavilion should be made thirty-two cubits in measure; its width should be eight [cubits], and the dressing room (nepathyagṛha) and other structures should be designed according to one's own intelligence in accordance with the specific requirements.
Two doors should be made according to those proportions,
and a third for the dressing room (nepathyagṛha) facing the stage.
They should be provided with equal intervals, equal pillars, and equal vestibules (alinda).

The auspicious pavilions (maṇḍapas) should have equal ears, be level, well-proportioned, and pleasing. A square structure should be provided with walls and, as desired, with an exit. The measurement should be based on the pillars and corners, while the wall should be situated outside that measurement.
The altar-maṇḍapa, with its decorations and so forth, may be situated either in the center or on the exterior;
however, if there is a desire for more space, it should be constructed in the middle of the wall's measurement.
In the largest [type], one should construct a four-square *bhadra* within a sixty-four-square grid.
In the center, there should be an auspicious area of eighty-one squares divided into five parts.
When divided into sections for the smallest [type], it should have continuous openings;
the corner projections (karṇas) should be made with two parts, and the pavilion should be provided with walls.
One should divide the *bhadra* and the *prāsāda* into parts resembling [the former], and likewise apportion the *karṇabhadra*.

One should protect the *kṣobhaṇa* on the exterior; in the opposite case, there would be a breaking apart (*pāṭana*). The *kṣaraka*, the *kumbha*, the *kalaśa*, and the *kapota* should be together with the *jaṅghā*.
In accordance with the proportions of the temple:
||38|| The *rucaka* should be four-cornered; the eight-cornered is called the *vajra*;
the sixteen-cornered is the *dvivajra*, and the one known as the *pratīta* is twice that [number of corners]. ||39||
In the Madhyapradeśa style, this pillar is proclaimed to be circular (vṛtta).
Now, one should construct pavilions (maṇḍapas) in another manner, in sixteen ways, with three, five, seven, or nine columns, being symmetrical on both sides.
The middle section [of the hall] should be one and a half parts, or indeed exactly two and a half parts, compared to the others;
this same rule should be applied even in a sixfold pavilion.
It should be situated within the interior of the temple's womb-chamber (garbha), or else it may be at its wall.
Along the path of the pillar-line, when the moment has arrived at the center of the pavilion,
the expansion of the *bhadra* should be performed by means of the interior of the main temple's sanctum;
the remaining moments should be established with an equal number of unbroken grains.
The pavilion (maṇḍapa) should be equal to the temple roof, including its one-third portion;
it should have similar dimensions and a level floor.
We shall now describe the height of the pavilion according to another method.
Half of that [measurement] should be placed in the middle of the *pada*; this is prescribed as auspicious for the temple. When the [length] is divided tenfold, it is equal to four and five cubits.
The pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) should consist of nine parts between the two northern beams (*uttarapaṭṭa*).
In a site measuring six, eight, or ten cubits, one-eighth part [is the door-width]; or in a seven-part site, it is not [so].
In sites of ten or eleven cubits, there should be six parts by count, including a half-part;
in sites of thirteen cubits, it is five and a half parts.
Furthermore, there should be fourteen parts of five [units] each, plus one-quarter;
above that, the height up to twenty [units] should consist of five parts.
One may arrange it so that it is joined or even so that it is detached, as one pleases.
The pillar of Śukanāsa and the pillar of the pavilion, though joined together, are clearly distinguished there;
likewise, the corner pillar of the palace and those swallowed by it, along with the swallowed pavilions, are distinct. (50–51)
They should emerge separately, adorned with the four auspicious features (caturbhadra):
the talapaṭṭa, the añcha, the śukanāsa, and the vyātala, as well as the bhūmiraṅgikā.
One should employ the talapaṭṭa below those pavilions (maṇḍapas).
In this manner, the wise man should make each subsequent level lower than the one preceding it;
or alternatively, he may make them level according to the measurement of the temple floor.
This applies likewise to those [deities] whose names begin with "Dhruva" and to those who have originated from Śrīkūṭa.
The names beginning with Rucaka and the various architectural divisions should be understood to apply to the pavilions as well, due to their connection with them, and not otherwise.
For the purpose of festivals in the temples, there are various distinct types of chariots (vimānas).

Above what is designated as the pavilion (maṇḍapa) and so forth, there should be twenty-seven [pillars] for the purpose of the deity's procession; likewise, one should arrange them accordingly. Furthermore, the pillars may exceed sixty-four in number according to the count of the squares (pada).
The components of the temple—along with the pavilion—should be [constructed] from those *kṣaṇas*;
the site of the *vāstu* should be understood and prepared using uneven *kṣaṇas*.
No fault arises therein; the artisan’s desire is the cause in this matter.
Now we shall describe the wooden construction (dārukalā) pertaining to the pavilion (maṇḍapa). Whatever the proportions of its level ground may be, those same proportions are stated here.
According to the division of the temple (prāsāda), the royal [pavilion] consists of one part.
The altar (vedī) is to be known as two parts; the two parts are for the *mattavāraṇa*.
Likewise, the *candrāvalokana* should be made with two parts.
The fillet (*paṭṭa*) is half a part, and the seat (*āsana*) is half a part.
One should fashion the capital and the pillar-base (kūṭastambha) with one and a quarter parts;
the crown (śīrṣaka) and the coping (bharaṇa) are likewise intended to be one and a quarter parts. This should be made on a level surface, though in some cases it may be uneven.
The fillet (paṭṭi) should be fashioned in another manner:
below the upper fillet and above the base fillet (talapaṭṭa),
it should be made as one-third of the module (pada) or in the middle of that third part for the purpose of viewing the moon.
Below that, a division should be made into five parts:
the *rājasena* should occupy one part, the *vedikā* two parts,
and the *mattavāraṇaka* should be made to measure two parts.
Alternatively, the world of the Moon (candraloka) should be made with four parts out of ten;
the altar (vedī) is made with two parts, and the mattavāraṇa is equal to that.
The rūpahāra is made with one part, and the kaṇṭhikā with one part.

The projection of the *mattavāraṇa* is one part less three-quarters [of the total width], or else it is half a part; the middle projection between those two is likewise. This measurement applies to the gabled pavilions (*kūṭāgāra*), as does this measurement for the seat-slab (*āsana-paṭṭaka*).
One should fashion the seat with an extent of two parts;
its *piṇḍa* (pedestal) shall be two parts, and the *mattavāraṇā* (the elephant-enclosure molding) shall be three parts less [than that].
On the altar (*vedī*), the *piṇḍa* together with the *paṭṭa* (fillet) should be likewise, as it is in the *kūṭāgāra* (pinnacled chamber).
The mass of the *rājasena* (the base) should be equal to the *kūṭāgāra* (the peaked roof).
The *kumbhikā* (the pitcher) should also have that same mass, and its height constitutes the seat (*āsana*).
One should know that the *kūṭaka* (the pinnacle), together with the pillar of the head (*śiraḥstambha*), [is formed]. ||71-72||
The *kumbhī* (pedestal) should be equal to the *rājasena*, and the *jaṅghā* (shaft) should be equal to the *vedi* (altar-base).

Thus, this [the *sūrpacchādya*] is declared in three ways; now the *sūrpacchādya* is described. One should divide the space from the bottom board (*adhaḥpaṭṭa*) to the end of the top board (*ūrdhvapaṭṭa*) into five parts.
One may worship with either two or three [images], for that is said to be the liberation [from rebirth].
Then, when divided into thirteen parts equal to the cloth, one should discard the upper portion of the winnowing-basket shape; the construction consists of twelve parts.
One should fashion the base of the winnowing fan (śūrpa) as one-fifth [of its height], or even a fifth part;
one should decorate the winnowing fan with cross-bars (daṇḍaka), avoiding a central bar.
In the center, there should be a pillar for the altar (vedi) and for the "intoxicated elephant" (mattavāraṇaka) motif.
The width of the fillet (paṭṭa) should be one-sixteenth part, or perhaps with a quarter added;
its thickness should be equal to one-sixth of its width.
The pillar (stambha) should be made equal to the fillet, and the capital (śīrṣaka) should be three times that.
The small pavilion (kūṭī) may be even greater than the pillar; the slab (paṭṭaka) may be even greater than the diamond-pattern (hīraka);
and the height of the Śukanāsa slab should be like that of the arm-band (bāhāpaṭṭa).
Alternatively, the altar (vedī) should be elevated by the mass of the band, or it may be greater than the band itself.
In the pavilion (maṇḍapa), the height of the pillar (tulā) should be measured by eight divisions;
it may be equal to the ground-floor temple, or even to the height of the plinth (pāta).
A wise man should cover the unevennesses using the application of decorative moldings (chedikā).

The wise should fashion Kaṇṭhaka with one-eighth [of the total height]; in the middle, pillars should be placed according to the method of cutting, being greater on the outside. At the fifty-sixth part from the hairline, there should be statues (sālabhañjikā).
Above the frieze, charioteers and śālabhañjikās should be placed;
in the center, a beautiful neck-piece (kaṇṭaka) or a lotus should be fashioned.
One should cover the base with various types of celestial palaces (vimānas). ||83-84||
In other moments, one should fashion radiant toraṇas;
otherwise, the form may be circular or, as in some cases, square.
It may be joined with an elephant’s palate, or above the fillet, it may indeed be octagonal.

One should construct an eight-sided figure in the center, and likewise rows on the outside. We shall describe the specific details for the covering; one should illuminate the pillar-lines with threads.
The heights are sixteen, twelve, eight, and four [units].
The feet should always be fashioned so as not to obstruct the sight of the craftsman;
the interval between the *paṭṭa* and the *ghaṇṭā* should be divided into twenty-three parts.
Above the *ghaṇṭā*, the *padmapatrī* is raised by one and a half parts.
Above that, the *dṛṣṭarī* should be one and a half parts in height.
The *kapota* (eaves), together with the *grāsa*, should be one and a half parts in height;
the *kaṇṭhaka* should be two parts, and the *amarā* should be two parts.
Two parts extend outwards at the three-fold elephant-palate (gajatāluka);
the raised eaves (ucchitakosala) shall occupy one part, and the *dhālikā* shall occupy one part.
The second [section] shall consist of two parts, and the third shall likewise consist of two parts.
Above that, a Valinī measuring half a part (ardhabhāgika) should be made.
The projection (nirgama) of each [component] shall be according to its own measurement along the path of the thread.
The corner of the womb (garbhakoṇa) should be at the end of the eyelash-leaf (pakṣmapatrī). ||92–93||
Having reflected, the architect himself should design the exit with symmetrical parts and petals, with formidable lotus-leaf ornaments,
elephant trunks, excellent arches, female statues, and small decorative finials.
The quadrangular courtyard should be adorned with *bhallika* arches,
with celestial garland-strings, and with various types of ritual canopies made of *mandāraka*, *śukti*, lotus, or *nāgapāśaka* designs. ||95-96||
The wise one should cover the pavilion; it is described as being outside [the main structure].
It may be double the size of the original door, or in some cases three-quarters of that double measure;
or it may be one-and-a-half parts, or in some cases double minus one-third.
In some cases, [the mandapa] should be made with three additional parts and four doors;
at the door, two gatekeepers (pratīhārau) should be fashioned, as well as bhallikas and arches (toraṇas).
And upon the two pillars, two varālas should be placed along with female figures (śālabhañjikā).

The *prāggrīva* and the *bhadra* should be auspicious, as should the *rathikā* and the outer *vedikā*. Above and below the pinnacle (*śikhara*) of the pavilion for the bridegroom, there should be a *chedapaṭṭa* measuring half a part; the remainder should be used for the enclosure (*saṃvṛti*).
One should cause the *śikhara* (spire) to be made with two parts of three [units], or less by one-quarter;
and in the temple, there should be a *śukanāsa* (gargoyle), or it may be present in the *sambhrama* (entrance hall);
furthermore, the elevation of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) should be below its own [level]. ||101-102||
The ten deities beginning with Vāmana and ending with Ananta, who were previously mentioned as belonging to the Upāyas,
should have their emergence arranged somewhere in the middle of the pavilion.
Having divided the emergence into three parts, one should have the Ghaṇṭā fashioned from one portion.

A *tilaka* (ornamental mark) is made with one-third of that measurement, and a *phaṃsanā* (a type of head-dress) with half of a *tilaka*. The construction is desired using three or five *śūrpa*s (winnowing baskets). This is declared as the left-side arrangement for the shoulder-covering (*skandhachādyavāsana*).
O auspicious lady, one should arrange the beauty in the ears according to the requirements,
with beautiful pathways, moon-chambers (candraśālās), and lion-ears (siṃhakarṇas),
as well as with chariot-pavilions (rathikās), excellent turrets (varālas), and lovely tilakas.
The decoration of the pavilion should be carried out by means of such types of figures as śukanāsas (fronton-like projections), elephants, lions, and others;
or alternatively, by means of three kinds of architectural elements: kūṭas (pinnacles), saṅghaṭas (arched niches), and kakṣakūṭakas (side-pinnacles). ||107-108||

The covering of the pavilion should be executed with decorative spots (tilakas), or with [ornamental] limbs (aṅgas), with hoof-enclosures (khuracchādyas), with joints (saghaṭṭakas), and with various types of projections such as horns (śṛṅgas).
The height of the pavilion must not exceed the height of the śukanāsa (the frontal pediment).
That which was described below should be executed without hesitation.
In a *valabhī* (pavilion), the height of the pavilion should extend up to the end of the *śukanāsā* (gargoyle);
the pavilion up to the end of the *śukanāsā* belongs to the *yogrāsakula*.
Nor, within that city, at the place where that pavilion stands,
should the sons, kinsmen, relatives, the builder, or the craftsmen [be harmed].
In buildings that are deficient or excessive in measurement, or situated far apart, [this does not apply].
If the materials used exceed the proper measure, there will be misfortunes at every step;
the city will not prosper, and there will be fear for the lord of the city.
When the pavilions have been thus constructed with correct proportions, endowed with beauty, and according to the true ritual, they bring success to the builder.
"Success, accomplishment, and even for the patron in this world, there shall be security and victory for the ruler of the earth.

Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Twenty-Seven Types of Pavilions," in the *Vāstuśāstra* named *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*, composed by the Great King of Kings, the Supreme Lord, the illustrious Bhojadeva.
Now begins the sixty-eighth chapter, titled "The Section on the Aggregate of the Limbs of the Jagatī."
For the prosperity of the abode of the thirty gods, for the sake of adorning the city,
for the enjoyment and liberation of men, for peace at all times,
for the dwelling of the deities, and for the accomplishment of the fourfold aims of human life.
And for the sake of attaining fame, longevity, and glory for wise men,
we shall here describe in detail the characteristics of the various types of buildings (jagatī).
Since they say that a temple (prāsāda) is a linga because it possesses three gateways (galla) and other features, [we shall now explain them].
Therefore, by virtue of being its support, the ground is considered the pedestal;
you should fashion it according to the height, while its width and length are determined by the [proportions of the] form.
Without that, there can be no arrangement of the primary and secondary limbs, nor even the sequence [of their placement].
O Bhadra, [describe] the division of the lotus-root tubers, their width and projection;
the water-reservoir, the entrance, the exit, and the ascent;
the numerical measurement of the halls, as well as their configuration, dimensions, and characteristics.
He [taught] their circumambulation, as well as their threefold designation,
their sixfold nature, and the cause of their origin;
he taught the classification of the root-halls and the exit from the circumambulatory path.
We shall now duly describe the *sañcaya*, the door, the staircase, the *muṇḍikā*, the *maṇḍa*, and their origins;
as well as the sanctuaries (*adhiṣṇya*) for two, three, or more deities, the *jagatī* enclosures, and the gateways (*toraṇa*),
all endowed with every characteristic.
A square, level, auspicious, and pleasing [hall] that slopes away on all sides,
with its directional quarters well-concealed by its proportions and connected to a palace, is auspicious. Likewise, it may be square and elongated, circular, or circular and elongated.
Alternatively, it should be made octagonal; having first purified the ground,
one should determine the temple of the gods according to its configuration, dimensions, and characteristics,
and then construct a surrounding platform (jagatī) at its side that corresponds to its shape.
It is of three kinds: the youngest (kanīyasī), the middle (madhyamā), and the eldest (jyeṣṭhā).
One should employ these [measures] starting from the smallest in the palaces, with Jagatī meters [consisting of] four, five, and six feet respectively.

The delightful [abodes] beginning with the Nānāśātiśānti and the Akaniṣṭha are considered to have halls corresponding in number to the primary and secondary members (aṅga-upāṅga) of the palace; their collective ritual procedure is now declared. ||14-15||

From twelve cubits upwards, the height [of the temple] shall extend up to twenty cubits; or again, from thirty-two cubits, it may be one-third or one-fourth of the hall (śālā). From half the height of the seat (āsana), the hall of the palace (prāsāda) shall extend up to fifty cubits.
Now, we shall describe here the various types of halls according to their application, starting from those with many temples following the proportions of the main palace:

those arising from the corner (karṇodbhavā), those with a circular elevation (bhramocchā), those arising from the bhadra-projection (bhadrajā), and those arising from the central core (garbhasambhavā). ||17-18||
There are six varieties of these [arches]: those arising from the middle, those arising from the sides, and so forth.

Among them, the *karṇajā* (ear-born) is first described by the ancient masters as having a specific width and length; the *bhramajā* (whirling-born), measured according to that same proportion, is encircled by a quarter [of its span].

The *bhadra* type is said to be one *jā* in height; the *karṇajā* is proclaimed to be one and a half *ayāmas*. The *garbhajā*, *madhyajā*, and *karṇajāyatasammite* (measured by the length of the ear-type) are likewise defined.
The *pārśvajā* and *bhramajā* are measured in *ayāmas*; now their respective positions are described.
The Karṇajā is known to be in the ears; the Bhramajā occurs in circular whirling.
The Bhadrajā is to be known in auspicious places, and the Garbhajā is within the three [circles].
That which is situated in the middle of the five is the Madhyajā.
The side-arrangement consists of four [shrines], two of which on each side are known as the *śāntā*s.
There should be two ears on both sides, and those too are born from the sides.
The circumambulatory path (*bhramantikā*) should be made half the width of the temple (*prāsāda*). ||23–24||

The wise one should fashion eight [lotuses] outside this [central lotus], starting from the root (kanda) and following the directions of the celestial abodes (the cardinal points). Beginning with Bhadra and Mālatī, he should continue up to the thirty-third triad.
From the nine-celled [grid] up to the thirty-first [cell] in sequence, the stalks (śālākanda) are traditionally taught;
they are divided into four groups.
Therein, that [grid] shall consist of four squares, and the circuit (bhrama) shall consist of twelve squares. ||26-27||
By this sequence, the work should be performed starting from the placement of the *śālā* and the *kanda*;

beyond that, however, there is no further rotation (*bhrama*) in the division of the *śālā*-groups. From the Rudras onwards, this rotation does not apply again for those who maintain the exit of the ears.
A circumambulation from the region of the ears should be performed, as in the case of the *rucaka* [temple type].
O auspicious lady, according to the proportions of the hall, the projection outside the base (*kandaka*) should be made by the wise with a width of four *pada*s. ||29-30||
In some cases, the width of the water-interval should be made one-quarter or one-half of the width of the *prajāṅga*;
the two *kṣobhaṇa* [pillars] should also be provided.
Having given the width of the temple (*prāsāda*) at the front, there should be an interval of water.
The two *gaṇḍa* (cheek) elements should be made following that same line, extending outward from the two feet by means of rotation.
For temples, these *gaṇḍas* emerging from the corner (*karṇa*) should be one, two, or three times the width [of the base], according to the superior, middling, and inferior [proportions].
At the summit, pavilions (suṇḍikā) should be constructed, with eaves extending from the side-chambers (karṇaśālā).
These should be provided with garlands and staircases, and filled with doorkeepers (pratīhāra).
Furthermore, a gateway (pratolī) should be made at the front, equipped with strong bolts and doors.
Now we shall describe the Jagatī-pīṭha (the base platform): a wise architect should construct it for a temple of one cubit [in height] with a height equal to its width;
for a temple of two cubits, it should be three-quarters [of that]; and for a temple of three cubits, it should be reduced by one-third. ||35-36||
When a four-cubit [structure] is to be made, it should be two and a half cubits high;
[for structures of] four, eight, and three [cubits],
one should arrange the smallest, middle, and largest elevations in sequence up to twelve cubits.
It should be half the size of the *karṇa-śālā*, or three-quarters, or equal to it; and by this same method, for the larger and medium-sized temples as well,
the *jagatī* should be raised according to the measurement of the *karṇa-prāsāda*.
One should divide the total height of the pedestal (pīṭha) [into parts]:
one part should be made for the *khuraka*, and one part for the path (*vartman*).
One part should be for the *kumbha* and its *khuraka*, and likewise two parts for the *kumbhaka*.
The *kalaśa* (dome) should be one part in height, and likewise the *antarapatraka* (inner leaf).
One should make the *varaṇḍī* (cornice) one part, and similarly the *paṭṭa* (band) one part.
From the *khuraka* (plinth) of the base (*jagatī*), the god [the architect] should project one part for the *pratiśoka*. ||41-42||
The *paṭṭa* [is measured] by one and a half parts; then the *pratiṣṭhā*, the *jagatī*, and the *khura*;
likewise the *khurakāra*, the *kumbha*, the *akiñcitkumbha*, and the *kṣaṇaka*;
as well as the *kaṇaka*, the *antarapatra*, and the *kapotālī*.
One should fashion the recesses of the moldings, as well as the curved projections of the nose-ornaments,
with delightful depressions and elevations;
[these should be adorned] with various diverse [moldings] and many-peaked pinnacles.
At the base of the pillars of the halls,

one should arrange very diverse works of art, well-proportioned and appropriate to their respective positions; the wise craftsman should execute these on the pedestals for the sake of the beauty of the palaces.
Just as a lion-throne for kings is adorned by the luster of jewels, so too the pedestal of the king of palaces should be fashioned with the finest works;
above the cloth-strip, an excellent *rājasenaka* should be constructed. ||47-48||
It should be joined with blooming lotuses and adorned with *bhāraputraka* flowers;
half of that should be provided with an altar (*vedikā*) crowded with various leaves. Then, it should be equipped with a *saṃghaṭaka* ornament and subsequently an *asamaghaṭṭaka*.
One should support it with many pillars;
above that, one should construct an excellent hand-projection (karavyāsana).
This should be situated between the corner halls (karṇaśālā), the base (tala), the foot (pāda), and the half-panels (ardhapaṭṭa). ||50-51||
One should construct the *rājasena* (the royal enclosure) for the altar (*vedi*) using one-third of its area;
or alternatively, the *rājasena* on the base may occupy half or one-third of the altar’s area.
Above the altar, the beautiful *kūṭāra* (the peaked roof structure) should be made with one-third of the altar’s measurement.
The *mattavāraṇa* (elephant-enclosure) should be constructed with a height of one *kara*;
it must have both an entrance and an exit for the sake of their comfortable play and feeding.
It should likewise be situated at the front of the *gandha* (fragrance chamber), at the front of the *sukā* (pleasure chamber), and similarly at the front of the *pratolī* (gate-tower).

The archway (toraṇa) should be known to be of three kinds: the smallest, the middling, and the largest. Thus has the proper measurement for the courtyard, the temple site, and the pedestal of the palace been fully prescribed.
"Do not describe this arrangement of the *jagatī* foundations in any other way than as it truly is,
along with its defining characteristics.

Thus ends the sixty-eighth chapter, titled "The Section on the Collection of Components of the *Jagatī*," in the *Vāstuśāstra* named *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*, composed by the illustrious Mahārājādhirāja Śrī Bhojadeva.
Now begins the sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Jagatī":
Vasudhā, Vasudhārā, Vahantī, and others;
Śrīdharā, Bhadrikā, Ekabhadra, and Dvibhadrikā.
Tribhadrī, Bhadramālā, Vaimānī, Bhramarāvalī,
Svastikā, Haramālā, Kulaśīlā, Mahīdharī,
Mandāramālikā, Anaṅgalekhā, and Utsavamālikā.
Nāgārāmā, Mārabhavyā, and likewise Makaradhvajā; Nandyāvartā, Bhūpālā, and Pārijātakamañjarī;
Cūḍāmaṇiprabhā, and likewise Śravaṇamañjarī. ||3-4||
Viśvarūpādikamalā, as well as Trailokyasundarī,
Gandharvabālikā, another Vidyādharakumārikā,
the one known as Subhadrā, and likewise Siṃhapañjarā.
The Vajrapakurava and others, as well as the Gandharvanagarī;
likewise, Amarāvatī should be known by name, and Ratnadhūmā;
also the assembly hall of the Lord of the Thirty-three, and another called Devayantrikā. ||6-7||
The second [group] consists of forty, less one by name;
they are bearers of twin garments, have three eyes, are fierce, and are white-skinned with mottled limbs.
Now, therefore, their classification is described exactly as it is.
The sequence for the *jagatī* [verses] and the halls is as previously described.
When the site has been made square and divided into six equal parts,
it may be arranged either with equal divisions or with half-units added, according to the desired quality or the length of the front.
One should construct the *jagatī* (pedestal/base) according to the proportions of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*).
Two parts should be for the middle region, the temple (*prāsāda*) should occupy one part, and there should be a circumambulatory path (*bhrama*).
Having removed [space] equal to the corner [measure] from both sides in front.
Śrīkhaṇḍikās are to be arranged for this temple;
it is joined with *mattavāraṇas* and adorned with gateways (*pratolī*) and other features.
This first *jagatī* is designated as Vasudhā. 12–13.
The *vasudhā* should be joined with a prominent *śālā* (hall) and a *vasudhārā*;
the exit should be made in front according to the dimensions of the temple. Likewise, the width should be made; one should divide that into four parts.
The *śramaṇī* should be made with one part, while the remaining hall (*śeṣaśālā*) should have two parts.
The *suṇḍikā* should also be as long as previously stated by that same measurement;
furthermore, the *vasudhā* and the *rājasiṃhikā* are formed by the two corner halls (*karṇaśālā*). ||15-16||

One should construct [the ornament] for both ears with half the height of the temple; one should likewise fashion the circular molding (bhramaṇī) for those two with half their own measurement. First, a pediment (suṇḍikā) should be made with a width equal to that of the root-temple.

When there is a *śālā* (a line of notes) on the earth (*vasudhā*) and royal swans (*rājahaṃsa*) in front, then it is the *Śrīdharī*; its *suroya* is as before. But when there are two *śālās* in the place of the *haṃsikā* at the two rear ears, [it is the same]. 18–19.
At that time, when it has that form and those dimensions, that Bhadrikā [shrine] shall come into being. When the field has been made square and divided into sixteen parts,
and prepared according to the previously mentioned sequence, it may be extended toward the front as desired.

When the length of the pavilion is divided into parts according to their respective proportions, a temple should be constructed in the center, provided with four squares (caturvargapada). Around it, on all sides, there should be a circumambulatory path (bhrama) with a width of two squares. ||21-22||
The *karṇa-śālā* (corner hall) should be made with a width of two *padas* and a length of three *padās* on each of the four sides, provided with a circumambulatory path (*pradik-bhramaṇa*).
A circumambulatory path (bhramaṇā) should be made, as well as beautiful Bhadra halls;
one should construct water-channels all around, situated between the two halls, entering one padika [in depth] and extending half of that [in width]. ||24-25||
In the rear of the hall, there may be one bay (ekabhadra) or two bays (dvibhadrikā);
with three bays formed by the corners, it is a "three-bayed" (tribhadra) hall. Furthermore, with three halls, there is the Jagatī, the Bhadra, and the Mālinī.
The four directions are each auspicious in one way.
When the field has been made square and divided into twenty-four parts,
the temple should be constructed in the center, endowed with the characteristics of six groups. Surrounding the temple, there should be a circumambulatory path consisting of three parts.
Then, the division of the halls (śālā) should be made according to the prescribed characteristics:
five parts in length and four parts in width in the middle, measured in padas.
Within that, the bhadra halls should be constructed, with a one-part circumambulatory path (bhrama) in their center.
On both sides of the Bhadra,
two halls (śālā) should be constructed, each measuring one hundred and twelve units in length and width;
the entrance into those two [halls] shall be one part at each of the two corners (karṇa).
In this manner, there shall be three [channels] each in the three directions beginning with the east;
likewise, six water-channels should be made, emerging from half a part [of the width],
and they should enter one part [of the width] in all three directions.
The two ears (karṇas) should be made in front, measuring two parts each.
This vimāna, worshipped by gods, asuras, and humans, possesses a suṇḍikā;
at the front of this suṇḍikā is a hall facing the prāsāda.
Then that row of bees (bhramarāvali) is praised by the Kinnaras and Siddhas;
it is devoid of a front hall (vaktraśālā) but provided with two side halls (pārśvaśālā). That which has the same form and the same dimensions as that is proclaimed as the Svastikī.
If the hall facing the temple should be situated on the Svastika plot itself,
then that ground is renowned on earth as Haṃsamālati.
When there is an intervening space of one part on both sides of the central [hall], ||37||

Having constructed the fierce [structure], one should effect the exit with the measurement of the *bhadra*. The cord should be equal to the temple (*prāsāda*), while the halls (*śālā*) are adorned with neck-ornaments (*galabhūṣita*).
In that state, there should be a turret (*śuṇḍikā*) at the entrance, even without the hall.
Then the Kulaśailas should be known as the refuge for the arrival of the rows of swans;
they are always favored by Maheśvara, and especially by Skanda.
When the hall (śālā) of this very [temple] is constructed in front of the Bhadra [shrine], [it is auspicious]. 39–40.
Then the Mahīdharī, who is dear to the heart of Mahīdhara, was proclaimed:
"In a square field divided into twenty-eight parts,
the wise man should construct a temple in the center consisting of sixty-four squares."
A four-footed circumambulatory path (bhrama) should be made all around the temple.
At the corners of the circumambulatory line, four halls should be constructed, each two paces long and wide, and surrounded by a one-part circumambulatory path. ||42-43||
Having abandoned four parts from their sides due to delusion,
one should construct a hall (śālā) with a length and width of one part each;
the corner (karṇa) of the side halls should have a width of one part.
In the middle section, there should be the water-path (jalādhvā), excluding the outer [portion] consisting of thirteen [units].
One should make that [water-path] two units wide and three units long;
O Bhadra, the water-path should be situated between the two water-residences on the sides.
And that [entrance], having entered from half a part in width and extending for exactly that same distance,
should be placed correctly in the middle of the *suṇḍikā* and the *kanda*, with its two openings (*tuṇḍau*) having a width equal to half of the temple (*prāsāda*), across the three directions.
And for those two as well, two halls adorned with the sequence of circular patterns should be made;
thus, the Mandāra hall shall be dear to the mind of Hara.
When its hall is completed in the Suṇḍikā [section], then— ||48-49||
When this same arrangement is made, but with a hall (śālā) added at the front, it becomes the Anaṅgalekhā, dear to Pārvatī; in this case,
there are two [structures] for the temple-towers (śuṇḍikā-gaṇḍa) and a series of staircases (sopāna-mālikā).
When that same [temple] is provided with a hall for the face, it becomes a Nāgāṅganā.
When the site has been made square and divided into thirty-two parts, a temple of sixty-four squares should be constructed in the center. ||51-52||
Its perimeter should be properly measured on all four sides;
however, when measuring the two legs, one must account for the curvature. The two auspicious ears, situated in the middle, should be fashioned according to their own proportions.
There should be sixteen squares for the *kandas*, and within them, four-legged halls (*śālās*). Furthermore, in all four corners, one should enter the squares formed by the circular lines;
likewise, the *bhadra* and the pair of halls should have a length of two squares.
It should be one-quarter less in width than its length, facing each other;
with a width of two parts and surrounded by a single part,
the *bhadra* hall should be constructed with a projection of three and a half parts.

There are three halls for the enemy of Mura (Viṣṇu) facing each of the directions—Saumya (North), Anila (West), and Vāruṇī (West), as well as Nairṛtī (Southwest) and Yāmya (South)—with no hall toward the southeast (Āgneyī) and other such quarters.
If there is a hall at the very entrance of this [central hall], it belongs to Makaradhvaja (Kāmadeva). ||57-58||
Having brought joy to the immortals by performing this rite, one shall attain liberation.
When, having abandoned the front hall, a hall is provided for each of the two ears,
that becomes the Nandyāvarta hall of the Lord of the Day (the Sun).
When there is a beautiful hall situated on the back of her mouth, extending for two parts in both length and width, with its front edge aligned with the Vikarṇa-kanda,
that hall shall stand facing the main hall. (60-61)
Then she should be known as Tāmramūlā, beloved by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara;
when her backbone is situated toward the south and west of the hands,
and two *śālā*s are made, then she should be known as Pārijātakamañjarī.

Situated at the four corners of the enclosure wall, it should face the hall. If the halls extend along the bamboo-beams (vaṃśa) in the east, south, and north directions, then that crest-jewel of the Lord shall be dear to all the gods. ||63-64||
When the site has been made square, it is square on all sides;
one-tenth part from both ends in the middle shall be the central temple-priest (prāsādanāyaka).
Likewise, this applies to the front and to both sides as well.
Its perimeters (bhrama) should be constructed with five steps.
The ear-roots (karṇakanda) should be made situated outside the perimeter-lines (bhramasūtra), measuring two parts in length and width, and adorned with four halls (catuḥśāla). ||66-67||
In this very same sequence,
the *bhadra* projections (*kandāḥ*) shall be increased by one-quarter (*pada*) for those bearing three garlands in the garlanded series of the main temple (*mūlaprāsāda*).
However, the halls (*śālāḥ*) situated at every corner (*karṇe karṇe*) shall have a length and width of two parts (*dvy-aṃśa*).
Having water-reservoirs occupying two parts, as well as circular perimeters of one part;
with water-channels entering the squares and joined by circular paths;
equal in all four corners and equal also in the three *bhadra* projections. ||69-70||

The *sṛga* and *bhrama* (spiral) features should be made with a width of two parts and a length of three parts, extending from the *bhrama-śālā* to the *diśānta*. The remainder, including the *śuṇḍikā* and the ornamentation of the *gaṇḍa*, should be executed as previously described.
This [structure] called Karṇamañjarī bestows joy upon the three worlds.
O auspicious lady, the Karṇamañjarikā is divided into ten sections;
one should construct a hall that is two parts in length and breadth and four parts in height. ||72-73||
One should fashion their mouths with water-pits (udaka-kṣaṇa) at the front;
the circumambulatory path (parikrama) for all of them together shall constitute one part on every side.
Two parts are for the auspicious ears (bhadra-kaṇa), and there is a contraction on both sides.
On the *bhadra* [projections], there should be another *karṇikā* (corner cell) with a width equal to one part;

it should be endowed with sixteen *pada*s and possess the graceful movement of various circular patterns (*bhrama*). There should also be a *catuṣkī* (quadrangular hall) on the *bhadra*, with its interior enclosed at the front. ||75-76||
One should construct a glorious pavilion adorned with many pillars,
surrounded by a moat dug according to this [measure], covered at the time of roofing, and provided with a door;
from its center, there should be the Viśvarūpa and Kasyāya in front.
With three sets of four squares (catuṣkikās), it becomes the Trailokyasundarī [mandala].
When the field has been made square and divided into twelve squares,
there is a four-faced hall in the center, with its length and width equal to three parts.
The path of squares should be made with one and a half parts on all sides;
within it, four halls should be arranged toward the east and north,
each measuring two parts in length and width, and made very beautiful.
This [ear-ornament] should be made with a portion of the *ālindaka* extending forward; it is not encircled.
Adorned with *karṇikās* occupying two parts at the positions of the *kakṣyās*, this very [ornament] is prescribed for the ear of the *karṇamañjarī*.
The *jagatī* is favored by Śiva; then there is the *gandharvamālikā*.
On the other side, in the fourth part, that which is accompanied by *śālī* should be known by the name *jagatī*, the *vidyādharakumārikā*.
On the western side, however, having omitted the fourth,
one should construct two walls for the Subhadrā, which is dear to the gods;
on each of the four Bhadrās, there should be five rafters.
If the Śālās are [arranged] like the moon and the stars, then it shall be a Siṃhapañjara.
When the site has been made square and divided into fourteen parts,
the temple of the deity should be situated in the center, with a length and width of three parts each.

Then, a circular enclosure (bhrama) should be made in three directions using one part (bhāga). In front of that, which is equal in length and width to the temple (prāsāda), there is a portico (mukhamaṇḍapa).
On both sides of the bhadra, the bhadra is extended outward.
A pair of halls (śālāyugma) should be constructed with a length and width of three padas, provided with a bhadra measuring one part and a maṇḍapa, if desired, according to the available space.
Alternatively, [a hall] may have a length and width of two parts, accompanied by a circumambulatory path (bhramaṇa) measuring one part.
Two *śāla* halls should be constructed in front, facing each other;
in this way, there will indeed be five *ala*s. When the *pṛṣṭhabhadra* is auspicious, there are two *bhadra*s and five *kañjara*s in the north-south four-*śāla* layout.
When there is a *pṛṣṭhabhadra* for this [house] with a middle hall (*madhyaśālā*),
and it is likewise joined with two *kakṣābhadrakas*, then it is a Gandharvanagarī.
There are five *bhadrakas* and three *bhadrakas* as well, provided with five halls (*pañcaśālā*).
The thirty-sixth [verse] beginning with *śiśutāt* should be known as the *jagatī* named Amarāvatī (93).
When, at the tip of its trunk, a certain hall is formed,
then that *jagatī*, beloved of the world, becomes Dantacūḍā (94).

These, namely the Śuṇḍikāśālā and the Gaṇḍaśālā provided with two [side-rooms], are to be known as the assembly halls (sabhā) of the Lord of the Thirty-three; they are equipped with a *suṇḍī* and a divine mechanical device (*devayantrikā*).
Thus are described the square [buildings] and their various elongated forms.
In a field seven parts long and five parts wide, there are two halls on the left and right, each two parts in length and width;
a quadrangle (catuṣkikā) one part in size should be situated in front of those two. ||96-97||
A circular path is prescribed in the middle and all around;
adorned with gateways (pratolī) and embellished with kiosks (khaṇḍaśuṇḍikā),
it is richly beautified by intoxicated elephants, and is proclaimed as the Yamālekhyā layout.
When the bulb (kanda) at the rear is three parts in width and extends three parts forward,
and is further divided into four parts,
the hall (śālā) shall have a length and width of two parts each, and the circumambulatory path (bhrama) shall be two parts. ||99-100||
Then, from the two front corners of the hall, there should be two *payodhara* (cloud) and *netra* (eye) [projections] at the front and back;
these, beginning with the *netra*, should constitute the body of the *cetya-śālā*.
From both of the two eastern [corners], a *kanda* (bulbous base) of the *sāman* [type] should emerge for one part.
And that portion which has entered within must also be divided as before.

(102) The same applies to the two *śāla* sections, the *anta*, the *māna*, and the *bhrama*, as well as the rotation on the two sides, provided there are two [sections] at the root-hall (*mūlaśālā*). (103)

The remainder is as previously described; all these are proclaimed as *dordaṇḍa* temples. Furthermore, if one constructs the two *śālā*s of the *rākṣasa* and *anilaya* types joined to the ears (*karṇa*) on both sides of the *dordaṇḍa*s, it becomes the *ākhaṇḍala*.
When a hall is constructed to the west of the Akhaṇḍālā hall, it is called Payo;
if it extends like the Sarayū river, it becomes Jagatī.
Or, if it is adorned with three halls, it is Śivā or Vāruṇī.
Then, in the Śuṇḍikārālaya, there was the Māhendrī Vaṃpakā; in Kokaiṇa, there were four halls belonging to Yamelā. O Bhadra, those three [halls] and those three [others] are my Pūrvabhadra-mamālaka.
Those which are the ears (karṇas) should extend out by two and a half parts.
When these are divided into four, the hall (śālā) shall consist of two parts;
there should be circular rotations (bhramaṇyas) of one part each, and these are the outer ear-halls (karṇa-śālās). ||108–109||
Three exits should be wide and spacious, situated outside the auspicious base (kanda).
There should be four walls with salas (pinnacles) and likewise a half-circumambulatory path (ardhabhrama).
A water-channel (jalapatha), measuring half a pada, is prescribed for the drains (kuṣṭha).
Its back-shoulder (pṛṣṭhasādhosikā) consists of two parts, and the kulāmodikā is one-eighth [of that].
Some praise the Jagatī-tilaka as being adorned with two rows of half-parts on the back-bhadra.
If there should be a *śālā* (hall) serving as an ornament for the face of this *śuṇḍikā*,
then that world arises which is named Pallava.
When two *śālās* occur upon the cheeks of the *tilakas*, [it is likewise].
Then she becomes a Vidyādharī facing Siddhārtha.
If the back wall-surface is three units wide and extends two units outward, then one should designate it as a Yakṣa in the Pṛṣṭhabhadra of the Vidyādharī. ||114-115||
On a site six parts wide and ten parts long,
a wise man should construct three halls, each two parts in length and width;
at their front, he should construct pavilions equal in size to those, or slightly larger.
One should perform [the design] according to one's desire for the sake of the splendor of the work.
One should create a circular division on the four sides of those [structures],
and also for the purpose of making special features using even the middle-sized halls.
Adorned with drinking-halls and decorated with the temples of elephants in rut,
this world-famous region of Trikūṭā is known as the city of Tṛpuṣa.
Trikūṭā is situated on the eastern ridge, measuring three parts in both length and breadth.
One should construct a pavilion hall (śālā) with a front face like that of a cow; it is called Citrakūṭikā.
If the hall is constructed such that its front is exactly like its rear, then it is known by the wise as a Saranikūṭī jagatī.
The *yuktā* consists of two *prāṇa*s (eight syllables) and is devoid of the *agraśālā*;
that *jagatī*, known on earth as the *upamevājottamā*, is joined with the *nairṛta*, *anala*, *vāyu*, *īśa*, *karṇa*, *prāsāda*, and *ka*. 122.
By means of three peaks, it becomes the Nandī-vibhakta-ṣaḍala [mandala].
The wise one should divide Citrakūṭā into two parts in sequence, as previously described for the Trikūṭā.
In its form and extent, the Siddhi-maṇḍala is twice the length and width of the Trikūṭā.
One should divide the bulb (kanda) placed from ear to ear into four parts:

with two parts there shall be the hall (śālā), and likewise with one part the circumambulatory path (bhramaṇa). Furthermore, the width at the base shall be half [of that], according to the measurement here.
On the north and south sides, it should extend four parts; one part should project outward. The *bhadra* should be provided with two parts.
As for the remainder, one should cause the circumambulation (*bhramaṇa*) to be made there at the middle and the sides.

Likewise, at the front as well, two *śāla* projections should be made on both sides of the door, extending out by one part (*bhāga*) and having a width of one part. Furthermore, a rear bay (*pṛṣṭhabhadra*) should be made with a width of two and a half parts.

It should be provided with a projection of two parts and a *śālā* (hall) of one and a half parts. Then, two *śālās* should be constructed to the south and north of this very [structure]. When the measurement has been correctly established, there should be an entrance into the [central] part.
The remaining one is the *bhrama*, situated in the middle of the seven halls;
this is the *śrayaṇī* of Śiva, beloved by all the hosts of gods.
When a hall arises at the very mouth of this [central hall], then—
