When it is well-constructed with a width of two and a half parts and a length of three and a half parts,
and when the two side-shālās (pārśva-bhadra) are each one part in width, the auspicious ground-plan known as Trivikrama arises. ||132-133||
In a structure associated with the virtuous, when it is provided with a circumambulatory path,
that hall becomes one attained through traditional succession;
moreover, at the front of the hall's porch, that very [circumambulatory path] arises as a triple junction.

The fourfold types have been declared; now the circular and polygonal forms are described. (135) When a square field has been prepared and divided into four parts, the temple is circular in the center, with a length and width of one and a half parts. (136)
Then, one should rotate the circular base (jagatī) by one-eighth of its total circumference;
on its sides, the *mattavāraṇa* (the elephant-enclosure) should be constructed according to the previously mentioned rule.
The circular base should be enriched with the beauty of the gate-towers (*gopura*).

Behind the *valaya* (enclosure), one should construct a hall (*śālā*) extending from the *kanda* (bulb-base) to the root, according to the previously mentioned rule; this hall should be half the size [of the former].
This is declared to be the *kalaśī*, a *jagatī* (pedestal) shaped like a water-pot (*kalaśa*). ||138-139||

Where there is a square area with four *karṇa-śālās* (corner halls), each measuring one *karṇa* in length and two *padas* in width, it is called the *Śātārmya*. [In this case], the square field is divided into seven parts on all sides.
One should first omit three parts, and then four parts on each side;
having abandoned three and a half parts on both sides, one should fashion the interior chamber (garbha).
The temple of the deity should be circular, with a length and width of two parts each.
One part should be made as a circumambulatory path (bhrama) all around it;
behind the circumambulatory path, the bulbous base (kanda) is adorned with a dimension of one part.
The hall (śālā) should be half of that, and the circumambulatory path (parikrama) half of that.

Within the womb, at the end of two parts between the directions of Īśāna and Agni, there are two parts that enter the bulb (kanda) by half a part each; these are located at the ends of the circles when a horizontal thread is placed above the back and the shoulder. 144–145.
Two pericarp-like sections (karṇikā) should be made in the directions of the Rākṣasa and Vāyu;
then one should construct the expenditure hall (vyayaśālā), equal in size to the rear hall (pṛṣṭhaśālā).
It should be situated within the womb of the pit (kandagarbha) from east to west by means of the junction of two threads.
One should fashion a sharp ear-ornament (karṇikā) on both sides as well.
All remaining procedures, such as the shaping of the trunk (śuṇḍikā), should be performed as before.
This Karavīrī [image], beloved by the gods beginning with Īśa, is thus described. 147–148.
When there are eight filaments situated behind this very [pattern],
and the two *vāmaśāla* are prescribed, then it becomes the *nalinī*.
It is drawn from the given portion by means of eight squares.
He should then cast the lines for that [mandala] in the cardinal and intermediate directions.

At the end of the circumambulation of the temple, he should fashion eight bulbous bases (kandas) on all sides at the eight points of intersection, each measuring two padas in length and breadth. ||150-151||
Having divided that [line] into four parts, one should likewise fashion the petals;
and between the bulbous bases (kandas), an eight-petaled pericarp (karṇikā) should be made.
When the thread is aligned with the region so that they correspond with one another, [the mandala is complete].

From both sides, the arrangement of the pericarp (karṇikā) should be of that same form. By dividing all the Bhadra sections in this way, the temple (surālaya) within the three-pada space becomes one with side-circumambulations (pārśvabhrama) and half-padas; this occurs when [the area] is divided tenfold. ||153-154||
And the bulbous bases (kandas) of the two-legged [pedestals] should be made in the cardinal and intermediate directions;
within them, the halls should be constructed facing one another as previously described.
One should behold those spears of Viṣṇu, who possesses incomparable majesty.
This is his task; they shall be known by the name Puṇḍarīka.
When a circle is fashioned in the place of its pericarp, then it becomes a parasol, and that [lotus] is to be made for Brahmā. ||156-157||
Having made the site square and elongated, one should divide it into ten squares;
in its center, a temple should be constructed occupying three squares.
On its sides, a circumambulatory path (bhrama) should be made measuring two and a half squares.
The outer circle should consist of two parts; therein one should perform this procedure:
one should divide that [area] into twelve equal measures, and each of those parts, in turn, should be divided into four.

A hall (śālā) measuring two parts in both length and width is prescribed for the center. There is a circular enclosure (bhrama) one part wide surrounding the three halls on both the left and right sides; these two halls are auspicious.

When those two have been arranged facing one another, the *śālā* (hall) should extend to the length of the *khuma*, and its width should be half of that half-part; by that same measure, the *saccāvā* (entrance) and the circumambulatory path (*bhramaṇa*) should be fashioned. ||162-163||
In this world, this [altar] is proclaimed by the name Cakravālā;
it should be made for the Sun together with the planets, or for the Moon, or again for Yama, who is praised in the three Vedas. 164.
When the field has been made square and divided into ten parts,
one should draw a circle on all sides using a thread extending from the corners of the central chamber (garbha).
Outside, one should fashion a bulbous base (kanda) with a width of three units and a height of four units.
In the two-legged hall (dvipadā), the width should be one and a half parts;
the remainder shall form a circumambulatory path (bhramaṇa) all around the Bhadra hall.
On both sides of the Bhadra, there should be circular projections (vṛtta), each two parts in length and width.
In the Śāla and Vṛtta types, there are three Bhadras on the southern, northern, and western sides, with their length and width equal to the interior portion;
they are provided with a curvature equal to half of that [dimension]. ||168-169||
Beautiful halls should be constructed in all four intermediate directions.
Having left the hall situated in the center of the *bhadra*, that [hall] shall be in the east.
Its length and width are equal, and it is provided with a circular enclosure (*bhramaṇa*) of half that size.
It should be performed for Soma together with the constellations for the sake of prosperity.
On a site made square and divided into ten parts,
one should construct a circular hall in the center, measuring five parts in length.
Two parts of the side-chamber (sādhā) should extend outside the temple;
one should know that there are side-halls (karṇaśālā) extending from the corners,
and having rotated the measurement of the corner externally in a circle, [the structure] should be made from the base (asāra).

One should design the halls for the Bhadra and Prabhadra types as being circular at the corners. One should construct the halls belonging to the Bhadra class with a length equal to two padas, a width of three padas,
and provided with a one-part (bhāgika) circular ambulatory (abhramaṇa).

One should construct two *bhadraka* (auspicious) halls on the two sides and two [halls] based on the *pratiratha* (corner-projections) within a half-circumference; their width should be one part, and from there,
two *halī* (plough-shaped) projections extending toward the half-corner should be made, each measuring one and a half parts.
Their circumambulation (parikrama) should be measured by half of that [unit].
Both the Bhadrā and the Pratiratha enter with a quarter-measure (padārdha).
Thus is described the Jagatī meter, known as Candra-maṇḍalā by its measurement. ||177-178||
Now, we shall describe the six *vṛtta* *jagatī* meters in their proper order:
[they consist of] five parts in length and four feet in width.
One should know that the *vṛtta* is elongated, with a portion of *bhava* (three) in the *camasa*.
In the middle, it should have three paces in length and two paces in width;
it should be joined with a *mattavāraṇa* (elephant-terrace), adorned with a gateway (*pratolī*), auspicious, and decorated at the edges of its staircases and spouts. ||180–181||
This [structure] called Mātuliṅgī has been described; it is beloved by the gods in this world.
When, on its very back, there is a hall with a length and width of two parts according to the previous sequence, then that should be known as Ghaṭī.
In that form, there are two halls, left and right, with a water-channel (jalāla) between them.
If there is also a western hall, then this is the Jagatī plan;
in all cases, the Ghaṭīkarṇas have a length and width of two parts each.
If the hall, joined with the *bhrama*, were divided as previously described,
one should construct two intermediate spaces (*antarikṣa*) and two *pṛṣṭha* sections;
this would indeed be the Kāliṅgī style, with its sides [extending] to the end of the *amṛta* measures.
But when, in this [type of] hall, the *śuṇḍikānana* is situated,
and the *jagatī* is constructed as circular and elongated— these are the circular and elongated [halls].
Now we shall describe the eight-cornered enclosures (jagatīs) possessing auspicious characteristics.
One should divide a square field into ten and one-quarter parts;
then, one should discard three parts along each diagonal line (karṇa). ||187-188||
One should leave four parts plus one-quarter remaining in the middle section;
it becomes perfected with eight corners, and half of that shall be the temple (surālaya).
Located in the middle portion of the eight-cornered [figure]—the remainder shall be the circular perimeter (bhramaṇa).

The temple should have four doors and be provided with four pavilions. One should install the Mukhaliṅga on the same axis as the temple, starting from half the height of the root-kanda and extending the kandas progressively toward the cardinal directions.
One should arrange eight circular halls of equal measurement, divided into four parts,
according to the sequence previously described;
they should be adorned with staircases, elephant-trunk-shaped projections, and gate-towers.
This is declared to be the Vava [plan] when it is endowed with Meru and has a span equal to the arms.
(193) Having made the field eight-sided as before, one should divide the Bhadra into two parts; one should make a half-part on the Bhadra and project it out from both sides. (194)

One should divide that width into six parts; the projection [of the portico] shall be three of those units. There should be a circumambulatory path on both sides, at the back, and in front. The remaining space for the hall (śālā) should be made twice as long, measuring two units.
The width of the *sādhabhāgika* (the portion consisting of one and a half parts) should be equal to the desired extent of the *saṃghāṭa*.
In this very manner, O auspicious lady, there shall be the *bhadra* (the projection).
The *karṇabhadra* (the corner-projection) should be constructed with a length and width of three *padas*.
When that [space] is divided into four parts, one part shall be for the circumambulatory path (bhramaṇa);
the remainder is to be known as the hall (śālā), with a length and width of two paces. This arrangement at all the corners of the intermediate directions is exceedingly beautiful.
The root-hall (mūlaśālā) is half the size of the bulb (kanda); from that, there is a circumambulatory path (bhrama) and then a lower circumambulatory path (adhībhrama).

This is declared to be the Mātṛkā [plan], which bestows the world, brings prosperity, and grants the desires of kinnaras. From the auspicious [measurements], it should extend out by three parts from the squares.
O Bhadra, when its width is four parts and the height of its plinth (anda) is three padas,
it is then called the Chekharā, adorned with three [elements],
serving as a dwelling place for many ever-joyful deities. 201.
First, in the field for Śrī, divided into four parts,
within a temple ten *bhramas* in length and breadth consisting of two parts,
one should arrange eight [sections] with equal width from the corners. ||202-203||
One should always construct those [sections] separately according to their respective proportions;

with an outward projection of four parts, they should be provided with a circular path (bhramaṇa) of one part. In the middle, there should be two halls (śālā), each measuring two parts in length and width.
"This [mudrā] is called Padmagarbheya; it is dear to the mind of Prajāpati.
It always brings clarity of mind to the noble goddesses and other deities.
Having prepared a field (kṣetra) with eight sides, measuring half a yojana in both length and width..."
In the center, a temple (devagṛha) should be constructed; outside, a circumambulatory path (bhrama) should be made half its size.
The *bhadra* projections should consist of twelve [units], and their outward extension should be four [units].
The outward extension of those *bhadras* should also be four units.
Their width is six padas; one should divide that [width] into four parts.
The *śālā* (hall) shall consist of half a part and be three parts in length. Furthermore, a circumambulatory path (*bhrama*) should be constructed on both its sides, measuring one part. ||208-209||
When the length and width of the hall are each two parts within the *padabhrama*,
this eight-sided (*jagatī*) structure, possessing auspicious characteristics, is called the Aṃśumatī. Having established the field as eight-cornered, its length and width are half [of that].

In the center, a temple (devagṛha) should be constructed, and outside of it, a circumambulatory path (bhrama) half its size. Having made the Bhadra [section] equal in width to the temple, one should then divide it;
its height shall be by fourteen [parts], and its width by ten of those same parts.
At the end of the primary circular movement,

a most beautiful hall (śālā) should be constructed, measuring three paces in length and width, and provided with a circular movement of one part. It should have a length and width of two paces and be endowed with a circular movement of one part.
On its two sides, two beautiful halls (śālās) should be constructed. Each hall should be five parts in width and three parts in depth, and it should extend into the central space by three parts.
Thus, each hall occupies one-third of the total area.
With a width of two parts and provided with a circular projection of one part,
there shall be two *karṇikās* on the sides of the *pratibhadra*, projecting by one part.
The *karṇas* should be one and a half parts in length and provided with a pair of *śālās*.
As previously described, the Śuṇḍikā and other types are also declared here as Kamalī.
One should arrange five distinct halls within the fourteen divisions of the seven Svastika layouts, with their lengths equal to the width of the exit. ||217-218||
"In the Agrabhadrā, however, three excellent halls (śālās) should be constructed.
Thus should it be understood; this has been fully described as the hall dear to the Wielder of the Thunderbolt (Vajradhara).
In this manner, the jagatī verses are arranged in a square formation.
The shanks, which are circular in their arrangement,
long and round, and well-proportioned, should always be fashioned by vigilant artisans. 220.
Thus ends the sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Jagatī," in the *Vāstuśāstra* named *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*, composed by the great king of kings, the illustrious Bhojadeva.
Now begins the seventieth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Liṅga, the Pedestal, and the Image. Now, the measurement and the characteristics of the *liṅgas* are being described.
The smallest [vessel] should be made with iron measuring one-third of a cubit.
In this manner, by increasing by two parts [of a cubit],
there should be three types— small, medium, and large— up to the measure of a full cubit, starting from the *akalpa* and so forth.
The temple should be constructed according to the names of the [auspicious] marks;
furthermore, those born of the Varuṇa class should be twice that measure,
and those born of the Mṛttikā class should be three times that.
By exchanging it for the position of its own minor [digit], the wise should apply the characteristic diminished by one in the path of the minor [digit].
Or, if it is in the seventh [position], it is like a water-jar tilted on its side. ||4-5||
The pillar-base (stambhadra) and the daityakaivalya are thus excluded by Viṣṇu;
the wing-line (pakṣarekhā) should be laid out for the purpose of extracting the characteristic marks.
When the field of the wings has been divided sixfold, it is encircled by portions of half a unit that have been set aside.
The *pakṣalekhā* is beneficial for those seeking sons and likewise for those seeking wealth today.
When this [number] is divided by eight or nine, the remainder below is the *pakṣalekhā*; when divided by six or seven, it grants desired objects.
Just as when divided by sixteen, excluding the two lower parts,

it is praised [when the remainder] is measured by the Paśu-rekhas (13), the arrows (5), the Nandās (9), the stars (27), and the Śakras (14); so too in the Liṅga, however many finger-breadths there are, they are measured by one-third of those same units.
The distance between the two marked lines [the *lakṣya*] should be equal to the width of the door; this is the task.

(10) Within the intervals between the lines, the wise man should make a hollow (*khāta*) equal to one part in the tenth part of the width, and he should make the width on the line equal to the previous measurement. (11)

One should not make a door-mark on a stone linga, one made of metal, one born of clay, a bāṇaliṅga, or a mobile (cala) linga; therefore, the mark should be made on a stationary (aja) one. Having divided the portion for worship into eleven equal parts from top to bottom, [one should proceed].
One should likewise divide the head into ninety-one parts transversely. With unequal steps, there shall be one thousand and one lingas;
this is called the Sahasralinga, consisting of the numbers five and two. ||13-14||
Having determined the proportions according to the measurement, one should fashion the entire [liṅga];
having set aside three parts from the top, one should arrange it by means of the remaining parts. Then, one should fashion the neck of the Śaka-liṅga with one part.
With two parts for the shoulder-sections and paired cloths,
and when it is established in the four directions situated upon flowers,
the four-faced liṅga becomes worshipped, granting all desires. ||16-17||
For the three-faced [deity], the limbs from the forehead onwards should be fashioned individually according to one part and a quarter; the formation of the shoulders is from the remaining parts.
However, for the single-wheeled [deity], one should fashion the forehead and other parts according to one and a half parts.
In the case of a nine-part division, one should discard two parts each from the two sides;
this is the rule for a four-faced [image] divided on both sides.
For a single-faced [image], one should discard one and a half parts each for the ornamentation of the half [of the face].
The head should be fashioned with a crescent moon as an ornament, bearing both peaks and non-peaks;
the formation of the head should be executed according to the path previously described.
There should be four [projections] on one side, and when extended, they constitute the emergence from the mouth.
Or it may be made with divisions called *rākendra* and *kāraka* in due order.
A face-liṅga (*mukhaliṅga*) should not be fashioned except for one that is entirely symmetrical to the [main] liṅga.
For all face-liṅgas, a two-part pedestal (*pīṭha*) is prescribed.
Thirty-three varieties of steel (taija) arise from those mentioned together;
likewise, there are those originating from iron (lauha), wood (dāru), stone (aśma), and earth (mṛt).
Among these, there are six others that are intermediate, such as yavana, vālīya, and so forth.
Beginning with four and increasing by four, [the temples] are measured in cubits, including the hand-span and the cubit.
Those palaces which are without supporting pillars (nirandhāra) contain nine liṅgas;
among those with supporting pillars, there are five [liṅgas] up to twelve, and so on, until fifty.

The stone temples are said to be constructed with heights of one cubit and so on, increasing by one cubit at a time; or else, according to the measurement of the interior of the temple, the best [size] is fifteen cubits,
the middling is fifteen minus five parts (ten), and the smallest would be half of that.
Through their internal subdivisions, each of these is further divided into three according to its appropriate application;
thus, there are six others, making nine lingas as before.
From those as well, when joined with the three types of intermediate subdivisions as previously described, [the total is reached]. ||28-29||
By this method, those made of wood—and likewise those made of metal—should be prepared.
When the length is divided into sixteen parts, the portion consisting of four parts is for the Liṅga worshipped by the gods;
it should not be less than that in width, being auspicious with its constituent parts.

It should be equal on all sides, square, and designated as the first [mandala] by means of six [lines]. (31) By marking the corners with a cord half the length of the diagonal and removing the remainder, it becomes eight-cornered; when divided into seven, there is another [division] for Hāni and Tuṇeśa. (32)
By drawing a circle using half the cord of the womb-limit (garbhasīmā), it is fashioned as a sphere;
the lower, middle, and upper portions should be square and so forth in sequence.
In the case of a liṅga, these are equal and excellent according to the length of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa respectively.
Among those [measures], two parts should be set aside from the *thuthubha* portion for the *liṅgas*;
these two parts, which are the bases for Brahmā and Śiva, are to be fashioned.
This width of the pedestal is prescribed according to the length of the *liṅga*.
Furthermore, another [measurement] is distinguished for the pedestal (pīṭha) on the side according to the width of the liṅga;
or, having removed [the portion] from the Brahmā-section equal to that [width], the Rudra-portion should be fashioned within the Brahmā-portion by virtue of that [measurement]. 36.
When this is done, the fault here will be avoided for you;

for both the maker and the employer, there shall be auspiciousness once that [fault] has been removed through the gift of one-third of the value and by providing maintenance, O Moon-like youth. (37–38)

When a copper vessel is produced with the thickness of four chicken eggs, it is called a *tuccha* when it is reduced by one-eighth; by giving half of that and adding [another] half, it is described as follows:
when this [remaining] eighth part is divided into four, it is stated by increasing the portion [successively].

The Puṇḍarīka, the Viśālākṣa, the Śrīvatsa, and the Śakrasarvānana—these should be fashioned as the door-ornaments (lakṣaṇas) upon the liṅgas; that [method] is now described. Having divided the portion of Rudra into three parts, one should extract the ornament by means of two [parts].
Even the characteristic of a long head is desired for the *liṅga*;
alternatively, a long face should be made in the sixth ninth-part (*navamāṃśaka*),
excluding the [portion] consisting of the syllable *vā*.
A square, three parts wide, is drawn along the side-lines;
as before, it has eight spokes and a circle, with a six-sided umbrella at its top, beautifully adorned by an umbrella known as "Enemy-Crusher" (Śatrumardana). ||43-44||
The Liṅga worshipped by Indra is praised for those desiring victory over the quarters;
this should be installed by one wishing to paralyze an enemy.
And with the world-protectors (Lokapālas), one should perform [the rite] characterized by three parts, half, and half again.
In the center of the Indra-square, a line for the wings of this [deity] is prescribed.

Its width should be five parts, consisting of half of its own length and the Rudras (eleven), while the middle is square and circular as before, according to the visualization of Citrabhānu. ||46-47||

It is circular, endowed with seven spokes, devoid of its own [original] arms, and its width extends to half the previous width; it has a mark at its uppermost head. Or, when divided by eleven, there are three [units] to be cut away on both sides.
That very [liṅga], raised by one part with the remaining parts omitted, is intended as a parasol.
Having fashioned this liṅga worshipped by Agni, one should place it toward the direction of Agni;
this should always be installed by one who desires to cause distress to his enemies.
One should construct the pit (kuṇḍa) with a width of five parts out of nine parts equal to half its own length; it should have eight corners and two sides, each formed by three [units].
Having divided [the area] into nine parts on all sides, one should omit the three [units] located at the corners.
One should likewise construct the weapon [mudrā]; thus, by means of three sides, it becomes circular in sequence.
Having divided the head into ten parts and omitting three portions, one should establish the two wings and create the elevation from a tenth part.
The characteristics [of the marks] should be understood as before, located at the tips of the staffs and the corners;
how this sign is [applied] in the various [positions] such as "yāni" and so forth by those desiring victory—
for the sake of slaying adversaries— has been honored by all the sons of Vivasvat.
Like that of Agni, the head of Viṣṇu is auspicious, yet it is characterized by the ten states of the seasons (55).
The head is said to be the zodiac sign of one's own [ascendant], measured at one and a half parts;
on its two sides there should be the gain of the signs, and it is praised when it resembles the tip of a sword (56).
Having established this Khaḍgabhidha-liṅga,
Nirṛti then beheld the state of the twice-born and the Śāṅkara yoga devoid of reality,
along with the sevenfold portion of all, the Liṅgin, and the one joined with the red-faced one.
He marked it with four signs resembling the tips of nooses and fashioned a sword-blade; having installed this emblem facing the northeast, Varuṇa attained the yoga of Īśvara,
yet this [linga] brings about peace and nourishment.
In the Svārddha [circle], with twelve parts and seven [units] in the Puva and Anila [sections],
one should apply the Viṣṇu-mark (13) divided by the Śoka (7) numbers, omitting two or three [units] as before;
the other circle is like the previous one, excluding the arrow and umbrella.
And its mark is like the tip of a banner;

furthermore, by means of this [mantra], one should perform the *sudīrgha* [rite] as well as the *śāmbhava-yoga*, which effects the eradication of enemies, their separation, and the causing of trembling in those who are hostile. 61–62.

This *liṅga* is to be installed; it was fashioned by the wise with the left eye [of the image] as the *kāryavāruṇa* [measure], yet the heavy state [of the proportions] has been exceeded. By the reduction of one-sixteenth part from the top of the head and the side-located portion of the feet... [63]
Its emblem should be a parasol, and it should resemble the tip of a mace.

Having fashioned this, Naneśvara, who was seated upon the essence of his own quarter, attained yoga for the sake of reaching the abode of Śiva and thereby obtained sovereign power (vibhūti). ||64-65||
Divide the square by six using six *śaṅkus* (measuring lines);
then, by omitting three parts on each side of the *bhava*-division, a triangle is formed.
The circle, however, should be made as before, and the head should resemble a hen’s egg.

With nine parts of *tryaṃśava* (three-part divisions), this becomes a "chicken-egg" (*kukkuṭāṇḍa*) shape. With nine *mūṣa* (molds) on the two sides, there are three *triśātana*s; the "chicken-egg" shape should be fashioned with three *aśri*s (angles) as the support for the portion of worship (*pūjābhāga*). ||67–68||
A mark resembling the tip of a trident should be made upon the Īśvara-liṅga;
this brings about the attainment of the sovereignty of yoga and knowledge.
In the Brāhma and Raudra types, the head of all [the liṅgas] should be like a lotus bud.
On this linga, there is a lotus-shaped mark belonging to the lotus-born [Brahmā].
Having installed this linga, Prajāpati attained the station of Prajāpati; therefore, this shall remain here as long as the instruction of the Vedas endures.
In the Vaiṣṇava [rite], everything is like the Raudra; on this [image], the head should be shaped like a spear.
For the Vaiṣṇava, the mark should be made equal to that of Bhavaja, or it may be produced from a sacred field for the twice-born and others by means of white [pigment] and so forth.
One should cause a stone substance to be collected from a woman who has been purified;
this may be either cooked or uncooked, containing within it iron and mercury.
The uncooked variety should be prepared for use as "vajralepa" (adamantine cement) and other such purposes by those seeking spiritual success.

For the sake of prosperity, one should worship a linga made of metal, excluding lead and tin, which is fashioned from gold, silver, copper, iron, and so forth. This [linga] possesses the characteristics described for a linga; it brings about the destruction of enemies for men and bestows elephants, horses, chariots, and other such things.
That which is produced from iron brings about the secret accomplishment of the Mothers and Guhyakas.
For monks, this [accomplishment] would be unstable; for those wishing to plunder, it is effective in the houses of others.
That which is born of diamond (vajra) is the best among all, and it cuts through all obstacles.
Padmarāga [ruby] is for great servants; pearls are for good fortune; puṣparāga [topaz] and mahānīla [sapphire] are for those born on the banks of the Yamunā;
and the sūryakānta [sun-stone] is for fame, the continuity of the lineage, and splendor.
Crystal (sphāṭika) grants all desires; śūlāraśma [is for] the destruction of enemies; maṇija [is] likewise for horripilation (pulaka);
sasyaka is for the production of crops; and bhojaga bestows divine accomplishments (divyasiddhi). ||79-80||

For those whose minds are intent on health, the best [linga] is one made of coral; likewise, those made of vaikrāntaka, saha, avarta, rāga, and magnetite are beneficial. That [linga], consecrated by mantras according to its specific class, is effective for the three types of minor ailments.
The quality of the fruit in other types of gems is to be inferred from their color,
name, shape, and specific characteristics by one who knows them.
[A gem] on the earth, or upon its pedestal, or no more than nine finger-breadths above it— ||82-83||
For the sake of success, [the placement] from the end of the *cara* up to the *dāra*, or from the *aśva* and *nakṣatra*, is praised.
If it is well-constituted and well-lit, even a downward-facing [configuration] does not produce a fault.
One endowed with subtle power and qualities is powerful and produces all faults.
The radiance of all gems produced from mountains is the cause of their presence;
this should be understood by the wise through the measures of māna, unmāna, and pramāṇa.
A stone [image] should be placed below the height of a cubit, and its installation in temples is highly commended.
Then they say that even a movable [image] is for women who have lost their support;
if, however, from this [fixed type], one intends to make a Suyavāṅka image on a pedestal,
there are two parts for the object (the image), and the remaining part is for the cavity of the pedestal.
Its three parts are circular, and its foundation should be established within the caves.
When this field has been taken possession of, there will be the destruction of the local ruler in that region;
the mandala, whose form is perfected and well-concealed, should be contemplated with focused intent.
When this has been washed with the juices of *siddhārtha* (white mustard) and *rāla*, it attains the state of perfected mercury (*siddharasa*).
Wherever its "embryo" (*garbha*) is said to be, by drawing it there, it becomes equal [to that].
With *karavīra*, *jaṭā*, *aṅkā*, yellow orpiment (*haritāla*), and *viṣṭibhiḥ*... [90]
When all these have been introduced, the region that was previously indistinct becomes clearly defined, as if it were being inscribed with a pen.
[This is achieved] with viṣa, rudrajaṭā, pathyā, brūvakaṇḍa, and vibhītaka. ||91-92||
Combined with *sudarśana*, *aśvamāra*, and *avidugdha*,
this is a plaster to be applied to the side for the purpose of manifesting the signs.
Now, the [application] of seats (*pīṭhas*) is likewise described here.
For the sake of establishing the distinction and non-distinction [of the deities] through their names, measures, and values:
||94|| This [mandala] possesses divisions such as Devī and so forth; however, the measure of the *garbha* (inner sanctum) is one *pada*.
Its accomplishment is declared by way of the [four] faces; [thus] the six limbs are for liberation. ||95||
Then, one should properly construct these [shrines], measuring them according to the dimensions of the *kārā* and other types of *liṅgas*, facing toward the north;
these are primarily taught for the sake of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Alternatively, one may fashion them correctly according to the measurement of the interior (*garbha*) of the *liṅga*.
The measurements for the length of the *liṅga* in various types of temples are equal to the measurement of the *viṣkaṃbha* (diameter) for those with unmanifest or detached *liṅgas*. Furthermore,
the dimensions of the *kārā* and other parts are determined in accordance with the measurement of the *liṅga*.

For the sake of devotion and liberation, one should construct a pedestal for the divine manifestations of that [deity], with a height and width equal to half of those [dimensions]. For the middling and lower types, one should construct a pedestal for the sake of success with a height and width equal to half of that [preceding measurement]. ||99||
Whether circular or square, it should conform to the characteristics of all temples.
A circular form is not beneficial for manifest [deities], as it leads to destruction and other evils.
According to the prescribed rite, the earth is known as "Pūrṇā" (the Full). 100–101.
Bhābhāvatī and Trapākṣī are also counted;
they should be assigned by name to the Liṅgas of the world-protectors beginning with Indra, in order, upon their pedestals.
On the Īśāna-liṅga, the Raudrīs [should be placed]—up to the pedestal that may exist.

Among these three, the others are said to bestow the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. Pāpā, Pāpāvarā, Vāpī, Vajrā, Candrakalā, and Saṃvartā are known as Nandikāvarta; these are considered common [to all].
Now, the characteristics of all these [pedestals] are described:

the *aindra* is marked by the phallic emblem (*liṅga*), the *vṛttā* is circular, and the *pṛthvī* is square at its base and so forth. One should divide the diagonal of the square into four parts and then further into eight.
Having divided this [line] into seven parts and calculating the inclusion of the fourth part,
the wise one should perform the rotation of two circles on the exterior sides of the two rear sections where the lines are situated. ||106-107||
In a square [mandala], by increasing the eight spokes from the central core-line,
one should mark the location of the petals and draw the lines from both sides.
By the removal of the abandoned portion, the pedestal (pīṭhikā) shall be formed.

The Āgneya-liṅga brings about the destruction of enemies and the burning away of their afflictions. In the field—having set aside one-twelfth part of this square—the remainder is the womb; from that, one should draw half of a circle.
This pedestal (pīṭhikā) for a southern liṅga becomes semi-circular in shape;
situated to the south of the city and other structures, it destroys [evil] influences.
By increasing half of the division on both sides of the square [base], [the form is achieved].
By the increase of the portion, she is surrounded by friends due to the application of two sūtras.
Following the sequence of the Raudrī [direction], Nairṛtī causes the death of women, hatred, and disease;
she has the form of the eastern moon, possesses a girdle, and belongs to Varuṇa.
Now, for rites of pacification (śāntika), nourishment (pauṣṭika), and the destruction of death, there is a pedestal;
having increased the western [side] by one-sixth— [from] that,
the four points of intersection produced by drawing a circle from the center [are established].
From those two points situated on the circumference,
one should draw a regular hexagon, or else a shape like a thunderbolt (vajra), by moving from ear to ear.
There should be a pedestal for the sky-dweller (Vāyu), and leaves for the Maruts in the direction of the wind.
The Yakṣī, who has three girdles and is circular in form, worshipped by Dhanada, should be employed by those desiring victory in rites such as eradication (uccāṭana) and for the attainment of wealth.
[She is] supported by the Gaṇas and possesses two girdles.

One should fashion the *khuraka* with one [unit] and the *jāḍyakumbha* with four; likewise, the *añja* with two and the entrance (*praveśa*) here with one. For the *jāḍyakumbha*, the insertion of those [units] is recommended with four; for the *añjūya*, with four; and for the *karṇikā*, with two units, O men.
From this [total], one part is for Kaṇṭhaka, one for Karṇikā,
six for the Vibhājiraṃpuśa, and then one for the Mekhalās.
The Padmayā pedestal is renowned as the bestower of all desires.
When the field is divided into sixteen parts, the *khuraka* shall consist of one part;
the *jarāta* consists of four parts, the *kumbha* of three, and the *karṇikā* of one.
The neck (*kaṇṭha*) consists of three parts, and the projection (*nirgama*) shall be four parts, as before. ||121-122||
This [pedestal]—among those with clearly defined characteristics—is the *payodharā* type;
such indeed would be the *apīṭha* as well, so what need is there to speak further regarding its definition?
When divided into twelve parts, the measurement of the pedestal (*pīṭha*) shall consist of two parts.
The *jagatī* is made with three [parts], the *kuśa* with two, and the *vedikā* with one;
the *kaṇṭha* with two and again the northern *vedikā* with one;
then, by means of each single part, there should be two *pīṭhikās*.
In this manner, the six-sided Vajrākṣa pedestal should be constructed by the wise.
The pedestal is divided into six parts of the field; one part shall be the base (khuraka).
Two parts shall be the shaft (jaṅghā), then one part for the altar (vedī), and two parts for the neck (kaṇṭhaka).

The exit from both [sides] is that; it becomes the crescent moon (candrakalā) according to the woman's desire. When the two [lines] extend toward the left and right, it is indeed the nectar-line (amṛtarekhā). From half of the six girdles (mekhalā), the upper neck (ūrdhvakaṇṭha) is then one part. ||127-128||
On the remaining area, there should be three strips with an interval between them;
this pedestal, worshipped by Rudra, is known by the name Saṃvarta.
Having constructed it, Saṃvarta and others ascended above Prakṛti.
The Rudras occupied that imperishable station known as Vothastara.
When the rise of the *pīṭha* is divided into six parts, there shall be three *paṭṭikās* (bands) for one part;
the neck (*kaṇṭha*) shall be by one part, and another *paṭṭikā* shall also be by one part.
Marked with the *nandyāvarta* [swastika], this is celebrated as *Nandyāvarta*;
it is common to all *liṅgas* and bestows all perfections (*siddhi*).
This *Siddhakhurā* is to be meditated upon as dwelling beautifully from the feet to the neck.
There are other pedestals (pīṭhikā) made of various materials;
however, those situated in the mind have not been described here due to their infinity.
For these [pedestals], the pit (garta) should be one-third [of the height] and the girdle (mekhalā) one-sixteenth.
And this [channel] should be led through the middle of the girdle into the cavity;
it should extend fifty-two tālas in length and width toward the north,
with an interval of two tālas.
At the edge, one should fashion two parts for the fear (the base), and at the front, a mouth that is double [in width].

The girdles should be made with one and a half parts; the life-channel (prāṇāla) should be according to its own measure in parts. On the linga, there should be three, three, and three [parts]; one should contemplate those as being like the falling leaves.

Whirlpools of beautiful form are auspicious; however, the pedestal (*pīṭha*) and the Brahma-stone (*brahmaśilā*) are always auspicious when they conform to the specific type of the *liṅga*. The Brahma-stone should measure one-fourth of the width of the inner sanctum (*garbha*).
Or else, the Brahma-stone may be equal in size to the ear [of the image].
The Brahma-stone, which is designated as the "Gone" (yātā), should be made from a portion of the Brahman;
the Karma-stone for it should be made by the wise to be even greater than that. ||139-140||

One should establish [the three deities] with three persons; one should place Śiva in the center, Brahmā to his right, and Puruṣottama to his left. By establishing them otherwise than this, a great transgression would occur.

The two [halves] should be reduced by one-third; the end of the navel-cord (kośānta) of the Discus-bearer (Cakrin) should be so formed. Reduced by one-third, the two [halves] should be so formed; the end of the navel-cord of the Discus-bearer should be so formed. From the height reduced by one-third, the end of the stalk (koka) of the Lotus-born (Padmajanman) should be so formed.
In the abode of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa—
the measurement for these who stand separately is two [units] at will.
Where Umā and Maheśvara are together, there Umā is like Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
The images intended for placement in the open air (ākāśa) should be forty-five cubits in height;
the medium-sized ones should be made three-quarters of that size, and the smaller ones half of that.
Furthermore, for the purpose of processions (yātrā), the image is prescribed according to the measurement of the doorway.
And having divided that door into three parts, one should fashion the pedestal (pīṭha) with one part;
the image should be made with two parts—such is the measurement for the largest [image].
For the medium-sized [image], one should divide the door into nine parts and omit one part.

Having divided the remaining portions into three, one should fashion the pedestal (pīṭha) with one portion. When the image is smaller than both [the temple and the pedestal], one should divide the door into eight parts; omitting one part, with the remainder— ||148–149||
One should arrange for the worship of that seated [deity] with those three from the pedestal (pīṭha).
Having divided half of the door into three parts, the pedestal is prescribed by means of two [parts].
Alternatively, having made the door either twofold or fourfold as previously described, one should set aside one [part].
Having divided the remainder into three parts, the pedestal (pīṭha) and the image (arcā) are to be fashioned as before.
Having divided the height of the door into fifteen parts, one part is set aside;
from that, the pedestal is made with one part and the image with two parts.

The pedestal may be prescribed as five parts, or alternatively, from a pair of parts; one should fashion the seated image with three parts. Having divided half of the door into three, the pedestal is prescribed by means of two [of those parts].
One should install the image according to the portion, the intention, and the size of the house, or by dividing half of the inner sanctum (garbha) of the temple into ten parts from the rear side;
therein one should establish the Piśācas, Rakṣasas, Danujas, Gandharvas, and Guhyakas. ||154-155||

The sequence of deities, beginning with Āditya and Candra and ending with Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Īśāna, follows the order of the six divisions within the womb [of the temple]. Alternatively, having excluded one part, the installation of all the deities is recommended in the fifth division. 156.
When the marks extending over the limbs and minor parts [of the body] are present,
one should know that the meaning of those [marks] is like a painting;
having understood even the linga with its pedestal as an image, it is highly esteemed.
"He shall become a king and be honored by all, even by those who are accomplished.

(157) Thus ends the seventieth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Limbs, the Pedestal, and the Images," in the *Vāstuśāstra* named *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*, composed by the Great King of Kings, the illustrious Bhojadeva.
Now begins the seventy-first chapter, titled "The Overview of Painting."
Now, O Priyavitta, we have undertaken this work of painting;
for painting is the foremost of all arts and is dear to the world.
Whether on every step or upon a wall, let the painting be executed according to our word.
One should practice drawing with fixed bonds so that the measurement of the lines is achieved; likewise,
one should master the clarity of color, the various sequences of brushwork,
the diverse methods of proportions and measurements, as well as the technique for the nine positions.

The arrangement of the hands, which is undoubtedly characterized by [auspicious] marks, belongs to both divine and human beings; that divine [arrangement] was produced by the one born from the mouth [of Brahmā].
Among those, the hunchbacks and dwarfs belong to the hosts of *gaṇas*, *rakṣasas*, and *kiṃnaras*.
The forms of conceptual constructions, as well as the shapes and structures of trees, shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, and spreading vines— [these are the results] for those of evil karma,
for the brave, for the ill-fated, and for wealthy kings. ||5-6||

In this [work], the physical appearance, characteristics, and attire of those of the Brahmin, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes who perform cruel deeds, as well as of the proud and of those who subsist by the stage,
are described; likewise, the beauty, marks, and dress of virtuous royal women are recounted.
The term *lakṣaṇā* is used for female slaves, female ascetics, and barren vines;
for girls, names of constellations, and breeds of elephants and horses;
as well as for crocodiles, serpents, lions, and those things employed in sacrifices. (8–9)
Without the division of night and the characteristics of the seasons,
how can it be determined here whether [a patient] is curable or palliable?
[Likewise,] the division of the deities and the characteristics of the lines [of the hand].
We shall now describe the characteristics of the five elements and their very commencement,
as well as the characteristics of the arrangement of variegated patterns for all animals such as wolves and the like, for birds, and for all aquatic creatures.
Since one performs various actions through the medium of action,
all its constituent parts are therefore explained here in detail:
first among them is the brush, and second is the binding of the ground.
The third is writing; here, the characteristics of the work of drawing lines are set forth.
The fifth is the work of engraving, the sixth is the sequence of modeling, the seventh is sketching and the execution of a drawing, and likewise the eighth is the two-fold work of calligraphy.
Thinking, "This is a compendium," and "This is a sūtra," one should indeed cultivate this according to its sequence and not fall into delusion.
And one becomes skilled in the art of painting.
Thus ends the seventy-first chapter, titled "The Section on Painting," in the *Vāstuśāstra* named *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*, composed by the great king of kings, the illustrious Bhojadeva.
Now begins the seventy-second chapter, titled "The Binding of the Ground."
Now the characteristics of the brush and the binding of the ground are described:
[one should work] in a beautiful field within a grove, on the bank of a river with lotuses,
in the thickets of mountains, or within a garden of ponds.
There may be lumps of salt found on the earth at the roots of trees.
Those that grow in these fields— firm, smooth, and white—
and which are obtained from soft soil or its margins, should be known as pungent sugar (kaṭu-śarkarā).
The auspicious clay from the sacred fields has been described in due order;
one should pound it after crushing it, and then prepare a paste.
Therein, a portion of cooked *śāli* rice should be added as prescribed.
In the summer season, one should bring [the oil] in the seventh part; in the winter season, in the fifth;
in autumn, in the sixth; and in the rainy season, one should bring it in the fourth part.
By that means, they come for the purpose of binding the wicks.
The *agrā* has the luster of a *śāliva-kra*; the *yavyā* is like a barley grain and is the house of happiness;
it resembles the tip of a cock's crest according to the differentiation of the portions of karma.
At the time of instruction, a pair of fingers is prescribed as the measure.
On the lines of the *kutha* (rug), brushes measuring three finger-breadths are recommended;
on the lines of the cloth (*paṭa*), one should use those measuring four finger-breadths.
Now we shall describe the procedure for binding the ground.
The *pakṣikā*, the *kūṭas*, and the cloth itself—
for each of these, the binding to the ground is now described.
[This should be done] on auspicious lunar mansions and days of the week, and on festive days.
The one who has been wounded, the one whose garment has been worn, the eater, the supporter, and the instructor—
having honored them with flowers of many colors,
with fragrances, and with various sweet-smelling incenses, one should begin that [rite]. ||11-12||
With water equal to that which is drawn from a new thread, soft, and fresh,
he who knows the sky-like [reality] performs no further action; he is like one who has attained a state of freshness,
observing the subtle threads of the signs nearby.
One should make it level with the ground, free from unevenness and ridges, as far as the earth extends;
having properly observed that it is well-established and does not waver when sprinkled with water, the wise one,
having performed these preparations for the site, should thereafter carry out the binding.
Having taken pure, stainless [substances] resembling grains of rice, one should grind them at a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) and prepare a paste (kalka). With that,
one should form a ball (piṇḍa) and dry it in the shade.
One should grind it into a paste with which one may smear [the body] from head to foot;
in this very manner, one should rub it seven times until the four corners [of the body] are reached,
and afterwards, one should massage it with the hand until it becomes like salt.
Alternatively, one should perform the binding on the ground for training;
one should apply the binding in the decoction of the previously mentioned paste in five parts, which is recommended during the summer seasons. (19)
In autumn, one should give three parts and a half; the meeting [of the seasons] consists of three parts.
It is certain that during the rainy season, one should give by means of a portion;
in summer, [it is] by the measure of five parts.
One who is not devoid of wisdom should apply this bandage preceded by the application of heat;
he should smear it with a tuft of hair, drying it layer by layer as it dries. When it has reached the desired consistency, it should be moistened with water by the skillful.
Thus, the excellent binding of the ground for the training area has been performed according to the rule.
Now, the binding of the wall-ground is described as it truly is:
one should procure *snuhī*, *vāstuka*, *kūśmāṇḍa*, and *kuddālī*.

One should place the milk of any one of these— apāmārga, ikṣuraka, or the seven [plants] mentioned in the Vāgasūtra— for seven nights. [Then there are] siṃha, pāsana, nimba, triphalā, vyādhighāta, and dyādi.
One should collect [the ingredients] as they are available, including the decoction of *kuṭaja* (26).
Having prepared a plaster with sea salt combined with astringent and alkaline substances,
one should first apply it to the wall and then sprinkle it thoroughly with the decoctions (27).
Taking smooth clay free from large stones,
he should place twice as much human excrement, river sand, and clay as that;
and likewise, the stalks of the *kakubha* tree, black gram, and *śālmalī* wood.
Likewise, one should provide the juice of *śrīphala* fruits according to the appropriate time.
The wise man, having gathered all that was previously prescribed for the binding of the earth along with sand, should place it together in a new vessel. (29–30)
One should scatter a quantity of earth equal to an elephant hide from the edge of the altar;
then, having cast away the impurities, one should make it resemble a conch shell—
pure, stainless, glossy, pale-white, soft, and radiant.
Having duly taken the thorny plant mentioned previously,
the wise man should pound and rub it to prepare a paste;
he should then add a portion of the previously mentioned cooked rice and the resinous exudations.
If one should apply it in all directions together with false sugar (kūṭasarkarā),
the wise man should smear the wall three times with the previously mentioned [substance].
Having smeared the hand with *hala*, one should apply the false *kūrtaka*.
By this procedure, the excellent construction of the wall is accomplished.
Now we shall describe the construction of the ground for the cloth-painting (paṭa);
having collected the seeds of the *bimba* plant and having removed their impurities, the wise [practitioner] should proceed. (35–36)
Having thus purified the flat beans or rice grains,
one should grind whichever of these is fine and cook it in a vessel.
Having applied a cloth bandage, one should perform the procedure as previously described.

Furthermore, the previously mentioned resinous exudates (niryāsa), along with sugar and *kaṭa*, should be ground with water; using that [mixture], one should paint the cloth. This method of binding is recommended for the work of painting.
One should perform the binding of the ground for the Sādās by another rite;
it should be provided with the resin of the *prādyadyāmika* palm. Then, one should provide three layers of straw and gravel mixed with resin.
This binding of the ground for the recitation should be diligently cleared away immediately thereafter with cow dung, straw mats, and the like, as well as with mats, gravel, and water,
using a broom.
Just as the binding of the ground and the covering of the edges follow after the painting has been described,
so too has the characteristic of the brushes here been explained,
along with the various types of single-footed walls and ground surfaces.
"He who understands all this both from the text and from its meaning,
by virtue of his connection with this delusion of the Creator,

speaks [thus]. (43) Thus ends the seventy-second chapter, titled "The Binding of the Ground," in the *Vāstuśāstra* named *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*, composed by the great king of kings, the illustrious Bhojadeva.
Now begins the seventy-third chapter, titled "The Art of Modeling (Leṣyakarman) and so forth.
The art of modeling, the characteristics of clay, the marks [of measurement], and the marks [of ornamentation] are described;
likewise, the construction of oblong ponds, wells, tanks, lotus-pools, and long reservoirs.
The foot of a tree, the bank of a river, lotus ponds, and likewise oblong ponds;
the foot of a tree, the bank of a river, and the midst of a thicket—
these are declared to be, in truth, the fields for [the collection of] earth.
Their colors are like white honey, fair (gaura), and tawny (kapila);
these glossy ones are recommended for the Brahmins and the other castes respectively.
The clay for the *indrākṣī* [vessel] should be taken, avoiding large stones.
One should pour into it the juice derived from śālmalī, māṣa, kakubha, madhūka, and the three myrobalans (triphalā), as well as the expressed juice of pippalī;
and also betel nut, chickpeas, bilva, and the hair of a horse.
One may apply cow-hair or the inner bark of a coconut;
having mixed it with clay, one should rub [the area] or apply double the amount of husks (tuṣa).
One should also mix sand, *tīvratī*, and *tapas* with the clay.
One should mix two parts of clay with a portion of cotton;
having combined those, one should place a third part of clay on top,
and then add the previously mentioned sand and gravel.

Having prepared a paste with cotton cloth and wrapped it around that form, one should carefully fashion the shape using that mixture of resin. The skillful artisan should then coat it with *kaṭaśarkarā* using a brush.

The application of a plaster made from a concentrated decoction of clay is recommended. One should cause a mass of iron to melt within a vessel of lime-mud; having joined it with the appropriate ingredients, one should apply it after it has been properly processed for a fortnight.
The determination of the clay for the plastering rite: that which is mixed with *anepaka* destroys the position of the performer.
The characteristics of vilekha are now correctly described.
First is kūrcana with a brush; second is the hand-brush (hastakūrcaka);
third is known as the bhāsa-brush; and fourth is the calla-brush. ||12-13||

The fifth [type of] application is considered to be the *vartanī*, the *kūrcamānya-kūrca*, and the *miṣya*. That is prescribed for the work of plastering (*lepyakarma*); they are not minute (*anāmaṇava*).
Here, the excellent *jalacūrṇaka* has been brought—[the rest of the verse is missing].
The wise man should carry a brush made from the hair of a bull's ears;
it may be fashioned from that [hair], or from bark, or even from coarse hair. ||15–16||
Whatever brush (kūrcaka) is prescribed here is praised;
the wise man should hold a brush made from the hair of a bull's ear.
A brush made of fibers is naturally superior for the work of scraping.
The first has the form of a sprout of speech; then follows that which has the shape of a clear sprout.
Another, the third, is like a needle of the *plakṣa* tree;
the fourth is proclaimed to have the form of a sprout of the *udumbara* tree. ||18-19||
One should not make the lines too thick, resembling the sprout of a banyan tree;
nor should one make them too thin, equal to the sprout of a Plakṣa tree.
Where the wise man [draws] in the form of an Aśvattha sprout from the hand...
The shape of an udumbara sprout is recommended for the work of modeling (lepyakarma).
The staff, made of bamboo, should be the eldest [in length], extending to eighteen finger-breadths.
Modeling (lepyakarma) [is thus described] in brief.
Following the rules for refinement, the clay is prepared;
herein the method of kneading is correctly described, as well as the fivefold fashioning of the brush. (22)

Thus ends the seventy-third chapter, titled "The Chapter on Plastering Work, Drawing, and Brushes," in the *Vāstuśāstra* named *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*, composed by the great king of kings, the supreme lord, the illustrious Bhojadeva.
Now begins the seventy-fourth chapter, titled "The Measurement of the Eggs" (*Aṇḍaka*).
Herein is described the procedure for fashioning the eggs (*aṇḍakavartanā*) as it follows in the sequence of the work.
And having drawn the proportions of the body, as well as the basis for the types of beings and so forth,
one should then place the stars;
having drawn three stars, there [is] the extent of the face.
They know that the length of the sphere (golaka) is its maximum dimension;
by means of that sphere, one should perform the measurement of both length and breadth.
The width of the face-sphere (mukhāṇḍaka) is equal to six layers of plaster.
The two lengths are seven globes, and the arrangement is that of a pond;
this excellent face-egg (mukhāṇḍaka) should be made in the art of painting.
The three-edged circular form should be drawn as a circular egg (vṛttāṇḍaka), according to the sequence.
Now we shall describe the egg-shapes of the planets;
the wise should calculate the dimensions of the Sun's sphere as being one and a half [yojanas] greater than a hemisphere.
A sphere measuring half a [yojana] in diameter is called the egg of Mars.
Its length should be nine *golakas*, and its opening at the mouth should be twice that [in width]. For men, the measurement taken from the base should be six [units], and its width five *golakas*.
The female organ (*aṇḍaka*) should be drawn resembling a coconut fruit.
In the art of painting, the egg-shaped form (aṇḍaka) for children should be made four *golaka*s in width and five *golaka*s in length;
one should distinguish its smiling faces by adding half-*golaka*s.

The egg of Ālasya is likewise, and its weeping is exactly like that. One should fashion the egg of Rākṣasa, which is six golakas in width and seven golakas in length, resembling the orb of the moon. ||10-11||
In the *Hāsyābhiprastava*, one should distinguish [the measurements] from half a *golaka*;
that is proclaimed here as the measure for *devāṇḍaka* in this context of indolence (*ālasya*).
Its width is six *golakas* and its length is eight *golakas*.
That which is circular and painted is known as the *divyāṇḍaka* (divine egg).
Now, the characteristics of the *divyamānuṣāṇḍaka* (divine-human egg) are described:
that [egg] should be more than half a *golaka* in measure, and it should be made according to human proportions.
Having fashioned the human face-egg (mukhāṇḍa) as five golakas in width and joined with the six-fold golaka-seam, the ketu is prescribed;
the face-egg of the Pramathas is according to the measurement of the child-egg (śiśukāṇḍaka).
The egg of the Yātudhānas should be according to the measure of the Rākṣasa egg;
one should fashion the egg of the Dānavas to resemble the face of a god, and the egg of the Gandharvas, Nāgas, and Yakṣas should be exactly like that. ||16-17||
The divine and human egg of the Vidyādharas is to be known;
some understand the meaning of the scriptures, while others perform ritual acts.
This latter pair, moreover, has a face like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand.
"One who knows the treatise does not know the practice, nor does one who knows the practice know the treatise;
he who knows both of these is indeed the preeminent master architect.
Thus ends the seventy-fourth chapter, titled "The Measurement of the Egg," in the *Vāstuśāstra* named *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*, composed by the great emperor, the illustrious Bhojadeva.
Now begins the seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Origin of Measurement.
We shall now describe the measures of length, beginning with the atom (*paramāṇu*):
an atom, a mote of dust, a hair, a nit, a louse-egg, a barley-corn, and a finger-breadth (*aṅgula*).
In this manner, the increase is eightfold in succession; thus the *mānāṅgula* (measurement-finger) is established.
A sphere (*golaka*) should be known as two *aṅgulas*, or they call that a *kalā*.
Two *kalās* are a *golaka* on the forearm; by that measurement, it is one part.
One who is learned in the science of painting should execute the figures so that their length and breadth are neither deficient nor excessive.
The body of the gods and other such beings should be eight parts in width,
and one who knows the treatise on painting should make it thirteen parts in length.
The lake of the Asuras should consist of portions joined with half-portions;
it is desired that its length be twenty-nine times its width.
Furthermore, the [lake] of the Rākṣasas is seven parts in width and long.
Furthermore, that which is divine and human shall consist of twenty-seven parts;
one should make it twenty-one spans long and six and a half parts wide.
In the case of birth as a mortal, the body should be made six parts wide.
One should divide [the length] into twenty-four parts plus a half.
This measurement has been declared by us for the best man;
for the middling man, however, it should be five parts plus a half in width.
Its length is said to be twenty [units] increased by two;
for the smallest dwarfs, the width is five parts.
Likewise, the length of this body should be made five parts of its width.
A length of twenty-two parts for this body is recommended.
For those who are hunchbacked, the length of the body should be made five parts less than its width;
likewise, one part should be allotted for the auspicious face.
The body of the Vāmana [incarnation] shall have a width of five parts;
likewise, one should make its length seven and a half parts.
This indeed is the measurement declared for the dwarf [forms].
The width of the expanding body is four parts;
furthermore, the length of the face is measured at six parts.
Thus, this line of measurement for the dimensions of the body has been stated separately. (14-15)
In this [work], the [genealogy] of the gods, asuras, and likewise of the rākṣasas;
of the divine, human, and mortal beings; and even of the hunchbacks and dwarfs;
of the kinnaras along with the bhūtas, has been set forth in due order. 16.
In this manner, the forest gradually expanded,
and its dimensions also increased according to the distinction of the species.

And having thus described the division according to its nature, that which is called the "wonderful wealth" (citravittama) has indeed been explained. Now, the origin of the Mānasa [lineage] is being duly related. 17–18.
The gods have three forms: Suraja, Kumbha, and Kau. The body of the divine-human [class] is one, being both divine and human. (19) The forms of the asuras are threefold: Cakra and likewise Uttīrṇaka.
Durdara, Śakaṭa, Kūrma, and Tridiva—these two [groups] belong to the Rakṣases. Furthermore, there are five forms of men; they are stated in order as follows:
Haṃsa, Sāma, Aprarūcaka, Bhakta, and Mālāvyaka. ||20-21||
The *kūya* and *svastika* types are to be known as having the form of a ram, and likewise the *vṛttakara*.
The *vāmana* types are to be known as threefold: the *sapiṇḍa*, the *sthāna*, and the *padmaka*.
First, there are the *kūṣmāṇḍaka* and *karvaṭa* [types], which are horizontal.
The mayūra, kurvaṭa, and kāśa—these three types of kinnara exist. The vālakā, pauruṣī, vṛttā, and likewise the daṇḍakā;
these three are said by those learned in the science of painting to be of five kinds in total. ||23–24||

The elephant is of four kinds: the noble (bhadra), the dull (manda), the deer-like (mṛga), and the mixed (miśra). They say that from birth there are three types: those dwelling in fire, treasure, mountains, rivers, or the lap of the earth. The various chariot-horses come from Pārśva in the north.
The lions are of four kinds, known as Śikhara, Bila, Durga, and Tṛṇa.
Sixteen types of beasts of prey (vyāla) are specified: the deer, the vulture, the parrot, the cock, the lion, the tiger, the wolf, the goat, the rhinoceros, and the elephant. (26–27)
The horse, buffalo, dog, monkey, and donkey—
these are the mounts of these [deities] in the eastern, southern, southwestern,
and western directions; that which is said to be in the northwestern and northern directions was born here as the weapon.
Then the elephant, the boar, and the dog; the goat, the cow, the ram, and the jackal; the elephant, the sheep, and the four-faced one (Brahmā);
and the horse, the lion, the tiger, and the ram—these are the sixteen here. 29–30.
One who has performed the birth-rites.
Clad in white garments, pure, skillful, and free from desire for women or Śūdras,
one should begin this work in a place that is partitioned and enclosed.
The commencement of the worship of deities should take place under the asterism Rohiṇī or under the Uttaras.
Or let it be effective; the commencement of the construction is now prescribed.
One should make the face one part, and the neck three parts from the face.
This face is known to extend to the hairline, measuring twelve finger-breadths.
This [face] shall again be twelve finger-breadths in width;
the forehead shall be one-third of that, and the nose one-third [of the forehead];
the forehead shall be one-third [of the face], and the mouth shall be three times [the height of] the elevation.
The two eyes should be two finger-breadths in length and slightly more than half of that in width.
They should be well-established with the pupil occupying one-third of the eye.
Then, in the center of the pupil, one should fashion the light with one-third of the pupil's size.
One should fashion the two eyebrows, free from excessive hair, upon the eye-sockets;
the syllables of the mantra should be raised and properly inscribed.
In this manner, according to the prescribed rule, every variety of form should be applied in its entirety. ||37||
The authority [for this] has been stated as being "by way of the castes.
Having clearly understood all that has been said regarding the divisions such as the *divya* and others,
whoever paints this in many wonderful ways— [to him belongs the fruit].
The assembly of painters bestows preeminence.
Thus ends the seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Origin of Measurement," in the *Vāstuśāstra* named *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*, composed by the great emperor, the illustrious Bhojadeva.
Now begins the seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Images."
Now we shall describe the characteristics and the materials for images. Gold, silver, copper, wood, stone, clay, and painting—
these are the seven types of materials prescribed for icons according to one's capacity.
One should know that gold brings about nourishment, and silver increases fame.
Copper produces an increase in progeny, and lead brings the conquest of the earth. The substance known as *dāvarava* bestows longevity, while objects used for writing and painting bring wealth.
The wise student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī), having conquered his senses, should begin according to the prescribed rule,
subsisting on a restricted diet of sacrificial offerings (havirya), devoted to recitation and burnt offerings (japa-homa),
and lying upon the surface of the earth with a bed of kusha grass spread thereon.
When [the measurement] has not yet been reached, the space between the two [eyes] should be five eye-units (pañcākṣi).
The distance between the eyes and the ears should be five finger-breadths (aṅgula).
The ears should be known to be equal to the eyes in width, and twice as long as their height.
It should extend as far as the edge of the ear, with its middle part shaped like a *piṣpalya* or a *kakūṭa*.
It should be twice the length of an *ulaka* and have a width of one finger-breadth at the base of the *piṣpalya*.
It should be known to be free of hair and shaped like a drawn bow.
The measurement of these [muscles] extending even to the back of the ear is as follows:
from the upper attachment to the lower attachment situated at the root of the ear, it should be known as one and a half *golakas*; and the same measurement applies to the posterior part.
The *karṇapippalī* should be made with a shape resembling a grain of husked barley;
it should be one finger-breadth in length and four barley-corns in width.
Between the *pippalī* and the *ādhāta*, there is that which is designated as the letter *la*.
It should be one and a half finger-breadths in length and one finger-breadth in width;
in the middle, there should be a depressed mark (lakāra) measuring four barley-corns.
At the base of the pippalikā, the ear-opening should be four barley-corns in size.
That which is a globular, swelling heat is proclaimed as *stūtikā*;
it should be half a finger-breadth in length and two barley-corns in width.
Situated between the two *lakāra* spirals, it is proclaimed as *pīyuṣī*.
It is two fingers in length and slightly more than one finger in width. That outer line of the ear is called the *āvarta*;
it should be six fingers in measure, curved, and oval in shape.

The root portion should be made half a finger-breadth (ardhāṅgula), and it should gradually decrease to two barley-corns (yava) in the middle; at the tip, it is prescribed to be one barley-corn in width. The space between the two 'la'-curves is known as the *uddhāta*.
In the lower part, the width of the *pīyūṣī* is three barley grains.
From above, the width of the ear is two barley grains more than the globule (*golaka*).
In the middle, the stalk is double [the width]; at the base, its measure is six barley grains.
In the measurement of the whole assembly, it should extend two finger-breadths in length from the ear-attachment; it should be fashioned with a division of depression and elevation.
The rear stalk should be one finger-breadth, and the front should be half a finger-breadth.
One should fashion two parts upon the tender stalk, extending over a length of two kalās.
This is the division of the ear as it has been correctly described; it should be measured neither less nor more, for such is praised, while otherwise it is defective.

The chin is known to be two finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in length; half of that is the lower lip, and the upper lip should be half of that again. The nostril is half a finger-breadth in height, and the two nostrils together are known to occupy one-fourth of the portion of the lips.

The two ends of those [ears] should be made auspicious and equal to the *karavīra* flower; the corners of the mouth (*sṛkvaṇī*) are said to be equal to the distance between the pupils. The nose should be four finger-breadths in length according to measurement.
The width at the edge of the forehead is two finger-breadths;
its width is eight finger-breadths, and it is also half that in length. Thus, the forehead is described as being endowed with the proper proportions and qualities.
Starting from the chin up to the hairline at the back,
the measurement of the head up to the crown should be thirty-two finger-breadths;
the distance between the two ears, measured across the forehead, should be eighteen finger-breadths.
The circumference of the two necks is twenty-four [aṅgulas]. From the neck, there should be the region of the chest, and from the chest, the navel; both of these should each consist of two parts. 28.

nābhyā adhaḥ śarīrasya bhāgāḥ ṣoḍaśa eva ca | jaṅghāyāḥ parīṇāho daśaiva ca caturuttarāḥ ||29 jānunoścaiva piṇḍau dvau pratyekaṃ dvādaśāṅgulau | jaṅghāyāśca tathā pṛṣṭhaṃ caturviṃśatiraṅgulam ||30 jaṅghāyāśca tathā pṛṣṭhaṃ caturviṃśatiraṅgulam | jaṅghāyāśca tathā pṛṣṭhaṃ caturviṃśatiraṅgulam ||31 jaṅghāyāśca tathā pṛṣṭhaṃ caturviṃśatiraṅgulam | jaṅghāyāśca tathā pṛṣṭhaṃ caturviṃśatiraṅgulam ||51 jaṅghāyāśca tathā pṛṣṭhaṃ caturviṃśatiraṅgul
The two thighs are equal, as are the shanks; the two knees are four finger-breadths [in length].
The two feet are recorded as being fourteen finger-breadths in measurement from end to end;
they are six finger-breadths in width and four finger-breadths in height.
The circumference [of the handle] should be five finger-breadths, and its length three finger-breadths.
The forefinger (pradeśinī) should be equal in length to the thumb;
the middle finger should be less than that by one-sixteenth part.
One should know that the ring finger is shorter than the middle finger by one-eighth part;
the little finger is to be known as shorter than that [ring finger] by one-eighth part.
A wise man should make the nail of the thumb three-quarters of an *aṅgula*.
One should fashion the nails of the fingers to be five and three-eighths finger-breadths in length;
one should make the height of the fingers one finger-breadth, with the little finger being three parts less than that.
The forefinger (pradeśinī) is one finger-breadth in height, and the remaining fingers are diminished in sequence accordingly.
The circumference at the middle of the shank should be eighteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas).
The circumference at the middle of the knee is twenty-one finger-breadths;
one should know that the kneecap (jānukapālaka) is one-seventh of that [circumference]. ||35-36||
The circumference at the middle of the thighs should be thirty-two aṅgulas.
The testicles should be half a part [of the length] and the penis situated below the testicles.
The circumference of the scrotum should be six aṅgulas, while the sheath itself is four aṅgulas.
The waist should be eighteen finger-breadths in width;
half a finger-breadth should be the space between the breasts,
and the circumference at the middle of the navel should be forty-six finger-breadths.
The distance between the two breasts is known to be exactly twelve finger-breadths (aṅgulas).
Above the breasts, the ends of the armpits are six finger-breadths [apart].
From the height [of the shoulders], the width of the back is twenty-four [finger-breadths].
The circumference from the chest together with the back is proclaimed [to be thirty-two finger-breadths].
It is certain that the measurements are in finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) derived from these six limbs;
the width is twenty-four finger-breadths and eight finger-breadths.
The neck should be made, and the length of the arm forty-six finger-breadths (aṅgulas).
The upper joint of the arm should be made eighteen finger-breadths;
the second joint is said to be exactly sixteen finger-breadths.
The circumference at the middle of the forearm should be eighteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas). The circumference of the wrist, however, is twelve finger-breadths;
its length, including the palm, is also declared to be twelve finger-breadths. ||44-45||
Devoid of finger-joints, it is declared by the wise to be seven fingers long;
it should be five fingers wide and marked with the characteristics of lines.
The middle finger should be made five fingers in measurement.
One should know that the middle finger is shorter than half a joint of the index finger;
the ring finger should be equal in length to the index finger;
and the little finger should be less by half a joint in its measurement.
The nails of all the fingers should be made equal to half a joint; their circumference is said to be equal to their length. The length of the thumb should be four finger-breadths.
The circumference [of the thumb] should be five finger-breadths (pañcāṅgula) and clearly marked with beautiful barley-grain lines;
the nails are considered to be slightly less than the height of the phalanges.
The space between the thumb and the forefinger should be two finger-breadths (dvyaṅgula).
For women as well, this same principle applies, though with a predominance of the breasts, thighs, and hips:
three, four, four, three, and four;
or eleven, eleven, and twenty-three, distributed across ten parts.
Twenty-three [palas] is proclaimed as the measurement for women; this is the smallest measurement. The medium measurement is eight [palas] plus one-third.
The best measurement is proclaimed to be eight and a half palas.
The width of their chest should be eighteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas),
and the width of the hips should be made twenty-four;
this is declared to be the measurement for images in brief.
