This measurement for all the limbs has been specified in due order;
it should always be performed by artisans on images produced from appropriate materials using golden rays [or golden proportions].
Thus ends the seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Images," in the *Vāstuśāstra* named *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*, composed by the great king of kings, the illustrious Bhojadeva.
Now begins the seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Forms, Weapons, and Equipment of the Gods and Others.
We shall now describe the forms and weapons of the thirty gods,
as well as those of the Daityas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas.
For the Vidyādharas and Piśācas— each according to their respective [class]—
one should fashion [the deity] with great brilliance, resembling the flame of the fire of Brahmā;
with stout limbs, white flowers, and wrapped in a white turban.
He should have a black antelope skin as an upper garment and white clothing, and be four-faced;
a staff and a water-pot should be placed in his two left hands;
likewise, he should hold a rosary and be girded with a belt of muñja grass.
One should increase the welfare of the world with one's right hand;
when this is done, security prevails everywhere in the world.
There is no doubt that the interests of the Brahmins will flourish through all their desires.
When the *kṛsodarī* belongs to those such as the Virūpas,
or when it is produced by Brahmins among the castes, it is not desired as it brings fear;
being fierce, it destroys the performer, and being of wretched form, it destroys the artisan.
A slender woman always brings about disease and destruction for the one who causes her to be made;
a woman with a sunken belly brings famine, while a deformed woman brings childlessness.
Having avoided these defects, she should be made very beautiful.
Or by means of a mantra of Brahmā, she was established in her first youth by those who know the ritual procedures.
Śambhu, the glorious one with a matted lock marked by the moon, the blue-throated one, well-restrained,
wearing a variegated crown, possesses a radiance equal to the moon.
Endowed with two, four, or eight arms,
holding a battle-axe in his hand and clad in a serpent-skin,
he is complete with all auspicious marks and adorned with three eyes.
Where Hara, the Lord of the World, endowed with such qualities as these resides, there shall be supreme prosperity for both the country and the king;
even if Maheśvara is established in a forest or on level ground. ||12-13||
In this manner, the image of the Maker (Viśvakarman) should then be fashioned as a bringer of auspiciousness:
it may have eighteen arms, or be endowed with twenty,
or perhaps a hundred arms, or even a thousand arms.
Fierce in form, surrounded by his hosts, with a lion’s skin as his upper garment;
with sharp-pointed fangs for teeth, adorned with a garland of heads;
his head marked by the moon, glorious, broad-chested, and of formidable appearance. ||15-16||

Maheśvara, residing in a cremation ground, should be fashioned with two arms; however, in a royal capital, he should have four arms. But when situated in the midst of a cremation ground or a forest, he should be made with twenty arms. (17)
O auspicious one, although the Blessed One is one, he is conceptualized through the differentiation of various abodes;
when performed by the wise, he may possess both a fierce and a gentle nature.
Just as the sun, though appearing gentle, rises as it does [with its various aspects], so too is the Blessed One.
Just as that very same sun becomes fierce when it has reached the meridian,
so too Śaṅkara, while constantly dwelling in the forest, is terrible;
yet when he abides in a gentle place, he remains established in gentleness.

Having learned all these locations, Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, should be propitiated by the Kimpuruṣas and others together with the Pramathas. Thus has the layout of the enemy of Tripura been correctly described.
Now the iconographic form of Kārttikeya is described:
resembling the rising sun, clad in red garments, and possessing the brilliance of fire;
having the appearance of a young boy, he is lovely, auspicious, and pleasing to behold.
With a serene countenance, glorious, radiant, majestic, and auspicious;
especially adorned with pearls and gems, and decorated with various jewels;
having either six faces or a single face, he bore a resplendent spear.
In a city, he should have twelve arms; in a village, he should have six arms;
and in a hamlet, he should be made with two arms by one desiring auspiciousness.
[His weapons are] the spear, the arrow, the sword, the mace, and the mallet.
One should display these weapons in his right hands.
One hand is extended, and the other is proclaimed as the sixth;
likewise, there are the four banners, the bell, the shield, and the cock.
In his left hands, the sixth is the one that destroys old age;
thus equipped with these weapons, he is ordained to stand in the midst of battle.
He should be fashioned as imperishable, yet endowed with playful sport.
Accompanied by goats and chickens, joined by peacocks, and enchanting to behold— Skanda should always be worshipped in cities by those desiring victory over enemies;
however, in a village, the six-faced one, radiant as fire, should be installed.
Likewise, he should be depicted with sharp weapons and adorned with garlands;
even in a village [form], he should be made two-armed, endowed with beauty and radiance.
His southern hand should be in the gesture of giving (varada), and in his [other] hand there should be a cock.
A very large and exceedingly beautiful image with variegated wings should be made.
In this manner, whether in a city, a small town, or a village,
the preceptor who is skilled in the scriptures should fashion the auspicious Kārttikeya.
In a village or excellent city where the planets are not in conflict,
one should diligently cause this temple of Kārttikeya to be built. There, the child-like deity, possessed of beautiful arms, glorious, and of great splendor, stands upon his banner.

His chest should be adorned with a forest garland (vanamālā), and his radiance should be equal to that of the moon. Holding a plow and a mace, he should be depicted as intensely intoxicated by divine joy.
He has four arms, a gentle face, and is clothed in blue garments. ||36-37||
The majestic forest deity should be depicted with hair adorned by a crown, embellished with passion,
and accompanied by Revatī.
Viṣṇu should resemble lapis lazuli, be clothed in yellow garments, and be graced by Śrī.
Varāha, Vāmana, and the terrifying Narasiṃha should be depicted;
or else Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, and the heroic son of Jamadagni.
He, the subduer of enemies, may have two arms, eight arms, or even four arms. ||39-40||

The omnipresent Lord, holding a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, powerful and endowed with splendor, should be fashioned in various forms after one has understood the specific requirements of the task.
Thus has Viṣṇu been described; let him be saluted by the gods and the immortals.
The lord of the thirty-three gods, thousand-eyed, wielding the thunderbolt with his strong arms, powerful, wearing a diadem, armed with a mace, glorious, clad in white garments,
and adorned with a great girdle and divine ornaments. ||42-43||
He should be appointed as one endowed with royal splendor and accompanied by a domestic priest;
he is to be known as Vaivasvata, the ultimate refuge of Kāla and Keśin.
Resplendent with brilliance like the sun, he is adorned with gold.
With a face like the full moon, dressed in yellow garments, and possessing auspicious eyes;
he should be depicted with a variegated crown and adorned with excellent armlets.
Resplendent with a brilliance equal to the sun, he should be made powerful and auspicious.
Dhanvantari, Bharadvāja, and likewise the Prajāpatis, as well as those for Dakṣa’s purpose, should be made similar; their forms should also be fashioned.
Arciṣmān and Jvalana should be made, whose throat is the wind of the horse.
Likewise, the embodied forms of Viṣṇu and Rudra should be made gentle.
All the Rākṣasas should be depicted wearing red garments, black in color, adorned with various ornaments, and equipped with many weapons. ||48-49||
With a face like the full moon, fair-complexioned, with lips like the *bimba* fruit and a beautiful smile,
she was lovely, wearing white garments and adorned with divine ornaments; she was radiant,
her left hand resting upon her hip.
Śrī, with a pure smile, should be depicted in her first youth, holding a lotus in her outstretched right hand; she has a serene face and holds a trident,
a club, a sword, a battle-axe, and a banner in her [other] hands.
Holding in her hand a light sword accompanied by a shield,
and bearing a single golden bell,
the terrible Kauśikī was clothed in yellow silk and mounted upon a lion.
Eight [deities] should be fashioned, wearing white garments, shining with crowns adorned with various jewels;
the two Aśvins, who bestow auspiciousness upon the world, should be made identical [to them]. ||54–55||
Wearing white garlands and garments, adorned with gold,
they possess the dark-blue luster of a swarm of bees;
some have the hue of lapis lazuli or bell-metal, and their beards are green.

The Piśācas and Bhūtas should be depicted as red, deformed, with blood-red eyes, and possessing many forms; their hair is entwined with serpents, and they wear garments and ornaments of various colors; they are harsh and speakers of untruth. ||57-58||
They should be fashioned as having many kinds of gentle laughter, being deformed with distorted faces, possessing terrible forms,
short, and variously colored;
they should be fearsome with most terrifying strides, formidable, and wearing sacred threads.
The wise should always fashion the spirits with armor and variegated garments;
even those [spirits] not mentioned here should be fashioned according to their specific requirements.
Whatever the characteristic mark of each particular asura or deva may be, [that should be provided].
Whether it be between a yakṣa and a rākṣasa, or even between various gandharvas,
he should be identified by that characteristic by one who understands correctly;
for generally, the dānavas are powerful and performers of cruel deeds.
And the Kirātins should be made with various weapons in their hands;
the Daityas should be made slightly smaller than them even in their qualities,
while the Yakṣas, inferior to the Daityas, should be made fierce with intoxication.
The Gandharvas are inferior even to them; the Pannagas are inferior to the Gandharvas; the Rākṣasas, who are prone to cruel transformations and wickedness, are inferior to the Nāgas;
and the Vidyādharas are known to possess bodies inferior to those of the Yakṣas.
Wearing variegated garlands and garments, with colorful shields and swords in their hands, these hosts of beings were terrible and fearsome, wearing various costumes;
they were more massive than Piśācas and likewise harsh in their splendor. ||66-67||
One should generally fashion them auspiciously, with proportions neither deficient nor excessive;
they should be endowed with divine seats and ornaments, and one should execute them exactly as described. 68.

Thus ends the seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Forms and Weapon-Combinations of Deities and Others," in the treatise on architecture named *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*, composed by the great king of kings, the illustrious Bhojadeva.
Now begins the seventy-eighth chapter, titled "The Determination of Faults and Virtues.
Now we shall describe the forms that are to be avoided in rites such as the installation of images.
As it has been said by those who know the truth of the treatises and who seek the welfare of cows and Brahmins:
"Even if it is produced by an artisan ignorant of the treatises and is thus fraught with defects, that which is endowed with sweetness should be accepted by those who know the scriptures. (1-2)
One with joints that do not meet, one who is disoriented, one who is crooked, and likewise one who is bent;
one who is unstable, one who is protruding, and likewise one with legs like those of a crow;
one deficient in limbs, one who is misshapen, and likewise one whose waist is sunken and knotted.
A wise man should certainly not have such a deity made for the sake of his welfare.
One should know that a deity with an unjoined neck-joint (sandhi) portends death; with a crooked one, confusion of place;
with a bent one, quarrel; and with a downward-facing one, the loss of life.
One should predict the loss of wealth for men by a [line] that is constantly unstable;
one should know fear and heart disease without doubt from a raised [line];
and constant travel to foreign lands is indicated by a crow's leg-shaped line.
If she is constantly deficient in some limb, the husband will remain childless.
From one with a deformed appearance, terrible danger is to be known;
likewise, from one with a downward face, there will be disease of the head.
One should diligently avoid an image endowed with these defects;

now we shall describe an image that is possessed of other defects as well. An image with a protruding base (piṇḍikā) brings suffering to its master. An image with a sword-like [sharp] edge brings suffering to its master.
If [the image] is situated in the belly, there will be widespread famine; if it is worshipped by hunchbacks, men will suffer from diseases.
If it is devoid of arms, it portends evil for the kingdom.
By means of the hall-seat, one gains a place; and by means of the female image, women [will prosper].
If the seat lacks a base, there will be bondage and displacement from one's position.
That which is joined with various kinds of wood, or that which is made of iron,
or that whose joints are not firmly secured, shall bring about fear of misfortune.
"Or perhaps with lead drawn by a magnet;
likewise, those conversant with the scriptures have declared that the joints of the image must be made of hard wood.
Furthermore, the joints should be joined very firmly by one who desires the prosperity [of the work]. (13-14)
One should bind it with copper, iron, gold, or silver, according to the procedure seen in the scriptures and by means of worship;
otherwise, it will cause disease and distress through the power of curses and *sāman* chants.
Therefore, with every effort, the master-architect (sthapati), well-versed in the scriptures,
should fashion the image according to the rules, well-proportioned and according to the prescribed measurements—
neither damaged, nor flawed, nor deficient. ||16-17||
It was not deficient in its limbs, nor lacking in its nose, feet, nails, and so forth;
it was well-proportioned, possessed of the proper height, with a serene face and auspicious appearance;
its joints and articulations were well-concealed, and it stood straight with even proportions.
For such [deities], one should offer this arghya, endowed with the proper measure and qualities.

(19) In brief, men whose limbs are well-developed with flesh, who possess the characteristics of the prescribed measurements, and who are adorned with garments and jewels, [attain these results]. (20)
Having conceived the virtues of patience and having discarded the multitude of faults, one should cultivate the aforementioned virtues with a mind free from pride.
Others, having become his disciples, worship him in various ways;
and craftsmen and those seeking renown praise him repeatedly.
Thus ends the seventy-eighth chapter, titled "The Chapter on Faults and Virtues," in the *Vāstuśāstra* named *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*, composed by the illustrious Bhojadeva, the Emperor of Emperors.
Now begins the seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Positions such as the Straight-Arrived" (ṛjvāgatādi).
Hereafter, I shall explain the sequence of rules for the positions of the *nevi* (the dancer's body);
for nine movements (*vṛtti*) arise from the *saṃpāti* and *ārūḍha* [techniques].
For them, the first [breath] is situated in the forehead; above that, it becomes situated in the throat;
then one should know the one situated in the heart; immediately after that is the one and a half eyes.
Those four, beginning with the one situated in the upper part, are the ones that have turned back.
Straight-approach and turn-back, then half-straight-approach and so forth;
the Śacīkṛta and turn-back, then preceded by the adhyardhākṣa;
and the ninth position, the pārśvāgata, which has the form of a wall-breaker.
Between the straight (ṛju) and the half-straight (ardharju) [channels], there are four intermediate ones;
and between the half-straight and the curved (sācīkṛta), there are three intermediate ones.
Between the two-and-a-half-straight (dvyardhārju) and the curved, there are two other intermediate ones.
Beyond that, there is one intermediate space with two and a half *kṣapa*s on its side, and another intermediate space for the *vyantara* [deities].

(6) There are ten intermediate spaces between those that have come straight, those that have turned back, and those that have approached from the side; there are also other locations for the *vyantara* [deities]. (7)
Having considered the straight, the middle, and the contracted [gazes]—the straight gaze has the remaining [gazes] as its future internal expenditures:
the half-cornered, the half-closed, and the half-of-a-half-closed. 8.1–2ab.
In the half-ardha-aṃśa as well, the *silīdavyantara* and *vyaya* are said [to be located];
then follows the *ardhasācīkṛta* and the *svastika*.
In the two *sācīkṛta* portions, the two aṃśas known as *dvyardhākṣa* are stated.
Those two, the *dvyardhākṣāṃśaparāvṛtta* and the *dvyardhākṣāṃsa*,
are declared by those expert in the various treatises to be located at the interval of two and a half akṣas within the *dvijvākṣa*.
Just as they have been described by name according to their positions at intervals of one and a half akṣas from the *ṛjvāgata*.
Likewise, when [the breath] has turned back, there would be the intermediate ones in their respective order.
The wise know that there is no variety on the wall; thus, they understand the variety of the painting.
In this way, by the path of differentiation, there are twenty-nine places.
A distance of one cubit (vaitasti) should be established between the feet, well-supported;
when the chin and the feet are both firmly placed upon the ground,
it is called "straight-approached" (ṛjvāgata), as previously described and defined by its measurement.
Then, one should observe this measurement for that which has come to the half-arch:
the Brahma-thread must be made passing through the very middle of the face; with the horizontal palm-span being equal to the line of the eyes, the face shall be formed. 15–16.
There should be a reduction of one-quarter of an aṅgula for the outer corner of the eye (apāṅga), the socket of the eye (akṣikūṭa), and the ear;
elsewhere, the measurement of the ear should be increased by half an aṅgula.
On the line of the eyes (dṛksūtra), there should be a space of one kalā from the Brahma-line (brahmalekhā).
The eye should be moistened with a drop of tears the size of a *yava*, and the other [parts] should likewise be reduced.

The white portion (*śvetabhāga*) should consist of three *yavas* according to the stated measurement, and the pupil (*tārā*) is also declared by that measure; the width of the white portion and the *karavīra* [portion] are also as previously stated.
The *parabhā* should be a *karavīra* flower's breadth from the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*), and likewise one finger-breadth from the *pūrvabhā*.
From the *karavīra* of the *pūrvabhā*, the junction (*saṅgama*) should be one finger-breadth;
the distance between the ear and the corner of the eye is said to be one and a half finger-breadths plus a *kalā*.
One should describe the supreme [measurement] as being without deviation in all directions from the eastern point.
From the Brahma-thread, the *puṭa* shall be one *aṅgula*, and from the cheek it shall be two *aṅgulas*.
In the east and elsewhere, the *puṭa* shall be half a *mātrā*; the remainder is as previously stated.
The distance from the outer edge [of the face] to the inner corner [of the eye] shall be one finger (aṅgula) plus two barley-corns (yava).
On the outer edge of the lower lip, six barley-corns are prescribed.
From the end of the lower lip, one digit (kalā) is the cheek; from the Brahma-thread (brahmasūtra), the jaw (hanu) extends further.
On the outer edge, there should be one and a half finger-breadths, and from that, a line for the face measuring one finger-breadth.
Whatever is to be executed on the raised surface must be carefully performed according to the instructions for the facial features and the surrounding lines. ||24-25||
When another thread is drawn from the middle of the foot upwards, the fourth part at the knee is to be omitted;
it does not increase beyond the previous measurement.
At the rear portion, the armpit-support (kakṣādhara) consists of five *golaka*s according to the thread-measurement.
One should know that the front portion is three [units] in measure according to the six globes (ṣaḍgola).
From the central thread, the side lines extend four units up to the jaw;
from the central thread of the chest, the armpit line occurs at nine units.

From that *dgaṃtalekhā*, you should fashion three parts for the breasts; one part for the sides, and either one part for the breast or a circular mandala for the breast. Beyond that, the hand (*hastaka*) should be fashioned according to the requirements of the ritual action.
All parts up to the sides should be adorned with six lotuses (30).
Likewise, the arrangement of the front hand should be fashioned according to the requirements; the ritual actions for the *abhaya* [mudrā] and others should be performed with the right hand (31).
In the middle, a line of six finger-breadths shall be outside the outer thread;
from the outer line on the eastern side, there should be a middle [line] of eight units.
On the other part at the region of the navel, that outer [line] shall be seven units.

The navel should be one *kalā* in measure; nine finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) from that [navel] toward the front, on the rear part, is the waist (*kaṭi*), measuring seven *mātrās* behind and ten toward the front.
The line of the thighs is in the middle of the measurement of the face, on the rear part. (33–34)
The outer line of the front portion [should be] from the knee of the rear [figure];
likewise, from the Indra-line and the Vāsta-line of the rear portion,
at an interval of one finger-breadth, there should be a line for the front of the *nalaka*.

The sixth parts of the rear section are the lines; two fingers ahead [of that], a ground-line for the other foot is established by the *nala* [measure]. Then, the big toe is one finger below, and the heel is half a finger above that. (36–37)
The tip of the thumb is five *mātrās* beyond the *brahmasūtra*;

its surface is recorded by those who know the supreme portion as being five finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) across. With the three *kalās* of the thumb-tip, there should be a span of three finger-breadths at the base of the palm.
All the fingers should extend from the thumb in successive order.
Due to the arrangement and the cloth, it measures two finger-breadths [from the thumb], while nine finger-breadths [extend] from the second finger.
As previously stated, the knee should first be four finger-breadths from the sūtra.
In the same manner, his two ankles (nalaka) are three finger-breadths apart from the thread;
the ankle-joint (akṣa) is three kalās [from the thread], while the big toe is three finger-breadths [from the joint].
The front big toe should extend one kalā below the ground-thread.
The thumb and the fingers, as well as everything else, are as previously described.
One should determine the measurements according to the stated proportions, taking into account the visible side-surface and the width of the middle surface, and assign them through proper reasoning.
This position, known as *ardharjvāgata*, is declared to be the most excellent.
Now, the characteristic mark of the *sācīkṛta* posture is described:
one should lay down the *brahmasūtra* for the sake of achieving the understanding of the previously mentioned postures.
The forehead should be at the rear portion, and likewise the line of hair (keśalekhā) should be a small fraction [of its length].
The line of the eyebrows is declared to be half [the length] of the rear portion.
The blackness (kālikā) of the eye-line is known to extend across two [parts]. 45–46.
In the upper portion of the light, a star is visible measuring one barley-corn (yava);
from that light, the star extends for two barley-corns.
Then there is the white Karavīra [star], according to the measurements previously stated.

One should know that the *kanīlikā* is the space between the root of the nose and the [outer corner of the eye], measuring one barleycorn (*yava*). From the measure of the root of the nose, the two upward-pointing globes (*golaka*) of the eyes should be known to be located three barleycorns from the *brahmasūtra* on the anterior side. 48–49.
One should know the outer corner of the eye (āpāṅga) to be at a distance of two golakas from the pupil;
from that point, the end of the ear is one part further away,
and the ear should be wide by two yavas less than one kalā, increased by the turning of the eye.
The whiteness of the first [cheek] together with the *karavīra* flower is three *yava*s;
the second [cheek’s] whiteness is said by the prescribed measurement to be one *dṛktārā* (pupil) and one *prasṛti*.
Beyond that, the line of the cheek (*kapolalekhā*) should be two *yava*s or one *kalā*.

From the Brahma-sūtra to the tip of the nose is seven barley-corns (yavas) in the upper part; the nostril on the front side should be one finger (aṅgula) plus a barley-corn. On the front side, the gojī is prescribed at the edge there to be one barley-corn.
The upper lip should have a superior portion and measure half a mātrā;
the lower lip should be three yavas in length, and the remainder is the reduction between the two.
A thread should be placed in the middle of the pālī, and the chin is beyond the pālī.
The line extending to the jaw should be half an aṅgula from the [central] thread;
the thread passing through the middle of the jaw should be circular on the other side,
clearly defined by a single thread reaching to the edge of the outer eye.
The lower lip should be above the chin, at the midpoint of the line extending to the edge of the mouth.
A skilled artist should create the sense of depth using these lines;
from there, at a distance of one finger-breadth above the thread-line, the neck is drawn as previously described. ||57-58||
Due to the connection with the thread, there is one finger-breadth (aṅgula) including a barley-corn (sayava) in the front;
the well-established [line] should be one and a half finger-breadths from the thread in the front.
Indeed, the outer line is eight finger-breadths beyond that thread.
The *tāla* is known as that which extends from the neck of the barley-grain (*yavonagrīvā*) to the neckless point (*nagrīvā*), while the *sūna* and *dūrvaka* are likewise defined [by these measures].
(60) Starting from the line of the *hikkā*, the portion up to the chest constitutes the *agrika*;
they say the *tara* is of that same measure, and one should indicate [the subsequent parts] starting from that point. (61)
Beyond the portion of the *hikkā-sūtra*, at a distance of five fingers, the breast should be marked;
a line indicating its end should be made, and the circle [of the nipple] should be one and a half fingers.
Immediately following that, one should specify the outer portion alone.
Starting from the *hikkāsūtra*, the breast is six *aṅgulas* in front;
at six *aṅgulas* from the breast, the eye is placed transversely, measuring two parts each.
Two *kalās* below the armpit, the outer line is prescribed.
The inner line is five finger-breadths from the breast;
within that space on the palm, they know the middle portion to be one part from the Brahma-sūtra.
From the middle, a further part of two kalās is divided transversely toward the other side.
The middle margin in the eastern part should be ten finger-breadths from the thread;
the region of the navel should extend transversely beyond the Brahma-thread by four fingers increased by four barley-corns. ||66-67||
That same [line], previously specified as eleven finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in length,
proceeds through the middle of the other thigh; the cord, resting within the navel,
extends from this [point] on the back side toward the front by one kalā.

From the lower part of the knee, by half a kalā and three yavas, [one reaches] the middle of the shank; from there, the line of the nalaka is attached. At its end is the vairava, and beyond that, a cord is desired at a distance of four [units]. ||69-70||
Following this very sequence, the outer lines are prescribed:
on the portion beyond the Brahma-sūtra, at a distance of five finger-breadths, is the hip;
that [line] is one span (āla) in width, and the tip of the penis is joined with the thread at its front.
From the cord,
at the base of the other thigh, there is a line two units (kalās) from the middle of the cord;
likewise, the base of the first thigh shall be one unit to the east of the cord.
The line of the front part should be understood by the knower as two kalās;
the knee is one and a half aṅgulas and a yava, and its side is half an aṅgula. By means of a cord, the central line of the foot is divided.
In the drawing of the beginning, middle, and end, the purification of the thread is proclaimed.
[75] From the thread, the front portion is at the mark; the end is five finger-breadths [away].
A reduction of half a finger-breadth should be made for the posterior parts of the thighs and shanks. [76]
The thread passing through the middle of the outer eye is established as extending down to the ground;
it is prescribed to be one finger-breadth forward from the edge of the outer foot.
From that thread, the sole of the front foot should be eight finger-breadths away.
On the undersides of the two soles, there should be a subtle line eighteen finger-breadths long.
From the thumb, the forefinger is successively longer by one finger-breadth.
The [lines] on the other sole are situated as before, beginning from the base of the thumb.
As stated in the Sūtra, that [line] is proclaimed as the "ground-line" (bhūmirekhā).
From the sūtra, at a distance of half a finger-breadth upwards, one should place the heel of the subsequent foot;
from the big toe, the fingers should fall [in such a way] according to the sequence of the preceding foot.
One should bend the *pradeśinī* (index finger) here from its position as an *upapradeśinī*;
then, one should gradually withdraw all the other fingers.
Thus has this posture, called *sācīkṛta*, been described according to its true nature.
Now they describe the position of the *adhyardhākṣa*;
having fixed the Brahma-thread at its starting point, the measurement is prescribed as follows:
from the thread, the hairline should be one *mātrā* plus a *yava*.
The Bhadra type has a broad chest, broad hips, rounded arms, and is well-proportioned;
he is naturally handsome with a round face.
The head of the Mālavya type should be three finger-breadths in measurement.
The forehead, the nose, the mouth, and the neck are each four mātrās in measure;
I shall state that the chest, the space between the navel and the genitals, and the abdomen are twelve mātrās.
The thighs are eighteen aṅgulas, and the shanks are likewise the same.
The two knees are four finger-breadths [apart]; the distance between the knees is four finger-breadths.
This total length of Mālavya is considered to be ninety-six finger-breadths;
his chest width is recorded as twenty-six measures.
The arms are sixteen mātras in length, and the forearms are likewise;
the two heels are twelve mātras, and this is the measurement for the Mālavas here.
He has muscular shoulders, long arms, a broad chest, and a slender waist.
The Mālava man is one whose thighs, hips, and shanks are well-rounded; he is the best among men. They say the face of a swan has broad cheeks, while that of a hare is thin and long.
The width and length of the *bhavaka* should be equal;
it should be well-rounded, auspicious, and curved here.
For the *mālāva* position, an application of lovely ointment should be used.
But embodied beings are endowed with various forms; they are possessed of all qualities through their actions.
That person who is measured as being "scattered" (kīrṇa) is indeed difficult to find; thus ends the sixth [chapter].
A woman whose neck veins are not visible due to a fleshy body, and whose limbs are well-fleshed and well-proportioned, is considered "Round" (vṛttā).
She who has a broad face, short hips, a short neck, and a large belly [is considered "Square"]. 94.

A woman who is like a *kāṇḍaka* plant in her masculine traits is considered to possess a masculine nature (*pauruṣī*). She whose body, head, and neck are small, whose limbs are light, and who is thin with little Brahmanic essence, is known as a *bālakī* woman. ||95-96||

A girl who has reached puberty while still in her childhood state due to contact with a male is called a *bālakī* by those expert in the characteristics of women. [97] The lines on the earth [of the palm] should measure one barleycorn in width and be as thin as a slender barleycorn in length.
Within this water-line, one should draw a semi-circle for the pupil;
its whiteness should be four barley-corns wide, and the remainder is the visible sclera.
Beyond that, the line of the eye-corner (kapota-rekhā) should be one finger-width minus one barley-corn.
The end of the thread at the front edge of the cloth should be half an *aṅgula* away [from the previous mark];
the end of the nose should be one *aṅgula* from the thread; and beyond that, the outer corner of the eye (*pāṅgula*) should be one *aṅgula*.
At the base, the nostril is with its margin; the thread goes through the middle of the "cow's bow" (*gojyā*).
The *gojī* (the upper lip of the following letter) should be half a *yava*;
it should be understood as measuring two *yavas* starting from the *brahmasūtra*. However, the line below the nose of the following letter should be half a finger-breadth (*ardhāṅgula*). ||101–102||
The measurement for the lower lip at its outer edge is considered to be one barley-corn (*yava*).
A thread is fixed at the center of the line extending to the jaw.
To the east of that thread, there should be a *karavīra* [mark] measuring two fingers minus two barley-corns.

That [mark] should be seen as half a barley-corn in length, and its whiteness should then be one and a half barley-corns. A star-like mark (tārā) is to be known as three barley-corns; the rest is according to the measurements already mentioned.
It is measured by the middle portion of the ear, located below the ear-convolution (karṇāvarta).

The width of the ear should be two finger-breadths, and from the ear-convolution (karṇāvarta), the line of the back of the head should be four barley-corns [in distance]; having understood this, one should act as prescribed.
One finger-breadth outside the ear-line, the neck should be fashioned.
The throat and the neck-joint are one finger-breadth beyond the *sūtra*;
likewise, the fleshy line (*aṃsalekhā*) is one finger-breadth above the *hikkāsūtra*.
The shoulder (*aṃsa*) is located two finger-breadths beyond the *brahmasūtra*.
The chest measures one finger-breadth from the Brahma-sūtra; there is no interval [between them].
At the mere distance of one part from the Kaksha-sūtra, the front of the breast occurs.
From the armpit, extending for three kalās, the line of the side (pārśvalekhā) is prescribed.
In front of that [central point], at a distance of eleven finger-breadths from the tip, there should be a thread for the middle of the palace according to the [prescribed] ritual procedure.
From that thread, the center of the rear section should be three finger-breadths away. ||110-111||
One finger-breadth beyond that, according to the measurement of the thread, the navel is desired;
the line of the abdomen should be known to be three finger-breadths from the navel.
The hips and ears should be at the navel, and the mouth should be increased by half a finger-breadth.
From the Brahma-sūtra, the hip is three parts [to the east] and three finger-breadths [to the west].
The penis-base (meḍhra) should be situated below and to the west of the Brahma-sūtra.
The previously mentioned middle line (madhya-rekhā) should be at an interval of one finger-breadth from that sūtra toward the west.
The root-line of that very [figure] is two finger-breadths (aṅgula) from the thread toward the front;
the root-line of the other thigh shall be two finger-breadths from the thread.
On the portion at the end of the knee, the upper line of the end is from the knee.
The two lines belonging to the outer portion of the thread are correctly established;
the line reaching the middle of the knee should rest upon the outer line.
The knee should measure one and a half mātras, and the lower line of that [knee] is as follows.
That [mark] is prescribed at half a finger-breadth (ardhāṅgula) from the thread toward the front;
beyond the thread, the tip of the big toe is one and three-quarter fingers (pādona-dvyaṅgula) from the base.
From the base, the tip of the big toe shall be three and a half fingers (sārdha-traya-aṅgula).

Beyond the sūtra, on the four-finger-width mark of the lower leg (jaṅghā), there should be a line; on the two-finger-width mark of that same lower leg, there should be a line for the front of the knee (pūrvajānu). One should measure one kalā for the front of the knee and execute the remainder as previously described.
The pillar that is firmly established horizontally upon the soles of the other two feet should extend upward from the eastern section by one and a half *kalās*.
The eastern bend is desired at the base of the big toe; there, the little finger is not its own.
A mere fraction [of the distance] from one's own thumb reaches the vertical plumb-line;
that which reaches the vertical plumb-line arising from the tip of the opposite finger,
and that which reaches the vertical plumb-line arising from the base of the opposite thumb.
That [position] consists of the connection of the big toe with the front part of the middle [foot];
one should place it three finger-breadths above the front of the heel.
The front foot is turned away from the other foot, which is behind the heel. (123–124)
One should draw the position according to the scripture with one and a half akṣas;
then the fifth position, situated on the side, is described as the name-position (nāmasthāna).
At the end of the turned face, the Brahma-thread (brahmasūtra) is prescribed.

One should show the external line of the forehead as touched by the string. From the string, the bridge of the nose extends two *akṣas* downward; the outer corner of the eye is two *kalās* from the string, and the ear is one and a half *aṃśas* and two *kalās*.
The ear is two finger-breadths in width, and from there, the back of the head is one kalā.
Then, one should establish a thread through its center; this represents half the mouth.
From that thread, the chin is one finger-breadth away, and the middle of the jaw is four yavas.
Then, at one and a half finger-breadths [from the center], the neck is curved at one finger-breadth;

then, at one finger-breadth from that, the *hikkā* [is located]; and at four [finger-breadths] from the *brahmasūtra*, the thread extends to the edge of the ear-lobes on the head—that is what is called the *sūtra*.
The middle line is said to be at the neck, measured by the middle finger.
At one *bhāga* from the middle line of the *hikkā*, the base of the stalk (*daṇḍamūla*) is located;
at two *kalās* and eight *mātrās*, the back [is situated], and the heart-line (*hṛllekhā*) is exactly the same.
From that, the circle of the breast is prescribed by means of one finger-breadth (aṅgula).
The armpit on the front side shall be five fingers from the thread;
on the other side, the armpit is prescribed at three measures (mātrā). ||132-133||
The wise say that the middle portion between the two ends is eight finger-breadths;
from the central line, the edge is ten finger-breadths away.
The back of the middle portion should be four [finger-breadths] and the back of the navel five.

The line within the navel is nine [aṅgulas]; the hip and back are known to be three kalās; the line at the edge of the abdomen is ten aṅgulas. From the [central] thread, the middle of the buttocks is said to be eight aṅgulas from the side.
The bladder-head is nine finger-breadths [from the perineum]; the end of the buttocks is eight finger-breadths;
the base of the penis is eight finger-breadths; the middle of the thigh is seven finger-breadths;
and the root of the side of the thigh is said to be five finger-breadths.
The middle of the hand is four and a half finger-breadths from behind;

they say that very same middle of the hand is five and a half finger-breadths from the front. The middle [of the hand] is prescribed at the center of the thread between the fingers of the middle of the hand.
The middle line should be at the midpoint of the thigh; from the knee, there should be a division and a line.
On both sides, there should be a line, and it is said that the shank is in the middle.
The shank is six finger-breadths [in length], and the line for the nalaka (ankle) should be in the middle.
On both sides, a nalaka (rein) two fingers wide should be made.
The heel is prescribed at four fingers from the central line;
likewise, the sole of the foot should be according to the stated measurement in finger-breadths. ||141-142||
This position, known as *bhittika*, is said to be one where [the hand] comes from the side.
This is the *pārśvāgata* position.
Henceforth, we shall describe the positions for turning back (parāvṛtta-sthānaka).
First, the straight-turned-back (ṛjvāgata-parāvṛtta) is described; in that position, two finger-breadths should be placed separately at each ear. 143–144.
The middle between the two heels should likewise be seven finger-breadths;
the two heels should each be made three and a half finger-breadths wide. One should display the four fingers—the little, ring, middle, and index fingers.
One should draw [the lines] between the thumb, the ring finger, the middle finger, and the little finger.
This remaining part should be indicated as turned back, while the rest should be described as proceeding straight.
Regarding those positions starting from one and a half akṣas and so forth, whatever [is to be done] in them—
Whatever belongs to one becomes his by virtue of that [transformation].
For whatever is visible to someone is said to be a limb of their state;
when that is transformed, it becomes invisible, and what was invisible is seen.
There will be locations among living beings and bipeds;
one should also know them among lifeless things, such as vehicles, seats, houses, and so forth.
In reality, these nine are the fundamental locations. (149–150)
Those which are situated in the twelve parts and their subdivisions, they know them as such;

when the gaze is seen fixed on the crown of the head, one should look at the straight and other [postures]. Whatever is the measurement of those positions, that is now described here from this [work].
One should lay out eighteen finger-breadths in width and double that in length;
the thread for the door-posts should be according to the divisions as is appropriate,
and its width at the front should be eight [finger-breadths] at half the distance of the total length.
One should moisten the region of the back and apply it;
one should lay down a thread extending through its middle, as long and wide as required. That shall be the limit for the emergence of the limbs, measuring eight *māṇakas*.
From the *Sūnatyoga* and the *Garbhasūtra*, and so forth:
"The interior of the breasts should be six finger-breadths wide according to the *Garbhasūtra*.
The lateral extent of the emergence of the breasts from the interior should be six finger-breadths. (155–156)
From the flank of the womb, the two sides of the back and the buttocks are ten finger-breadths [in width];
the spinal column is nine finger-breadths; the distance between the two buttocks is seven finger-breadths;
and from the root of the armpit to the womb, it is ten finger-breadths in length.
Its projection forward is one finger-breadth, and seven fingers-breadths behind the central line (sūtra).
From the central line, the transverse measurement is one-quarter part, which is eighteen finger-breadths;
and from the center, the region of the jaw (yava-pradeśa) shall be five finger-breadths.
The belly [is measured] from the womb by eight [aṅgulas], as well as from both sides and from the front.
The back of the abdomen is seven and a half aṅgulas behind it.
Furthermore, the root of the thighs is considered to be twelve and a half aṅgulas.
The protrusion [of the perineum] should be five finger-breadths, and seven behind it.
From the back of the root of the thigh, the buttocks project three finger-breadths.
Then, the penis should be known to be six finger-breadths from the line of the womb at its tip.
From the horizontal thread, the side of the knee measures nine and a half finger-breadths;
from the longitudinal thread, it is four finger-breadths at the back and front of the end of the knee.
The nalaka should extend six finger-breadths horizontally from its interior.
From the *garbhasūtra*, the *nalaka* extends four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) toward the back;
from the end of the *sūtra* to the tip of the finger, it measures six and a half finger-breadths.
The axle (*akṣa*) should be one and a half finger-breadths from the *sūtra*, as seen from its width.
In this [measurement], the foot is proclaimed to be fourteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in length;
from the inner edge (garbha), its tip is eight finger-breadths, and at the back it is six finger-breadths. Furthermore, the distance between the two knees should be one finger-breadth.
One finger-breadth is prescribed for the thighs, and four finger-breadths for the two shoulders.
This is declared to be "straightly positioned" when it does not deviate from the central axis of the torso.
Even if it rotates around the finger-breadth [measurement], it should still be reduced by two finger-breadths.
Therefore, that [line] should be rotated by one and a half finger-breadths;
this procedure is declared for the wall-line (*bhittika*) even when it is turned back. Those known as *ṛjvāgatārdha*, *ṛjuka*, *sāci*, *adhyardhākṣa*, and *pārśvāgata*— [End of verse 169]
"And their fourfold revolution, as well as the twenty intermediate [positions], have been declared.

Thus ends the seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Positions such as the Straight-Arrived (*ṛjvāgata*)," in the *Vāstuśāstra* named *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*, composed by the Great King of Kings, the illustrious Bhojadeva.
Now begins the eightieth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Positions such as the Vaiṣṇava."
Now, other numerous positions for movement are described,
knowing which those who are discerning and skilled do not become deluded:
the Vaiṣṇava, the Samapāda, the Vaiśākha, and likewise the Maṇḍala.
Pratyālīḍha and ālīḍha— these are the postures (sthāna) and their characteristics. When a woman strides like a horse, spanning the three worlds,
the distance between her two feet should be two tālas and a half-tāla.
Of these two, one is endowed with symmetry while the other stands with three corners;
the former has slightly bent shanks and is joined with a beautiful body and face.
This indeed is the Vaiṣṇava posture, and Viṣṇu is the presiding deity here.
In the *samapāda* stance, the two feet are equal and positioned one *tāla* apart;
they are endowed with natural grace, and Brahmā is the presiding deity here.
The distance between the two feet shall be three *tālas* and half a *tāla*.
One should draw one foot in a relaxed posture and the second foot positioned on the side;
when the thighs are thus not level, this stance is indeed known as Vaiśākha.
The Blessed Viśākha is the presiding deity of this stance.
The *aindra* (Indra) posture consists of a circular base with the two feet situated four *mūla*s apart;
the thighs are positioned like the sides of a triangle, and the hips are level with the knees.
Then, extending the right foot, it is placed at a distance of five *tāla*s.
One should assume the *ālīḍha* stance; Rudra is the presiding deity here. Having bent the right leg and extended the left foot, by reversing this [stance] it is known as *pratyālīḍha*.
In that [stance], the right foot is even, while the other, situated on the side, is triangular;
with the left hip raised, it is called *āvahittha*.
One foot is placed evenly, while the second has its sole turned forward. ||11-12||
The wind that has reached the extremities of the wheels is called *śūdraviddha*.
These three locations may occur in women and sometimes in men as well:
the waist, the sides, the hands, the face, the chest, the neck, and the head. (13)
In all the [theoretical] positions, this matter follows the sequence of ritual action (kriyā).
However, because actions are infinite, it is not possible to describe them in their entirety;
nevertheless, we shall demonstrate merely a general indication (diṅmātra) of them.
When a joyful beloved woman or a man stands near their lover, her or his posture consists of three parts; we shall now describe that.
It is when the *brahmasūtra* (the plumb line from the navel) remains straight even as she moves toward the mother’s side [the left].
We shall now describe that [process] sequentially, according to the division of its parts:
first, it is cold in the nostrils, the lips, and the corners of the mouth;
then at the edge of the throat, preceded by the nipples; and finally, after an interval of a *kalā*, in the navel. (17–18)
O beautiful lady, the movement of the thread is prescribed as being at three parts [of the body]: behind the thighs, between the hips, and likewise at the end of the western ankle;
in this stance called *tribhaṅga*, the two feet should be placed at a distance of one *tāla* apart.
In the space between sixteen and twenty finger-breadths, the father’s staff is placed on the right;
they say there are three types of movement— quick, medium, and slow— distinguished by their tempo,
occurring at the positions known as the half-eye and the walls within the three movements.
At the edge [of the mouth], then at the end of the *karavīra* [the palate], and at the end of the lips;
at the end of the throat, at the far side of the breasts, and at the end of the *guladruma*; near the navel, in the middle of the penis, and likewise at the other end of the *nalaka*.
When the *vajra* has reached the extremity during the movement, there occurs the movement of the *brahmasūtra*.
However, during the upward movement, it is indeed in the two nostrils (*locana-khīraka*) at the front;
likewise, it is at the edge of the chin, in the middle of the nipple, and at the navel. ||23-24||
In the middle of the penis, at its end, and sequentially down to the other knee,
and at the base of the other big toe— this is to be known as the *brahmasūtra*. Likewise, it is established by standing on the other foot, and so too during the forenoon.
One should form the palm here at half the cord of the ground-level, raised by one *gula*.
At the edge of the ground, at the outer corner, the portion of the chin is within the sphere; due to the subsequent cord from the navel, it is to the east, ending at half the other eye.
When the configuration is situated on the side, the hind leg here consists of seven *golās*.
We have described the movement for traveling two and a half *akṣas*; now we shall explain the movement for traveling along the side.
[In the case of] an *āvarta*, a *kūṭa*, or the edge of the cheek, [it concerns] the part of the corner of the mouth.
The thread from the two throat-convolutions (galavartau) in the middle of the breasts, passing through the space between the three circles (golatrika), to the navel;
and the thread from the buttocks (sphic), the sides, the back, and the knees, to the front of the right knee—these should be known as the threads for the *itthoni* (the female organ). 29–30.
One should subtract the elapsed portion of the day from the previously stated measure of one's own [shadow];
here, for the forenoon, the thumb should be made to rest upon the ground-line.
Subsequently, the tip of the thumb should be closely joined when the gait is slow.

From the *brahmasūtra* at the thumb and the little finger, [the distance] to the middle of the palm is sixteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). In the *drutagati* (fast gait), the tip of the thumb must be placed there;
from that point, the front foot is lifted up while the hind foot remains on the ground. ||32-33||
Thus, in all cases regarding the places of movement and stationing,
a wise man should establish the arrangement of these lineages (gotras) according to what is appropriate,
through their placement, expansion, contraction, and the disposition of their eyes, hands, and so forth. //34//
Now, because of the mention of the four positions [of the practitioner] as those who desire to enter, other rites that may occur here for men should also be written down;
for the sake of the disciples' understanding, he should set forth three sūtras. (35–36)
When the thread has reached the Brahma-line and those situated at the sides,
one should apply three upward threads across the various positions;
among these, that which is in the center is called the Brahma-thread.
Furthermore, regarding the wall, it is considered that the Brahma-sūtra, which stands at the side in relation to another portion, is indeed situated in the middle due to its functional purpose;
those two [lines] on both sides are known as the sūtras. ||38-39||
Whatever is desired here for the completion of a specific part or limb,
a thread should be laid out there according to the horizontal and vertical directions;
one should attend to as many [threads] as are required for the successful manifestation of each individual limb.
One should apply that many horizontal lines for the sake of establishing the manifestation of the parts;
three vertical lines should follow from the horizontal ones. Thus, the positions beginning with the Vaiṣṇava have been correctly described.
Endowed with a gait that flashes like a triple-bend,
and having correctly described the method for laying out the thread,
one who knows this becomes the most excellent among those who bear the thread. (42)

Thus ends the eightieth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Positions of Vaiṣṇava and Others," in the *Vāstuśāstra* named *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*, composed by the great king of kings, Śrī Bhojadeva.
Now begins the eighty-first chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Five Men and Women.
[Concerning] the bodily proportions of the five principal types of men, beginning with the Haṃsa...
We shall now describe separately those women headed by Daṇḍinī.
There are five types of men: Haṃsa, Śaśa, Rucaka, Bhadra, and Mālavya; among these, the measurement of the Haṃsa is described first.

The length of the swan is proclaimed to be eighty-eight finger-breadths (aṅgulas). The increase for the other four [types] should be understood to proceed by increments of two finger-breadths each. Of that [swan], the beak and the nose measure two and a half finger-breadths.
The neck and the face together shall be eleven finger-breadths (aṅgulas).
Likewise, the distance from the navel to the genitals is ten;
the thighs are twenty finger-breadths, and the shanks, knees, and [the lower part of the shanks] are three each.
The hairline is three finger-breadths above the [forehead] measure, and the hair itself occupies two finger-breadths;
this measurement of the hairline for all [figures] should be greater than their own [standard] proportion.
The chest should be twenty finger-breadths in width.
One should specify that the width of the upper arm is twelve finger-breadths;
the forearms and likewise the hands are ten finger-breadths each.
Furthermore, the hips should be thick with individual fingers [in width] accordingly.
By the nature of a swan, his nose is distinct from the [other] parts;
the remaining [portion] is three finger-breadths, as are the nose and the mouth.
The neck is also of that same measure, while the chest is eleven finger-breadths.
Likewise, the belly, the navel, and the space between the genitals and the anus are ten [finger-breadths] each;
the two thighs of the hare are proclaimed to be twenty finger-breadths in measure;
the knees are three finger-breadths, and the shanks are twenty finger-breadths in length.
The two ankles shall be three fingers in length, and the head shall be of that same measure;
thus, the total length of the hare shall be measured at ninety fingers.
Its chest is declared to be twenty-two fingers in width.
The forearms, the upper arms, and the hands of even a hare should be like those of a swan;
he should possess the proper proportions and a slender waist by nature.
Likewise, his hair, thighs, and shanks should be well-formed, as determined by the wise.
The neck of the rucaka [type of pillar] is said to be ten and a half aṅgulas in height;
its width is declared to be three and a half aṅgulas.
Its circumference, according to the measurement previously established, is eleven aṅgulas.
His abdomen is exactly that much; the space between his navel and genitals is ten [aṅgulas].
His thighs are twenty aṅgulas, and his knees are three aṅgulas.
One should specify that the length of his shanks is twenty aṅgulas.
The ankles and its head should each be three finger-breadths;
the *rucaka* is proclaimed to have a length of ninety-two finger-breadths.
Thus is its length; its width at the chest is twenty finger-breadths.
The two arms are ten finger-breadths in length, and the forearms are exactly the same;
his hands are proclaimed to be eleven finger-breadths in width.
He has broad shoulders and muscular arms, with graceful gait and movements.
The *vṛttabāhu* (rounded-armed) type should be strong and shaped like a *rucaka* (bracelet);
they say the length of the head for the *bhadra* type is three finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
The neck is eleven finger-breadths long and three and a half finger-breadths wide.
His chest and abdomen together measure eleven and one-quarter finger-breadths (ekādaśāṅgula-sapāda).
One should know that the interval between his navel and genitals is ten and a half finger-breadths (sārdhadaśāṅgula),
and the length of his two thighs should be known as twenty and one-quarter finger-breadths (viṃśati-sapādāṅgula).
The two calves are as long as [the torso], and the distance from the knee to the ankle is three *mātrās*.
With four folds and beautiful, this is proclaimed to be the *candrasa* (moon-like) type. This length is the width of the chest, which is twenty-one [units].
His two arms are eleven finger-breadths long;
this has been stated thus for [the images of] the Haṃsa and other male deities,
or else according to the measurement of their specific characteristics.
And he who correctly understands the sources of happiness for women shall be honored by kings.

Thus ends the eighty-first chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Five Types of Men and Women," in the treatise on architecture named *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*, composed by the great emperor, the illustrious Bhojadeva.
Now begins the eighty-second chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Rasas and Dṛṣṭis.
Next, we shall describe the characteristics of the rasas and the dṛṣṭis,
for upon them depends the manifestation of the emotions (bhāvas) in painting.
The erotic, the comic, the pathetic, the furious, the lovable,
the fearful, the heroic, the wondrous, the odious, the marvelous,
and likewise the tranquil— these eleven are declared to be the aesthetic sentiments (rasas) by those expert in the science of poetry.
The definition of each of these is now stated in sequence:

Where there is a trembling of the eyebrows, a swaying of the hips, and movements characterized by beloved gracefulness, accompanied by the qualities of love, that is known as the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa).
That which possesses playful, graceful outer corners of the eyes, a gentle quivering of the lips,
and is accompanied by sportiveness is called the comic sentiment (hāsya-rasa).
[5] That which has the edges of the cheeks moistened with tears and eyes contracted by grief...
That which is joined with mental anguish is called the pathetic sentiment (karuṇa-rasa).
He whose forehead is wiped clean, whose eyes are bloodshot and rolling,
and who bites his lower lip with his teeth— that is said to be the furious sentiment (raudra-rasa).
The aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) arising from the gain of wealth, the birth of a son, or the joy of seeing a beloved, in which a thrill of horripilation has appeared— that is called *pramā* (cognition).
[In contrast,] one whose eyes are wandering in agitation due to the terror caused by seeing an enemy—

The *bhayānaka* (terrifying) rasa is to be known as arising from the agitation of the heart. The *vīra* (heroic) rasa is traditionally defined as that which arises from steadfastness, courage, and strength, and which is produced by the contraction and expansion of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*). 9–10.
When one perceives a matter that is only slightly sown with seed and possesses a steady pupil,
yet is worthy of being honored, the marvelous rasa (adbhuta-rasa) arises.
[This occurs] through the various transformations of the eyebrows, eyes, face, and so forth, which are serene.
"That which arises from the absence of passion toward sense objects is known as the sentiment of tranquility (śānta-rasa).
Thus have these sentiments been described with their defining characteristics in connection with dramatic composition;
having placed human beings at the forefront, one should apply them to all living beings.
Thus end the aesthetic sentiments (rasas).

Now we shall describe the gazes: the playful, the joyful, the blossoming, the distorted, the frowning, the expressive, the contracted, the one with the neck bent forward, the upward-turned, the yogic, the wretched, and the gaze that trembles in various ways in the sky.

There may be the *Aṅkitā*, the *Abhidhānā*, the *Vivikhyā*, the *Jihmā*, the *Madhyasthā*, and likewise another called the *Sthirā*; thus eight [types] have been indicated. Now, the definition of these such as they are shall be stated in order. ||15-16||
The glance that is blossoming, bold, agitated, and accompanied by the casting of side-long glances,
arising from the sentiment of love (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*), is to be known as "graceful" (*lalitā*).
[When directed] toward a beloved object, it is serene, with hair standing on end and the outer corners of the eyes dilated.

The gaze born from the tip of the nose is declared to be the "Joyful" (hṛṣṭā) glance. ||18|| The "Expanded" (vikāsitā) glance is characterized by the corners of the eyes being wide open, as are the outer regions of the eyes, the cheeks, and the surface of the face; it is endowed with a playful form and belongs to the aesthetic flavor of laughter (hāsyarasa). ||19||
That gaze which is renowned as "altering joy," with pupils that are clearly visible and wandering,
should be known by those skilled in dramatic expression as the "terrible" (bhayānakā) look, characterized by agitation and fear. Furthermore,
the "fierce" (dīptā) look has wide-open eyes, is bloodshot, and is characterized by a slow or dull vision.
A gaze directed upward with knitted brows is proclaimed as *bhrūkuṭi*. A gaze that is steady, firm in its aim, graceful, with clearly visible pupils, gentle,
and extended by a network of rays from the corners of the eyes is called *vibhrama*.
Filled with the intoxication of passion, with the pair of her eyelids opened by the sensation of touch,
and endowed with the blissful joy of a flower tree, this gaze is called "contracted" (asaṅkucitā).
When it is free from modification, she gazes at the tip of her nose for a moment.
That gaze called *yoginī* arises from the application of the mind to reality (*tattva*).
With its upper eyelid half-lowered, its pupils slightly constricted, moving slowly, and tearful, it is described as "miserable" (*dīnā*) in the context of sorrow. (24–25)
That gaze which, when the pupils are steady and wide-open, appears as if emitting vitality and is born of enthusiasm;
and that gaze whose eyelids and lashes are drooping, which is slack and slow-moving— [these are the two types]. (26)
The gaze that has entered the corners of the eyes and is agitated is known as *tāmalā*.
A gaze that is slightly moving, somewhat steady, wide-open, directed askance, dull, startled in its pupils, and apprehensive is considered the *śaṅkitā* (suspicious) look. ||27-28||

That gaze in which the eyelashes are contracted and the lids are likewise contracted, and in which the pupil moves slightly within them, is called the "contracted" (kuñcitā) gaze. That which has drooping half-lids, a sideways glance, and a slow, harsh look is [the "hanging" (lambitā) gaze].
The gaze that is hidden, with pupils concealed and slanted, is called *jihmā* (the averted).
The gaze that has upright pupils, straight eyelids, is serene, free from passion, and indifferent toward sense objects, is called *madhyasthā* (the neutral). ||30-31||

The gaze is proclaimed to be steady when it is level, with even eyelids and even eyebrows, unchanging, helpful, and free from agitation. Indicating the meaning with the hand and establishing it with the gaze—
One should appear as if alive through the observation of all forms of dramatic representation (abhinaya).
This is called the means (sādhana) in both the physical (āṅgika) and the pictorial (citra). Therefore, in this context, the pictorial [representation] should be based upon these two.
View.
Thus has been declared here the definition of the tastes (rasas) and of the glances (dṛṣṭis) in brief;
by means of this, the mind never falls into doubt regarding the various internal details of painting that are to be known.

Thus ends the eighty-second chapter, titled "The Definition of Tastes and Glances," in the treatise on architecture named *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra*, composed by the great king of kings, the illustrious Bhojadeva.
Now begins the eighty-third chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Sixty-Four Hand-Gestures (Hastas) beginning with Patākā.
Herein, the sixty-four hand-gestures are now described,
along with their characteristics and applications, according to the distinction between their proper and improper usage.
The *patāka*, the *tripatāka*, and thirdly the *kartarīmukha*;
likewise the *ardhacandra*, the *ārāla*, and another, the *śukatuṇḍa* (parrot-beak);
the *muṣṭi*, the *śikhara*, the *kapittha*, and the *khaṭakāmukha*.
The needle-mouthed, the lotus-bud-headed, the deer-head,
the kāṅgala-lotus, the kola, the fourfold, the bee, the swan-mouthed, the swan-winged, the forceps, and the bud-shaped [are the types of nozzles]. ||3-4||
The spider (*ūrṇanābha*) and the copper-crested bird (*tāmracūḍa*): this [section] is endowed with four [subdivisions].
The characteristics and functions of those twenty hands are now described.
Indeed, he whose fingers are joined together with their tips extended—
When the thumb is likewise bent, it is known as the *patāka* (banner) hand. Furthermore,
when the head is raised by the hand, and the body is again slightly bent to the left with the eyebrows curved into a frown— ||7||
One should indicate a blow with eyes slightly opened;
likewise, one who has arisen [in anger] indicates the *pratāpana* strike with a fierce gaze.
Similarly, with a face unchanged, the hand placed on the forehead and moved slightly [indicates the same].
With eyes darting like banners and eyebrows knitted in a frown,
those who are experts in the science of painting should manifest the pride of thinking "I am capable";
and they should employ this [expression] in conjunction with the subjects that are about to be described.
That hand which is joined with the second hand is known as *saṃyuta*.
Therein, having moved upward from the front and then from the right,
it should be extended upwards with its two fingers moving.
Thus has the description of the rain-showers been set forth.
However, she should show those two [hands] reaching out as far as the limit;
with her fingers slightly trembling at the falling of the shower of flowers. (12-13)

The two hands should be curved with a span of two *kārṣas*; here, three [fingers] are even more prominent. Having placed the *svastika* with the palms facing upward, the wise one, performing its release, should display the *palvala* mudrā.

Raising her left eyebrow slightly and tilting her head a little, she should form that same pair of hands [as previously described] with an unaltered facial expression, toward the offerings of flowers, the young grass, and whatever objects are situated upon the ground. (15–16)
With that same [instrument], the joining of the parts should be performed face-downward;
it should be closed, firm, and well-adhered.
The face in this [performance] should always be shown as unaltered. ||17||
The two soles should be placed one upon the other, neither raised nor pressed down;
with the head slightly inclined, the palms should be turned downward,
held firmly against each other, while the lotus-face remains free from any alteration of expression.
With the chest forward and the two hands turned upward,
one should demonstrate the *manasāśakti* with effort;
it is to be concealed by the left hand held in a guarded position, while the head is slightly bowed.
One should display the left eyebrow slightly contracted,
using the two parts of the hand— the index finger and thumb— as a *patāka* (flag) gesture held at the side,
while the other two hands form a *patāka* gesture raised above. ||21-22||
Then, greeting the person of authority, he should direct his breath toward their face;
with his head slightly bowed and his eyebrows knit in a frown,
the wise one should indicate both the time and the earth with his two hands.
With his left hand placed in front and his right hand [supporting him], the man,
with his head slightly raised as he moves forward like a serpent,
should constantly demonstrate speed while maintaining an unchanging facial expression.
Thus, with two trembling hands,
and likewise with the head following them,
one who is skilled in hand gestures (hastābhinaya) should perform this gesture of agitation for one with a distorted face.
One who has been struck from below should be represented by the face turned downward; this also serves another purpose.
[This] should be performed with the *patāka* hand, slightly knitting the brows, positioned at the side, and repeatedly moving the fingers upward. (27–28)
One should perform encouragement by raising the neck;
by drawing [the bow] sideways, one should indicate "abundant.
A grand gesture should be made for a "great" [object], with the hand moving upward from the sides.
With the face turned upwards and not lowered, one should represent a lion by means of the *siṃha* hand;
with the hand raised high and acting as a banner,
moving here and there, one should show the striking of the lotus.
One should perform the movement with the face turned away from the seven [positions], and with the mouth;
one should display it by moving it obliquely while stationed at the sides.
One should constantly perform the action of raising the wings with a distorted face.
With the left hand held upward and the other [right hand] extended forward,
washed with the palm pressed down, and then rubbed again with a frown while the gaze follows the hands. ||33-34||
By rubbing with one form while the second extends [over it],
and by that hand being placed upon it, [the gesture] is performed.
One should display the *piṣṭa* (ground) through mutual friction and by means of the brow-frown (*bhrukuṭī*).
Standing at the side with the mountain-king [the *mudrā*] extended far, one should slowly raise the creeper-like eyebrow of Umā;
then, facing each other and capable of supporting one another, they perform the holding of the mountain (*śailadhāraṇa*). ||36-37||
Then, having drawn him in from both sides with his chin tucked and brows knitted,
he performed the uprooting of mountains while holding him aloft;
and with his head positioned high above, he held him far extended upward.
"The act of lifting a mountain should be performed with raised eyebrows.
Thus ends the description of the *patāka* hand gesture.
When, however, the ring finger of the *patāka* hand is curved, it should be known as the *tripatāka*; its function is now described.
This [hand]—with the middle and little fingers not moving...
In this case, one should perform the rite with the head slightly raised, but not so much as to touch the crown;
rather, one should perform the act of descending with the head bowed while its front part is lifted upward. 41–42.
The dismissal [of the enemy] should be performed by him as he glides along the side,
or by frowning fiercely at those who have turned their backs;
likewise, the warding off [of an attack] is done while stationed on the side, and the entry [into the formation] by one bent downwards.
While entering, one should perform the *ākāra* [mudrā], which is straight and without distortion;
with this pair of raised fingers turned upward and with a face free from distortion, the act of raising [the head] should be performed. (44–45)
One should perform it by bowing from the side with the head bent forward;
likewise, there is the illustration of the upturned [hand] with the tips of the fingers pointing upward,
and again, the connection of the rite before the face that has been extended forward.
With the breathless (lifeless) ring finger, having grasped auspicious objects with the finger called the nameless (anāmikā), their touching is prescribed;
likewise, with the head turned away and moving along the region of the head. ||47-48||
One should display the arrangement of the head with this hand;
all these [gestures] should be shown with faces free from distortion,
while the two hands are positioned close to the hair on both sides.
One should visualize that [the deity] attains the uṣṇīṣa, the crown, and so forth.
This mudrā, which destroys the [adversaries'] necks, should be performed according to the ritual procedure near [the deity].
The hand, with a frown formed, has two fingers raised there.
One should show [this] with two downward-pointing fingers;
or with two moving, bud-like hands, one may show the lotuses of this very hand.
At times, with both hands, one should show small birds.
And likewise other objects such as the wind—
one should indicate these by means of both hands with moving fingers,
or by lowering the face, or by pointing forward with a gliding motion.
With his two hands positioned above like the stream of the Gaṅgā and resembling a thread, and with one hand bending downward to point the way,
he moved forward with a distorted face.
The wise performer should make the gesture of a snake with the hand.
With two fingers turned downwards, he should perform the wiping away of tears;
with the little finger curved toward the corner of the eye, he should assume a downward-turned face.
Then, with the ring finger, one should apply a mark on the forehead with sandalwood paste;
with the index finger, one should fashion a beautiful tilaka upon the creeper-like eyebrows; and with the ring finger, the application of *rocanā* (yellow pigment) should be performed.
Having taken the yellow pigment (rocanā), one should likewise scatter it upon the head;
in the same manner, the display of the *alaka* [forehead mark] should be performed with the hand raised and the fingers forming the *tripatāka* gesture while laughing.
By moving two fingers horizontally at the tip of the *cadaneśya* hand,
and by moving the fingers of the *tripatākā* hand forward in front of the chest,
one should represent the peacock, the *śārikā* bird, the cuckoo, and so forth.
One should cause the hand to perform the "Trailokyavijaya" gaze following it. (62) Thus ends the Tripatāka mudrā.
When the *tripatāka* hand is turned backward in the palm,
with the index finger [extended] against the middle finger, that is the *kartarīmukha* (scissors-mouth) gesture.
Moving about here and there with steps joined by bowing down—
Indeed, by that [measure], the length of the yoke (yuga) is established; its measurement is as follows:
the downward-facing part should be made with a curvature, while the horn-like projection situated on the forehead should be joined and elevated. 64–65.
One should indicate a written document by scratching it with raised eyebrows;
likewise, one should indicate falling down by looking downward with a single eyebrow slightly bent, and similarly,
death by moving downward.
One should show the *namate* gesture, which is free from the movement of Śakra;

with the hand moving, the eyebrows knitted and the head bowed, one should display it as if casting down [an object] for a specific purpose, while restraining the gaze and likewise performing the expulsion (*nirghāṭana*). ||67-68||
The *kartarīmukha* (scissors-mouth) [hand-gesture] is formed when the fingers are plump and the little finger follows the thumb.

That hand whose fingers, together with the thumb, are bent like a bow is called the *ardhacandra* (half-moon); its function is now described. With one such hand, one may display the crescent moon by raising the eyebrows.
One should likewise carry out the banishment of one whose measures are moderate. Others say that when he is thus joined [with the ritual],
fatness, young trees, conch-shells, jars,
and bracelets should be displayed.
By means of this [hand gesture], the girdle, earrings, and so forth, as well as the leaf-pattern ornament, should be indicated;
likewise, the hips and loins should be expressed by the hand positioned at those respective places.
Furthermore, the gaze should always be made to follow that [gesture] by the dancers in every instance.
The crescent moon is its [form].
In the *ārāla* [hand gesture], the first finger (the index) is bent like a bow, the thumb is likewise contracted,
and the remaining fingers are known to be separated, turned upward, and curled.
It is formed with the hand slightly raised and turned toward the chest.
The dancer should display courage, magnanimity, depth, fortitude, and grace;
even when facing divine beings or those who are half-evil, he should show them with an unaltered face, with raised eyebrows, and using this hand gesture. ||75-76||
Bestowing blessings upon women, seizing their hair,
and gazing at all the limbs of oneself—
all such acts of self-exaltation must be performed by one with raised eyebrows.
With both hands moving in a clockwise direction, one should indicate marriage, sexual union, and many festive ceremonies;
likewise, by forming a svastika with the tips of the fingers joined together. ||78-79||
One should demonstrate circumambulation by moving in a circular path;
likewise, by this [path], one should demonstrate the great water and whatever substance has been fashioned upon the surface of the earth in a circular configuration. (80)
Giving, warding off, and summoning are likewise expressed by various words;
one should indicate these with that hand when it is not joined [with the other].
