With that same hand, the removal of sweat and the smelling of fragrances should be performed.
This [hand] is generally employed by those skilled in dance with the hand placed upon the region of the hips,
and also in relation to women. One should always perform all these actions with the *tripatāka* hand.
One should not act with the thought "I am not," nor should one remain in a state of dejection;
rather, one should direct the gaze to follow her and likewise adjust the eyebrows.
This is the *itara* (or *arāla*) glance.
When the ring finger of the *arāla* hand is curved, it should be known as the *śukatuṇḍa* (parrot-beak). Its function is now described:
one should indicate "not you" by extending this [hand] sideways. ||85-86||
One should indicate that "there is no further duty" with a hand turned away;
one should perform the invocation by extending the hand forward and repeatedly bowing toward it,
and the dismissal by turning the hand sideways.

One should observe that there is no purpose served by a hand that is turned away; rather, it is praised when turned toward the pouring of the libation. One should employ this hand so that its fingers and eyebrows follow [the movement]. 88–89.
Thus ends the section on the parrot’s beak.
That hand whose fingers are positioned with their tips toward the center of the palm,
and over which the thumb is placed, is called a fist (muṣṭi).
This should be employed in striking and athletic exercises by those with faces contorted by frowns.
"With the pair of hands positioned at the sides, it is prescribed for the act of exiting.
(91) Thus ends the *muṣṭi* [mudrā]. It is used for seizing a sacrificial post, for half-pressing, and for pressing the breasts.
Likewise, it should be formed unjoined for one who possesses right view.
When the thumb is raised from this very same fist, that hand is then to be known by practitioners as the *śikhara* (peak) mudrā. ||92-93||
This left [hand] should be employed in the fourfold manner of the *kuśara* rays;
both hands are occupied with the act of grasping the goad.
However, for the discharge of the spear and the javelin, the right hand is employed.
When applying collyrium to the feet or lips, the big toe should be moved;
when lifting the hair-ornament, one should remain positioned in that same region and likewise direct the gaze toward the pair of eyebrows following it. ||95-96||
Thus ends the section on the pinnacle.
When the index finger of this very same mudrā called Śikhara is bent and pressed down by the two thumbs, it is then known as Kapittha.
[With it, one employs] the bow, the javelin, the discus, the sword, the spear, the mace, and the club. ||97||
By this [method], the wise man should represent all other weapons as well.
Even while performing the representation, he should repeatedly brandish [the weapon];
here too, the movement of the eyes and eyebrows following the hand is recommended.
Thus is the kapittha [hand].
But when that same [hand] is raised and curved, it should be made the kanīyasī;
however, this very kapittha has a face consisting of six parts of a pada. 100.
By this, the oblation, the offering, and the food are prescribed through salutation.
By two [verses], the drawing [of the bow], the umbrella, the rim, the reins, and the display are shown.
By this, neither the mirror nor the jaw is [to be] seized again.
Lowering and raising are performed with the [hand] turned away,
while crushing is to be executed with it rotating;
likewise, the seizing of a long staff and the grasping of a six-finger span [of cloth] are done in the same manner.
When grasping a bundle of kuśa grass, hair, and the like, or when taking up a garland or a wreath,
the hand joined with the gaze and the eyebrows should be employed by the wise.
Thus ends the *khaṭakāmukha* [hand gesture].
When the index finger is extended in the hand known as *khaṭaka*,
it should then be recognized by practitioners as the hand named *sūcīmukha*.
The operation of its index finger occurs almost exclusively [in this manner].
Bent slightly forward, trembling, with the delusions of a child’s marriage ceremony—
such a one is fit for that ritual there.
One should represent the wheel of delusion (bhrumaya) by means of this yawning and movement.
With her flickering [hand], she [held] the banners and so forth;
with the two eyebrows, she [formed] a cluster of flowers from the sprouts and young leaves drenched with incense and lamps.
With her swaying gait, she moves in a curved manner, her crest-like hair rising upward.
O Creator, the wise call her "Budhā" (the Awakened), for she has half-shaken feet;
she is like a creeping vine of incense and lamps, with sprouts that are young serpents.
With this [gaze] previously well-established, one should show the crest-lock, the circle,
and the eye with an upward-glancing movement;
then, with a downward-bending motion, the right [eye] should be shown as slightly lowered.
With a horizontal circle, one should display the entire world with it. One should fashion this [line] as elevated according to the prescribed rules for the initial long [measure];
then, one should make it inclined again when displaying the afternoon.

This finger, characterized by being slightly curved and expanded, should be placed near the mouth by those who know the principles of dance when defining the meaning of a statement. When pointing out something as "this is that," it should be extended, turned upward, and shaken.
With her fingertips trembling in anger and her hand raised high, it is not intended that the hand with extended fingers be used for depicting perspiration, nor for depicting the hair,
armlets, cheeks, or earrings. ||115-116||
The twenty-sixth movement, *prācalatī*, should be performed swiftly;
it is turned upward and concealed by the forehead, and is employed for the representation of an elephant. Alternatively, when extended and raised, it is prescribed for aiming at enemies.
When anger is about to manifest, that gaze should be directed slightly upward;
even when pointing out "Who is this?", it should be cast obliquely.
When hearing a sound, it should be directed toward the ear-tip, relying on the father [the teacher]. ||118-119||
In the *kārya* [gesture], the fingers of both hands are joined together facing each other;
in *viyoga*, they are separated; in *kalahe*, they are formed in the shape of a *svastika*;
and in *caturdhanitā*, they are pressed against one another. (120)
While describing whatever must be done, as far as the upward-pointing movement [of the hand] is concerned,
the wise man should make the gaze and the eyebrows follow that hand;
thus is the *sūcīmukha* (needle-mouth) gesture.
When the fingers are spread apart and bent by the thumb,
and are turned upward with their tips joined together, that is the *padmakośaka* (lotus-bud) gesture;
one should represent the grasping of a *śrīphala* or a wood-apple (*kapittha*) with it.
One should perform the depiction of other fruits as well, primarily the citron (*bījapūraka*),
with a form similar to that [of the previous fruit] and positioned upright;
one should represent the breasts of a woman with an open mouth spread wide.
The wise one should direct his gaze and eyebrows toward this hand;
this is the Padmakoṇaka.
That [hand] whose fingers are all joined together with the thumb [is the next].

Likewise, when it is directed downwards, that hand with the serpent-head should be used for sprinkling and offering water; however, when moving, it should be turned face down like a serpent. (126–127)
The performer of the Vidhāta [mudrā] should place his left hand, doubled over, below the shoulder-blade;
with the hand having a serpent’s head, he should perform the action of slapping.
Thus, knitting his brows and holding his head askance, he should act in this manner.
One should not look down in front; one should perform the *ālana* [movement].
The gaze, together with the eyebrows, should follow the hand.
This is the *sarpaśiras* (serpent-head) [mudrā].
When the three fingers are turned downward and the little finger and thumb are joined together,
with the little finger and thumb pointing upward, that is the *mṛgaśīrṣaka* (deer-head) mudrā;
one should employ it here and now when saying "so it is" or "yes."

If one obtains an umbrella, there should be a fall from the state of animals; if one casts down the previous eye, one should wipe away the sweat while facing downwards, and that [action] should be performed with a downward gaze.
In the case of *kuṭṭamita*, he should be made to move about while facing downwards.
"Her following gaze and her hands should also do so;
thus is the *mṛgaśīrṣaka*."
The middle, index, and thumb fingers are held together in the form of the three sacrificial fires (tretāgni).
The ring finger is bent at the tip, and the little finger is likewise raised upward.
With this "tretā" gesture, one should display the karkandhū fruit and other such objects.
Young fruits, other light objects, whatever else is small,
the words of women uttered with gestures of their fingers in anger,
and the display of gems such as pearls and emeralds— [these are the things that attract bees]. (135–136)
"With this hand, one should touch the eyebrows when they have reached the back [of the head];
thus says Kāṅgūla."
When the fingers curl inward toward the palm, it is indeed called the *alapa* (lotus) hand; when positioned at the side and spread out,
this hand should be held obliquely in front for the purpose of prohibition.
When a wise man says, "To whom do you belong? or "I have no one," and when he remains silent, the women's minds should not waver from their assigned mission.
Furthermore, his gaze should follow [the messenger], and likewise his eyebrows should be raised.
Thus spoke Padma.
The three fingers [index, middle, and ring] are extended, and the little finger is likewise turned upward;
the thumb is positioned between them—this hand is known as *catura*.
When it is turned downward and moved, it is called *matasya*, and with that, one tells various stories.

This [gesture] should be performed by one skilled in dramatic representation according to the rules of *vinaya* (restraint) and *naya* (guidance). Having made the eyebrows raised and auspicious through versatility,
one should again place the hand, turned upward, in a graceful manner during the act of restraint.
However, one should not act crookedly toward discipline;
one should show the child with the hand facing downwards.
In showing the child, one should keep the neck slightly bent.
Therefore, immediately after the patient,
this hand is prescribed for both truthfulness and consent, when it is turned upward, extended horizontally, and placed outside with the face of the hand unchanged.

In this very manner, the middle *paryaṅka* posture should be employed when joined with two [hands] or with one; likewise, it should be performed while standing in a circle (*maṇḍala*). Furthermore, the *vicārita*, *vihṛta*, and *lajjita* [gestures] should be employed in the same way. ||146-147||
In that [gesture], the face of the lady with arched brows should be made motionless;
the chest should be slightly raised and held in a circular position,
while the face is turned downward in front and likewise drawn apart.
In that [pose], the face should be unaltered, with the eyebrows raised;
the head, moreover, should be bent toward the left.
With both eyes, one should display the ears of a deer.
The task should be performed by those experts residing in that region with a knitting of the eyebrows;
or else, with the hand held open and joined, one should display the shape of a leaf. Having slightly lowered the eyebrow, the clever one [acts] in the sky with the hand.
Līlā, Rati, Smṛti, Buddhi, Saṃjñā, Āyā, Vicāraṇā,
Saṅgata, Praṇaya, Śauca, Āvartī, Bhāva, Akṣamā,
Puṣṭi, Savicā, Śīla, Cāturya, Mārdava, and Sukha. ||152-153||
Inquiry, news, dress, logic, courtesy, youth, wealth and lack of wealth, slight, sexual union, the excellent, the gentle (154),
virtue and vice, the home, wives, and various castes based on different supports.
All of these should be represented by the skillful actor as is appropriate:
at times through power, at times through wandering, and at times through gentleness—whichever means produces the comprehension of each particular meaning in whatever manner it may be. ||155-156||
The wise should likewise represent [the drinking] on the head with the hand as prescribed;
the eyebrows, the gaze, the eyes, and the face should be managed accordingly.
With the hand positioned in the *maṇḍala* gesture, one should indicate that [the drink] is yellow or red.
With her eyebrows slightly arched and her head turned in a circle, she should indicate Kṛṣṇa by touching [the area] with the blue-black [color];
and she should indicate the clever pigeon-colored and other natural complexions with [her hand]. ||158-159||
Thus, there are four.
With the middle finger and thumb joined like a pair of tongs, the forefinger bent,
and the other fingers extended upwards and scattered— this is the *bhramara* hand; with this hand, one performs the grasping of the kumuda, utpala, and padma lotuses.
In the same manner, one should fashion other [ornaments] such as those with long stalks;
moreover, an ear-ornament (karṇapūra) should be fashioned, positioned in the region of the ear. Their eyes and eyebrows should be made continuous, following the movement of the hands.
Thus ends the section on the bee.
The index, middle, and thumb fingers should be joined together without gaps, positioned like fire;
for the Haṃsavaktra [mudrā], the remaining fingers should be extended.
Slightly vibrating the thumb and raising the eyebrows with it—[this is the mudrā]. 163.
One should display it as devoid of essence, slight, subtle, soft, and light;
and in the enactment of what is to be performed, these [qualities] reside in the eyes, the eyebrows, and the hands.
Thus ends the Haṃsavaktra [hand gesture].
The three fingers [other than the thumb] are extended, and the little finger is likewise raised;
the thumb is bent—it is known as the *saṃsapakṣa* [hand]. With the palm turned upward, it is placed obliquely on the outside, adorning the neck and the water-vessel.
He must perform the ritual turning of the head for the sake of the body's health;
he should keep this person lying on his back during meals and when receiving gifts, as well as during the act of sipping water (ācamana) for the twice-born. 167.
One should place this [actor] at the bottom of the two ends, joined with the svastika gesture.
With the head slightly bent, he should move around according to the rasa;
by these two [hands], held sideways on both sides, there is the "display of the pillar" (stambha-darśana).

One should produce horripilation with a single hair on the left arm during massage or the application of unguents, as well as upon touching that specific area. In the case of women’s despondency or amorous playfulness, the milk situated there is like the [sublime] aesthetic flavor (rasa).
One should apply the lower surface [of the hand] in the same way for supporting the jaw;
likewise, one should direct the gaze following the hand and the eyebrows.
This is the Haṃsapakṣa [mudrā].
When there is a pinching with the index finger and the thumb for the purpose of weeping, and the middle of the palm is slightly bent, that is known as the *sandaṃśa* (pinch) gesture;
it is of three types, distinguished by its position at the tip, the face [of the fingers], or the side. ||172-173||
One should employ it for gathering flowers, stringing them, and for grasping grass or leaves; likewise, others use it for hair, thread, and so forth.
For grasping a portion of a craft object, however, one uses a firm pair of forceps.
Likewise, in attraction, in drawing [something] black, in plucking a flower from its stalk,
in the examination of a probe, in anger, and in the utterance of the word "fie," one should employ this [glance] directed toward the outer part. ||175-176||

That which is accumulated through sacrifice is attained by standing in that region with the palms turned upward, joined at the front of the chest, slightly bent, and with the face cast downward. 177. This is the speech of Valahā.
One should demonstrate the seizing of the string of qualities, the aiming at the target, and the meditation and yoga with that which resides in the region of the heart.
Those [arrows] which are slightly separated should be made joined together in front of the target. ||178-179||
In cases of reproach, toward those who are tender, and regarding words that are offensive,
the left [hand] should have its tip turned back and be slightly opened; likewise in the fashioning of coral,
in taking up a wick, and in the coloring of the eyes.
And he should be depicted in a painting likewise during the pressing of lac-dye;
then one should make his eyebrows and gaze follow [the object].
Thus ends the section on the *sandaṃśa* (tongs).
When the fingers are brought together and joined at their tips so that they point upwards like the beak of a swan, that hand becomes the *mukula* (bud) mudrā;
it should be held closed for [representing] lotus buds and the like. ||182-183||
Having crept forward, one should rise up and act as a "lascivious kisser" (viṭacumbaka);
thus says Mukula.

When the fingers of the lotus-bud hand are contracted, it is to be known as the Ūrṇanābha; it is used for seizing thieves by the hair and similar acts. For seizing a thief by the hair, this hand should be turned downwards.
In the examination of the disease of leprosy (kuṣṭha), while scratching the head,
the practitioner should remain facing downwards and frequently move about in various directions, assuming the forms of lions, tigers, and other such creatures. 186.
The seizing of this [victim] should be performed with a frowning face and with restraint;
here too, the movement of the eyes and eyebrows is prescribed just as before.
Thus ends the section on Ūrṇanābha.

With the middle finger and thumb joined like a pincer and the forefinger bent, this hand gesture is to be employed for inspiring confidence in wild beasts such as tigers and for holding a child; likewise, when combined with a frown, it is used for threatening. ||188-189||
When joined with lions, tigers, and the like, it becomes expressive of [fear] when displaced;
the wise should apply the gaze and eyebrows in accordance with its specific nature.
This hand, when cut by others, is proclaimed by the learned as being known as "Chiditā" (the Cut).
Thus ends the story of Tāmracūḍa.
Twenty-four unjoined hands have been described.
Now, thirteen joined hands are being told according to their names and characteristics:
the *añjali*, the *kapota*, the *karkaṭa*, and likewise the *svastika*. ||191-192||
The *khaṭakāvardhamāna*, the *utsaṅga*,
the *niṣadhana*, the *ḍola*, the *puṣpapuṭa*, as well as the *makara* and the *gajadantaka*—
these ten are declared to be the *varittha* (hand postures) that are bound (*saṃyata*), according to their names and characteristics.

The añjali, the kapota, the karkaṭa, and likewise the svastika—these thirteen hands are declared to be known as "joined" (saṃyukta). When the two hands, both in the patāka position, are brought into contact, that is remembered as the añjali. ||194-195||
The head should be slightly bowed there; this is what must be done by the wise man.
One should perform the salutation to the teacher while remaining close to his face. No regard is paid to friends, nor is there any restriction regarding one's position.
Thus [ends] the *añjali* [gesture].
When both hands grasp each other at the sides, that hand is called *kapota*; its application is now described:
one should perform a salutation with it placed upon the chest, but not with the head bowed down.
One should converse with the teacher; by that, cold and likewise fear [are dispelled].
When accepting discipline, this is called "this" (ayam).
With that very hand, which has been released while being rubbed with the fingers—
He speaks thus to them: "This is not the time for action," and he should demonstrate that he is blind.
Such is the form and appearance of this pigeon. Thus ends the section on the pigeon.
That hand whose fingers are interlaced within one another is to be known as the *karkaṭa* (crab) hand; its function is now described.
With the veins slightly raised and the eyebrows somewhat lifted, it performs the gesture of yawning (*jṛmbhaṇa*).
By this very [method], one should diagnose body aches in those afflicted by desire;
thus ends the section on Karkaṭa.
With both feet turned upward and placed on the left side, it is proclaimed as the Svastika posture.
Above that, it is spread out on all sides like forests;
the seasons, the sky, and the clouds—by that [posture], one moves toward the goal.
Thus ends the Svastika [mudrā].
The *khaṭaka* placed upon the *khaṭaka* is the *khaṭakāvardhamānaka*; it should be employed for the purpose of erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*). Another, the *parāvṛtta*, should likewise be used.
In the gait of a libertine (*viṭa*), it should be performed with the head slightly bowed, according to its proper measure.
Thus ends the section on the *khaṭaka* [hand gesture].

When the two hands are inverted and turned upward, they are known as the *vardhamānaka*; this is to be understood as the *utsaṅga* (lap) hand, used for the perception of touch. The two hands bearing the name *utsaṅga* are thus described, and their function is now stated.
The application of these two should be performed by a beginner with a single stroke.
These two hands should likewise be employed by women in a state of jealousy;
one should place either the right or the left hand so that it rests upon the middle of the elbow.
Thus ends the section on the lap.
When the two flags (patākās) are loosened, released,
and hanging down in this manner within the *karaṇa*, it is known as *dola*.
Thus ends *dola*.
That which is called *sarpaśiras* (serpent-head) has its fingers held close together;
when joined along the second side, it is the *puṣpapuṭa* (flower-bud). Furthermore, whatever other objects one wishes to display, they should be shown by means of this [mudrā].
One should perform the taking up and pouring out of water—
thus ends the "flower-cup" (puṣpapuṭa).
When the two hands are in the *patāka* position, with the thumbs pointing upward and the palms facing downward,
placed one above the other, that is the *makaradhvaja* (the dolphin-bannered) [mudrā]. Thus ends the *makara*.
When the two hands, joined at the wrists, are shaped like the heads of serpents, that hand is to be known as the *gajadanta* (elephant-tusk); and its function is as follows: 213.
Thus ends the *gajadanta*.
Having formed the hands like parrot-beaks (śukatuṇḍa) and brought them forward and curved toward the chest,
slowly lowering them face-downward, this is known as the *saubha* hand-position. One should perform the gestures for the throat and other parts with this hand.
Thus ends the *avahittha* [gesture].
He is to be known as Vardhamāna, and his ritual action is now declared.
By means of this [mantra], the utterance of truth, the grasping, and the seizing must be performed; likewise, by this [mantra] when it is pressed down, the counting of kalpas must be accomplished.

By this [definition] as well, these [hands] of theirs— namely, the two *krauñca* hands, the *nalinī* lotus-bud hand, and likewise the *garuḍapakṣaka*— are established. Although these belong to the category of *nṛttahasta* (dance hands), they are useful for the purpose of dramatic expression (*abhinaya*).
One should personally infer and apply the *samā* [mudrā] therein.
The application may also be performed by means of movement with a limb or the hand, or even by means of the cheeks, lips, nose, sides of the face, thighs, feet, gait, water, and so forth. ||218–219||

In whatever manner a representation may be intended, one should strive accordingly; [this concludes] the imitation of what has been performed. Now, the definition of the dance hands (nṛttahasta) is being stated.
The square (caturaśra), the raised (udvṛtta), the svastika, the scattered (viprakīrṇaka),
those called the lotus-bud (padmakośa), the arāla, the khaṭakāmukha, the āviddhavaktra, and those known as the needle (sūcī) and the mallet (mudgara). ||221-222||
Then there are the two known as *ardharecita*, likewise *uttānavañcita*,
those called *pallava*, *nirāva*, *keśabandha*,
*latākara*, *karihasta*, and thereafter those called *pakṣavañcita*.
In one wing [of the formation], there are the Pradyotakarins; likewise, there are the Garuḍapakṣakas (224).
Then follow those called Daṇḍapakṣakas, then the Ūrdhvamaṇḍalins, then the Pārśvamaṇḍalins, and similarly the Romaṇḍalins (225).
Immediately thereafter, the two hands should be known as the chest-side half-circle (uraḥpārśvārdhamaṇḍala),
the fist-cross (muṣṭikasvastika), the lotus (nalinī), and the lotus-bud (padmakośaka). Following that, the two hands are described as the prominent bud-like sprout (alapallavaka).
The two *lalita* and the one called *valita*—these twenty-nine have been described.

When the two hands are placed eight finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in front of the chest, level with the nipples, facing each other, and shaped like *khaṭakāmukha*, they are [known as *lalita*]. (227–228)
These two are called *caturaśrau* by those skilled in the art of dance-hands.
Thus ends the section on the *caturaśrau*.
Those same two hands, known as *haṃsapakṣa*, when turned outward and rotated, are subsequently brought to the state of *svastika* and extended from the wrists;
they are then called *viprakīrṇa* by those skilled in dramatic gesture (*nṛttābhinaya*). ||229–230||
Thus it is scattered.

Having performed the action of turning back those very two hands known as the "swan's wings," they are brought to the state of "sprout-like" (alapa) palms; then they are turned over. Having made the two hands face upwards, they should be formed into the shape of lotus buds (padmakośaka).
Thus are the two lotus-bud hands.

Having performed the *punarvivartita* and then the *parivartanaka*, one should make the right hand *arāla* and the left hand comfortably as a *khaṭaka*. These three hands, known as *khaṭaka*, are prescribed for their own respective domains (*svakṣetra*). ||232-233||
The *itara* and *khaṭakāmukha* [hand gestures] are thus.
When both hands are curved and rotated together with the arms and elbows,
with their palms facing downwards, and are both tossed upwards and bent,
one should know them by the name *vinata*; they are crooked and are used for expressing dejection.
And the *āviddha* and *vakraka* [positions] are formed through the application of the encirclement of the mace (*gadāveṣṭana*).
Thus are the *ita-viddha* and *vakraka*.
When the two hands, with their thumbs resting on the palms, are formed into the shape of a serpent’s head and turned upward,
and the tips of the fingers are extended, that is the placement of the trident (śūlanyāsa), which brings prosperity. 236.
Thus [are described] the two Sūcīmukhas.
The two hands, with fingers like needle-points, released from the wrist-joint,
are then rotated by means of outward and inward revolutions (vyāvṛtti and parivṛtti).
Having brought them to the state of swan-wings (haṃsapakṣa), one should perform the lotus-rotation (kamalavartita).
Likewise, having performed rapid rotations, the two hands are slowly extended to the sides;
these are to be known as *recita* by those skilled in hand gestures.
Thus ends the description of *recita*.
The two hands, turned by means of withdrawal and rotation like a square, with the elbows and shoulders drawn together, are brought to the state of the *tripatāka* [gesture];
these two, remaining slightly apart, should be known as "upturned. (239–240)
Thus [are defined] the *uttāna* and *vañcita* [hand gestures].
Having performed the action of the initial turning with the *bāhuvartanā* (arm-turning) movement,
when the square [hand] has been formed by means of two square rotations (*caturaśrakaparivṛtti*),
then the left hand and its opposite [the right] perform the *itarecita* (alternately raised) gesture among these.
These two should then be understood by the wise as having the name *ardharecita* (half-turned).
Thus ends the section on *ardharecita*.
[They are performed] either by the rotation of the arms or by the turning away from the tops of the shoulders.
When the two hands have emerged from the *karaṇa* position, or have come near it in a measured manner,
they are designated as the *pallava* hands;
thus are the *pallavas*.

The two known as *keśabandha* (hair-binding) are situated on both sides of the head in the posture of standing, with the head turned by the winding of a cloth and shaped like a sprout. Thus end the hair-bindings. (244)
When both are positioned facing forward on the ground according to the sequence of movement,
with hands like sprouts at both sides, they are known as the *latā* (creeper) hands.
Thus ends the description of the *latā* hands.
With both hands turned away, the right hand is a *latāhasta* (creeper-hand),
while the left hand is raised, shaken, and formed as a *tripatāka* (three-fold banner). Thus is the *karihasta* (elephant-trunk gesture).

When the two hands, joined with the *tripatāka* [mudrā] facing each other through a twisting and turning motion, are positioned like the trunk of an elephant, they are then called *pakṣavañcitaka*. Thus ends the description of the *pakṣavañcitaka*.
Those same hands in the *tripatāka* position, with their tips placed near the hips and head,
are called by the name *pakṣapracyotaka* due to the prescribed method of turning them back.
Thus ends the *pakṣapracyotaka*.
The two hands with three branches, facing downwards, are to be known as the "Garuda-wings";
thus [ends] the Garuda-wings.
When the haṃsapakṣaka hands are formed by the actions of *āvartita* and *parivartita*, and when the two *upakṣa* hands—
having the form of wings and their tips raised—
are extended, and if they take on a circular shape through the application of *vyāvartita* and *parivartita*, [they constitute the *gamana* gesture]. (249–250)
When the two hands are turned upwards like a snake that has been struck, they are known as *ūrdhvamaṇḍalinau*;
likewise, having performed the turning (*āvartita*) and the crossing-over (*parivartitakaraṇa*), they are designated as *ūrdhvamaṇḍalisaṃjñau*.
Thus [are described] the *pārśvamaṇḍalinau* (side-circular gestures).
When both [arms] are wound around and then rotated as one over the region of the chest, they both become *uraḥ-maṇḍalinas*;
those who know [the art] should recognize them as such at that time.
(252) Thus ends the section on the *uraḥ-maṇḍalinas*.
The *pallava* (sprout) hand is likewise [formed], as is the one called *ārālā*;
the former is produced by turning away, while the other arises from wrapping around.
These two are positioned respectively through the joining of the upper part of the chest and the joining of the side of the chest. (253)
The wise man should recognize these two as the *uraḥpārśvārdhamaṇḍala* (the half-circle of the chest and side).
Thus ends [the section on] the *uraḥpārśvārdhamaṇḍala*.
May there be auspiciousness.
